sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Operator precedence is the grammatical order of operations in programming (like PEMDAS/BODMAS in algebra). When multiple operators appear in a single statement without parentheses, Java uses strict precedence tiers and associativity rules to decide which operation binds to which operands first.

sections.title: Complete Java Operator Precedence Hierarchy (Highest to Lowest)
Precedence vs Order of Evaluation (Critical Distinction)
sections.content:
Precedence determines which operators group with which operands. However, operand evaluation in Java ALWAYS proceeds strictly from Left-to-Right.

Example:
`int result = getA() + getB() * getC();`

1. Evaluation Order: Java executes `getA()`, then `getB()`, then `getC()` in strict left-to-right sequence.
2. Precedence Binding: The returned value of `getB()` is multiplied by `getC()` first, and then added to `getA()`.

sections.title: Parentheses and Precedence in Practice
sections.explanation: Always use explicit parentheses when mixing bitwise, logical, and relational operators to guarantee clarity and avoid compiler errors.

sections.title: Try It: Complex Expression Precedence
sections.explanation: For x: 3 * 4 = 12, then 12 / 2 = 6, then 2 + 6 = 8, then 8 - 1 = 7. For cond: '&&' runs before '||', so false && false = false, then true || false = true.

iterations.description: Multiplication '*' (level 3) runs: 3 * 2 = 6.
Addition '+' (level 4) runs: 5 + 6 = 11.
Relational '>' (level 6) runs: 11 > 10 is true.
Equality '==' (level 7) runs: 4 == 4 is true.
Logical AND '&&' (level 11) runs: true && true evaluates to true.

sections.title: Defensive Coding Standard
items: Do not rely on obscure precedence rules. If there is any ambiguity, use explicit parentheses '()'.
Parentheses carry zero performance penalty at runtime and make your intentions immediately clear to other engineers and code reviewers.

traps.question: Why does 'System.out.println(1 + 2 + " = " + 1 + 2);' output '3 = 12'?
traps.trap: Thinking it outputs '3 = 3' or '12 = 12'.
traps.solution: Because '+' is left-associative: 1 + 2 evaluates to integer 3. Then 3 + " = " evaluates to String "3 = ". Once a String operand exists, all subsequent '+' operations perform String concatenation: "3 = " + 1 = "3 = 1", and "3 = 1" + 2 = "3 = 12".

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which operator has the lowest precedence among the following?
sections.explanation: Assignment operators (=, +=, etc.) have the lowest precedence among standard operators, ensuring the entire right-hand expression is fully calculated before being stored.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Precedence order: Postfix > Unary > Multiplicative (* / %) > Additive (+ -) > Shift > Relational > Equality > Bitwise > Logical (&& before ||) > Ternary > Assignment.
Operands are always evaluated strictly Left-to-Right in Java.
Use parentheses to override precedence and eliminate ambiguity in complex conditions.

content.theory:
When an expression contains several operators, precedence and associativity decide which operations happen first. `2 + 3 * 4` is 14 because multiplication has higher precedence than addition. Most of the time precedence matches mathematical intuition, but some rules, especially around logical, bitwise, ternary and assignment operators, produce surprises. This lesson presents Java's precedence table, associativity, evaluation order, and the practical rule that parentheses beat memorization.

## Precedence table

From highest to lowest:

| Level | Operators | Associativity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Postfix `x++ x--` | Left to right |
| 2 | Prefix and unary `++x --x + - ! ~`, casts | Right to left |
| 3 | Multiplicative `* / %` | Left to right |
| 4 | Additive `+ -` | Left to right |
| 5 | Shift `<< >> >>>` | Left to right |
| 6 | Relational `< > <= >= instanceof` | Left to right |
| 7 | Equality `== !=` | Left to right |
| 8 | Bitwise AND `&` | Left to right |
| 9 | Bitwise XOR `^` | Left to right |
| 10 | Bitwise OR `|` | Left to right |
| 11 | Logical AND `&&` | Left to right |
| 12 | Logical OR `||` | Left to right |
| 13 | Ternary `? :` | Right to left |
| 14 | Assignment `= += -= *=` and others | Right to left |

A useful memory aid: unary, arithmetic, shift, comparison, bitwise, logical, ternary, assignment.

## Precedence in action

~~~java
int r1 = 2 + 3 * 4;          // 14
int r2 = (2 + 3) * 4;        // 20
int r3 = 10 - 2 - 3;         // 5: left-associative, (10 - 2) - 3
int r4 = 20 / 2 * 5;         // 50: (20 / 2) * 5, same level, left to right
boolean b = 5 > 3 && 2 > 4;  // false: comparisons first, then &&
~~~

## Associativity

When operators share a level, associativity decides grouping:

- **left to right** for most binary operators: `a - b - c` is `(a - b) - c`
- **right to left** for unary operators, ternary and assignment: `a = b = c` is `a = (b = c)`, and `-~x` is `-(~x)`

Nested ternaries group from the right: `a ? b : c ? d : e` means `a ? b : (c ? d : e)`.

## Precedence is not evaluation order

Precedence decides grouping, not the order operands are computed. Java always evaluates operands **left to right**:

~~~java
int i = 2;
int r = i * (i = 5);   // 2 * 5 = 10: the left operand i is read before the assignment
~~~

In `a() + b() * c()`, the multiplication groups first, but the methods are called in the order a, b, c. This distinction matters when operands have side effects.

## Classic traps

**Integer division before multiplication**:

~~~java
double pct = 1 / 4 * 100;      // 0.0: 1 / 4 is 0 in integer division
double ok = 100.0 * 1 / 4;     // 25.0
~~~

**Concatenation is left to right**:

~~~java
System.out.println("Sum: " + 2 + 3);    // "Sum: 23"
System.out.println("Sum: " + (2 + 3));  // "Sum: 5"
System.out.println(2 + 3 + " total");   // "5 total"
~~~

**Bitwise below comparison**:

~~~java
if ((flags & MASK) != 0)    // parentheses required
~~~

Without them, `flags & MASK != 0` parses as `flags & (MASK != 0)`, which doesn't compile for ints.

**&& before ||**:

~~~java
boolean r = true || false && false;   // true: && binds first, true || (false && false)
~~~

**Ternary below everything except assignment**:

~~~java
String s = "Score: " + score > 50 ? "pass" : "fail";   // compile error
~~~

The `+` runs first, producing a String, which can't be compared with `>`. Write `"Score: " + (score > 50 ? "pass" : "fail")`.

**Casts bind tightly**:

~~~java
double avg = (double) total / count;    // casts total, then divides: correct
double bad = (double) (total / count);  // divides in int first: truncated
~~~

## Parentheses are free

Parentheses cost nothing at runtime and make intent explicit. Professional style guides recommend them whenever an expression mixes operator families, such as arithmetic with bitwise, or `&&` with `||`. Code is read far more often than it's written; nobody should need the precedence table to understand your expressions.

## Solving precedence puzzles

1. add parentheses according to the table, highest precedence first
2. apply associativity for operators at the same level
3. evaluate operands left to right, applying side effects as they occur
4. track types: integer division, promotion and String concatenation

## How interviewers test this

Expect output questions such as `1 / 4 * 100`, `"a" + 1 + 2`, `true || false && false` and expressions mixing ternary with `+`. Group operators using the table, distinguish grouping from left-to-right operand evaluation, and recommend parentheses for readability.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Think of your computer as having three standard pipes (streams) connected to your program: Standard Input (`System.in`), Standard Output (`System.out`), and Standard Error (`System.err`). Printing output is the act of pushing formatted character bytes into the Standard Output pipe so your operating system terminal can display them.

sections.title: Standard Streams in Java
sections.content:
Java provides two built-in output streams in the `java.lang.System` class:
• `System.out` (Standard Output): Buffered output stream for normal application messages, results, and prompts.
• `System.err` (Standard Error): Unbuffered output stream dedicated to error messages, warnings, and stack traces, ensuring errors appear immediately even if the main output buffer is full.

sections.title: The Core Output Methods in Action
sections.explanation: System.out is an instance of java.io.PrintStream. It handles byte-to-character encoding automatically based on your system console.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Output Stream Sequence
sections.explanation: 'A' prints with no newline. 'B' prints right after 'A' on line 1, then moves cursor to line 2. 'C' prints on line 2, and 'D' prints after 'C' before moving to line 3.

iterations.description: Prints 'Loading'. Cursor stays at end of word on Line 1.
Appends ': '. Cursor remains on Line 1.
Prints '100%' and sends newline separator, advancing cursor to start of Line 2.

sections.title: Common Output Mistakes
items: Excessive string concatenation inside tight loops: 'System.out.println("val: " + a + ", " + b)' creates multiple temporary String objects.
Assuming System.out and System.err print in exact chronological order on the console: Because System.err is unbuffered and System.out is buffered, their output lines can interleave unpredictably.
Forgetting that System.out.println() with no arguments prints a clean blank newline.

traps.question: What is 'System.out' in terms of Java class hierarchy?
traps.trap: Calling it a method or keyword.
traps.solution: 'System' is a final class in 'java.lang'. 'out' is a public static final field of type 'java.io.PrintStream'. Methods like 'println()' are member methods of the PrintStream class.

traps.question: Can System.out.println() ever throw an IOException?
traps.trap: Thinking all I/O operations must declare 'throws IOException'.
traps.solution: No! Unlike standard Java I/O streams, PrintStream methods (print, println, printf) suppress and catch internal IOExceptions, storing an error flag accessible via 'System.out.checkError()'.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the return type of System.out.println("Hello")?
sections.explanation: System.out.println() has a 'void' return type because its sole purpose is performing the side effect of writing bytes to the console stream.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: System.out is a PrintStream for standard output; System.err is an unbuffered stream for diagnostics.
print() stays on the same line; println() appends a newline.
PrintStream methods never throw checked IOExceptions.

sections.content: Next, we compare print() vs println() vs printf(), mastering formatted output specifiers (%d, %f, %s, %n), precision control, and column alignment.

content.theory:
Printing output is how a program communicates results: to a user at a terminal, to a log file, or to you while debugging. Java's `System.out` provides `print`, `println` and `printf`, plus `String.format` for building formatted text. Formatting numbers, aligning columns and producing exactly the expected output are everyday tasks, and on coding platforms, output must match character for character. This lesson covers how printing works, string concatenation, formatted output, and printing efficiently.

## System.out

`System.out` is a `PrintStream` object connected to the program's **standard output**, usually the terminal. Its methods convert values to text and write them:

~~~java
System.out.println("Hello");     // text, then a newline
System.out.println(42);          // numbers are converted to text
System.out.println(3.5);
System.out.println(true);
System.out.println('A');
~~~

There's also `System.err`, the **standard error** stream, intended for error messages. Terminals usually show both, but they can be redirected separately: `java App > out.txt` captures only standard output.

## Concatenation

The `+` operator joins strings with other values:

~~~java
String name = "Asha";
int score = 92;
System.out.println("Student: " + name + ", score: " + score);
~~~

Watch the left-to-right rule: `"Total: " + 5 + 3` prints "Total: 53". Wrap arithmetic in parentheses: `"Total: " + (5 + 3)`.

## How objects print

Printing an object calls its `toString()` method. Classes without a custom `toString` print something like `Student@1b6d3586`. Arrays are the classic trap:

~~~java
int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(nums);                    // [I@6d06d69c
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums));   // [1, 2, 3]
~~~

`Arrays.toString` prints a one-dimensional array; `Arrays.deepToString` prints nested arrays. Collections such as ArrayList already print their contents.

## Formatted output with printf

`printf` takes a format string with placeholders, followed by values:

~~~java
System.out.printf("%s scored %d marks%n", "Ravi", 88);
System.out.printf("Average: %.2f%n", 87.456);   // Average: 87.46
~~~

Common format specifiers:

| Specifier | Meaning | Example | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%d` | Integer | `printf("%d", 42)` | 42 |
| `%f` | Decimal (6 places default) | `printf("%f", 3.5)` | 3.500000 |
| `%.2f` | Decimal with 2 places | `printf("%.2f", 3.14159)` | 3.14 |
| `%s` | String (or any object) | `printf("%s", "hi")` | hi |
| `%c` | Character | `printf("%c", 'x')` | x |
| `%b` | Boolean | `printf("%b", true)` | true |
| `%n` | Platform newline | | |
| `%%` | Literal percent sign | `printf("100%%")` | 100% |

`printf` doesn't add a newline automatically; end the format with `%n`.

## Width and alignment

A number between `%` and the letter sets a minimum width:

~~~java
System.out.printf("%-10s|%5d|%n", "Asha", 92);
System.out.printf("%-10s|%5d|%n", "Ravi", 8);
// Asha      |   92|
// Ravi      |    8|
~~~

A minus sign left-aligns. `%05d` pads with zeros: `printf("%05d", 42)` prints 00042. `%,d` adds grouping separators: 1,000,000.

## String.format

`String.format` uses the same syntax but returns a String instead of printing, useful for building messages:

~~~java
String msg = String.format("%s has %d new messages", user, count);
String price = String.format("%.2f", amount);
~~~

Since Java 15, `"%s scored %d".formatted(name, score)` does the same thing as an instance method.

## Rounding when printing

`%.2f` rounds for display (HALF_UP behaviour) without changing the stored value. For calculations that need exact decimal rounding, such as invoices, use `BigDecimal` with `setScale`.

## Printing efficiently

Each `System.out.println` call is relatively slow, because output is synchronized and may be flushed. Printing hundreds of thousands of lines one at a time can make competitive programming solutions time out. Build the output in a `StringBuilder` and print once:

~~~java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) sb.append(i).append('\n');
System.out.print(sb);
~~~

A `PrintWriter` wrapped around `System.out` with a buffer is another common approach.

## Matching expected output exactly

Online judges compare output strictly. Common causes of "wrong answer" despite correct logic:

- extra or missing spaces, especially trailing spaces
- a missing final newline, or an extra blank line
- printing `3.5` when `3.50` was expected
- debug prints left in the code

## Printing for debugging

Temporary prints such as `System.out.println("i=" + i + " sum=" + sum);` reveal what a program is doing. Remove them before submitting. Real applications use logging frameworks, which add timestamps and levels and can be switched off without code changes.

## How interviewers test this

Expect formatting tasks such as printing to two decimal places or aligning a table, the array-printing trap, and concatenation puzzles. Show printf specifiers including width and precision, use Arrays.toString for arrays, and mention StringBuilder for large outputs.

items: Using '\n' instead of '%n' in printf: '\n' hardcodes Unix linebreaks, while '%n' respects the host OS line separator (important on Windows servers).
Mismatching specifier types (e.g. passing a double to '%d'): Throws a runtime 'java.util.IllegalFormatConversionException'.
Forgetting that printf() does NOT automatically add a newline at the end.

traps.question: What happens if you run: System.out.printf("%d", 3.14);?
traps.trap: Thinking it truncates 3.14 to 3.
traps.solution: Throws runtime 'IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double'! Unlike casting, printf() does not perform narrowing conversions—the format specifier must match the argument type.

traps.question: What does 'System.out.printf("%b", "hello");' print?
traps.trap: Thinking it causes a format error or prints false.
traps.solution: Prints 'true'! In Java printf, '%b' evaluates any non-null object or string as 'true', and null as 'false'. It only tests boolean values directly if a boolean primitive is passed.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which format specifier prints a floating-point number with exactly 3 decimal digits?
sections.explanation: '%.3f' instructs printf to format a floating point number with a precision of 3 digits after the decimal point.

items: print() = no newline; println() = automatic newline; printf() = parameterized formatting.
Key specifiers: %d (int), %f (float/double), %s (string), %n (portable newline), %,d (comma grouping).
Mismatching format specifiers throws runtime IllegalFormatConversionException.

An escape sequence uses the backslash as an 'escape key', telling the compiler: 'Do not treat the next character as code syntax; treat it as a literal or control character inside the string.'

sections.title: Common Escape Sequence Traps

Unicode escapes '\uXXXX' are processed by the Java preprocessor BEFORE lexical parsing. Even inside comments, an invalid '\u' sequence causes compile errors!
Confusing single quote escapes: inside strings '"' needs '\"', inside chars '\'' needs '\''.

traps.question: Why does this comment cause a compile error: // Look at folder: C:\users\new?

traps.question: How do you represent a newline portably across Windows and Linux in Java?
traps.trap: Thinking '\n' works identically everywhere.
traps.solution: While '\n' works on modern terminals, the standard OS-independent line separator is obtained via 'System.lineSeparator()' or '%n' in printf().

sections.explanation: '\t' is the escape sequence for a horizontal tab.

content.theory:
Some characters can't be typed directly inside a string literal: a double quote would end the string, a newline would break the line of code, and a backslash has special meaning. **Escape sequences** solve this with a backslash followed by a code, such as `\n` for a newline or `\"` for a quote. This lesson covers Java's escape sequences, Unicode escapes, text blocks for multi-line strings, and the common mistakes with backslashes in file paths and regular expressions.

## Java's escape sequences

| Sequence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\n` | Newline (line feed) |
| `\t` | Tab |
| `\"` | Double quote |
| `\'` | Single quote |
| `\\` | Backslash |
| `\r` | Carriage return |
| `\b` | Backspace |
| `\f` | Form feed |
| `\s` | Space (Java 15+) |
| `\0` to `\377` | Octal character value, such as `\0` for the null character |

Any other character after a backslash, such as `\d` in a normal string, is a compile error: "illegal escape character".

## Newlines and tabs

~~~java
System.out.println("Line one\nLine two");
// Line one
// Line two

System.out.println("Name\tScore\nAsha\t92");
// Name    Score
// Asha    92
~~~

Tabs jump to the next tab stop, often every 8 columns, so tab-aligned output can still look uneven when values have different lengths. For reliable alignment, use `printf` with widths, such as `%-10s`.

## Quotes inside strings

~~~java
System.out.println("She said \"hello\"");    // She said "hello"
System.out.println("It's fine");               // single quotes need no escape in strings
char quote = '\'';                            // but they do in char literals
char dq = '"';                                 // double quote needs none in a char literal
~~~

## Backslashes

A literal backslash must be doubled:

~~~java
String path = "C:\\Users\\asha\\notes.txt";   // C:\Users\asha\notes.txt
~~~

Writing `"C:\Users\new"` causes problems: `\U` is an illegal escape, and `\n` would silently become a newline. Two practical alternatives: use forward slashes, which Java accepts on Windows for file paths, or build paths with `Path.of("C:", "Users", "asha")`.

## Escapes and regular expressions

Regular expressions use backslashes too, so they double up. The regex for "one or more digits" is `\d+`; in a Java string literal it becomes `"\\d+"`:

~~~java
boolean allDigits = "12345".matches("\\d+");
String[] words = sentence.split("\\s+");   // split on whitespace
~~~

Matching a literal dot needs `"\\."`, because a bare `.` in regex means "any character". `"a.b.c".split(".")` returns an empty array, a classic surprise; `split("\\.")` gives the three parts.

## Unicode escapes

`\u` followed by four hex digits represents a Unicode character:

~~~java
System.out.println("\u20B9 500");   // ₹ 500
char omega = '\u03A9';               // Ω
~~~

Unicode escapes are processed **before** the compiler parses anything else, even inside comments. A comment containing `\u000A` (a newline) can end the comment early, which leads to strange compile errors. This is a well-known Java puzzle.

## Text blocks

Java 15 added **text blocks** for multi-line strings, delimited by three double quotes:

~~~java
String json = """
    {
      "name": "Asha",
      "score": 92
    }
    """;
~~~

Inside a text block, newlines are kept as written, double quotes don't need escaping, and common leading indentation is removed automatically. They're ideal for JSON, SQL, HTML and test data. A backslash at the end of a line joins it with the next line, and `\s` preserves a trailing space that would otherwise be stripped.

## Carriage return and backspace

`\r` moves the cursor to the start of the line without advancing, which terminals use for progress indicators that overwrite themselves. `\b` moves back one character. Their visible effect depends on the terminal and is rarely needed in application code.

## Counting characters

An escape sequence is written with two or more characters but represents one character in the string:

~~~java
System.out.println("a\nb".length());   // 3
System.out.println("\\".length());     // 1
~~~

## Escapes in char literals

Char literals use the same escapes: `'\n'`, `'\t'`, `'\\'`, `'\''`. Comparing characters with these is common when processing input, such as `if (c == '\n')`.

## How interviewers test this

Expect output questions with `\n`, `\t` and `\"`, string length puzzles involving escapes, and "Why does `split(".")` return nothing?" List the main sequences, explain double escaping in paths and regex, mention that Unicode escapes are processed before parsing, and show text blocks for multi-line strings.

items: Calling 'scanner.close()' closes the underlying stream 'System.in'. Once closed, System.in CANNOT be reopened for the lifetime of your JVM process!

traps.question: Is Scanner thread-safe in Java?

When you type a number and press Enter on the keyboard, you are actually sending TWO pieces of data into the input stream: the digits of the number (e.g. `2` and `5`) followed by the newline character `

sections.title: Common Input Parsing Traps
items: Forgetting to discard invalid input in validation loops: If 'sc.hasNextInt()' is false, you MUST call 'sc.next()' to discard the bad token, otherwise your loop spins forever!

Assuming nextDouble() accepts commas or dots universally: Scanner uses system locale (some European locales expect '3,14' instead of '3.14'). Use 'sc.useLocale(Locale.US)' to enforce standard decimal dots.

traps.question: Why does an input validation loop with 'if (!sc.hasNextInt()) continue;' create an infinite loop?
traps.trap: Thinking continue resets the scanner.
traps.solution: 'hasNextInt()' only inspects the token without consuming it. If the token is invalid (e.g. "abc"), it stays in the buffer forever unless explicitly discarded using 'sc.next()'.

traps.question: How does BufferedReader compare to Scanner for competitive programming input?
traps.trap: Saying they are identical.
traps.solution: BufferedReader is significantly faster than Scanner because it uses a large internal 8KB buffer and performs no regex parsing. In competitive programming, 'BufferedReader + StringTokenizer' is preferred for processing hundreds of thousands of inputs within time limits.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Token methods (nextInt, nextDouble) leave the trailing newline character in the buffer.
Always consume the leftover newline with an extra sc.nextLine() or use Integer.parseInt(sc.nextLine()).
Use hasNextInt() / hasNextDouble() for crash-proof input validation.
Discard bad tokens in validation loops using sc.next() to avoid infinite loops.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: Before learning control flow, you should understand variables, data types, arithmetic and logical operators, and standard console output.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: By default, a computer program is a single straight train track: the CPU's Program Counter (PC) executes instructions one by one from top to bottom (Sequential Execution). Control flow statements are the railroad switches and loop-tracks that allow the train to branch onto different paths (Selection) or circle back to repeat a track section (Iteration) based on real-time track signals (Boolean Conditions).

sections.title: The 3 Pillars of Structured Programming
sections.content:
In 1966, mathematicians Corrado Böhm and Giuseppe Jacopini proved that ANY computable algorithm can be constructed using only three control structures:
1. Sequence: Execute statements in orderly top-to-bottom succession.
2. Selection: Choose between alternative paths based on a condition (`if`, `if-else`, `switch`).
3. Iteration: Repeat a block of code while a condition remains true (`for`, `while`, `do-while`).

sections.title: How the CPU & JVM Handle Branching Internally
sections.content:
Under the hood, the JVM compiles selection statements into low-level conditional branch bytecode instructions (such as `ifeq`, `ifne`, `if_icmpeq`) and unconditional jump instructions (`goto`).

When the CPU evaluates a condition:
• If the condition is met, the Program Counter jumps directly to the memory offset of the targeted branch.
• If not met, execution simply falls through to the next sequential instruction.

sections.explanation: Combining selection and iteration allows programs to make complex real-world decisions and process arbitrary amounts of data.

sections.title: Fundamental Control Flow Rules
items: In Java, conditions MUST evaluate to a boolean primitive (`true` or `false`). Numeric values like `if (1)` or `if (0)` are compilation errors.
Always use braces `{}` even for single-statement branches to avoid maintenance bugs and accidental dangling statements.

traps.question: Can C/C++ style truthy/falsy integers (e.g. if (1)) be used in Java control flow?
traps.trap: Assuming non-zero integers are implicitly true in Java.
traps.solution: No! Java is strictly type-safe. The condition in 'if', 'while', and 'do-while' must be of type 'boolean' or 'Boolean' (autounboxed). Writing 'if (1)' results in a compile error: 'incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean'.

sections.explanation: A while loop is an iteration structure that repeatedly executes a block of statements while its condition remains true.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Control flow alters default top-to-bottom sequential execution.
Three main structures: Sequence, Selection (decision branching), and Iteration (loops).
Java conditions must strictly evaluate to boolean expressions.

content.theory:
Control flow is the order in which a program's statements execute. Without it, a program would run every line once, top to bottom, and could never make decisions or repeat work. Control flow statements let a program choose between paths, repeat steps, and jump out early. Every algorithm, from validating a password to searching a database, is built from three basic structures: sequence, selection and iteration. This lesson introduces those structures, Java's control flow statements, and how to reason about the paths through a program.

## The three basic structures

Computer scientists showed that any algorithm can be expressed using three structures, a result known as the **structured program theorem**:

1. **Sequence**: statements run one after another, in order
2. **Selection**: the program chooses which statements to run based on a condition
3. **Iteration**: the program repeats statements while a condition holds

~~~java
int marks = 72;                       // sequence
if (marks >= 40) {                    // selection
    System.out.println("Pass");
}
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {        // iteration
    System.out.println("Attempt " + i);
}
~~~

## Java's control flow statements

| Category | Statements | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Selection | `if`, `if-else`, `else if`, `switch`, ternary `? :` | Choose a path |
| Iteration | `for`, enhanced `for`, `while`, `do-while` | Repeat work |
| Jump | `break`, `continue`, `return` | Leave a loop, skip an iteration, exit a method |
| Exceptions | `try`, `catch`, `finally`, `throw` | Handle errors by jumping to handlers |

Each gets its own lesson in this module.

## Conditions drive control flow

Selection and iteration depend on **conditions**: expressions that evaluate to `true` or `false`. They're built from relational operators (`<`, `==`), logical operators (`&&`, `||`, `!`), boolean variables and methods that return booleans:

~~~java
if (age >= 18 && hasId) { ... }
while (!queue.isEmpty()) { ... }
~~~

Java requires conditions to be genuine booleans. `if (count)` with an int doesn't compile, which prevents a family of bugs common in C.

## Blocks

A **block** is a group of statements in braces. Control flow statements apply to the single statement or block that follows them:

~~~java
if (marks >= 40)
    System.out.println("Pass");
    System.out.println("Well done");   // always runs: not part of the if
~~~

The indentation suggests both lines belong to the if, but only the first does. Always using braces, even for one statement, prevents this bug. Variables declared inside a block exist only within it.

## Flowcharts

A **flowchart** draws control flow: rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions, arrows for the order of execution. Flowcharts and pseudocode help plan logic before coding, and drawing one for a confusing function often reveals a missing case.

## Paths through a program

Each decision splits execution into paths. A method with two independent if statements has up to four paths; with ten, up to 1,024. This growth is why:

- testing must cover important paths, especially boundary cases
- deeply nested conditions are hard to understand
- small methods with few decisions are easier to get right

A metric called **cyclomatic complexity** counts the independent paths in a method; tools flag methods where it gets high.

## Tracing execution

To understand control flow, trace a program by hand with concrete values: track each variable and note which branch runs and how many times each loop repeats. A trace table with one column per variable and one row per step is a reliable way to find logic errors and to solve output questions in interviews.

## Structured versus unstructured flow

Early languages used `goto` to jump anywhere, producing tangled "spaghetti code". Java reserves the word `goto` but doesn't implement it. Its jump statements are restricted: `break` and `continue` affect only loops and switches, and `return` exits only the current method. These limits keep control flow readable.

## Choosing the right structure

- one condition, one optional action: `if`
- two alternatives: `if-else`
- several ranges or unrelated conditions: `else if` ladder
- one value compared against fixed options: `switch`
- choosing between two values in an expression: ternary
- repeat a known number of times: `for`
- repeat until something happens: `while`
- run at least once: `do-while`

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What are the types of control statements in Java?", output questions that require tracing branches and loops, and bugs caused by missing braces. Name sequence, selection and iteration, list Java's statements by category, and demonstrate tracing with a table of variable values.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand boolean expressions, relational operators (==, !=, <, >), and logical operators (&&, ||, !).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: An `if` statement is a security checkpoint. Before allowing the program to enter and execute a block of code, it inspects a boolean credential (the condition). If the credential is `true`, the gate opens and the code runs; if `false`, the checkpoint is bypassed completely.

The if Statement in Action

sections.title: The Dangerous Dangling Semicolon Trap
Braceless if Statements & Historical Bugs
sections.content:
If braces `{}` are omitted, the `if` statement guards ONLY the single immediately following statement:

```java
if (score >= 90)
    System.out.println("Passed");
    System.out.println("Grade A"); // NOT part of if! Always executes!
```

Industry Best Practice:
Always include curly braces `{}` even for single-line statements. The famous Apple SSL security bug (CVE-2014-1266 / "goto fail") was caused by a duplicated unbraced statement.

sections.title: Try It: The Semicolon Bug
sections.explanation: Because of the semicolon after 'if (num > 0);', the block '{ num = 100; }' is an independent block and executes regardless of num being negative.

iterations.description: Initial cart state.
Condition evaluates to true.
Body of if executes: apply 20 discount.
Program continues with discounted total.

sections.title: Common if Statement Pitfalls
items: Accidental semicolon after if: 'if (x > 5);' causes the following block to run unconditionally.
Omission of curly braces causing misleading indentation bugs.
Accidental assignment: 'if (flag = false)' assigns false to boolean variable flag and evaluates to false.

traps.question: What is the output of: boolean b = false; if (b = true) System.out.println("TRUE"); else System.out.println("FALSE");?
traps.trap: Thinking it prints 'FALSE' because b was false.
traps.solution: Prints 'TRUE'! 'b = true' is an assignment expression that mutates b to true and returns the value 'true' to the if statement condition. To prevent this, always use '==' for comparison or simply 'if (b)'.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.explanation: Without braces, only 'x = 20;' belongs to the if statement. 'x = 30;' executes unconditionally, setting x to 30.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: if statements execute code blocks only when their boolean condition is true.
Never place a semicolon after the if condition header.
Always use explicit curly braces `{}` to guarantee safety and clarity.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand basic `if` statements, boolean logic, and block scoping.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: An `if-else` statement is a fork in the road. You must choose exactly one path: if the primary road is open (condition is `true`), you take the `if` route; otherwise (condition is `false`), you are forced onto the alternate `else` route. You can never take both roads, and you can never skip both roads.

sections.title: Mutual Exclusivity Principle
sections.content:
In an `if-else` construct, the two code blocks are mutually exclusive:
• `if` block executes ⇔ condition is `true`
• `else` block executes ⇔ condition is `false`
One and only one block will execute on every pass.

sections.title: Common if-else Mistakes
items: Attempting to attach a condition to 'else': 'else (x < 0)' is a SYNTAX ERROR (use 'else if' for conditional alternatives).
Declaring a variable inside if and attempting to read it after the if-else block.
Writing redundant else blocks after a return statement (e.g. 'if (cond) return a; else return b;' can be simplified to 'if (cond) return a; return b;').

traps.question: Why does this fail to compile: int res; if (flag) { res = 10; } System.out.println(res); vs with an else block?
traps.trap: Assuming 'res' defaults to 0.
traps.solution: In Java, local variables must be definitely assigned before access. Without an 'else' block, the compiler detects that if 'flag' is false, 'res' remains uninitialized, causing a compile error: 'variable res might not have been initialized'. Adding an 'else { res = 20; }' guarantees assignment across all code paths.

sections.question: Can both the if block and the else block execute in the same pass?
options: Yes, if the condition changes inside the if block
Yes, if no break statement is used
sections.explanation: The if and else blocks are strictly mutually exclusive. Exactly one block executes depending on the boolean condition.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: if-else provides guaranteed two-way binary branching.
Variables declared inside branch blocks have local scope.
Compilers use if-else for definite assignment verification of local variables.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `if` and `if-else` statements, relational comparisons, and logical operators.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: An `else-if` ladder is a multi-tier sieve or waterfall. You drop a value in from the top. It tests against tier 1; if it matches, it gets caught and processed, and the rest of the waterfall is skipped. If it doesn't match, it falls to tier 2, then tier 3, until either a match is found or it hits the catch-all bucket at the bottom (the final `else`).

sections.title: Waterfall Execution Rule
sections.content:
Conditions in an else-if ladder are evaluated sequentially from TOP to BOTTOM:
• The FIRST condition that evaluates to `true` executes its block.
• All subsequent `else if` and `else` blocks are IMMEDIATELY SKIPPED.
• If NO conditions match, the optional fallback `else` block executes.

sections.title: Common else-if Mistakes
items: Inverting range checks so broader conditions shadow specific conditions.
Using multiple independent 'if' statements instead of 'else if', causing multiple blocks to execute and overwrite results.
Omitting the final fallback 'else' when unexpected inputs could leave variables unassigned.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Independent if vs else-if Ladder

traps.question: What is the difference in execution between 4 sequential 'if' statements vs an 'else if' ladder?
traps.trap: Thinking they behave identically if conditions are mutually exclusive.
traps.solution: In 4 independent 'if' statements, the CPU evaluates ALL 4 conditions unconditionally, potentially executing multiple blocks. In an 'else if' ladder, evaluation short-circuits on the FIRST true match, skipping all remaining conditions for superior performance and safety.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How many code blocks can execute in an else-if ladder with a final else?
sections.explanation: With a final 'else' clause present, exactly one block is guaranteed to execute (the first matching condition, or the default else).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: else-if ladders evaluate sequentially from top to bottom.
The first true match executes its block and terminates the ladder.
Order conditions from most specific/restrictive to least specific.
Always include a final default else for defensive robustness.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Nested conditions represent hierarchical decision trees. Think of entering a high-security vault: Gate 1 checks if you have a valid ID badge (outer `if`). ONLY if Gate 1 opens can you walk forward to Gate 2, which scans your biometric fingerprint (inner `if`). If Gate 1 fails, you never even reach Gate 2.

sections.title: When to Nest vs When to Combine with &&
sections.content:
• Use `&&` (flat condition): When both checks are simple, independent criteria for the same action (e.g. `if (age >= 18 && hasTicket)`).
• Use Nested `if`s (hierarchical): When the inner check is only valid or meaningful after the outer check succeeds (e.g. checking if an object is non-null before checking its properties, or providing distinct error messages at each level).

traps.question: In this unbraced code, what prints: int x = 5, y = 2; if (x > 10) if (y > 1) System.out.println("A"); else System.out.println("B");?
traps.trap: Thinking 'else' belongs to the outer 'if (x > 10)' and prints 'B'.
traps.solution: Prints NOTHING! In Java grammar, an 'else' always binds to the closest preceding unmatched 'if' (which is 'if (y > 1)'). Because the outer 'if (x > 10)' is false, the entire inner if-else structure is skipped!

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How do you refactor deeply nested conditions into clean, readable code?
options: Use while loops instead of if
Place all conditions on one line
sections.explanation: Guard clauses test for failure conditions first and return early, keeping the happy path flat and readable.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Nested if statements model multi-level decision hierarchies.
An unbraced 'else' always binds to the closest preceding 'if' (Dangling Else problem).
Refactor deep nesting into flat guard clauses with early returns.

lessons.title: switch Statement
lessons.description: A switch statement is an indexed direct-dial telephone switchboard or lookup router. In an else-if ladder, the CPU evaluates condition 1, then condition 2, then...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `if-else` ladders, relational comparisons, literal constants, and basic data types.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: A `switch` statement is an indexed direct-dial telephone switchboard or lookup router. In an `else-if` ladder, the CPU evaluates condition 1, then condition 2, then condition 3 sequentially ($O(N)$ comparisons). In a `switch` statement, the expression is evaluated once, and the runtime jumps directly to the matching `case` label ($O(1)$ direct branch via bytecode jump tables).

sections.title: Permitted Data Types in switch
sections.content:
Java allows switching ONLY on specific data types:
• Primitives & Wrappers: `byte`, `short`, `char`, `int` (and `Byte`, `Short`, `Character`, `Integer`)
• Strings: `String` (supported since Java 7)
• Enums: `enum` constants (supported since Java 5)

❌ Types NOT allowed: `long`, `float`, `double`, `boolean` (cannot switch on continuous decimals, 64-bit longs, or simple boolean flags).

sections.title: Classic switch with Fallthrough & Modern Enhanced switch
sections.explanation: In classic switch, omitting 'break' causes execution to fall through into subsequent cases. Modern enhanced switch expressions use arrow syntax '->' which eliminates fallthrough bugs and returns values cleanly.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Case Fallthrough
sections.content:
In a classic switch statement, the `case` labels act merely as entry markers. Once execution enters a matching case, it executes all statements sequentially across subsequent cases until it encounters an explicit `break;` statement or reaches the end of the switch block.

While intentional fallthrough is useful for grouping multiple values (like matching cases 6 and 7 for weekends), unintentional fallthrough caused by a forgotten `break;` is one of the most infamous sources of bugs in software engineering.

sections.title: Try It: Quarter Identifier
sections.explanation: Month 4 matches case 4, falls through to assign 'quarter = Q2', and breaks out of the switch.

iterations.description: Input code is 2.
Direct jump to case 2. Prints 'TWO'. No break present!
Execution falls through into case 3! Prints 'THREE'. No break present!
Falls through into default! Prints 'OTHER'. Exits.

sections.title: Common switch Statement Pitfalls
items: Forgetting `break;` at the end of a case, causing silent fallthrough logic corruption.
Attempting to use variables in case labels: `case x:` is illegal. Case values must be compile-time constants (literals or `final` variables).
Switching on a `null` String or Object: throws `NullPointerException` immediately upon evaluating the switch expression header.
Attempting to test boolean expressions or ranges (`case score >= 90:` is a syntax error in Java).

traps.question: How does the JVM optimize switch statements under the hood compared to else-if chains?
traps.trap: Thinking switch is just syntactic sugar for a series of if-else statements.
traps.solution: The Java compiler generates specialized bytecode instructions: `tableswitch` (when case values are densely packed integers, enabling an $O(1)$ direct array index jump) or `lookupswitch` (when case values are sparse, performing an $O(\log N)$ binary search on sorted keys). This makes switch significantly faster than long $O(N)$ else-if chains.

traps.question: What happens if a String switch variable is null: String s = null; switch(s) { case "A": break; }?
traps.trap: Thinking it jumps to the default case.
traps.solution: It throws a `NullPointerException` at the `switch(s)` header line before inspecting any case labels because Java calls `s.hashCode()` internally to evaluate String switches.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which of the following data types CANNOT be used in a switch statement?
sections.explanation: Floating-point numbers (`float` and `double`) are not permitted in switch statements due to precision and rounding ambiguities.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: switch provides fast, direct O(1) multi-way branch selection for exact constant matches.
Permitted types: byte, short, char, int, String, and enums (no float, double, long, boolean).
In classic switch, every case requires a break to prevent fallthrough.
Case values must be compile-time constants.

lessons.title: Ternary Operator
lessons.description: The ternary operator (? :) is an inline binary selector or compact valve. While an if-else construct is a statement (it executes a block of actions but does not...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `if-else` branching, boolean conditions, and the difference between expressions and statements.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The ternary operator (`? :`) is an inline binary selector or compact valve. While an `if-else` construct is a *statement* (it executes a block of actions but does not return a value on its own), the ternary operator is an *expression*—it evaluates to a concrete value that can be assigned directly to a variable or passed as an argument.

sections.title: Syntax Structure
sections.content:
`variable = (booleanCondition) ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse;`

1. Operand 1: The condition to evaluate (must yield a boolean).
2. `?`: The decision separator.
3. Operand 2: The value/expression returned if condition is `true`.
4. `:`: The alternate separator.
5. Operand 3: The value/expression returned if condition is `false`.

sections.title: Ternary Operator in Action
sections.explanation: Ternary expressions compress simple 5-line if-else assignment blocks into a single, highly readable line.

sections.title: Type Promotion and Type Unification in Ternary Expressions
Try It: Absolute Value Calculator
sections.explanation: Because n (-25) is < 0, the true branch (-(-25) = 25) evaluates and assigns 25 to absVal.

iterations.description: Input age is 20.
Condition evaluates to true.
Returns left value; right operand ("Minor") is never evaluated.
Value assigned to status variable.

sections.title: Common Ternary Mistakes
items: Deeply nesting ternary operators: `a ? b : c ? d : e ? f : g` creates unreadable 'spaghetti code' (use an `else-if` ladder instead).

Auto-unboxing NullPointerException: mixing primitive and wrapper types where the wrapper is null: `boolean flag = false; Integer x = null; int y = flag ? 10 : x;` throws NPE when Java unboxes null `x` into primitive `int`.

Using ternary operators for statements with side-effects instead of value returns: `flag ? System.out.println("A") : System.out.println("B")` is a SYNTAX ERROR in Java (the operands must be expressions with values).

traps.question: What is printed by: System.out.println(true ? Integer.valueOf(1) : Double.valueOf(2.0));?
traps.trap: Thinking it prints '1' because the true branch is an Integer.
traps.solution: It prints '1.0'! Because one operand is an Integer and the other is a Double, Java's ternary type promotion rules unbox the Integer to int and promote it to double (1.0) to match the Double operand.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the key functional difference between an if-else statement and a ternary operator?
options: Ternary is an expression that yields a value; if-else is a statement block
Ternary can execute multiple statement blocks
sections.explanation: Ternary is an expression returning a value for direct assignment; if-else is a statement construct for executing blocks of code.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Ternary operator `condition ? trueVal : falseVal` is the only 3-operand operator in Java.
Use ternary for clean, concise single-line conditional assignments.
Avoid nesting ternary expressions.
Beware of numeric type promotion and unboxing NullPointerExceptions.

sections.content: Next, we explore Jump Statements starting with the break Statement, understanding how to escape loops and switch blocks immediately.

content.theory:
The ternary operator, `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`, is a compact if-else that produces a value. It's Java's only operator with three operands, and it shines when choosing between two values for an assignment, a return or an argument. Overused or nested, it becomes hard to read. Its type rules also cause surprising results when the two branches have different types. This lesson covers syntax, when to use it, nesting, type rules and common traps.

## Syntax

~~~java
result = condition ? expression1 : expression2;
~~~

If the condition is true, the whole expression evaluates to expression1; otherwise to expression2. Only the chosen branch is evaluated.

~~~java
int a = 7, b = 12;
int max = a > b ? a : b;                         // 12
String parity = n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd";
String label = count == 1 ? "item" : "items";
System.out.println(count + " " + label);
~~~

## Ternary versus if-else

The equivalent if-else for `max` takes five lines:

~~~java
int max;
if (a > b) {
    max = a;
} else {
    max = b;
}
~~~

The ternary is better when:

- both branches produce a value of the same kind
- the expressions are short
- the result goes directly into an assignment, return or method argument

if-else is better when branches perform actions (printing, updating several variables), contain multiple statements, or need explanatory comments. The ternary is an **expression**, not a statement: `x > 0 ? print("pos") : print("neg");` doesn't compile as a standalone statement.

## Common uses

~~~java
return list.isEmpty() ? 0 : list.get(0);                 // safe default
String name = input != null ? input : "Guest";            // null fallback
System.out.println("Status: " + (active ? "on" : "off")); // inline in output
int abs = x < 0 ? -x : x;                                 // absolute value
~~~

For null fallbacks, `Objects.requireNonNullElse(input, "Guest")` expresses the same idea by name.

## Precedence and parentheses

The ternary has low precedence, below arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, but above assignment. Inside a concatenation, it must be wrapped in parentheses:

~~~java
System.out.println("Result: " + score > 40 ? "pass" : "fail");     // compile error
System.out.println("Result: " + (score > 40 ? "pass" : "fail"));   // correct
~~~

Without parentheses, `"Result: " + score` happens first, producing a String, which can't be compared with `>`.

## Nested ternaries

The ternary is right-associative, so nesting chains from the right:

~~~java
String grade = marks >= 90 ? "A"
             : marks >= 75 ? "B"
             : marks >= 40 ? "C"
             : "F";
~~~

Formatted one condition per line, this reads like a ladder. Nested ternaries inside the **true** branch, or on one long line, quickly become unreadable. Many teams allow at most one level; an else-if ladder or switch expression is clearer beyond that.

## Type rules

Both branches must produce compatible types, and the result type is determined by both:

~~~java
System.out.println(true ? 1 : 2.0);    // prints 1.0
~~~

When one branch is int and the other double, numeric promotion makes the whole expression a double, even when the int branch is chosen.

A more dangerous case mixes a wrapper and a primitive:

~~~java
Integer cached = null;
int value = flag ? cached : 0;          // NullPointerException when flag is true
~~~

Because one branch is the primitive 0, Java unboxes `cached` to int, and unboxing null throws. Such bugs are hard to spot in code review.

## Side effects

Only the selected branch runs, so side effects in the other branch don't happen:

~~~java
int x = 5;
int y = x > 3 ? x++ : x--;   // y = 5, x = 6; x-- never runs
~~~

Keep side effects out of ternaries; they make code harder to follow.

## The conditional operator in other contexts

Ternaries work anywhere an expression is allowed: array indices, method arguments, lambda bodies and field initializers. That flexibility is useful but tempting: if a reader needs to stop and parse it, an if-else is probably kinder.

## Switch expressions as an alternative

For choosing among many values based on one variable, a switch expression is cleaner than nested ternaries:

~~~java
String dayType = switch (day) {
    case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "Weekend";
    default -> "Weekday";
};
~~~

## How interviewers test this

Expect output questions like `true ? 1 : 2.0`, precedence errors with concatenation, "find the max of three numbers using the ternary operator" and rewrites between if-else and ternary. Explain that only one branch is evaluated, the numeric promotion rule, the unboxing NullPointerException, and when if-else is more readable.

lessons.title: break Statement
lessons.description: The break statement is an Emergency Stop Button on an industrial conveyor belt. When triggered, it immediately halts the entire enclosing loop or switch constru...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand loops (`for`, `while`, `do-while`), `switch` blocks, and basic control flow.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `break` statement is an Emergency Stop Button on an industrial conveyor belt. When triggered, it immediately halts the entire enclosing loop or switch construct and transfers execution directly to the first line of code outside that structure.

sections.title: Where break is Permitted
sections.content:
In Java, `break` can ONLY be used inside:
1. Loops (`for`, `while`, `do-while`) — to abort loop execution early.
2. `switch` statements — to prevent fallthrough.
3. Labeled blocks — to break out of named scopes.

❌ Using `break` inside a regular `if` statement that is NOT inside a loop or switch produces a compile-time error.

sections.title: Early Loop Termination & Labeled Break
sections.explanation: Unlabeled break terminates the immediate innermost loop. Labeled break allows escaping multiple nested loop levels in a single jump without maintaining complex boolean flags.

sections.title: Innermost Scope Rule vs Labeled Breaks
sections.content:
When loops are nested 2, 3, or more levels deep, a standard `break;` statement applies strictly to the innermost enclosing loop. The outer loops will continue running unless you either:
• Use a **labeled break** (`break labelName;`), or
• Set a shared `boolean isDone = true` flag checked by all outer loops, or
• Return directly from the enclosing method.

sections.title: Try It: Breaking on Threshold
sections.explanation: When i reaches 10, sum becomes 55 (> 50). The if condition triggers break, terminating the loop early.

sections.title: Early Exit Loop Trace with break

iterations.description: sum < 50, continue loop.
sum < 50, continue loop.
sum > 50 condition triggers!
Loop terminates immediately. Remaining 90 iterations skipped.

sections.title: Common break Mistakes
items: Expecting `break` to exit an outer loop when used in nested loops (only exits innermost loop unless labeled).
Unreachable code error: placing statements directly after an unconditional `break;` inside a block.
Using `break` in a standalone `if` block outside of any loop or switch (syntax error).

sections.title: Interview Traps: break with finally Blocks

traps.question: If a loop contains a try-finally block and executes break inside try, does the finally block execute?
traps.trap: Thinking break bypasses the finally block.
traps.solution: YES, the finally block is GUARANTEED to execute before the break transfers control outside the loop. The JVM ensures cleanup in finally blocks executes whenever a scope is exited via break, continue, or return.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What does an unlabeled break statement do inside a nested loop?
options: Terminates only the innermost enclosing loop
Skips to the next iteration of the inner loop
sections.explanation: An unlabeled break statement only terminates the nearest enclosing (innermost) loop.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: break halts loop or switch execution immediately.
Unlabeled break exits only the innermost enclosing structure.
Labeled break `break label;` allows escaping multi-level nested loops directly.
Crucial for optimizing linear searches and preventing switch fallthrough.

sections.content: Next, we explore the continue Statement, learning how to skip specific iterations without terminating the entire loop.

lessons.title: continue Statement
lessons.description: The continue statement is the 'Skip Track' button on a music player. It doesn't turn off the music player (unlike break which halts everything); it simply aband...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `for`, `while`, and `do-while` loops, and the difference between `break` and `continue`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `continue` statement is the 'Skip Track' button on a music player. It doesn't turn off the music player (unlike `break` which halts everything); it simply abandons the remainder of the currently playing song and immediately cues up the next song in the playlist.

sections.title: Where Does continue Jump?
sections.content:
• In a `for` loop: `continue` jumps directly to the **update step** (`i++`), and then re-evaluates the condition.
• In a `while` / `do-while` loop: `continue` jumps directly to the **boolean condition check**.

⚠️ CRITICAL DANGER: In a `while` loop, if your variable increment (`i++`) is placed *after* the `continue` statement, it will be skipped, causing a permanent **INFINITE LOOP**!

sections.title: Filtering Iterations with continue & The while Loop Pitfall
sections.explanation: In for loops, continue reliably triggers the increment clause. In while loops, developers must ensure the loop counter is updated before invoking continue.

sections.title: Using continue as a Loop Guard Clause
Try It: Skip Multiples of 3
sections.explanation: When n is 3, 6, and 9, continue triggers, skipping the print statement and moving straight to n++.

iterations.description: Prints '1'.
continue encountered! Jumps straight to i++.
Prints '3'.
continue encountered! Jumps straight to i++.

sections.title: Common continue Mistakes
items: Creating accidental infinite while loops by placing counter increments after the continue statement.
Confusing `break` (aborts entire loop) with `continue` (aborts current iteration only).
Attempting to use `continue` inside a `switch` block (continue belongs only to loops).

sections.title: Interview Traps: continue in while Loops

traps.question: What happens when this code runs: int i = 0; while (i < 5) { if (i == 3) continue; i++; }?
traps.trap: Thinking it prints numbers 0 to 4 except 3.
traps.solution: It hangs in an INFINITE LOOP! When `i` reaches 3, `continue` jumps to the condition `while (i < 5)`. Because `i++` was skipped, `i` remains 3 indefinitely, re-triggering continue forever.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: When continue executes inside a for loop `for(int i=0; i<10; i++)`, what executes next?
options: The statement immediately after the loop
The update step `i++`, then the condition `i < 10`
The condition check `i < 10` without incrementing i
sections.explanation: In a for loop, continue jumps directly to the update expression (i++), and then evaluates the loop termination condition.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: continue abandons the rest of the current iteration and begins the next.
In for loops, continue jumps to the update step.
In while loops, ensure the loop variable is incremented before continue to prevent infinite loops.
Use continue as a guard clause to flatten deeply nested loop bodies.

lessons.title: return Statement
lessons.description: The return statement is the Exit Door & Delivery Parcel of a method. It halts all execution within the current method immediately, pops the method's stack frame...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand method declarations, return types (`void` vs data types), and control flow structures.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `return` statement is the Exit Door & Delivery Parcel of a method. It halts all execution within the current method immediately, pops the method's stack frame off the execution call stack, and hands control (and any resulting parcel / value) back to the calling function.

sections.title: Rules of the return Statement
sections.content:
1. **In `void` methods**: `return;` (with no value) is optional at the end, but can be used anywhere to exit early.
2. **In non-void methods**: `return value;` is MANDATORY. The returned value must be assignment-compatible with the declared return type.
3. **Definite Assignment & Return**: The compiler verifies that EVERY possible execution path produces a return statement.
4. **Unreachable Code**: Any code placed directly after an unconditional return produces a compile error.

sections.title: Guaranteed Return Paths & Early Exit Guard Clauses
sections.explanation: Early returns simplify complex method logic by rejecting invalid inputs immediately at the top.

sections.title: The Definite Return Rule & Unreachable Code
Try It: Number Clamp Function
sections.explanation: Because val (150) is greater than max (100), the method returns max (100) immediately.

sections.title: Call Stack Trace with return Statement

iterations.description: New stack frame pushed for clamp().
First guard clause skipped.
Second guard clause matched: returns max (100).

variables.stack: clamp() frame popped, control returns to main()

iterations.description: main() receives value 100.

sections.title: Common return Statement Mistakes
items: Missing return statement in one branch of an if-else structure.
Attempting to return a value from a method declared with `void` return type.
Placing executable statements immediately after a `return`, causing an 'unreachable code' compile error.

sections.title: Interview Traps: return vs finally Block

traps.question: What is returned by this method: public static int test() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }?
traps.trap: Thinking it returns 1 or throws an error.
traps.solution: It returns 2! When a `finally` block contains a `return` statement, it silently discards and overrides any return value or pending exception from the `try` block. (Warning: placing a return inside a finally block is a severe anti-pattern).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Can a method with a `void` return type include a return statement?
options: No, return is forbidden in void methods
Yes, but only 'return;' without any value to exit early
sections.explanation: A void method can use 'return;' with no attached value to terminate execution early.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: return exits the current method immediately and returns control to the caller.
Non-void methods must return a compatible value across every possible path.
Code directly following an unconditional return is flagged as unreachable.
Guard clauses with early returns keep methods flat, clean, and readable.

lessons.title: Why Loops?
lessons.description: Loops are the Automation Engines of computing. Why do computers exist? Humans tire quickly and make errors when repeating tasks; computers can execute identical...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand sequential execution, variables, control flow branching (`if`/`else`), and arithmetic increment operators (`++`, `+=`).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Loops are the Automation Engines of computing. Why do computers exist? Humans tire quickly and make errors when repeating tasks; computers can execute identical mathematical operations millions of times per second with 100% precision. Without loops, processing 10,000 bank accounts would require copy-pasting 10,000 identical lines of code—creating an unmaintainable codebase.

sections.title: The 3 Fundamental Invariants of Every Loop
sections.content:
Regardless of programming language or syntax, EVERY loop relies on three essential elements:
1. **Initialization**: Setting up the starting state or counter variable before looping begins.
2. **Termination Condition**: A boolean expression evaluated on each cycle. When `true`, loop continues; when `false`, loop terminates.
3. **Update / Step**: Mutating the state on every iteration so the program moves closer to the termination condition.

⚠️ If the update step is missing or faulty, the condition never becomes `false`, resulting in an **Infinite Loop** that freezes the CPU thread.

sections.title: The Problem: Manual Duplication vs Loop Automation
sections.explanation: Loops decouple the volume of data being processed from the physical length of your source code.

sections.title: The Three Loop Archetypes in Java
sections.content:
Java provides three distinct looping mechanisms tailored for specific programming scenarios:

• `for` loop: Used for **Definite / Counted Iteration** where the number of steps or collection bounds are known in advance.
• `while` loop: Used for **Indefinite / State-Driven Iteration** where execution continues until a dynamic condition or sentinel value is met.
• `do-while` loop: Used for **Post-Tested Iteration** where the loop body must execute at least once (e.g. interactive user prompts).

sections.title: Try It: Predict Iteration Count
sections.explanation: The loop runs for step = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 (5 iterations total).

iterations.description: Init: i=1. Condition check passes. Executes body: prints 1.
Update: i becomes 2. Condition check passes. Executes body: prints 2.
Update: i becomes 3. Condition check passes. Executes body: prints 3.
Update: i becomes 4. Condition check FAILS. Loop terminates immediately.

sections.title: Common Loop Pitfalls
items: **Off-by-One Errors (Fencepost Problem)**: Using `<` instead of `<=` (or starting at 1 vs 0), causing the loop to run 1 too many or 1 too few times.
**Missing Update Step**: Forgetting to increment the loop variable in `while` loops, causing permanent thread hangs.
**Modifying Loop Variable inside Body**: Mutating `i` both in the loop header and inside the loop body, causing unpredictable skip bugs.

traps.question: What is the primary operational difference between a loop and recursion in Java?
traps.trap: Thinking they have identical memory overhead.
traps.solution: Loops execute iteratively within a single stack frame, using $O(1)$ constant stack memory. Recursion pushes a brand new stack frame onto the Call Stack for EVERY iteration. If recursion runs 10,000+ levels deep without tail-call optimization (which Java does not support), it will throw a `StackOverflowError`, whereas a loop can run billions of iterations safely.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What are the three essential components required by every well-formed loop?
sections.explanation: Every loop requires Initialization (starting state), a Termination Condition (exit criteria), and an Update step (progress towards exit).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Loops automate repetitive computational tasks with O(1) code size.
Every loop must have: Initialization, Condition, and Update.
Choose `for` for counted iterations, `while` for indeterminate conditions, and `do-while` for at-least-once execution.

sections.content: Next, we deep-dive into the for Loop, examining its 4-phase execution lifecycle, block scoping, and multi-variable headers.

content.theory:
Loops let a program repeat work without repeating code. Printing a times table, summing a list of prices, reading every line of a file and checking every user in a database all follow the same idea: do something for each item, or keep doing something until a condition changes. Computers excel at repetition, and loops are how you harness that. This lesson explains why loops exist, the parts every loop has, the kinds of loops Java offers, and how to think about loop correctness and cost.

## The problem without loops

Printing the numbers 1 to 5 without a loop takes five statements:

~~~java
System.out.println(1);
System.out.println(2);
System.out.println(3);
System.out.println(4);
System.out.println(5);
~~~

Printing 1 to 1,000 this way is absurd, and printing 1 to n, where n comes from user input, is impossible: you can't know at writing time how many statements to write. A loop handles any count with the same few lines:

~~~java
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}
~~~

## The parts of every loop

Whatever the syntax, a loop has four parts:

1. **Initialization**: set up the starting state, such as `int i = 1`
2. **Condition**: a boolean test checked before (or after) each repetition; the loop continues while it's true
3. **Body**: the statements that repeat
4. **Update**: change the state so the condition eventually becomes false, such as `i++`

If the update never brings the condition to false, the loop runs forever: an **infinite loop**.

## Java's loops

| Loop | Best for | Condition checked |
|---|---|---|
| `for` | A known number of repetitions, counting | Before each iteration |
| enhanced `for` (for-each) | Visiting every element of an array or collection | Implicitly, per element |
| `while` | Repeating until something happens, count unknown | Before each iteration |
| `do-while` | Running at least once, such as menus | After each iteration |

All loops are interchangeable in principle; choosing the one that matches the situation makes code easier to read.

## Iterations and tracing

Each pass through the body is an **iteration**. Tracing a loop means tracking variables across iterations:

~~~java
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    sum += i;
}
~~~

| Iteration | i | sum after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 6 |
| 4 | 4 | 10 |

After the fourth iteration, `i` becomes 5, the condition `5 <= 4` fails, and the loop ends. Trace tables like this solve most loop output questions.

## Loop invariants

A **loop invariant** is a statement that's true before and after every iteration. For the sum loop: "sum equals 1 + 2 + ... + (i - 1)". If the invariant holds at the start, each iteration preserves it, and the loop ends, then the result is correct. Thinking in invariants is the most reliable way to write loops that work the first time, and it's how binary search and sorting algorithms are proven correct.

## Off-by-one errors

The most common loop bug is running one time too many or too few:

- `i <= n` versus `i < n`
- starting at 0 versus 1
- array indices run from 0 to length - 1

Always check the first and last iterations explicitly: what is i on the first pass, and on the last?

## Infinite loops

~~~java
int i = 0;
while (i < 10) {
    System.out.println(i);   // forgot i++: prints 0 forever
}
~~~

Sometimes infinite loops are intentional, such as a server waiting for requests or a game loop, written as `while (true)` with a break or return inside. Unintentional ones freeze the program; in a terminal, Ctrl+C stops it.

## The cost of loops

Loops are where programs spend their time. A loop over n items does work proportional to n, written O(n). A loop inside a loop over the same items does about n × n work, O(n²). For n = 100,000, that's ten billion steps, far too slow. Recognizing loop structures and estimating their cost is the foundation of algorithm analysis and of passing time limits in coding rounds.

## Alternatives to explicit loops

Java offers higher-level tools that loop internally:

~~~java
int total = Arrays.stream(prices).sum();
list.forEach(System.out::println);
~~~

Streams and library methods such as `Arrays.fill` and `Collections.max` express intent concisely. Recursion is another way to repeat, covered in the problem-solving module. Understanding plain loops first makes these tools easier to understand.

## Choosing the right loop

- know the count in advance: `for`
- visiting every element without needing the index: for-each
- waiting for a condition, such as valid input or the end of a file: `while`
- the body must run at least once: `do-while`

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Why do we need loops?", "Difference between while and do-while?", trace-the-output questions, and spotting infinite loops or off-by-one errors. Name the four loop parts, explain when each loop type fits, trace with a table, and estimate cost for nested loops.

lessons.description: The for loop is an Odometer / Fixed-Interval Stepper. When you know in advance how many times an operation should run (e.g. counting from 1 to 100, visiting eve...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `why-loops`, increment/decrement operators (`++`, `--`), and relational comparisons (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `for` loop is an Odometer / Fixed-Interval Stepper. When you know in advance how many times an operation should run (e.g. counting from 1 to 100, visiting every element in an array of size $N$, or counting down by 5s), the `for` loop packages the initialization, condition, and step update into a single, compact header line.

sections.title: The 4-Phase Execution Lifecycle
sections.content:
Syntax: `for (Phase 1: Init; Phase 2: Condition; Phase 4: Update) { Phase 3: Body }`

1. **Phase 1 (Initialization)**: Executes EXACTLY ONCE when the loop is first encountered.
2. **Phase 2 (Condition Evaluation)**: Evaluated BEFORE every iteration. If `false`, loop terminates immediately.
3. **Phase 3 (Body Execution)**: All statements inside `{}` execute.
4. **Phase 4 (Update Step)**: Executes AFTER the body finishes. Control then jumps directly back to **Phase 2**.

sections.title: Versatile for Loop Patterns in Practice
sections.explanation: The for loop header supports multiple variable declarations of the same type and multiple step expressions separated by commas.

sections.title: Loop Variable Scope & Optional Header Clauses
sections.content:
Variables declared inside the `for` header have **block scope**—they exist only within the loop construct and are discarded once the loop ends:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { ... }
// System.out.println(i); // COMPILE ERROR: 'i' cannot be resolved to a variable
```

All three header clauses are optional:
• `for (;;)` is valid Java syntax creating an **infinite loop** (equivalent to `while (true)`).
• Initialization can occur outside the loop if the variable must outlive the loop.

sections.title: Try It: Sum of First N Even Numbers
sections.explanation: Calculates 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30.

sections.title: 4-Phase Lifecycle Trace: for (int i=0; i<3; i++)

iterations.description: Init runs once. Condition true -> executes body.
Body finishes. Update increments i to 1.
Condition true. Body runs. Update increments i to 2.
Condition true. Body runs. Update increments i to 3.
Condition fails. Control jumps past the loop body.

sections.title: Common for Loop Mistakes
items: **Accidental Semicolon after Header**: `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++); { ... }` runs an empty loop 5 times, then executes the `{}` block ONCE unconditionally.
**Array Index Out of Bounds**: `for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)` causes `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at `i == arr.length` (use `< arr.length`).
**Using Floating-Point Counters**: `for (double d = 0.0; d != 1.0; d += 0.1)` enters an infinite loop because IEEE 754 floating-point inaccuracies prevent `d` from ever equaling exactly `1.0`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Unreachable Code in for Loops

traps.question: Why does `for (int i=0; false; i++) { System.out.println(i); }` fail compilation?
traps.trap: Thinking the loop simply skips execution without error.
traps.solution: In Java, if the compiler can determine at compile time that a loop condition is constant `false`, the statements inside the body are marked as UNREACHABLE CODE, triggering a compile-time error: 'unreachable statement'.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: When does the update expression (e.g. `i++`) in a for loop execute?
options: At the very beginning of the loop cycle
At the end of each iteration, after the body finishes
sections.explanation: The update step executes strictly at the end of each iteration after the loop body has finished, just before re-checking the condition.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: for loop packages Init, Condition, and Update into a single compact header.
Execution order: 1. Init -> 2. Condition -> 3. Body -> 4. Update -> repeat from 2.
Variables declared in the header have block scope restricted to the loop.
Never place a semicolon directly after the for header.
