content.theory:
The `for` loop packs initialization, condition and update into a single line, making it the natural choice when the number of iterations is known or can be computed: counting from 1 to n, visiting every array index, or stepping through a range. Java also has an enhanced for loop for visiting each element of an array or collection directly. This lesson covers the classic for loop's anatomy and execution order, counting patterns, scope of the loop variable, the enhanced for loop, and common mistakes.

## Anatomy

~~~java
for (initialization; condition; update) {
    body
}
~~~

~~~java
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    System.out.println("Line " + i);
}
~~~

## Execution order

1. **Initialization** runs once: `int i = 1`
2. **Condition** is checked; if false, the loop ends immediately
3. **Body** runs
4. **Update** runs: `i++`
5. Back to step 2

The condition is checked before every iteration, including the first. If it's false from the start, as in `for (int i = 10; i < 5; i++)`, the body never runs.

## Counting patterns

~~~java
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)        // 0 to n-1: n iterations, array indices
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)       // 1 to n: n iterations, human counting
for (int i = n; i >= 1; i--)       // n down to 1
for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2)     // 0, 2, 4, ...: even indices
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)    // 1, 2, 4, 8, ...: about log2(n) iterations
~~~

The last pattern doubles each time, so it runs about log₂(n) times. Recognizing it matters for estimating complexity.

## Scope of the loop variable

A variable declared in the initialization exists only inside the loop:

~~~java
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { ... }
System.out.println(i);   // compile error: i isn't in scope
~~~

If you need the final value after the loop, declare the variable before it:

~~~java
int i;
for (i = 0; i < arr.length && arr[i] != target; i++) { }
// i is now the index of target, or arr.length if not found
~~~

## Multiple variables

The initialization and update can hold several comma-separated parts, useful for two-pointer techniques:

~~~java
for (int left = 0, right = arr.length - 1; left < right; left++, right--) {
    int tmp = arr[left];
    arr[left] = arr[right];
    arr[right] = tmp;
}
~~~

This reverses an array in place by swapping from both ends toward the middle.

## Optional parts

All three parts are optional. `for (;;)` is an infinite loop, equivalent to `while (true)`. Omitting parts usually signals that a while loop would be clearer.

## The enhanced for loop

The for-each loop visits every element of an array or any `Iterable` collection:

~~~java
int[] scores = {78, 92, 85};
int total = 0;
for (int s : scores) {
    total += s;
}

List<String> names = List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera");
for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println(name);
}
~~~

Read it as "for each `s` in `scores`". It removes index bookkeeping and off-by-one errors.

## Limits of for-each

The enhanced for loop gives you each element's **value**, not its position. Use a classic for loop when you need to:

- know the index, such as printing "Item 3"
- modify array elements: assigning to the loop variable changes only the local copy
- traverse backwards or skip elements
- compare adjacent elements (`arr[i]` and `arr[i + 1]`)
- iterate over two arrays in parallel

~~~java
for (int s : scores) {
    s = s + 5;            // changes the local copy only; the array is unchanged
}
for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) {
    scores[i] += 5;       // changes the array
}
~~~

Removing items from a collection inside a for-each loop throws `ConcurrentModificationException`; use an Iterator's `remove` method or `list.removeIf(...)` instead.

## Common mistakes

**Off by one**: `for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)` reads `arr[arr.length]` and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

**Stray semicolon**:

~~~java
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++);   // empty body runs 5 times
{
    System.out.println("Hi");  // prints once
}
~~~

**Modifying the loop variable in the body**: changing `i` inside the body as well as in the update makes the iteration count hard to reason about.

**Floating-point counters**: `for (double x = 0; x != 1.0; x += 0.1)` may never end, because 0.1 added ten times isn't exactly 1.0. Use integer counters and compute the double from them.

**Recomputing expensive conditions**: `for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++)` is fine for ArrayList, but calling an expensive method in the condition on every iteration can waste time; compute it once before the loop when it doesn't change.

## for versus while

Any for loop can be written as a while loop and vice versa. Prefer for when initialization, condition and update all concern one counter; prefer while when the loop waits for a condition unrelated to counting.

## How interviewers test this

Expect output questions tracing for loops with different updates, off-by-one bugs, the stray semicolon trap, and "when can't you use for-each?" Explain the execution order, scope of the loop variable, counting patterns including doubling, and the value-copy limitation of the enhanced for loop.

lessons.title: while Loop
lessons.description: The while loop is a Guarded Sentry Gate. It checks credentials before granting entry. You use a while loop when you do NOT know how many times the code needs to...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand boolean conditions, relational operators, and basic iteration concepts.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `while` loop is a Guarded Sentry Gate. It checks credentials *before* granting entry. You use a `while` loop when you do NOT know how many times the code needs to repeat beforehand—such as reading data until a network connection closes, finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers, or extracting digits until a number becomes 0.

sections.title: Pre-Condition Testing Principle
sections.content:
In a `while` loop, the boolean condition is evaluated **BEFORE** entering the body:
• If the condition is `true`, the body executes, then loops back to re-evaluate.
• If the condition is `false` initially, the loop body executes **ZERO times**.

⚠️ State Invariant: Something inside the loop body MUST eventually mutate the variables involved in the condition, otherwise the loop runs forever.

sections.title: Classic while Loop Patterns: Digit Extraction & Sentinel Control
sections.explanation: Digit processing algorithms naturally fit while loops because the number of digits is state-dependent rather than a static pre-counted range.

sections.title: Mechanical Equivalence: for vs while
Try It: Sum of Digits
sections.explanation: Extracts 6 (sum=6, num=45), 5 (sum=11, num=4), and 4 (sum=15, num=0). Loop terminates.

sections.title: Digit Extraction Trace: while (n > 0) for n = 35

iterations.description: Condition passes. digit = 35 % 10 = 5. n becomes 35 / 10 = 3.
Condition passes. digit = 3 % 10 = 3. n becomes 3 / 10 = 0.
Condition FAILS (0 > 0 is false). Loop exits immediately.

sections.title: Common while Loop Pitfalls
items: **The Semicolon Lock**: `while (count < 10); { count++; }` creates an infinite empty loop because the semicolon terminates the header.
**Variable Leakage**: Unlike `for` loops, variables initialized before a `while` loop persist in the outer scope, potentially causing name collisions.
**Missing State Progression**: Forgetting to update loop variables inside complex conditional branches within the while loop.

traps.question: How many times does this loop execute: int x = 10; while (x < 5) { x++; }?
traps.trap: Assuming it executes at least once.
traps.solution: Zero times! Because `while` is a pre-test loop, `10 < 5` evaluates to false immediately on entry, skipping the entire body.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the minimum number of times a while loop body can execute?
sections.explanation: If the condition evaluates to false on the very first check, the body executes 0 times.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: while loops evaluate their condition before each iteration (pre-test loop).
Can execute 0 times if condition is initially false.
Ideal for indeterminate iteration, digit manipulation, and sentinel checks.
Ensure the body updates state to avoid infinite loops.

sections.title: Connection to Next Lesson
sections.content: Next, we explore the do-while Loop, where code is guaranteed to execute at least once before testing the condition.

lessons.title: do-while Loop
lessons.description: The do-while loop is a 'Try First, Ask Later' / Post-Test Gate. Unlike while (which checks your ticket before letting you ride), a do-while loop lets you ride o...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `while` loops, boolean expressions, and user input/menu logic.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `do-while` loop is a 'Try First, Ask Later' / Post-Test Gate. Unlike `while` (which checks your ticket before letting you ride), a `do-while` loop lets you ride once first, and only checks if you want/qualify to ride again *after* the ride finishes.

sections.title: Post-Condition Testing Principle
sections.content:
In a `do-while` loop, the boolean condition is evaluated **AFTER** executing the body:
• The loop body is **GUARANTEED to execute at least 1 time**, even if the condition is `false` from the beginning.
• Syntax Requirement: The trailing semicolon `while (condition);` is **MANDATORY** in Java grammar.

sections.title: Interactive CLI Menu & Input Validation Pattern
sections.explanation: Input validation and menu systems naturally require running the prompt at least once before knowing whether to re-prompt.

sections.title: The Variable Scoping Trap in do-while
Try It: Post-Test Execution Guarantee
sections.expectedOutput:
Executes even though condition is false: 100
Loop finished.
sections.explanation: Even though 100 is not < 50, the body runs once before the condition is checked.

sections.title: do-while Post-Condition Trace: False Condition on Startup

iterations.description: Enters do body unconditionally.
Prints output and increments val to 101.
Condition evaluates to false.
Control continues past the loop after exactly 1 iteration.

sections.title: Common do-while Mistakes
items: **Omitting the Trailing Semicolon**: `do { ... } while (cond)` without a semicolon `;` is a compile error.
**Declaring Variables inside the `do` Block**: The `while(...)` condition cannot access variables declared inside the `{}` body.

**Using do-while when 0 iterations may be required**: If processing an empty collection or null stream, `do-while` will attempt to process the first element and potentially crash with a `NullPointerException`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Comparison of Minimum Loop Iterations

traps.question: What are the minimum possible execution counts for `for`, `while`, and `do-while` loops in Java?
traps.trap: Confusing `while` and `do-while` minimums.
traps.solution:
• `for` loop: Minimum = 0
• `while` loop: Minimum = 0
• `do-while` loop: Minimum = 1 (Guaranteed at least one execution because the condition check is deferred until after the body completes).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Why is a do-while loop preferred over a while loop for interactive CLI menus?
options: It runs faster in the JVM
The menu must be displayed to the user at least once before checking their selection
It does not require boolean conditions
sections.explanation: CLI menus require rendering options to the user at least once before evaluating whether they chose to exit.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: do-while guarantees at least ONE execution of the loop body (post-test loop).
Must terminate with a semicolon: `while (condition);`.
Variables used in the condition must be declared outside the do block.
Ideal for menus, input re-prompts, and retry loops.

lessons.title: Nested Loops
lessons.description: Nested loops are like the Hands of a Clock (Hour Hand vs Minute Hand). For every single tick/advance the slow Hour Hand makes (the outer loop), the fast Minute ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `for` and `while` loops, 2D Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$, and basic time complexity intuition.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Nested loops are like the Hands of a Clock (Hour Hand vs Minute Hand). For every single tick/advance the slow Hour Hand makes (the outer loop), the fast Minute Hand must complete a full 360-degree rotation of 60 ticks (the inner loop). The inner loop starts over from the beginning on every single iteration of the outer loop.

sections.title: The Multiplicative Iteration Rule
sections.content:
If an outer loop runs $N$ times and its inner loop runs $M$ times, the statements inside the inner loop execute a total of:
$$\text{Total Operations} = N \times M$$

• For quadratic loops ($N = M$): Runs $N^2$ times ($O(N^2)$ time complexity).
• For 3 nested loops of size $N$: Runs $N^3$ times ($O(N^3)$ cubic complexity).

sections.title: 2D Matrix Traversal & Multiplication Tables
sections.explanation: The outer loop controls vertical row progression, while the inner loop scans horizontally across columns.

sections.title: Independent vs Dependent Nested Loops
sections.content:
• **Independent Inner Loops**: The inner loop bounds are constant and do not depend on the outer variable (e.g. `for(int j=0; j<M; j++)`). Total work = $N \times M$.
• **Dependent Inner Loops**: The inner loop bound varies based on the current outer variable `i` (e.g. `for(int j=0; j<=i; j++)`). Total operations form an arithmetic series: $1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + N = \frac{N(N+1)}{2} \approx \frac{N^2}{2}$, which is still $O(N^2)$ time complexity.

sections.title: Try It: Coordinate Pair Generator
sections.explanation: Outer x=1 pairs with y=1,2,3. Then x=2 pairs with y=1,2,3.

sections.title: Nested Iteration Trace: 2 Rows x 2 Columns

iterations.description: Outer row 1 starts. Inner col 1 runs -> prints (1,1).
Outer row 1 continues. Inner col 2 runs -> prints (1,2). Inner loop ends.
Outer row 2 starts. Inner col resets to 1 -> prints (2,1).
Outer row 2 continues. Inner col 2 runs -> prints (2,2). All loops finish.

sections.title: Common Nested Loop Pitfalls
items: **Variable Name Shadowing / Re-use**: Accidentally using `i` for both outer and inner loops, corrupting the loop counter.
**Forgetting Newline between Rows**: Printing all elements on a single unreadable line by omitting `System.out.println()` after the inner loop.
**Unintentional Complexity Explosions**: Nesting 3 or 4 loops over large collections ($1000^3 = 10^9$ operations), freezing the application.

traps.question: What is the time complexity of: for(int i=0; i<n; i++) for(int j=0; j<=i; j++) { sum++; }?
traps.trap: Thinking it is O(N) because the inner loop only goes up to i.
traps.solution: It is $O(N^2)$! The number of inner iterations is $1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n^2 + n}{2}$. Dropping lower-order terms and constants yields $O(N^2)$ quadratic time complexity.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: If an outer loop runs 5 times and an inner loop runs 4 times per outer iteration, how many total times does the inner loop body execute?
sections.explanation: Total executions = Outer count × Inner count = 5 × 4 = 20.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Inner loops complete their entire lifecycle for every single tick of the outer loop.
Total iterations equal the product of outer and inner loop counts ($N \times M$).
Essential for 2D matrix manipulation, image processing, and pattern printing.
Use distinct, descriptive variable names (e.g., `row` and `col`).

lessons.description:
Think of break and continue as precision flight controls for loops:
• break is the Emergency Ejection Seat: It aborts the entire flight mission immediately and ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand single and nested `for`/`while` loops, and basic jump statement mechanics.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of `break` and `continue` as precision flight controls for loops:
• `break` is the **Emergency Ejection Seat**: It aborts the entire flight mission immediately and lands outside the loop.
• `continue` is the **Skip Waypoint Thruster**: It abandons the current waypoint coordinates and flies directly to the next scheduled flight path.

sections.title: The Innermost Enclosure Rule vs Labeled Controls
Search Optimization with Labeled break and continue
sections.explanation: Labeled breaks avoid the need to maintain cumbersome boolean flags (`boolean stopAll = true`) across multiple nested levels.

sections.title: Performance Benefits of Early Search Aborts
sections.content:
In a dataset with $1,000,000$ elements, searching for a key that appears at index $5$ takes:
• Without `break`: $1,000,000$ iterations (wasteful CPU burn).
• With `break`: Exactly $6$ iterations (99.9994% reduction in CPU time!).

sections.title: Try It: Filter & Early Stop
sections.explanation: Prints odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7. When i reaches 9 (> 7), break terminates the loop before printing.

iterations.description: No match. Continues inner loop.
Match found! 'break gridSearch' executed.
Both inner and outer loops terminate in a single step.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls with Loop Jumps
items: Placing labels on statements that are not loops (labels can only be applied to blocks or loops).
Using `continue` inside a `while` loop without incrementing the counter variable first (causes infinite loop).
Overusing labeled breaks instead of decomposing complex nested code into small, focused helper methods with `return` statements.

sections.title: Interview Traps: break vs return in Nested Loops

traps.question: When should you use a labeled break vs extracting the loops into a method and using 'return'?
traps.trap: Assuming labeled break is always the preferred clean code approach.
traps.solution: Modern clean coding standards generally recommend extracting deeply nested search loops into a dedicated helper method (e.g. `findCoordinates()`) and using `return new Point(r, c);`. Labeled break is useful for localized algorithmic scripts, but helper methods with returns provide cleaner abstraction.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: In a 2-level nested loop without labels, what happens when 'continue' executes inside the inner loop?
options: It skips to the next iteration of the outer loop
It skips the rest of the inner loop body and advances the inner loop
It restarts the outer loop from zero
sections.explanation: An unlabeled continue applies strictly to the innermost loop, advancing its iteration.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: break halts execution immediately; continue skips to the next iteration.
Unlabeled jump statements affect strictly the innermost enclosing loop.
Labeled break/continue allows surgical multi-level navigation.
Early termination via break transforms O(N) worst-case into O(1) best-case for searches.

lessons.title: Counting & Accumulation Patterns
lessons.description:
Think of these two patterns as Turnstile Clickers vs Cash Register Drawers:
• Counter Pattern (Clicker): Starts at $0$. Whenever an event of interest occurs (e....

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand loops (`for`/`while`), compound assignment operators (`+=`, `*=`), and primitive data types.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of these two patterns as Turnstile Clickers vs Cash Register Drawers:
• **Counter Pattern (Clicker)**: Starts at $0$. Whenever an event of interest occurs (e.g., encountering a negative number or passing a test), you click `count++`.
• **Accumulator Pattern (Cash Register)**: Starts with a neutral identity value ($0$ for additions, $1$ for multiplications). Every incoming item is absorbed into the running total: `sum += item` or `product *= item`.

sections.title: The Identity Value Invariants
sections.content:
Choosing the correct initial value before the loop begins is critical:
• **Summation Accumulator**: Start at `0` (Additive Identity: $x + 0 = x$).
• **Product Accumulator**: Start at `1` (Multiplicative Identity: $x \times 1 = x$. Starting at 0 makes everything 0!).
• **Minimum Finder**: Start at `Integer.MAX_VALUE` (or array's first element).
• **Maximum Finder**: Start at `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (or array's first element).

sections.title: The 4 Core Accumulation Blueprints in Practice
sections.explanation: These four patterns form the algorithmic building blocks for data aggregations, statistics, and business calculations.

sections.title: The Reset Trap in Nested Accumulators
Try It: Count Multiples of 5
sections.explanation: 10, 15, 25, and 30 are divisible by 5, giving a count of 4.

sections.title: Accumulator Running State Trace: Sum of [10, 20, 30]

iterations.description: sum becomes 0 + 10 = 10.
sum becomes 10 + 20 = 30.
sum becomes 30 + 30 = 60.
Loop terminates; 60 available for downstream processing.

sections.title: Common Accumulator Mistakes
items: **Initializing Product to 0**: Setting `int product = 0;` causes the result to remain `0` forever.
**Integer Division in Averages**: Writing `double avg = sum / count;` where both are integers truncates decimals (e.g. `7 / 2` yields `3.0` instead of `3.5`).
**Integer Overflow**: Summing many large integers exceeds `2,147,483,647`, silently wrapping to negative numbers (use `long`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Division by Zero on Empty Datasets

traps.question: What happens when calculating the average of an empty array: int[] arr = {}; double avg = (double) sum / arr.length;?
traps.trap: Assuming it returns 0.0.
traps.solution: Because `arr.length` is 0 and double division by zero is defined in IEEE 754, `0.0 / 0` results in `Double.NaN` (Not a Number)! In production code, always guard with `if (arr.length == 0) return 0.0;`.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What should a product accumulator variable be initialized to?
sections.explanation: A product accumulator must start at 1 (the multiplicative identity). Starting at 0 would multiply everything by 0.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Counters tally events (`count++`); Accumulators aggregate values (`sum += val`).
Initialize sum to 0, product to 1, min to MAX_VALUE, max to MIN_VALUE.
Cast to double before division to preserve decimal precision in averages.
Reset nested accumulators inside outer loops.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand nested loops, row-by-row iteration, and `System.out.print()` vs `System.out.println()`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Pattern printing is like a Dot Matrix / CRT Printer. The printer print head sweeps horizontally across Row 1 character by character (using `System.out.print()`). When the row ends, it issues a carriage return newline (`System.out.println()`) to drop down to Row 2. You can NEVER jump backwards to an earlier row or column.

sections.title: The 4-Step Universal Pattern Formula
sections.content:
Every geometric pattern can be solved using this standard structure:
1. **Outer Loop**: Controls the row number `r` (typically `1` to `N`).
2. **Inner Loop 1 (Leading Spaces)**: Prints spaces for right-aligned or symmetric pyramid shapes.
3. **Inner Loop 2 (Symbols/Numbers)**: Prints characters based on a formula relating current row `r` to column `c`.
4. **Row Terminator**: Execute `System.out.println()` after all inner loops finish to begin the next line.

sections.title: Classic Geometries: Triangle, Inverted, and Centered Pyramid
sections.explanation: Analyzing the mathematical relationship between the row index 'r' and the column counts (stars & spaces) unlocks any 2D pattern.

sections.title: Number Patterns: Floyd's Triangle & Binary Alternating Triangles
Try It: Number Repeater Triangle
sections.explanation: Row 1 prints '1', Row 2 prints '22', Row 3 prints '333'.

sections.title: Pattern Matrix Dry Run: Centered Pyramid n = 3

iterations.description: Prints '    * ' and newline.
Prints '  * * * ' and newline.
Prints '* * * * * ' and newline.

sections.title: Common Pattern Mistakes
items: **Accidental `println()` in Inner Loop**: Using `println` instead of `print` inside the inner loop breaks the shape into a vertical line.
**Forgetting Outer Loop `println()`**: All rows print on a single continuous horizontal line.
**Space Width Mismatch**: Using 1 space for padding when star characters are printed with trailing spaces (`* ` requires `  ` 2 spaces).

traps.question: How do you construct a symmetrical diamond pattern of size N without duplicating code?
traps.trap: Attempting to create complex condition formulas inside a single inner loop.
traps.solution: Deconstruct the diamond into two distinct halves: Top Pyramid (rows 1 to N) followed by Bottom Inverted Pyramid (rows N-1 down to 1). This separation makes loop bounds trivial and avoids error-prone conditional branching inside inner loops.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: For a right-angled triangle of height N, how many stars are printed in row index r (1-indexed)?
sections.explanation: In a standard right-angled triangle, row 1 has 1 star, row 2 has 2 stars, ..., and row r has exactly r stars.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Outer loop controls rows; inner loops control spaces and characters.
Use `System.out.print()` inside inner loops, and `System.out.println()` after each row.
Derive algebraic formulas relating row index `r` to column counts.
Pattern problems build essential muscle memory for nested coordinate traversals in DSA.

content.theory:
Pattern problems ask you to print shapes, such as triangles, pyramids, diamonds and number grids, using nested loops. They look like puzzles, but they're excellent practice for the core skill of loop design: relating the row number to how many spaces, stars or numbers that row needs. They're common in campus placement tests and first interview rounds. This lesson gives a systematic method for any pattern and works through the classic shapes.

## The systematic method

1. **Count rows**: the outer loop runs once per row, usually `for (int row = 1; row <= n; row++)`
2. **Analyse each row**: write down, for rows 1, 2, 3, how many spaces and how many symbols appear, and what values are printed
3. **Find formulas** in terms of `row` and `n`: for example, row r has r stars, or n - r spaces
4. **One inner loop per segment**: spaces first, then symbols
5. **End each row** with `System.out.println()`

Writing a small table before coding turns a visual puzzle into arithmetic.

## Right triangle

~~~
*
* *
* * *
* * * *
~~~

Row r has r stars.

~~~java
for (int row = 1; row <= n; row++) {
    for (int s = 1; s <= row; s++) {
        System.out.print("* ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}
~~~

## Inverted triangle

Row r has n - r + 1 stars, or count rows downward:

~~~java
for (int row = n; row >= 1; row--) {
    for (int s = 1; s <= row; s++) System.out.print("* ");
    System.out.println();
}
~~~

## Right-aligned triangle

~~~
      *
    * *
  * * *
* * * *
~~~

| Row | Spaces (units) | Stars |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 |
| r | n - r | r |

~~~java
for (int row = 1; row <= n; row++) {
    for (int sp = 1; sp <= n - row; sp++) System.out.print("  ");
    for (int s = 1; s <= row; s++) System.out.print("* ");
    System.out.println();
}
~~~

Each star is printed as two characters ("* "), so each space unit is also two characters to keep alignment.

## Pyramid

~~~
   *
  ***
 *****
*******
~~~

Row r has n - r spaces and 2r - 1 stars.

~~~java
for (int row = 1; row <= n; row++) {
    for (int sp = 1; sp <= n - row; sp++) System.out.print(" ");
    for (int s = 1; s <= 2 * row - 1; s++) System.out.print("*");
    System.out.println();
}
~~~

## Diamond

A diamond is a pyramid followed by an inverted pyramid without repeating the middle row: run the pyramid for rows 1 to n, then the same formulas for rows n - 1 down to 1.

## Number patterns

~~~
1
1 2
1 2 3
~~~

Print the inner loop variable: `System.out.print(col + " ");`

~~~
1
2 2
3 3 3
~~~

Print the row number instead: `System.out.print(row + " ");`

~~~
1
2 3
4 5 6
~~~

Floyd's triangle uses a counter that keeps increasing across rows:

~~~java
int num = 1;
for (int row = 1; row <= n; row++) {
    for (int col = 1; col <= row; col++) {
        System.out.print(num++ + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}
~~~

The counter is declared outside both loops so it doesn't reset each row.

## Alternating and conditional patterns

Patterns such as a 0-1 triangle or a hollow square use conditions inside the inner loop:

~~~java
// Hollow square: stars on the border only
for (int r = 1; r <= n; r++) {
    for (int c = 1; c <= n; c++) {
        boolean border = r == 1 || r == n || c == 1 || c == n;
        System.out.print(border ? "* " : "  ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}
~~~

`(row + col) % 2` produces alternating 0s and 1s for checkerboard patterns.

## Character patterns

~~~
A
A B
A B C
~~~

Use char arithmetic: `System.out.print((char) ('A' + col - 1) + " ");`

## Debugging patterns

- check the first row, the last row and one middle row against your formulas
- print row numbers temporarily to see where a shape goes wrong
- confirm whether the expected output uses "* " or "*", since spacing changes alignment
- watch for println inside the inner loop, which prints one symbol per line

## Why these problems matter

Pattern problems train the same thinking used in matrix traversal, dynamic programming tables and image processing: mapping coordinates (row, column) to values by formula. They also test attention to detail, because one wrong space breaks the expected output.

## How interviewers test this

Expect pyramids, inverted triangles, diamonds, Floyd's triangle and hollow shapes, usually for a given n. Show the row table before coding, derive space and symbol counts as formulas of row and n, use one inner loop per segment, and explain where counters must be declared so they don't reset.

lessons.title: What is an Array?
lessons.description: An array is a Contiguous Apartment Complex on the Heap. Instead of creating 100 separate detached houses (individual variables scattered randomly across memory)...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand primitive variables, data types, stack vs heap memory models, and reference variables.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: An array is a Contiguous Apartment Complex on the Heap. Instead of creating 100 separate detached houses (individual variables scattered randomly across memory), an array builds a single continuous block of identical units lined up side-by-side. The array variable `arr` on your Call Stack is simply the street address (reference pointer) pointing to the front door of Apartment 0.

sections.title: The 3 Invariants of Java Arrays
sections.content:
1. **Homogeneous Data**: All elements inside an array must be of the EXACT same data type (e.g. all `int`, all `double`, or all `String`).
2. **Fixed Capacity**: Once allocated in heap memory with `new dataType[size]`, an array's length is strictly **immutable** and cannot grow or shrink.
3. **Contiguous Memory**: Elements occupy consecutive, unbroken byte addresses in RAM, enabling $O(1)$ instantaneous random access.

sections.title: Array Instantiation, Default Values & Length Property
sections.explanation: In Java, arrays are real heap objects. When instantiated, the JVM automatically wipes the memory block and fills it with type-safe default values.

sections.title: Automatic Default Initialization Values on the Heap
sections.content:
When you allocate an array with `new`, Java automatically initializes every cell to its standard zero-equivalent:

| Element Data Type | Default Initial Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long` | `0` / `0L` |
| `float`, `double` | `0.0f` / `0.0d` |
| `boolean` | `false` |
| `char` | `'\u0000'` (null character) |
| Object References (`String`, `Object`, custom classes) | `null` |

sections.title: Try It: Inspecting Default Values
sections.explanation: Primitive boolean arrays default to false; object reference arrays (like String) default to null.

iterations.description: Array allocated at memory address 0x1000.
Index 0 requires 0 bytes offset. Direct access in O(1).
Index 3 computed instantly via simple arithmetic: Base + (Index * 4).

sections.title: Common Array Pitfalls
items: **`length` vs `length()`**: Array size is an immutable property field (`arr.length`), whereas String size is a method call (`str.length()`).
**Assuming Dynamic Resizing**: Arrays cannot expand. If you need dynamic resizing, use `ArrayList<T>` or create a new larger array and copy elements.
**Printing Array Directly**: `System.out.println(arr)` prints the object type hash code (e.g. `[I@1b6d3586`) instead of contents (use `Arrays.toString(arr)`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Array Type Hierarchy & Object Identity

traps.question: Is an array a primitive or an Object in Java? Does `int[]` inherit from `Object`?
traps.trap: Thinking primitive arrays are primitives because they hold primitives.
traps.solution: In Java, EVERY array (even primitive arrays like `int[]` or `boolean[]`) is a first-class **Object** residing on the Heap. It inherits directly from `java.lang.Object`, implements `Cloneable` and `java.io.Serializable`, and has an object header with class metadata (e.g. `[I` for `int[]`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the time complexity of accessing any arbitrary element in an array by its index `arr[i]`?
sections.explanation: Because memory is contiguous, the CPU calculates the target byte address via a single arithmetic operation `Base + (i * size)`, achieving O(1) constant time access.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Arrays are fixed-size, homogeneous collections stored in contiguous heap memory.
Instantaneous O(1) random access via arithmetic index offsets.
Allocated arrays are automatically filled with type-safe default values.
Size is accessible via the immutable `arr.length` field.

sections.title: Connection to Next Lesson
sections.content: Next, we explore Array Declaration & Initialization, comparing dynamic allocation, array literals, and anonymous inline arrays.

content.theory:
An array is a fixed-size, ordered collection of values of the same type, stored in one contiguous block of memory and accessed by numeric index. Arrays let one variable hold a hundred test scores or a million pixels, and they're the foundation that lists, strings, matrices, heaps and hash tables are built on. This lesson explains what arrays are, why contiguous storage makes index access fast, their fixed-size limitation, how they live in memory in Java, and when to choose a list instead.

## Why arrays exist

Without arrays, storing the marks of five students needs five variables:

~~~java
int m1 = 78, m2 = 92, m3 = 85, m4 = 64, m5 = 71;
~~~

Computing the average means writing every name, and handling 500 students or a number chosen at runtime is impossible. An array stores them all under one name:

~~~java
int[] marks = {78, 92, 85, 64, 71};
int sum = 0;
for (int m : marks) sum += m;
~~~

The same loop works for 5 students or 5 million.

## Key properties

- **Same type**: every element has the declared type, such as `int` or `String`
- **Fixed size**: the length is set when the array is created and never changes
- **Indexed from 0**: the first element is `marks[0]`, the last is `marks[marks.length - 1]`
- **Contiguous**: elements sit next to each other in memory
- **Ordered**: elements keep their positions until you change them

## Why index access is fast

Because elements are contiguous and equally sized, the computer finds any element with arithmetic:

~~~
address of marks[i] = start address + i × element size
~~~

Reading `marks[0]` or `marks[999999]` takes the same time: **O(1)**, constant time. This **random access** is arrays' defining strength. Contiguity also helps CPU caches, which load neighbouring memory together, so looping through an array is extremely fast in practice.

## The cost of fixed size

An array can't grow or shrink. To add an element to a full array, you must create a bigger array and copy everything over, which is O(n). Inserting or deleting in the middle requires shifting later elements, also O(n).

| Operation | Array |
|---|---|
| Read or write by index | O(1) |
| Search unsorted array | O(n) |
| Search sorted array (binary search) | O(log n) |
| Insert or delete in the middle | O(n), shifting elements |
| Grow beyond capacity | O(n), copy to a new array |

## Arrays are objects in Java

In Java, an array is an object on the heap. The variable holds a reference to it:

~~~java
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = a;          // b refers to the same array
b[0] = 99;
System.out.println(a[0]);   // 99
~~~

Assigning an array variable copies the reference, not the elements. Passing an array to a method lets the method modify the caller's elements. Every array also carries its length in a field, `a.length` (no parentheses; it's a field, not a method).

## Bounds checking

Java checks every index access. Reading `marks[5]` on a five-element array throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, as does a negative index. In C, the same mistake silently reads or overwrites neighbouring memory, a major source of security vulnerabilities. Java's check costs a little time but prevents that class of bug.

## Default values

A new array's elements are initialized automatically: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, `'\u0000'` for char, and null for object types such as String. An array of Strings created with `new String[3]` holds three nulls, not three empty strings, so calling a method on an element throws NullPointerException until you assign it.

## Arrays of objects

An array of objects holds **references**, each pointing to a separate object elsewhere on the heap:

~~~java
String[] names = {"Asha", "Ravi"};
~~~

The array stores two references; the String objects live separately.

## Arrays versus ArrayList

| | Array | ArrayList |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Fixed at creation | Grows automatically |
| Element types | Primitives or objects | Objects only (Integer, not int) |
| Syntax | `arr[i]`, `arr.length` | `list.get(i)`, `list.size()` |
| Performance | Slightly faster, less memory for primitives | Boxing overhead for numbers |
| Utilities | `Arrays` class | Many built-in methods |

Use arrays when the size is known and fixed, for primitive data where performance matters, and in algorithm problems; use ArrayList when the number of elements changes. ArrayList is itself built on an array that it replaces with a larger one when full.

## Where arrays appear

Arrays underpin strings (an array of characters internally), images (arrays of pixels), matrices, buffers for files and networks, and data structures such as stacks, queues, heaps and hash tables. Most algorithm interview questions start with "given an array".

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is an array and why is access O(1)?", "Array vs ArrayList?", "What are default values in a new array?" and aliasing output questions. Explain contiguous storage and address arithmetic, fixed size and O(n) insertion, references and `length`, and bounds checking.

lessons.title: Array Declaration & Initialization
lessons.description:
Think of the creation steps as Blueprint vs Construction vs Furnished Move-In:
• Declaration (int[] arr;): Registering the architectural blueprint on the stack ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-an-array`, reference variables, and heap allocation.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of the creation steps as Blueprint vs Construction vs Furnished Move-In:
• **Declaration (`int[] arr;`)**: Registering the architectural blueprint on the stack (currently pointing to `null`).
• **Dynamic Allocation (`arr = new int[5];`)**: Constructing the physical building on the heap (unfurnished, filled with default 0s).
• **Array Literal (`int[] arr = { 10, 20, 30 };`)**: Constructing, sizing, and moving into a fully furnished building in a single concise line.

sections.title: The 4 Array Creation Paradigms
sections.content:
1. **Declare then Allocate**: `int[] arr; arr = new int[5];`
2. **Declare and Allocate in One Step**: `int[] arr = new int[5];`
3. **Array Initializer Literal**: `int[] arr = { 10, 20, 30 };` (size inferred automatically as 3)
4. **Anonymous Array Instantiation**: `new int[] { 10, 20, 30 }` (used when passing arrays inline to methods without naming a variable)

sections.title: All 4 Initialization Syntaxes in Action
sections.explanation: Array literals can only be used on the line of declaration. To reassign an existing array variable or pass inline to a method, use the anonymous array syntax 'new int[] { ... }'.

sections.title: Bracket Placement: Java Style vs C-Style
sections.content:
Java permits two syntactic styles for declaring array references:

```java
int[] a, b; // PREFERRED JAVA STYLE: Both 'a' and 'b' are integer arrays (int[])
int a[], b; // C-STYLE LEGACY: 'a' is an integer array (int[]), but 'b' is a single int!
```

Always place brackets directly after the type (`int[] arr`) to ensure clarity and avoid subtle multi-variable declaration bugs.

sections.title: Try It: Array Literal vs Anonymous Array
sections.explanation: primes is initialized with 5 elements. primes[2] accesses the 3rd element (index 2 = 5).

iterations.description: Declaration: 'int[] arr;' creates reference on stack holding null.
Allocates 12 bytes on heap. Initializes elements to default 0.
Assigns heap memory address to arr reference variable.

sections.title: Common Initialization Mistakes
items: **Illegal Size Specification with Literals**: `int[] arr = new int[3]{1, 2, 3};` is a COMPILE ERROR (do not specify size when providing literal values).
**Reassigning with Literal Syntax**: `int[] arr; arr = {1, 2, 3};` is a COMPILE ERROR (must use `arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3};` when separating assignment from declaration).
**Negative Array Size**: `int[] arr = new int[-5];` compiles, but throws `NegativeArraySizeException` at runtime.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Array Declaration Multi-Variable Trap

traps.question: In `int[] a, b[];`, what are the data types of variable `a` and variable `b`?
traps.trap: Thinking both are 1D arrays.
traps.solution: `a` is a 1-Dimensional array (`int[]`), but `b` is a 2-Dimensional array (`int[][]`)! The base type `int[]` applies to both, and the trailing `[]` on `b` adds a second dimension.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which of the following creates and initializes a valid 3-element integer array?
sections.explanation: `int[] arr = { 10, 20, 30 };` is valid array literal syntax. Specifying `[3]` alongside `{ ... }` produces a compile-time error in Java.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Use `int[] arr = { ... }` for known static data on declaration.
Use `new int[size]` when allocating blank arrays of known dynamic capacity.
Use anonymous syntax `new int[]{ ... }` when reassigning or passing inline to methods.
Prefer `dataType[] arr` over legacy C-style `dataType arr[]`.

content.theory:
Before using an array, you declare a variable to hold it and create the array object, either with a size or with initial values. Java offers several syntaxes for this, and the differences matter: some create default-filled arrays, some fill values directly, and some only work at declaration. This lesson covers declaration styles, creating arrays with `new`, array literals, default values, filling and copying arrays, and common errors.

## Declaring an array variable

~~~java
int[] scores;        // preferred style: the type is "int array"
int scores2[];       // also legal, inherited from C; avoid it
~~~

A declaration creates only a reference variable, initially with no array. Using it before assigning an array is a compile error for local variables, or a NullPointerException for fields left null.

## Creating an array with new

~~~java
int[] scores = new int[5];          // five ints, all 0
String[] names = new String[3];     // three nulls
boolean[] seen = new boolean[100];  // 100 falses
~~~

The size can be any int expression evaluated at runtime:

~~~java
int n = sc.nextInt();
int[] data = new int[n];
~~~

A negative size throws `NegativeArraySizeException`. A size of zero is legal and creates an empty array, useful as a return value meaning "no results" instead of null.

## Default values

| Element type | Default |
|---|---|
| `int`, `long`, `short`, `byte` | 0 |
| `double`, `float` | 0.0 |
| `char` | `'\u0000'` |
| `boolean` | false |
| Any object type | null |

## Array literals

When you know the values, list them in braces:

~~~java
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11};
String[] days = {"Mon", "Tue", "Wed"};
~~~

The length is inferred from the number of values. This short form works only in a declaration. To assign a new array to an existing variable, include the type:

~~~java
primes = {13, 17};                 // compile error
primes = new int[]{13, 17};        // correct
~~~

The `new int[]{...}` form also works for passing an array directly to a method: `printAll(new int[]{1, 2, 3});`. You can't give both a size and values: `new int[3]{1, 2, 3}` is an error.

## Filling an array

~~~java
int[] dist = new int[n];
Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);   // every element set to the same value

int[] squares = new int[10];
for (int i = 0; i < squares.length; i++) {
    squares[i] = i * i;                 // computed values
}
~~~

`Arrays.setAll(squares, i -> i * i)` does the computed version in one line.

## Copying arrays

Assignment copies only the reference:

~~~java
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = a;              // same array
~~~

To copy the elements, use one of these:

~~~java
int[] c = a.clone();                       // full copy
int[] d = Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length);      // full copy
int[] e = Arrays.copyOf(a, 5);             // copy and pad with zeros: {1, 2, 3, 0, 0}
int[] f = Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, 3);     // {2, 3}: from index 1 up to, not including, 3
System.arraycopy(a, 0, target, 0, a.length);   // copy into an existing array
~~~

For arrays of objects, these copies are **shallow**: the new array holds the same object references.

## Comparing arrays

`a == b` checks whether two variables refer to the same array. `a.equals(b)` does the same, because arrays don't override equals. To compare contents, use `Arrays.equals(a, b)`, or `Arrays.deepEquals` for nested arrays.

## Printing arrays

`System.out.println(arr)` prints something like `[I@1b6d3586`. Use `Arrays.toString(arr)` to see `[1, 2, 3]`.

## Arrays of objects need two steps

~~~java
Student[] students = new Student[3];   // three null references
students[0] = new Student("Asha");     // each element needs its own object
~~~

Forgetting the second step leads to NullPointerException when calling methods on elements.

## var with arrays

`var nums = new int[]{1, 2, 3};` works, but `var nums = {1, 2, 3};` doesn't, because an array literal alone has no type to infer.

## Choosing a size

When the count isn't known up front, either read it first (`n`, then the elements), over-allocate with a maximum and track how many slots are used, or use an ArrayList and convert at the end with `list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray()`.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What are the ways to initialize an array?", "What are default values?", "How do you copy an array?" and "Why does `arr1 == arr2` return false for equal contents?" Show new with size, literals and `new int[]{...}`, list defaults, contrast reference assignment with clone and Arrays.copyOf, and use Arrays.equals and Arrays.toString.

lessons.description: Array indexing is Distance / Offset from the Starting Gate. An index is not an arbitrary label; it represents how many element-sized steps forward the CPU must ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand array allocation, the `.length` property, and memory references.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Array indexing is Distance / Offset from the Starting Gate. An index is not an arbitrary label; it represents how many element-sized steps forward the CPU must travel from the array's base memory address:
• Index `0`: $0$ steps forward (you are standing right at the front door).
• Index `1`: $1$ step forward (the 2nd element).
• Index $N-1$: $N-1$ steps forward (the last element).

sections.title: Valid Index Boundaries & Runtime Safety
sections.content:
For an array of size $N$ (`arr.length == N`):
• **First Valid Index**: `0`
• **Last Valid Index**: `arr.length - 1`

⚠️ If you attempt to access an index $< 0$ or $\ge N$, the JVM halts execution and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` immediately.

sections.explanation: Element swapping requires a temporary storage variable 'temp' to prevent overwriting values before they can be copied.

sections.title: Common Indexing Pitfalls
items: **Accessing `arr[arr.length]`**: The last valid index is `arr.length - 1`. `arr[arr.length]` always throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
**Negative Indexing**: Unlike Python or JavaScript, Java does NOT support negative indexing (e.g. `arr[-1]` throws an exception).
**1-Based Indexing Confusion**: Assuming the 3rd element is at index 3 (the 3rd element is at index 2).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Bounds Checking Overhead & Hardware Optimization

traps.question: Does the JVM perform bounds checking on every single array access? Can it be optimized?
traps.trap: Thinking bounds checking makes Java arrays significantly slower than C++ arrays.
traps.solution: Yes, the Java runtime checks bounds to prevent buffer overflow vulnerabilities. However, modern JIT (Just-In-Time) compilers perform **Bounds Check Elimination (BCE)**: when a standard `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)` loop is analyzed, the JIT proves that `i` cannot exceed array bounds and completely removes the runtime checks, matching raw C-speed.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: For an array `int[] arr = new int[8];`, what is the last accessible valid index?
sections.explanation: For an array of length 8, valid indices run from 0 to 7 (length - 1).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Array indices are 0-based memory offsets running from 0 to `length - 1`.
Always access the last element dynamically using `arr[arr.length - 1]`.
In-place swapping requires a 3-step temporary variable handshake.
Invalid indices immediately trigger `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

content.theory:
Every element of an array has an index: its position, counting from zero. Indexing is how you read and write individual elements, and getting indices right is the difference between a working program and an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. This lesson explains zero-based indexing and why it exists, valid index ranges, reading and writing elements, index arithmetic for neighbours and the middle, using values as indices, and the classic off-by-one mistakes.

## Zero-based indexing

~~~java
String[] colors = {"red", "green", "blue"};
System.out.println(colors[0]);   // red
System.out.println(colors[2]);   // blue
~~~

For an array of length n, valid indices are **0 to n - 1**. The last element is always `arr[arr.length - 1]`.

Why start at zero? The index is an **offset** from the array's start: the first element is zero steps from the beginning. The address calculation, start + index × size, needs no adjustment. Most mainstream languages, including C, Java, Python and JavaScript, use zero-based indexing.

## Reading and writing

~~~java
int[] scores = new int[4];
scores[0] = 85;              // write
scores[3] = scores[0] + 5;   // read, then write: 90
scores[1]++;                 // increment in place
~~~

An indexed element behaves like an ordinary variable: it can be assigned, incremented, passed to methods or used in expressions.

## Out of bounds

~~~java
int[] a = new int[3];
a[3] = 10;     // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
a[-1] = 10;    // also out of bounds
~~~

Java checks every access at runtime. The exception message names the bad index and the length, which tells you exactly what went wrong. These checks can't be turned off, and they prevent the memory corruption that out-of-bounds writes cause in C.

## Index arithmetic

Many algorithms compute indices:

~~~java
int first = arr[0];
int last = arr[arr.length - 1];
int mid = arr[arr.length / 2];         // middle (upper middle for even lengths)
int prev = arr[i - 1];                 // valid only when i >= 1
int next = arr[i + 1];                 // valid only when i <= length - 2
int mirror = arr[arr.length - 1 - i];  // element at the same distance from the end
~~~

Before using `i - 1` or `i + 1`, check that the result stays within 0 to length - 1. Loops comparing neighbours usually run `i` from 1, or stop at `length - 1`:

~~~java
for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] < arr[i - 1]) System.out.println("Drop at index " + i);
}
~~~

## Circular indexing

The remainder operator wraps indices around, treating the array as a ring:

~~~java
int nextIndex = (i + 1) % arr.length;                    // after the last comes the first
int prevIndex = (i - 1 + arr.length) % arr.length;       // before the first comes the last
~~~

Adding `arr.length` before taking the remainder avoids a negative result, since Java's `%` keeps the sign of the left operand. Circular indexing is used in rotating arrays, ring buffers and round-robin scheduling.

## Using values as indices

When values fall in a small known range, they can serve as indices into a counting array:

~~~java
int[] count = new int[101];          // marks from 0 to 100
for (int m : marks) count[m]++;      // count[m] = how many students scored m

int[] letters = new int[26];
for (char c : word.toCharArray()) letters[c - 'a']++;   // 'a' maps to 0
~~~

This technique, the basis of **counting sort** and frequency tables, gives O(1) lookups without a map. Validate values first, since an unexpected value becomes an out-of-bounds index.

## Index versus value

A frequent bug mixes up the position and the content:

~~~java
int[] nums = {10, 20, 30};
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);         // prints 0, 1, 2: indices
    System.out.println(nums[i]);   // prints 10, 20, 30: values
}
~~~

When a problem asks to "return the index of the maximum", track the index, not the value.

## Off-by-one errors

- `for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)`: one iteration too many
- `for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++)`: skips index 0 by accident
- `arr[arr.length]` instead of `arr[arr.length - 1]` for the last element
- computing a range `[start, end]` but looping with `< end`, which skips the last element

Check the first and last index of every loop explicitly. Many APIs use **half-open ranges**, where the start is included and the end excluded, such as `Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, 3)` and `substring(1, 3)`. With half-open ranges, the length is `end - start`, and adjacent ranges such as [0, 3) and [3, 6) don't overlap.

## Index of the middle

For a range from `low` to `high`, the middle index `(low + high) / 2` can overflow for large values; `low + (high - low) / 2` is the safe form used in binary search.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Why do arrays start at 0?", out-of-bounds output questions, neighbour comparisons, circular rotation, and frequency counting with an array. Explain indices as offsets, the valid range 0 to n - 1, boundary checks before `i - 1` and `i + 1`, the circular formula with `%`, and half-open ranges.

lessons.title: Traversing Arrays
lessons.description: Traversing an array is like an Inspector on an Assembly Line. The inspector walks down the conveyor belt systematically visiting every single box from index $0$...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand array indexing, `for` loops, and the `.length` property.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Traversing an array is like an Inspector on an Assembly Line. The inspector walks down the conveyor belt systematically visiting every single box from index $0$ to $N-1$ to examine, log, update, or aggregate its contents.

sections.title: Traditional for vs Enhanced for-each Loop
sections.content:
• **Traditional Indexed `for` Loop**: `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)`
  - Full control: Access to index position `i`, allows modifying array elements in-place, supports reverse and custom-step traversals.
• **Enhanced `for-each` Loop**: `for (int val : arr)`
  - Clean, idiomatic, read-only iteration: Eliminates off-by-one errors and bounds risks. Cannot mutate array elements or access index numbers.

sections.title: Array Traversals: Inspection, Mutation, and Reverse Iteration
sections.explanation: Enhanced for-each loops are ideal for reading data; traditional for loops are required whenever you need to write/mutate array elements or iterate in reverse.

sections.title: Why for-each Cannot Modify Array Elements
Try It: Count Elements Above Threshold
sections.explanation: 68 and 89 are >= 50, so count is 2.

iterations.description: Starts at last index. Prints 30. Decrements i.
Prints 20. Decrements i.
Prints 10. Decrements i to -1.
Condition fails. Reverse loop terminates cleanly.

sections.title: Common Traversal Pitfalls
items: **Using `<=` in Forward Loop**: `for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)` crashes at the last step (use `< arr.length`).
**Wrong Initialization in Reverse Loop**: `for (int i = arr.length; ...)` crashes immediately with `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` (must start at `arr.length - 1`).
**Attempting In-Place Mutation via for-each**: Trying to initialize or modify array contents inside an enhanced for-each loop.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Modifying Objects vs Primitives in for-each

traps.question: Can an enhanced for-each loop modify the state of objects inside an object array (`Person[]`)?
traps.trap: Assuming for-each can never mutate anything because it can't mutate primitives.
traps.solution: Yes, for object reference arrays! While `person = new Person()` only reassigns the local reference copy, calling a setter method `person.setName("Alice")` mutates the actual heap object referenced by the array.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which loop construct should you use to multiply every element in an integer array by 2 in-place?
options: Traditional indexed for loop `for(int i=0; i<arr.length; i++)`
sections.explanation: In-place modification requires write access by index `arr[i] = ...`, which is only provided by traditional indexed loops.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Use enhanced `for-each` for clean, safe read-only operations.
Use traditional `for` when you need index positions, mutations, or reverse stepping.
Forward loops run `i = 0; i < arr.length; i++`.
Reverse loops run `i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--`.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `Scanner` input, dynamic memory allocation `new dataType[N]`, and standard `for` loops.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Think of taking array input as Sizing the Container before Filling. Because arrays in Java cannot resize once created, you must first ask the user/stream 'How many items are coming?' ($N$), construct an empty container of exact size $N$ on the Heap, and then run a loop $N$ times to fill each slot sequentially from index $0$ to $N-1$.

sections.title: The 3-Step Array Input Pipeline
sections.content:
1. **Read Capacity**: Read the total element count $N$ from input (`int n = sc.nextInt();`).
2. **Instantiate on Heap**: Allocate memory of size $N$ (`int[] arr = new int[n];`).
3. **Populate via Loop**: Iterate from index `0` to `n - 1`, reading each token into `arr[i]`.

sections.title: Dynamic Array Input: Numeric Data & String Buffer Clearance
sections.explanation: When reading Strings after numeric inputs, always call 'sc.nextLine()' to clear the leftover newline character in the input buffer before reading String tokens.

sections.title: Defensive Validation of Array Capacity
Try It: Array Population Logic
sections.explanation: Array is sized to 3 and populated sequentially with 10, 20, 30.

sections.title: Array Input Buffer Trace: Reading 3 Integers [45, 88, 92]

iterations.description: Allocates 3-element integer array.
First token read into scores[0].
Second token read into scores[1].
Third token read into scores[2]. Loop terminates.

sections.title: Common Input Mistakes
items: **Attempting to Allocate before Reading Size**: Writing `int[] arr = new int[n];` before initializing `n` with `sc.nextInt()`.
**The Phantom Newline Bug**: Forgetting `sc.nextLine()` between `sc.nextInt()` and `sc.nextLine()` causes the first String to be read as an empty string `""`.
**Not Handling Non-Numeric Input**: Throws `InputMismatchException` if a user enters text when an integer is expected.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Time & Space Complexity of Array Reading

traps.question: What is the time and space complexity of reading an array of size N from standard input?
traps.trap: Thinking reading input has no algorithmic complexity.
traps.solution: Reading $N$ elements requires $O(N)$ Time Complexity (must process $N$ tokens) and $O(N)$ Auxiliary Space Complexity (allocates a contiguous heap buffer of size $N$).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Why must array size N be read before instantiating an array in Java?
options: Java syntax requires all arrays to be constant size
Arrays have immutable capacity that must be allocated on the heap during instantiation
Scanner cannot operate without array size
sections.explanation: Because Java arrays have fixed heap capacity, the JVM requires the exact size at creation time to allocate the contiguous memory block.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Array input workflow: 1. Read size N -> 2. Allocate `new int[N]` -> 3. Loop `0` to `N-1`.
Clear leftover newlines with `sc.nextLine()` when switching from numeric to String input.
Validate that $N \ge 0$ to prevent `NegativeArraySizeException`.
Array input has O(N) time and O(N) space complexity.

lessons.title: Searching Arrays
lessons.description: Searching an array is like Finding a Key in a Row of Lockers. You start at Locker 0, open it, and compare its contents with your target key. If it matches, you ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand array traversal, boolean equality operators, and the `break` keyword.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Searching an array is like Finding a Key in a Row of Lockers. You start at Locker 0, open it, and compare its contents with your target key. If it matches, you record the locker index and stop searching immediately. If you inspect every locker to the very end ($N-1$) without finding a match, you report failure by returning the standard sentinel `-1`.

sections.title: The Sentinel -1 Convention
sections.content:
Valid array indices are strictly non-negative integers ($0, 1, 2, \dots, N-1$).

Therefore, returning `-1` is the universally accepted standard in computer science to signal: **Target Element Not Found** (e.g. `String.indexOf()`, `List.indexOf()`).

sections.title: Linear Search Algorithm for Primitives & Objects
sections.explanation: Linear search inspects elements sequentially from left to right. Returning immediately upon finding a match minimizes CPU time.

sections.title: Linear Search Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
• **Best Case ($O(1)$)**: Target is located at index `0` (terminates on the very first check).
• **Worst Case ($O(N)$)**: Target is at the last index $N-1$, or does not exist in the array (must inspect all $N$ elements).
• **Average Case ($O(N)$)**: On average, inspects $\approx \frac{N}{2}$ elements.
• **Auxiliary Space ($O(1)$)**: Uses constant additional memory.

sections.title: Try It: Search for Target
sections.explanation: 35 does not exist in nums, so idx remains -1.

sections.title: Linear Search Trace: Searching for 73 in [45, 88, 73, 99]

iterations.description: No match. Advances to index 1.
No match. Advances to index 2.
Match found! Returns index 2 immediately. Remaining elements skipped.

sections.title: Common Search Mistakes
items: **Returning 0 for 'Not Found'**: Index 0 represents the first valid element! Returning 0 creates severe false-positive bugs (always return -1).
**Using `==` for String Search**: Comparing strings with `==` checks reference addresses, causing searches to fail even when text contents are identical (always use `.equals()`).
**Forgetting to `break` or `return`**: Continuing to iterate through the entire array after finding the element, wasting CPU time.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Linear Search vs Binary Search

traps.question: When is Linear Search preferred over Binary Search?
traps.trap: Assuming Binary Search ($O(\log N)$) is always superior.
traps.solution: Binary Search REQUIRES the dataset to be strictly sorted. Sorting an unsorted array takes $O(N \log N)$ time. Therefore, if you only need to perform a single search on an unsorted dataset, Linear Search ($O(N)$) is significantly faster than sorting first.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Why is -1 returned when a target is not found in an array?
options: It is the only negative integer supported by Java
Valid array indices start at 0, making -1 an unambiguous indicator of absence
sections.explanation: Because all valid array indices are non-negative (0 to N-1), -1 unambiguously signals that the element was not found.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Linear search inspects elements sequentially in O(N) time.
Returns the matching index on success, or `-1` on failure.
Exit immediately via `return` or `break` upon finding a match.
Always use `.equals()` when searching String or object arrays.

lessons.title: Min, Max & Sum
lessons.description: Think of this algorithm as the Scorekeeper & The Scale. As data elements arrive one-by-one from the array, the scorekeeper keeps track of three statistics simul...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand array traversal, accumulator patterns, and primitive numeric types.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Think of this algorithm as the Scorekeeper & The Scale. As data elements arrive one-by-one from the array, the scorekeeper keeps track of three statistics simultaneously: the smallest value seen so far (`min`), the largest value seen so far (`max`), and the running cumulative weight (`sum`).

sections.title: The First-Element Initialization Rule
sections.content:
⚠️ **CRITICAL BUG TRAP**: NEVER initialize `max = 0` or `min = 0`!
• If an array contains only negative numbers (e.g. `[-15, -8, -22]`), an initial `max = 0` will incorrectly return `0` instead of `-8`.
• **Rule**: Always initialize both `min` and `max` to the first element `arr[0]` (or `Integer.MAX_VALUE` / `Integer.MIN_VALUE`).

sections.title: Single-Pass O(N) Min, Max, Sum & Average Calculation
sections.explanation: Computing min, max, sum, and average in a single unified loop traversal avoids scanning memory multiple times, maximizing CPU cache efficiency.

sections.title: Preventing Integer Overflow & Truncation
sections.content:
• **Integer Overflow**: In Java, adding two large positive `int`s that exceed $2,147,483,647$ wraps around into negative numbers. Accumulate sums into `long sum = 0L;`.
• **Decimal Truncation**: Writing `double avg = sum / arr.length;` performs integer division before assignment (e.g. `7 / 2 = 3.0`). Always cast one operand: `(double) sum / arr.length`.

sections.title: Try It: Min and Max with Negative Numbers
sections.explanation: Because max was initialized to scores[0] (-15), it correctly identifies -3 as the highest score.

iterations.description: Initialized state.
Process 20: sum becomes 20.
Process -5: min updated to -5, sum becomes 15.
Process 40: max updated to 40, sum becomes 55.

sections.title: Common Min/Max/Sum Mistakes
items: **Initializing `max = 0`**: Fails completely when all numbers in the array are negative.
**Missing Empty Array Guard**: Accessing `arr[0]` on an empty array (`new int[0]`) immediately throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
**Integer Division Bug**: Forgetting to cast `(double)` when calculating averages.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Minimum Number of Comparisons for Min & Max

traps.question: What is the theoretical minimum number of comparisons needed to find both min and max in an array of size N?
traps.trap: Thinking it requires 2N comparisons.
traps.solution: Standard independent checks take $2N - 2$ comparisons. However, by processing elements in **pairs** (compare pairs first, then compare the larger with `max` and smaller with `min`), the total comparisons drop to $\approx 3N/2$ (1.5N comparisons), a common algorithmic optimization interview question.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Why should min and max be initialized with `arr[0]` instead of 0?
options: Because index 0 runs faster in the JVM
To ensure correct results when arrays contain all negative or all non-zero numbers
Because Java forbids initializing min to 0
sections.explanation: Initializing max to 0 fails if all elements are negative (e.g. max would stay 0 instead of -3). Initializing to arr[0] guarantees correctness across all numeric ranges.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Always initialize min and max with `arr[0]` to safely handle all-negative arrays.
Use `long` for sum accumulators to defend against integer overflow.
Cast `(double)` before division to prevent integer truncation in averages.
Compute min, max, and sum in a single O(N) pass.

lessons.description: In Java, a 2D array is an Array of Arrays (Master Reference Array). It is NOT a single flat contiguous grid like in C/C++. Instead, it is a master array on the ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand 1D arrays, nested loops, heap memory models, and reference variables.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: In Java, a 2D array is an **Array of Arrays** (Master Reference Array). It is NOT a single flat contiguous grid like in C/C++. Instead, it is a master array on the Heap whose elements are reference pointers, each pointing to an independent 1D array representing a single row.

sections.title: Matrix Dimension Properties
sections.content:
For a 2D array `int[][] matrix = new int[3][4];`:
• **Number of Rows**: `matrix.length` (gives 3)
• **Number of Columns in Row `r`**: `matrix[r].length` (gives 4)
• **Element Access**: `matrix[row][col]`

sections.title: 2D Rectangular Matrix & Dynamic Jagged Arrays in Action
sections.explanation: Because each row is an independent heap array, Java supports jagged arrays where individual rows have completely different lengths.

sections.title: Memory Architecture: Array of References
sections.content:
```
Stack (matrix) ---> Heap Master Array (Pointers)
                     [0] ---> [ 10 | 20 | 30 ] (Row 0 Heap Array)
                     [1] ---> [ 40 | 50 | 60 ] (Row 1 Heap Array)
```
Because rows can reside in completely separate regions of Heap RAM, accessing `matrix[r][c]` performs two pointer dereferences: first to locate Row `r`, then to locate Column `c`.

sections.title: Try It: Sum Elements of a 2D Matrix

iterations.description: Reads row 0, col 0.
Reads row 0, col 1. Row 0 complete.
Reads row 1, col 0.
Reads row 1, col 1. Traversal complete.

sections.title: Common 2D Array Pitfalls
items: **Confusing `matrix.length` with Columns**: `matrix.length` gives total ROWS. To get columns of row 0, use `matrix[0].length`.
**Inverted Index Order**: Writing `matrix[c][r]` instead of `matrix[r][c]` causes out-of-bounds exceptions or data corruption.
**Assuming Fixed Column Widths**: Forgetting that jagged arrays have variable `matrix[r].length` per row.
**Accessing Unallocated Jagged Rows**: Calling `jagged[0][0]` before allocating `jagged[0] = new int[...]` throws `NullPointerException`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Cache Locality in Row-Major vs Column-Major Traversal

traps.question: Why is row-major traversal (`matrix[r][c]`) faster than column-major traversal (`matrix[c][r]`) in hardware?
traps.trap: Thinking iteration order has identical speed.
traps.solution: Modern CPUs load contiguous memory into high-speed CPU L1/L2 caches in blocks called Cache Lines. Traversing elements in row order reads consecutive memory slots (Cache Hit). Traversing down columns jumps across different row arrays in heap memory on every step, causing frequent **Cache Misses** that degrade performance.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How do you determine the number of columns in row index 2 of a 2D array?
sections.explanation: `matrix[2].length` returns the exact number of column elements in row 2, which is safe for both rectangular and jagged arrays.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: 2D arrays in Java are arrays of 1D array reference pointers on the heap.
`matrix.length` = number of rows; `matrix[r].length` = number of columns in row r.
Supports jagged/ragged arrays with variable row lengths.
Row-major traversal `matrix[r][c]` provides superior CPU cache performance.

lessons.title: What is a String?
lessons.description: A Java String is an Immutable Stone Tablet. Once a String is constructed on the Heap, its character sequence is permanently carved in stone—no thread or method ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand primitive types (`char`), objects vs references, heap memory, and array fundamentals.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: A Java `String` is an Immutable Stone Tablet. Once a String is constructed on the Heap, its character sequence is permanently carved in stone—no thread or method can mutate its contents in-place. When you call a method like `str.toUpperCase()`, Java does NOT alter the original tablet; it chisels a brand-new stone tablet with uppercase letters and returns a new reference pointer.

sections.title: The 4 Critical Reasons for String Immutability
sections.content:
1. **Security**: Sensitive parameters like database URLs, usernames, passwords, and file paths cannot be hijacked or corrupted by malicious code.
2. **Thread Safety**: Multiple concurrent threads can safely read the same String instance simultaneously without synchronization locks.
3. **Hash Code Caching**: Because the content never changes, `str.hashCode()` is calculated once and cached forever, making Strings ultra-fast keys in `HashMap` and `HashSet`.
4. **String Constant Pool Optimization**: Enables memory sharing where millions of identical string literals point to a single shared heap object.

sections.title: Demonstrating String Immutability in Java
sections.explanation: Every String manipulation method in the Java Standard Library returns a freshly allocated String object, preserving the immutable integrity of the original instance.

sections.title: Internal Representation: Compact Strings (Java 9+)
Try It: Predict Immutability Output
sections.explanation: Because the return values of concat() and replace() were not reassigned, 'word' remains 'planet'.

iterations.description: Initial literal created in String Pool.
New String object 0x200 created on Heap. Return value discarded.
greeting pointer remains locked onto 0x100.

sections.title: Common String Mistakes
items: **Ignoring Return Values**: Calling `str.trim()`, `str.replace()`, or `str.toLowerCase()` without reassigning the variable.
**String Concatenation in Heavy Loops**: Using `str += i` inside a 10,000-iteration loop creates 10,000 temporary garbage objects (use `StringBuilder` instead).
**Confusing String with Primitive Types**: `String` is a reference class (`java.lang.String`), not a primitive.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why is String Final in Java?

traps.question: Why is the `String` class declared as `public final class String` in Java?
traps.trap: Thinking it's just to prevent developers from adding helper methods.
traps.solution: If `String` were not `final`, a subclass could override methods like `equals()` or `hashCode()` to make Strings mutable or bypass security checks (e.g. altering a file path after permission verification). Declaring it `final` guarantees that no subclass can ever violate its immutability and security guarantees.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What happens when you invoke `str.concat(" world")` on a variable `String str = "hello";`?
options: A new String "hello world" is created and returned; `str` remains "hello"
sections.explanation: Because Strings are immutable, concat() returns a brand-new String object containing the combined text, leaving the original variable unchanged.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Strings in Java are completely immutable reference objects.
Immutability guarantees security, thread safety, hash code caching, and literal pooling.
All transformation methods return new String instances.
Backed by a compact `byte[]` array in modern Java.
