content.theory:
A string is a sequence of characters: a name, a sentence, a password, a line of a file, a JSON document. Text is everywhere in software, so strings are among the most used types in any language. In Java, `String` is a class, not a primitive, and its objects are **immutable**: once created, their contents never change. That single design choice explains how strings behave, why `==` misleads, and why building text in loops needs `StringBuilder`. This lesson introduces strings, their immutability, the string pool, and how Java stores them.

## Strings in Java

~~~java
String name = "Asha";
String greeting = "Hello, " + name + "!";
System.out.println(greeting);          // Hello, Asha!
System.out.println(greeting.length()); // 12
~~~

`String` lives in `java.lang`, so it needs no import. Although it's a class, Java gives it special support: literals in double quotes, and `+` for concatenation.

## Characters and strings

A `char` holds a single character in single quotes, `'A'`; a `String` holds zero or more characters in double quotes, `"A"`. They're different types: `'A' == "A"` doesn't compile. The **empty string** `""` has length zero and is a valid object, unlike `null`, which means no object at all:

~~~java
String empty = "";
String none = null;
empty.length();   // 0
none.length();    // NullPointerException
~~~

## Immutability

String objects can't be changed. Methods that seem to modify a string return a **new** string:

~~~java
String s = "hello";
s.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(s);          // hello: unchanged
s = s.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(s);          // HELLO: s now refers to a new object
~~~

Forgetting to use the returned value is one of the most common string bugs.

Why immutable?

- **safe sharing**: many variables can refer to the same string without one changing it for the others
- **string pool**: identical literals can share one object
- **hash keys**: a string's hash code can be cached and never goes stale, which makes strings fast and reliable HashMap keys
- **security**: a file path or URL checked for safety can't be altered afterwards
- **thread safety**: immutable objects can be shared between threads without locks

## The string pool

String literals are stored in a special area of the heap called the **string pool**. Identical literals refer to the same object:

~~~java
String a = "java";
String b = "java";
String c = new String("java");
System.out.println(a == b);       // true: same pooled object
System.out.println(a == c);       // false: new creates a separate object
System.out.println(a.equals(c));  // true: same characters
~~~

Strings created at runtime (by concatenating variables, reading input, or `new String`) aren't pooled automatically. `intern()` returns the pooled version, though application code rarely needs it.

The lesson: `==` compares object identity, which depends on how the strings were created. **Always compare contents with `equals`.**

## Concatenation

`+` joins strings, converting other values to text:

~~~java
String info = "Age: " + 21 + ", active: " + true;
~~~

Because strings are immutable, each `+` in a loop creates a new string and copies all previous characters:

~~~java
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    result += i;          // creates 10,000 intermediate strings: O(n²) copying
}
~~~

`StringBuilder` is a mutable sequence of characters designed for building text:

~~~java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    sb.append(i);
}
String result = sb.toString();
~~~

For a handful of concatenations in one expression, `+` is fine; the compiler optimizes it.

## How strings are stored

Internally, a String holds an array of bytes plus an encoding flag. Since Java 9 (**compact strings**), text containing only Latin-1 characters uses one byte per character, and other text uses two bytes per character in UTF-16. This halves memory for typical English text. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as many emoji, take two `char` values (a surrogate pair), so `length()` counts UTF-16 units, not visible characters.

## Strings and arrays

A string behaves like a read-only array of characters: you can read the character at an index with `charAt`, get its length, and convert it with `toCharArray()` when you need to modify characters. The following lessons cover indexing, length, charAt and substring in detail.

## Useful methods at a glance

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `length()` | Number of characters |
| `charAt(i)` | Character at index i |
| `substring(a, b)` | Part of the string |
| `indexOf(s)` | Position of a substring, or -1 |
| `equals`, `equalsIgnoreCase` | Compare contents |
| `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase` | Change case |
| `trim`, `strip` | Remove surrounding whitespace |
| `split(regex)` | Break into parts |
| `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith` | Test contents |
| `replace(a, b)` | Replace occurrences |
| `isEmpty`, `isBlank` | Test for empty or whitespace-only |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Why are strings immutable in Java?", "== vs equals for strings?", "What is the string pool?" and "String vs StringBuilder?" Explain immutability with its benefits, show the pool example with literals and `new String`, and explain the O(n²) cost of `+=` in loops.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-a-string`, heap memory, and reference equality.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of String creation as The Public Library (String Constant Pool) vs Buying an Unshared Copy (`new String()`):
• **String Literal (`"Java"`)**: You visit the public library. If 'Java' is already on the shelf, the JVM gives you a shared library card pointing to that exact instance.
• **Constructor (`new String("Java")`)**: You demand a brand-new, private copy printed on private paper in general Heap RAM, completely bypassing the shared library.

sections.title: String Constant Pool (SCP) Mechanics
sections.content:
The **String Constant Pool** is a specialized hash-table cache inside Heap memory:
• When a string literal is encountered, the JVM checks the pool.
• If found → returns the existing pooled reference ($O(1)$ memory savings).
• If not found → creates a new object in the pool and caches it.

⚠️ **Best Practice**: ALWAYS use string literals (`String s = "text";`). Avoid `new String("text")` unless you explicitly require unshared object identity.

sections.title: String Literals vs new String() & The intern() Method
sections.explanation: The '==' operator checks if two references point to the exact same memory address. The '.equals()' method checks if the character contents match.

sections.title: Constructing Strings from Character & Byte Arrays
sections.content:
Java provides specialized constructors to convert arrays into Strings (essential for cryptography, network I/O, and file streams):

```java
char[] charArray = { 'J', 'a', 'v', 'a' };
String fromChars = new String(charArray); // "Java"

byte[] utf8Bytes = { 72, 101, 108, 108, 111 }; // ASCII for 'H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'
String fromBytes = new String(utf8Bytes, java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8); // "Hello"
```

sections.title: Try It: Reference Equality vs Content Equality
sections.explanation: 'a' is in the String Pool while 'b' is a separate Heap object. Hence '==' is false, but '.equals()' is true.

sections.title: Common Creation Mistakes
items: **Using `new String("literal")`**: Creates redundant heap objects, wasting memory and defeating the String Pool.
**Using `==` to Check Equality**: `==` checks reference addresses, causing intermittent false negatives on Strings created dynamically.
**Creating Strings in Tight Loops**: Concatenating strings with `+` in loops spawns millions of transient objects.

sections.title: Interview Traps: How Many Objects Are Created?

traps.question: How many objects are created by the statement: `String s = new String("Hello");`?
traps.trap: Answering 1 object.
traps.solution:
It creates **2 objects** (assuming "Hello" is not already in the String Pool):
1. One object is created in the **String Constant Pool** for the literal `"Hello"`.
2. One object is created in **General Heap Memory** by the `new String(...)` constructor.
The reference `s` points to the Heap object.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.explanation: Both literals point to the exact same pooled object in the String Constant Pool, so `s1 == s2` evaluates to true.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Always prefer string literals `String s = "text";` to leverage the String Constant Pool.
`new String()` forces unpooled heap allocations.
Use `.equals()` for content comparison; `==` compares memory addresses.
`intern()` retrieves the canonical pooled reference.

content.theory:
Java gives you several ways to create strings: literals, the `new` keyword, conversion from other types, building from characters or arrays, concatenation, formatting, and `StringBuilder`. Each has different effects on memory and performance, and interviewers frequently ask how many objects a given line creates. This lesson covers each creation method, the string pool's role, converting values to strings, multi-line text blocks, and choosing the right approach. ## String literals ~~~java String city = "Pune"; ~~~ The JVM looks for an identical string in the **string pool**. If one exists, the variable refers to it; otherwise the literal is added to the pool. Using literals is the normal, preferred way to create fixed text. ## The new keyword ~~~java String city = new String("Pune"); ~~~ This always creates a new String object on the heap, separate from the pooled literal `"Pune"`. The literal itself is also in the pool. So this line involves up to two objects: the pooled literal (if not already there) and the new heap object. There's almost never a reason to write `new String("...")` in application code; it wastes memory and makes `==` comparisons behave differently from literals. ## Compile-time constant folding The compiler combines concatenations of literals and compile-time constants: ~~~java String a = "Hel" + "lo"; // folded to "Hello" at compile time: pooled String b = "Hello"; System.out.println(a == b); // true String part = "Hel"; String c = part + "lo"; // computed at runtime: a new object System.out.println(c == b); // false ~~~ If `part` were declared `final String part = "Hel";`, it would be a compile-time constant, and `c == b` would be true. These cases appear in output-prediction questions; the practical rule remains: compare strings with `equals`. ## From other types ~~~java String s1 = String.valueOf(42); // "42" String s2 = Integer.toString(42); // "42" String s3 = "" + 42; // "42": works, but less clear String s4 = String.valueOf(3.5); // "3.5" String s5 = String.valueOf(true); // "true" String s6 = String.valueOf('x'); // "x" String s7 = obj.toString(); // object's text form ~~~ `String.valueOf(obj)` returns "null" for a null reference, while `obj.toString()` throws NullPointerException, so valueOf is safer when values might be null. ## From characters and arrays ~~~java char[] letters = {'j', 'a', 'v', 'a'}; String s1 = new String(letters); // "java" String s2 = String.valueOf(letters); // "java" String s3 = new String(letters, 1, 2); // "av": offset 1, count 2 String s4 = String.valueOf('x').repeat(3); // "xxx" ~~~ Converting a string to a char array, modifying it, and creating a new string is the standard way to "edit" characters, since strings themselves are immutable: ~~~java char[] chars = word.toCharArray(); chars[0] = Character.toUpperCase(chars[0]); String capitalized = new String(chars); ~~~ ## Concatenation ~~~java String full = first + " " + last; String joined = String.join(", ", List.of("a", "b", "c")); // "a, b, c" String concat = first.concat(last); ~~~ `String.join` places a separator between items without a trailing one, handy for output formatting. ## Formatting ~~~java String line = String.format("%-10s %5.2f", name, price); String msg = "%s scored %d".formatted(name, marks); // Java 15+ ~~~ Formatting creates readable text from several values with precise control over width and decimals. ## StringBuilder When building text step by step, especially in loops, use StringBuilder: ~~~java StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (String word : words) { if (sb.length() > 0) sb.append(' '); sb.append(word); } String sentence = sb.toString(); ~~~ StringBuilder is mutable: `append`, `insert`, `delete`, `reverse` and `setCharAt` change it in place, and `toString()` produces the final immutable String. `StringBuffer` is an older, synchronized version; StringBuilder is preferred unless multiple threads share one builder. ## Text blocks For multi-line text (Java 15+): ~~~java String html = """
  • One
  • Two
"""; ~~~ Text blocks keep line breaks, need no escaped quotes, and strip common indentation. ## Repeating and padding ~~~java String line = "-".repeat(20); // 20 dashes String padded = String.format("%5s", "ab"); // " ab" ~~~ ## Counting objects: a classic question `String s = new String("hi");` creates one heap object, plus the pooled literal "hi" if it isn't already in the pool: one or two objects. `String a = "hi"; String b = "hi";` creates at most one object. Interviewers ask these to check understanding of the pool. ## Choosing a creation method | Need | Use | |---|---| | Fixed text | Literal | | Number or other value as text | `String.valueOf` | | A few pieces joined once | `+` | | A list with separators | `String.join` | | Building in a loop | `StringBuilder` | | Precise formatting | `String.format` or `formatted` | | Multi-line text | Text block | | Edit individual characters | `toCharArray`, modify, `new String(chars)` | ## How interviewers test this Expect "Literal vs new String?", "How many objects does this line create?", "Why use StringBuilder?" and output questions on compile-time constant folding. Explain the pool, the extra heap object from `new`, folding of literal concatenation, valueOf versus toString for null safety, and StringBuilder for loops.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `string-creation`, zero-based indexing, and primitive `char` types.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: String indexing is a Row of Numbered Character Slots. A String is an ordered sequence of character boxes numbered strictly from $0$ to $\text{length}() - 1$. Box 0 holds the initial letter, and Box $\text{length}() - 1$ holds the final letter.

sections.title: No Square Bracket Access in Java Strings
sections.content:
⚠️ **CRITICAL SYNTAX RULE**: Unlike arrays, C++, Python, or JavaScript, Java does **NOT** permit square brackets for String indexing:
• ❌ `char ch = str[0];` → **COMPILE ERROR!**
• ✅ `char ch = str.charAt(0);` → **Correct Java Method Call**

sections.title: Accessing Characters via charAt() & Boundary Validation
sections.explanation: The charAt(i) method performs direct index access into the underlying byte/char storage array in O(1) constant time.

sections.title: StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Mechanics
sections.content:
The JVM verifies bounds on every `charAt(index)` call:
• Valid indices: $0 \le \text{index} < \text{str.length}()$
• Accessing index $< 0$ or index $\ge \text{str.length}()$ throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`:

```java
String s = "Hi"; // length is 2 (indices 0 and 1)
char c = s.charAt(2); // THROWS StringIndexOutOfBoundsException!
```

sections.title: Try It: Extract First and Last Initials
sections.explanation: word.charAt(0) is 'A', and word.charAt(8) is 'm'.

iterations.description: Initial character.
Second character.
Third character.
Final character.

sections.title: Common Indexing Pitfalls
items: **Attempting `str[i]`**: Square bracket indexing is only valid for arrays, not String objects.
**Using `charAt(str.length())`**: The maximum valid index is `str.length() - 1`.
**Attempting to Mutate via charAt**: Writing `str.charAt(0) = 'B';` is a compile error because Strings are immutable.

sections.title: Interview Traps: UTF-16 Surrogate Pairs & Code Points

traps.question: What does `"😀".length()` and `"😀".charAt(0)` return in Java?
traps.trap: Assuming length is 1 because it is a single emoji.
traps.solution: Because emojis and rare scripts reside outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), Java encodes them as **2 UTF-16 surrogate chars**. Therefore, `"😀".length()` returns **2**, and `charAt(0)` returns the high-surrogate char `'\uD83D'`. To handle supplementary characters correctly, use `str.codePointAt(0)`.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is returned by `"Pathway".charAt(4)`?
sections.explanation: Indices: P(0), a(1), t(2), h(3), w(4), a(5), y(6). Index 4 is 'w'.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Strings use 0-based character indexing running from 0 to `length() - 1`.
Must use `str.charAt(i)` method (not `str[i]`).
Out-of-bounds indices throw `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
Accessing characters is an O(1) constant time operation.

sections.title: Connection to Next Lesson
sections.content: Next, we explore the length() Method, contrasting String method calls with array fields and mastering empty vs blank checks.

content.theory:
Like arrays, strings are indexed from zero: the first character is at index 0, and the last is at index `length() - 1`. Indexing is the basis of almost every string algorithm: reversing, checking palindromes, counting characters, finding patterns and parsing input. Unlike arrays, Java strings don't support square-bracket access; you read characters with `charAt(i)`. This lesson covers how string indices work, reading characters, searching for positions with indexOf, traversal, half-open ranges and the errors that out-of-range indices cause.

## Zero-based positions

~~~
String s = "CODE";
index:  0   1   2   3
char:  'C' 'O' 'D' 'E'
~~~

~~~java
System.out.println(s.charAt(0));               // C
System.out.println(s.charAt(s.length() - 1));  // E
~~~

`s[0]` doesn't compile in Java; strings aren't arrays. Use `charAt`.

## Out-of-range indices

~~~java
"CODE".charAt(4);    // StringIndexOutOfBoundsException: index 4, length 4
"".charAt(0);        // also throws: an empty string has no characters
~~~

Always check that an index is between 0 and `length() - 1` before reading, especially when computing indices like `i + 1` or `length() - 1` on a possibly empty string.

## Finding positions with indexOf

`indexOf` searches for a character or substring and returns the index of the first match, or -1 if it isn't found:

~~~java
String email = "asha@studyhub.dev";
int at = email.indexOf('@');            // 4
int dot = email.indexOf('.');           // 13
int missing = email.indexOf('#');       // -1
int second = "banana".indexOf('a', 2);  // 3: start searching from index 2
int last = "banana".lastIndexOf('a');   // 5
~~~

Checking `indexOf(x) != -1` tells you whether x occurs; `contains(x)` expresses that more readably. Combining indexOf with substring extracts parts of structured text:

~~~java
String user = email.substring(0, at);           // "asha"
String domain = email.substring(at + 1);        // "studyhub.dev"
~~~

Handle the -1 case before using the result as an index; `substring(0, -1)` throws.

## Counting occurrences with indexOf

~~~java
int count = 0, from = 0;
while ((from = text.indexOf("ab", from)) != -1) {
    count++;
    from += 1;          // move past this match (use += 2 to skip overlaps)
}
~~~

## Traversing characters

~~~java
String word = "level";
for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) {
    char c = word.charAt(i);
    System.out.println(i + ": " + c);
}
~~~

Or convert to an array for a for-each loop:

~~~java
for (char c : word.toCharArray()) {
    if ("aeiou".indexOf(c) != -1) vowels++;
}
~~~

`toCharArray()` creates a copy, costing O(n) memory; `charAt` in an indexed loop avoids that.

## Index arithmetic patterns

~~~java
char first = s.charAt(0);
char last = s.charAt(s.length() - 1);
char mirror = s.charAt(s.length() - 1 - i);   // character at the same distance from the end
char middle = s.charAt(s.length() / 2);
~~~

The mirror index is the key to palindrome checks and reversals:

~~~java
boolean isPalindrome = true;
for (int i = 0; i < s.length() / 2; i++) {
    if (s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(s.length() - 1 - i)) {
        isPalindrome = false;
        break;
    }
}
~~~

Looping only to `length() / 2` compares each pair once.

## Characters as numbers

`charAt` returns a `char`, which is a numeric type, so characters support arithmetic:

~~~java
int digit = s.charAt(i) - '0';          // '7' becomes 7
int letterIndex = s.charAt(i) - 'a';    // 'c' becomes 2
char shifted = (char) (s.charAt(i) + 1);
~~~

These conversions power frequency arrays and parsing numbers digit by digit.

## Half-open ranges

String methods taking a range use a **start inclusive, end exclusive** convention: `substring(1, 4)` returns indices 1, 2 and 3. The length of the result is `end - start`. The convention lets ranges join cleanly: `s.substring(0, k) + s.substring(k)` always rebuilds `s`.

## Unicode caveat

Indices count UTF-16 code units, not visible characters. An emoji such as 😀 occupies two indices, so `"😀".length()` is 2 and `charAt(0)` returns half of it. For most interview problems, which use ASCII letters and digits, this doesn't matter; for user-facing text, `codePoints()` handles full characters correctly.

## Strings are read-only

You can read any index, but you can't assign to one: there's no `setCharAt` on String. To change characters, use a `char[]` or a `StringBuilder` (`sb.setCharAt(i, 'x')`), then convert back to a String.

## How interviewers test this

Expect palindrome checks, counting vowels or digits, finding the first non-repeating character, and extracting parts with indexOf. Explain zero-based indexing and charAt, the -1 result of indexOf, mirror indices, char arithmetic, half-open ranges and StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `string-indexing`, method invocation syntax, and `null` reference handling.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: The `length()` method is a Digital Character Caliper. It measures the string and returns the exact count of 16-bit `char` code units in the sequence. Spaces, punctuation marks, digits, and escape sequences all count as real characters.

sections.title: The 3 Size Access Paradigms in Java
sections.content:
• **Arrays**: `arr.length` → Public immutable **field property** (NO parentheses).
• **Strings**: `str.length()` → Public **method call** (REQUIRES parentheses `()`).
• **Collections (`ArrayList`, `HashMap`)**: `list.size()` → Public **method call**.

sections.title: String Length, Empty vs Blank Checks & Defensive Null-Guards
sections.explanation: Never invoke .length() on a reference without verifying that it is non-null, or a NullPointerException will be thrown.

sections.title: Escape Sequences and Character Count
sections.content:
Escape sequences represent a single character in byte storage:
• `"\n".length()` is **1** (newline character)
• `"\t".length()` is **1** (tab character)
• `"\\\"".length()` is **2** (one backslash + one double quote)

sections.title: Try It: Length of Escape Strings
sections.code:
String text = "A\nB\tC";
System.out.println("Length: " + text.length());

iterations.description: String with letters, space, and digits.
7 total slots.
length() returns 7; last index is 6.

sections.title: Common length() Mistakes
items: **Omitting Parentheses**: Writing `str.length` (compile error; arrays use `.length`, strings use `.length()`).
**NullPointerException**: Calling `str.length()` when `str == null`.
**Confusing `isEmpty()` with `isBlank()`**: `" ".isEmpty()` is `false` (length is 1), but `" ".isBlank()` is `true`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Time Complexity of String.length()

traps.question: What is the time complexity of `str.length()` in Java? Does it count characters on every call?
traps.trap: Assuming it loops through the string like C's strlen() in O(N).
traps.solution: In Java, `str.length()` is strictly **$O(1)$ constant time**. The length is stored as a pre-computed internal field in the String object header and returned immediately without any character counting.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the length of the string `"Hi\n"`?
sections.explanation: 'H' (1) + 'i' (1) + '\n' (1) = 3 characters total.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `str.length()` returns total 16-bit char code units in O(1) time.
Requires parentheses `()`, unlike array `arr.length`.
Empty string `""` has length 0; whitespace characters count toward length.
Always perform null checks before calling `.length()`.

content.theory:
The `length()` method returns the number of characters in a string. It's the most called string method, because nearly every string algorithm needs it to set loop bounds, find the last character, check for empty input or compare sizes. Its rules are short but precise: it's a method with parentheses (unlike an array's `length` field), it counts UTF-16 units, and it throws on null. This lesson covers its behaviour, its uses in loops and validation, related methods such as isEmpty and isBlank, and the traps.

## Basic use

~~~java
String word = "Placement";
System.out.println(word.length());   // 9
System.out.println("".length());     // 0
System.out.println(" ".length());    // 1: a space is a character
System.out.println("a b".length());  // 3
~~~

`length()` counts every character, including spaces, punctuation, digits and escape-sequence characters such as `\n` (which counts as one).

## Method versus field versus size

Java uses three different spellings for "how many", a frequent source of compile errors:

| Type | Syntax |
|---|---|
| String | `s.length()`: a method |
| Array | `arr.length`: a field, no parentheses |
| Collection (List, Set) | `list.size()`: a method |

`s.length` without parentheses and `arr.length()` with them both fail to compile.

## Loop bounds

The valid indices of a string are 0 to `length() - 1`:

~~~java
for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char c = s.charAt(i);
}
~~~

Using `i <= s.length()` reads one past the end and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Calling `length()` in the loop condition is fine: it returns a stored value in constant time, so there's no need to cache it in a variable for performance.

## The last character

~~~java
char last = s.charAt(s.length() - 1);
~~~

On an empty string, `length() - 1` is -1, and charAt throws. Check emptiness first when input may be empty.

## Empty and blank checks

~~~java
s.isEmpty()     // true only for "" (length 0)
s.isBlank()     // true for "", "   ", "\t\n": empty or whitespace only (Java 11+)
~~~

For user input, `isBlank()` is usually the right check, because a field containing only spaces isn't meaningful. `s.length() == 0` is equivalent to `isEmpty()`.

## Null versus empty

~~~java
String a = "";
String b = null;
a.length();      // 0
b.length();      // NullPointerException
~~~

An empty string is an object with zero characters; null is no object. Safe checks put the null test first, relying on short-circuit evaluation:

~~~java
if (s == null || s.isBlank()) {
    System.out.println("Please enter a value");
}
~~~

## Trimming before measuring

User input often carries stray spaces:

~~~java
String input = "  asha  ";
input.length();           // 8
input.trim().length();    // 4
input.strip().length();   // 4: strip also handles Unicode whitespace
~~~

Trim or strip before validating length requirements, such as a minimum username length.

## Validation examples

~~~java
boolean validPin = pin.length() == 4 && pin.chars().allMatch(Character::isDigit);
boolean validPassword = password.length() >= 8;
boolean fitsTweet = message.length() <= 280;
~~~

## Comparing lengths

Comparing lengths is a cheap first step in many algorithms: two strings of different lengths can't be equal, anagrams or rotations of each other.

~~~java
static boolean isRotation(String a, String b) {
    return a.length() == b.length() && (a + a).contains(b);
}
~~~

`Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)` sorts strings by length.

## Unicode and length

`length()` counts UTF-16 code units, not the characters a person sees:

~~~java
"café".length();     // 4
"😀".length();       // 2: one emoji, two code units
"😀".codePointCount(0, "😀".length());   // 1
~~~

Accented letters may also be represented as two code points (a letter plus a combining accent), depending on normalization. For user-visible length limits, `codePointCount` is closer to what users expect. For typical interview problems using ASCII, `length()` is exactly right.

## StringBuilder length

`StringBuilder` has `length()` too, and `setLength(n)` truncates or pads it, `setLength(0)` clears the builder for reuse.

## Performance

`length()` runs in O(1): the string stores its size. Interview complexity analysis often uses n to mean the string's length.

## A quick summary

`length()` returns the number of UTF-16 characters in O(1), including spaces and punctuation. Loop with `i < s.length()`, check for null before calling it, trim user input before validating lengths, and prefer `isBlank()` when a value made only of spaces should count as missing.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "length vs length() vs size()?", off-by-one loops with `<=`, empty and null input handling, and validation tasks. State that length() is O(1) and counts all characters including spaces, show null-safe checks with short-circuiting, distinguish isEmpty and isBlank, and mention the emoji caveat.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `string-indexing`, 0-based coordinate systems, primitive `char` data types, and boundary conditions.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Think of `charAt(index)` as a **Precision Microscopic Probe**. You provide a single non-negative integer coordinate, and the probe directly inspects the internal contiguous byte/char array at that exact offset and retrieves the primitive `char` residing in that cell in $O(1)$ constant time.

sections.title: Method Signature & Return Type
sections.content:
• **Signature**: `public char charAt(int index)`
• **Return Value**: Returns a primitive `char` (16-bit Unicode unit), NOT a `String` object.
• **Immutability Constraint**: `charAt()` is strictly **read-only**. You cannot assign to it (e.g., `str.charAt(0) = 'X'` is a compilation error).

sections.title: Reading Characters, Boundary Checks & Iteration
sections.explanation: Iterate from i = 0 up to i < title.length(). At each iteration, title.charAt(i) safely extracts the character at index i.

sections.title: charAt() Index vs Character Value Map: "JAVA"
Try It: Extract First Letters for an Acronym
sections.explanation: Extracts character at index 0 of each word and concatenates them into the acronym 'SQL'.

iterations.description: Initial consonant 'C' evaluated.
Vowel 'o' matches; count incremented to 1.
Consonant 'd' evaluated.
Vowel 'e' matches; count incremented to 2.

sections.title: Common charAt() Traps
items: **The `<= length()` Off-by-One**: Writing `for (int i = 0; i <= str.length(); i++)` crashes on the final iteration because valid indices end at `str.length() - 1`.
**Attempting to Assign**: `str.charAt(0) = 'Z';` is illegal because String objects are immutable in Java.
**Ignoring Null Checks**: Calling `.charAt()` on a `null` reference throws `NullPointerException` before any index checking happens.
**Confusing char with String**: `str.charAt(0)` produces primitive `char` `'A'`, which cannot be compared using `.equals()` (use `==` for primitives, or `String.valueOf(ch)`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Fast Character Frequency Array using charAt()

traps.question: How do you count character frequencies of lowercase English letters in $O(N)$ time without using a HashMap?
traps.trap: Using a heavy HashMap<Character, Integer> with object boxing overhead.
traps.solution: Use a fixed-size integer array `int[] count = new int[26];` and index directly with `count[str.charAt(i) - 'a']++`. Because `char` arithmetic computes the zero-based offset in $O(1)$ memory without allocations.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What exception is thrown by `"Java".charAt(4)`?
sections.explanation: Because "Java" has length 4, valid indices are 0, 1, 2, and 3. Requesting index 4 throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `str.charAt(index)` retrieves the primitive `char` at the given 0-based index in $O(1)$ time.
Valid indices strictly range from $0$ to $\text{str.length}() - 1$.
Strings are immutable; `charAt()` cannot be used as an assignment target.
Combine `str.charAt(i)` with `Character` utility methods like `Character.isDigit()` and `Character.toUpperCase()` for robust character processing.

sections.title: Connection to Next Lesson
sections.content: Next, we examine the substring() Method, learning how to slice contiguous sub-sequences using half-open index intervals.

content.theory:
`charAt(index)` returns the character at a given position in a string. It's the basic tool for examining text one character at a time: checking whether a character is a digit, counting vowels, comparing characters from both ends, or converting digits to numbers. Because it returns a `char`, a numeric type, it also enables arithmetic tricks that appear in many problems. This lesson covers how charAt works, character classification, char arithmetic, frequency counting, comparisons, and its exceptions.

## Basic use

~~~java
String s = "Java21";
char first = s.charAt(0);    // 'J'
char digit = s.charAt(4);    // '2'
~~~

Valid indices run from 0 to `length() - 1`. Anything else throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. charAt runs in O(1) time.

## Iterating with charAt

~~~java
int digits = 0, letters = 0, spaces = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char c = s.charAt(i);
    if (Character.isDigit(c)) digits++;
    else if (Character.isLetter(c)) letters++;
    else if (Character.isWhitespace(c)) spaces++;
}
~~~

## The Character class

`Character` provides static methods for classifying and converting:

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Character.isDigit(c)` | 0 to 9 (and other Unicode digits) |
| `Character.isLetter(c)` | Any letter |
| `Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)` | Alphanumeric |
| `Character.isUpperCase(c)`, `isLowerCase(c)` | Case tests |
| `Character.isWhitespace(c)` | Space, tab, newline |
| `Character.toUpperCase(c)`, `toLowerCase(c)` | Case conversion |
| `Character.getNumericValue(c)` | Digit value |

These methods handle Unicode correctly and read better than range comparisons.

## char is a number

A `char` is a 16-bit unsigned integer holding a UTF-16 code unit, so characters can be compared and combined arithmetically:

~~~java
char c = 'C';
int code = c;                     // 67
boolean upper = c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z';
int pos = c - 'A';                // 2: position in the alphabet
char next = (char) (c + 1);       // 'D'
~~~

Key ASCII values to remember: `'0'` is 48, `'A'` is 65, `'a'` is 97. Lowercase and uppercase letters differ by 32.

## Converting digit characters

~~~java
char ch = '7';
int value = ch - '0';             // 7
~~~

Subtracting `'0'` maps '0' through '9' to 0 through 9, because digit characters are consecutive in the character table. This is how numbers are parsed digit by digit:

~~~java
int number = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < str.length(); i++) {
    number = number * 10 + (str.charAt(i) - '0');
}
~~~

A common bug: `int value = ch;` gives 55, the character code, not 7.

## Frequency counting

~~~java
int[] freq = new int[26];
for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) {
    char c = Character.toLowerCase(word.charAt(i));
    if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') freq[c - 'a']++;
}
~~~

`c - 'a'` maps 'a' to index 0 and 'z' to index 25. With this array, checking anagrams, finding the first non-repeating character and counting distinct letters all take O(n). For arbitrary characters, use an array of size 128 (ASCII) or 256, or a `HashMap<Character, Integer>`.

## Comparing characters

Characters are primitives, so `==` compares them correctly:

~~~java
if (s.charAt(i) == 'a') { ... }
if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)) { ... }
~~~

Be careful mixing char and String: `s.charAt(0) == "a"` doesn't compile. For case-insensitive comparison, convert both with `Character.toLowerCase`.

## Concatenation trap

Adding chars produces an int, not a string:

~~~java
System.out.println('a' + 'b');        // 195: 97 + 98
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b');   // ab
System.out.println('a' + "b");        // ab
~~~

When either operand of `+` is a String, concatenation happens; with two chars, arithmetic happens.

## Building a result from characters

~~~java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = s.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    sb.append(s.charAt(i));
}
String reversed = sb.toString();
~~~

## Case conversion manually

~~~java
char lower = 'g';
char upper = (char) (lower - 32);            // 'G', ASCII only
char upper2 = Character.toUpperCase(lower);  // preferred: handles all alphabets
~~~

Toggling case with `c ^ 32` works for ASCII letters, a bit trick that appears in puzzles.

## charAt versus toCharArray

`charAt` reads characters without copying. `toCharArray()` creates a new array, useful when you need to modify or sort characters:

~~~java
char[] chars = word.toCharArray();
Arrays.sort(chars);
String sorted = new String(chars);    // "listen" becomes "eilnst"
~~~

Sorting characters gives a canonical form for anagram checks.

## How interviewers test this

Expect counting vowels, consonants, digits and spaces; converting a numeric string to an int without parseInt; anagram checks with a frequency array; and output puzzles like `'a' + 'b'`. Explain char arithmetic with `- '0'` and `- 'a'`, the Character helper methods, and the difference between char addition and string concatenation.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `string-indexing`, `length-method`, and half-open mathematical intervals $[\text{start}, \text{end})$.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content: Think of `substring(beginIndex, endIndex)` as a **Cookie Cutter Window**. The cutter drops over the string starting at the left boundary `beginIndex` (inclusive) and lifts up just before `endIndex` (exclusive). The characters inside the window are sliced out and encapsulated into a brand-new String object.

sections.title: The Golden Formula: Result Length = endIndex - beginIndex
sections.content:
Whenever you call `str.substring(beginIndex, endIndex)`:
• The resulting substring length is always exactly **`endIndex - beginIndex`**.
• Example: `"Developer".substring(0, 4)` → Length is $4 - 0 = 4$ (`"Deve"`).
• Example: `"Developer".substring(3, 3)` → Length is $3 - 3 = 0$ (`""` empty string).

sections.title: Two Overloads of substring() in Action
sections.explanation: substring(beginIndex) extracts from beginIndex all the way to string end. substring(beginIndex, endIndex) excludes the character at endIndex.

sections.title: Try It: Extract Email Domain Name
sections.explanation: indexOf('@') finds the @ symbol at index 7. substring(8) extracts everything after it.

iterations.description: Full string has length 5: S(0), T(1), U(2), D(3), Y(4).
Start slice at beginIndex 1.
Continue through index 2.
Continue through index 3.
Hit endIndex 4; stop immediately. Return new String "TUD".

sections.title: Common Substring Mistakes
items: **Assuming endIndex is Inclusive**: Writing `str.substring(0, 4)` extracts 4 characters (indices 0, 1, 2, 3), NOT 5.
**Inverted Indices (`beginIndex > endIndex`)**: Calling `str.substring(5, 2)` crashes with `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
**Exceeding String Length**: `endIndex` can be at most `str.length()`. Any value $> \text{length}()$ throws an exception.
**Expecting Original String Mutation**: `str.substring(2)` returns a new string; it does NOT mutate `str`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Java 6 vs Java 7+ Substring Memory Leak

traps.question: How did Java 6's `substring()` implementation differ from modern Java (Java 7u6+), and what interview bug did it cause?
traps.trap: Assuming `substring()` has always copied character arrays identically.
traps.solution: In Java 6, `substring()` did not create a new character array; it shared the parent string's massive internal `char[]` and merely stored a new `offset` and `count`. If you extracted a 3-character substring from a 100MB file string and cached the substring, the entire 100MB array stayed in memory, creating a catastrophic memory leak. In Java 7u6+, `substring()` always allocates a fresh, compact `char[]`/`byte[]` array containing only the sliced characters.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is returned by `"HelloWorld".substring(2, 6)`?
sections.explanation: Indices extracted are 2 ('l'), 3 ('l'), 4 ('o'), 5 ('W'). Index 6 is excluded. Length is 6 - 2 = 4. Result is "lloW".

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `substring(start)` extracts from `start` to string end.
`substring(start, end)` extracts characters in the half-open interval $[\text{start}, \text{end})$.
Resulting length is strictly $\text{endIndex} - \text{beginIndex}$.
Valid boundaries are $0 \le \text{beginIndex} \le \text{endIndex} \le \text{length}()$.

sections.title: Connection to Next Lesson
sections.content: Next, we explore String Comparison, mastering the critical differences between reference equality (==), value equality (.equals()), and lexicographical ordering (.compareTo()).

content.theory:
`substring` extracts part of a string as a new string. It's how programs pull a username from an email, an extension from a file name, a year from a date, or every window of characters in a sliding-window algorithm. Its range is half-open (start included, end excluded), a convention that confuses beginners but makes calculations cleaner. This lesson covers both forms of substring, the half-open convention, combining it with indexOf, its exceptions, its cost, and related methods.

## Two forms

~~~java
String s = "Programming";
s.substring(3);        // "gramming": from index 3 to the end
s.substring(0, 7);     // "Program": indices 0 to 6
s.substring(3, 7);     // "gram": indices 3, 4, 5, 6
~~~

- `substring(begin)`: from `begin` to the end
- `substring(begin, end)`: from `begin` up to, but not including, `end`

## The half-open convention

The end index is **exclusive**. That seems odd at first, but it has useful properties:

- the length of the result is `end - begin`: `substring(3, 7)` has 4 characters
- `substring(0, k)` gives the first k characters
- adjacent ranges join without overlap: `s.substring(0, k) + s.substring(k)` always equals `s`
- `substring(i, i)` is the empty string

Most Java APIs that take ranges, such as `Arrays.copyOfRange` and `List.subList`, follow the same convention.

## Valid ranges

The rules are `0 <= begin <= end <= length()`. Violations throw `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`:

~~~java
"hello".substring(2, 10);   // end beyond length
"hello".substring(3, 1);    // begin after end
"hello".substring(-1);      // negative begin
"hello".substring(5);       // "": begin equal to length is allowed
~~~

## Combining with indexOf

Many extraction tasks find a delimiter, then cut around it:

~~~java
String email = "ravi.k@college.edu";
int at = email.indexOf('@');
String user = email.substring(0, at);         // "ravi.k"
String domain = email.substring(at + 1);      // "college.edu"

String file = "report.final.pdf";
String ext = file.substring(file.lastIndexOf('.') + 1);   // "pdf"
~~~

Always handle the case where the delimiter isn't found: indexOf returns -1, and `substring(0, -1)` throws. Note the `+ 1` to skip the delimiter itself.

## Common patterns

~~~java
String firstChar = s.substring(0, 1);
String lastChar = s.substring(s.length() - 1);
String withoutFirst = s.substring(1);
String withoutLast = s.substring(0, s.length() - 1);
String capitalized = s.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase() + s.substring(1).toLowerCase();
~~~

Each assumes the string isn't empty; guard with a length check when it might be.

## Generating all substrings

~~~java
for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    for (int j = i + 1; j <= s.length(); j++) {
        System.out.println(s.substring(i, j));
    }
}
~~~

A string of length n has n(n + 1) / 2 non-empty substrings. Note `j <= s.length()`, because the end index is exclusive. Brute-force solutions that check every substring are O(n²) substrings, each taking up to O(n) to create or check: O(n³) overall. Techniques such as sliding windows exist to avoid that.

## Sliding windows

Fixed-size windows move across a string:

~~~java
int k = 3;
for (int i = 0; i + k <= s.length(); i++) {
    String window = s.substring(i, i + k);
}
~~~

The condition `i + k <= s.length()` ensures the last window fits.

## Cost of substring

Since Java 7, `substring` copies the selected characters into a new string, costing O(k) time and memory for a result of length k. (Older Java versions shared the original's array, which could leak memory when a small substring kept a huge string alive.) In tight loops, compare characters with `charAt` or use index-based methods like `regionMatches` and `startsWith(prefix, offset)` instead of creating many substrings.

## Strings are immutable

`substring` doesn't change the original string; it returns a new one. `s.substring(1);` on its own line does nothing useful; assign the result: `s = s.substring(1);`.

## Related methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `startsWith(prefix)`, `endsWith(suffix)` | Test the beginning or end without extracting |
| `contains(part)` | Test for a substring anywhere |
| `indexOf(part)` | Find where a substring starts |
| `split(regex)` | Cut a string into many parts at delimiters |
| `subSequence(a, b)` | Same as substring, typed as CharSequence |
| `StringBuilder.substring` | Extract from a builder |

For structured formats like CSV lines, `split` is often clearer than repeated indexOf and substring.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "what does substring(2, 5) return?", extracting usernames or extensions, generating all substrings, and questions on exceptions. Explain the half-open range and its length rule, combine indexOf with substring while handling -1, count n(n + 1) / 2 substrings, and mention that substring copies characters in modern Java.

lessons.description:
Think of String comparison as Three Different Types of Inspection:
1. Address Inspection (==): Checks if two people live at the exact same GPS building coordina...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-a-string`, `string-creation`, String Constant Pool interning, and reference vs value equality.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of String comparison as Three Different Types of Inspection:
1. **Address Inspection (`==`)**: Checks if two people live at the exact same GPS building coordinates (same RAM pointer).
2. **Content Inspection (`.equals()`)**: Checks if two distinct letters contain the exact same words written inside them.
3. **Alphabetical Dictionary Ranking (`.compareTo()`)**: Checks which word appears earlier or later in a standard dictionary index.

sections.title: The #1 Rule of Java Strings
sections.content:
⚠️ **NEVER USE `==` TO COMPARE STRING CONTENT!**
• `==` tests **reference identity** (whether both variables point to the same object in RAM).
• `.equals()` tests **value equality** (whether both objects contain the identical sequence of characters).
• Using `==` will cause subtle, intermittent bugs whenever strings are constructed dynamically from user input, network sockets, or database queries.

sections.title: The 4 Essential String Comparison Methods
sections.explanation: .equals() checks character-by-character. compareTo() calculates the numerical difference between the first mismatched Unicode code points.

sections.title: Comparison Method Matrix
rows: Checking if two references point to the exact same object.
Verifying passwords, IDs, codes, exact text.
Command inputs, email logins, search queries.

sections.title: Try It: Yoda Condition to Avoid NullPointerException
sections.explanation: Calling .equals() on the literal string "ADMIN" is completely null-safe; it safely returns false without throwing an exception.

iterations.description: First characters match; proceed to next index.
Second characters match; proceed to next index.
Characters mismatch! 't'(116) - 'r'(114) = +2.
Positive integer indicates "cat" comes after "car" in dictionary order.

sections.title: Common String Comparison Mistakes
items: **Using `==` for String logic**: Causes catastrophic bugs when comparing strings from Scanner, JSON, or DB.
**Calling `.equals()` on Null References**: `userRole.equals("ADMIN")` throws `NullPointerException` if `userRole` is null. Use `"ADMIN".equals(userRole)` or `Objects.equals(userRole, "ADMIN")`.
**Misunderstanding `compareTo()` return value**: `compareTo()` returns a negative, zero, or positive integer (e.g. -5, 0, 12), NOT specifically -1 or 1. Check `result < 0` or `result == 0`.
**Case Sensitivity in Sorting**: In Unicode ASCII, uppercase letters ('A'=65) come BEFORE lowercase letters ('a'=97). Hence `"Zebra".compareTo("apple")` returns a negative number.

traps.question: How do `Objects.equals(s1, s2)` and `s1.equals(s2)` handle `null` arguments differently?
traps.trap: Assuming they behave identically.
traps.solution: `s1.equals(s2)` throws `NullPointerException` if `s1` is null. In contrast, `java.util.Objects.equals(s1, s2)` first evaluates `(s1 == s2 || (s1 != null && s1.equals(s2)))`. It safely returns `true` if both are null, and `false` if only one is null, never throwing an NPE.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.explanation: `s1 == s2` is false because `new` creates two distinct Heap objects. `s1.equals(s2)` is true because both contain identical character contents "hello".

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Always use `.equals()` to compare String text content; never use `==`.
Use `.equalsIgnoreCase()` when matching case-insensitive strings.
Use `.compareTo()` to determine lexicographical ordering (<0, 0, >0).
Put literals on the left (`"CONST".equals(variable)`) or use `Objects.equals()` to prevent NullPointerExceptions.

sections.content: Next, we synthesize everything into Basic String Problems, implementing String Reversal, Palindrome Validation, and Anagram Checks with optimal time and space complexity.

content.theory:
Comparing strings looks trivial but is one of the most common sources of bugs in Java. `==` compares whether two variables refer to the same object, not whether they contain the same text. Correct comparison uses `equals`, `equalsIgnoreCase` and `compareTo`, each with its own purpose. This lesson explains reference versus content equality, case-insensitive comparison, lexicographic ordering with compareTo, null-safe comparisons, and comparing prefixes and regions.

## == compares references

~~~java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");
String d = sc.nextLine();          // user types hello

System.out.println(a == b);   // true: same pooled literal
System.out.println(a == c);   // false: c is a separate object
System.out.println(a == d);   // false: input creates a new object
~~~

`==` happens to work for literals because of the string pool, which tricks beginners into thinking it compares text. It fails for strings from input, concatenation at runtime, or `new`. Code using `==` for strings is a bug even when tests pass.

## equals compares contents

~~~java
System.out.println(a.equals(c));   // true
System.out.println(a.equals(d));   // true
~~~

`equals` checks that both strings have the same length and the same characters in the same order. It's case-sensitive: `"Java".equals("java")` is false.

## Case-insensitive equality

~~~java
"YES".equalsIgnoreCase("yes");     // true
~~~

Use it for user commands, yes or no answers, and file extensions. Alternatively, normalize first: `input.trim().toLowerCase().equals("yes")`.

## Null safety

Calling a method on null throws NullPointerException:

~~~java
String input = null;
input.equals("admin");        // NullPointerException
"admin".equals(input);        // false: safe
Objects.equals(input, "admin"); // false: safe, handles both sides null
~~~

Putting the known non-null literal first, sometimes called a Yoda condition, avoids the exception. `Objects.equals(a, b)` is the clearest when either side might be null.

## Lexicographic ordering with compareTo

`compareTo` orders strings the way a dictionary does, character by character:

~~~java
"apple".compareTo("banana");   // negative: apple comes first
"banana".compareTo("apple");   // positive
"apple".compareTo("apple");    // 0
~~~

It returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. Only the sign is meaningful; don't rely on specific values such as -1.

How it works:

1. Compare characters at index 0, 1, 2 and so on
2. At the first difference, return the difference of those characters' codes: `'a' - 'b'` is -1
3. If one string runs out first, the shorter one comes first: `"app".compareTo("apple")` is negative, returning the length difference

## Uppercase sorts before lowercase

Character codes put all uppercase letters (65 to 90) before lowercase letters (97 to 122):

~~~java
"Zebra".compareTo("apple");    // negative: 'Z' (90) < 'a' (97)
"Zebra".compareToIgnoreCase("apple");   // positive
~~~

For human-friendly sorting, use `compareToIgnoreCase` or `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`. For language-aware sorting (accents, local alphabets), use `java.text.Collator`.

## Numbers as strings

String comparison isn't numeric:

~~~java
"10".compareTo("9");   // negative: '1' < '9'
~~~

Sorting `{"10", "9", "100"}` as strings gives `{"10", "100", "9"}`. Parse to numbers when numeric order matters.

## Sorting strings

~~~java
String[] names = {"Ravi", "asha", "Meera"};
Arrays.sort(names);                                  // [Meera, Ravi, asha]
Arrays.sort(names, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);   // [asha, Meera, Ravi]
names = Arrays.stream(names).sorted(Comparator.comparing(String::length)).toArray(String[]::new);
~~~

## Comparing parts

~~~java
url.startsWith("https://");
file.endsWith(".pdf");
text.contains("error");
a.regionMatches(true, 0, b, 0, 3);   // compare the first 3 chars, ignoring case
~~~

These avoid creating substrings only to compare them.

## contentEquals

`s.contentEquals(sb)` compares a String with a StringBuilder or other CharSequence. `s.equals(sb)` is always false, because equals requires the other object to also be a String.

## Switch on strings

A switch on a String uses `equals` internally, so it compares contents correctly. It throws NullPointerException if the string is null.

## Hash codes

Equal strings always have equal hash codes, which is why strings work reliably as HashMap and HashSet keys. Different strings can share a hash code, so maps still call equals to confirm matches.

## A quick summary

Use `equals` for exact text, `equalsIgnoreCase` when case shouldn't matter, and `compareTo` or `compareToIgnoreCase` for ordering. Never compare strings with `==`, even when it seems to work for literals. Put a known literal first or use `Objects.equals` when either side may be null, and parse numeric strings before comparing them as numbers. When sorting text for people to read, choose a case-insensitive or locale-aware comparator so the order matches what readers expect.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "== vs equals?", output questions with literals, `new String` and runtime concatenation, "how does compareTo work?", sorting with mixed case, and null-safe comparison. Explain reference versus content equality, the pool's misleading effect, lexicographic comparison including the length rule, uppercase-before-lowercase, and `Objects.equals` or literal-first equals for null safety.

lessons.title: Basic String Problems
lessons.description:
Think of String algorithms as Pattern Pipelines. Every core interview question relies on one of three fundamental machinery patterns:
1. Two-Pointer Convergence...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `charat-method`, `substring-method`, `string-comparison`, `for` loops, and array manipulation.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of String algorithms as **Pattern Pipelines**. Every core interview question relies on one of three fundamental machinery patterns:
1. **Two-Pointer Convergence**: Scanning characters from both ends inward (Palindromes, In-Place Reversals).
2. **Frequency Bucketing**: Accumulating character counts into fixed 26/128-element frequency arrays (Anagrams, Duplicates).
3. **Mutable Buffer Accumulation (`StringBuilder`)**: Assembling new text dynamically without triggering quadratic $O(N^2)$ memory garbage.

sections.title: The StringBuilder Performance Imperative
sections.content:
⚠️ **CRITICAL INTERVIEW INSIGHT**: Because Strings are immutable, concatenating characters with `str += ch` inside an $N$-step loop creates $N$ intermediate String objects, degrading performance to **$O(N^2)$ time** and thrashing the Garbage Collector.

Always use **`StringBuilder`** for iterative string creation ($O(N)$ amortized time, single contiguous resizable buffer).

sections.title: Problem 1: String Reversal (Two-Pointer char[] vs StringBuilder)
sections.explanation: Converting to char[] allows in-place swapping using two pointers until left >= right, avoiding repetitive String allocations.

sections.title: Problem 2: Palindrome Verification (Ignoring Case & Non-Alphanumeric)
sections.explanation: Two pointers converge toward the center in O(N) time and O(1) extra space without allocating cleaned copy strings.

sections.title: Classic String Interview Problems & Optimal Complexities
rows: Allocating new regex-cleaned strings instead of skipping in-place.
Sorting strings in $O(N \log N)$ instead of counting in $O(N)$.

sections.title: Try It: Valid Anagram Checker
sections.explanation: Counts of each character in 's' are cancelled out by 't'. If all entries in counts are 0, they are anagrams.

iterations.description: Left 'r' == Right 'r'. Matches! Increment left to 1, decrement right to 3.
Left 'a' == Right 'a'. Matches! Increment left to 2, decrement right to 2.
left == right. Pointers crossed. Loop terminates successfully -> Palindrome is TRUE.

sections.title: Common String Problem Traps
items: **String Concatenation in Loops**: Writing `for (...) { res += s.charAt(i); }` is an automatic red flag in coding interviews. Always use `StringBuilder`.
**Ignoring Case Differences**: Forgetting `Character.toLowerCase()` before comparing causes false negatives in palindrome and anagram verification.
**Forgetting Length Checks**: In Anagram questions, always guard with `if (s.length() != t.length()) return false;` immediately.
**Negative Array Indices in Frequency Arrays**: Always ensure input characters are in the expected range before doing `char - 'a'`, or use a 128/256-size array to support full ASCII.

sections.title: Interview Traps: In-Place String Mutation in Java

traps.question: An interviewer asks: 'Write an in-place string reversal algorithm that operates with $O(1)$ auxiliary space in Java.' How should you answer?
traps.trap: Claiming you can mutate the Java `String` directly in-place without memory allocation.
traps.solution: Explain that because Java `String` instances are immutable and their internal byte arrays are private final fields, true in-place reversal of a `String` object without allocating a `char[]` or `StringBuilder` is impossible by language design. You can perform $O(1)$ space in-place reversal on a `char[]` or `StringBuilder`, but converting back to `String` will always require $O(N)$ memory.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Why is `StringBuilder` preferred over `+` string concatenation in loops?
options: `StringBuilder` modifies a mutable buffer in O(N) amortized time instead of creating O(N) intermediate immutable objects in O(N^2) time
sections.explanation: String concatenation creates a brand-new String on every iteration copying previous characters ($O(N^2)$ time), whereas StringBuilder appends to a resizable buffer in $O(1)$ amortized time ($O(N)$ total time).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Use two-pointer techniques for string reversal and palindrome verification.
Use fixed-size frequency arrays (`int[26]` or `int[256]`) for $O(N)$ anagram and character frequency counting.
Always use `StringBuilder` rather than `+` string concatenation when building strings iteratively.
Java Strings are immutable; all mutation operations create new objects.

sections.title: Module Completion Summary
sections.content: 🎉 **Congratulations! You have completed Module 8: Strings.** You have mastered String immutability, the String Constant Pool, zero-based indexing, length measurement, character slicing with `substring()`, reference vs content equality, and standard algorithmic string manipulation patterns.

sections.title: Prerequisites

Think of a Method as a **Specialized Kitchen Appliance (e.g., a Digital Blender)**:
• **Inputs (Parameters)**: You pour in raw ingredients (e.g., milk, fruit, ice).

• **Output (Return Value)**: The appliance dispenses a finished smoothie (a computed result value) or sounds a completion beep (a `void` method).

sections.title: Formal Definition & Anatomy
sections.content: A **method** is a named, self-contained sub-routine within a class that encapsulates a specific set of instructions. It takes optional input parameters, performs computations or actions, and optionally returns a single result value back to the caller.

sections.title: Method Definition, Invocation & Program Flow
sections.explanation: When calculateRectangleArea(12, 10) is called, the CPU jumps from main() into calculateRectangleArea, executes its instructions, and substitutes the return value 120 back into room1.

sections.title: The 6 Core Components of a Java Method
rows: Controls which other classes can invoke this method.
Declares that the method belongs to the Class rather than individual object instances.
Declares the data type of the result returned. Use `void` if no value is returned.
Unique identifier following camelCase naming conventions.
Comma-separated input variables enclosed in parentheses `()`.
The block of statements enclosed in curly braces `{}`.

sections.explanation: (10000 * 7.5 * 3) / 100 = 2250.0. The computed double value is returned and printed.

Call invoked: A new Stack Frame for calculateArea is pushed. Local parameters length=12 and width=10 are allocated.
area computed. return statement transfers 120 back to caller.
calculateArea stack frame is popped. Execution resumes in main() with room1 initialized to 120.

sections.title: Common Method Pitfalls
items: **Declaring Methods Inside Methods**: Java does NOT allow direct nested method declarations inside another method body.
**Missing Return in Non-Void Methods**: If a method declares a return type like `int`, every reachable execution path MUST terminate with a `return <int_value>;`.
**Defining but Never Calling**: Writing a method does nothing until it is explicitly invoked by an active execution thread.
**Ignoring Return Values**: Calling `calculateArea(10, 20);` without assigning or printing the result causes the return value to be discarded.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Method Signature vs Method Header

traps.question: What exact elements constitute a Java 'Method Signature', and does it include the return type?
traps.trap: Thinking access modifiers and return types are part of the method signature.
traps.solution:
In Java, a **Method Signature** strictly consists of only two things:
1. The **Method Name**
2. The **Parameter List** (types, number, and order of parameters).

Modifiers, return types, and `throws` clauses belong to the **Method Header**, but are NOT part of the signature. This is why two methods differing only by return type cannot coexist in the same class.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which of the following is NOT part of a Java method signature?
sections.explanation: In Java, the method signature consists solely of the method name and parameter types/order. The return type is part of the method header, not the signature.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Methods encapsulate reusable, modular blocks of business logic.
Invoking a method creates a new Stack Frame on the JVM Call Stack.
Methods have a return type (`void` for no result, or a specific data type).
Method signatures consist strictly of the Method Name and Parameter Types.

content.theory:
A method is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be run whenever it's needed by calling its name. Methods are the basic unit of organization in Java programs: `main` is a method, `System.out.println` is a method, and every useful program is built from many small methods that call each other. This lesson explains what a method is, how calling and returning work, the parts of a method, built-in versus user-defined methods, and how methods relate to functions in other languages.

## A first method

~~~java
public class Greeter {
    static void greet(String name) {
        System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        greet("Asha");
        greet("Ravi");
    }
}
~~~

`greet` is **defined** once and **called** twice. Each call runs the method's body with a different value for `name`.

## Definition versus call

- A **method definition** (or declaration) describes what the method does: its name, inputs, output type and body. Defining a method doesn't run it
- A **method call** (or invocation) runs it: `greet("Asha");`

You can define a method once and call it from many places, which is the point of having methods.

## What happens during a call

1. The arguments are evaluated: `"Asha"`
2. Their values are copied into the method's parameters: `name = "Asha"`
3. Control jumps to the first statement of the method body
4. The body runs until it reaches a `return` statement or the closing brace
5. Control returns to the point right after the call, bringing back a return value if there is one

Behind the scenes, each call gets its own **stack frame** holding its parameters and local variables. When the method returns, the frame is discarded.

## Parts of a method

~~~java
public static int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}
~~~

| Part | In the example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Access modifier | `public` | Who can call it |
| `static` | `static` | Belongs to the class; callable without an object |
| Return type | `int` | Type of the value sent back, or `void` for none |
| Name | `add` | How callers refer to it |
| Parameter list | `(int a, int b)` | Inputs, with types |
| Body | `{ return a + b; }` | The statements that run |

The name plus the parameter types form the method's **signature**. The method syntax lesson covers each part in detail.

## Methods that compute versus methods that act

- Some methods **return a value**: `Math.max(3, 7)` returns 7, which the caller can store or use
- Some methods **perform an action** and return nothing (`void`): `System.out.println` prints text

A well-designed method usually does one or the other: it answers a question or it changes something. Mixing both, such as a method that prints and also returns a computed value, makes code harder to reuse.

## Built-in and user-defined methods

Java's standard library provides thousands of methods: `Math.sqrt`, `String.length`, `Arrays.sort`, `Integer.parseInt`. Learning to find and use library methods saves time and avoids bugs. **User-defined** methods are the ones you write for your own program's tasks, like `calculateGrade` or `isPrime`.

## Static and instance methods

`static` methods belong to the class and are called through the class name or directly from other static methods: `Math.max(a, b)`. **Instance** methods belong to objects and are called on an object: `name.length()`, `list.add(x)`. At this stage, most methods you write will be static, called from `main`. The OOP course covers instance methods in depth.

## Methods and functions

Other languages call similar constructs **functions** (C, Python, JavaScript) or **procedures** (functions that return nothing). In Java, every method belongs to a class; there are no standalone functions, though static methods behave much like them. The underlying idea is the same everywhere: package a computation behind a name.

## The main method

`public static void main(String[] args)` is the entry point the JVM calls to start a program. It's an ordinary static method with a special signature. `args` holds command-line arguments. Programs grow by having main call other methods rather than putting all code inside main.

## Naming methods

Methods use **camelCase** names that start with a verb, describing what they do: `calculateTotal`, `printReport`, `findMax`. Methods returning booleans read as questions: `isEven`, `hasAccess`, `canVote`. A good name lets readers understand a call without reading the body.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a method?", "What is a method signature?", "Difference between a parameter and an argument?" and tracing calls in output questions. Explain definition versus call, the call steps including the stack frame, the parts of a method, and the difference between returning a value and performing an action.

lessons.title: Why Use Methods?
lessons.description:
Think of software without methods as a Monolithic Spaghetti Skyscraper vs with methods as Modular Interchangeable Lego Blocks:
• Without Methods: Writing 5,000 ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-a-method`, loops, and basic procedural logic.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of software without methods as a **Monolithic Spaghetti Skyscraper** vs with methods as **Modular Interchangeable Lego Blocks**:
• **Without Methods**: Writing 5,000 lines of code inside `main()` means if you find a bug in your email validation formula, you must hunt down and manually edit 40 duplicate copy-pasted sections, inevitably introducing inconsistencies.
• **With Methods**: You write `isValidEmail()` once. 40 different caller classes invoke it. Fixing a bug in that single 5-line method instantly fixes the entire enterprise application.

sections.title: The 5 Pillars of Method Design
sections.content:
1. **DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)**: Eliminate duplicate logic across the codebase.
2. **Abstraction**: Callers use functionality by name without needing to understand underlying complexities.
3. **Single Responsibility (SRP)**: Each method focuses on executing one specific task reliably.
4. **Automated Testing**: Small, isolated methods are simple to test with unit tests.
5. **Maintainability**: Code changes and optimizations are localized to one file and method.

sections.title: Refactoring: Repetitive Monolith vs Modular Methods
sections.explanation: Extracting the net income calculation into calculateNetIncome() makes the code self-documenting, eliminates copy-paste bugs, and allows instant updates if tax formulas change.

sections.title: Monolithic Code vs Modular Methods
rows: Slow (must search across thousands of lines)
Fast (isolated stack traces pinpoint exact method)
Effortless (isolated unit testing of inputs & outputs)
Frequent merge conflicts on monolithic files
High (developers work on independent modular methods)

sections.title: Try It: Modular Greeting Formatter
sections.explanation: formatGreeting standardizes role casing and whitespace trimming across all user greetings.

sections.title: Maintainability Trace: Updating Tax Formula from 20% to 22%

iterations.description: Developer must manually find, edit, and verify 40 separate lines. High risk of human error.
Developer changes 1 line inside calculateNetIncome().
Every caller across the application immediately reflects the updated 22% tax rate.

sections.title: Common Modularization Pitfalls
items: **God Methods**: Writing massive 200-line methods that perform database access, validation, calculation, and UI printing all at once.
**Over-Abstraction**: Creating one-line methods for trivial operations that are used only once and obscure readability.
**Vague Method Names**: Naming methods `doWork()`, `handle()`, or `processData()` rather than specific verbs like `calculateDiscount()`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Does Calling Methods Slow Down Java?

traps.question: Does splitting code into dozens of small methods reduce Java runtime performance compared to writing one giant loop?
traps.trap: Believing method invocation stack frame overhead will degrade CPU performance.
traps.solution: No. The JVM **HotSpot JIT (Just-In-Time) Compiler** identifies frequently executed 'hot' methods and performs **Method Inlining** at runtime. It replaces the method call with the method's raw bytecode instructions directly at the call site, completely eliminating stack frame allocation overhead while keeping the source code perfectly modular.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What software engineering principle states that logic should have a single, unambiguous representation in a codebase?
sections.explanation: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) is the core principle emphasizing the reduction of code repetition by extracting shared logic into reusable methods.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Methods promote DRY architecture and single responsibility.
Methods provide abstraction by separating public interface contracts from internal algorithms.
JIT compiler inlining ensures modular methods run at blazing bare-metal speeds.
Always choose expressive, self-documenting method names.

sections.content:
Think of Method Syntax as an **Official Legal Contract Header**. Every keyword in the header establishes strict rules:
• **Who can call it?** (Access Modifier: `public` vs `private`)
• **Does it need an instance object?** (Modifier: `static` vs instance)
• **What does it produce?** (Return Type: `int`, `String`, or `void`)
• **What is its legal name?** (Identifier: `calculateTotal`)
• **What inputs must the caller provide?** (Parameters: `(double subtotal, double tax)`)
• **What happens inside?** (Body `{ ... }`)

sections.title: The Universal Java Method Header Pattern
Diverse Method Syntax Configurations
sections.explanation: Notice how each method specifies its exact return type (double, String, or void) and matching parameter definitions.

sections.title: Common Java Access & Property Modifiers for Methods
rows: Accessible from any class in any package across the entire application.
Accessible ONLY within the declaring class (internal helper methods).
Accessible within the same package and by derived subclasses.
Package-private: accessible only within the declaring package.
Belongs to the class directly; callable without instantiating an object (`ClassName.method()`).
Cannot be overridden by any child subclass.

sections.title: Common Syntax Traps
items: **Shorthand Parameter Type Omission**: Writing `(int x, y)` instead of `(int x, int y)` is a compilation error in Java.
**Accidental Semicolon on Method Header**: Writing `public static void run(); { ... }` treats the header as an abstract method declaration and breaks the body block.
**Omitting Parentheses on Zero-Parameter Methods**: Calling `printDivider;` instead of `printDivider();` fails to invoke the method.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can a Method Return Multiple Values in Java?

traps.question: How can a single Java method return multiple values simultaneously?
traps.trap: Attempting syntax like `return a, b;` or using output parameters like C# out/ref.
traps.solution: A Java method can return strictly **only one value or reference**. To return multiple values, you must bundle them into a container object: an array (`int[]`), a standard Java Collection (`List`), a custom `class`, or modern Java 14+ `record Pair(int min, int max)`.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which of the following method declarations is syntactically INVALID in Java?
options: int calculate(int x, y) { return x + y; }
public static String[] getNames() { return new String[0]; }
sections.explanation: In Java, every formal parameter must explicitly state its type. `int calculate(int x, y)` fails because parameter `y` lacks a type declaration.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Every parameter must explicitly declare both its data type and variable name.
Non-void methods must return a value compatible with the declared return type.
Static methods can be invoked directly from class scope (`Class.method()`).
Bundle multiple return values into classes, records, or arrays.
