lessons.title: The 'this' Keyword & Self-Reference
lessons.description:
Think of the this keyword as an Identity Badge & Personal Mirror ("Me, Myself, and I"):
• When a method executes, it needs to know which specific physical objec...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `fields-and-methods`, `classes-and-objects`, and method parameter passing.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of the `this` keyword as an **Identity Badge & Personal Mirror ("Me, Myself, and I")**:
• When a method executes, it needs to know *which* specific physical object on the heap called it.
• If Alice calls `alice.display()`, inside that method, `this` is Alice's identity badge.
• If Bob calls `bob.display()`, inside that method, `this` is Bob's identity badge.
• `this` provides a direct, unambiguous pointer back to the currently executing object instance.

sections.title: The 4 Core Use Cases of `this` in Java
sections.content:
1. **Disambiguating Variable Shadowing**: Distinguishing instance fields from method parameters with identical names (`this.age = age`).
2. **Constructor Chaining (`this(...)`)**: Calling another constructor in the same class to eliminate duplicate initialization code (MUST be the 1st line).
3. **Method Chaining (Fluent Interface)**: Returning `this` from setter methods (`return this;`) to allow chained calls (`user.setName("A").setAge(25)`).
4. **Passing Current Object as Parameter**: Passing self-reference to external methods (`eventListener.register(this)`).

sections.title: Comprehensive `this` Usage: Shadowing, Chaining & Fluent APIs
sections.explanation: this(username, ...) reuses constructor logic. setEmail() returns 'this', enabling elegant fluent dot-chaining.

sections.title: The 4 Usages of `this` in Java
rows: Essential when parameter and field share identical identifiers.
MUST be the absolute first statement in the constructor body.
Method return type must match the class type.
Passes current object reference to an outside service or callback.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Shadowing Bug Output
sections.explanation: Because 'val = val' assigns the local parameter to itself without 'this.', the instance field obj.val remains 10.

sections.title: Stack Frame Trace: `this` in Slot 0 during `user.setEmail("...")`

iterations.description: JVM automatically places invoking object pointer (0x4A2F) into Stack Frame Slot 0 as 'this'.
Dereferences 0x4A2F and assigns the email pointer.
Pushes pointer 0x4A2F back onto Operand Stack for the next chained method call.

sections.title: Common `this` Compiler Errors
items: **Using `this` Inside Static Methods**: Writing `this.name` inside `public static void main` throws compile error: *non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context* (static methods belong to the class, not any instance).
**Placing `this()` After Other Statements**: Calling `this("default");` on line 2 of a constructor throws compile error: *constructor call must be the first statement in a constructor*.
**Recursive Constructor Invocation**: Constructor A calling `this()` which calls Constructor A causes compile error: *recursive constructor invocation*.

traps.question: Can you reassign `this` to point to a different object inside an instance method, like `this = new MyClass();`?
traps.trap: Thinking it replaces the current object.
traps.solution: NO, **`this` is an immutable `final` reference value managed exclusively by the JVM**. Writing `this = ...` produces a compile-time error: *cannot assign a value to final variable this*. You can mutate fields of `this` (`this.age = 20`), but you cannot change the address `this` points to.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Where must constructor chaining `this(...)` be placed inside a constructor body?
options: As the absolute first statement in the constructor
At the very end of the constructor
sections.explanation: Java language specification strictly requires `this(...)` (or `super(...)`) to be the very first statement in a constructor.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `this` is an immutable reference pointing to the current executing object instance.
Stored automatically in Slot 0 of non-static instance method Stack Frames.
Used to resolve variable shadowing: `this.field = param`.
Used for constructor chaining: `this(args)` must be the first line.
Cannot be used in `static` contexts because static methods have no instance receiver.

sections.content: Next, we explore Stack vs Heap Memory for Objects, understanding object reference aliasing, pass-by-value mechanics, and NullPointerExceptions.

lessons.title: Object Memory Model: Stack vs Heap Deep Dive
lessons.description:
Think of Object References as TV Remote Controls and Television Sets:
• The Heap Object (The Physical 65-inch TV): Mounted on the wall in the living room (Heap)...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `the-this-keyword`, `stack-memory`, `heap-memory`, and reference variables.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Object References as **TV Remote Controls and Television Sets**:
• **The Heap Object (The Physical 65-inch TV)**: Mounted on the wall in the living room (**Heap**). It has state (Channel 7, Volume 25, Power ON).
• **The Stack Reference (The Remote Control)**: Held in your hand at your desk (**Stack Frame**). The remote is not the TV; it merely holds the frequency code (**Memory Pointer**) to control the TV.
• **Aliasing (Multiple Remotes)**: If you buy a second remote control (`Remote r2 = r1;`), you do NOT get a second TV! Both remotes control the exact same physical television on the wall. Changing the channel with Remote 2 changes what you see with Remote 1.

sections.title: The Invariant of Reference Copying (Aliasing)
sections.content: In Java, assigning one object variable to another (`Car b = a;`) **NEVER copies the object payload**. It strictly copies the 64-bit reference address pointer. Both `a` and `b` now point to the exact same object in Heap memory.

sections.title: Object Aliasing & Method Parameter Mutation in Action
sections.explanation: reassignReference() changes its own local parameter 'b' to point to a new Box(500). The caller's box1 pointer on the main() stack remains completely unchanged pointing to the original Box(99).

sections.title: Primitive Variables vs Reference Variables in Memory
rows: What is stored in Stack slot?
Directly inside Stack Frame (or inside enclosing object).
Copies the raw value; completely independent.
Copies the pointer address; both point to same object.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Aliasing and Mutation Result
sections.explanation: n1 and n2 point to the same object (val=5, n1==n2 is true). n3 is a separate heap object (val=1, n1==n3 is false).

sections.title: Step-by-Step Memory Map Trace: `Box box1 = new Box(10); Box box2 = box1;`

iterations.description: new Box(10) allocates heap object at 0x88AA; box1 stack slot stores pointer 0x88AA.
box2 = box1 copies the pointer 0x88AA into box2 stack slot (Aliasing).
Dereferences 0x88AA and updates width to 20. box1 observes this change immediately.
box1 reference severed; object at 0x88AA remains alive because box2 still points to it.

sections.title: Common Memory Model Traps
items: **The NullPointerException (NPE)**: Attempting to access fields or methods on a reference holding `null` (`box = null; box.width = 10;`) crashes at runtime with `NullPointerException`.
**Assuming `a = b` Duplicates an Object**: Modifying `b` unexpectedly mutates `a` because both reference the same heap memory.
**Unintentional Object Retention**: Keeping static references to objects prevents the Garbage Collector from freeing their heap memory.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Is Java Pass-By-Value or Pass-By-Reference?

traps.question: Does Java pass objects to methods by reference or by value?
traps.trap: Claiming Java passes primitives by value and objects by reference.
traps.solution:
Java is **100% STRICTLY PASS-BY-VALUE, ALWAYS!**
• When you pass an `int`, a copy of the primitive value is passed.
• When you pass an `Object`, a **copy of the 64-bit reference pointer (memory address)** is passed by value.
• Because the method receives a copy of the address, you can mutate the object's fields (`b.width = 99`), but if you reassign the parameter (`b = new Box(500)`), the caller's reference outside the method remains completely unchanged!

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: If `Box a = new Box(10); Box b = a;`, what happens if you execute `a = null;`?
options: The Box object is immediately garbage collected
The Box object remains alive in Heap memory because `b` still references it
sections.explanation: Setting `a = null` only clears the `a` pointer on the stack. `b` still holds the heap address 0x88AA, keeping the object alive and reachable from GC Roots.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Reference variables on the Stack store memory addresses pointing to Object payloads on the Heap.
Assigning reference variables (`b = a`) aliases the object without copying the underlying heap data.
Java is strictly 100% Pass-by-Value; passing an object copies the reference pointer.
An object is eligible for Garbage Collection only when zero live GC Roots hold its reference address.

sections.title: Connection to Next Module
sections.content: Next, we enter Module 2: Encapsulation, mastering data hiding, access modifiers (private, protected, public), and defensive getter/setter architecture.

content.theory:
When a Java program runs, its data lives in two main memory areas: the stack, which holds method calls and local variables, and the heap, which holds objects. Knowing which goes where explains how references work, why Java passes arguments the way it does, what causes StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError, and when objects are garbage collected. This lesson builds a clear picture of both areas.

## The stack

Each thread has its own **stack**. Every method call pushes a **frame** holding the method's parameters, local variables and return address. When the method returns, its frame is popped and all its locals disappear instantly.

- Allocation and cleanup are extremely fast: moving a pointer
- Size is limited, often 512 KB to 1 MB per thread by default
- Data is private to the thread

## The heap

The **heap** is a single large area shared by all threads, where every object and array is allocated. Objects live there until no references reach them, and the garbage collector reclaims them later.

- Can hold gigabytes, sized with JVM options such as `-Xmx`
- Allocation is fast in modern JVMs, but cleanup requires garbage collection
- Shared between threads, so concurrent access needs care

## What goes where

~~~java
void demo() {
    int count = 5;                 // primitive local: on the stack
    Car car = new Car();           // reference 'car' on the stack; Car object on the heap
    car.speed = 60;                // field 'speed' lives inside the object, on the heap
}
~~~

| Item | Location |
|---|---|
| Local primitive variables | Stack (inside the method's frame) |
| Local reference variables | Stack (the reference itself) |
| Objects and arrays | Heap |
| Instance fields, including primitives | Heap, inside their object |
| Static fields | With the class's data in the heap (in modern JVMs) |

A common misconception is that primitives always live on the stack. An `int` field of an object lives on the heap with that object; only local primitives live on the stack.

## Java passes references by value

Java always passes arguments **by value**. For objects, the value copied is the reference, so the method gets its own copy of the address pointing to the same object:

~~~java
void rename(Car c) {
    c.model = "Baleno";   // changes the shared object: visible to the caller
    c = new Car();        // rebinds the local copy only: caller unaffected
}
~~~

The method can modify the object the caller passed, but it can't make the caller's variable point to a different object. This is why Java has no pass-by-reference, despite objects behaving that way for field changes. Swapping two objects inside a method, for the same reason, doesn't affect the caller.

## StackOverflowError

Each call adds a frame. Deep or infinite recursion keeps pushing frames until the stack's fixed size runs out, throwing `StackOverflowError`. Missing base cases are the usual cause. Recursion depth of tens of thousands can overflow even when correct, which is why deep traversals are often rewritten with an explicit stack data structure on the heap.

## OutOfMemoryError

If the heap fills with reachable objects and garbage collection can't free enough space, the JVM throws `OutOfMemoryError`. Causes include loading huge datasets into memory and **memory leaks**: objects that are no longer needed but still referenced, often from a static collection or a cache that never evicts.

## Garbage collection basics

The garbage collector finds objects that can't be reached from any **GC root**: local variables in active stack frames, static fields, and a few JVM internals. Unreachable objects are freed, even when they form cycles that reference each other. Most objects die young, so the JVM uses **generational** collection: a young generation collected often and cheaply, and an old generation for long-lived objects. You can't force collection; `System.gc()` is only a suggestion.

## Escape analysis

Modern JVMs analyse whether an object ever escapes the method that creates it. If it doesn't, the JIT compiler may avoid heap allocation entirely, replacing the object with its fields in registers or on the stack. This is an optimization, not a language rule, so you still reason about objects as heap-allocated.

## Strings and the pool

String literals are stored in a shared **string pool** on the heap, so identical literals refer to one object. `new String("hi")` always creates a separate heap object, which is why `==` between them is false.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Where are objects and local variables stored?", "Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?" and "What causes StackOverflowError versus OutOfMemoryError?" Draw the stack frame holding a reference to a heap object, explain that references are passed by value, and connect each error to its memory area.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-oop`, `classes-and-objects`, and `fields-and-methods`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Encapsulation as an **Automated Bank ATM Machine**:
• **The Inner Vault (Private State)**: Millions of dollars in cash are locked inside a thick steel safe (`private double cashVault`). No customer can reach in and grab bills directly.
• **The Keypad & Dispenser (Public Interface)**: Customers interact with the machine strictly through controlled public buttons (`insertCard()`, `enterPin()`, `withdraw()`).
• The ATM validates preconditions (Is PIN correct? Is vault balance sufficient? Is daily limit exceeded?) before dispensing cash, ensuring the internal cash vault is never corrupted or stolen.

sections.title: The 2 Core Tenets of Encapsulation
sections.content:
1. **Data Bundling**: Unifying state (fields) and the behaviors (methods) that operate on that state within a single cohesive class.
2. **Data Hiding & Protection**: Restricting direct external access to internal fields using the `private` access modifier, allowing access only through validated public methods.

sections.title: Vulnerable Public Fields vs Encapsulated BankAccount
sections.explanation: In SecureAccount, the balance field is private. External callers cannot arbitrarily alter or corrupt account funds without passing through withdraw() validation rules.

sections.title: The 4 Pillars of Encapsulation
rows: Prevents unauthorized external reads and arbitrary modifications.
Provides controlled, read-only visibility into state.
Enables state updates only after verifying business rules.
Guarantees the object never enters an invalid or illegal state.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Encapsulated Mutation Guard
sections.explanation: Because 50 is outside the valid range [10, 35], setTemperature(50) rejects the change, leaving the temperature at its initial value of 20.

iterations.description: Invokes member method with amount = 1200.0.
Passes positive amount validation.
Insufficient funds guard triggers. Prints denial message.
Aborts transaction without mutating internal balance. Returns false.

sections.title: Common Encapsulation Anti-Patterns
items: **Blindly Generating Getters & Setters**: Automatically creating getters and setters for all private fields without asking if callers need write access destroys encapsulation.
**Public Fields with Separate Validation Methods**: Keeping `public int age;` and writing `validateAge()` does nothing to prevent code from bypassing validation.
**Exposing Internal Data Structures**: Returning direct references to mutable collections or arrays from getters allows external callers to mutate them secretly.

traps.question: What is the precise difference between Encapsulation and Abstraction in Object-Oriented Design?
traps.trap: Confusing data hiding with complexity hiding.
traps.solution:
• **Encapsulation (Information Hiding & Protection)**: Focuses on **HOW** an object guards its internal data and implementation. Solves the problem of data security and invalid states (achieved via `private` fields and getters/setters).
• **Abstraction (Complexity Hiding & Interface Design)**: Focuses on **WHAT** an object does rather than how it does it. Solves the problem of high cognitive load and code coupling (achieved via `abstract class` and `interface`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the primary objective of data hiding in Encapsulation?
options: To encrypt source code files on disk
To prevent unauthorized direct access and ensure object invariants cannot be corrupted
To make the program execute with zero RAM usage
To eliminate the need for methods
sections.explanation: Data hiding protects internal object fields from direct outside manipulation, ensuring all state changes are validated through class methods.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Encapsulation binds state and behavior together and protects data via `private` access.
Getters provide read access; setters validate updates before modifying state.
Encapsulation prevents objects from ever entering invalid or inconsistent states.
Encapsulation is about data protection; Abstraction is about interface simplicity.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `understanding-encapsulation`, Java package structures, and basic class declarations.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Java Access Modifiers as **Security Clearance Badges in a Corporate Campus**:
• **`private` (Personal Safe Deposit Box)**: Only you (the exact enclosing class) have the key. Nobody else in the building or outside can see inside.
• **`default` (Department Floor / Package-Private)**: Anyone working inside your immediate department (**Same Package**) can enter freely. Outsiders and other floors are blocked.
• **`protected` (Family & Subsidiary Access)**: Open to your department (**Same Package**) PLUS any of your official child subsidiaries (**Subclasses**), even if they are located in another city (**Different Package**).
• **`public` (Public Street Reception)**: Anyone anywhere in the world can access it.

sections.title: The 4 Java Access Modifiers Hierarchy
sections.content:
From strictest to most accessible:
$$\text{private} \longrightarrow \text{default (no keyword)} \longrightarrow \text{protected} \longrightarrow \text{public}$$
Access modifiers can be applied to fields, methods, constructors, and nested classes. Top-level classes can only be `public` or `default`.

sections.title: Access Modifiers in Action Across Classes & Packages
sections.explanation: Demonstrates the 4 access levels declared inside a single class. Their visibility changes depending on the caller's package and inheritance relationship.

sections.title: The Definitive Java Access Modifiers Matrix
Try It: Predict Modifier Access Error
sections.explanation: 'secret' is private to Parent and inaccessible in Child. 'shared' is protected and accessible to subclasses, printing 200.

sections.title: Compiler Access Verification Trace: Accessing `protected double transactionFee`

iterations.description: Same class access -> ALLOWED (private, default, protected, public).
Same package non-subclass -> ALLOWED (default, protected, public).
Different package subclass -> ALLOWED for protected via 'super.transactionFee' or 'this.transactionFee'.
Different package non-subclass -> BLOCKED by compiler! Only public is allowed.

sections.title: Common Access Modifier Pitfalls
items: **Declaring Top-Level Classes `private` or `protected`**: Top-level classes in `.java` files can ONLY be `public` or `default` (package-private). Declaring `private class App {}` causes a compile error.
**Overusing `protected` for Convenience**: Making fields `protected` exposes them to any class in the same package and any subclass worldwide, weakening encapsulation.
**Accidental Default Access**: Omitting a modifier (e.g. `int count;`) does NOT mean public; it means package-private, causing confusing compile errors when imported into other packages.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can Method Overriding Reduce Visibility?

traps.question: If a superclass defines `protected void calculate()`, can a subclass override it as `private void calculate()` or `void calculate()` (package-private)?
traps.trap: Thinking a subclass can restrict access to its own methods.
traps.solution:
NO! **A subclass cannot reduce the visibility of an inherited method** (Compile Error: *cannot assign weaker access privileges*). In Java method overriding:
• You can **widen** visibility (`protected` → `public`).
• You **CANNOT narrow** visibility (`public` → `protected` → `default` → `private`) because it would violate Liskov Substitution Principle (polymorphism would fail if a caller using the parent reference cannot access the overridden child method).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which access modifier allows access within the same package and by subclasses located in different packages?
sections.explanation: `protected` grants access to all classes in the same package, plus subclasses in any package via inheritance.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Java has 4 access levels: `private`, `default` (package-private), `protected`, and `public`.
Top-level classes can only be `public` or `default`.
`private` is the foundation of encapsulation (class-only visibility).
Method overriding can widen access privileges but can never narrow them.

content.theory:
Access modifiers control which code can see a class, field, method or constructor. Java has four levels: private, package-private (no modifier), protected and public. Choosing the narrowest level that works is how encapsulation is enforced by the compiler. This lesson explains each level precisely, the subtle rules of protected, what applies to top-level classes, and how to choose.

## The four levels

| Modifier | Same class | Same package | Subclass in another package | Any other class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | Yes | No | No | No |
| (none) package-private | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| `protected` | Yes | Yes | Yes (through inheritance) | No |
| `public` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Each level includes everything the narrower levels allow. Package-private is the default when you write no modifier, and it's often misunderstood as "public within the project"; it's only public within the same package.

## private

Private members are visible only inside the class that declares them, including its nested classes. Use private for all fields by default, and for helper methods that are implementation details. Private members aren't inherited in a usable way: a subclass object contains the parent's private fields, but subclass code can't access them directly.

Note that private is per class, not per object. One Account object's method can read another Account's private balance:

~~~java
boolean hasMoreThan(Account other) {
    return this.balance > other.balance;   // allowed: same class
}
~~~

## Package-private

With no modifier, a member is visible to every class in the same package. It's useful for classes that collaborate closely within one package while hiding them from the rest of the codebase, and for test code placed in the same package. Many library implementation classes are package-private so users can't depend on them.

## protected

Protected members are visible within the same package and to subclasses in other packages. The subclass rule has a subtlety: code in a subclass in another package can access a protected member only through references of its own type or subtypes, not through an arbitrary parent-type reference.

~~~java
package animals;
public class Animal { protected int age; }

package pets;
public class Dog extends animals.Animal {
    void test(Dog d, animals.Animal a) {
        this.age = 3;   // allowed
        d.age = 4;      // allowed: Dog reference
        a.age = 5;      // compile error: Animal reference from another package
    }
}
~~~

Protected is part of a class's API for subclasses, so it's a commitment: changing a protected member can break subclasses you don't control. Use it deliberately, not as a halfway house between private and public.

## public

Public members are visible everywhere. Everything public becomes part of the contract other code depends on, and changing it later can break callers. Keep the public surface small: the methods others genuinely need.

## Top-level classes

A top-level class can only be `public` or package-private. A public class must be declared in a file with the same name, so each file has at most one public top-level class. Nested classes can use all four levels; a private nested class is a common way to hide a helper type, such as a linked list's Node.

## Overriding and access

An overriding method can't reduce visibility: if the parent method is public, the override must be public. Widening is allowed, such as overriding a protected method as public. This rule preserves substitutability: code that can call the parent method must be able to call the override.

## Access and constructors

Constructors take access modifiers too:

- a **private constructor** prevents outside instantiation, used by singletons, utility classes such as `Math`, and static factory methods
- a **protected constructor** lets subclasses create instances while preventing direct creation by unrelated code

## Modules add a layer

Since Java 9, the module system restricts access further. A public class in a package that its module doesn't **export** isn't accessible to other modules. This lets libraries hide internal packages completely, which earlier Java could only suggest by convention.

## Choosing a level

Start with the most restrictive level and open up only when needed:

1. Fields: private, almost always
2. Helper methods: private
3. Collaborators within a package: package-private
4. Extension points for subclasses: protected, deliberately
5. The intended API: public

## How interviewers test this

Expect the access table, "What is the default access level?", "Can a top-level class be private?" and protected subtleties. Recite the table, explain that package-private isn't project-wide, explain the protected-through-subclass-reference rule, and note that overrides can't narrow visibility.

lessons.title: Getters, Setters & Defensive Copying
lessons.description:
Think of Defensive Copying as a Security Desk at an Embassy (Certified Photocopy vs Original Document):
• If a visitor asks to view a secret government record, ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `understanding-encapsulation`, `access-modifiers-deep-dive`, and `stack-vs-heap-objects`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Defensive Copying as a **Security Desk at an Embassy (Certified Photocopy vs Original Document)**:
• If a visitor asks to view a secret government record, the security clerk does NOT hand over the original physical ledger book (**Internal Mutable Object**). If they did, the visitor could take a pen and scribble over the numbers.
• Instead, the clerk places the ledger on a Xerox machine, makes a certified duplicate photocopy (**Defensive Copy**), and hands the copy to the visitor. The visitor can shred or scribble on their copy without affecting the master ledger.

sections.title: The Mutable Reference Leak Bug
sections.content:
Making fields `private` is NOT enough if the field is a **Mutable Reference Type** (e.g. `java.util.Date`, `int[]`, `ArrayList`, custom objects)!
• If your getter returns `return this.birthDate;`, the caller receives a direct pointer to your internal heap object and can do: `person.getBirthDate().setYear(1900);`, silently corrupting your private field!

sections.title: The Mutable Reference Leak & The Defensive Copying Solution
sections.explanation: Defensive copying in both constructor and getter prevents external callers from ever obtaining a direct mutable pointer to internal state.

sections.title: Safe vs Vulnerable Return Types in Getters
rows: Safe to return directly (passed by value).
Safe to return directly (internal state cannot be modified).
MUST return a clone / defensive copy: `new Date(d.getTime())`.
MUST return a cloned copy: `return arr.clone();`.
Return unmodifiable wrapper: `Collections.unmodifiableList(list)` or defensive copy.

sections.title: Try It: Predict UnmodifiableList Mutation Result
sections.explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList throws UnsupportedOperationException if any code attempts to mutate it.

iterations.description: EmployeeRecord holds private Date object at 0x1111.
Allocates brand-new Date object on Heap at 0x2222 with identical timestamp.
Caller receives pointer to 0x2222.
Mutates 0x2222. Internal object at 0x1111 remains completely untouched and pristine.

sections.title: Getter and Setter Traps
items: **Returning Direct Array References**: Writing `public int[] getScores() { return this.scores; }` allows callers to do `scores[0] = 999;`, destroying encapsulation.
**Defending Only in Getters but Not Constructors**: If you make defensive copies in getters but forget constructor defensive copies, the caller can mutate the object passed to the constructor.

**Using Modern `java.time` Instead of `java.util.Date`**: In modern Java (Java 8+), use immutable `LocalDate`, `LocalTime`, and `Instant` instead of `java.util.Date` to eliminate the need for defensive date copying.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Is Returning Arrays Dangerous in Java?

traps.question: Why is `public int[] getNumbers() { return this.numbers; }` considered a critical security vulnerability even if `numbers` is declared `private final`?
traps.trap: Thinking `final` makes the array elements immutable.
traps.solution: `final int[] numbers` only makes the **reference pointer unmodifiable** (you cannot reassign `numbers = new int[5]`). However, the **array elements inside the heap object remain 100% mutable**! Any caller can do `obj.getNumbers()[0] = -1;` to corrupt internal state. Fix: `return this.numbers.clone();`.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How should a getter safely return a private `List<String>` without allowing callers to modify the internal list?
sections.explanation: `Collections.unmodifiableList()` wraps the internal list in a read-only decorator that throws an exception upon any mutation attempt.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Defensive copying creates isolated duplicates to prevent external reference mutation.
Always defend on BOTH input (constructors/setters) and output (getters) for mutable types.
Never return raw array references; return `arr.clone()`.
Use `Collections.unmodifiableList()` or immutable types (`LocalDate`, `String`, records) to simplify design.

sections.content: Next, we explore Encapsulation in Practice & Immutability, learning the 5 rules for creating 100% immutable classes and modern Java Records.

lessons.title: Encapsulation in Practice & Immutability
lessons.description:
Think of an Immutable Class as a Solid Gold Minted Coin:
• Once stamped at the mint (Constructor Initialization), its weight, purity, and engravings can never b...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `getters-and-setters-best-practices`, `access-modifiers-deep-dive`, and defensive copying.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of an Immutable Class as a **Solid Gold Minted Coin**:
• Once stamped at the mint (**Constructor Initialization**), its weight, purity, and engravings can never be altered by anyone.
• If you need a coin with a different value or date, you cannot melt and repaint the existing coin; you must mint a completely brand-new coin (**Creating a New Object**).
• Multiple people (threads) can hold and inspect the coin simultaneously with zero fear of data corruption or race conditions.

sections.title: The 5 Rules for Creating a 100% Immutable Class in Java
sections.content:
1. **Declare the class `final`**: Prevents subclasses from overriding methods and introducing mutable state.
2. **Make all fields `private` and `final`**: Enforces data hiding and prevents reassignment after construction.
3. **Do not provide any setter / mutator methods**.
4. **Initialize all fields in the constructor using Defensive Copies** for any mutable parameters.
5. **Return Defensive Copies (or unmodifiable views)** in all getter methods for any mutable fields.

sections.title: Classic Immutable Class vs Modern Java Record (Java 14+)
sections.explanation: Java 14+ Records eliminate boilerplate while providing immutable data carriers. List.copyOf() ensures the record's list cannot be modified.

sections.title: Encapsulation Architecture: Mutable Class vs Immutable Class vs Record
rows: Domain Value Objects, Security Tokens, Cache Keys

sections.title: Try It: Predict Record Immutability
sections.explanation: Records provide value-based equality out of the box. p1.equals(p2) is true because both have identical components (5, 10).

sections.title: Encapsulation in JDK: How `java.util.ArrayList` Maintains Internal Invariants

variables.Internal State: private Object[] elementData; private int size = 0;

iterations.description: ArrayList stores elements in private heap array.
get() performs bounds checking before accessing elementData.
add() automatically handles dynamic array reallocation behind the scenes.

variables.Result: Client sees clean O(1) list interface

iterations.description: Encapsulation achieves full separation between API interface and internal memory management.

sections.title: Common Immutability Mistakes
items: **Omitting the `final` Keyword on Class**: If an immutable class is not `final`, a subclass could override getters to return mutable static fields.
**Assuming `List.of()` or `Arrays.asList()` Can Be Mutated**: `List.of()` creates an immutable list; calling `.add()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.
**Modifying Fields via Reflection**: While reflection can technically override private fields, it violates JVM safety and will fail under Java Platform Module System (JPMS) strong encapsulation.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Is `String` Immutable in Java?

traps.question: Why was `java.lang.String` designed to be completely immutable in Java?
traps.trap: Only giving a single reason like 'security'.
traps.solution:
1. **String Constant Pool (SCP)**: Immutability allows multiple variables to share the exact same string literal in the SCP, saving massive amounts of Heap memory.
2. **Security & Parameter Integrity**: Strings are used for database connection URLs, file paths, and network sockets. If String were mutable, a malicious thread could change the file path between verification and file opening (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition).
3. **Thread Safety**: Immutable strings can be shared across threads with zero synchronization overhead.
4. **Hash Code Caching**: String caches its `hashCode` during creation, making HashMap and HashSet key lookups extremely fast.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which of the following is NOT required to make a custom Java class fully immutable?
options: Make all fields private and final
Declare the class `final` so it cannot be extended
sections.explanation: Implementing `Serializable` is for object persistence/serialization, not a requirement for immutability.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Immutable classes cannot be modified after construction and are inherently thread-safe.
Follow the 5 rules: `final class`, `private final fields`, no setters, constructor defensive copies, getter defensive copies.
Java 14+ Records (`record`) provide concise immutable data carriers with auto-generated getters, `equals`, and `hashCode`.
`String` immutability powers the String Constant Pool, thread safety, and secure API parameters.

lessons.title: What is a Constructor? Object Initialization
lessons.description:
Think of a Constructor as a Quality-Control Assembly Inspector at a Car Factory:
• When a new car rolls off the welding robots (new Car()), it cannot be driven ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `classes-and-objects`, `fields-and-methods`, and the `new` keyword.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of a Constructor as a **Quality-Control Assembly Inspector at a Car Factory**:
• When a new car rolls off the welding robots (`new Car()`), it cannot be driven onto public roads until the commissioning inspector:
  1. Installs the steering wheel and odometer (`field initialization`).
  2. Fills the engine with oil and brake fluid (`mandatory invariant setup`).
  3. Validates the VIN number (`parameter validation`).
• The constructor is the mandatory gateway code that runs automatically every time an object is born, guaranteeing it starts in a valid, usable state.

sections.title: The 3 Inviolable Rules of Java Constructors
sections.content:
1. **Exact Name Match**: A constructor MUST have the exact same identifier name as its enclosing class (case-sensitive).
2. **NO Return Type**: A constructor must NOT declare any return type—not even `void`!
3. **Invoked via `new`**: A constructor cannot be called like a standard method; it is executed automatically by the JVM during object instantiation.

sections.title: Constructor Anatomy vs Regular Method
sections.explanation: The constructor BankCustomer(String, int) sets fields and computes isVerified upon creation, ensuring c1 is ready for immediate use.

sections.title: Constructor vs Regular Method: Comparison
rows: Initialize state and invariants of a new object.
Perform operations, business logic, or transformations.
MUST declare a return type (`void`, `int`, `String`, etc.).
Invoked implicitly by JVM via `new` operator.
Constructors are NOT inherited by subclasses.
Methods are inherited by subclasses (unless private).

sections.title: Try It: The Phantom Method Trap
sections.explanation: Adding 'void' turned TrapDemo() into a regular method. When 'new TrapDemo()' ran, it executed the default constructor, leaving x = 10.

iterations.description: JVM allocates contiguous memory for object header + fields on Heap.
JVM sets all instance fields to default zero/null values.
Executes Object superclass constructor.
Executes constructor body statements.
Assigns completed object pointer to stack reference variable.

sections.title: Common Constructor Traps
items: **Declaring `void` on Constructor**: Writing `public void Car() {}` does NOT produce a compiler error; it secretly creates a regular method that is never called during `new Car()`!
**Overriding Constructors**: Constructors cannot be overridden because they belong strictly to the enclosing class and are not inherited.
**Throwing Exceptions Without Cleanup**: Throwing exceptions inside constructors aborts object creation; partially initialized state is discarded for garbage collection.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can a Constructor be Marked `private`?

traps.question: Can a constructor be declared with the `private` access modifier? What is the practical architectural use case?
traps.trap: Thinking private constructors are useless because no objects could ever be created.
traps.solution:
YES, **private constructors are widely used in professional architecture**:
1. **Singleton Pattern**: Restricts instantiation so only one global instance can be created internally (e.g. `DatabaseConnection.getInstance()`).
2. **Utility / Helper Classes**: Prevents instantiating purely static classes (e.g. `java.lang.Math`, `java.util.Collections`).
3. **Factory Method Pattern**: Forces callers to use named static factory methods (e.g. `ComplexNumber.fromCartesian(x, y)`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What happens if you write `public void Point(int x, int y)` in a class named `Point`?
options: Compilation error: constructors cannot have parameters
It defines a valid constructor that returns void
It defines a regular member method named Point; it is NOT a constructor
Throws a RuntimeException upon class loading
sections.explanation: Declaring a return type (like `void`) causes the Java compiler to treat it as a regular instance method, not a constructor.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Constructors initialize state and enforce invariants during object instantiation.
Must match the class name exactly and cannot declare any return type.
Executed automatically during the `new` lifecycle.
Private constructors are used in Singletons, utility classes, and static factories.

content.theory:
A constructor is a special block of code that runs when an object is created, putting it into a valid starting state. Good constructors make it impossible to create a half-initialized or invalid object. This lesson explains how constructors differ from methods, what happens step by step during object creation, how field initializers and initializer blocks fit in, and how to design constructors that protect invariants.

## Constructor syntax

A constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even `void`:

~~~java
public class Student {
    private final String name;
    private final int rollNo;

    public Student(String name, int rollNo) {
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
        this.name = name;
        this.rollNo = rollNo;
    }
}

Student s = new Student("Asha", 42);
~~~

If you add a return type, it's no longer a constructor but an ordinary method that happens to share the class name, which compiles and causes confusing bugs.

## Constructors versus methods

| | Constructor | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Name | Same as the class | Any valid name |
| Return type | None | Required (or void) |
| Called | Automatically by `new` | Explicitly by name |
| Inherited | No | Yes (unless private or static) |
| Purpose | Initialize a new object | Perform behaviour |

Constructors aren't members in the inheritance sense: a subclass doesn't inherit its parent's constructors, though it calls one through `super(...)`.

## What happens during new

Creating an object runs these steps in order:

1. Memory is allocated on the heap, and every field gets its default value (0, false, null)
2. The constructor is called; its first action is calling a parent constructor, explicitly with `super(...)` or implicitly with `super()`, all the way up to `Object`
3. After the parent constructor returns, this class's **field initializers** and **instance initializer blocks** run, in the order they appear in the source
4. The rest of the constructor body runs
5. `new` returns the reference

Knowing this order explains output questions with print statements in constructors, initializers and parent classes.

## Field initializers and initializer blocks

Fields can be initialized where they're declared, and instance initializer blocks run code for every constructor:

~~~java
public class Counter {
    private int count = 10;                 // field initializer
    private final List<String> log;

    {                                       // instance initializer block
        log = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    public Counter() {
        count++;                            // runs after the initializer: count becomes 11
    }
}
~~~

Initializer blocks are rare in modern code; field initializers or a shared private method are clearer. Static initializer blocks, marked `static { }`, run once when the class is first loaded, not per object.

## Constructors should establish invariants

A constructor's main job is making sure every object starts valid:

- require all mandatory data as parameters, rather than allowing "empty" objects to be filled in later
- validate arguments and throw `IllegalArgumentException` for bad input
- initialize every final field, which the compiler enforces

If a constructor throws, no object is created, and the caller never receives a reference to invalid data.

## Avoid heavy work and overridable calls

Constructors should be quick and predictable. Avoid:

- **Expensive work** such as network calls or reading large files: callers expect `new` to be cheap, and failures are harder to handle. Use a factory method or a separate `load()` step
- **Calling overridable methods**: if a constructor calls a method that a subclass overrides, the override runs before the subclass's own fields are initialized, and may see null or zero values
- **Leaking this**: passing the half-built object to other code, as the this keyword lesson explains

## Static factory methods

An alternative to public constructors is a static method that returns an instance:

~~~java
public static Student of(String name, int rollNo) { return new Student(name, rollNo); }
~~~

Factories can have descriptive names (`LocalDate.of`, `List.of`), return cached instances, or return a subtype. Many JDK APIs prefer them for these reasons.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a constructor?", "Constructor vs method?", "Can a constructor be private?" and output questions about initialization order. Give the comparison table, walk through the five creation steps including the implicit `super()`, explain that private constructors enable singletons and factories, and warn against calling overridable methods from constructors.

lessons.title: Default vs Parameterized Constructors
lessons.description:
Think of Constructor Types as Ordering Furniture (Standard Catalog vs Custom-Built):
• The Default Constructor (Standard Catalog): You order "Table 101" with ze...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-a-constructor`, field initializations, and method signatures.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Constructor Types as **Ordering Furniture (Standard Catalog vs Custom-Built)**:
• **The Default Constructor (Standard Catalog)**: You order "Table #101" with zero custom options (`new Table()`). The factory builds it using standard factory defaults (Plain wood, 4 standard legs).
• **The Parameterized Constructor (Custom Commission)**: You order "Table #101" with explicit dimensions and finishes (`new Table("Mahogany", 6, true)`). You specify the exact state at the moment of creation.

sections.title: The Law of the Disappearing Default Constructor
sections.content:
⚠️ **CRITICAL JAVA RULE**: If you write **ZERO** constructors in your class, the Java compiler automatically synthesizes an empty, no-argument **Default Constructor** for you.
• HOWEVER, the instant you define even **ONE** custom parameterized constructor, the compiler **immediately revokes and deletes the automatic default constructor**!

sections.title: The Disappearing Default Constructor in Action
sections.explanation: In CustomProduct, if we did not manually write 'public CustomProduct()', calling 'new CustomProduct()' would fail with a compile error.

sections.title: Default Constructor vs Explicit No-Arg vs Parameterized
rows: ONLY when NO other constructors exist in source code.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Missing Constructor Error
sections.explanation: Because Item defined a parameterized constructor, the default no-arg constructor ceased to exist. Only 'new Item("Coffee")' compiles.

iterations.description: Zero constructors written -> Compiler injects 'public A() { super(); }'.
One parameterized constructor written -> Compiler generates NOTHING extra. B has only B(int).
Both written explicitly -> C has both no-arg and parameterized constructors available.

sections.title: Enterprise Framework Reflection Warning
items: **Framework Crash (Spring / Hibernate / Jackson)**: ORM and JSON serialization libraries use Java Reflection to instantiate objects using the no-arg constructor (`Class.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`). If you create a parameterized constructor and forget to write an explicit no-arg constructor, serialization will crash with `NoSuchMethodException`.

**Subclass Invariant Failure**: Subclass constructors implicitly call `super()`. If the parent class loses its no-arg constructor, all child classes will fail to compile unless they explicitly call `super(args)`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Does the JVM Provide a Default Constructor?

traps.question: Does the JVM at runtime provide a default constructor if none is present in the `.class` bytecode file?
traps.trap: Confusing the JVM runtime with the javac compiler.
traps.solution: NO! The **JVM does not generate constructors**. It is the **Java Compiler (`javac`)** at compile time that inserts the default constructor into the `.class` bytecode file. If the compiler does not insert it (because another constructor was written), the bytecode contains no default constructor, and attempting to call one throws a compile error.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: When does the Java compiler automatically generate a default no-argument constructor for a class?
options: Only when the class is marked public
Only when the programmer has not declared ANY constructor in the class
Only when the class implements an interface
sections.explanation: The compiler provides a default no-argument constructor if and only if the class contains zero explicitly written constructors.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: The compiler synthesizes a no-arg constructor only when no constructors are written.
Declaring any custom constructor deletes the automatic default constructor.
Always include an explicit no-arg constructor in classes used with frameworks (Spring, JPA, Jackson).
Parameterized constructors guarantee mandatory state is supplied at creation time.

lessons.title: Constructor Overloading & Multiple Initialization Paths
lessons.description:
Think of Constructor Overloading as Multiple Ticket Options for an Airline Flight:
• Economy Ticket: new FlightBooking("Alice") → Provides name; seat and m...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `default-vs-parameterized-constructors`, `the-this-keyword`, and method overloading basics.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Constructor Overloading as **Multiple Ticket Options for an Airline Flight**:
• **Economy Ticket**: `new FlightBooking("Alice")` → Provides name; seat and meals are assigned standard defaults.
• **Business Ticket**: `new FlightBooking("Bob", "Seat 2A")` → Specifies name and seat.
• **First-Class Ticket**: `new FlightBooking("Charlie", "Seat 1A", "Vegan", true)` → Specifies full custom configuration.
• All ticket tiers ultimately create a valid `FlightBooking` object on the same plane, but each offers a tailored initialization pathway.

sections.title: Constructor Overloading Rules
sections.content:
A class can have multiple constructors as long as their **parameter lists differ in**:
1. **Number of parameters** (e.g. 1 param vs 3 params).
2. **Data types of parameters** (e.g. `int` vs `String`).
3. **Order of parameter types** (e.g. `(int, String)` vs `(String, int)`).
*Note: Constructors do not have return types, so return type is never a factor.*

sections.title: Overloaded Constructors with Master Canonical Delegation
sections.explanation: The Master Constructor Pattern centralizes all validation logic in one place. Overloaded constructors delegate defaults using this(...) without duplicating code.

sections.title: Constructor Overloading Valid vs Invalid Signatures
rows: Swapped parameter order (`int, String` vs `String, int`).
Identical parameter types `(String, int)` (only variable names changed).

sections.title: Try It: Predict Constructor Resolution
sections.explanation: The compiler matches constructor signatures based on exact parameter types: int -> DOUBLE -> STRING.

iterations.description: Enters 1-arg constructor Book(String).
Delegates immediately to 4-arg master constructor.
Runs centralized validation and initializes all 4 fields.

variables.Completion: Returns to 1-arg constructor -> Returns to caller

iterations.description: Object fully initialized and delivered to main().

sections.title: Constructor Overloading Traps
items: **Duplicating Validation Code**: Writing validation logic inside every constructor creates maintenance bugs; always delegate to a single master constructor using `this(...)`.
**Ambiguous Overloading with `null`**: If you have `User(String s)` and `User(Integer i)`, calling `new User(null)` causes a compile error: *reference to User is ambiguous*.
**Telescoping Constructor Anti-Pattern**: Having 8 overloaded constructors with dozens of optional parameters becomes unreadable. Use the **Builder Pattern** for complex objects.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can Constructors Be Overridden?

traps.question: Can a constructor be overloaded in Java? Can a constructor be overridden?
traps.trap: Saying yes to both.
traps.solution:
• **Overloaded**: **YES!** A class can have many constructors with different parameter signatures.
• **Overridden**: **NO!** Method overriding applies strictly to inherited methods. Because constructors are NOT inherited by subclasses and have names matching their specific class, a subclass can never override a parent constructor.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Can two constructors in the same class have the signatures `MyClass(int a, String b)` and `MyClass(int count, String name)`?
options: Yes, because the parameter names are different
No, because the parameter type sequence (int, String) is identical, causing a duplicate constructor error
Yes, if one is public and the other is private
Yes, if they have different annotations
sections.explanation: Java differentiates overloaded methods and constructors strictly by parameter types, order, and count—parameter variable names are completely ignored.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Constructor overloading provides multiple initialization options for callers.
Overloads must differ in parameter type, count, or sequence.
Use the Master Canonical Constructor pattern with `this(...)` to avoid duplicate validation logic.
Constructors can be overloaded but NEVER overridden.

lessons.title: Constructor Chaining: `this()` and `super()`
lessons.description:
Think of Constructor Chaining as Constructing a Skyscraper Floor by Floor:
• You cannot build the 10th floor penthouse (Subclass) until the ground foundation an...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `the-this-keyword`, `constructor-overloading`, and basic class inheritance (`extends`).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Constructor Chaining as **Constructing a Skyscraper Floor by Floor**:
• You cannot build the 10th floor penthouse (**Subclass**) until the ground foundation and structural columns (**Superclass**) are completely poured and set.
• When a child constructor runs, its very first action is to call up to its parent (`super()`), which calls its grandparent, all the way up to `java.lang.Object`.
• The foundations initialize top-down ($Object \to Parent \to Child$), ensuring the child inherits a rock-solid, fully initialized base.

sections.title: The Inviolable First-Statement Rule
sections.content:
In Java, a constructor's first statement MUST be either:
1. `this(...)`: To call another constructor in the **same class**.
2. `super(...)`: To call a constructor in the **direct superclass**.
• If you do not explicitly write either, the Java compiler automatically inserts `super();` as the first statement for you!

sections.title: Constructor Chaining in an Inheritance Hierarchy
sections.explanation: Calling new GamingLaptop("Asus") delegates via this() to GamingLaptop(3-args) -> calls super() to Computer -> calls super() to Device -> outputs 1, 2, 3 in hierarchical order.

sections.title: `this()` vs `super()` Constructor Invocations
rows: Calls another constructor in the SAME class.
Calls a constructor in the DIRECT SUPERCLASS.
MUST be the 1st statement in constructor.
MUST be the 1st statement in constructor.
NO (Cannot have both `this()` and `super()` on line 1).
NO (Cannot have both `this()` and `super()` on line 1).
Compiler inserts `super();` automatically if neither is present.
Recursive chaining (`A -> B -> A`) is a compile error.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Chaining Order
sections.explanation: new Derived() calls this(5) -> Derived(5) calls implicit super() -> Base() prints 'A ' -> Derived(5) prints 'C ' -> Derived() prints 'B '.

iterations.description: Invokes 1-arg constructor. Executes this("Asus", 16, "RTX 4060").
Executes super("Asus", 16) calling Computer constructor.
Executes super("Asus") calling Device constructor.
Calls Object() -> Sets brand="Asus" -> Prints '1. Device'.
Sets ramGB=16 -> Prints '2. Computer'.
Sets gpuModel="RTX 4060" -> Prints '3. GamingLaptop'.

sections.title: Common Constructor Chaining Traps
items: **Writing Both `this()` and `super()`**: Putting both `this("default");` and `super();` in the same constructor is a compile error because both demand to be the first statement.

**Parent Missing No-Arg Constructor**: If a superclass defines `Parent(int x)` without a no-arg constructor, child classes with default constructors will fail to compile because the compiler's implicit `super();` call finds no match.

**Accessing Instance Members Inside `this()` / `super()` arguments**: You cannot pass instance fields or call instance methods as arguments to `this(field)` or `super(method())` because the object has not finished being constructed.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Implicit `super()` and Compilation Failures

traps.trap: Thinking Truck has a syntax error in its constructor.
traps.solution: Because `Truck()` does not explicitly call `super(...)`, the compiler automatically inserts `super();` on line 1. However, `Vehicle` has ONLY a parameterized constructor `Vehicle(String)` and NO no-arg constructor `Vehicle()`. The implicit `super();` fails to find a matching constructor in `Vehicle`, producing a compile error: *constructor Vehicle in class Vehicle cannot be applied to given types*. Fix: Write `Truck() { super("Heavy"); }` or add `Vehicle() {}`.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What statement does the Java compiler automatically insert on line 1 of a constructor if you write neither `this(...)` nor `super(...)`?
sections.explanation: The compiler automatically inserts an explicit zero-argument `super();` call to invoke the parent class's no-argument constructor.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `this(...)` delegates to another constructor in the same class; `super(...)` invokes the parent constructor.
Either `this(...)` or `super(...)` must be the absolute first statement in any constructor body.
Constructors initialize hierarchical state top-down from `Object` down to the leaf subclass.
If a parent class has no zero-arg constructor, child constructors MUST explicitly call `super(args)`.

lessons.title: Copy Constructors & Object Cloning
lessons.description:
Think of Copying Objects as Cloning an Experimental Laboratory Drone:
• Shallow Copy (Shared Remote Control): You assemble a second drone frame, but you wire bo...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `stack-vs-heap-objects`, `getters-and-setters-best-practices`, and `constructor-overloading`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Copying Objects as **Cloning an Experimental Laboratory Drone**:
• **Shallow Copy (Shared Remote Control)**: You assemble a second drone frame, but you wire both drones to the exact same shared lithium battery pack (**Shared Heap Object**). If Drone 1 discharges the battery, Drone 2 immediately loses power and crashes.
• **Deep Copy (Complete Independent Replica)**: You manufacture an entirely new drone frame AND build a brand-new, isolated lithium battery pack for it. Drone 1 and Drone 2 can fly, charge, and crash independently without affecting each other.

sections.title: What is a Copy Constructor?
Shallow Copy Vulnerability vs Deep Copy Constructor
sections.explanation: Because Employee(Employee other) deep-copied both address and projects, changing emp2 does not corrupt emp1.

sections.title: Copy Constructors vs `Object.clone()`
rows: ❌ Bypasses constructors completely via native JVM magic.
⚠️ Deprecated / Avoid due to architectural flaws.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Shallow vs Deep Copy Output
sections.explanation: Because t2 performed a deep copy of the members list, adding 'Dev2' to t2 leaves t1 with size 1 and t2 with size 2.

sections.title: Memory Trace: Deep Copy Constructor Allocation

iterations.description: Original employee graph in memory.
Allocates brand-new Employee container at 0x5000.
Allocates brand-new Address object at 0x6000.
Allocates brand-new ArrayList object at 0x7000.

variables.Isolation Verification: 0x5000 has zero shared mutable pointers with 0x1000

iterations.description: Full independent isolation achieved.

sections.title: Common Copying Mistakes
items: **Shallow Copying Collections**: Doing `this.list = other.list;` copies the reference pointer, meaning both objects share the exact same list on the Heap.

**Using `Object.clone()` in New Code**: `Object.clone()` has numerous design flaws (bypasses constructors, requires Cloneable interface, shallow by default). Prefer Copy Constructors or Static Factory Methods (`User.copyOf(other)`).
**Circular References in Deep Copying**: If Object A points to Object B and Object B points to Object A, a naive deep copy constructor will enter infinite recursion and throw `StackOverflowError`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why is `Object.clone()` Considered Broken in Java?

traps.question: Why do senior Java architects and authors like Joshua Bloch advise against implementing `Cloneable` and using `Object.clone()`?
traps.trap: Only stating that it creates shallow copies.
traps.solution:
1. **Bypasses Constructors**: `clone()` creates objects without invoking any constructor, violating language consistency and invariant checks.
2. **Incompatible with `final` Fields**: `clone()` cannot assign new copies to `final` fields because `final` fields can only be initialized in constructors or declarations.
3. **Checked Exception Overhead**: Declares checked `CloneNotSupportedException`.
4. **Unsafe Interface Design**: `Cloneable` is a marker interface that does not even declare the `clone()` method (it remains protected in `Object`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the primary difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy of an object?
options: Shallow copy copies primitives; deep copy does not
Shallow copy duplicates nested objects; deep copy shares references
Shallow copy copies reference pointers (sharing nested objects); deep copy recursively duplicates nested objects into new memory
Deep copy only works with String objects
sections.explanation: A shallow copy shares nested heap references, whereas a deep copy creates distinct, independent copies of all nested mutable objects.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Copy Constructors create a new instance initialized from an existing instance.
Deep copies recursively allocate new objects for all mutable nested fields to prevent reference leaking.
Immutable fields (`String`, primitives) are safe to copy directly by reference/value.
Copy Constructors and Static Factory Methods are preferred over Java's legacy `Cloneable` / `clone()`.

lessons.title: What is Inheritance? The 'Is-A' Relationship
lessons.description:
Think of Inheritance as Biological Genetics & Smartphone Lineage:
• The Parent Class (Generic Smartphone): Defines fundamental genetic traits: touch screen, cel...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `classes-and-objects`, `access-modifiers-deep-dive`, and constructors.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Inheritance as **Biological Genetics & Smartphone Lineage**:
• **The Parent Class (Generic Smartphone)**: Defines fundamental genetic traits: touch screen, cellular radio, battery management, and an operating system kernel.
• **The Child Class (iPhone 15 Pro)**: Inherits all base smartphone traits automatically without re-inventing the wheel, while adding specialized features: titanium frame, satellite SOS, and an action button.
• An iPhone 15 Pro **"Is-A"** Smartphone. Any code designed to work with a Smartphone will seamlessly accept an iPhone 15 Pro.

sections.title: The 'Is-A' Relationship vs 'Has-A' Composition
sections.content:
• **Inheritance ('Is-A')**: A Dog *is-a* Mammal; a Car *is-a* Vehicle (`class Car extends Vehicle`). Use when the child is a true specialized subtype of the parent.
• **Composition ('Has-A')**: A Car *has-an* Engine (`class Car { private Engine engine; }`). Use when an object contains another object as a component part.
⭐ **Industry Best Practice**: *Favor Composition over Inheritance* unless a genuine, immutable 'Is-A' taxonomic relationship exists.

sections.title: Inheritance in Action: Vehicle & ElectricCar Hierarchy
sections.explanation: ElectricCar extends Vehicle, instantly inheriting brand, maxSpeed, startEngine(), and displaySpecs() without writing duplicate code.

sections.title: Inheritance ('Is-A') vs Composition ('Has-A')
rows: Tight coupling (Child depends on parent implementation)
Loose coupling (Components can be swapped at runtime)
Inherits all non-private fields and methods automatically
Reuses code by delegating method calls to internal objects
Use when child satisfies Liskov Substitution Principle
Preferred standard for 90% of software engineering design

sections.title: Try It: Predict Inherited Method Output
sections.explanation: Dog inherits speak() from Animal and defines bark(). Calling both outputs 'Sound Woof! '.

iterations.description: Allocates single contiguous heap object containing both Vehicle fields (brand, maxSpeed) and ElectricCar fields (batteryKWh).
JVM checks ElectricCar class for displaySpecs(); not found, traverses up to Vehicle superclass.
Runs inherited method using the current object's fields.
JVM finds method directly on ElectricCar subclass and executes immediately.

sections.title: Inheritance Traps to Avoid
items: **Inheriting for Code Reuse Without 'Is-A'**: Extending a class just to grab a couple of helper methods (e.g. `Stack extends Vector` in legacy Java) is an architectural flaw; use Composition instead.

**Assuming Private Fields are Inaccessible in Memory**: Private superclass fields ARE present in the heap object payload, but child class code cannot access them directly by name (must use inherited getters/setters).
**Circular Inheritance**: Class A extending Class B while Class B extends Class A causes a compile error: *cyclic inheritance involving A*.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Are Constructors and Private Members Inherited?

traps.question: Are constructors, private fields, and private methods of a superclass inherited by its subclass in Java?
traps.trap: Saying yes to all, or saying private fields don't exist in the child object.
traps.solution:
• **Constructors**: **NEVER inherited**. A child class must define its own constructors (which invoke parent constructors via `super()`).
• **Private Members**: **NOT inherited in scope**. The child class cannot access `private` fields/methods directly by name. However, the private fields **DO exist in memory inside the child object's heap footprint**, accessible indirectly through inherited public/protected methods.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which keyword is used in Java to establish class inheritance?
sections.explanation: In Java, the `extends` keyword is used to inherit from a superclass (e.g. `class Dog extends Animal`). `implements` is used for interfaces.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Inheritance models an 'Is-A' hierarchy using the `extends` keyword.
Subclasses inherit all public and protected fields and methods from the superclass.
Constructors and private members are not inherited.
Favor Composition ('Has-A') over Inheritance ('Is-A') for flexible, loosely coupled architecture.

sections.title: Connection to Next Lesson
sections.content: Next, we explore Types of Inheritance & The Diamond Problem, learning why Java supports single and multilevel inheritance but forbids multiple class inheritance.

content.theory:
Inheritance lets one class build on another: a subclass receives the fields and methods of its superclass and adds or changes behaviour. It models "is-a" relationships, such as a SavingsAccount is an Account, and enables polymorphism. Used carelessly, it also creates some of the most rigid code in object-oriented systems. This lesson explains what inheritance gives you, what it doesn't, the is-a test, and why many designers prefer composition.

## The extends keyword

~~~java
public class Account {
    protected double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) { balance += amount; }
    public double getBalance() { return balance; }
}

public class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    private final double rate;

    public SavingsAccount(double rate) { this.rate = rate; }

    public void addInterest() { deposit(balance * rate); }
}
~~~

A SavingsAccount object has everything an Account has, plus `rate` and `addInterest`. Code written once in Account is reused by every subclass.

## What is inherited

A subclass inherits:

- public and protected fields and methods
- package-private members, if the subclass is in the same package

It does **not** inherit:

- **constructors**: each class declares its own and calls a parent constructor with `super(...)`
- **private members** in a usable way: the fields exist inside the object, but subclass code can't name them directly
- **static members** in the polymorphic sense: they're accessible through the subclass, but they're hidden, not overridden

## The is-a test

Inheritance should model a true "is-a" relationship, where every subclass object can stand in for a superclass object anywhere. A Dog is an Animal; a Car is a Vehicle. Failing the test produces trouble:

- a `Stack extends ArrayList` inherits `add(index, element)`, which lets callers insert into the middle of a stack, breaking its rules. Java's own `java.util.Stack extends Vector` has this flaw
- a `Square extends Rectangle` breaks when code sets width and height independently, which the SOLID module discusses as the Liskov substitution principle

If a subclass needs to disable or contradict inherited behaviour, the relationship probably isn't is-a.

## Inheritance versus composition

**Composition** means a class holds a reference to another object and delegates to it, a "has-a" relationship:

~~~java
public class Car {
    private final Engine engine;          // Car has an Engine
    public void start() { engine.ignite(); }
}
~~~

| | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship | is-a | has-a |
| Coupling | Tight: subclass depends on parent internals | Loose: depends only on the public API |
| Flexibility | Fixed at compile time | Parts can be swapped at runtime |
| Exposure | Subclass inherits the whole parent API | Expose only what you choose |

"Favour composition over inheritance" is a widely followed guideline from the Gang of Four and Effective Java. Inheritance remains the right tool for genuine type hierarchies, especially when designed for extension, as with abstract base classes.

## The fragile base class problem

Subclasses depend on the parent's implementation details, not only its public contract. Suppose a parent's `addAll` calls `add` internally, and a subclass overrides `add` to count insertions. If the parent later changes `addAll` to stop calling `add`, the subclass's count breaks, though the subclass didn't change. Changes to a base class can silently break subclasses, which is why classes not designed for extension are often marked `final`.

## Single inheritance of classes

A Java class extends exactly one class. Every class without an explicit `extends` extends `Object`, so all classes form a single tree rooted at Object. Multiple inheritance of type comes through interfaces, which a class can implement in any number. The types of inheritance lesson explains why Java made this choice.

## Benefits worth naming

- **Code reuse**: shared behaviour lives in one place
- **Polymorphism**: code written against the parent type works with every subclass
- **Hierarchical modelling**: domain concepts with real is-a structure map naturally onto class trees

## When to reach for inheritance

Use it when the is-a relationship is real and stable, the parent is designed for extension (documented, with protected hooks), and you need polymorphic substitution. Otherwise, start with composition and an interface; you can always introduce a base class later if repetition appears.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is inheritance?", "What isn't inherited?" and "Composition vs inheritance?" Define is-a, list constructors and private members as not inherited, give the Stack-extends-Vector example of misuse, and explain why composition is usually preferred for flexibility.

lessons.title: Types of Inheritance & The Diamond Problem
lessons.description:
Think of Inheritance Topologies as Organizational Hierarchy Trees vs The Deadly Two-Boss Dilemma:
• Single Inheritance (One Direct Manager): You report to one l...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-inheritance`, class definitions, and method dispatch.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Inheritance Topologies as **Organizational Hierarchy Trees vs The Deadly Two-Boss Dilemma**:
• **Single Inheritance (One Direct Manager)**: You report to one lead engineer. Instructions are 100% clear.
• **Multilevel Inheritance (Chain of Command)**: Junior Dev → Senior Dev → Tech Lead → CTO. Orders flow cleanly down the chain.
• **Multiple Inheritance with Classes (The Two-Boss Disaster / The Diamond Problem)**: You report simultaneously to Manager A and Manager B. Manager A tells you to "Delete the database (`reset()`); Manager B tells you to "Keep the database (`reset()`). When you are told `reset()`, **WHICH manager's code should you execute?** Java bans multiple class inheritance to prevent this exact chaos.

sections.title: The 5 Inheritance Topologies
sections.content:
1. **Single Inheritance**: Class B extends Class A (✅ Supported in Java).
2. **Multilevel Inheritance**: Class C extends Class B, which extends Class A (✅ Supported in Java).
3. **Hierarchical Inheritance**: Class B and Class C both extend Class A (✅ Supported in Java).
4. **Multiple Inheritance**: Class C extends Class A and Class B (❌ Forbidden with Classes in Java; ✅ Allowed via Interfaces).
5. **Hybrid Inheritance**: Combination of multiple types (❌ Forbidden with Classes; ✅ Allowed via Interfaces).

sections.title: Inheritance Depth & Fragile Base Class Pitfall
items: **Fragile Base Class Problem**: Creating deep multilevel chains (e.g. 6 tiers: `A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F`) means modifying a single line in Class A can unexpectedly break subtle invariants in Class F.
**Attempting `class C extends A, B`**: Causes compile error: *'{' expected* (Java syntax does not allow comma-separated superclasses).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Does Java Allow Multiple Interface Inheritance but Not Multiple Class Inheritance?

traps.question: Why does Java forbid multiple inheritance with classes, but allows a class to implement multiple interfaces (`implements A, B`)?
traps.trap: Saying interfaces cannot have conflicting methods.
traps.solution:
1. **State Ambiguity (Instance Variables)**: Classes have instance state (fields). If Class B and Class C both inherit a field `int count` from Class A, and Class D extends B and C, Class D would have two conflicting copies of `count` in its heap layout.
2. **Pure Interface Contracts**: Interfaces historically contained no state and no method bodies, meaning if Interface A and Interface B both declared `void run()`, the implementing Class C supplied the single concrete body, eliminating all ambiguity.
3. **Interface Default Methods (Java 8+)**: If Interface A and Interface B both define identical `default void run()`, Java forces the programmer to explicitly resolve the conflict via `InterfaceA.super.run()` or override it, preventing silent ambiguity.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the primary reason Java disallows multiple inheritance with classes?
options: To prevent the compiler from taking more than 5 seconds
To avoid the Diamond Problem and state/method ambiguity
Because Java does not have interfaces
sections.explanation: Multiple inheritance with classes introduces the Diamond Problem, where method resolution and instance state become ambiguous between duplicate parent branches.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Java supports Single, Multilevel, and Hierarchical class inheritance.
Java disallows Multiple and Hybrid inheritance with classes to eliminate the Diamond Problem.
Multiple inheritance is achieved safely in Java through Interfaces (`implements A, B`).
Keep class hierarchies shallow (2-3 levels) to avoid the Fragile Base Class problem.

sections.content:
1. **Invoking Superclass Methods**: Calling a parent method that was overridden in the child class (`super.displayDetails()`).
2. **Accessing Shadowed Superclass Fields**: Referencing a parent field when the child class declares a field with the exact same identifier (`super.maxSpeed`).
3. **Invoking Superclass Constructors**: Delegating initialization to the parent constructor (`super(name, age)`), which must be line 1 of the child constructor.
