sections.title: Common `super` Traps
items: **Attempting `super.super.method()`**: You CANNOT chain `super.super`. Java strictly enforces that a subclass can only see its direct immediate parent to preserve encapsulation boundaries.

**Using `super` in a `static` Method**: `super` relies on the current heap object instance; calling `super.print()` inside `public static void main` causes a compile error: *non-static variable super cannot be referenced from a static context*.
**Field Shadowing Anti-Pattern**: Re-declaring a field with the exact same name in a child class creates confusing bugs; prefer giving fields unique names or keeping them private.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can You Access Grandparent Methods via `super.super`?

traps.question: Is `super.super.method()` valid syntax in Java to bypass an immediate parent's overridden method and call the grandparent's version?
traps.trap: Assuming Java allows multi-level super navigation like C++ scope resolution.
traps.solution: NO! **`super.super` is a compile-time syntax error in Java**. The language designers intentionally banned `super.super` to prevent child classes from violating the encapsulation invariants established by the immediate parent class.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How can a subclass method invoke its parent's version of an overridden method named `calculate()`?
sections.explanation: `super.calculate()` explicitly directs the JVM to invoke the parent class implementation of `calculate()`, bypassing the child's override.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `super` references the immediate superclass part of the current object.
Used to call overridden parent methods: `super.method()`.
Used to access shadowed parent fields: `super.field`.
Used in constructor chaining: `super(args)` on line 1.
`super.super` is illegal in Java.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-inheritance`, `super-keyword`, and method signatures.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Method Overriding as **Upgrading a Smartphone App with a Specialized Driver**:
• The base operating system defines a universal button: **"Navigate to Work"** (`mapApp.navigate()`).
• If you are driving a gasoline car, the navigation app calculates standard highway routes.
• If you are driving an Electric Car (**Subclass**), the app **overrides** the navigation algorithm to automatically route through Tesla Superchargers (**Specialized Child Behavior**).
• The user presses the exact same button (`navigate()`), but the system executes the specific child implementation tailored to the runtime object.

sections.title: The 5 Inviolable Rules of Method Overriding
sections.content:
1. **Exact Signature Match**: Method name, parameter count, and parameter types MUST be identical.
2. **Covariant Return Type**: The return type can be identical OR a subtype of the parent's return type.
3. **Access Visibility Rule**: The child method CANNOT reduce visibility (can widen: `protected` → `public`; cannot narrow: `public` → `private`).
4. **Exception Handling Rule**: The child method cannot throw broader or new checked exceptions than the parent.
5. **Forbidden Overrides**: `private`, `static`, and `final` methods CANNOT be overridden.

sections.title: Method Overriding Traps
items: **Omitting `@Override`**: If you misspell the method name (e.g. `public double getarea()`) without `@Override`, the compiler treats it as a brand-new method instead of an override, and polymorphism will fail silently.
**Static Method Hiding (Not Overriding)**: Re-declaring a static method in a subclass hides the parent method; it is bound at compile-time by reference type, NOT dynamically at runtime.
**Narrowing Access Modifier**: Changing `public void move()` in parent to `protected void move()` in child causes compile error: *cannot reduce visibility of inherited method*.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can You Override `static` Methods in Java?

traps.question: Can a `static` method be overridden in Java? What happens if a subclass defines a static method with the exact same signature as the parent?
traps.trap: Thinking static methods participate in runtime polymorphism.
traps.solution:
NO! **Static methods cannot be overridden; they can only be HIDDEN (Method Hiding)**.
• Method overriding relies on dynamic runtime dispatch based on the **actual heap object** (`invokevirtual`).
• Static methods belong to the class and are resolved at compile-time based on the **reference variable's declared type** (`invokestatic`).
• If `Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod();` executes, it will run `Parent.staticMethod()`, NOT `Child.staticMethod()`!

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: If a superclass defines `protected Object getItem()`, which return type is legally allowed for a subclass overriding this method?
options: `String` (because String is a subtype of Object - Covariant Return Type)
None; the return type must strictly be `Object`
sections.explanation: Java allows Covariant Return Types: an overriding method can declare a return type that is a subtype (like `String`) of the parent method's return type (`Object`).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Method Overriding enables runtime polymorphism (dynamic method dispatch).
Always annotate overriding methods with `@Override` for compiler validation.
Signatures must match; return types can be covariant subtypes.
Access visibility can be widened but never narrowed.
`static`, `private`, and `final` methods cannot be overridden.

content.theory:
Method overriding lets a subclass provide its own implementation of a method inherited from its parent. When the method is called through a parent-type reference, Java runs the subclass version, chosen at runtime. Overriding is the mechanism behind runtime polymorphism. This lesson covers the rules an override must follow, the @Override annotation, covariant return types, exception rules, and what can't be overridden.

## A basic override

~~~java
class Animal {
    public String sound() { return "..."; }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String sound() { return "Woof"; }
}

Animal a = new Dog();
a.sound();   // "Woof": the Dog version runs
~~~

The reference type is Animal, but the object is a Dog, and the object's type decides which method runs.

## The rules for a valid override

An overriding method must:

1. **Have the same name and parameter types** as the parent method. Different parameters create an overload, not an override
2. **Have a compatible return type**: the same type, or a subtype for reference types (covariant return)
3. **Not reduce visibility**: a public method can't be overridden as protected
4. **Not throw broader checked exceptions**: it may throw the same, narrower or no checked exceptions
5. **Be an instance method** that the subclass can see and that isn't final

| Parent method | Allowed in override | Not allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `protected Number get()` | `public Integer get()` | `private Number get()` |
| `void read() throws IOException` | `void read() throws FileNotFoundException` | `void read() throws Exception` |

Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted.

## Why the rules exist

All the rules protect **substitutability**. Code holding an Animal reference expects to call `sound()` with the parent's visibility, get back the declared return type, and handle only the declared checked exceptions. An override that narrowed visibility, returned an unrelated type, or threw a new checked exception would break that caller.

## The @Override annotation

`@Override` tells the compiler you intend to override. If the method doesn't actually override anything, compilation fails:

~~~java
class Point {
    @Override
    public boolean equals(Point other) { ... }   // compile error: doesn't override equals(Object)
}
~~~

Without the annotation, this silently creates an overload, and collections calling `equals(Object)` never use it. Always use `@Override`; it turns a subtle runtime bug into a compile-time error.

## Covariant return types

Since Java 5, an override may return a subtype of the parent's return type:

~~~java
class Animal { Animal reproduce() { return new Animal(); } }
class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override Dog reproduce() { return new Dog(); }   // narrower return type
}
~~~

Callers holding a Dog reference get a Dog back without casting. `clone()` overrides commonly use this to return the specific type.

## What can't be overridden

- **final methods**: the parent forbids it
- **private methods**: not visible to the subclass; declaring a same-named method creates a new, unrelated method
- **static methods**: a same-signature static method in a subclass **hides** the parent's, and which one runs depends on the reference type, not the object
- **constructors**: they aren't inherited at all

~~~java
class Parent { static String id() { return "P"; } }
class Child extends Parent { static String id() { return "C"; } }

Parent p = new Child();
p.id();   // "P": static methods are resolved by reference type
~~~

This hiding behaviour is a frequent output question.

## Overriding versus overloading

| | Overriding | Overloading |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Subclass redefines a parent method | Same class (or subclass) adds a method with the same name |
| Parameters | Must match | Must differ |
| Resolved | At runtime, by object type | At compile time, by argument types |
| Polymorphism type | Runtime (dynamic) | Compile-time (static) |

## Calling the parent version

An override can still use the parent's logic with `super.method()`, which lets it extend behaviour instead of replacing it entirely.

## Overriding Object methods

The most common overrides in real code are `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` from Object. The Object class lesson covers their contracts, which are stricter than they look.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What are the rules of method overriding?", "Can you override static or private methods?" and "Overriding vs overloading?" List the five rules with the reason behind them, explain static method hiding with an output example, show how @Override catches the `equals(Point)` mistake, and contrast runtime and compile-time resolution.

sections.title: Prerequisites

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of the `final` Keyword as a **Security Tamper-Proof Seal on a Certified Legal Contract**:
• **`final` Variable (Immutable Stamped Value)**: Once written with ink, the number cannot be crossed out or altered (`final int MAX = 100`).
• **`final` Method (Non-Negotiable Core Procedure)**: The security protocol for bank vault authentication is sealed. Subclasses may customize their lobby decor, but they are strictly forbidden from overriding the authentication security algorithm.
• **`final` Class (Sealed Standard Specification)**: The class is 100% complete and sealed (`final class String`). Nobody can subclass it to inject spyware or modify its behavior.

sections.title: The 3 Scopes of `final` in Java
sections.content:
1. **`final` Variable**: Cannot be reassigned after its initial assignment (constant value / pointer).
2. **`final` Method**: Cannot be overridden by any subclass (locks core algorithm).
3. **`final` Class**: Cannot be extended / subclassed by any class (locks entire hierarchy).

sections.title: The `final` Keyword Across Variables, Methods & Classes
sections.explanation: SecurityToken cannot be extended. SecureBankAccount allows subclasses to override printSummary(), but forbids overriding auditTransaction().

sections.title: Summary of `final` Keyword Behaviors
rows: Cannot be overridden in any subclass.
Protect critical algorithms; enable JIT inlining.
Guarantee complete security; prevent subclass tampering.

Compiler inspects superclass header -> detects ACC_FINAL flag.

sections.title: Common `final` Misconceptions
items: **Confusing `final` Reference with Object Immutability**: Declaring `final int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};` prevents `arr = new int[5]`, but `arr[0] = 999;` is 100% valid! `final` locks the pointer, not the heap object payload.

**Final Variables Must Be Initialized**: A `final` instance variable must be initialized either at declaration or inside every constructor; otherwise, the compiler throws *variable might not have been initialized*.
**Overusing `final` Classes in Extensible Frameworks**: Marking every class `final` prevents users of your library from mocking or extending classes in unit tests.

traps.question: What catastrophic security and architectural bugs would occur if `java.lang.String` were NOT declared `final` in Java?
traps.trap: Only citing performance optimizations.
traps.solution:
If `String` were not `final`, an attacker could create a malicious subclass `MutableString extends String`:
1. **Security Bypass**: If a security manager checks `if (str.equals("/safe/path")) openFile(str);`, the attacker could override `toString()` or mutate internal state between the check and file opening, gaining unauthorized root file access.
2. **String Constant Pool Corruption**: Subclasses could mutate pooled literals, corrupting strings across unrelated application threads.
3. **HashMap & HashSet Key Invalidation**: Changing hash values after insertion would corrupt hash table lookup trees.

sections.explanation: The `final` keyword explicitly forbids subclasses from overriding the method, producing a compile-time error.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `final` variables cannot be reassigned after initialization.
`final` methods cannot be overridden, protecting business invariants.
`final` classes cannot be extended, locking down security and immutability.
`final` on reference variables locks the memory pointer, NOT the object payload.
Core Java classes (`String`, `Integer`, `Math`) are `final` for security and stability.

content.theory:
The `final` keyword closes doors. A final class can't be extended, a final method can't be overridden, and a final variable can't be reassigned. Choosing what to make final is a design decision about which parts of a class are fixed and which are open for extension. This lesson covers final classes and methods, why the JDK makes classes such as String final, sealed classes as a finer-grained alternative, and the design principle "design for inheritance or prohibit it".

## Final classes

~~~java
public final class Money {
    // ...
}

class Coins extends Money { }   // compile error: cannot inherit from final Money
~~~

A final class has no subclasses, so its behaviour is exactly what its own code says. JDK examples include `String`, `Integer` and the other wrapper classes, `LocalDate` and `Math`.

## Why String is final

If String could be subclassed, a malicious or buggy subclass could override methods to return different contents over time, breaking:

- **immutability**, which the string pool and hash map keys depend on
- **security checks**, such as validating a file path and then using it, if the subclass changed its value between check and use
- **performance assumptions** the JVM makes about String's behaviour

Making the class final guarantees every String behaves like a String.

## Final methods

A final method can't be overridden, while the rest of the class stays extensible:

~~~java
public abstract class Payment {
    public final void process() {       // the algorithm is fixed
        validate();
        charge();
        sendReceipt();
    }
    protected abstract void charge();   // the step subclasses customize
    protected void validate() { }
    protected void sendReceipt() { }
}
~~~

This is the **template method** pattern: the parent fixes the sequence of steps, and subclasses fill in individual steps. Making `process` final stops a subclass from skipping validation or receipts.

Final methods are also appropriate when a constructor must call a method: making it final (or private) prevents a subclass override from running on a half-built object.

## Design for inheritance or prohibit it

Effective Java's guideline: a class should either be carefully designed and documented for extension, or be made final. Designing for inheritance means:

- documenting which methods call which overridable methods (self-use)
- providing protected hooks deliberately
- testing by writing subclasses

Without that work, subclasses depend on undocumented implementation details and break when the parent changes, the fragile base class problem. Many teams default to final and remove it when a real extension need appears.

## Alternatives to final

- **Private constructors** with static factories prevent subclassing from outside the class, since a subclass constructor must call a parent constructor it can't access
- **Package-private constructors** allow subclasses only within the package

## Sealed classes (Java 17)

Sealed classes sit between final and fully open: they list exactly which classes may extend them.

~~~java
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Rectangle { }

public final class Circle implements Shape { ... }
public final class Square implements Shape { ... }
public non-sealed class Rectangle implements Shape { ... }
~~~

Each permitted subclass must declare itself `final`, `sealed` (with its own permits list) or `non-sealed` (open again). Sealing lets the compiler know every possible subtype, so a `switch` over a sealed type can be checked for exhaustiveness without a default branch. Sealed hierarchies suit closed sets of variants, such as payment methods or expression nodes.

## Final variables, briefly

`final` on a variable means it's assigned exactly once:

- **final fields** must be assigned by the end of construction
- **final local variables and parameters** can't be reassigned
- **final references** can't point elsewhere, but the object they refer to can still change

The final keyword advanced lesson covers these in depth, including effectively final variables in lambdas.

## Performance myths

Older advice claimed final methods were faster because they could be inlined. Modern JIT compilers inline non-final methods too, using class hierarchy analysis. Use final for design reasons, not speed.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What are the uses of final?", "Why is String final?" and "Can an abstract class be final?" Cover final classes, methods and variables, explain String's immutability and security reasons, show the template method use of final methods, mention sealed classes, and note that abstract and final together don't compile, because an abstract class needs a subclass.

lessons.title: The 'Object' Class: Root of the Java Hierarchy
lessons.description:
Think of java.lang.Object as the Universal Cellular DNA of Java:
• In biology, every living animal cell shares foundational DNA for cellular respiration and div...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-inheritance`, `method-overriding-basics`, and reference equality (`==`).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of `java.lang.Object` as the **Universal Cellular DNA of Java**:
• In biology, every living animal cell shares foundational DNA for cellular respiration and division, whether it's an eagle or a blue whale.
• In Java, **EVERY SINGLE CLASS** (whether written by Oracle, Spring, or you) directly or indirectly extends `java.lang.Object`.
• This guarantees that every object in Java inherently possesses universal abilities: printing its identity (`toString()`), checking value equality (`equals()`), generating hash buckets (`hashCode()`), and thread synchronization (`wait()`/`notify()`).

sections.title: The Inviolable Contract Between `equals()` and `hashCode()`
sections.content:
1. **Consistency**: If `a.equals(b)` is `true`, then `a.hashCode()` and `b.hashCode()` **MUST return the exact same integer**!
2. **Inequality**: If `a.equals(b)` is `false`, their `hashCode()` values are NOT required to be distinct (though distinct hash codes improve `HashMap` performance).
⭐ **Rule of Thumb**: *If you override `equals()`, you MUST ALWAYS override `hashCode()`!*

sections.title: Overriding `toString()`, `equals()`, and `hashCode()` Correctly
sections.explanation: u1 and u2 have different heap addresses (u1 == u2 is false), but logical value equality u1.equals(u2) is true. HashSet correctly deduplicates them to size 1.

sections.title: The 3 Equality Checks in Java
rows: Reference addresses (Are both pointing to exact same heap address?)
Generates hash code using same fields as `equals()`.

sections.title: Try It: The Broken HashSet Bug
sections.explanation: Because hashCode() was NOT overridden, the two equal objects produced different random hash codes, landing in different buckets. HashSet failed to detect the duplicate and inserted both (Size = 2)!

iterations.description: Calculates bucket index = 981247 % 16 = Bucket #7. Stores value in Bucket #7.
Calculates bucket index = 442199 % 16 = Bucket #3. Looks in Bucket #3.
HashMap returns null even though an equal User(101) exists in Bucket #7! Object lost.

sections.title: Common `Object` Method Traps
items: **Overloading `equals` Instead of Overriding**: Declaring `public boolean equals(User other)` creates an overload. When passed to a `HashSet`, it calls `equals(Object o)` and bypasses your method! Always write `@Override public boolean equals(Object o)`.

**Using Mutable Fields in `hashCode()`**: If you change an object's field after inserting it into a `HashSet`, its hash code changes, making it permanently unfindable and impossible to remove from the set (Memory Leak!).
**Comparing Floating Point with `==` in `equals`**: Use `Double.compare(d1, d2) == 0` to properly handle `NaN` and `-0.0` vs `+0.0`.

traps.question: What happens if two objects return `true` for `a.equals(b)`, but return DIFFERENT values for `a.hashCode()` and `b.hashCode()`?
traps.trap: Saying Java throws an Exception.
traps.solution:
No exception is thrown, but it causes **catastrophic silent data corruption in Hash Collections (`HashMap`, `HashSet`, `Hashtable`)**:
• `HashSet` uses `hashCode()` to find the array bucket first, and only checks `equals()` if the bucket has items.
• Because their hash codes differ, equal objects will be placed into different buckets.
• `set.contains(new User(101))` will return `false`, `set.add()` will insert duplicate keys, and `map.get()` will return `null`!

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: If `a.equals(b)` is `true`, what MUST be true according to the Java specification?
sections.explanation: The `equals`-`hashCode` contract strictly mandates that two equal objects must produce the exact same integer hash code.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: `java.lang.Object` is the universal superclass of all classes in Java.
Override `toString()` for human-readable diagnostic logging.
Override `equals(Object o)` for logical value equality.
Always override `hashCode()` whenever you override `equals()` to prevent hash collection corruption.
Never use mutable fields in `hashCode()` calculations.

sections.content: Next, we enter Module 5: Polymorphism, mastering dynamic method dispatch, runtime vs compile-time polymorphism, covariant returns, and instanceof pattern matching.

content.theory:
Every Java class ultimately extends `java.lang.Object`, so every object inherits its methods. Three of them, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`, are overridden in almost every serious class, and getting `equals` and `hashCode` wrong breaks hash-based collections in silent, confusing ways. This lesson covers Object's methods, the equals and hashCode contracts, and how to implement them correctly.

## Object's methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `equals(Object)` | Logical equality; defaults to reference equality |
| `hashCode()` | Hash value for hash tables; consistent with equals |
| `toString()` | Text representation; defaults to `ClassName@hexHash` |
| `getClass()` | Runtime class of the object (final) |
| `clone()` | Protected field-by-field copy, with Cloneable |
| `wait()`, `notify()`, `notifyAll()` | Thread coordination on the object's monitor (final) |
| `finalize()` | Deprecated cleanup hook; don't use it |

## toString

The default output, such as `Student@1b6d3586`, is useless in logs. Override it to show meaningful state:

~~~java
@Override
public String toString() {
    return "Student[name=" + name + ", rollNo=" + rollNo + "]";
}
~~~

`System.out.println(obj)` and string concatenation call `toString` automatically. Avoid including sensitive data such as passwords.

## The equals contract

The default `equals` compares references. Override it when two distinct objects with the same values should count as equal. The documented contract requires equals to be:

- **Reflexive**: `x.equals(x)` is true
- **Symmetric**: `x.equals(y)` equals `y.equals(x)`
- **Transitive**: if x equals y and y equals z, then x equals z
- **Consistent**: repeated calls give the same result if nothing changes
- **Non-null**: `x.equals(null)` is false

## A correct equals

~~~java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;                       // same object
    if (!(o instanceof Point other)) return false;    // type check (also handles null)
    return x == other.x && y == other.y;              // compare significant fields
}
~~~

Notes:

- the parameter must be `Object`, or it's an overload that collections never call; `@Override` catches this
- compare floating-point fields with `Double.compare`, and object fields with `Objects.equals`, which handles nulls
- using `instanceof` allows subclass instances to be equal to parent instances, which can break symmetry if a subclass adds fields; using `getClass() != o.getClass()` avoids that but rejects subclasses entirely. Making the class final sidesteps the dilemma

## The hashCode contract

If two objects are equal by `equals`, they **must** have the same hash code. Unequal objects may share a hash code, though fewer collisions mean faster hash tables.

~~~java
@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(x, y);
}
~~~

## Why overriding only equals breaks HashMap

A HashMap finds a key by first computing its hash code to choose a bucket, then calling equals within that bucket. If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal points get different default hash codes, land in different buckets, and the map never compares them:

~~~java
Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new Point(1, 2));
set.contains(new Point(1, 2));   // false without hashCode
~~~

The set ends up holding "duplicates", and lookups fail. This is one of the most asked Java interview bugs.

## Mutable keys

If a field used in hashCode changes after the object is put in a HashMap, the object sits in a bucket for its old hash and becomes unreachable by lookup. Use immutable objects as keys, or never mutate key fields.

## Records do this for you

A record generates `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` from its components, following the contracts correctly. For value-like data, records remove a common source of bugs. IDEs and Lombok can also generate these methods.

## getClass and the other methods

`getClass()` returns the runtime class and is final. `wait`, `notify` and `notifyAll` support low-level thread coordination; modern code usually uses `java.util.concurrent` instead. `finalize` is deprecated for removal because it ran unpredictably; use try-with-resources or `Cleaner` for cleanup.

## A quick checklist

Whenever a class represents a value, override `toString` for readable logs, and override `equals` and `hashCode` together using the same fields. Add `@Override` to each, so a wrong parameter type fails at compile time. If the class is plain data, prefer a record and let the compiler write all three.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What methods does Object have?", "What's the equals and hashCode contract?" and "What happens if you override equals but not hashCode?" List the methods, state the five equals properties and the hashCode rule, walk through the HashSet bug bucket by bucket, and mention records as the modern way to get these right.

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-inheritance`, `method-overriding-basics`, and `the-this-keyword`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Polymorphism as a **Universal Power Button on Electronic Devices**:
• You press the universal power button (**Single Uniform Interface**) on a Smartphone, a Laptop, or an Air Conditioner.
• The Smartphone turns on its OLED screen, the Laptop spins its CPU cooling fans, and the Air Conditioner starts its refrigerant compressor (**Many Diverse Forms of Behavior**).
• You do not need 3 different remote controls with 3 different button names; you issue a single instruction, and each object executes its own specialized behavior.

sections.title: The 2 Branches of Polymorphism in Java
sections.content:
1. **Compile-Time Polymorphism (Static Binding / Early Binding)**: Resolved at compile time by the Java compiler. Achieved via **Method Overloading**.
2. **Runtime Polymorphism (Dynamic Binding / Late Binding)**: Resolved at runtime by the JVM based on the actual heap object. Achieved via **Method Overriding** and **Upcasting**.

sections.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism in Action
sections.explanation: calc.add() is resolved at compile time based on parameter types. p1.playMedia() is resolved at runtime based on the actual object (SpotifyPlayer) on the Heap.

sections.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism
rows: Negligible vtable pointer lookup (~1 CPU cycle)

sections.title: Try It: The Non-Polymorphic Field Trap
sections.explanation: In Java, variables and fields are NEVER polymorphic! Field access is resolved at compile-time based on the reference type (Parent), printing 'ParentName'.

Dynamic dispatch invokes SpotifyPlayer's overridden implementation.

sections.title: Polymorphism Pitfalls
items: **Believing Fields are Polymorphic**: Instance variables in Java do NOT participate in runtime polymorphism. Only non-static, non-private methods are polymorphic.
**Static Methods are Not Polymorphic**: Static methods belong to classes and use Method Hiding (resolved by reference type), not dynamic dispatch.
**Calling Subclass-Specific Methods via Parent Reference**: If `Animal a = new Dog();` and `Dog` has a new method `fetch()`, calling `a.fetch()` fails compilation (must downcast `((Dog) a).fetch()`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Are Variables Polymorphic in Java?

traps.question: If Class B extends Class A, and both define `int x = 10` and `int x = 20` respectively, what does `A obj = new B(); System.out.println(obj.x);` print?
traps.trap: Answering 20, assuming fields are polymorphic like methods.
traps.solution: It prints **10**! In Java, **variables (fields) are NOT polymorphic**. Field access is resolved strictly at compile time based on the **declared type of the reference variable** (`A obj`), NOT the actual runtime object (`new B()`). Runtime polymorphism applies exclusively to instance methods.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which of the following participates in dynamic runtime polymorphism in Java?
options: Public and protected non-static instance methods
sections.explanation: Only non-static, non-private instance methods participate in runtime polymorphism via dynamic virtual method dispatch.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Polymorphism allows one interface to control multiple underlying implementations.
Compile-time polymorphism is achieved via method overloading (static binding).
Runtime polymorphism is achieved via method overriding and upcasting (dynamic binding).
Instance fields and static methods are never polymorphic.

content.theory:
Polymorphism means "many forms": one interface, many implementations. In Java, a variable of a parent type can refer to objects of any subclass, and calling a method on it runs the version that belongs to the actual object. This lets you write code once against an abstraction and have it work with types that don't exist yet. This lesson explains the two kinds of polymorphism, how dynamic dispatch works, and why polymorphism is central to extensible design.

## The core idea

~~~java
abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }
class Circle extends Shape {
    final double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
class Square extends Shape {
    final double s;
    Square(double s) { this.s = s; }
    double area() { return s * s; }
}

double total(List<Shape> shapes) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (Shape s : shapes) sum += s.area();   // the right formula for each object
    return sum;
}
~~~

`total` knows nothing about circles or squares. Add a Triangle class tomorrow, and `total` works with it unchanged.

## Two kinds of polymorphism

| | Compile-time (static) | Runtime (dynamic) |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Method overloading | Method overriding |
| Decided by | Compiler, from argument types | JVM, from the object's actual type |
| Also called | Static binding, early binding | Dynamic dispatch, late binding |
| Example | `print(int)` vs `print(String)` | `shape.area()` on a Circle or Square |

When people say "polymorphism" in OOP, they usually mean runtime polymorphism. Generics are sometimes called parametric polymorphism, a third form.

## Reference type versus object type

Every polymorphic call involves two types:

- the **reference type** (compile-time type): the declared type of the variable, such as Shape
- the **object type** (runtime type): the class of the object actually created, such as Circle

~~~java
Shape s = new Circle(2);
~~~

The **compiler** uses the reference type to decide which methods you may call: only methods declared in Shape. The **JVM** uses the object type to decide which implementation runs. That's why `s.area()` compiles (Shape declares it) and runs Circle's version.

## How dynamic dispatch works

The JVM typically gives each class a **virtual method table** (vtable): an array of pointers to the implementations of its overridable methods. A subclass's table copies the parent's entries and replaces those it overrides. A call like `s.area()` looks up the slot for `area` in the object's table and jumps there. The JIT compiler often optimizes this further, inlining the call when only one implementation is loaded, so polymorphism rarely costs measurable performance.

## What isn't polymorphic

- **Fields**: resolved by reference type. A field declared in both parent and child is chosen by the variable's declared type
- **Static methods**: resolved by reference type; they're hidden, not overridden
- **Private and final methods**: can't be overridden, so they're bound at compile time

## Upcasting

Assigning a subclass object to a parent reference is **upcasting**. It's implicit and always safe, because every Circle is a Shape:

~~~java
Shape s = new Circle(2);   // implicit upcast
~~~

Going the other way, downcasting, requires an explicit cast and can fail at runtime; the downcasting lesson covers it.

## Why polymorphism matters

- **Open for extension**: new types plug in without changing existing code, the open-closed principle
- **Removes type switches**: instead of `if (type == CIRCLE) ... else if (type == SQUARE) ...` scattered everywhere, each class carries its own behaviour
- **Enables frameworks**: a web framework calls your controller through an interface it defined years before your class existed
- **Testability**: code depending on an interface can be tested with a fake implementation

## Polymorphism through interfaces

Interfaces are the most flexible form, because unrelated classes can implement the same interface. `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()` is polymorphism: code depends on List, and you can switch to LinkedList by changing one line. Programming to interfaces rather than concrete classes is a widely recommended habit.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is polymorphism?", "Compile-time vs runtime polymorphism?" and output questions mixing reference and object types. Define one interface with many implementations, contrast overloading and overriding, explain that the compiler checks the reference type while the JVM dispatches on the object type, and note that fields and static methods aren't polymorphic.

• A device plugs into the charger requesting electricity.
• The charger te...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-polymorphism`, primitive widening, wrapper classes, and varargs.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Overload Resolution as a **Smart Power Brick Charger Negotiating with Devices**:
• A device plugs into the charger requesting electricity.
• The charger tests protocols in strict priority order:
  1. **Exact Protocol Match**: Is it a native 20V USB-C Laptop? (Exact Type Match).
  2. **Widening**: Can we safely step up voltage without data loss? (`int` → `long` → `double`).
  3. **Packaging**: Can we wrap it into a smart packet? (`int` → `Integer` Autoboxing).
  4. **Universal Fallback**: Can we deliver variable low-power pulses? (Varargs `int...`).
• The compiler always picks the **most specific, least costly conversion** available.

sections.title: The 4-Tier Compiler Overload Priority Ladder
sections.content:
When resolving an overloaded method call, `javac` checks candidates in this exact order:
$$\text{1. Exact Match} \longrightarrow \text{2. Primitive Widening} \longrightarrow \text{3. Autoboxing/Unboxing} \longrightarrow \text{4. Varargs}$$

sections.title: Tracing the Overload Resolution Priority Ladder
sections.explanation: If process(int) is commented out, process(long) executes (Widening). If process(long) is commented out, process(Integer) executes (Autoboxing). Finally, process(int...) is the last resort.

sections.title: The 4 Overload Resolution Tiers
rows: Safe numeric widening without loss of magnitude.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Widening vs Autoboxing
sections.explanation: Primitive widening (Tier 2: int -> long) takes precedence over Autoboxing (Tier 3: int -> Integer), printing 'LONG '.

iterations.description: Proceeds to Tier 2.
Match found! Halts search immediately.
Compile-time binding locked to test(long).

sections.title: Overloading Ambiguity Traps
items: **Widening + Autoboxing Incompatibility**: Java can do `int -> long` (widening) OR `int -> Integer` (boxing), but it will NEVER do `int -> Long` (autoboxing + widening combined in a single step is illegal!).
**Ambiguity on Two-Parameter Conversions**: Having `void add(int a, double b)` and `void add(double a, int b)` called with `add(5, 5)` causes compile error: *reference to add is ambiguous*.
**Passing `null` to Sibling Types**: If a class has `print(String s)` and `print(Integer i)`, calling `print(null)` fails compilation because neither is more specific than the other.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Does Widening Beat Autoboxing?

traps.question: Why does Java prioritize primitive widening (`int -> long`) over autoboxing (`int -> Integer`) during method overload resolution?
traps.trap: Assuming autoboxing is newer so it should take precedence.
traps.solution: For **Strict Backward Compatibility**! Widening was part of the original Java 1.0 language specification in 1995. Autoboxing was introduced later in Java 5.0 (2004). If autoboxing took precedence, existing legacy code written for Java 1.4 would suddenly change method execution targets and break production systems upon upgrading.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Given `void show(long a)` and `void show(Integer a)`, which method executes when calling `show(5)` with an `int` literal?
options: `show(Integer a)` because Integer is an object
`show(long a)` because primitive widening takes precedence over autoboxing
sections.explanation: Primitive widening (`int -> long`) is Tier 2, which takes priority over autoboxing (`int -> Integer`, Tier 3).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Method Overloading resolution follows the 4-tier priority ladder: Exact Match → Widening → Autoboxing → Varargs.
Widening always takes precedence over autoboxing for backward compatibility.
Java cannot widen and autobox simultaneously (`int` cannot become `Long`).
Overloaded calls with `null` can cause ambiguity if multiple sibling references exist.

sections.content: Next, we explore Runtime Polymorphism & Virtual Method Tables (vtable), uncovering how the JVM dispatches overridden methods dynamically in O(1) time.

content.theory:
Method overloading means defining several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in one class. The compiler picks which one to call from the argument types, which is why overloading is called compile-time polymorphism. Overloading makes APIs pleasant, as with `println` accepting any type, but its resolution rules around widening, boxing, varargs and null produce classic interview puzzles. This lesson explains the rules and the traps.

## Valid overloads

Methods overload when their parameter lists differ in number, types or order:

~~~java
int max(int a, int b) { ... }
double max(double a, double b) { ... }
int max(int a, int b, int c) { ... }
~~~

What doesn't count:

- **return type alone**: `int parse(String s)` and `long parse(String s)` can't coexist
- **parameter names**: `f(int a)` and `f(int b)` are the same signature
- **checked exceptions or access modifiers**: they're not part of the signature
- **generic type arguments after erasure**: `f(List<String>)` and `f(List<Integer>)` both erase to `f(List)` and clash

## How the compiler chooses

When several overloads could apply, the compiler works in phases and stops at the first phase that finds a match:

1. **Exact match or widening of primitives** (int to long, float to double) and subtype references, without boxing or varargs
2. **Boxing and unboxing** allowed (int to Integer)
3. **Varargs** allowed

Within a phase, it picks the **most specific** method. If no single most specific method exists, the call is ambiguous and doesn't compile.

## Widening beats boxing

~~~java
void f(long x) { System.out.println("long"); }
void f(Integer x) { System.out.println("Integer"); }

f(5);   // prints "long"
~~~

Phase 1 finds `f(long)` by widening int to long, so boxing to Integer is never considered. This rule preserved the behaviour of pre-Java-5 code when autoboxing arrived.

## Boxing beats varargs

~~~java
void g(Integer x) { System.out.println("Integer"); }
void g(int... xs) { System.out.println("varargs"); }

g(5);   // prints "Integer"
~~~

Varargs is the last resort, used only when nothing else fits.

## Most specific wins

~~~java
void h(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }
void h(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }

h("hi");   // String
h(null);   // String: null fits both, and String is more specific
~~~

Add a third overload `h(Integer i)` and `h(null)` becomes ambiguous: String and Integer are both more specific than Object, but neither is more specific than the other. The fix is a cast: `h((String) null)`.

## Overloading uses the compile-time type

Overload selection uses the **declared** type of the argument, not its runtime type:

~~~java
void describe(Object o) { System.out.println("object"); }
void describe(String s) { System.out.println("string"); }

Object x = "hello";
describe(x);   // "object": x's declared type is Object
~~~

This is the sharpest contrast with overriding, where the runtime type decides. People expecting "string" here have confused the two mechanisms.

## The remove trap in lists

`List<Integer>` has `remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)`:

~~~java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
list.remove(1);                    // removes index 1 (the value 20)
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(10));  // removes the value 10
~~~

`remove(1)` picks the int overload in phase 1 without boxing. This real API pitfall appears in interviews and production bugs alike.

## Overloading and inheritance

A subclass can overload an inherited method by adding a version with different parameters. Combined with overriding, this gets confusing: a subclass method with a different parameter type looks like an override but is an overload, and it isn't called polymorphically. The `@Override` annotation catches this.

## Designing overloads well

- overloads should do the same conceptual thing, differing only in input form
- avoid overloads with the same number of parameters where types could convert into each other
- when overloads would be confusing, use distinct names instead, as in `writeInt` and `writeLong`
- `println` is the classic good example: one concept, many input types

## A quick summary

Overloading is resolved once, by the compiler, from the declared types of the arguments. The compiler tries widening first, then boxing, then varargs, and picks the most specific match in the first phase that succeeds. When two candidates are equally specific, the call is ambiguous, and a cast settles it.

## How interviewers test this

Expect output questions with widening versus boxing, `null` arguments, and declared versus runtime types, plus "Can you overload by return type?" Walk through the three phases, explain most-specific selection and ambiguity, and emphasize that overloading is resolved at compile time from declared types.

lessons.title: Runtime Polymorphism & Virtual Method Tables (vtable)
lessons.description:
Think of Runtime Polymorphism as an International Credit Card Terminal at a Store:
• The cash register checkout system only knows the abstract concept: "Process...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-polymorphism`, `method-overriding-basics`, and JVM execution engine architecture.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Runtime Polymorphism as an **International Credit Card Terminal at a Store**:
• The cash register checkout system only knows the abstract concept: **"Process Payment"** (`PaymentProcessor.pay(amount)`).
• A customer swipes a **Visa**, an **Amex**, or an **Apple Pay device** (**Dynamic Concrete Subclasses**).
• The cash register does NOT have a giant 50-line `if/else` block hardcoded for every bank in the world.
• Instead, it sends the `pay()` message to whichever card is swiped, and the card's internal chip executes its own payment protocol (**Dynamic Virtual Method Dispatch**).

sections.title: How the JVM Executes Dynamic Dispatch: The Virtual Method Table (vtable)
sections.content:
When a class is loaded into Metaspace, the JVM constructs a **Virtual Method Table (vtable)**:
• A vtable is an array of direct memory pointers to the executable machine code of each method.
• Subclasses inherit parent vtable slot indices. If the subclass overrides a method, it overwrites that slot with the pointer to its own child method code.
• At runtime, `invokevirtual` jumps to `vtable[slot_index]` in **$O(1)$ constant time**, achieving polymorphic flexibility with virtually zero CPU overhead!

sections.title: Polymorphic Payment Processing Architecture
sections.explanation: CheckoutService.completeOrder() accepts any PaymentGateway. When new payment methods (e.g. PayPalGateway) are created, CheckoutService requires zero code modifications (Open/Closed Principle).

sections.title: Procedural Switch vs Polymorphic Dynamic Dispatch
rows: Must find and modify 10+ `switch` statements across the codebase.
Just create a new subclass `class X extends Base`; zero existing code modified.
High coupling (Master function knows all concrete types).
Loose coupling (Master function knows only base interface).
High (Easy to forget a `case` branch in one switch).
Zero (Compiler enforces implementation of abstract methods).

sections.title: Try It: Polymorphic Array Processing
sections.explanation: Iterating through the polymorphic array invokes the correct overridden drive() method on each concrete instance: Car -> Bike -> Drive.

iterations.description: Instruction targets method slot 4.
Inspects receiver object's runtime class definition in Metaspace.
Retrieves machine code pointer for CreditCardGateway.processPayment().
Executes credit card verification logic.

sections.title: Runtime Polymorphism Mistakes
items: **Overriding Private Methods**: Subclasses cannot override `private` methods. If a child declares a method with the same name, it is a completely unrelated method, and polymorphism will not work.

**Constructors Calling Overridden Methods**: Calling an overridable method inside a superclass constructor executes the child's overridden method BEFORE the child's fields have been initialized, causing `NullPointerException`!
**ClassCastException on Unsafe Downcasting**: Assuming a parent reference is always a specific child without checking `instanceof`.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why You Should Never Call Overridable Methods in Constructors

traps.question: What is dangerous about calling an overridden method inside a Superclass constructor?
traps.trap: Assuming the superclass version executes.
traps.solution:
Because **dynamic dispatch executes the Child's overridden method before the Child constructor has initialized its fields**!
• Trace: `Parent()` constructor runs → calls `init()` → JVM dynamically dispatches to `Child.init()` → `Child.init()` tries to read `this.databaseUrl` → `this.databaseUrl` is still `null` because `Child()` constructor hasn't executed yet! → Crashes with `NullPointerException`.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How does the JVM achieve O(1) constant time method resolution for dynamic polymorphism?
options: By searching all source code files sequentially
Using Virtual Method Tables (vtables) containing direct pointers to executable bytecode for each slot
By converting all classes to static methods
sections.explanation: The JVM uses Virtual Method Tables (vtables) in Metaspace, allowing `invokevirtual` to jump directly to the target method address in O(1) time.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Runtime polymorphism decouples high-level orchestrators from concrete low-level implementations.
Dynamic dispatch is executed by the JVM in $O(1)$ time using vtables.
Eliminates fragile `switch` statements and adheres to the Open/Closed Principle.
Never call overridable methods inside constructors to prevent uninitialized field access.

lessons.title: Casting Objects & Pattern Matching for instanceof
lessons.description:
Think of Object Casting as Military Rank & ID Badge Verification:
• Upcasting (Promotion / General View): A Navy SEAL is also a Soldier (Soldier s = new NavySEA...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-polymorphism`, `method-overriding-polymorphism`, and reference type hierarchy.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Object Casting as **Military Rank & ID Badge Verification**:
• **Upcasting (Promotion / General View)**: A Navy SEAL is also a Soldier (`Soldier s = new NavySEAL()`). Upcasting is implicit and 100% safe because every SEAL is guaranteed to be a Soldier.
• **Downcasting (Demotion / Specialized Mission)**: You have a generic Soldier reference `s` and want them to pilot a submarine (`pilotSubmarine()`). Only a Navy SEAL can pilot a submarine!
• **The Security Check (`instanceof`)**: Before ordering them into the submarine, you inspect their security badge (`if (s instanceof NavySEAL)`). If you blindly downcast an Army Cook to a Navy SEAL, the system crashes in flames (`ClassCastException`).

sections.title: Upcasting vs Downcasting Rules
sections.content:
• **Upcasting (Child → Parent)**: Implicit, automatic, and 100% safe (`Animal a = new Dog()`).
• **Downcasting (Parent → Child)**: Explicit and risky (`Dog d = (Dog) a`). MUST always be guarded with `instanceof` to prevent runtime `ClassCastException`.

sections.title: Classic `instanceof` vs Modern Java Pattern Matching (Java 14+)
sections.explanation: Java 14+ Pattern Matching eliminates the redundant manual cast '(Developer) emp', binding the typed variable 'dev' directly in the if-block.

sections.title: Upcasting vs Downcasting Comparison
rows: Treat diverse objects uniformly through base interface
Access specialized child methods not present in parent

sections.title: Try It: Predict Pattern Matching Scope
sections.explanation: Pattern variable 's' is immediately available in the right-hand condition (s.length() > 5) and inside the if-block.

variables.emp1: Points to Developer object on Heap

iterations.description: Passes Employee reference into method.
JVM validates heap type -> evaluates to TRUE.
Binds strongly typed variable 'dev'.
Executes developer-specific method safely with zero exceptions.

sections.title: Casting Traps
items: **Unchecked Downcasting**: Writing `Developer dev = (Developer) emp;` without `instanceof` will crash in production with `ClassCastException` the moment an unexpected subtype is passed.
**Downcasting Unrelated Types**: Attempting `String s = (String) new Integer(5);` is rejected by the compiler because String and Integer have no hierarchical relationship.
**Using Pattern Variables Outside Scope**: Pattern variable `dev` in `if (emp instanceof Developer dev)` is NOT in scope inside the `else` block.

sections.title: Interview Traps: What Does `null instanceof AnyClass` Return?

traps.question: What is the result of `null instanceof String` and `null instanceof Object` in Java? Does it throw a `NullPointerException`?
traps.trap: Thinking it throws NPE or returns true for Object.
traps.solution: It evaluates to **`false` in all cases without throwing any exception**! The Java Language Specification explicitly guarantees that `null instanceof AnyType` always returns `false`. This makes `if (obj instanceof String)` completely safe against null pointers.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What happens if you execute `String s = (String) (Object) Integer.valueOf(42);` at runtime?
options: Converts the integer 42 into the string "42"
sections.explanation: At runtime, the heap object is an Integer. Attempting to cast an Integer to String throws a `ClassCastException`.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Upcasting is implicit and safe; Downcasting is explicit and risky.
Always guard downcasts with `instanceof` to prevent `ClassCastException`.
Java 14+ Pattern Matching for `instanceof` combines type checking and casting in a single clean expression.
`null instanceof Type` safely evaluates to `false` without throwing NPE.

lessons.title: Polymorphism in System Design: The Strategy Pattern
lessons.description:
Think of the Strategy Pattern as an Interchangeable Camera Lens Mount System:
• The high-end DSLR camera body (Context / Orchestrator) contains the sensor, shut...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `method-overriding-polymorphism`, `downcasting-and-instanceof`, and interfaces.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of the Strategy Pattern as an **Interchangeable Camera Lens Mount System**:
• The high-end DSLR camera body (**Context / Orchestrator**) contains the sensor, shutter, and battery.
• The camera body does NOT hardcode physical glass optics inside its metal casing.
• Instead, it exposes a universal bayonet mount (**Strategy Interface**).
• The photographer can hot-swap a **Wide-Angle Lens**, a **Macro Lens**, or a **Telephoto Lens** (**Polymorphic Concrete Strategies**) at runtime depending on whether they are shooting landscapes or distant wildlife.

sections.title: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
sections.content:
The **Open/Closed Principle** (the 'O' in SOLID) states:
$$\text{Software entities should be OPEN for extension, but CLOSED for modification.}$$
Polymorphism is the primary mechanism to achieve OCP: You add new system capabilities by creating a *new subclass or interface implementor* without altering a single line of existing, battle-tested production code.

sections.title: Strategy Design Pattern: Multi-Channel Notification Dispatcher
sections.explanation: AlertService delegates sending to NotificationStrategy. To add Discord or Slack notifications, you create a new class implementing NotificationStrategy with ZERO edits to AlertService.

sections.title: Monolithic Code vs Strategy Pattern Architecture
rows: High (Class contains 500 lines of SMS, Email, and Push logic).
Loose (Each strategy is isolated in its own testable class).
Must edit existing class and add `else if (type == DISCORD)`.
Easy (Unit test each strategy class in isolation).
Strategies can be swapped dynamically on the fly.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Strategy Swap Output
sections.explanation: Swapping the strat reference from RegularDiscount to VIPDiscount changes the calculation dynamically from 10% off to 30% off.

iterations.description: Invokes triggerSecurityAlert().
Dispatches dynamically to EmailStrategy.sendAlert(). Outputs email log.
Replaces strategy pointer on context.
Dispatches dynamically to SMSStrategy.sendAlert(). Outputs SMS log.

sections.title: System Design Polymorphism Traps
items: **Over-Engineering Simple Logic**: Do not create 10 strategy classes for simple boolean toggles; use the Strategy Pattern when behaviors vary independently and have meaningful complexity.
**Leaking Concrete Types in Client Code**: If your client code constantly casts strategies back to concrete types (`((SMSStrategy) strategy).getTwilioSid()`), your interface abstraction is flawed.
**Stateless Strategy Sharing**: If a Strategy class holds no mutable state, share a single instance (Singleton) across threads rather than allocating `new Strategy()` on every request.

sections.title: Interview Traps: How Does Polymorphism Enable Dependency Inversion (DIP)?

traps.question: How does Polymorphism enable the Dependency Inversion Principle (the 'D' in SOLID)?
traps.trap: Confusing Dependency Inversion with Dependency Injection.
traps.solution:
• **Without Polymorphism (Direct Dependency)**: High-level business logic (`OrderService`) directly instantiates and depends on low-level database classes (`MySQLDatabase`). If database changes, business logic breaks.
• **With Polymorphism (Inverted Dependency)**: High-level business logic depends on an **Abstract Interface** (`DatabaseRepository`). Both `OrderService` and `MySQLDatabase` depend on the interface. The direction of dependency is inverted, decoupling business logic from infrastructure.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which SOLID design principle states that software should be open for extension but closed for modification?
sections.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP) states that classes should allow new behavior to be added via extension (polymorphism) without modifying existing source code.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Strategy Pattern encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface.
Polymorphism enables the Open/Closed Principle (OCP) and Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP).
Allows runtime swapping of behaviors without modifying orchestrator classes.
Decouples high-level business workflows from low-level third-party integrations.

lessons.title: What is Abstraction? Hiding Complexity
lessons.description:
Think of Abstraction as the Dashboard & Pedals of a Modern Car:
• When you press the accelerator pedal (Clean Abstract Interface), the car moves forward.
• You ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-oop`, `understanding-encapsulation`, and `method-overriding-polymorphism`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Abstraction as the **Dashboard & Pedals of a Modern Car**:
• When you press the accelerator pedal (**Clean Abstract Interface**), the car moves forward.
• You do not need to know fuel injection timing, spark plug ignition firing orders, crankshaft rotational physics, or transmission gear ratios (**Hidden Implementation Complexity**).
• Abstraction allows human developers to manage massive, millions-of-lines enterprise systems by interacting with simple, high-level conceptual interfaces while hiding dizzying low-level machinery.

sections.title: WHAT vs HOW: The Core Principle of Abstraction
sections.content:
• **Abstraction defines WHAT an object does** (Exposes public method contracts).
• **Implementation defines HOW it does it** (Hidden inside concrete classes).
In Java, Abstraction is implemented through **Abstract Classes** (partial abstraction) and **Interfaces** (pure abstraction).

sections.title: Abstraction in Action: High-Level Audio Processing Pipeline
sections.explanation: MusicPlayer is decoupled from specific audio formats. It interacts with the clean AudioDecoder abstraction.

sections.title: Abstraction vs Encapsulation: The Deep Comparison
rows: Hide complexity by exposing essential features.
Hide data to guard integrity and prevent corruption.
Focuses on **HOW** the object protects internal state.
External Design (How collaborators see the object).
Internal Implementation (How the class organizes its fields).
A Car's steering wheel and brake pedal.
A Car's fuel tank sealed with a lockable gas cap.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Abstract Contract Output
sections.explanation: Client code holds a CloudStorage abstraction pointer and calls upload(), executing AWSStorage's implementation.

iterations.description: Invokes method with polymorphic AudioDecoder parameter.
Dynamic dispatch resolves call to FlacDecoder.class.
Decodes audio and returns raw PCM bytes.
MusicPlayer plays sound with zero knowledge of FLAC mathematics.

sections.title: Abstraction Traps
items: **Leaking Implementation Details**: Naming an abstract method `queryMySQLDatabase()` leaks technical details; name it `loadUserRecord()` so implementations can switch to MongoDB or Redis seamlessly.

**Premature Abstraction**: Creating 5 interfaces and abstract factories for simple 10-line scripts adds unnecessary boilerplate; abstract when code has multiple implementations or evolving requirements.
**Confusing Abstraction with Encapsulation**: Saying 'encapsulation is hiding data, abstraction is hiding code' is imprecise: Encapsulation protects state; Abstraction reduces conceptual complexity.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can an Abstract Class Have Zero Abstract Methods?

traps.question: Can a class be declared `abstract` if it contains zero `abstract` methods (i.e. all methods are 100% concrete)?
traps.trap: Assuming abstract classes must have at least one abstract method.
traps.solution: YES! **An abstract class does NOT require any abstract methods**. Programmers intentionally declare a fully concrete class `abstract` to **prevent direct instantiation with `new`**, forcing developers to extend it (e.g. `java.awt.event.MouseAdapter`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What is the primary difference between Abstraction and Encapsulation?
options: Abstraction protects data; Encapsulation hides complexity
Abstraction hides implementation complexity (WHAT); Encapsulation protects internal data integrity (HOW)
Abstraction requires static methods; Encapsulation requires final classes
They are identical concepts with different names
sections.explanation: Abstraction simplifies interfaces by hiding complex details (WHAT), while Encapsulation guards internal state using access modifiers (HOW).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Abstraction exposes clean interfaces while hiding complex internal implementations.
Defines WHAT an object does rather than HOW it does it.
Implemented in Java via Abstract Classes and Interfaces.
Enables loose coupling and high architectural maintainability.

content.theory:
Abstraction means showing what something does while hiding how it does it. You drive a car through a steering wheel and pedals without knowing how fuel injection works; you call `list.sort()` without knowing which sorting algorithm runs. In Java, abstraction is expressed with abstract classes and interfaces, but it's first a way of thinking about design. This lesson explains abstraction as a concept, how it differs from encapsulation, its levels, and how to find the right abstractions.

## The idea

An abstraction is a simplified model that keeps the details a user needs and hides the rest. A good abstraction:

- has a small, clear interface
- hides complexity that callers don't need
- stays stable while the implementation changes

`java.util.Map` is an abstraction: put, get, remove. Whether it's a hash table, a red-black tree or a concurrent structure is hidden behind the interface.

## Abstraction in Java

Java offers two main tools:

- **Abstract classes**: partial implementations with some methods left abstract for subclasses
- **Interfaces**: pure contracts describing capabilities, optionally with default methods

~~~java
public interface Storage {
    void save(String key, byte[] data);
    byte[] load(String key);
}
~~~

Code using Storage doesn't know whether files go to local disk, Amazon S3 or a database. Each implementation hides its own details.

Methods and classes are abstractions too. A well-named method like `calculateTax(order)` hides its steps; callers read the name instead of the code.

## Abstraction versus encapsulation

These are related but distinct, and the difference is asked constantly:

| | Abstraction | Encapsulation |
|---|---|---|
| Focus | What an object does: the design-level view | How data is protected: the implementation-level mechanism |
| Goal | Reduce complexity for users | Protect invariants and internal state |
| Java tools | Interfaces, abstract classes | private fields, access modifiers, getters and setters |
| Question it answers | What can callers do? | What can callers touch? |

They work together: an interface defines the abstraction, and a class encapsulates its state while implementing it. A class can be encapsulated but poorly abstracted (private fields, but a confusing API with fifty methods), or vice versa.

## Levels of abstraction

Systems are built in layers, each hiding the one below:

1. Hardware and machine instructions
2. The JVM, hiding the operating system and CPU
3. The Java standard library, hiding data structures and I/O
4. Your service layer, hiding database queries behind business operations
5. Your API, hiding the service layer from clients

Good code keeps each method at one level. A method that mixes `placeOrder` logic with raw SQL string building is hard to read because it jumps between levels.

## Leaky abstractions

Every non-trivial abstraction leaks some detail. An ORM hides SQL, but performance problems such as the N+1 query issue force you to understand the SQL anyway. A remote call that looks like a local method can fail with network timeouts. Knowing where your abstractions leak is part of using them well.

## Finding good abstractions

- **Look for what varies**: if there are or will be several payment providers, abstract the payment step behind an interface
- **Name by role, not implementation**: `MessageSender`, not `SmtpEmailSender`, for the interface
- **Keep interfaces small**: callers should need most of what an interface offers
- **Don't abstract too early**: an interface with one implementation and no foreseeable second one adds indirection without benefit. Wait until a second case or a test double appears

## Benefits

- callers deal with less complexity
- implementations can change or be swapped without affecting callers
- teams can work in parallel against agreed interfaces
- testing is easier with fake implementations

## A worked example

An ATM shows a handful of operations: check balance, withdraw, deposit and change PIN. Behind them sit card readers, network calls to the bank, cash dispensers and audit logs. Customers never see those parts, and the bank can replace a dispenser model or switch networks without retraining anyone. In code, an `AtmService` interface plays the same role: callers depend on its few methods while implementations change freely.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is abstraction?", "Abstraction vs encapsulation?" and "How do you achieve abstraction in Java?" Use a real-world example (a car, an ATM), show an interface with hidden implementations, give the comparison table, and mention abstract classes and interfaces as Java's two mechanisms.

lessons.title: Abstract Classes & Template Method Pattern
lessons.description:
Think of an Abstract Class as an Incomplete Architectural Housing Foundation Template:
• A master construction firm pours the concrete slab foundation, installs...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-abstraction`, `what-is-inheritance`, and `super-keyword`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of an Abstract Class as an **Incomplete Architectural Housing Foundation Template**:
• A master construction firm pours the concrete slab foundation, installs standard plumbing pipes, and wires the electrical fuse box (**Concrete Shared Methods & State**).
• However, the master architect leaves the exterior facade, roof tiles, and interior paint (**Abstract Hook Methods**) blank.
• You cannot move into the raw foundation (`new HouseTemplate()` is illegal); a builder must create a finished subclass (`ModernVilla extends HouseTemplate`) that completes all unfinished rooms.

sections.title: The Inviolable Rules of Abstract Classes
sections.content:
1. **Cannot Be Instantiated**: Writing `new AbstractClass()` causes a compile error.
2. **Can Have Constructors & State**: Has instance fields and constructors (invoked by child constructors via `super()`).
3. **Contains Both Concrete and Abstract Methods**: Can provide shared common logic while forcing subclasses to implement abstract methods.
4. **First Concrete Subclass Must Implement All Abstract Methods**: If a child class fails to implement all inherited abstract methods, the child class itself MUST be declared `abstract`.

sections.title: The Template Method Design Pattern with Abstract Classes
sections.explanation: DataParser defines the immutable process() template workflow. CSVParser and JSONParser supply only the custom parseContent() step.

sections.title: Abstract Class Rules & Modifiers Matrix
rows: Shared implementations inherited by all subclasses.
Declared with `abstract`; must NOT have a body `{}`.
Compile error: *class is abstract; cannot be instantiated*.
Compile error! Abstract methods must be visible to be overridden.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Abstract Class Compilation
sections.explanation: new Square() invokes Shape() constructor initializing colorCode to 5. s.draw() executes Square's overridden draw() method.

iterations.description: Invokes super("users.csv") in DataParser; sets sourceFile.
Executes concrete openFile() from DataParser.
Dispatches dynamically to CSVParser.parseContent().
Executes concrete closeFile() from DataParser.

sections.title: Abstract Class Traps
items: **Illegal Modifier Combinations**: Marking an abstract method `private abstract`, `static abstract`, or `final abstract` causes a compile error (because private, static, and final methods cannot be overridden!).
**Empty Method Body `{}` on Abstract Method**: Writing `abstract void run() {}` produces a compile error: *abstract methods cannot have a body* (must end with a semicolon `;`).
**Forgetting Constructors in Abstract Classes**: Abstract classes should define constructors to initialize base fields cleanly.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Do Abstract Classes Have Constructors?

traps.question: If an Abstract Class cannot be instantiated with the `new` keyword, why does Java allow it to have constructors?
traps.trap: Thinking constructors in abstract classes are dead code.
traps.solution:
Because **Constructors in Abstract Classes initialize the superclass state of concrete subclass objects**!
• When a child class is instantiated (`new CSVParser()`), the child constructor calls `super("users.csv")` to execute the abstract parent's constructor.
• This guarantees that all private/protected fields and invariant checks in the abstract class are properly initialized before child code executes.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which modifier combination is ILLEGAL on a method in Java?
sections.explanation: `final abstract` is a contradictory compile error: `abstract` mandates that the method MUST be overridden, while `final` strictly forbids overriding.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and can contain both abstract and concrete methods.
Abstract classes have constructors executed via `super()` during subclass creation.
The Template Method Pattern uses abstract classes to define fixed algorithm skeletons with customizable hook steps.
`abstract` methods cannot be `private`, `static`, or `final`.

sections.content: Next, we explore Interfaces: Contracts & Multiple Inheritance, mastering pure contract design, default constant fields, and implementing multiple interfaces.

lessons.title: Interfaces: Contracts & Multiple Inheritance
lessons.description:
Think of a Java Interface as a Standard Universal Electrical Wall Outlet (USB-C / 120V Socket):
• The power grid company publishes a precise physical interface ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-abstraction`, `types-of-inheritance`, and method overriding.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of a Java Interface as a **Standard Universal Electrical Wall Outlet (USB-C / 120V Socket)**:
• The power grid company publishes a precise physical interface specification (**The Interface**).
• Any device manufacturer—whether making a toaster, a laptop charger, or a Tesla car charger—can implement the matching prongs (`implements PowerConsumer`).
• The power grid outlet does not care about the internal circuitry or brand of the device; as long as the device implements the standard plug contract, electricity flows flawlessly.

sections.title: Implicit Modifiers in Java Interfaces
sections.content:
By default in Java interfaces:
• **All Fields** are implicitly `public static final` (Constant values).
• **All Non-Default Methods** are implicitly `public abstract` (Public contracts).
*You can omit these keywords in source code, but the compiler injects them automatically.*

sections.title: Multiple Interface Implementation in Action
sections.explanation: AutonomousDrone implements Flyable, GPSNavigable, and CameraEquipped, achieving clean multiple inheritance of type and capabilities.

sections.title: Interface Rules & Invariants Summary
rows: Must be initialized at declaration; cannot be modified (Constants).
No body `{}`; must be implemented by concrete classes with `public` modifier.
Can be used as polymorphic reference types (`Flyable f = new Drone()`).
A class can implement unlimited interfaces.
An interface can extend multiple other interfaces using `extends`!

sections.title: Try It: Predict Interface Constant Output
sections.explanation: Interface fields are static constants accessed via InterfaceName.FIELD.

sections.title: Interface Method Dispatch Trace: `Flyable f = new AutonomousDrone("DJI"); f.takeOff();`

iterations.description: Upcasts AutonomousDrone instance to Flyable interface reference.
Issues interface method invocation opcode.
Locates concrete takeOff() method implementation in AutonomousDrone.

variables.Execution: Drone rotors spinning up. Taking off!

iterations.description: Executes drone takeOff logic.

sections.title: Interface Implementation Traps
items: **Omitting `public` on Overriding Methods**: Writing `void takeOff() {}` in the implementing class causes compile error: *attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public* (because interface methods are implicitly public!).
**Constants Anti-Pattern**: Using interfaces solely to hold constant variables (`interface Constants { ... }`) is an anti-pattern. Use `final class` with private constructors or `enum` instead.
**Interface Names**: Prefer adjectives ending in '-able' (`Runnable`, `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `AutoCloseable`) or clear nouns (`Repository`, `PaymentGateway`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can an Interface Extend Multiple Other Interfaces?

traps.question: Can an interface extend multiple other interfaces using the `extends` keyword?
traps.trap: Thinking multiple inheritance is never allowed with extends.
traps.solution:
YES! **An interface CAN extend multiple interfaces** using the `extends` keyword:
```java
interface SmartDevice extends WifiConnectable, BluetoothConnectable, PowerManageable {}
```
Multiple inheritance is forbidden for *classes* (because of state/constructor conflicts), but fully supported for *interfaces*.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What are the implicit modifiers applied to every field declared inside a Java interface?
sections.explanation: All fields in a Java interface are automatically `public static final` constants.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Interfaces define pure contracts of behavior.
A class can implement multiple interfaces (`implements A, B, C`).
All interface fields are implicitly `public static final` constants.
All standard interface methods are implicitly `public abstract`.
Implementing methods MUST be declared `public`.
