lessons.title: Abstract Class vs Interface & Modern Java Features
lessons.description:
Think of the choice between an Abstract Class and an Interface as Biological Identity vs Skill Certifications:
• Abstract Class (Species / Identity / "Is-A"): A...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `abstract-classes`, `interfaces-in-java`, and `what-is-inheritance`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of the choice between an Abstract Class and an Interface as **Biological Identity vs Skill Certifications**:
• **Abstract Class (Species / Identity / "Is-A")**: A Bird (`abstract class Bird`). It has physical state (feathers, beak, internal body temperature) and shared genetics.
• **Interface (Capabilities / Certifications / "Can-Do")**: Flying (`interface Flyable`). A Bird can fly, an Airplane can fly, a Drone can fly, and a Superhero can fly. None of them share biological genetics, but all implement the `Flyable` capability contract.

sections.title: The Modern Evolution of Java Interfaces
sections.content:
• **Java 8 `default` Methods**: Allows interfaces to provide backward-compatible default method implementations without breaking existing implementing classes.
• **Java 8 `static` Methods**: Allows utility helper methods directly inside interfaces (`List.of()`, `Comparator.comparing()`).
• **Java 9 `private` Methods**: Allows sharing common internal helper code between multiple default methods without exposing them to implementing classes.

sections.title: Modern Interface with `default`, `static`, and `private` Methods (Java 9+)
sections.explanation: Demonstrates modern Java interface features: default methods, private helper methods, and static factory methods.

sections.title: The Definitive Matrix: Abstract Class vs Interface
rows: Can have instance fields (`private int age;`).
Easy to add concrete methods without breaking code.
Can add `default` methods without breaking code.
Fast ($O(1)$ itable jump with JIT inline caching).

sections.title: Try It: Resolving Default Method Conflicts
sections.explanation: When two interfaces provide conflicting default methods, the implementing class MUST override the method and explicitly choose or combine them.

sections.title: Decision Framework: Should I Use an Abstract Class or an Interface?

variables.Question: Do you need to share mutable instance state or constructors?

iterations.description: YES → Use ABSTRACT CLASS (Interfaces cannot hold instance fields).

variables.Question: Do you want unrelated classes to implement a common capability?

iterations.description: YES → Use INTERFACE (`Comparable`, `Serializable`, `AutoCloseable`).

variables.Question: Do you need multiple inheritance of type?

iterations.description: YES → Use INTERFACE (Java allows `implements A, B, C`).

variables.Question: Do you want to design clean public API contracts (e.g. Spring Service)?

iterations.description: YES → Use INTERFACE (Enables mocking, dependency injection, and proxying).

sections.title: Common Architectural Mistakes
items: **Overusing Default Methods to Turn Interfaces into Abstract Classes**: Interfaces should remain lightweight contracts; do not dump 500 lines of business logic into interface default methods.
**Creating Abstract Classes for Pure Contracts**: If your abstract class has zero instance fields and zero constructors, convert it into an `interface` to allow multiple inheritance.
**Interface Default Diamond Conflicts**: Forgetting to resolve duplicate default methods causes compile error: *class inherits unrelated defaults for method from types Alpha and Beta*.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Were Default Methods Added in Java 8?

traps.question: Why did Java 8 introduce `default` methods in interfaces? What major problem did it solve in the Java standard library?
traps.trap: Thinking it was just to make interfaces act like abstract classes.
traps.solution:
To provide **Non-Breaking API Evolution for Java 8 Lambdas and Streams**!
• In Java 8, Oracle wanted to add `stream()`, `parallelStream()`, and `forEach()` to `java.util.Collection`.
• If interfaces only supported abstract methods, adding `stream()` to `Collection` would have instantly **broken millions of custom collections in production code worldwide** (because every custom collection would fail compilation for not implementing `stream()`).
• Default methods allowed Oracle to add `default Stream<E> stream()` directly to `Collection` with zero breaking changes!

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: When must you choose an Abstract Class over an Interface in Java?
options: When you want to implement multiple inheritance
When you need non-static instance fields or constructor initialization of base state
When designing a functional interface for lambdas
When you need public static methods
sections.explanation: Interfaces cannot hold instance variables or define constructors. If your design requires non-static fields or constructor execution, you MUST use an Abstract Class.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Use Abstract Classes for 'Is-A' relationships with shared state and constructors.
Use Interfaces for 'Can-Do' capabilities across unrelated classes.
Java 8 introduced `default` and `static` interface methods for non-breaking API evolution.
Java 9 added `private` interface methods for internal helper code sharing.
Conflicting default methods are resolved explicitly using `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

content.theory:
"Abstract class or interface?" is among the most asked OOP interview questions, and the honest answer changed with Java 8, when interfaces gained default methods. The differences that remain are about state, constructors, inheritance limits and intent. This lesson lays out the precise technical differences, the design guidance for choosing, and how the two combine in real code such as the Java collections framework.

## The technical differences

| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Instance fields (state) | Yes, any kind | No; only `public static final` constants |
| Constructors | Yes | No |
| Method bodies | Concrete methods of any access | Default, static and private methods (Java 8+, 9+) |
| Abstract method access | public, protected or package-private | Implicitly public |
| How many a class can use | Extends one | Implements many |
| Keyword | `extends` | `implements` (classes), `extends` (interfaces) |
| Relationship expressed | is-a, with shared identity | can-do, a capability |
| Lambdas | No | Yes, if functional (one abstract method) |

## The differences that matter most

**State.** Only abstract classes can hold instance fields. If subclasses share data, such as an id, a name or a creation timestamp, with logic around it, an abstract class can manage it once.

**Constructors.** An abstract class can enforce initialization rules for every subclass through its constructor. An interface can't require anything at construction time.

**Single versus multiple.** A class can extend only one class. Using an abstract class spends that one slot, which can block future designs. Interfaces don't have this cost.

**Evolution.** Adding an abstract method to either breaks existing implementations. Adding a default method to an interface, or a concrete method to an abstract class, doesn't. Since Java 8, both can evolve this way.

## Choosing: the guidance

Prefer an **interface** when:

- you're defining a capability that unrelated classes might share, such as Comparable or AutoCloseable
- you want implementations to remain free to extend some other class
- you want lambdas to implement it
- you're defining the type that callers will depend on

Prefer an **abstract class** when:

- subclasses share state and the code that manages it
- you need constructors to enforce invariants
- you need non-public methods as part of the contract with subclasses, such as protected hooks
- you're implementing the template method pattern with a fixed final algorithm

A common rule of thumb: **define types with interfaces; share implementation with abstract classes.**

## Using both together

The JDK's collections show the combination:

~~~java
public interface List<E> extends Collection<E> { ... }        // the type
public abstract class AbstractList<E> implements List<E> { ... } // skeletal implementation
public class ArrayList<E> extends AbstractList<E> implements List<E> { ... }
~~~

Callers depend on `List`. Implementers can extend `AbstractList` to get most methods for free, or implement `List` directly if they need to extend a different class. You get the flexibility of the interface and the code reuse of the abstract class.

## A worked example

Designing notification senders:

~~~java
public interface NotificationSender {
    void send(String to, String message);
}

public abstract class RetryingSender implements NotificationSender {
    private final int maxAttempts;
    protected RetryingSender(int maxAttempts) { this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts; }

    @Override
    public final void send(String to, String message) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= maxAttempts; i++) {
            try { deliver(to, message); return; }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { if (i == maxAttempts) throw e; }
        }
    }
    protected abstract void deliver(String to, String message);
}
~~~

Code depends on the interface. Senders needing retries extend RetryingSender, which holds state (`maxAttempts`) and a fixed algorithm. A sender wrapping a third-party SDK class can implement the interface directly.

## Interface default methods don't replace abstract classes

Default methods can't access instance state, because interfaces have none; they can only call other interface methods. They suit convenience methods built on the abstract ones, such as `describe()` calling `area()`, not behaviour that needs fields. Treating interfaces with many defaults as abstract classes misses this limit.

## A quick decision checklist

1. Do implementations need shared fields or constructor logic? Yes leads to an abstract class
2. Might implementers need to extend another class? Yes leads to an interface
3. Is it a capability unrelated types share? Interface
4. Want both a public type and reusable code? Interface plus an abstract skeletal class

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Differences between abstract class and interface?", "When would you use each?" and "After Java 8, why still use abstract classes?" Give the table, emphasize state, constructors and single inheritance as the lasting differences, state the rule of thumb, and show the List plus AbstractList pairing.

lessons.title: Nested & Inner Classes: Member vs Static Nested
lessons.description:
Think of Nested Classes as Car Components (Engine vs Spare Tire):
• Non-Static Member Inner Class (The Engine): Tightly bound to a specific car chassis (Outer.t...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `classes-and-objects`, `access-modifiers-deep-dive`, and `the-this-keyword`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Nested Classes as **Car Components (Engine vs Spare Tire)**:
• **Non-Static Member Inner Class (The Engine)**: Tightly bound to a specific car chassis (`Outer.this`). An engine cannot exist or operate without being mounted inside a physical car instance.
• **Static Nested Class (The Spare Tire in the Trunk)**: Packaged inside the car's compartment for organizational convenience, but it does NOT depend on the car's engine or battery. You can take the spare tire and use it anywhere without needing the original car running.

sections.title: The 4 Types of Nested Classes in Java
sections.content:
1. **Static Nested Class**: Declared `static` inside an outer class (no outer instance reference).
2. **Non-Static Member Inner Class**: Declared inside an outer class (holds implicit reference to enclosing outer instance `Outer.this`).
3. **Local Inner Class**: Declared inside a method or block.
4. **Anonymous Inner Class**: Inline class declaration and instantiation without an identifier name.

sections.title: Static Nested Class vs Non-Static Member Inner Class
sections.explanation: Static nested classes are instantiated with 'new Outer.StaticNested()'. Non-static inner classes require an enclosing outer object: 'outerInstance.new Inner()'.

sections.title: Non-Static Member Inner Class vs Static Nested Class
rows: No reference to outer instance (Clean decoupling).
Can access all outer instance fields and private members.
Can access ONLY outer `static` fields and methods.
High (Can prevent outer instance from being garbage collected).

sections.title: Try It: Predict Inner Class State Output
sections.explanation: 'val' resolves to Inner's local field (20), while 'Outer.this.val' resolves to the enclosing outer instance's field (10).

sections.title: Memory Trace: Non-Static Inner Class Allocation

iterations.description: Allocates enclosing outer instance.
JVM compiler injects hidden 'this$0' pointer inside Account pointing back to outer 0x1000.
Even though bank is null, outer object at 0x1000 cannot be GC'd because Account at 0x2000 retains its hidden this$0 pointer!

sections.title: Inner Class Memory Leak Traps
items: **Asynchronous Memory Leaks (Android / Handlers)**: Passing a non-static inner class (like a `Runnable` or `Handler`) to a background thread prevents the entire outer UI Activity / Service from being garbage collected until the thread finishes.
**Prefer `static` Nested Classes by Default**: Unless an inner class strictly needs access to the outer instance's non-static fields, always declare nested classes `static` (Effective Java Item 24).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Does the Compiler Inject `this$0`?

traps.question: How does a non-static inner class access private fields of its enclosing outer class? What is `this$0`?
traps.trap: Thinking the JVM has special syntax permissions.
traps.solution: The Java compiler synthesizes a hidden synthetic field named **`final Outer this$0;`** inside the non-static inner class and passes the outer instance reference to the inner constructor during `outer.new Inner()`. It also creates synthetic package-private accessor methods in the outer class to allow the inner class to read outer private fields.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How do you instantiate a static nested class named `Builder` declared inside `Database`?
sections.explanation: Static nested classes do not require an outer instance; they are instantiated directly via `new Outer.StaticNested()`.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Member inner classes hold an implicit reference `Outer.this` to their enclosing outer instance.
Static nested classes do not hold an outer reference and are decoupled.
Always prefer static nested classes by default to eliminate memory leak risks.
Use `Outer.this.field` to disambiguate outer fields from inner shadowed fields.

lessons.title: Local & Anonymous Inner Classes
lessons.description:
Think of Anonymous Inner Classes as Hiring a One-Day Specialized Freelance Consultant:
• You have a one-time event (A button was clicked, or a background worker...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `nested-and-inner-classes`, `interfaces-in-java`, and variable scope.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Anonymous Inner Classes as **Hiring a One-Day Specialized Freelance Consultant**:
• You have a one-time event (A button was clicked, or a background worker needs to run for 5 seconds).
• You do NOT want to file corporate incorporation paperwork to create a permanent company (`class PermanentButtonHandler implements ActionListener`).
• Instead, you hire a temporary contractor on the spot (`new ActionListener() { ... }`), write their custom instructions inline, execute the task, and dismiss them.

sections.title: The Law of Effectively Final Captured Variables
sections.content:
Any local variable declared inside a method that is accessed by a Local or Anonymous Inner Class **MUST be `final` or effectively final** (its value is never modified after initialization).
• *Why?* Because when the method finishes executing, its stack frame is popped. The inner class (living on the Heap) makes a **copy** of the local variable. If the local variable could change, the stack and heap values would fall out of sync!

sections.title: Anonymous Inner Class vs Modern Lambda Expression
sections.explanation: Both patterns capture the effectively final variable 'prefix' and implement TaskExecutor inline without declaring a separate named class file.

sections.title: Anonymous Inner Class vs Lambda Expression
rows: Can extend abstract/concrete classes OR implement interfaces.
Can ONLY implement Functional Interfaces (Single Abstract Method).
`this` refers to the anonymous inner class instance.
`this` refers to the enclosing outer class instance (Lexical Scope).
Can declare its own instance fields and multiple methods.

sections.title: Try It: The Non-Final Mutation Trap
sections.explanation: Because 'name' is not mutated after initialization, it is effectively final and safely accessible inside the anonymous inner class.

iterations.description: Local variable allocated in method stack frame.
Compiler injects synthetic field inside 0x55FF holding a copy of 'prefix'.
Method finishes; stack variable destroyed. Heap object at 0x55FF retains its captured copy intact.

sections.title: Anonymous Inner Class Traps
items: **Attempting to Mutate Captured Variables**: Writing `count++;` inside an anonymous inner class on a method local variable will not compile; use an `AtomicInteger` or 1-element array `int[] count = {0}` if mutation is needed.
**Constructors are Impossible in Anonymous Classes**: Anonymous classes have no name, so you cannot write a constructor (must use instance initialization blocks `{ ... }` instead).
**Class File Proliferation**: Anonymous inner classes generate separate `.class` files on disk; use Lambdas where possible.

sections.title: Interview Traps: What Does `this` Refer to Inside an Anonymous Class vs a Lambda?

traps.question: What does the `this` keyword point to inside an Anonymous Inner Class compared to inside a Lambda Expression?
traps.trap: Assuming `this` behaves identically in both.
traps.solution:
• **Inside an Anonymous Inner Class**: `this` refers to the **Anonymous Inner Class instance itself**.
• **Inside a Lambda Expression**: `this` refers to the **Enclosing Outer Class instance** (Lambdas use **Lexical Scoping** and do not create a new scope for `this`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Why must a local variable accessed by an anonymous inner class be final or effectively final?
options: To prevent the variable from consuming CPU cache
Because Java copies the variable value to the heap object, and changing it on the stack would cause desynchronization
Because anonymous classes only accept numbers
sections.explanation: Local stack variables are destroyed when methods return. The inner class captures a copy on the heap, requiring immutability to prevent desynchronization.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Anonymous Inner Classes declare and instantiate one-off classes inline without a name.
Captured local variables must be `final` or effectively final.
In anonymous classes, `this` refers to the anonymous instance; in lambdas, `this` refers to the outer class.
Use modern Lambda expressions when implementing Functional Interfaces.

sections.content: Next, we explore Lambda Expressions & Functional Interfaces, mastering the SAM contract, Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, and method references.

lessons.title: Lambda Expressions & Functional Interfaces
lessons.description:
Think of Lambda Expressions as Passing a Pure Action Verb Instead of a Heavy Physical Appliance:
• Pre-Java 8 (The Heavy Box): To tell a worker to filter apples...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `local-and-anonymous-inner-classes`, `interfaces-in-java`, and method signatures.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Lambda Expressions as **Passing a Pure Action Verb Instead of a Heavy Physical Appliance**:
• **Pre-Java 8 (The Heavy Box)**: To tell a worker to filter apples, you manufactured a physical wooden box (`new AppleFilter() { boolean test(Apple a) { ... } }`), placed the rule inside, and carried the box across the room.
• **Modern Java (The Laser Pointer)**: You pass the raw action formula directly: `apple -> apple.getWeight() > 150`.
• Lambdas treat code as data, passing concise executable behaviors as function parameters.

sections.title: What is a Functional Interface?
sections.content:
A **Functional Interface** is an interface that contains **EXACTLY ONE Single Abstract Method (SAM)**.
• Annotated with `@FunctionalInterface` (compiler enforces the single abstract method rule).
• It can contain any number of `default` or `static` methods, but only ONE abstract method.

sections.title: The 4 Core Built-In Functional Interfaces (`java.util.function`)
sections.explanation: The 4 pillars of java.util.function: Predicate (boolean test), Function (transformation), Consumer (accepts input with no return), Supplier (produces output without input).

sections.title: The 4 Core Standard Functional Interfaces
rows: Transform input T to output R

sections.title: Try It: Method References
sections.explanation: f converts 'JAVA ' to 'java ', and consumer c prints it to the console.

iterations.description: JVM invokes bootstrap method LambdaMetafactory.

variables.CallSite Linkage: Generates lightweight SAM wrapper in memory

iterations.description: Dynamically links lambda expression to target method.
Executes boolean check directly with zero class-file generation overhead.

sections.title: Lambda Pitfalls
items: **Adding Multiple Abstract Methods to `@FunctionalInterface`**: Causes compile error: *Unexpected @FunctionalInterface annotation: interface is not a functional interface*.
**Overusing Multi-Line Lambdas**: If a lambda exceeds 3-4 lines of code, extract it into a dedicated helper method and use a Method Reference (`this::helperMethod`) to maintain readability.
**Confusing Method Reference Forms**: `String::length` (instance method on arbitrary object) vs `System.out::println` (instance method on specific object) vs `Math::max` (static method).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can a Functional Interface Have Multiple Methods?

traps.question: Can an interface annotated with `@FunctionalInterface` have 10 methods?
traps.trap: Answering no, thinking it can only have one method total.
traps.solution: YES, **it can have 10 methods**, provided that **EXACTLY ONE is abstract** and the other 9 are `default` or `static` methods (or abstract methods that override public methods from `java.lang.Object` like `equals()`).

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Which functional interface should be used to test whether a number is prime (taking an `Integer` and returning a `boolean`)?
sections.explanation: `Predicate<T>` accepts an input of type `T` and returns a `boolean` (via `boolean test(T t)`).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A Functional Interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM).
The 4 core interfaces are `Predicate` (test), `Function` (transform), `Consumer` (accept), and `Supplier` (produce).
Method References (`Class::method`) provide concise shorthand for lambdas that simply call existing methods.
Lambdas use `invokedynamic` for lightweight runtime linkage.

content.theory:
Lambda expressions, added in Java 8, let you treat behaviour as a value: pass a function to a method, store it in a variable, or return it. They work with functional interfaces, interfaces with exactly one abstract method. Together with method references and streams, lambdas changed how idiomatic Java is written. This lesson covers lambda syntax, functional interfaces, the standard ones in java.util.function, method references, and the rules around captured variables.

## Lambda syntax

A lambda is a parameter list, an arrow and a body:

~~~java
(a, b) -> a + b                        // two parameters, expression body
s -> s.isBlank()                       // one parameter: parentheses optional
() -> System.out.println("hi")         // no parameters
(String s) -> s.length()               // explicit parameter type
(a, b) -> {                            // block body needs return
    int sum = a + b;
    return sum * 2;
}
~~~

Parameter types are usually inferred from the context, the functional interface the lambda is assigned to.

## Functional interfaces

A lambda has no type of its own; it takes the type of the functional interface it's assigned to:

~~~java
@FunctionalInterface
interface DiscountRule {
    long apply(long pricePaise);
}

DiscountRule tenPercent = p -> p * 90 / 100;
long finalPrice = tenPercent.apply(50000);
~~~

The annotation is optional but makes the compiler reject a second abstract method. Default and static methods don't count. Pre-existing interfaces such as `Runnable`, `Comparator` and `Callable` are functional interfaces too, which is why lambdas work with them.

## The standard functional interfaces

The `java.util.function` package covers most needs:

| Interface | Method | Shape | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Predicate<T>` | `test(T)` | T to boolean | `s -> s.isEmpty()` |
| `Function<T, R>` | `apply(T)` | T to R | `s -> s.length()` |
| `Consumer<T>` | `accept(T)` | T to nothing | `s -> System.out.println(s)` |
| `Supplier<T>` | `get()` | nothing to T | `() -> new ArrayList<>()` |
| `UnaryOperator<T>` | `apply(T)` | T to T | `s -> s.trim()` |
| `BinaryOperator<T>` | `apply(T, T)` | (T, T) to T | `(a, b) -> a + b` |
| `BiFunction<T, U, R>` | `apply(T, U)` | (T, U) to R | `(name, age) -> name + age` |

Primitive specializations such as `IntPredicate` and `ToIntFunction` avoid boxing costs. Many have useful default methods for composition: `predicate.and(other)`, `predicate.negate()`, `function.andThen(next)`.

## Method references

When a lambda only calls an existing method, a method reference is shorter:

| Kind | Syntax | Equivalent lambda |
|---|---|---|
| Static method | `Integer::parseInt` | `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)` |
| Instance method of a particular object | `System.out::println` | `x -> System.out.println(x)` |
| Instance method of an arbitrary object | `String::toUpperCase` | `s -> s.toUpperCase()` |
| Constructor | `ArrayList::new` | `() -> new ArrayList<>()` |

## Lambdas with streams

Lambdas made the Streams API practical:

~~~java
List<String> topScorers = students.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.marks() >= 90)
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::marks).reversed())
    .map(Student::name)
    .toList();
~~~

Each step takes a functional interface: `filter` a Predicate, `map` a Function, `sorted` a Comparator.

## Capturing variables

Like anonymous classes, lambdas can use local variables from the enclosing scope only if they're **effectively final**. Lambdas can freely read and modify instance fields, since those live on the heap with the object, though modifying shared state from lambdas, especially in parallel streams, invites race conditions.

## this inside a lambda

A lambda doesn't introduce a new scope for `this`: inside a lambda, `this` refers to the enclosing instance. This differs from anonymous classes, where `this` is the anonymous object.

## Checked exceptions

Standard functional interfaces don't declare checked exceptions, so a lambda calling a method that throws IOException doesn't compile in `map` or `forEach`. Options are catching inside the lambda, wrapping in an unchecked exception, or defining your own functional interface that declares the exception.

## Lambdas and OOP

Lambdas complement objects rather than replacing them. The Strategy pattern becomes a one-line lambda when the strategy has one method. Classes still model concepts with state and multiple behaviours; lambdas handle small pieces of behaviour passed between them.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a functional interface?", "Name the core java.util.function interfaces", "Types of method references" and "Why effectively final?" Give the Predicate, Function, Consumer and Supplier shapes, the four method reference kinds, explain captured copies, and contrast `this` in lambdas with anonymous classes.

lessons.description:
Think of static Members as the Classroom Whiteboard vs Students' Personal Notebooks:
• Instance Fields (Personal Notebooks): Each of the 30 students in the clas...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `memory-execution-overview`, `fields-and-methods`, and `constructors`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of `static` Members as the **Classroom Whiteboard vs Students' Personal Notebooks**:
• **Instance Fields (Personal Notebooks)**: Each of the 30 students in the class has their own notebook on their desk. Student A writing in their notebook does not affect Student B's notebook.
• **Static Fields (The Classroom Whiteboard)**: There is only ONE whiteboard mounted at the front of the room. It belongs to the **Classroom (The Class in Metaspace)**, not any individual student. If any student writes on the whiteboard, every single person in the room immediately sees the change.

sections.title: The 4 Applications of `static` in Java
sections.content:
1. **Static Fields**: Shared class-level variables living in Metaspace (only 1 copy exists across all instances).
2. **Static Methods**: Utility functions called via `ClassName.method()` without creating an object.
3. **Static Blocks (`static { ... }`)**: Initialization code executed ONCE when the class is first loaded into memory.
4. **Static Nested Classes**: Nested classes decoupled from outer instance references.

sections.title: Complete JVM Execution Order: Static vs Instance vs Constructor
sections.explanation: Static blocks execute ONCE on class loading. Instance blocks and constructors execute on every 'new' instantiation.

sections.title: The 4-Step JVM Initialization Order
rows: Class is first referenced / loaded by JVM

sections.title: Try It: Predict Static Execution Order
sections.explanation: Static block runs once (+10). Instance 1 adds instance block (+5) and constructor (+1) = 16. Instance 2 adds instance block (+5) and constructor (+1) = 22.

sections.title: Class Loading & Static Block Memory Trace

iterations.description: Allocates static memory in Metaspace.
Prints Step 1 and Step 2 logs.
Instance block runs -> Constructor runs (Prints Step 3, 4, 5).
Static block is SKIPPED. Instance block -> Constructor runs again.

sections.title: Static Traps
items: **Accessing `this` or `super` in Static Methods**: Static methods have no instance receiver, so calling `this.name` or `super.toString()` causes a compile error.
**Static Memory Leaks**: Holding object references inside a `static List` or `static Map` prevents them from ever being garbage collected, causing `OutOfMemoryError`.
**Non-Thread-Safe Static State**: Modifying a static variable from multiple concurrent threads causes race conditions without proper synchronization.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can a `static` Method Be Synchronized?

traps.question: Can you declare a `static` method with the `synchronized` keyword? What lock does it acquire?
traps.trap: Thinking synchronization only works on instances (`this`).
traps.solution: YES! **A static method can be synchronized**. While an instance synchronized method locks on the current object instance (`this`), a **synchronized static method locks on the `Class` object in Metaspace (`ClassName.class`)**, serializing execution across all threads application-wide.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: When is a `static` initialization block executed in Java?
options: Exactly once when the class is first loaded into memory by the ClassLoader
Every time a static method is invoked
sections.explanation: Static blocks execute exactly once when the class is initially loaded into memory by the JVM ClassLoader.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Static members belong to the Class in Metaspace, shared across all instances.
Static blocks run exactly once on class load; instance blocks run on every `new`.
Static methods cannot access `this`, `super`, or non-static instance fields.
Beware of memory leaks when storing objects in static collections.

lessons.title: Advanced 'final' Keyword: Blank Finals & Concurrency
lessons.description:
Think of Blank Finals and Final Fields in Concurrency as an Engraved Official Notary Seal on a Certificate:
• Blank Final (Unsigned Certificate): A certificate ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `preventing-inheritance-final`, `constructors`, and `static-keyword-deep-dive`.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Blank Finals and Final Fields in Concurrency as an **Engraved Official Notary Seal on a Certificate**:
• **Blank Final (Unsigned Certificate)**: A certificate is printed with a blank signature line. It is invalid until the certified notary fills it in during the commissioning ceremony (**Constructor Body**). Once signed, it can never be rewritten.
• **The Final Field Freeze (Concurrency Safety)**: When you mail the sealed certificate to another city (**Another Thread**), the notary guarantees the ink is completely dry and immutable before the envelope leaves the building, preventing other threads from seeing half-written or corrupted data.

sections.title: The Java Memory Model (JMM) Final Field Freeze Guarantee
sections.content:
Under the Java Memory Model:
• When an object is constructed with `final` fields, the JVM enforces a **StoreStore memory barrier** at the end of the constructor.
• This guarantees that all other threads reading the object reference are **100% guaranteed to see the fully initialized, correct values of all `final` fields** without needing `volatile` or `synchronized` locks!

sections.title: Blank Final Fields & Constructor Definite Assignment
sections.explanation: Blank final fields allow runtime parameterization while guaranteeing immutability after constructor completion.

sections.title: Final Field Types and Initialization Requirements
rows: Constant value fixed at compile/declaration time.
Must be assigned exactly ONCE in every constructor path.
Must be assigned exactly ONCE during class loading.
At method call site (`void log(final String msg)`)
Parameter cannot be reassigned inside method body.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Blank Final Compilation
sections.explanation: Because 'x' is definitely assigned in both if and else branches, the blank final compiles cleanly and sets x to 0.

sections.title: Compiler Definite Assignment Check on Blank Finals

variables.Code: final int x; Constructor(int v) { if (v > 0) x = v; }

iterations.description: Compiler analyzes control flow graph.
Discovers path where 'x' remains unassigned.
Rejects code: *variable x might not have been initialized*.

sections.title: Blank Final Traps
items: **Missing Branch in Constructor**: If any `if/else` or `switch` branch fails to initialize a blank final, compilation fails.
**Reassigning Final Parameters**: Writing `final int count` in a method header and executing `count++` causes compile error: *cannot assign a value to final variable count*.

sections.title: Interview Traps: The Final Field Freeze in Multi-Threading

traps.question: Why is a class with `final` fields thread-safe to publish across threads without synchronization, while a class with non-final fields can suffer from visibility bugs?
traps.trap: Thinking all object reads are equal.
traps.solution: Under the **Java Memory Model (JMM)**, non-final fields can suffer from CPU instruction reordering, where Thread B sees the new object reference before Thread A's constructor has finished writing field values (observing default zeros/nulls). **Final fields enforce a memory freeze barrier**, guaranteeing that any thread seeing the object reference is guaranteed to see the fully written final field values.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Where can a non-static blank final instance field be initialized in Java?
options: At declaration or inside constructor bodies
sections.explanation: Blank finals must be initialized either at their declaration point or inside constructors via definite assignment.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Blank finals allow instance-specific immutability initialized via constructors.
The compiler enforces Definite Assignment across all constructor branches.
Final method parameters prevent accidental variable reassignment.
The JMM Final Field Freeze guarantees thread-safe visibility without locks.

content.theory:
`final` means "assigned once" for variables, "can't be overridden" for methods, and "can't be extended" for classes. The variable case has more depth than it first appears: blank finals, final references to mutable objects, effectively final variables for lambdas, and the special memory-model guarantee that final fields give to multithreaded code. This lesson covers each in detail, along with common misconceptions.

## Final local variables

A final local variable can be assigned only once:

~~~java
final int max = 10;
max = 20;   // compile error
~~~

It doesn't have to be assigned at declaration, as long as every path assigns it exactly once before use:

~~~java
final String label;
if (score >= 90) label = "A";
else label = "B";
~~~

The compiler's definite assignment analysis checks this.

## Final parameters

`void process(final Order order)` prevents reassigning `order` inside the method. Some teams use it everywhere for clarity; others consider it noise because reassigning parameters is already discouraged. It has no effect on callers.

## Final fields and blank finals

A final field must be assigned exactly once by the end of construction. A **blank final** is declared without an initializer and assigned in every constructor:

~~~java
public class Account {
    private final String id;          // blank final

    public Account(String id) { this.id = id; }
    public Account() { this(UUID.randomUUID().toString()); }
}
~~~

If any constructor path fails to assign it, compilation fails. A static final field must be assigned at declaration or in a static block.

## Final references versus immutable objects

The most common misconception: `final` freezes the **reference**, not the **object**.

~~~java
final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Asha");           // allowed: the list changes
names = new ArrayList<>();   // compile error: the reference can't change
~~~

For an unmodifiable list, use `List.of(...)` or `List.copyOf(...)`. An immutable class needs final fields **and** immutable or defensively copied contents.

## Effectively final

A local variable that's never reassigned after initialization is **effectively final**, even without the keyword. Lambdas, anonymous classes and local classes can only capture effectively final variables:

~~~java
int limit = 5;
list.removeIf(x -> x > limit);   // fine: limit is effectively final
limit++;                         // makes the lambda above fail to compile
~~~

Since Java 8, you don't need to write `final` for captured variables; the compiler infers it.

## Final and the memory model

Final fields have a special guarantee in the Java Memory Model: once a constructor finishes, any thread that obtains a reference to the object sees the correctly initialized values of its final fields, without synchronization. Non-final fields don't have this guarantee; another thread could see default values if the object was published unsafely.

This is why immutable objects with final fields are safe to share between threads. The guarantee breaks if `this` escapes during construction, for example by registering the object with a listener inside its constructor.

## Final methods and classes, briefly

- **final methods** can't be overridden, used in template methods and for methods called from constructors
- **final classes** can't be extended, used for immutable value types and security-sensitive classes such as String

## final, finally and finalize

A classic interview trick question compares three unrelated words:

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| `final` | Keyword: assign once, no override, no subclass |
| `finally` | Block after try/catch that runs whether or not an exception occurred |
| `finalize()` | Deprecated Object method once called before garbage collection; don't use it |

## Where final isn't allowed

- constructors can't be final (they aren't inherited, so there's nothing to prevent)
- abstract methods can't be final (they must be overridden)
- a class can't be both abstract and final
- interface methods can't be final

## Using final well

- make fields final by default, and remove it only when mutation is required
- use final classes for value types and anything not designed for extension
- don't rely on final for performance; modern JITs optimize non-final code well

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What does final mean for variables, methods and classes?", "Can a final list be modified?" and "final vs finally vs finalize?" Show that final freezes the reference not the object, explain blank finals and effectively final variables, and mention the memory-model guarantee for immutable objects.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of a Java Enum as a **Certified Fixed Menu of Elite Specialized Objects**:
• In C/C++, enums are just primitive integers in disguise (`0, 1, 2`).
• In Java, **an Enum is a full-fledged Object-Oriented Class**!
• Each enum constant (`PENDING`, `SHIPPED`, `DELIVERED`) is a `public static final` instance of the enum class living on the Heap, complete with its own private fields, constructors, and custom methods.

sections.title: Core Invariants of Java Enums
sections.content:
• Every enum implicitly extends `java.lang.Enum` (cannot extend another class, but CAN implement interfaces).
• Enum constructors are **implicitly `private`** (cannot be called with `new`).
• Enums are type-safe and evaluated at compile time.
• Optimized with specialized collections: **`EnumSet`** (bit-vector $O(1)$ operations) and **`EnumMap`**.

sections.title: Custom Enum with Fields, Methods & Abstract Calculations
sections.explanation: OrderStatus encapsulates custom status codes and descriptions. DatabaseConnectionPool implements a 100% thread-safe Singleton with zero boilerplate.

sections.title: Legacy `public static final int` vs Java `enum`
rows: ❌ NO (Can pass any random integer like `999999`).
Cannot attach fields or methods to ints.

sections.title: Try It: Enum Values & Ordinal
sections.explanation: name() returns 'HIGH', and ordinal() returns its 0-indexed declaration position (2).

iterations.description: ClassLoader loads OrderStatus into Metaspace.
Runs private constructor for each declared constant.

variables.Result: 4 static final instances cached on Heap

iterations.description: Zero additional instances can ever be created.

sections.title: Enum Traps
items: **Relying on `ordinal()` in Business Logic**: `ordinal()` returns the declaration position index. If someone reorders constants, ordinal values change, breaking persisted database data! Always use explicit custom field codes (`statusCode`).
**Attempting to Subclass Enums**: Enums implicitly extend `java.lang.Enum` and cannot be extended via `extends`.
**Calling Enum Constructors with `new`**: `new OrderStatus(100, "...")` produces a compile error: *enum types may not be instantiated*.

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why is Enum the Best Singleton Implementation?

traps.question: Why does Joshua Bloch state in Effective Java that a single-element enum is the best way to implement a Singleton in Java?
traps.trap: Only citing simplicity.
traps.solution:
Because **Enums provide 3 ironclad guarantees automatically**:
1. **Free Thread-Safety**: The JVM guarantees thread-safe class loading and instantiation.
2. **Reflection Attack Immune**: `Constructor.newInstance()` explicitly throws `IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects`.
3. **Free Serialization Safety**: Standard serialization creates duplicate objects; the JVM handles enum serialization specially, guaranteeing zero duplicate instances upon deserialization.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: Can an enum in Java implement an interface?
options: Yes, an enum can implement one or more interfaces
Only if all methods are static
sections.explanation: While enums cannot extend other classes (they already extend `java.lang.Enum`), they can implement multiple interfaces.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Java enums are type-safe classes extending `java.lang.Enum`.
Enum constants can have custom fields, constructors, and methods.
Never rely on `ordinal()` for database persistence; use explicit code fields.
A single-element enum is the gold standard for implementing Singletons in Java.

lessons.title: Java Records: Modern Immutable Data Carriers
lessons.description:
Think of a Java Record as a Machine-Stamped Official Identification Card:
• In legacy Java, creating a simple data transfer object (DTO) required writing 80 lin...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `encapsulation-in-practice`, `the-object-class`, and immutability.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of a Java Record as a **Machine-Stamped Official Identification Card**:
• In legacy Java, creating a simple data transfer object (DTO) required writing 80 lines of boilerplate: private final fields, constructors, getters, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`.
• With **Java Records (Java 14+)**, you write a 1-line blueprint specification (`record Point(int x, int y) {}`).
• The Java compiler automatically manufactures a 100% immutable, thread-safe data carrier with all standard methods pre-built.

sections.title: What the Java Compiler Generates for a Record
sections.content:
Given `public record User(int id, String name) {}`, the compiler automatically generates:
1. `private final int id;` and `private final String name;`.
2. Public Canonical Constructor `public User(int id, String name)`.
3. Component Accessors `id()` and `name()` (Note: NO 'get' prefix!).
4. Value-based `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`.
5. Implicit `extends java.lang.Record` and `final` class modifier.

sections.title: Java Record with Compact Constructor & Custom Validation
sections.explanation: Compact constructors allow clean validation and normalization without duplicate 'this.field = field' boilerplate.

sections.title: Java Record Rules & Invariants
rows: Records are final and sealed in hierarchy.
CAN implement multiple interfaces (`implements A, B`).
CANNOT declare extra instance fields outside header.
All instance state must be declared in component header.
CAN declare `static` fields and static methods.
Useful for constants, factories, and loggers.
Clean modern syntax; not JavaBeans getter style.

sections.title: Try It: Predict Record Accessor Output
sections.explanation: Record component accessors are invoked using p.x() and p.y().

sections.title: Record Creation & Compact Constructor Execution Trace

iterations.description: Enters compact constructor.
Validation guards pass.
Normalizes currency parameter.
Compiler automatically assigns final fields and seals object.

sections.title: Java Record Mistakes
items: **Attempting to Declare Instance Fields**: Writing `private int extraCount;` inside a record body causes compile error: *instance field is not allowed in record*.
**Calling Getters with 'get' Prefix**: Calling `tx.getOrderId()` fails compilation; records use `tx.orderId()`.
**Mutable Components Leak Immutability**: If a record holds an `ArrayList`, external callers can still mutate list contents unless you use defensive copying (`List.copyOf(items)`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Can Records Be Subclassed?

traps.question: Can a Java Record be extended by another class using `class MyClass extends MyRecord`?
traps.trap: Assuming records behave like normal classes.
traps.solution: NO! **All Java Records are implicitly `final` and cannot be extended** (compile error). Additionally, records implicitly extend `java.lang.Record` and cannot extend any other superclass. They are designed strictly as transparent immutable data carriers.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: How are component accessor methods named in a Java record `record User(String username)`?
sections.explanation: Record accessors match the exact component identifier name without any 'get' prefix (e.g. `user.username()`).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Records provide concise immutable data carriers with zero boilerplate.
Auto-generates private final fields, canonical constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString`.
Use Compact Constructors for clean validation and normalization.
Records are implicitly `final` and extend `java.lang.Record`.

lessons.title: Java Generics Basics: Type Safety & Erasure
lessons.description:
Think of Java Generics as Precision-Labeled Shipping Containers:
• Pre-Generics (Raw Unlabeled Crates): You pack objects into a generic wooden crate (ArrayList ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `the-object-class`, `downcasting-and-instanceof`, and compile-time type checking.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
Think of Java Generics as **Precision-Labeled Shipping Containers**:
• **Pre-Generics (Raw Unlabeled Crates)**: You pack objects into a generic wooden crate (`ArrayList list = new ArrayList()`). The crate accepts anything: apples, books, and live dynamite. When unpacking (`(Apple) list.get(0)`), if someone packed dynamite, your code explodes at runtime (`ClassCastException`).
• **Generics (Precision Label `<Apple>`)**: The crate has an electronic scanner at the door (`List<Apple>`). It forbids anything other than Apples from entering at compile time, guaranteeing 100% unpacking safety with zero manual type casts.

sections.title: What is Type Erasure?
sections.content:
Java Generics are a **Compile-Time Safety Feature**:
• The compiler validates all generic types at build time.
• Once compilation succeeds, the compiler performs **Type Erasure**, removing all generic type parameters (`<T>`) and replacing them with raw `Object` (or the bounding superclass) in the `.class` bytecode.
• This guarantees 100% backward compatibility with pre-Java 5 legacy bytecode.

sections.title: Generic Classes, Generic Methods & Bounded Type Parameters
sections.explanation: KeyValuePair<K, V> provides compile-time type safety. calculateSum(<T extends Number>) restricts arguments to subclasses of java.lang.Number.

sections.title: Standard Generic Type Parameter Naming Conventions
Try It: Predict Bounded Type Safety
sections.explanation: Generics eliminate manual downcasting: b.getItem() returns String directly.

variables.Source Code: class Box<T extends Number> { T val; }

iterations.description: Programmer writes bounded generic class.
Compiler rejects: String does not extend Number!
Replaces 'T' with bounding type 'Number': 'class Box { Number val; }'.

variables.Bridge Casts: Emits synthetic checkcasts at call sites

iterations.description: Ensures type safety in bytecode without modifying JVM runtime architecture.

sections.title: Common Generics Traps
items: **Cannot Use Primitives with Generics**: `List<int>` is illegal; you must use wrapper classes `List<Integer>`.
**Cannot Instantiate Generic Types with `new`**: `new T()` or `new T[10]` is illegal because `T` is erased to `Object` at runtime.
**Cannot Check `instanceof` on Parameterized Types**: `if (obj instanceof List<String>)` is illegal due to type erasure (use `if (obj instanceof List<?>)`).

sections.title: Interview Traps: Why Can't You Create Generic Arrays (`new T[10]`)?

traps.question: Why does Java forbid creating generic arrays, such as `T[] arr = new T[10];`?
traps.trap: Thinking it's just missing syntax.
traps.solution:
Because **Java Arrays are Reified (retain type at runtime), while Generics are Erased (type removed at compile time)**!
• Arrays enforce type safety at runtime by checking every store (`arr[0] = item`).
• Because `T` is erased to `Object`, `new T[10]` would create an `Object[]` array in memory, breaking array runtime type safety guarantees.

sections.title: Quick Check
sections.question: What does the Java compiler do to generic type parameters during compilation (Type Erasure)?
options: Creates a separate .class file for every type parameter
Erases type parameters and replaces them with their bounding type (or Object) in bytecode
Converts all objects to C++ pointers
sections.explanation: Type Erasure strips generic type information at compile time, replacing `<T>` with its bound (e.g. `Number` or `Object`) for JVM backward compatibility.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Generics provide compile-time type safety and eliminate manual type casts.
Bounded type parameters (`<T extends Number>`) restrict allowed types to specific hierarchies.
Type Erasure removes generic type parameters in bytecode for backward compatibility.
Cannot use primitive types (`List<int>` is illegal; use `List<Integer>`).

content.theory:
Generics let classes and methods work with any type while keeping compile-time type safety. Before generics, a List held Objects, and every retrieval needed a cast that could fail at runtime. With `List<String>`, the compiler guarantees only strings go in and strings come out. This lesson covers generic classes and methods, bounded types, wildcards and the PECS rule, type erasure, and the restrictions erasure causes.

## The problem generics solve

~~~java
List list = new ArrayList();      // raw type, pre-Java 5 style
list.add("hello");
list.add(42);                     // nothing stops this
String s = (String) list.get(1);  // ClassCastException at runtime
~~~

With generics, the mistake moves to compile time:

~~~java
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(42);                     // compile error
String s = list.get(0);           // no cast needed
~~~

## Generic classes

~~~java
public class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    public void set(T value) { this.value = value; }
    public T get() { return value; }
}

Box<Integer> b = new Box<>();     // diamond operator infers Integer
b.set(5);
int n = b.get();
~~~

`T` is a **type parameter**. Conventional names: `T` (type), `E` (element), `K` and `V` (key and value), `R` (return). Type arguments must be reference types: `Box<int>` isn't allowed, so use `Box<Integer>`.

## Generic methods

A method can declare its own type parameters, before the return type:

~~~java
public static <T> T firstOrDefault(List<T> list, T fallback) {
    return list.isEmpty() ? fallback : list.get(0);
}

String s = firstOrDefault(names, "none");   // T inferred as String
~~~

## Bounded type parameters

`extends` restricts a type parameter to a type and its subtypes, which lets you call that type's methods:

~~~java
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> list) {
    T best = list.get(0);
    for (T item : list) if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;
    return best;
}
~~~

Without the bound, `compareTo` wouldn't compile, because an arbitrary T might not have it. Multiple bounds use `&`: `<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>`.

## Generics aren't covariant

A `List<Integer>` is **not** a `List<Number>`, even though Integer is a Number:

~~~java
List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>();
List<Number> nums = ints;    // compile error
~~~

If it were allowed, you could add a Double through `nums` and corrupt the list of integers. Arrays are covariant, `Integer[]` is a `Number[]`, and that's why arrays throw ArrayStoreException at runtime.

## Wildcards

Wildcards provide flexibility where invariance is too strict:

- `List<?>`: a list of some unknown type; you can read Objects but can't add anything except null
- `List<? extends Number>`: a list of Number or some subtype; you can **read** Numbers but can't add
- `List<? super Integer>`: a list of Integer or some supertype; you can **add** Integers but reads give Object

~~~java
double sum(List<? extends Number> nums) {      // accepts List<Integer>, List<Double>
    double total = 0;
    for (Number n : nums) total += n.doubleValue();
    return total;
}

void fill(List<? super Integer> out) {          // accepts List<Integer>, List<Number>, List<Object>
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) out.add(i);
}
~~~

## PECS

The rule to remember: **Producer Extends, Consumer Super**. If a parameter produces values for you to read, use `extends`; if it consumes values you write, use `super`. `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` shows both.

## Type erasure

Generics exist only at compile time. The compiler checks types, inserts casts, and then **erases** type parameters, replacing them with their bounds (Object if unbounded). At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both plain `List`. This kept compatibility with pre-generics code.

Consequences:

- `new T()` isn't allowed: the type isn't known at runtime
- `new T[10]` and `new List<String>[10]` aren't allowed
- `obj instanceof List<String>` doesn't compile; only `instanceof List<?>` does
- overloads differing only in type arguments clash after erasure
- static fields can't use the class's type parameter, since one static field is shared by all parameterizations

A common workaround for creating instances is passing a `Class<T>` or a `Supplier<T>`.

## Raw types

Using `List` without a type argument is a **raw type**, kept for legacy compatibility. It disables generic checks and produces unchecked warnings. Don't use raw types in new code.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Why use generics?", "What is type erasure?", "Is List<Integer> a List<Number>?" and "Explain wildcards and PECS." Show the compile-time safety benefit, explain invariance with the corrupted-list argument, give PECS with `Collections.copy`, and list erasure's restrictions.
