lessons.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) & Cohesion
lessons.description:
Think of class design as Kitchen Gadgets:
• The God Object Anti-Pattern (Swiss Army Knife): A single gadget with scissors, corkscrew, flashlight, knife, and mag...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `classes-and-objects`, `fields-and-methods`, `encapsulation-in-practice`, and `understanding-encapsulation`.

sections.title: Mental Model: The Swiss Army Knife vs The Specialist Tool
sections.content:
Think of class design as **Kitchen Gadgets**:
• **The God Object Anti-Pattern (Swiss Army Knife)**: A single gadget with scissors, corkscrew, flashlight, knife, and magnifying glass. If the corkscrew breaks or needs sharpening, you have to risk damaging the blade and flashlight just to open it up. If 3 chefs need different tools at the same time, they collide over the same knife.
• **Single Responsibility (Specialist Tools)**: You have a chef's knife, a wine bottle opener, and a torch. Each tool has **only one reason to change** (improving knife alloy only changes the knife, not the bottle opener). High cohesion makes maintenance, unit testing, and team collaboration clean and bug-free.

sections.title: Robert C. Martin's Definition of SRP
sections.content:
"A class should have one, and only one, reason to change."

In practical software engineering, a 'reason to change' maps directly to a **specific stakeholder or business actor**. If an `Invoice` class handles calculating totals (accounting actor), rendering PDF layout (design/UI actor), and writing to SQL database (DB administrator actor), it has THREE separate reasons to change!

sections.title: Violation of SRP vs Clean SRP Separation in Java
sections.explanation: By isolating Invoice (state & calc), InvoicePrinter (view), and InvoiceRepository (DB storage), each component can be modified, refactored, or mock-tested in complete isolation without breaking the others.

sections.title: Cohesion vs Coupling in OOP Architecture
rows: All methods and fields inside a class are closely related to its single purpose.
Easy to understand, reuse, and unit test without complex mock setups.
Classes have minimal direct dependencies on the internal implementation of other classes.
Changing Class A does not ripple breaking bugs across Classes B, C, and D.
A monolithic class that knows or does everything (5000+ lines, 50+ methods).
Impossible to test safely; changes create unexpected side effects across entire app.
Making 1 small business change forces edits across 15 different classes.
Indicates responsibilities are scattered rather than centralized in one cohesive class.

sections.title: Over-Engineering Trap: Don't Atomize into Single-Method Classes
sections.content: SRP does NOT mean every class should have only one method! Cohesion means a class manages **one coherent concept**. An `ArrayList` has `add()`, `remove()`, `get()`, `size()`, and `clear()`. It has multiple methods, but they all serve the single responsibility of managing a dynamically resizing array in memory.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Architectural Impact of SRP

steps.explanation: Tax law introduces tiered tax brackets based on transaction volume.
In clean SRP, you update `Invoice.calculateTotalWithTax()` or inject a `TaxCalculatorStrategy`.
`InvoicePrinter` and `InvoiceRepository` have zero diff in Git, zero regression risk, and need no re-verification.
Unit tests for printing and DB continue passing 100% without modification.

traps.question: How does SRP differ from creating single-method classes?
traps.trap: Creating hundreds of single-method micro-classes (e.g. InvoiceValidator, InvoiceSaver), destroying code readability.
traps.solution: Group cohesive behaviors that change for the same business actor under one class. Separate only when different business actors or systems drive changes.

traps.question: Should logging and database transactions be written directly inside business domain entities?
traps.trap: Mixing Logging, Security, and Caching directly inside Core Entities violates SRP and tightly couples business logic to infrastructure.
traps.solution: Use Decorator Pattern, Proxy Pattern, or Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP / Interceptors) for cross-cutting infrastructure concerns.

sections.question: Which of the following scenarios is the clearest violation of the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
options: A `UserManager` class that validates user credentials, generates JWT tokens, formats HTML welcome emails, and writes raw SQL queries to insert user records into PostgreSQL.
A `MathUtil` class containing static methods `factorial()`, `gcd()`, and `isPrime()`.
sections.explanation: Option B is a classic God Object anti-pattern: authentication, token generation, email templating, and SQL persistence are 4 distinct responsibilities with 4 different reasons to change.

items: SRP states that a class should have only one reason to change (one primary actor/responsibility).
Aim for high cohesion (closely related methods) and low coupling (minimal direct dependencies).
Symptoms of SRP violation include God Classes, fragile tests, and high merge conflict rates during teamwork.
SRP does not mean one method per class; it means one unified domain purpose.

content.theory:
The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), the S in SOLID, says a class should have only one reason to change. It's often misread as "a class should do one thing", but its real focus is on who requests changes: each class should answer to one source of requirements. Classes that mix responsibilities become hard to change, hard to test and prone to unrelated breakages. This lesson explains SRP precisely, how to spot violations, how to split classes, and how to avoid overdoing it.

## The principle

Robert C. Martin, who popularized SOLID, phrases SRP as "a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor", where an actor is a group of people who request changes. If the finance team and the operations team can both force changes to the same class for unrelated reasons, that class has two responsibilities.

## A violation

~~~java
public class Invoice {
    private final List<LineItem> items;

    public long total() { ... }                       // business rules: finance
    public String toHtml() { ... }                    // presentation: UI team
    public void saveToDatabase(Connection c) { ... }  // persistence: platform team
    public void emailTo(String address) { ... }       // delivery: operations
}
~~~

Problems:

- a change to the HTML layout risks breaking the tax calculation, because both live in one file
- testing `total()` drags in database and email dependencies
- two developers changing unrelated features conflict in the same class
- reusing the calculation in a mobile app also pulls in HTML and SQL code

## Splitting the responsibilities

~~~java
public class Invoice {                        // business rules only
    private final List<LineItem> items;
    public long total() { ... }
}

public class InvoiceHtmlRenderer {            // presentation
    public String render(Invoice invoice) { ... }
}

public interface InvoiceRepository {          // persistence
    void save(Invoice invoice);
}

public class InvoiceMailer {                  // delivery
    private final EmailClient client;
    public void send(Invoice invoice, String to) { ... }
}
~~~

Each class now changes for one reason. The core Invoice class has no I/O dependencies and can be tested in isolation.

## Spotting violations

- **The "and" test**: describing the class needs "and": "it calculates totals and renders HTML and saves to the database"
- **Vague names**: `Manager`, `Processor`, `Helper`, `Utils` often hide many responsibilities
- **Mixed imports**: a class importing both `java.sql` and HTML or HTTP libraries
- **Size**: a class of thousands of lines, or methods that don't share fields, often called low cohesion
- **Change history**: if one file shows up in commits for many unrelated features, it's doing too much

## Cohesion

SRP is closely related to **cohesion**: how strongly a class's members belong together. In a cohesive class, most methods use most fields. If one group of methods uses fields A and B while another group uses C and D, the class is two classes sharing a file.

## SRP at other levels

The idea applies beyond classes:

- **methods**: a method should do one thing at one level of abstraction
- **modules and packages**: group code that changes together
- **microservices**: each service owns one business capability

## Don't over-split

SRP doesn't mean one method per class. Splitting too far creates many tiny classes with heavy coordination, where following a single feature means opening a dozen files. Split along **real axes of change**, ones that have changed or clearly will. A small class that does a few closely related things for one actor is fine.

## SRP and other principles

- splitting responsibilities often reveals interfaces, such as `InvoiceRepository`, that support dependency inversion
- focused classes are easier to extend without modification, supporting open-closed
- smaller interfaces follow naturally, supporting interface segregation

## A worked example

A `UserService` that registers users, hashes passwords, sends welcome emails and writes audit logs answers to product, security, marketing and compliance teams. Splitting it gives `UserRegistration` for the workflow, a `PasswordHasher` owned by security, a `WelcomeMailer` owned by marketing and an `AuditLog` owned by compliance. Each piece now changes only when its own team asks, and the registration workflow reads as a short sequence of calls.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Explain SRP with an example", "How do you identify a violation?" and low-level design reviews where a god class must be split. Use the "one reason to change, one actor" definition, show the Invoice split into calculation, rendering, persistence and delivery, and mention cohesion and the risk of over-splitting.

lessons.title: Open-Closed Principle (OCP) & Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
lessons.description:
Think of OCP and LSP in terms of USB-C Standards:
• Open-Closed Principle (OCP): A computer's USB-C port is closed for modification (you don't tear open the lap...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `what-is-polymorphism`, `method-overriding-polymorphism`, `abstract-classes`, and `interfaces-in-java`.

sections.title: Mental Model: Hardware Ports & Plug-in Adapters
sections.content:
Think of OCP and LSP in terms of **USB-C Standards**:
• **Open-Closed Principle (OCP)**: A computer's USB-C port is **closed for modification** (you don't tear open the laptop motherboard and re-solder chips every time you want to plug in a webcam) but **open for extension** (anyone can engineer a new USB-C microphone, display, or flash drive that plugs right in).
• **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)**: If a device claims to be a USB-C device, plugging it in must NEVER short-circuit your motherboard, blow a fuse, or throw unexpected hardware panics. Subtypes must honor the exact behavioral contract of the parent type.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.content:
• **Open-Closed Principle (OCP)**: Software entities (classes, modules, functions) should be *open for extension, but closed for modification*.
• **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)**: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness or intended behavior of the program ($S \subseteq T$ implies objects of type $T$ may be replaced with objects of type $S$).

sections.title: Open-Closed Principle: Eliminating Switch / If-Else Cascades
sections.explanation: When marketing introduces a 'BlackFridayDiscount', we simply create a new class implementing DiscountStrategy without touching CheckoutService or existing discount classes.

sections.title: The Classic LSP Violation: Square Inheriting from Rectangle
sections.explanation: Square breaks the post-conditions and behavior expected of a Rectangle (setting width independently of height). A Square is NOT a behavioral subtype of Rectangle in OOP mutability.

sections.title: LSP Behavioral Contract Rules (Barbara Liskov)
rows: Subclass cannot require stricter input conditions than parent.
Parent allows negative numbers; child throws `IllegalArgumentException` on negative.
Subclass must guarantee at least as much as parent.
Parent guarantees `balance >= 0`; child allows overdraft into negative balance.
State invariants of parent must be preserved by child.
Rectangle invariant (independent width/height) broken by Square.
Child cannot mutate immutable state defined by parent.
Child adds mutator method to an ostensibly immutable collection/record parent.
Child overridden method cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions.
Child method signature adds `throws Exception` not declared in parent.

sections.title: Execution Trace: Why Square Breaks Rectangle's Contract
sections.code:
Rectangle r = new Square();
r.setWidth(5);  // Square sets width=5 AND height=5
r.setHeight(10); // Square sets width=10 AND height=10
int area = r.getArea(); // 10 * 10 = 100 instead of 5 * 10 = 50

steps.explanation: Caller passes reference `r` typed as `Rectangle` to `resize()`.
`r.setWidth(5)` runs. Overridden Square implementation silently sets BOTH width=5 and height=5.
`r.setHeight(10)` runs. Square overrides and mutates BOTH width=10 and height=10.
`r.getArea()` returns $10 \times 10 = 100$. Caller expected $5 \times 10 = 50$. The client code fails or produces corrupt financial data.

traps.question: Why does throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass break LSP?
traps.trap: Subclasses like ReadOnlyArrayList throwing UnsupportedOperationException on add() crash callers expecting standard List behavior.
traps.solution: Split into segregated interfaces: ReadableCollection and MutableCollection instead of forcing read-only classes to inherit mutating methods.

traps.question: Is using instanceof checks in client code an acceptable workaround for subclass differences?
traps.trap: Using instanceof checks in client code (e.g. if shape instanceof Square) violates both OCP and LSP.
traps.solution: Rely exclusively on polymorphic method dispatch defined in the common interface.

sections.question: An engineer creates an abstract class `Bird` with method `fly()`. They create `Ostrich extends Bird` and implement `fly()` by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException("Ostriches cannot fly!")`. Which principle is violated?
sections.explanation: This is a textbook LSP violation. Any client expecting a `Bird` and invoking `fly()` will crash at runtime when passed an `Ostrich`. `Bird` should not enforce flying as a universal behavior for all avian species.

items: OCP states systems should allow adding new features by writing new classes, not editing existing battle-tested code.
LSP mandates that subclasses must behave seamlessly in place of parent classes without breaking client invariants or throwing unexpected exceptions.
The Square-Rectangle paradox proves that real-world 'is-a' relationships do not always translate to OOP mutable inheritance.
Never override a parent method with `throw new UnsupportedOperationException()`—use interface segregation instead.

lessons.title: Interface Segregation (ISP) & Dependency Inversion (DIP)
lessons.description:
Think of ISP and DIP as Modern Electronics & Wall Sockets:
• Interface Segregation (ISP - Slim Ports): Instead of one massive 50-pin master port on your smartph...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should understand `interfaces-in-java`, `abstract-class-vs-interface`, `downcasting-and-instanceof`, and `open-closed-and-liskov`.

sections.title: Mental Model: Power Outlets & Slim Interfaces
sections.content:
Think of ISP and DIP as **Modern Electronics & Wall Sockets**:
• **Interface Segregation (ISP - Slim Ports)**: Instead of one massive 50-pin master port on your smartphone (charging + audio + video + antenna + biometric + keyboard), you have focused, segregated interfaces (USB-C for power/data, Bluetooth for audio). Clients only connect to the capabilities they actually need.
• **Dependency Inversion (DIP - Wall Outlets)**: Your lamp does NOT solder its power wires directly into the high-voltage electrical grid transformer down the street (tight coupling to low-level details). Instead, both the lamp and the power grid depend on an **abstraction (the standard 120V/230V wall socket interface)**. You can unplug a desk lamp and plug in a laptop charger without rebuilding your house.

sections.title: Formal Definitions
sections.content:
• **Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)**: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer many small, client-specific interfaces over one 'fat/polluted' general-purpose interface.
• **Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)**:
  1. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions (interfaces/abstract classes).
  2. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details (concrete implementations) should depend on abstractions.

sections.title: Interface Segregation Principle: Refactoring Fat Interfaces
sections.explanation: Segregating interfaces ensures clients are never forced to provide empty dummy implementations or throw UnsupportedOperationExceptions.

sections.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) & Dependency Injection (DI)
sections.explanation: NotificationService no longer instantiates concrete senders with 'new'. By accepting the MessageService interface via constructor injection, the high-level business service is decoupled and 100% testable with mock services.

sections.title: Complete Summary of All 5 SOLID Principles
rows: A class should have 1 reason to change.
God classes, huge bloated files with 20+ unrelated methods.
Open for extension, closed for modification.
Subtypes must preserve base type contracts.
Segregate interfaces, check invariants, avoid fake inheritance.
Clients shouldn't depend on unused methods.
Forced empty dummy method overrides across implementing classes.
Split fat interfaces into small role interfaces.
Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes.
Hardcoded `new ConcreteClass()` inside high-level business logic.

sections.title: Dependency Inversion in Unit Testing & Mocking

steps.explanation: Test creates a `MockMessageService` that does not send real network packets or incur API costs.
`NotificationService` accepts the mock without knowing or caring that it is a test double.
`testService.notifyUser()` executes in <1ms completely offline in memory.
Unit test asserts `mock.wasSent == true` reliably and deterministically.

traps.question: What is the key difference between Dependency Inversion (DIP) and Dependency Injection (DI)?
traps.trap: Confusing DIP with DI in technical system design interviews.
traps.solution: DIP is the architectural principle (depend on abstractions). Dependency Injection (DI) is the concrete pattern/technique (passing dependencies via constructor/setter) used to satisfy DIP.

traps.question: Why are monolithic 'Mega-Repository' interfaces considered bad practice?
traps.trap: Creating one gigantic repository interface forces lightweight UI consumers to depend on unneeded destructive operations (violates ISP).
traps.solution: Break large interfaces into small role-focused query/command interfaces (e.g. UserReader, UserWriter).

sections.question: Which code snippet best demonstrates the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)?
options: `public class OrderService { private MySQLDatabase db = new MySQLDatabase(); }`
`public class OrderService { private DatabaseConnection db; public OrderService(DatabaseConnection db) { this.db = db; } }` (where `DatabaseConnection` is an interface)
`public class OrderService extends MySQLDatabase { public void process() { super.insert(); } }`
`public class OrderService { public void save() { MySQLDatabase.getInstance().insert(); } }`
sections.explanation: Option B depends on the `DatabaseConnection` interface and receives the dependency via constructor injection, completely decoupling `OrderService` from specific DB implementations like MySQL, Mongo, or PostgreSQL.

items: ISP advocates for small, role-focused interfaces (`Printable`, `Closeable`, `AutoCloseable`, `Comparable`) rather than monolithic super-interfaces.
DIP decouples high-level policy logic from low-level infrastructure details by inserting an interface abstraction between them.
Dependency Injection (DI) is the primary programmatic mechanism used to achieve DIP without hardcoding `new` operator calls.
Adhering to SOLID principles produces software that is scalable, easy to extend, simple to test, and resistant to architectural rot.

lessons.title: OOP Design Patterns, Anti-Patterns & Technical Interview Traps
lessons.description:
Think of Design Patterns as Civil Engineering Blueprints for Recurring Architectural Challenges:
• Creational (How to build): E.g., Factory Method & Singleton. ...

sections.title: Prerequisites
sections.content: You should have completed all prior OOP modules: Fundamentals, Encapsulation, Constructors, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction, and Advanced OOP.

sections.title: Mental Model: Design Patterns as Architectural Blueprints
sections.content:
Think of Design Patterns as **Civil Engineering Blueprints for Recurring Architectural Challenges**:
• **Creational (How to build)**: E.g., **Factory Method & Singleton**. How objects are instantiated without coupling client code to exact constructor signatures or creating duplicate shared state.
• **Structural (How to assemble)**: E.g., **Adapter & Decorator**. How classes and objects compose to form larger structures (like a power plug adapter bridging UK plugs to US sockets).
• **Behavioral (How to communicate)**: E.g., **Observer & Strategy**. How algorithms, responsibilities, and events are distributed cleanly among collaborating objects.

sections.title: The Top 3 Must-Know Design Patterns for Placement Coding Rounds
sections.content:
1. **Singleton Pattern**: Ensures a class has only ONE instance and provides a global access point (e.g., ThreadPool, Logger, DB Connection Manager).
2. **Factory Method Pattern**: Defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses or factories decide which class to instantiate.
3. **Strategy Pattern**: Defines a family of interchangeable algorithms and makes them selectable at runtime.

sections.title: Thread-Safe Singleton with Double-Checked Locking in Java
sections.explanation: The 'volatile' keyword is mandatory: it prevents JVM compiler reordering where memory is allocated and assigned to 'instance' before the constructor finishes executing.

sections.title: Factory Method & Strategy Patterns in Action
sections.explanation: Strategy decouples routing algorithms from the Navigator client, and Factory centralizes instantiation logic so clients never call concrete constructors directly.

sections.title: OOP Anti-Patterns Every Placement Candidate Must Recognize
rows: A 4000-line class holding 80% of entire application state.
Zero modularity, merge conflict nightmare, untestable.
Extract classes following Single Responsibility Principle.
Old legacy methods kept 'just in case' with TODOs from 2021.
Confuses new developers, increases cognitive load.
Delete aggressively; Git history preserves old code.
Tangled control flow with circular dependencies between classes.
Changing class A breaks class B which breaks class A.
Establish clear layered architecture (UI -> Service -> Repository).
Using one favorite design pattern (e.g., Singleton or Factory) everywhere.
Adds massive unnecessary boilerplate for simple 10-line scripts.
Apply patterns only when architectural pain justifies them.
Deep inheritance hierarchies (8+ levels: A extends B extends C...).
Reading a method requires jumping up and down 10 source files.
Favor Object Composition over deep inheritance hierarchies.

sections.title: Interview Question Breakdown: Composition vs Inheritance

steps.explanation: Inheritance creates tight compile-time coupling (fragile base class problem: modifying superclass can silently break subclasses).
Inheritance exposes superclass internal implementation details to child classes (breaks encapsulation).
Java allows only Single Inheritance: extending a class consumes the class's only inheritance slot.
Composition allows swapping behavior dynamically at runtime (e.g. `car.setEngine(new ElectricEngine())`) while keeping engine internals private.

traps.question: Why is synchronizing the entire getInstance() method an anti-pattern for Singletons?
traps.trap: Synchronizing the entire getInstance() method introduces a major thread bottleneck on every single read call.
traps.solution: Use Double-Checked Locking with volatile or an Initialization-on-Demand Holder / Enum Singleton.

traps.question: How can standard Java Singletons be broken via Reflection or Serialization?
traps.trap: Standard Singletons can be bypassed by setting constructor accessibility to true via Reflection, or deserializing duplicate objects.
traps.solution: Implement readResolve() for serialization and throw exceptions in constructor, or use a single-element enum which JVM natively protects.

traps.question: When does applying design patterns become an anti-pattern (Premature Abstraction)?
traps.trap: Creating abstract factories, visitors, and mediators for trivial scripts introduces massive unnecessary cognitive overhead.
traps.solution: Write simple, clean code first; refactor to design patterns only when real business variation or complexity requires it.

sections.question: Which of the following is the most robust, thread-safe, reflection-proof way to implement a Singleton in Java?
options: Eager initialization with a `public static final` field.
Lazy initialization with `synchronized public static Singleton getInstance()`.
sections.explanation: As noted in Joshua Bloch's Effective Java, a single-element enum is the gold standard: it provides 100% thread safety, handles serialization automatically, and the JVM strictly prohibits reflection-based instantiation of enum constants.

items: Creational patterns handle instantiation, Structural patterns handle composition, and Behavioral patterns handle object communication.
Always use Double-Checked Locking with `volatile` or an `enum` when building Singletons.
Favor composition over inheritance to avoid fragile base class coupling and maintain flexible runtime behavior.
Avoid common anti-patterns like God Classes, Yo-Yo Inheritance hierarchies, and Premature Abstraction in interview rounds.

content.theory:
Design patterns are named, proven solutions to recurring design problems. Knowing the common ones lets you communicate designs in a word ("use a strategy here") and recognize them in frameworks. OOP interviews combine pattern questions with tricky output puzzles that test precise knowledge of the language. This lesson surveys the patterns interviewers ask about most, with when to use each, and then collects the classic OOP traps from across the course.

## Pattern categories

The Gang of Four book (1994) grouped 23 patterns into three families:

| Category | Concern | Common examples |
|---|---|---|
| Creational | How objects are created | Singleton, Factory Method, Builder, Prototype |
| Structural | How objects are composed | Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite |
| Behavioural | How objects interact | Strategy, Observer, Command, Template Method, State |

## Singleton

Ensures one instance with global access. Thread-safe options:

~~~java
public enum Clock { INSTANCE; }                          // simplest, reflection-safe

public final class Config {                              // lazy holder idiom
    private Config() { }
    private static class Holder { static final Config I = new Config(); }
    public static Config get() { return Holder.I; }
}
~~~

Caution: singletons are global state, which hides dependencies and complicates testing. Prefer one instance managed by a DI container where possible. A classic follow-up asks about double-checked locking, which requires the field to be `volatile`.

## Factory Method and Builder

**Factory** centralizes object creation, returning an interface type so callers don't depend on concrete classes. **Builder** constructs complex objects step by step with named settings, avoiding telescoping constructors, as in `HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(...).GET().build()`.

## Adapter, Decorator and Proxy

- **Adapter** converts one interface to another, such as wrapping a third-party SMS SDK to match your `MessageSender` interface
- **Decorator** wraps an object with the same interface to add behaviour, as with `new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file))`
- **Proxy** stands in for another object to control access, add caching, or load lazily; Spring uses proxies for transactions

All three wrap objects, but their intents differ: change the interface, add behaviour, or control access.

## Strategy, Observer and Command

- **Strategy**: interchangeable algorithms behind one interface; often a lambda today
- **Observer**: subjects notify registered listeners of changes, as in event systems and UI frameworks
- **Command**: requests as objects, enabling undo stacks, queues and logging

## Patterns aren't goals

Patterns solve specific problems. Applying them without the problem adds indirection: a factory for one class, or a strategy with one implementation. Interviewers value candidates who can explain why a pattern fits and when it doesn't.

## Classic OOP traps

These questions recur constantly. Each was covered earlier in the course:

1. **Fields aren't polymorphic.** `Parent p = new Child(); p.name` reads Parent's field; `p.getName()` runs Child's override
2. **Static methods are hidden, not overridden.** A static call through a parent reference runs the parent's version
3. **Overloads are chosen at compile time.** `Object o = "hi"; print(o)` calls `print(Object)`, not `print(String)`
4. **Widening beats boxing beats varargs.** `f(5)` prefers `f(long)` over `f(Integer)`
5. **Constructors call overridable methods dangerously.** A parent constructor calling an override sees the child's fields uninitialized
6. **equals without hashCode breaks HashSet.** Equal objects land in different buckets
7. **`equals(Point)` doesn't override `equals(Object)`.** Use @Override to catch it
8. **== compares references.** Two `new String("a")` are `==`-different but `equals`-same
9. **final freezes references, not objects.** A final list can still be modified
10. **Private methods can't be overridden.** A same-named subclass method is unrelated
11. **Java is pass-by-value.** A method can change an object's fields but not the caller's reference
12. **Integer caching.** `Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b` is true, but with 128 it's typically false, because only -128 to 127 are cached. Always compare wrappers with `equals`
13. **Adding any constructor removes the default one.** Subclasses relying on implicit `super()` then fail to compile
14. **Abstract classes have constructors; interfaces don't.**

## Answering design questions

For low-level design rounds (parking lot, elevator, library system):

1. clarify requirements and scope
2. identify core entities (nouns) and their responsibilities
3. define interfaces where variation exists, applying SOLID
4. name the patterns you use and why
5. discuss extensions: how a new vehicle type or payment method fits without modifying existing classes

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Implement a thread-safe singleton", "Difference between Adapter, Decorator and Proxy?", rapid output puzzles from the trap list, and a low-level design problem. Know two singleton implementations and their trade-offs, distinguish wrappers by intent, trace traps with the reference-type versus object-type rule, and justify every pattern you use with the problem it solves.

description: From your first SELECT to window functions and the most-asked placement queries. Every example runs in the built-in SQL Lab against its preloaded employees and departments tables.

modules.description: Introduction to RDBMS, tables, and fundamental database concepts.

lessons.title: What is a Database: Flat Files vs DBMS
lessons.description:
Imagine tracking millions of bank transactions using a single shared Excel spreadsheet (Flat File System):
• Data Redundancy & Anomaly: Customer addresses are c...

sections.title: Mental Model: The Ledger Spreadsheet vs The Vault Filing System
sections.content:
Imagine tracking millions of bank transactions using a single shared **Excel spreadsheet (Flat File System)**:
• **Data Redundancy & Anomaly**: Customer addresses are copy-pasted across 10,000 rows. When a customer moves, updating 9,999 rows leaves 1 row stale (Update Anomaly).
• **Concurrency Collisions**: Two bank tellers open the Excel file at 9:00:00 AM. Teller A deposits $100; Teller B withdraws $50. Whoever clicks 'Save' last overwrites the other's work entirely (Lost Update Problem).
• **Security & Integrity Violations**: Anyone with file access can accidentally type 'FREE MONEY' into a balance cell because text files lack strict mathematical constraint validation.

A **Database Management System (DBMS)** is an ACID-compliant engine that acts as a secure, high-throughput financial vault: it guarantees atomic operations, enforces strict schema types, handles 50,000 concurrent read/write queries per second with multi-version concurrency control (MVCC), and ensures catastrophic crash recovery.

sections.title: Formal Definition of DBMS
sections.content: A **Database Management System (DBMS)** is specialized system software designed to define, create, query, update, administer, and protect structured data. It abstracts low-level operating system disk block allocations and buffer pool caching behind declarative query interfaces (like SQL).

sections.title: Flat File System vs Database Management System (DBMS)
rows: High. Duplicated data leads to update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.
Primitive file-level locks. Simultaneous writes corrupt or overwrite data.
Granular row-level locks and Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC).
System crash during file write causes file corruption or half-written records.
Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and redo/undo logs guarantee crash resilience.
No automatic type safety (e.g. string allowed in numeric price column).
Enforced via strict constraints: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, NOT NULL.
O(N) full linear scans through entire files.
O(log N) B+ Tree index lookups, query planners, and buffer cache pools.

sections.title: Demonstrating Data Integrity Enforcement in SQL
sections.code:
-- Creating a structured table with strict domain constraints
CREATE TABLE bank_accounts (
    account_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_holder VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0.00),
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- 1. Valid insertion
INSERT INTO bank_accounts (account_id, account_holder, balance)
VALUES (101, 'Alice Smith', 1500.50);

-- 2. INVALID INSERTION: Negative balance triggers CHECK constraint rejection!
-- Result: ERROR: new row for relation "bank_accounts" violates check constraint "bank_accounts_balance_check"
INSERT INTO bank_accounts (account_id, account_holder, balance)
VALUES (102, 'Bob Jones', -250.00);
sections.explanation: Unlike flat files where bad data silently corrupts systems, an RDBMS actively rejects illegal states at the engine level before data hits disk.

sections.title: Execution Trace: The Lost Update Problem in Flat Files vs DBMS Isolation
sections.code:
-- Scenario: Initial account balance = $1000
-- Teller 1 deposits $200. Teller 2 withdraws $300 at the exact same millisecond.

steps.explanation: Flat File: Teller 1 and Teller 2 both read balance = $1000 into local memory buffers simultaneously.

Flat File: Teller 1 computes $1000 + $200 = $1200 and writes to disk at t=10ms. Teller 2 computes $1000 - $300 = $700 and writes to disk at t=12ms. Final file balance = $700 (The $200 deposit was completely erased!).
DBMS (Transactions): Teller 1 begins transaction and acquires row lock. Teller 2 is queued.
DBMS: Teller 1 updates balance to $1200 and commits. Row lock releases. Teller 2 reads authoritative new balance $1200, subtracts $300, and commits balance = $900. Total integrity preserved.

sections.title: Common Novice Assumption: A Database is NOT Just a Place to Dump JSON
sections.content: Beginners often ask: 'Why not just use MongoDB or JSON files for everything?' Relational databases provide mathematical guarantees of referential integrity and joins that document stores cannot enforce natively across collections. Use relational DBMS for financial, transactional, and relational domain models.

traps.question: What are the 3 major anomalies caused by data redundancy in flat file storage?
traps.trap: Listing generic bugs like 'slow performance' or 'file size too big'.
traps.solution: The formal database anomalies are: 1. Insertion Anomaly (cannot record an entity without creating a dummy parent), 2. Deletion Anomaly (deleting one piece of info inadvertently wipes out unrelated historical data), 3. Update Anomaly (modifying data in one row leaves inconsistent copies elsewhere).

traps.question: Why can't operating system file locks replace a DBMS transaction manager?
traps.trap: Thinking OS file locks provide ACID properties.
traps.solution: OS locks are coarse-grained (entire file or byte-range), lack atomic multi-file coordination, have no undo/redo write-ahead logs for crash rollback, and do not provide SQL isolation levels (Read Committed, Serializable).

sections.question: Which of the following scenarios describes an Update Anomaly in a poorly structured database or flat file system?
options: A query runs out of memory while computing an average.
A customer's phone number is updated in the orders table, but remains outdated in the shipping table because the data was duplicated.
Two users attempt to insert records with the same primary key.
A hard drive failure wipes uncommitted transaction logs.
sections.explanation: An update anomaly occurs when data redundancy causes inconsistent data copies across different records after a partial modification.

items: DBMS solves the 4 critical flaws of flat files: redundancy anomalies, concurrency collisions, lack of integrity constraints, and crash vulnerability.
Relational databases enforce strict mathematical schemas with declarative SQL interfaces.
Concurrency control mechanisms (like MVCC and locking) prevent lost updates and race conditions during high-volume operations.
Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) ensures full durability and recovery even during power outages.

content.theory:
A database is an organized collection of data, and a database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores it, retrieves it and keeps it correct while many users work at once. Before databases, applications kept data in their own files, which led to duplication, inconsistency and lost updates. This lesson explains what goes wrong with flat files, what a DBMS adds, the main kinds of databases in use today, and where SQL fits.

## The flat-file approach

Imagine a college keeping student records in spreadsheets: one file for admissions, another for the library, another for fees. Each office maintains its own copy of each student's name, phone number and address. Problems follow quickly:

- **Redundancy**: the same facts are stored many times, wasting space
- **Inconsistency**: when a student changes their phone number, one office updates it and others don't, so the files disagree
- **Hard queries**: answering "which students with unpaid fees borrowed library books?" means writing a custom program to cross-reference files
- **No concurrency control**: two clerks editing the same file at once can overwrite each other's changes
- **Weak security**: file permissions are all-or-nothing, so you can't let the library see names without also seeing fee records
- **No recovery**: a crash in the middle of saving can leave a file half-written

## What a DBMS provides

A DBMS solves these problems by putting all access to the data through one system:

| Problem with files | What the DBMS does |
|---|---|
| Redundancy and inconsistency | Stores each fact once, with constraints that reject invalid data |
| Hard queries | Offers a query language, SQL, that answers new questions without new programs |
| Concurrent edits | Uses transactions and locking so simultaneous users don't corrupt data |
| Security | Grants permissions per table, column or action |
| Crashes | Logs changes so it can recover to a consistent state |

## Data independence

A key benefit is **data independence**: applications describe what data they want, not how it's stored. The DBMS can add an index, move data to a faster disk or change file formats without any application changing. This separation, between the logical view of data and its physical storage, is one of the main reasons databases replaced hand-written file code.

## The three-schema architecture

Databases separate three levels of description:

- **External level**: the views different users see, such as a library view that shows names and borrowed books only
- **Conceptual level**: the full logical structure, meaning all tables, columns and relationships
- **Internal level**: how data is physically stored, including files, pages and indexes

Changes at one level shouldn't force changes at the levels above it.

## Kinds of databases

Relational databases dominate, but other models serve particular needs:

| Type | Data model | Examples | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relational | Tables with rows and columns | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Oracle, SQL Server | Business data, transactions, most applications |
| Document | JSON-like documents | MongoDB, Couchbase | Flexible or nested records |
| Key-value | Keys mapped to values | Redis, DynamoDB | Caching, sessions, fast lookups |
| Wide-column | Rows with flexible column families | Cassandra, HBase | Massive write-heavy workloads |
| Graph | Nodes and edges | Neo4j | Social networks, recommendations |

Non-relational systems are often grouped as **NoSQL**. Many trade some of the guarantees relational databases give, such as strict consistency or joins, for easier horizontal scaling or a more flexible schema. In practice, most companies use a relational database as their main system of record, and add others for specific jobs.

## Where SQL fits

SQL, the Structured Query Language, is the standard language for relational databases. It's **declarative**: you describe the result you want, and the DBMS's query optimizer decides how to compute it, such as which index to use or in which order to join tables. Compare writing a loop that scans files and merges records with writing one line:

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM students WHERE fees_due > 0;
~~~

SQL was developed at IBM in the 1970s and became an ANSI standard in 1986. It remains one of the most widely used programming languages, and nearly every backend, data or analyst role expects it.

## Database, DBMS and database system

These terms are often mixed up:

- **Database**: the data itself
- **DBMS**: the software managing it, such as PostgreSQL
- **Database system**: the DBMS together with its databases and the applications using them

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a DBMS and why use one instead of files?" and "SQL versus NoSQL?" List the file-system problems (redundancy, inconsistency, concurrency, security, recovery), explain data independence, and compare relational and non-relational databases by data model and scaling trade-offs rather than declaring one better.

sources.title: SQLite: SQL As Understood By SQLite
E. F. Codd, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (1970)

lessons.title: The Relational Model & Codd's Foundations
lessons.description: In 1970, Dr. Edgar F. Codd revolutionized computing with a radical proposal: separate how data is physically stored on magnetic tape/disk from how humans logica...

sections.title: Mental Model: Mathematical Sets and Cartesian Grids
sections.content:
In 1970, Dr. Edgar F. Codd revolutionized computing with a radical proposal: **separate how data is physically stored on magnetic tape/disk from how humans logically view and query it**.
• In the Relational Model, data is represented as **Relations (Tables)**.
• A relation is mathematically a **set of tuples (unordered rows)** where every element in a tuple corresponds to an **attribute (column)** belonging to a specific domain (data type).
• Because a relation is a mathematical set: **row order does NOT matter, duplicate rows are forbidden by definition, and column order is irrelevant**.

sections.title: Codd's Relational Terminology vs Everyday SQL Terms
sections.content:
• **Relation** $\leftrightarrow$ **Table**
• **Tuple** $\leftrightarrow$ **Row / Record**
• **Attribute** $\leftrightarrow$ **Column / Field**
• **Domain** $\leftrightarrow$ **Data Type / Set of Permitted Values**
• **Cardinality** $\leftrightarrow$ **Total Number of Rows ($N$)**
• **Degree (Arity)** $\leftrightarrow$ **Total Number of Columns ($K$)**

sections.title: Relational Theory vs SQL Implementation Nuances
rows: Relations are pure sets (no duplicate tuples allowed).
Tables are multisets/bags (duplicates allowed unless PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint is defined).
Eliminating duplicates on every query has high performance overhead ($O(N \log N)$ sort/hash).
Row order is undefined unless explicit `ORDER BY` is specified.
Query engines return rows according to disk storage layout or parallel execution threads.
Columns have primitive datatypes (INT, VARCHAR, DATE), with modern extensions for JSONB/Arrays.
Guarantees predictable joins and relational algebra operations.
Data Access via Relational Calculus / Algebra.
Allows query optimizer to rewrite queries into optimal execution plans.

sections.title: Cardinality and Degree in Action
sections.code:
-- Creating a relation 'students'
-- Degree (Arity) = 4 (student_id, full_name, email, gpa)
CREATE TABLE students (
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    gpa DECIMAL(3, 2) CHECK (gpa >= 0.0 AND gpa <= 4.0)
);

-- Inserting 3 tuples -> Cardinality = 3
INSERT INTO students (student_id, full_name, email, gpa) VALUES
(1, 'Aditi Sharma', 'aditi@univ.edu', 3.85),
(2, 'Rahul Verma', 'rahul@univ.edu', 3.60),
(3, 'Sneha Patel', 'sneha@univ.edu', 3.92);

-- Querying metadata in PostgreSQL to verify Degree and Cardinality
SELECT COUNT(*) AS cardinality FROM students; -- Result: 3
SELECT COUNT(*) AS degree FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'students'; -- Result: 4
sections.explanation: Degree is the static column count (4). Cardinality is the dynamic row count (3) which changes as records are inserted or deleted.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Relational Set Operations

steps.explanation: Engine scans relation A and emits `(1, 'Alice')` and `(2, 'Bob')` into temporary hash set.
Engine scans relation B and evaluates `(2, 'Bob')`. Since it already exists in the set, it is deduplicated.
Engine evaluates `(3, 'Charlie')` and adds it to the hash set.
Final result set contains 3 unique tuples: `{(1, 'Alice'), (2, 'Bob'), (3, 'Charlie')}`.

traps.question: What is the difference between Cardinality and Degree of a table?
traps.trap: Swapping the two terms or confusing degree with relationship cardinality (1:N).
traps.solution: Degree (or Arity) is the number of **columns/attributes** in a relation. Cardinality is the number of **rows/tuples** currently stored in the relation.

traps.question: Does SQL guarantee that `SELECT * FROM table;` will return rows in insertion order?
traps.trap: Saying 'Yes, it always returns rows in the order they were inserted'.
traps.solution: NO! In the relational model and SQL standard, table rows are an unordered set. Without an explicit `ORDER BY` clause, row return order is non-deterministic (dependent on vacuuming, index scans, or parallel worker execution).

sections.question: If a database table `employees` has 5 columns and 1,200 rows, what is its Degree and Cardinality?
sections.explanation: Degree is the number of columns (5) and Cardinality is the number of tuples/rows (1200).

items: The Relational Model separates logical data structures from physical disk storage.
A Relation is a set of Tuples; SQL Tables are multisets that permit duplicate rows unless constrained.
Degree = Number of columns (attributes); Cardinality = Number of rows (tuples).
Without an explicit ORDER BY clause, SQL query result order is fundamentally non-deterministic.

content.theory:
The relational model, proposed by Edgar F. Codd at IBM in 1970, represents all data as relations: tables of rows and columns, connected by values rather than by pointers. Its mathematical foundation, set theory and logic, is what makes SQL possible and why relational databases still dominate more than fifty years later. This lesson explains relations, tuples and attributes, the properties that make a table a relation, relational algebra, and Codd's idea of a fully relational system.

## Before the relational model

Earlier databases used hierarchical and network models, where records were linked by physical pointers. To find data, programs navigated those links step by step. If the structure changed, programs broke. Codd's insight was that data should be accessed by its values alone, with the system handling how to find it. That separation of logical structure from physical storage is the relational model's core contribution.

## Relations, tuples and attributes

The model uses mathematical terms that map onto familiar ones:

| Formal term | Common term | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Relation | Table | A set of tuples sharing the same attributes |
| Tuple | Row | One record |
| Attribute | Column | A named property of each tuple |
| Domain | Data type | The set of allowed values for an attribute |
| Degree | Number of columns | How many attributes a relation has |
| Cardinality | Number of rows | How many tuples a relation has |

A relation's **schema** names it and lists its attributes and domains, such as `employees(id, name, dept_id, salary)`.

## Properties of a relation

A true relation has properties that follow from being a set:

- **No duplicate tuples**: a set can't contain the same element twice, so every row must be distinguishable, which is why every relation has a key
- **No inherent row order**: sets are unordered, so a query without `ORDER BY` can return rows in any order
- **No inherent column order**: attributes are identified by name, not position
- **Atomic values**: each cell holds a single value from its domain, not a list or nested table, which is first normal form

SQL tables relax some of these. A table without a primary key can contain duplicate rows, and `SELECT` returns duplicates unless you add `DISTINCT`. Knowing where SQL departs from the pure model explains several behaviours that surprise beginners.

## Relationships through values

Relations connect through shared values, not stored links. An employee row stores `dept_id = 10`, and the department with `id = 10` is found by matching values. A **foreign key** constraint guarantees the referenced value exists. Because connections are values, any relationship can be queried in any direction, including ones the original designers never planned.

## Relational algebra

Relational algebra is the set of operations on relations that underlies SQL. Each operation takes relations as input and produces a relation as output, so operations combine freely:

| Operation | Symbol | Effect | SQL equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Selection | σ | Keep rows meeting a condition | `WHERE` |
| Projection | π | Keep chosen columns | The `SELECT` list |
| Union | ∪ | Rows in either relation | `UNION` |
| Difference | − | Rows in the first but not the second | `EXCEPT` |
| Cartesian product | × | Every pairing of rows | `CROSS JOIN` |
| Rename | ρ | Rename a relation or attribute | `AS` |
| Join | ⋈ | Product filtered by a matching condition | `JOIN ... ON` |

The query optimizer works in these terms. It rewrites your SQL into an algebra expression, then rearranges it into an equivalent but cheaper form, for example by filtering rows before joining instead of after. This rearrangement is safe because algebraic laws guarantee the result doesn't change.

## Closure

Because every operation returns a relation, the output of one query can be the input of another. This property, called **closure**, is why SQL supports subqueries, views and common table expressions: each is a relation that other queries can use as if it were a table.

## Codd's rules

In 1985, Codd published twelve rules (numbered 0 to 12) defining what a fully relational DBMS must do, partly to call out products that added a SQL layer over non-relational storage. Among them:

- **Information rule**: all data is represented as values in tables
- **Guaranteed access**: every value is reachable by table name, primary key and column name
- **Systematic treatment of nulls**: missing information is represented uniformly, independent of data type
- **Physical and logical data independence**: storage changes and many schema changes don't break applications

No commercial product satisfies every rule, but they remain a useful description of what "relational" means.

## RDBMS products

A relational database management system (RDBMS) implements the model. PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and SQLite are the most widely used. They share the core model and SQL, and differ in features, performance characteristics, licensing and dialect details.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is the relational model?", "What's the difference between a relation and a table?" and "What is relational algebra?" Define relations, tuples and attributes, explain why relations have no duplicate rows or ordering, list the core algebra operations with their SQL equivalents, and mention closure as the reason queries compose.

lessons.description:
To understand relational database architecture, distinguish between Schema and Instance:
• Database Schema (Intension / Blueprint): The structural skeleton defi...

sections.title: Mental Model: The Architectural Blueprint vs The Occupied Building
sections.content:
To understand relational database architecture, distinguish between **Schema** and **Instance**:
• **Database Schema (Intension / Blueprint)**: The structural skeleton defined at design time. It dictates table names, column data types, field lengths, default values, and foreign key relationships. Schemas change rarely via DDL (`ALTER TABLE`).
• **Database Instance (Extension / State)**: The actual snapshot of data inhabiting the database at an exact point in time (e.g. at 14:02:15 UTC on Sept 30). Instances change thousands of times a second via DML (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`).

sections.title: Three-Schema Architecture (ANSI/SPARC Framework)
sections.content:
1. **External Schema (View Level)**: Tailored views for specific end-users (e.g., HR sees employee salaries; Team Lead sees employee projects but salaries are hidden).
2. **Conceptual Schema (Logical Level)**: The complete relational design of all tables, columns, and constraints (Entity-Relationship design).
3. **Internal Schema (Physical Level)**: How bytes are stored on disk (B+ Tree page files, block sizes, compression, heap files).

sections.title: Common SQL Data Types Matrix
rows: High-volume transactional event logs, globally unique IDs.
Financial balances, prices, currency (NO floating-point rounding errors).
Fixed-length codes: ISO country codes (`CHAR(2)`), currency codes (`CHAR(3)`).
Audit logs (`created_at`), event scheduling across global zones.

sections.title: Defining Schemas and Querying Schema Metadata
sections.code:
-- 1. Defining the Schema (Logical Structure)
CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    sku CHAR(8) NOT NULL UNIQUE,          -- E.g. 'PROD1092'
    product_name VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    unit_price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,   -- Up to $99,999,999.99 exact
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- 2. Creating an Instance (Populating with dynamic data)
INSERT INTO products (sku, product_name, unit_price) 
VALUES ('TECH4091', 'Noise-Cancelling Headphones', 199.99);

-- 3. Schema Evolution (Altering structure)
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN stock_quantity INT DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock_quantity >= 0);
sections.explanation: Notice the strict precision of DECIMAL(10,2) for financial math and CHAR(8) for fixed-length SKUs to optimize disk alignment and indexing.

sections.title: Why Float/Double Must NEVER Be Used for Currency in SQL

steps.explanation: Float utilizes binary fractional approximation ($1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8...$). 0.1 cannot be represented precisely in binary base-2.
`float_sum` evaluates to `0.30000000000000004`.
`decimal_sum` uses base-10 packed decimal arithmetic and evaluates to exact `0.30`.
In banking, accumulating millions of float rounding errors results in financial reconciliation failure.

traps.question: When should you use CHAR(N) instead of VARCHAR(N)?
traps.trap: Using VARCHAR for everything or using CHAR(255) for variable names.
traps.solution: Use CHAR(N) ONLY when values have a strictly fixed length across all rows (e.g. SHA-256 hash `CHAR(64)`, US State Code `CHAR(2)`, UUID without dashes `CHAR(32)`). For varying lengths, VARCHAR avoids space-padding wasted bytes.

traps.question: What is the difference between Schema Independence (Physical vs Logical)?
traps.trap: Confusing physical disk storage changes with view alterations.
traps.solution: Physical Data Independence: Changing physical storage (creating indexes, changing file paths) does not affect conceptual schema or application SQL queries. Logical Data Independence: Changing the conceptual schema (adding columns/tables) does not break external views.

sections.question: Which data type should always be chosen for storing monetary transactions and account balances in a production database?
sections.explanation: DECIMAL/NUMERIC stores exact fixed-point numbers with exact decimal precision, preventing floating-point rounding errors.

items: Schema is the structural blueprint (static design); Instance is the database state at a specific point in time (dynamic data).
The 3-schema architecture provides Physical and Logical Data Independence.
Always use DECIMAL/NUMERIC for monetary values; never use FLOAT/DOUBLE for financial transactions.
Use CHAR for strictly fixed-length codes and VARCHAR for variable-length text.

content.theory:
Tables are where relational data lives. Each table has a structure that changes rarely, the schema, and contents that change constantly, the instance. Designing tables well means choosing columns, data types and constraints that describe the data accurately. This lesson explains schema versus instance, how columns and data types work, how to create and inspect tables, and the design choices that matter most.

## Schema versus instance

A table's **schema** is its definition: the table name, each column's name and data type, and its constraints. The **instance**, or state, is the set of rows it holds at a particular moment.

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    dept_id    INTEGER REFERENCES departments(id),
    salary     NUMERIC(10, 2) CHECK (salary > 0),
    hire_date  DATE NOT NULL
);
~~~

This statement defines the schema. Each `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` changes the instance. Schemas change through `ALTER TABLE`, usually as deliberate, versioned migrations, while instances change every second in a busy application. The analogy: the schema is a form's blank template, and the instance is the stack of filled-in forms.

## Rows and columns

A **row** represents one entity or event, such as one employee or one order. A **column** represents one property of every row, such as salary. Every row has a value, possibly `NULL`, for every column. Rows have no guaranteed order: a database may return them in insertion order today and a different order after an update or a vacuum, so always use `ORDER BY` when order matters.

## Data types

Every column has a data type, which restricts the values it accepts and decides how they're stored and compared. The main families:

| Family | Common types | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Integers | `SMALLINT`, `INTEGER`, `BIGINT` | Use `BIGINT` for IDs that may exceed about 2.1 billion |
| Exact decimals | `NUMERIC(p, s)`, `DECIMAL(p, s)` | Required for money; p is total digits and s is digits after the point |
| Floating point | `REAL`, `DOUBLE PRECISION` | Approximate; 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 |
| Text | `CHAR(n)`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `TEXT` | `CHAR` pads with spaces; `VARCHAR` enforces a maximum length |
| Date and time | `DATE`, `TIME`, `TIMESTAMP`, `TIMESTAMPTZ` | Store times with a time zone when users span zones |
| Boolean | `BOOLEAN` | MySQL stores it as a tiny integer |
| Others | `UUID`, `JSON`, `JSONB`, arrays | Vary by database |

Choosing the right type prevents whole classes of bugs. Storing dates as text allows values such as `'2024-02-30'` and sorts `'10/01/2024'` before `'9/01/2024'`. Storing money as floating point causes rounding errors in totals. Storing phone numbers as integers drops leading zeros and breaks on `+91`.

## Type systems differ

PostgreSQL enforces types strictly: inserting `'abc'` into an `INTEGER` column fails. SQLite uses **type affinity**: a column's declared type is a preference, and by default it can store a value of any type in any column. MySQL, depending on its SQL mode, may silently convert or truncate invalid values. Knowing your database's behaviour matters when moving data between systems.

## Inspecting tables

Each database has commands to see a table's structure. PostgreSQL's `psql` uses `\d employees`, MySQL uses `DESCRIBE employees`, and SQLite uses `PRAGMA table_info(employees)`. The SQL standard way, supported by PostgreSQL and MySQL, queries the catalog:

~~~sql
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'employees';
~~~

## Naming conventions

Consistent naming makes schemas readable. Common conventions: lowercase `snake_case` names, which avoid quoting since PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase; one consistent choice of plural or singular table names; an `id` primary key; and foreign keys named after the referenced table, such as `dept_id`. Avoid reserved words such as `order`, `user` or `group` as table names, because they need quoting everywhere.

## Design choices

A few habits produce better tables:

- **One table per entity type**: employees and departments are separate tables, not columns in one wide table
- **Atomic columns**: store first and last names separately if you'll sort or search by either; don't store comma-separated lists in a column
- **Constraints as documentation**: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK` and foreign keys state the rules of the data where every application must follow them
- **Narrow over wide**: a table with dozens of mostly empty columns usually hides several entities that belong in separate tables

## Degree and cardinality

The **degree** of a table is its number of columns, and the **cardinality** is its number of rows. The employees table above has degree 5. Its cardinality changes with every insert and delete. The term "cardinality" also describes relationships, such as one-to-many, and the number of distinct values in a column, which affects index usefulness, so use it with context.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What's the difference between a schema and an instance?" and data type questions such as "CHAR versus VARCHAR?" and "Why not store money as FLOAT?" Explain schema as structure and instance as current data, justify type choices with concrete failure examples, and mention that SQL databases differ in how strictly they enforce types.

lessons.title: Keys in Relational Databases: Primary, Foreign & Candidate
lessons.description:
Think of relational keys as National Identity & Family Registry:
• Super Key (Any set of identifiers that uniquely identifies a citizen): {SSN}, {SSN, Favorite ...

sections.title: Mental Model: Government Identification & Passport Linkage
sections.content:
Think of relational keys as **National Identity & Family Registry**:
• **Super Key (Any set of identifiers that uniquely identifies a citizen)**: `{SSN}`, `{SSN, Favorite Color}`, `{SSN, Hair Color, Full Name}`. All can uniquely find a person, but many contain useless clutter.
• **Candidate Key (A minimal Super Key)**: Stripped of all redundant attributes. Examples: `{SSN}` or `{Passport_Number}` or `{Driver_License_No}`.
• **Primary Key (The chosen representative)**: The database architect picks ONE candidate key (e.g., `{SSN}` or auto-incrementing `user_id`) as the official unique row identifier.
• **Alternate Key**: The remaining candidate keys that were not chosen as Primary Key (e.g. `{Passport_Number}`). They are enforced with `UNIQUE NOT NULL`.
• **Foreign Key (The Parent Reference)**: A child's birth certificate lists `{Mother_SSN}`. The child's record cannot reference a mother who does not exist in the citizen database (Referential Integrity).

sections.title: The Mathematical Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
$$\text{Primary Key} \subseteq \text{Candidate Keys} \subseteq \text{Super Keys}$$
• Every Candidate Key is a Super Key.
• Not every Super Key is a Candidate Key (because Super Keys may contain non-essential columns).
• The Primary Key is chosen from the set of Candidate Keys and automatically enforces `UNIQUE` and `NOT NULL` invariants.

sections.title: Relational Key Classifications
rows: Authoritative unique row identifier; automatically creates clustered/primary index.
Eligible minimal super keys capable of serving as Primary Key.
Candidate keys not chosen as the Primary Key (enforced with UNIQUE constraint).
Enforces Referential Integrity by referencing a Primary/Unique Key in a parent table.
A key composed of 2 or more columns (e.g. `order_id + item_id`).

sections.title: Primary Key, Foreign Key & Referential Actions in SQL
sections.code:
-- 1. Parent Table (Departments)
CREATE TABLE departments (
    dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dept_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

-- 2. Child Table (Employees) with Foreign Key
CREATE TABLE employees (
    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL, -- Alternate Candidate Key
    dept_id INT NOT NULL,
    
    -- Enforcing Referential Integrity with CASCADE delete rule
    CONSTRAINT fk_employee_department
        FOREIGN KEY (dept_id)
        REFERENCES departments(dept_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT      -- Blocks deleting department if employees exist!
        ON UPDATE CASCADE       -- Updates child dept_id if parent dept_id changes
);

-- Inserting valid parent and child
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (10, 'Engineering');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (101, 'Kavita Rao', 'kavita@co.com', 10);

-- ILLEGAL: Attempting to insert employee for non-existent Department 99
-- Result: ERROR: insert or update on table "employees" violates foreign key constraint
-- INSERT INTO employees VALUES (102, 'Dev Patel', 'dev@co.com', 99);
sections.explanation: Foreign key constraints make it physically impossible for orphaned records to exist in the child table.

sections.title: ON DELETE / ON UPDATE Referential Actions
headers: Behavior When Parent Row Is Deleted / Updated
rows: Rejects the parent deletion and throws foreign key constraint error.
Protecting critical parents (cannot delete Department if employees still assigned).
Automatically deletes all child rows referencing the deleted parent row.
Parent-Child composition: Deleting an `Order` automatically deletes all `OrderItems`.
Sets child foreign key column to `NULL` (FK column must be nullable).
Non-mandatory references: Deleting a `Manager` sets employee's `manager_id` to NULL.
Sets child foreign key column to its defined column default.

traps.question: Can a Primary Key consist of multiple columns (Composite Primary Key)?
traps.trap: Thinking a table can have multiple Primary Keys.
traps.solution: A table can only have ONE Primary Key, but that single Primary Key can be composed of multiple columns (e.g. `PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)`). This is a Composite Primary Key.

traps.question: Can a Foreign Key reference a column that is NOT a Primary Key in the parent table?
traps.trap: Answering 'No, foreign keys must always reference the primary key'.
traps.solution: A Foreign Key can reference ANY column in the parent table, provided that column has a `UNIQUE` constraint or is a `PRIMARY KEY` (referential target must be guaranteed unique).

traps.question: What is the difference between Surrogate Key and Natural Key?
traps.trap: Confusing artificial IDs with business domain identifiers.
traps.solution: A Natural Key is a real-world attribute with business meaning (e.g. SSN, ISBN, VIN). A Surrogate Key is an artificial, system-generated integer/UUID (e.g. `id BIGSERIAL`) that has zero business meaning and never changes.

sections.question: Given a relation with candidate keys {A, B} and {A, C}. Which statement is TRUE regarding Super Keys?
options: {A, B, D} is a Super Key.
{B, C} is guaranteed to be a Candidate Key.
The table cannot have a Primary Key.
sections.explanation: Since {A, B} is a candidate key (minimal super key), any superset containing {A, B} (such as {A, B, D}) is by definition a Super Key.

items: Super Key = Any set of attributes uniquely identifying a tuple.
Candidate Key = Minimal Super Key with zero redundant attributes.
Primary Key = The chosen candidate key (enforces Unique + Not Null); exactly 1 per table.
Foreign Key enforces Referential Integrity between tables, preventing orphaned child rows.
Referential actions (CASCADE, RESTRICT, SET NULL) define child behavior when parent records change.

content.theory:
Keys identify rows and connect tables. A primary key gives every row a unique identity, a foreign key links a row to a row in another table, and candidate keys are all the column sets that could serve as an identity. Getting keys right prevents duplicate records and orphaned references. This lesson defines every kind of key, explains how foreign keys enforce referential integrity, and compares natural and surrogate keys.

## Superkeys

A **superkey** is any set of columns whose values are unique across all rows. In an employees table, `{id}` is a superkey, and so is `{id, name}`, because adding columns to a unique set keeps it unique. Superkeys can contain unnecessary columns.

## Candidate keys

A **candidate key** is a minimal superkey: no column can be removed without losing uniqueness. If both `id` and `email` are unique for every employee, then `{id}` and `{email}` are both candidate keys. `{id, name}` isn't, because `name` can be removed. A table can have several candidate keys, and each could serve as the primary key.

## Primary keys

The **primary key** is the candidate key chosen as the main identifier. It must be unique and can never be `NULL`. Each table has at most one primary key, though it can span several columns:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
    student_id INTEGER,
    course_id  INTEGER,
    grade      CHAR(2),
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
~~~

Here neither column alone is unique, since a student takes many courses and a course has many students, but the pair is. A multi-column key like this is a **composite key**. Most databases automatically create an index on the primary key, which makes lookups by key fast.

## Alternate keys

Candidate keys not chosen as the primary key are **alternate keys**. Enforce them with `UNIQUE` constraints. If `id` is the primary key, declaring `email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL` keeps emails unique too. Without that constraint, two employees could end up with the same email, and nothing would stop it.

A `UNIQUE` column allows `NULL` unless also declared `NOT NULL`. In PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite, multiple `NULL` values are allowed in a unique column, because `NULL` isn't equal to `NULL`. SQL Server allows only one. PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` to change this behaviour.

## Foreign keys

A **foreign key** is a column, or set of columns, whose values must match a key in another table, called the referenced or parent table:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    dept_id INTEGER REFERENCES departments(id)
);
~~~

Every non-null `dept_id` must exist in `departments.id`. Inserting an employee with `dept_id = 99` when no department 99 exists fails. This guarantee is **referential integrity**: no row references something that doesn't exist. A foreign key can be `NULL`, which means "no department yet", unless you declare it `NOT NULL`.

The referenced columns must be a primary key or have a unique constraint, so each reference points to exactly one row.

## Referential actions

Foreign keys also decide what happens when a referenced row is deleted or its key is updated:

| Action | On deleting the parent row |
|---|---|
| `RESTRICT` / `NO ACTION` | Reject the delete while child rows exist (the default) |
| `CASCADE` | Delete the child rows too |
| `SET NULL` | Set the child's foreign key to `NULL` |
| `SET DEFAULT` | Set the child's foreign key to its default value |

`ON DELETE CASCADE` suits parts that can't exist alone, such as order items when an order is deleted. It's dangerous elsewhere: cascading from departments would silently delete every employee in a deleted department. The same options exist for `ON UPDATE`.

## Self-referencing keys

A foreign key can reference its own table. An employees table with a `manager_id` column referencing `employees.id` models a reporting hierarchy. The top manager has `manager_id = NULL`. Self-joins and recursive queries, covered later, query such hierarchies.

## Natural versus surrogate keys

A **natural key** is a real-world attribute that's unique, such as an email address, a national ID or an ISBN. A **surrogate key** is an artificial value with no meaning, such as an auto-incrementing integer or a UUID.

| | Natural key | Surrogate key |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Has business meaning | Meaningless |
| Stability | Can change (emails change) | Never changes |
| Size | Often long strings | Compact integer or UUID |
| Uniqueness | May fail in edge cases | Guaranteed by the database |

Most schemas use surrogate primary keys for stability and compact foreign keys, and enforce natural keys with `UNIQUE` constraints. Changing a natural primary key means updating every foreign key that references it.

Generate surrogate keys with `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` in PostgreSQL (the older `SERIAL` also works), `AUTO_INCREMENT` in MySQL, or `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` in SQLite. UUIDs suit distributed systems where several servers create rows without coordinating.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Primary key versus unique key?", "What is a candidate key?", "What is referential integrity?" and "Natural versus surrogate keys?" Build up from superkey to candidate key to primary key, explain foreign keys with a failing insert, describe the referential actions and the danger of cascading deletes, and recommend surrogate primary keys with unique natural keys.
