lessons.title: The UPDATE Statement: In-Place Mutations & Safeguards
lessons.description:
Think of UPDATE as A Precision Surgical Tool:
• UPDATE employees SET salary = salary  1.10 WHERE empid = 104; surgically targets a single employee's file and ap...

sections.title: Mental Model: The Targeted Modification vs The Catastrophic Flood
sections.content:
Think of `UPDATE` as **A Precision Surgical Tool**:
• `UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE emp_id = 104;` surgically targets a single employee's file and applies a 10% raise.
• If you forget the `WHERE` clause: `UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10;` (The dreaded catastrophe!). The surgical tool becomes a flood: EVERY single employee in the entire company—from interns to the CEO—gets their salary modified in one sweep.
• In production database engineering, senior engineers always verify the row count with `SELECT` before executing an `UPDATE`, or use database **Safe Update Mode** (`--safe-updates`).

sections.title: Golden Rule of Production Database Modification
Atomic Increments, Multi-Column Updates, and Safe Transactions
sections.code:
-- 1. Atomic In-Place Counter Increment (Prevents Race Conditions!)
-- Never do: balance = [read_val] + 50. Always do balance = balance + 50 directly in SQL!
UPDATE bank_accounts 
SET balance = balance + 250.00, 
    last_transaction_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE account_id = 101 AND is_frozen = FALSE;

-- 2. Multi-Column Update with Subquery
UPDATE employees
SET salary = salary * 1.05,
    title = 'Senior Software Engineer'
WHERE department_id = (SELECT dept_id FROM departments WHERE dept_name = 'Cloud Engineering')
  AND hire_date < '2022-01-01';

-- 3. UPDATE with RETURNING (Inspect mutated state instantly)
UPDATE inventory
SET stock_qty = stock_qty - 1
WHERE product_id = 409 AND stock_qty > 0
RETURNING product_id, stock_qty AS remaining_stock;
sections.explanation: Performing calculations directly inside the SET clause (balance = balance + 250) is atomic at the row lock level, preventing lost updates in concurrent environments.

sections.title: Safe vs Unsafe UPDATE Practices
rows: Always filter on Primary Key or Indexed Unique column.
Directly running bare UPDATE on production console.
Accidental execution without WHERE wipes entire column.

sections.title: Why Atomic SQL Updates Prevent Lost Updates

steps.explanation: Tx1 acquires exclusive row lock on `item_id = 5`. Evaluates `stock > 0` (1 > 0 = TRUE).
Tx1 sets `stock = 1 - 1 = 0` and commits. Lock releases.
Tx2 acquires row lock. Evaluates predicate `stock > 0` on the authoritative new state (0 > 0 = FALSE).
Tx2 updates 0 rows and returns affected count = 0. The inventory is never oversold into negative numbers!

traps.question: What is the return value of an UPDATE statement if no rows match the WHERE condition?
traps.trap: Thinking it throws an error or exception.
traps.solution: An UPDATE statement that matches 0 rows is completely valid syntax; it simply returns `UPDATE 0` (Affected rows: 0). Application code should inspect the affected row count to verify success.

traps.question: What is MySQL 'Safe Updates Mode' (SQL_SAFE_UPDATES)?
traps.trap: Not knowing how database engines protect against unconstrained updates.
traps.solution: When `SET sql_safe_updates = 1;` is enabled, MySQL rejects any `UPDATE` or `DELETE` that does not include a `WHERE` clause with a key/indexed column or a `LIMIT` clause.

sections.question: An engineer writes: `UPDATE products SET price = 99.99;`. What is the result of executing this statement?
options: Only the first product is updated to 99.99.
The database throws a syntax error because WHERE is mandatory.
EVERY single product in the table has its price changed to 99.99.
sections.explanation: In SQL, omitting the WHERE clause applies the UPDATE to every row in the table unconditionally.

items: Never execute an unconstrained UPDATE without a WHERE clause unless you intentionally wish to modify all rows.
Use atomic in-place increments (`SET count = count + 1`) to eliminate concurrency race conditions.
Always wrap manual production updates in transaction blocks with verification queries before committing.
Inspect affected row count in application backend code to detect missing target records.

content.theory:
`UPDATE` changes values in existing rows. It's one of the most dangerous statements in SQL, because a missing or wrong `WHERE` clause silently changes every row in a table. This lesson explains the syntax, updating from expressions and other tables, how updates interact with constraints and concurrency, and the safeguards that prevent disasters, including transactions, previews and safe update modes.

## The basic form

~~~sql
UPDATE employees
SET salary = 95000
WHERE id = 101;
~~~

`SET` lists columns and their new values; `WHERE` selects which rows change. The database reports how many rows were affected. Checking that number is a quick sanity test: an update meant for one employee that reports 4,000 rows changed signals a problem.

## The missing WHERE disaster

Without `WHERE`, every row changes:

~~~sql
UPDATE employees SET salary = 95000;   -- every employee now earns 95,000
~~~

This is one of the most common and costly SQL mistakes. Running a statement with only part of it selected in a SQL editor, so the `WHERE` line isn't included, produces the same result.

## Expressions and multiple columns

`SET` can use expressions, including the column's current value, and can change several columns at once:

~~~sql
UPDATE employees
SET salary = salary * 1.10,
    last_raise_date = CURRENT_DATE
WHERE dept_id = 10;
~~~

All expressions on the right are evaluated using the row's values **before** the update. So `SET a = b, b = a` swaps the two columns in PostgreSQL, SQLite and the SQL standard. MySQL evaluates assignments left to right, using already-updated values, so the same statement sets both columns to the original b. That's a subtle dialect difference worth knowing.

## Conditional updates with CASE

Different rows can receive different values in one statement:

~~~sql
UPDATE employees
SET salary = CASE
    WHEN performance = 'excellent' THEN salary * 1.15
    WHEN performance = 'good' THEN salary * 1.08
    ELSE salary
END
WHERE dept_id = 10;
~~~

The `ELSE salary` keeps other rows unchanged. Without it, `CASE` returns NULL for unmatched rows, wiping their salaries.

## Updating from another table

Often new values come from a related table. PostgreSQL uses `UPDATE ... FROM`:

~~~sql
UPDATE employees e
SET salary = e.salary + b.amount
FROM bonuses b
WHERE b.employee_id = e.id;
~~~

MySQL writes it as `UPDATE employees e JOIN bonuses b ON ... SET ...`. A correlated subquery works everywhere:

~~~sql
UPDATE employees
SET dept_name = (SELECT d.name FROM departments d WHERE d.id = employees.dept_id);
~~~

With the subquery form, rows that find no match get NULL, which may not be what you want; add a `WHERE EXISTS` condition to limit the update to rows that have a match. With a join form, if the source table has several matching rows for one target row, the result is unpredictable, so make sure the join is one-to-one.

## Safeguard 1: preview with SELECT

Before running an update, run a `SELECT` with the same `WHERE` clause and check the rows and their count:

~~~sql
SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 10;
~~~

If the result looks right, change `SELECT ... FROM` to `UPDATE ... SET`, keeping the `WHERE` clause identical.

## Safeguard 2: use a transaction

Wrap manual updates in a transaction, check the result, then commit or roll back:

~~~sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dept_id = 10;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 10;   -- verify
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK if something looks wrong
~~~

Until `COMMIT`, other sessions don't see the change, and `ROLLBACK` restores everything. Keep these transactions short, because the updated rows stay locked against other writers until you finish.

## Safeguard 3: safe update modes and RETURNING

MySQL's `sql_safe_updates` setting, enabled by default in MySQL Workbench, rejects `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statements without a key-based `WHERE` or `LIMIT`. PostgreSQL and SQLite support `RETURNING`, which shows the changed rows:

~~~sql
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dept_id = 10
RETURNING id, name, salary;
~~~

## Safeguard 4: backups and permissions

Mistakes still happen, so production databases need tested backups and, ideally, point-in-time recovery. Restrict who can run ad-hoc updates in production, and route routine changes through reviewed scripts or application code.

## Updates and constraints

An update must leave every row satisfying every constraint. Changing a salary to a negative value fails a `CHECK`, and changing an employee's `dept_id` to a nonexistent department fails the foreign key. Updating a referenced primary key either fails or cascades to child rows, depending on the foreign key's `ON UPDATE` action. If any row violates a constraint, the entire statement fails and no rows change.

## Updates and concurrency

An update locks each row it changes until the transaction ends, so concurrent updates to the same row wait. The pattern `SET quantity = quantity - 1` is safe under concurrency, because the database reads and writes the current value atomically. Reading the value into an application, subtracting there and writing it back risks lost updates when two sessions do it at once. Use atomic expressions, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to lock rows before reading, or a version column for optimistic locking.

## How interviewers test this

Expect to write updates with conditions and joins, and questions such as "How do you update a table from another table?" and "How do you protect against accidental mass updates?" Preview with SELECT, use transactions, mention safe update mode and `RETURNING`, and explain atomic increments versus read-modify-write.

lessons.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP: Destruction Deep Dive
lessons.description:
To understand data removal in relational databases, compare the 3 Levels of Destruction:
• DELETE (The Pencil Eraser): You open the ledger, flip through pages o...

sections.title: Mental Model: Eraser vs Shredder vs Demolition Wrecking Ball
sections.content:
To understand data removal in relational databases, compare the **3 Levels of Destruction**:
• **DELETE (The Pencil Eraser)**: You open the ledger, flip through pages one by one, locate specific lines with your eraser, rub them out, write an audit log entry for every erased line, and leave the page numbering intact. Can be rolled back. Slow for huge tables.
• **TRUNCATE (The Office Paper Shredder)**: You take the entire stack of papers inside the binder, dump them straight into the shredder, and place a brand new empty notepad inside the binder. Fast; resets auto-increment counters; bypasses row-level audit triggers.
• **DROP (The Demolition Wrecking Ball)**: You demolish the entire filing cabinet, melt the metal, and erase the office address from the city map. The table data AND its schema definition cease to exist entirely.

sections.title: The Ultimate Placement Comparison: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
sections.content: This is one of the **top 3 most frequently asked SQL interview questions** across all technical rounds. Interviewers expect you to know: 1. Command Category (DML vs DDL), 2. Rollback Capability, 3. Trigger Execution, 4. Performance Mechanisms (Row log vs Page deallocation), and 5. Identity Reset behavior.

sections.title: Detailed Comparison Matrix: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
rows: Slow for large tables ($O(N)$ row-by-row logging)
Rollable back in PostgreSQL; No in MySQL/Oracle
Cannot be rolled back in MySQL/Oracle
YES (`ON DELETE` triggers fire for every row)
RESETS counter back to 1 / Seed value

sections.title: Demonstrating DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP in SQL
sections.explanation: Use DELETE for targeted row cleanup with business triggers. Use TRUNCATE to reset staging/test tables. Use DROP to decommission schema objects.

sections.title: Why TRUNCATE is 1,000x Faster Than DELETE on a 10-Million Row Table

steps.explanation: DELETE: Scans 10,000,000 rows. For EVERY single row, it writes a detailed undo log entry to WAL, marks row header as dead, updates 4 separate indexes, and checks foreign key constraints. Total Time: ~45 seconds.
TRUNCATE: Modifies the database data dictionary pointers. It marks the storage allocation extents/data pages as free and points the table root to a new empty page. Total Time: ~12 milliseconds.

traps.question: Can TRUNCATE be rolled back?
traps.trap: Giving a flat 'No, TRUNCATE can never be rolled back' without qualifying the engine.
traps.solution: In MySQL and Oracle, TRUNCATE is DDL that auto-commits, so it CANNOT be rolled back. In **PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server**, TRUNCATE is fully transaction-safe and CAN be rolled back if executed inside `BEGIN ... ROLLBACK;`!

traps.question: What happens if you try to TRUNCATE a table that is referenced by an active Foreign Key?
traps.trap: Thinking TRUNCATE cascades automatically like DELETE.
traps.solution: The database will REJECT the TRUNCATE statement with a foreign key constraint violation, even if the referencing child table is empty (unless `CASCADE` is explicitly specified in PostgreSQL or the FK is disabled).

sections.question: You need to empty all 5,000,000 rows from a temporary staging table, reset its auto-increment ID counter back to 1, and ensure the operation finishes in milliseconds. Which command should you choose?
sections.explanation: `TRUNCATE TABLE` empties all rows via page deallocation, resets the auto-increment identity seed, preserves table schema, and executes in milliseconds.

items: DELETE is DML: Row-by-row removal, supports WHERE, fires triggers, keeps auto-increment counter.
TRUNCATE is DDL: Fast page deallocation, deletes all rows, resets auto-increment seed, bypasses row triggers.
DROP is DDL: Completely eradicates data, table structure, indexes, and schema definitions.
TRUNCATE is transaction-safe in PostgreSQL/SQL Server, but auto-commits in MySQL/Oracle.

content.theory:
`DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and `DROP` all remove data, but they work at different levels and behave in distinct ways. `DELETE` removes chosen rows, `TRUNCATE` empties a whole table quickly, and `DROP` removes the table itself. Choosing the wrong one can cost hours of recovery. This lesson explains each statement, compares their speed, logging, rollback, triggers and identity behaviour, and covers soft deletes as an alternative.

## DELETE: remove chosen rows

~~~sql
DELETE FROM employees WHERE id = 101;
~~~

`DELETE` removes rows matching the `WHERE` clause, or every row if there's no `WHERE`. It's DML: it processes rows one by one, fires row-level `DELETE` triggers, checks foreign keys for each row and can be rolled back inside a transaction.

Deleting many rows is slow on large tables, because every row deletion is logged and every index is updated. In MVCC databases such as PostgreSQL, deleted rows aren't removed physically right away; they're marked dead and cleaned up later by `VACUUM`, so a mass delete doesn't immediately shrink the table on disk. Large deletes are often done in batches, such as 10,000 rows at a time, to keep transactions short and avoid long locks.

## TRUNCATE: empty a table

~~~sql
TRUNCATE TABLE logs;
~~~

`TRUNCATE` removes all rows at once. Instead of deleting rows individually, it releases the table's storage and starts fresh, so it takes about the same time for a hundred rows or a hundred million. It's classified as DDL. Key behaviours:

- no `WHERE` clause: it's all rows or nothing
- row-level `DELETE` triggers don't fire
- it resets auto-increment counters in MySQL and SQL Server; PostgreSQL resets them only with `TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY`
- it fails if another table references this one through a foreign key, unless you use `CASCADE` in PostgreSQL, which also truncates the referencing tables
- it needs a stronger lock than `DELETE`, blocking all other access to the table while it runs

## Can TRUNCATE be rolled back?

It depends on the database. In PostgreSQL and SQL Server, `TRUNCATE` inside a transaction can be rolled back. In MySQL and Oracle, it causes an implicit commit and can't be undone. SQLite has no `TRUNCATE` statement; a `DELETE` without `WHERE` is optimized into a fast table clear when no triggers are involved. This variation is a common interview follow-up.

## DROP: remove the table

~~~sql
DROP TABLE employees;
~~~

`DROP` removes the table entirely: its data, structure, indexes, constraints, triggers and permissions. Queries referencing it fail afterwards. It's DDL, and only PostgreSQL and SQLite, with transactional DDL, can roll it back within a transaction. `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` avoids an error when the table doesn't exist, which is useful in setup scripts. If other objects depend on the table, such as views or foreign keys, the drop fails unless you add `CASCADE`, which removes the dependents too.

## Comparing the three

| | DELETE | TRUNCATE | DROP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Removes | Chosen rows | All rows | The whole table |
| Category | DML | DDL | DDL |
| WHERE clause | Yes | No | No |
| Speed on large tables | Slow, row by row | Fast | Fast |
| Row triggers fire | Yes | No | No |
| Structure kept | Yes | Yes | No |
| Identity reset | No | Usually (database-dependent) | Table is gone |
| Rollback | Yes | Database-dependent | Database-dependent |
| Space reclaimed | Later (vacuum or reuse) | Immediately | Immediately |

## Choosing between them

- To remove specific rows, use `DELETE` with `WHERE`
- To empty a staging or log table quickly while keeping its structure, use `TRUNCATE`
- To remove a table that's no longer needed, use `DROP`

## Soft deletes

Many applications never physically delete business records. Instead, they mark rows as deleted:

~~~sql
UPDATE customers SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE id = 42;
~~~

Queries then filter with `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Soft deletes allow recovery from mistakes, keep history for audits, and preserve foreign key references from old orders. The costs: every query must remember the filter, unique constraints need adjusting so a deleted email can be reused (a partial unique index in PostgreSQL handles this), and the table keeps growing. Some systems use a separate archive table instead.

Privacy law can require real deletion. Under rules such as the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, users can request erasure of personal data, so soft-deleted personal data may still need to be purged or anonymized.

## Recovering from mistakes

After an accidental `DELETE` without `WHERE`, rollback only helps if you were inside an uncommitted transaction. Otherwise, recovery depends on backups. Point-in-time recovery, available in PostgreSQL through archived write-ahead logs and in MySQL through binary logs, can restore the database to the moment before the mistake. Test restores regularly: a backup that's never been restored isn't a reliable backup.

## How interviewers test this

"DELETE versus TRUNCATE versus DROP" is one of the most frequently asked SQL questions. Use the comparison table: scope, category, speed, triggers, identity reset and rollback behaviour, noting that rollback for TRUNCATE varies by database. Mention soft deletes to show you think about recoverability.

sections.title: Mental Model: Writing Code vs How the Engine Actually Compiles It
sections.content:
In English or Java, you read code from top to bottom. In SQL, **the order in which you WRITE a query is completely different from the order in which the database ENGINE EXECUTES it**:
• You write `SELECT` first at the top of your query text.
• But the database engine executes `SELECT` **almost last (at Step 6 of 8)**!

Understanding this 8-stage logical pipeline is the single most important conceptual superpower for writing bug-free SQL, mastering aliases, filtering aggregations, and optimizing query performance.

sections.title: The 8-Stage Logical Query Execution Pipeline
sections.content:
1. **FROM & JOIN**: Gather source tables and build Cartesian / joined row streams.
2. **WHERE**: Filter individual base rows before grouping.
3. **GROUP BY**: Bucket remaining rows into aggregate groups.
4. **HAVING**: Filter aggregated groups.
5. **SELECT**: Evaluate expressions, window functions, and project final column list.
6. **DISTINCT**: Deduplicate projected rows.
7. **ORDER BY**: Sort the final result set.
8. **LIMIT / OFFSET**: Paginate and slice the output window.

sections.title: Written Order vs Logical Execution Order
headers: Why It Happens at This Stage
rows: Engine must identify and combine source tables before it can read any data.
Eliminate unqualified individual rows early before doing expensive groupings.
Group surviving rows into summary buckets.
Compute expressions, assign column aliases, and evaluate window functions.
Remove duplicate rows from the projected columns.
Sort the projected rows (can now reference column aliases!).
Discard rows outside the requested pagination window.

sections.title: Traced SQL Query Demonstrating the Complete Execution Pipeline
sections.code:
-- A complex analytical query
SELECT 
    department_id,
    COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
    AVG(salary) AS avg_dept_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'        -- Step 2: Filter base rows
GROUP BY department_id                  -- Step 3: Bucket into departments
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3                   -- Step 4: Keep only depts with >= 3 hires
ORDER BY avg_dept_salary DESC          -- Step 7: Sort by alias (Valid because SELECT already ran!)
LIMIT 5;                               -- Step 8: Return top 5
sections.explanation: Trace how each clause executes in sequence: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Resolution of Common Aliasing & Filtering Errors

steps.explanation: In Query A, the engine attempts to evaluate `WHERE avg_sal > 50000` at Step 2.
Failure 1: `avg_sal` alias is created in `SELECT` at Step 5. The engine has not reached Step 5 yet!
Failure 2: `AVG(salary)` is an aggregate function. Aggregates cannot be computed before `GROUP BY` (Step 3).
In Query B, `HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000` runs at Step 4 (after GROUP BY), which is mathematically and syntactically valid.

traps.question: Why can't you use aggregate functions (like `SUM()` or `COUNT()`) in a `WHERE` clause?
traps.trap: Saying 'it's just a syntax rule'.
traps.solution: Because the `WHERE` clause executes at Step 2 on individual base rows, BEFORE rows are grouped into buckets at Step 3 (`GROUP BY`). Aggregates only exist after grouping, which is why group filtering must be placed in `HAVING` (Step 4).

traps.question: Why does `ORDER BY` allow using column aliases defined in `SELECT`?
traps.trap: Thinking ORDER BY runs first or in parallel.
traps.solution: Because `SELECT` executes at Step 5, assigning all column aliases. `ORDER BY` executes at Step 7, so all aliases created in Step 5 are fully in scope and accessible.

sections.question: Which of the following represents the correct logical execution order of clauses in a SQL query?
options: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
FROM → SELECT → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
WHERE → FROM → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → LIMIT
sections.explanation: The engine first reads source tables (FROM), filters rows (WHERE), groups them (GROUP BY), filters groups (HAVING), calculates projection and aliases (SELECT), and finally sorts (ORDER BY).

items: SQL is written in lexical order (SELECT ... FROM), but executed in logical order (FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT).
WHERE filters raw individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated groups after grouping.
Column aliases created in SELECT are invisible to WHERE and HAVING, but are fully accessible in ORDER BY.
Window functions and DISTINCT are evaluated during/after the SELECT stage.

content.theory:
SQL is written in one order and evaluated in another. You write `SELECT` first, but the database logically processes `FROM` first and `SELECT` near the end. Understanding this logical order explains rules that otherwise seem arbitrary: why aliases don't work in `WHERE`, why aggregates can't appear in `WHERE`, and why `HAVING` exists. This lesson walks through each step of the pipeline, explains the rules that follow, and separates logical order from how the database physically executes a query.

## Written order versus logical order

A full query is written like this:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 60000
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
LIMIT 5;
~~~

But it's logically evaluated in this order:

| Step | Clause | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `FROM` and `JOIN` | Build the source rows, combining tables |
| 2 | `WHERE` | Filter individual rows |
| 3 | `GROUP BY` | Group rows sharing values |
| 4 | `HAVING` | Filter groups |
| 5 | `SELECT` | Compute output columns and aliases; window functions run here |
| 6 | `DISTINCT` | Remove duplicate output rows |
| 7 | `ORDER BY` | Sort the result |
| 8 | `LIMIT` / `OFFSET` | Keep a slice of the sorted rows |

Each step takes the output of the previous one as its input.

## Step 1: FROM and JOIN

The database first assembles the rows to work with. For a single table, that's every row. With joins, it's the combined rows that satisfy the join conditions. Subqueries in `FROM` and common table expressions are evaluated here too, producing tables the rest of the query uses.

## Step 2: WHERE

`WHERE` keeps individual rows where the condition is true. It sees only the columns from step 1. Since grouping hasn't happened, aggregate functions don't exist yet, so this fails:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id FROM employees WHERE AVG(salary) > 60000;   -- error
~~~

Filtering early is also efficient: every row removed here is one row fewer to group, sort and return.

## Step 3: GROUP BY

`GROUP BY` collapses rows into groups sharing the same values in the grouping columns. After this step, the query works with groups, not rows. Every later step can reference only the grouping columns and aggregates computed over each group, which is why selecting a column that's neither grouped nor aggregated is an error in standard SQL.

## Step 4: HAVING

`HAVING` filters groups, and it can use aggregates because groups now exist:

~~~sql
HAVING AVG(salary) > 60000
~~~

The rule of thumb: conditions on individual rows go in `WHERE`; conditions on aggregates go in `HAVING`. Putting a row condition in `HAVING` works but wastes effort, since rows that could have been discarded early get grouped first.

## Step 5: SELECT

Only now does the database compute the select list: expressions, function calls and aliases. Window functions such as `ROW_NUMBER()` are computed here, after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`. That's why you can't filter on a window function's result in `WHERE`; you wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.

## Why aliases aren't visible earlier

An alias defined in `SELECT` doesn't exist during steps 1 to 4, so `WHERE annual_salary > 1000000` fails when `annual_salary` is an alias. `ORDER BY` comes after `SELECT`, so it can use aliases:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY annual_salary DESC;   -- works
~~~

Some databases relax the rule: MySQL and SQLite allow aliases in `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, and PostgreSQL allows them in `GROUP BY`. The portable approach repeats the expression or uses a subquery.

## Steps 6 to 8: DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT

`DISTINCT` removes duplicate output rows. `ORDER BY` sorts, and it's the only step that guarantees an order. `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` come last, so `LIMIT 5` returns the top five rows **after** sorting. Without `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` returns an arbitrary five rows, which may differ between runs.

## Logical order versus physical execution

The logical order defines what result a query must produce. The database doesn't have to execute it that way. The optimizer is free to rearrange work as long as the result is the same. It might apply a `WHERE` condition while reading an index, push filters below joins, use an index that's already sorted to skip the `ORDER BY` step, or stop early once `LIMIT` rows are found. Use `EXPLAIN` to see the physical plan the database chose.

## Using the order to debug

When a query misbehaves, build it up in logical order. Start with `SELECT * FROM ...` plus joins and check the rows. Add `WHERE` and check again. Add grouping and aggregates. This isolates which step introduces the problem, such as a join that multiplies rows before an aggregate inflates the totals.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is the order of execution of a SQL query?" and follow-ups such as "Why can't you use an alias in WHERE?" and "WHERE versus HAVING?" Recite the eight steps, then derive the rules from them: aggregates need groups, so they belong in HAVING; aliases are created in SELECT, so only ORDER BY sees them. Mention that the optimizer may physically reorder work.

lessons.description: Filter rows with =, <>, <, >, <=, >= and understand how WHERE is evaluated row by row.

sections.title: Run It Yourself
sections.content: Open Practice → SQL Lab. It comes preloaded with two tables: employees(id, name, department, salary, hire_date) with 8 rows, and departments(id, name, budget) with 4 rows. Every query in this lesson runs there exactly as written.

sections.title: How WHERE Works
sections.content: WHERE tests a condition against each row. Rows where the condition is TRUE are kept; rows where it is FALSE or UNKNOWN (because of NULL) are discarded. WHERE runs before SELECT, so it can't use column aliases defined in the SELECT list.

sections.title: Example
sections.explanation: Returns Alice (85000), Bob (78000) and Fiona (92000).

sections.title: Predict the Output
sections.code:
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2023-01-01' AND department <> 'Engineering';
sections.explanation: Hired in 2023 or later: Alice, Charlie, Evan, George. Removing Engineering drops Alice. ISO dates (YYYY-MM-DD) stored as text compare correctly as strings.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using double quotes for text: `"Sales"` is an identifier (a column name) in standard SQL. Use single quotes: `'Sales'`.
Comparing numbers stored as text: '9' > '10' is TRUE as strings. Store numbers in numeric columns.
Referencing a SELECT alias in WHERE: `SELECT salary*12 AS annual ... WHERE annual > 900000` fails. Repeat the expression or use a subquery.

sections.question: How many employees have a salary of at least 72000?
sections.explanation: Fiona 92000, Alice 85000, Bob 78000, Diana 72000. That's 4 (>= includes 72000).

items: WHERE filters rows before SELECT runs.
Text uses single quotes; ISO dates compare correctly as text.
You can't use SELECT aliases inside WHERE.

content.theory:
The `WHERE` clause filters rows, keeping only those that satisfy a condition. It's how a query narrows a million-row table down to the handful of rows you care about. This lesson explains how `WHERE` evaluates conditions, the comparison operators, how comparisons behave for numbers, text and dates, and how to write filters that can use indexes.

## How WHERE works

`WHERE` evaluates its condition once for each row produced by `FROM`. Rows where the condition is TRUE stay; rows where it's FALSE or UNKNOWN are dropped.

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 80000;
~~~

The condition can reference any column of the source tables, including columns not in the select list. It can't reference column aliases from `SELECT` or aggregate functions, because both are computed later in the query's logical order.

## Comparison operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `=` | Equal | `dept_id = 10` |
| `<>` or `!=` | Not equal | `status <> 'terminated'` |
| `<`, `>` | Less than, greater than | `salary > 50000` |
| `<=`, `>=` | At most, at least | `hire_date >= '2023-01-01'` |

`<>` is the SQL standard; `!=` is accepted by all major databases. SQL uses a single `=` for comparison, not `==` as in many programming languages.

## Comparing numbers

Numeric comparisons behave as expected, with two cautions. Floating-point columns store approximations, so `WHERE price = 0.3` can miss a value computed as 0.1 + 0.2. Use exact `NUMERIC` types for values you'll compare for equality, such as money. And comparisons between an integer column and a decimal literal convert types; `WHERE quantity > 2.5` works, but understand that the database converts one side.

## Comparing text

Text comparisons follow the column's **collation**, the rules for ordering and equality. In a typical collation, `'apple' < 'banana'` because comparison goes character by character. Two details catch people out:

- **Case**: PostgreSQL compares case-sensitively, so `'Alice' = 'alice'` is false. MySQL and SQL Server usually use case-insensitive collations, so it's true there. For portable case-insensitive matching, compare `LOWER(name) = 'alice'`
- **Trailing spaces**: values in `CHAR(n)` columns are padded with spaces, and comparisons with `CHAR` usually ignore trailing spaces, while `VARCHAR` comparisons may not, depending on the database

Text literals use single quotes. Double quotes mean an identifier in standard SQL, so `WHERE name = "Alice"` looks for a column named `Alice` in PostgreSQL. A single quote inside a string is escaped by doubling it: `'O''Brien'`.

## Comparing dates

Date literals in ISO format, `'2024-03-15'`, work in every major database. Because ISO dates sort as text in date order, comparisons such as `hire_date >= '2024-01-01'` are reliable even in SQLite, which stores dates as text.

Timestamps need care with ranges. To find everything on 15 March 2024, this misses most of the day:

~~~sql
WHERE created_at <= '2024-03-15'          -- means up to 00:00:00 on the 15th
~~~

Use a half-open range instead, including the start and excluding the next day:

~~~sql
WHERE created_at >= '2024-03-15' AND created_at < '2024-03-16'
~~~

Half-open ranges work for any precision of timestamp and never overlap or leave gaps between consecutive periods.

## NULL in comparisons

Every comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, so `WHERE manager_id = NULL` and `WHERE manager_id <> NULL` both return no rows. Use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`. Remember also that `WHERE salary <> 50000` excludes rows where salary is NULL, which surprises people expecting "everything except 50,000".

## Filters and indexes

An index on a column lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table, but only when the condition is written so the index can be used. The rule: keep the indexed column alone on one side of the comparison.

| Can use an index on `salary` | Can't use it |
|---|---|
| `salary > 50000` | `salary * 12 > 600000` |
| `salary BETWEEN 40000 AND 60000` | `salary + bonus > 60000` |

The same applies to functions: `WHERE YEAR(hire_date) = 2024` or `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x'` hides the column inside a function, so a plain index on it can't help. Rewrite as a range, `hire_date >= '2024-01-01' AND hire_date < '2025-01-01'`, or create an index on the expression itself, which PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL 8 support. Conditions that can use an index are sometimes called **sargable**, short for "search argument able".

## Implicit type conversion

Comparing a column with a value of a different type forces a conversion. In MySQL, comparing a text column holding phone numbers with a number, `WHERE phone = 9876543210`, converts every row's text to a number, which prevents index use and can match unexpected values. Always compare with a literal of the column's own type.

## Parameterized filters

In application code, filter values come from users. Never concatenate them into SQL strings; use parameters, `WHERE email = ?`, so the database treats input strictly as data. This prevents SQL injection and lets the database reuse the query plan.

## How interviewers test this

Expect filtering queries with numeric, text and date conditions, and questions such as "Why does WHERE x = NULL return nothing?" and "Why isn't my index used?" Use `IS NULL`, half-open date ranges and sargable conditions that keep indexed columns bare, and mention collation when comparing text.

lessons.title: AND, OR, NOT, IN and BETWEEN
lessons.description: Combine conditions correctly, avoid precedence bugs, and use IN and BETWEEN for cleaner filters.

sections.title: Precedence
sections.content: NOT is evaluated first, then AND, then OR, just like × before + in arithmetic. When you mix AND and OR, always add parentheses to make your intent explicit.

sections.title: The Classic Precedence Bug
sections.code:
-- Intended: Sales or HR employees earning at least 60000
-- BUG: AND binds tighter, so this means
--   department = 'Sales' OR (department = 'HR' AND salary >= 60000)
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Sales' OR department = 'HR' AND salary >= 60000;
-- returns Charlie, Diana, George   (George earns 58000!)

-- Correct
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE (department = 'Sales' OR department = 'HR') AND salary >= 60000;
-- returns Charlie, Diana

-- Cleaner with IN
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE department IN ('Sales', 'HR') AND salary >= 60000;
sections.explanation: IN (a, b, c) is shorthand for = a OR = b OR = c, and it avoids the precedence trap.

sections.title: BETWEEN (inclusive on both ends)
sections.code:
SELECT name, salary FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 65000 AND 72000;
sections.explanation: Returns Charlie 65000, Diana 72000, Evan 68000, Hannah 71000. Both 65000 and 72000 are included.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Writing `BETWEEN 72000 AND 65000` (high value first) returns nothing; the lower bound must come first.
For timestamps, `BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'` misses times later on Jan 31. Prefer `>= '2024-01-01' AND < '2024-02-01'`.
`NOT IN` with a list containing NULL returns no rows at all (see the NULL lesson).

sections.question: Which query returns employees NOT in Engineering or Sales?
sections.explanation: Option B is always true (every value differs from at least one of the two). NOT IN expresses 'neither' correctly.

items: Precedence: NOT > AND > OR. Use parentheses whenever you mix them.
IN is a clean multi-value equality; BETWEEN is inclusive.

content.theory:
Real filters combine several conditions: employees in engineering **and** hired this year, orders that are pending **or** on hold, products **not** discontinued. SQL's logical operators combine conditions, and `IN` and `BETWEEN` express common combinations more compactly. This lesson explains `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, operator precedence and why parentheses matter, `IN` and `BETWEEN` with their edge cases, and how NULL changes the results.

## AND, OR and NOT

`AND` requires both conditions to be true; `OR` requires at least one; `NOT` inverts a condition:

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 10 AND salary > 70000;

SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE status = 'on_leave' OR status = 'suspended';

SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE NOT (dept_id = 10);
~~~

## Precedence and parentheses

`NOT` binds tightest, then `AND`, then `OR`. So this query doesn't mean what it appears to:

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 10 OR dept_id = 20 AND salary > 70000;
~~~

Because `AND` binds first, it means `dept_id = 10 OR (dept_id = 20 AND salary > 70000)`: everyone in department 10, plus well-paid people in department 20. If you meant well-paid people in either department, write:

~~~sql
WHERE (dept_id = 10 OR dept_id = 20) AND salary > 70000;
~~~

Use parentheses whenever a condition mixes `AND` and `OR`, even when precedence happens to give the right answer. They make intent clear to readers and prevent bugs when someone edits the query later.

## De Morgan's laws

Negating a combined condition flips the operator:

- `NOT (A AND B)` equals `NOT A OR NOT B`
- `NOT (A OR B)` equals `NOT A AND NOT B`

So "not in department 10 or 20" is `NOT (dept_id = 10 OR dept_id = 20)`, which equals `dept_id <> 10 AND dept_id <> 20`. A common mistake is writing `dept_id <> 10 OR dept_id <> 20`, which is true for every row, since no value equals both 10 and 20.

## IN

`IN` tests membership in a list:

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IN (10, 20, 30);
~~~

It's shorthand for `dept_id = 10 OR dept_id = 20 OR dept_id = 30`, shorter and easier to read. The list can also be a subquery: `WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE location = 'Bengaluru')`.

## NOT IN and NULL

`NOT IN` is shorthand for a chain of `<>` comparisons joined by `AND`. If the list contains NULL, one comparison is always UNKNOWN, so the whole condition is never TRUE:

~~~sql
WHERE dept_id NOT IN (10, NULL)   -- returns no rows, ever
~~~

With literal lists, this is rare. With subqueries, it's a real danger: if the subquery can return a NULL, `NOT IN` silently returns nothing. Use `NOT EXISTS`, or add `WHERE column IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery. Also, rows where the tested column itself is NULL are never returned by `IN` or `NOT IN`.

## BETWEEN

`BETWEEN` tests whether a value falls in a range, **inclusive** of both ends:

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000;   -- 50,000 and 80,000 both included
~~~

It's equivalent to `salary >= 50000 AND salary <= 80000`. The lower bound must come first: `BETWEEN 80000 AND 50000` matches nothing in standard SQL. `NOT BETWEEN` matches values outside the range.

## BETWEEN with timestamps

Because `BETWEEN` is inclusive, it's risky with timestamps:

~~~sql
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-03-01' AND '2024-03-31'
~~~

The upper bound means midnight at the start of 31 March, so almost all of that day is excluded. Changing it to `'2024-03-31 23:59:59'` misses fractional seconds. The reliable form is a half-open range: `created_at >= '2024-03-01' AND created_at < '2024-04-01'`. Use `BETWEEN` for integers and dates without times, and half-open ranges for timestamps.

## Short-circuit evaluation

Programming languages usually evaluate `A AND B` left to right and skip B when A is false. SQL doesn't promise any evaluation order: the optimizer may evaluate conditions in whatever order it estimates is cheapest. Don't rely on order for safety. This can fail if the optimizer evaluates the division first:

~~~sql
WHERE quantity <> 0 AND total / quantity > 10
~~~

Write `total / NULLIF(quantity, 0) > 10` instead, or use a `CASE` expression, which does guarantee evaluation order in most databases.

## Logical operators and NULL

Three-valued logic applies: `TRUE AND UNKNOWN` is UNKNOWN, `FALSE AND UNKNOWN` is FALSE, `TRUE OR UNKNOWN` is TRUE, and `NOT UNKNOWN` is UNKNOWN. In practice, a condition like `WHERE bonus > 1000 OR dept_id = 10` returns department 10 employees even if their bonus is NULL, because the OR's second branch is TRUE.

## OR and performance

Conditions joined by `OR` on different columns, such as `WHERE email = ? OR phone = ?`, can be harder to optimize than `AND`. Some databases combine two index scans; others fall back to a full table scan. Rewriting as a `UNION` of two indexed queries sometimes helps on large tables. Check with `EXPLAIN`.

## How interviewers test this

Expect filters mixing `AND` and `OR`, and questions such as "Is BETWEEN inclusive?" and "Why does NOT IN return nothing?" Use parentheses, apply De Morgan's laws correctly, prefer half-open ranges for timestamps, and recommend `NOT EXISTS` when NULLs might appear in a subquery.

lessons.title: LIKE and Pattern Matching
lessons.description: Use % and _ wildcards, understand case sensitivity, and know when LIKE can't use an index.

sections.title: Filtering Dates Stored as Text
sections.explanation: This works because ISO dates are text in SQLite. A range (`>= '2023-01-01' AND < '2024-01-01'`) is usually better, because it can use an index on hire_date.

sections.title: Database Differences
items: SQLite and MySQL (with default collations) compare LIKE case-insensitively for ASCII letters; PostgreSQL's LIKE is case-sensitive (use `ILIKE` there).
A leading wildcard (`'%son'`) can't use a B+ tree index, so the database scans every row.
To match a literal % or _, use an escape character: `LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\'`.

sections.question: Which pattern finds names that contain the letter 'o' anywhere?
sections.explanation: % on both sides allows any characters before and after: Bob, Fiona and George match.

items: % = any number of characters; _ = exactly one.
Case sensitivity depends on the database.
Leading wildcards can't use indexes.

content.theory:
`LIKE` matches text against a pattern with wildcards, answering questions such as "which customers have a Gmail address?" or "which products start with 'Pro'?" It's flexible but has performance traps, since some patterns can't use an index. This lesson explains the two wildcards, escaping, case sensitivity across databases, how patterns interact with indexes, and the alternatives for more powerful matching: regular expressions and full-text search.

## The two wildcards

`LIKE` supports two wildcards:

| Wildcard | Matches | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%` | Any sequence of characters, including none | `'A%'` | Anything starting with A |
| `_` | Exactly one character | `'_at'` | `'cat'`, `'bat'`, not `'at'` |

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
SELECT name FROM products WHERE code LIKE 'PRD-____';   -- PRD- plus four characters
~~~

The pattern must match the **whole** value. `LIKE 'son'` matches only the exact string `'son'`, not `'Johnson'`. For "contains", wrap the text in percent signs: `LIKE '%son%'`.

## Common patterns

| Goal | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Starts with "Pro" | `LIKE 'Pro%'` |
| Ends with ".pdf" | `LIKE '%.pdf'` |
| Contains "data" | `LIKE '%data%'` |
| Exactly five characters | `LIKE '_____'` |
| Second character is "a" | `LIKE '_a%'` |

`NOT LIKE` returns rows that don't match. Like other comparisons, `LIKE` with a NULL value returns UNKNOWN, so rows with NULL in the column are excluded by both `LIKE` and `NOT LIKE`.

## Escaping wildcards

To match a literal `%` or `_`, escape it. The `ESCAPE` clause names an escape character:

~~~sql
SELECT code FROM discounts WHERE code LIKE '%50!%%' ESCAPE '!';   -- contains "50%"
~~~

Here `!%` means a literal percent sign. PostgreSQL and MySQL also treat backslash as the default escape character. Escaping matters with user input: a search box that passes `_` or `%` straight into a pattern lets users run broader matches than intended, and patterns starting with `%` can force expensive scans.

## Case sensitivity

Whether `LIKE` ignores case depends on the database:

| Database | Default `LIKE` behaviour |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | Case-sensitive; use `ILIKE` for case-insensitive matching |
| MySQL | Follows the collation, usually case-insensitive |
| SQL Server | Follows the collation, usually case-insensitive |
| SQLite | Case-insensitive for ASCII letters only |

The portable approach is `LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER('%alice%')`, though wrapping the column in a function prevents a plain index from helping.

## LIKE and indexes

A B-tree index stores values in sorted order, like a dictionary. It can find all words starting with "Pro" quickly by jumping to that section, but it can't find all words containing "pro" somewhere, any more than a dictionary helps you find words with "pro" in the middle.

| Pattern | Can use a B-tree index? |
|---|---|
| `'Pro%'` (prefix) | Yes, as a range scan |
| `'%pro'` (suffix) | No |
| `'%pro%'` (contains) | No, full scan |

In PostgreSQL, prefix matching with an index needs the `C` collation or a `text_pattern_ops` index. For suffix searches, a trick is to index the reversed string and search for the reversed pattern as a prefix. For "contains" searches on large tables, PostgreSQL's `pg_trgm` extension builds trigram indexes that make `LIKE '%pro%'` and `ILIKE` fast.

## Regular expressions

When wildcards aren't enough, databases offer regular expressions:

~~~sql
-- PostgreSQL: phone numbers of exactly 10 digits
SELECT phone FROM customers WHERE phone ~ '^[0-9]{10}$';

-- MySQL 8 equivalent
SELECT phone FROM customers WHERE phone REGEXP '^[0-9]{10}$';
~~~

PostgreSQL uses `~` for case-sensitive and `~*` for case-insensitive matching; MySQL uses `REGEXP` or `REGEXP_LIKE()`. SQLite defines the `REGEXP` operator but needs an extension to supply its implementation. Regular expressions are powerful but generally can't use ordinary indexes, so they suit validation and smaller tables.

## SIMILAR TO

The SQL standard's `SIMILAR TO` operator mixes `LIKE` wildcards with some regular expression syntax. PostgreSQL supports it, but it's rarely used; most people choose `LIKE` for basic patterns and full regular expressions for complex ones.

## Full-text search

Searching documents for words is a different problem from pattern matching. Searching for "running" should also find "run", rank better matches higher, and handle large text quickly. `LIKE '%run%'` does none of that and also matches "prune". Full-text search tokenizes text into words, reduces them to their stems and builds a specialized index:

~~~sql
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT title FROM articles
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'database & index');
~~~

MySQL offers `FULLTEXT` indexes with `MATCH ... AGAINST`, and SQLite offers the FTS5 extension. Large search features often use dedicated engines such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.

## How interviewers test this

Expect queries such as "names starting with A", "emails from a domain" and "names whose second letter is a". Know `%` versus `_`, that patterns must match the whole value, how to escape wildcards, and why a leading `%` prevents index use. Mention `ILIKE`, regular expressions and full-text search as the next tools.

lessons.title: Working With NULL
lessons.description: Three-valued logic, IS NULL, COALESCE, NULLs in aggregates, and the NOT IN trap.

sections.title: What NULL Means
= NULL Never Works
sections.code:
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE bonus = NULL;    -- 0 rows (always UNKNOWN)
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE bonus IS NULL;   -- Charlie, Diana, Evan, George, Hannah
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE bonus <> 5000;   -- 0 rows! NULL <> 5000 is UNKNOWN too
sections.explanation: To include rows with a NULL bonus in that last query, write `bonus <> 5000 OR bonus IS NULL`.

sections.title: Replacing NULLs With COALESCE
sections.code:
SELECT name, salary + COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS total
FROM employees
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 3;
-- Fiona 97000, Alice 90000, Bob 83000
sections.explanation: Without COALESCE, `salary + bonus` would be NULL for everyone without a bonus: arithmetic with NULL gives NULL.

traps.question: Why does `WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t)` sometimes return nothing?
traps.trap: Blaming the data or the join.
traps.solution: If the subquery returns even one NULL, then `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` means `x <> ... AND x <> NULL`, which is never TRUE. Use NOT EXISTS, or filter out NULLs with `WHERE y IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

traps.question: Is AVG(bonus) the same as SUM(bonus) / COUNT(*)?
traps.trap: Saying yes.
traps.solution: No. AVG divides by the count of non-NULL values. To treat missing values as 0, use AVG(COALESCE(bonus, 0)).

sections.question: What does `SELECT NULL = NULL` return?
sections.explanation: Two unknown values can't be known to be equal, so the result is unknown. Use IS NULL (or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM where supported).

items: Test for NULL with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never with = or <>.
Aggregates (except COUNT(*)) skip NULLs.
COALESCE(x, default) replaces NULL; NOT IN with NULLs is a trap, so prefer NOT EXISTS.

content.theory:
NULL represents a missing value, and it behaves differently from every other value in SQL. Comparisons with it are unknown, arithmetic with it produces NULL, and aggregates skip it. Writing correct queries means handling NULL deliberately in filters, calculations, sorting and joins. This lesson is a practical guide: how to test for NULL, replace it, compare values that might be NULL, and avoid the most common NULL bugs.

## Testing for NULL

Only `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` test for NULL correctly:

~~~sql
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;       -- top-level managers
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE phone IS NOT NULL;        -- has a phone number
~~~

`= NULL` and `<> NULL` always produce UNKNOWN and return no rows. Some tools, such as SQL Server with a legacy setting, once allowed `= NULL`, which spread a bad habit; never rely on it.

## NULL in arithmetic and strings

Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: `salary + bonus` is NULL for every employee without a bonus. String concatenation with the standard `||` operator also gives NULL: `first_name || ' ' || middle_name` is NULL when `middle_name` is NULL. MySQL's `CONCAT()` likewise returns NULL if any argument is NULL, while `CONCAT_WS()` skips NULL arguments. PostgreSQL's `CONCAT()` treats NULL as an empty string. Oracle treats empty strings as NULL, the opposite surprise.

## COALESCE

`COALESCE` returns its first non-NULL argument, making it the main tool for substituting defaults:

~~~sql
SELECT name,
       salary + COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS total_pay,
       COALESCE(mobile, office_phone, 'no contact') AS contact
FROM employees;
~~~

It's standard and works in every major database. Older, dialect-specific functions do similar jobs: `IFNULL(a, b)` in MySQL and SQLite, `ISNULL(a, b)` in SQL Server, `NVL(a, b)` in Oracle. Prefer `COALESCE` for portability, and note it accepts any number of arguments.

## NULLIF

`NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when a equals b, and a otherwise. Its main use is preventing division by zero:

~~~sql
SELECT region, revenue / NULLIF(orders, 0) AS revenue_per_order
FROM sales;
~~~

When `orders` is 0, the division becomes `revenue / NULL`, which is NULL instead of an error. Wrap it in `COALESCE(..., 0)` if you'd rather show zero. `NULLIF` also converts placeholder values into real NULLs, such as `NULLIF(phone, '')` for empty strings left by an old form.

## Comparing values that might be NULL

To check whether two nullable columns hold the same value, `a = b` fails when both are NULL. The standard solution is `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, which treats two NULLs as equal:

~~~sql
SELECT * FROM staging s JOIN employees e
ON s.middle_name IS NOT DISTINCT FROM e.middle_name;
~~~

PostgreSQL and SQLite (as `IS`) support it; MySQL uses the null-safe operator `<=>`. Without these, write `(a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL))`.

## NULL in negated filters

`WHERE status <> 'active'` excludes rows where status is NULL, because `NULL <> 'active'` is unknown. If those rows should be included, say so explicitly:

~~~sql
WHERE status <> 'active' OR status IS NULL
-- or, in PostgreSQL:
WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'active'
~~~

Similarly, `NOT IN` with a NULL in its list returns no rows. Prefer `NOT EXISTS` for subqueries.

## NULL in aggregates

Aggregates skip NULLs, and the results can mislead:

| Expression | With bonuses 1000, 3000 and NULL |
|---|---|
| `COUNT(*)` | 3 |
| `COUNT(bonus)` | 2 |
| `SUM(bonus)` | 4000 |
| `AVG(bonus)` | 2000 (sum over 2 non-NULL rows) |
| `AVG(COALESCE(bonus, 0))` | 1333.33 (sum over all 3 rows) |

Decide whether a missing value means "unknown, leave it out" or "zero", and write the query to match. `SUM` over no rows, or only NULLs, returns NULL rather than 0, so report totals as `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)`.

## NULL in sorting

Databases disagree on where NULLs sort. PostgreSQL and Oracle treat NULL as larger than any value, so NULLs come last in ascending order. MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server treat it as smaller, putting NULLs first. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite (since 3.30) support explicit control:

~~~sql
SELECT name, last_login FROM users ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS LAST;
~~~

In MySQL, emulate it with `ORDER BY last_login IS NULL, last_login DESC`, since the boolean expression sorts false before true.

## NULL in joins and grouping

Rows with NULL join keys never match in an inner join, because `NULL = NULL` isn't true. Outer joins produce NULLs in the columns of the unmatched side, which is how you find missing matches: `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_table.id IS NULL`. `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT` treat all NULLs as one group.

## Designing to avoid NULL problems

Declare columns `NOT NULL` unless absence is meaningful, and use defaults where a sensible one exists. When NULL is allowed, document what it means. Avoid using placeholder values such as `-1`, `'N/A'` or `'1900-01-01'` to mean "missing": they corrupt averages, comparisons and sorts in ways that are harder to detect than NULL.

## How interviewers test this

Expect questions on `IS NULL`, `COALESCE` versus `ISNULL`/`NVL`, `NULLIF` for division by zero, and how NULL affects `COUNT` and `AVG`. Show the aggregate table, handle negated filters explicitly, and mention `IS DISTINCT FROM` for null-safe comparison.

lessons.title: ORDER BY, LIMIT / OFFSET and DISTINCT
lessons.description: Sort by several columns, paginate results, and remove duplicate rows.

sections.title: Multi-Column Sorting
sections.explanation: Sorts by department first; within each department, the highest salary comes first.

sections.title: Top-N and Pagination
sections.explanation: SQL Server uses `TOP n` or `OFFSET ... FETCH NEXT`; Oracle uses `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`. The idea is the same.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary set of rows, which may change between runs.
Large OFFSETs are slow, because the database still reads and discards the skipped rows. For deep pagination use keyset pagination: `WHERE salary < :last_seen ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 20`.
`DISTINCT` applies to the whole selected row, not just the first column: `SELECT DISTINCT department, name` returns 8 rows.

sections.question: SELECT name FROM employees ORDER BY salary ASC LIMIT 1 returns:
sections.explanation: Ascending order puts the lowest salary first: George with 58000.

items: Always ORDER BY when you use LIMIT.
OFFSET pagination gets slow on deep pages; keyset pagination scales.
DISTINCT de-duplicates whole rows.

content.theory:
Without `ORDER BY`, a database returns rows in whatever order is convenient, which can change from one run to the next. `ORDER BY` sorts results, `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` return a slice, and together they power leaderboards, "top 10" lists and paginated screens. This lesson explains sorting rules, ties and determinism, `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` across dialects, why deep offsets are slow, and keyset pagination as the scalable alternative.

## ORDER BY basics

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;
~~~

`ASC` (ascending) is the default; `DESC` sorts descending. Multiple sort keys break ties in order:

~~~sql
ORDER BY dept_id ASC, salary DESC, name ASC
~~~

This sorts by department, then by highest salary within each department, then alphabetically among equal salaries. Each key has its own direction.

## What you can sort by

`ORDER BY` runs after `SELECT` in the logical order, so it can use column aliases and expressions:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary * 12 AS annual FROM employees ORDER BY annual DESC;
SELECT name FROM employees ORDER BY LENGTH(name), name;
~~~

You can also sort by column position, `ORDER BY 2 DESC`, meaning the second column in the select list. It's handy interactively but fragile in code, since adding a column shifts positions. You can sort by columns not in the select list, except with `SELECT DISTINCT`, where most databases require the sort keys to be selected.

## No ORDER BY, no order

Relational tables are unordered sets. A query without `ORDER BY` might return rows in insertion order today and a different order tomorrow, after an update, a vacuum, a parallel scan or a new index. Any code that depends on row order must specify `ORDER BY`. This includes `LIMIT`: `SELECT * FROM employees LIMIT 5` returns an arbitrary five rows.

## Ties and deterministic order

If several rows share the same sort value, their relative order is undefined. For a "top 3 salaries" list where the third and fourth employees earn the same, either might appear, and the choice can change between runs. That causes bugs in pagination, where a row can appear on two pages or none. Make ordering **deterministic** by adding a unique column as the last tiebreaker:

~~~sql
ORDER BY salary DESC, id
~~~

## Sorting text and NULLs

Text sorts according to the column's collation, which decides whether uppercase sorts before lowercase and how accented characters compare. Numbers stored as text sort as text, so `'10'` comes before `'9'`; store numbers in numeric columns, or cast when sorting. NULL placement varies: last in ascending order in PostgreSQL and Oracle, first in MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server. Use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` where supported.

## LIMIT and OFFSET

`LIMIT` restricts the number of rows returned, and `OFFSET` skips rows first:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;     -- rows 21 to 30
~~~

Syntax varies by database:

| Database | First 10 rows |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite | `LIMIT 10` |
| SQL Server | `SELECT TOP 10 ...` or `OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY` |
| Standard SQL, Oracle 12c+, PostgreSQL | `FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY` |

MySQL also accepts `LIMIT 20, 10`, meaning offset 20 and count 10, an order that people often confuse.

## Page numbers

For page number p, counting from 1, with s rows per page, the offset is (p − 1) × s. Page 3 with 10 rows per page uses `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20`.

## Why deep offsets are slow

`OFFSET` doesn't jump to a position. The database must produce and discard every skipped row. `OFFSET 100000` reads 100,010 rows to return 10. Pages near the end of a large result get progressively slower, and a crawler walking through every page can overload a server.

Offsets also shift when data changes. If a new row is inserted at the top while a user moves from page 1 to page 2, the last row of page 1 is pushed onto page 2 and appears twice.

## Keyset pagination

Keyset pagination, also called the seek method, remembers where the previous page ended and continues from there:

~~~sql
-- first page
SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, id
LIMIT 10;

-- next page: continue after the last row seen (salary 72000, id 418)
SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees
WHERE (salary, id) < (72000, 418)
ORDER BY salary DESC, id
LIMIT 10;
~~~

With an index on `(salary, id)`, each page costs about the same regardless of depth, and inserted rows don't cause duplicates. The trade-off is that you can't jump directly to page 50; you can only move forward or backward. That fits infinite scrolling and "load more" buttons, which is why large sites use it. The row-value comparison `(salary, id) < (...)` works in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite; in other databases, expand it into `salary < 72000 OR (salary = 72000 AND id < 418)`.

## Sorting cost

Sorting n rows costs O(n log n) and may spill to disk when results exceed the database's sort memory. An index whose order matches the `ORDER BY` lets the database read rows already sorted and stop after `LIMIT` rows, turning a full sort into a quick index walk. For "top N" queries, many databases use a partial sort that keeps only the best N rows in memory.

## DISTINCT with ORDER BY and LIMIT

The logical order is `SELECT`, then `DISTINCT`, then `ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT`. So `SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees ORDER BY dept_id LIMIT 3` deduplicates first, then returns the three smallest department IDs.

## How interviewers test this

Expect top-N queries, pagination and "Why is my pagination slow?" Always pair `LIMIT` with `ORDER BY`, add a unique tiebreaker, know the dialect differences, explain why large offsets scan skipped rows, and describe keyset pagination with its trade-off.

lessons.title: String Functions
lessons.description: UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTR, concatenation, REPLACE, TRIM and INSTR, with dialect differences.

sections.title: Common String Functions (SQLite)
sections.code:
SELECT UPPER(name), LOWER(department), LENGTH(name), SUBSTR(name, 1, 3)
FROM employees WHERE id <= 3;
-- ALICE  engineering  5  Ali
-- BOB    engineering  3  Bob
-- CHARLIE sales       7  Cha

SELECT name || ' (' || department || ')' AS label
FROM employees WHERE id IN (1, 4);
-- Alice (Engineering)
-- Diana (HR)
sections.explanation: SUBSTR is 1-indexed: SUBSTR(name, 1, 3) means 3 characters starting at position 1.

sections.title: Predict the Output
sections.code: SELECT INSTR(name, 'a') FROM employees WHERE name = 'Hannah';
sections.explanation: INSTR returns the 1-based position of the first match: H-a-n-n-a-h, so 'a' is first found at position 2. It returns 0 if there is no match.

sections.question: SUBSTR('Engineering', 3, 4) returns:
sections.explanation: Start at position 3 ('g') and take 4 characters: g-i-n-e.

items: String positions are 1-based in SQL.
Concatenation syntax differs: || in SQLite/PostgreSQL, CONCAT in MySQL.
Wrapping a column in a function inside WHERE usually prevents index use.

content.theory:
String functions clean, transform and extract text: trimming stray spaces, standardizing case, pulling a domain out of an email, or formatting names for a report. Function names vary more across databases than most of SQL, so knowing the standard forms and the common dialect differences matters. This lesson covers length and case, concatenation, trimming, extracting substrings, searching and replacing, padding, and the performance cost of functions in filters.

## Length and case

~~~sql
SELECT name,
       LENGTH(name)  AS chars,
       UPPER(name)   AS upper_name,
       LOWER(email)  AS normalized_email
FROM employees;
~~~

`LENGTH` counts characters in PostgreSQL and SQLite, but bytes in MySQL, where `CHAR_LENGTH` counts characters. The difference matters for non-ASCII text: `'नमस्ते'` has 6 characters but 18 bytes in UTF-8. SQL Server uses `LEN`, which ignores trailing spaces. `UPPER` and `LOWER` are standard everywhere. PostgreSQL adds `INITCAP` for title case.

## Concatenation

Joining strings uses different syntax across databases. The SQL standard, PostgreSQL, SQLite and Oracle use the double-pipe operator:

~~~sql
SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM employees;
~~~

MySQL treats `||` as logical OR by default and uses `CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)` instead. SQL Server uses `+` or `CONCAT`.

`CONCAT` is available in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, making it the most portable choice. NULL handling differs: `||` returns NULL if any part is NULL, MySQL's `CONCAT` returns NULL if any argument is NULL, and PostgreSQL's `CONCAT` skips NULLs. `CONCAT_WS(separator, ...)`, in PostgreSQL and MySQL, joins values with a separator and skips NULLs, which suits building addresses from optional parts.

## Trimming

`TRIM` removes leading and trailing spaces, or other characters:

~~~sql
SELECT TRIM('  Asha  ');                 -- 'Asha'
SELECT LTRIM('  Asha'), RTRIM('Asha  ');  -- left only, right only
SELECT TRIM(BOTH '0' FROM '000123');      -- '123'
~~~

Stray spaces from imported data cause failed matches: `'Asha '` doesn't equal `'Asha'` in a `VARCHAR` comparison. Trimming during import, or with a `CHECK` constraint that rejects untrimmed values, prevents these bugs.

## Extracting substrings

`SUBSTRING` extracts part of a string by position, counting from 1:

~~~sql
SELECT SUBSTRING('StudyHub' FROM 1 FOR 5);   -- 'Study' (standard form)
SELECT SUBSTRING('StudyHub', 6, 3);          -- 'Hub' (common shorthand)
~~~

SQLite and Oracle use `SUBSTR`. `LEFT(s, n)` and `RIGHT(s, n)` take characters from either end in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server. SQL strings are 1-indexed, unlike most programming languages; using position 0 is a common bug.

## Searching

Finding the position of a substring is essential for extracting variable-length parts:

| Database | Function | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, MySQL, standard | `POSITION('@' IN email)` | Position, or 0 if absent |
| MySQL, SQLite, Oracle | `INSTR(email, '@')` | Position, or 0 |
| SQL Server | `CHARINDEX('@', email)` | Position, or 0 |

Extracting an email's domain combines search and substring:

~~~sql
SELECT SUBSTRING(email FROM POSITION('@' IN email) + 1) AS domain
FROM customers;
~~~

PostgreSQL also offers `SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2)`, and MySQL offers `SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1)`, both more readable for this task.

## Replacing and padding

`REPLACE(s, from, to)` replaces every occurrence of a substring:

~~~sql
SELECT REPLACE(phone, '-', '') FROM customers;   -- '98-765-43210' becomes '9876543210'
~~~

`LPAD` and `RPAD` pad a string to a length: `LPAD('42', 5, '0')` gives `'00042'`, useful for fixed-width codes. PostgreSQL and MySQL also offer `REVERSE` and `REPEAT`, and regular expression functions such as `REGEXP_REPLACE` for complex cleanup.

## Aggregating strings

Combining values from many rows into one string is a frequent reporting need, such as listing every employee in each department:

| Database | Function |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2017+, standard | `STRING_AGG(name, ', ')` |
| MySQL | `GROUP_CONCAT(name SEPARATOR ', ')` |
| SQLite | `GROUP_CONCAT(name, ', ')` |

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, STRING_AGG(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS team
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

MySQL truncates `GROUP_CONCAT` output at 1,024 bytes by default, controlled by the `group_concat_max_len` setting, a silent limit that surprises people.

## Converting between types

`CAST(expr AS type)` converts values: `CAST(42 AS VARCHAR)`, `CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE)`. PostgreSQL also accepts `'42'::INTEGER`. Casting text that isn't a valid number raises an error in PostgreSQL but may silently produce 0 in MySQL, depending on its SQL mode.

## Functions in WHERE clauses

Applying a function to a column in `WHERE` usually prevents index use:

~~~sql
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'asha@example.com'   -- a plain index on email can't help
~~~

The database must compute `LOWER(email)` for every row. Solutions: store data normalized when it's written, such as lowercased emails; create an index on the expression, `CREATE INDEX ON customers (LOWER(email))`, supported in PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL 8; or use a case-insensitive collation or PostgreSQL's `citext` type.

## Cleaning data with string functions

Real datasets need cleanup before analysis: trimming spaces, normalizing case, removing punctuation from phone numbers, splitting full names. Doing it once with an `UPDATE` and adding constraints to keep data clean is better than repeating the cleanup in every query.

## How interviewers test this

Expect tasks such as "extract the domain from an email", "find names longer than 10 characters", "list employees per department as a comma-separated string" and "format names as Last, First". Use the right function for your dialect, remember 1-based positions, handle NULL in concatenation, and mention expression indexes when filtering on functions.

lessons.title: Numeric Functions and Integer Division
lessons.description: ROUND, ABS, modulo, CAST, and the integer-division trap.

sections.title: Arithmetic on Salaries
sections.code:
SELECT name, salary,
       ROUND(salary * 1.075)      AS raised,       -- 91375.0
       salary / 12                AS monthly_int,  -- 7083  (integer division!)
       ROUND(salary / 12.0, 2)    AS monthly       -- 7083.33
FROM employees WHERE id = 1;
sections.explanation: When both operands are integers, SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server do integer division and drop the fraction. Make one operand decimal (12.0) or CAST it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Calculating percentages as `count / total * 100` with integers gives 0. Write `100.0 * count / total`.
MySQL's `/` always returns a decimal; use `DIV` there for integer division. Know which database the interviewer means.
Storing money as FLOAT causes rounding errors. Use DECIMAL(12, 2), or integer paise or cents.

sections.question: In SQLite, what does SELECT 5 / 2 * 2 return?
sections.explanation: 5 / 2 = 2 (integer division), then 2 × 2 = 4.

items: Integer / integer = integer in most databases; multiply by 1.0 or 100.0 first.
Use DECIMAL for money.

content.theory:
Numeric functions round values, compute remainders, find absolute values and perform the arithmetic behind reports. They look straightforward, but integer division, rounding rules and floating-point precision cause wrong answers that are hard to spot. This lesson explains arithmetic operators and integer division, rounding functions and their differences, modulo, choosing numeric types, and the precision traps in money and percentages.

## Arithmetic operators

SQL supports `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and modulo, written `%` in most databases or `MOD(a, b)` in the standard and Oracle. Standard precedence applies: multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, so use parentheses when combining them. Arithmetic with NULL produces NULL.

## Integer division

When both operands are integers, many databases perform **integer division**, discarding the remainder:

~~~sql
SELECT 7 / 2;      -- 3 in PostgreSQL, SQLite and SQL Server; 3.5000 in MySQL
SELECT 7 / 2.0;    -- 3.5 everywhere
~~~

This is the most common numeric bug in SQL. A query computing a percentage as `completed / total * 100` returns 0 for any fraction below 1 in PostgreSQL, because `completed / total` truncates to 0 before the multiplication. Force decimal division by making one operand decimal:

~~~sql
SELECT completed * 100.0 / total AS pct;
SELECT CAST(completed AS NUMERIC) / total * 100 AS pct;
~~~

Putting the multiplication first, `completed * 100.0 / total`, also preserves precision. MySQL's `/` always returns a decimal, and its `DIV` operator performs integer division.

## Rounding functions

| Function | Behaviour | 2.5 | -2.5 | 2.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROUND(x)` | Nearest integer, halves away from zero (for exact types) | 3 | -3 | 2 |
| `CEIL(x)` / `CEILING(x)` | Smallest integer ≥ x | 3 | -2 | 3 |
| `FLOOR(x)` | Largest integer ≤ x | 2 | -3 | 2 |
| `TRUNC(x)` | Drop the fractional part, toward zero | 2 | -2 | 2 |

`ROUND(x, n)` rounds to n decimal places: `ROUND(3.14159, 2)` gives 3.14. A negative n rounds to the left of the decimal point: `ROUND(1234, -2)` gives 1200. `TRUNC` is called `TRUNCATE(x, n)` in MySQL; SQL Server uses `ROUND(x, n, 1)`.

## Rounding rules differ

For exact `NUMERIC` values, PostgreSQL and MySQL round halves away from zero. For floating-point values, PostgreSQL's `ROUND` on `double precision` follows the platform, typically rounding halves to the nearest even number, so `ROUND(2.5::float8)` gives 2. Floating-point values such as 2.675 can't be represented exactly, so `ROUND(2.675, 2)` may give 2.67. When rounding must be predictable, as with money, use `NUMERIC`.

## CEIL and FLOOR in practice

`CEIL` answers "how many containers do I need?" questions. To find how many pages 47 items fill at 10 per page:

~~~sql
SELECT CEIL(47 / 10.0);   -- 5
~~~

With integer division, `CEIL(47 / 10)` gives 4, because `47 / 10` truncates to 4 before `CEIL` sees it. An integer-only alternative is `(47 + 10 - 1) / 10`. `FLOOR` groups values into buckets: `FLOOR(salary / 10000) * 10000` groups salaries into ranges of 10,000.

## Modulo

The remainder after division is useful for parity, cycles and bucketing:

~~~sql
SELECT id FROM employees WHERE id % 2 = 0;           -- even IDs
SELECT id, id % 4 AS shard FROM employees;           -- assign to 4 groups
~~~

For negative numbers, `%` in most databases takes the sign of the dividend: `-7 % 3` is -1, not 2. Normalize with `((x % n) + n) % n` when you need a non-negative remainder.

## Other useful functions

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ABS(x)` | Absolute value; differences regardless of direction |
| `POWER(x, y)` | x raised to the power y |
| `SQRT(x)` | Square root |
| `SIGN(x)` | -1, 0 or 1 by sign |
| `GREATEST(a, b, ...)` / `LEAST(...)` | Largest or smallest of several values in a row |
| `RANDOM()` / `RAND()` | A random number (PostgreSQL and SQLite / MySQL) |

`GREATEST` and `LEAST` compare values across columns in one row, unlike `MAX` and `MIN`, which aggregate down a column. Their NULL handling differs: PostgreSQL ignores NULL arguments, while MySQL returns NULL if any argument is NULL. SQL Server added them only in 2022.

## Choosing numeric types

| Type | Exact? | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `INTEGER`, `BIGINT` | Yes | Counts, IDs, quantities |
| `NUMERIC(p, s)` / `DECIMAL(p, s)` | Yes | Money, rates, anything compared for equality |
| `REAL`, `DOUBLE PRECISION` | No | Scientific measurements, where tiny errors are acceptable |

Floating-point types store binary approximations, so `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3` is false in `DOUBLE PRECISION`. Summing millions of floating-point amounts accumulates visible errors. Store money as `NUMERIC(12, 2)`, or as an integer count of the smallest unit, such as paise.

## Overflow

Integer arithmetic can overflow. `INTEGER` holds values up to about 2.1 billion; summing large values or multiplying two big numbers can exceed it. PostgreSQL raises an error on overflow, which is safe but can break reports. `SUM` of an integer column returns a `BIGINT` or `NUMERIC` in PostgreSQL to reduce this risk. Cast to `BIGINT` before multiplying large integers.

## Percentages and averages

`AVG` of an integer column returns a decimal in PostgreSQL and MySQL but may truncate in SQL Server. A percentage of total combines aggregates and division: `100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'done' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)`. Round only for display, at the end, because rounding intermediate values compounds errors.

## How interviewers test this

Expect percentage calculations, rounding questions and "Why does this division return 0?" Explain integer division and fix it with a decimal operand, know `ROUND`, `CEIL`, `FLOOR` and `TRUNC` with negative inputs, and recommend `NUMERIC` for money.
