sections.title: SQLite Date Functions
sections.code:
-- Extract year and month
SELECT name, strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS yr, strftime('%m', hire_date) AS mon
FROM employees WHERE id IN (1, 6);
-- Alice 2023 01
-- Fiona 2020 03

-- Whole years of service as of 2025-01-01
SELECT name,
       CAST((julianday('2025-01-01') - julianday(hire_date)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) AS years
FROM employees ORDER BY years DESC LIMIT 3;
-- Fiona 4, Diana 3, Bob 2

-- Date arithmetic
SELECT date('2024-03-15', '-10 days'),        -- 2024-03-05
       date('2024-02-10', 'start of month');  -- 2024-02-01
sections.explanation: SQLite has no DATE type: dates are stored as ISO text and handled by date(), strftime() and julianday().

sections.title: The Same Tasks in Other Databases
Predict the Output (an edge case)
sections.code: SELECT date('2024-01-31', '+1 month');
sections.explanation: SQLite adds one to the month (giving 2024-02-31), then normalizes the invalid date by overflowing into March. PostgreSQL would return 2024-02-29. Month arithmetic near the end of a month differs between databases, so test it.

sections.question: Which SQLite expression returns the hire month as text like '05'?
sections.explanation: strftime('%m', ...) gives a zero-padded month. SUBSTR(hire_date, 6, 2) would also work; SUBSTR(..., 1, 2) gives the century digits.

items: Store dates in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).
Date functions differ most across databases; learn your target database's set.
Watch end-of-month arithmetic.

content.theory:
Dates and times drive most business reporting: sales by month, users who signed up this week, orders older than 30 days. Date handling is also where SQL dialects differ most, and where time zones cause subtle bugs. This lesson covers the date and time types, getting the current date, extracting parts, date arithmetic, truncating to periods, formatting, time zones, and writing date filters that use indexes.

## Date and time types

| Type | Stores | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `DATE` | Calendar date | `2024-03-15` |
| `TIME` | Time of day | `14:30:00` |
| `TIMESTAMP` | Date and time, no time zone | `2024-03-15 14:30:00` |
| `TIMESTAMPTZ` (PostgreSQL) | An absolute instant, shown in the session's zone | `2024-03-15 14:30:00+05:30` |
| `INTERVAL` | A duration | `3 days`, `2 hours` |

MySQL has `DATE`, `DATETIME` and `TIMESTAMP`, where its `TIMESTAMP` converts to UTC for storage. SQLite has no date types; it stores dates as ISO-8601 text, Julian day numbers or Unix timestamps, and provides functions to work with them.

## The current date and time

~~~sql
SELECT CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;
~~~

These standard forms work in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite. Alternatives include `NOW()` in PostgreSQL and MySQL, `GETDATE()` in SQL Server and `SYSDATE` in Oracle. In PostgreSQL, `NOW()` returns the transaction's start time, so it stays constant throughout a transaction; `clock_timestamp()` returns the actual current time.

## Extracting parts

The standard `EXTRACT` function pulls out a component:

~~~sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS yr,
       EXTRACT(MONTH FROM hire_date) AS mon,
       EXTRACT(DOW FROM hire_date) AS weekday   -- PostgreSQL: 0 = Sunday
FROM employees;
~~~

MySQL also offers `YEAR()`, `MONTH()`, `DAY()` and `DAYOFWEEK()` (where 1 is Sunday). SQLite uses `strftime('%Y', hire_date)`, which returns text. Weekday numbering differs by database and function, so check before filtering on day-of-week values.

## Date arithmetic

Adding and subtracting time intervals varies most across dialects:

| Task | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add 30 days | `d + INTERVAL '30 days'` | `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 30 DAY)` | `date(d, '+30 days')` |
| Subtract 1 month | `d - INTERVAL '1 month'` | `DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)` | `date(d, '-1 month')` |
| Days between dates | `d2 - d1` (for DATE values) | `DATEDIFF(d2, d1)` | `julianday(d2) - julianday(d1)` |

SQL Server uses `DATEADD(day, 30, d)` and `DATEDIFF(day, d1, d2)`, with the argument order reversed compared with MySQL's `DATEDIFF`.

Month arithmetic has edge cases: adding one month to 31 January gives 29 February in a leap year in PostgreSQL and MySQL, clamping to the month's last day. Adding then subtracting a month doesn't always return the original date.

## Age and differences

PostgreSQL's `AGE(d2, d1)` returns a human-readable interval such as "3 years 2 mons 5 days". To compute tenure in whole years, `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(CURRENT_DATE, hire_date))` works in PostgreSQL, and `TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CURDATE())` in MySQL. Subtracting years with `EXTRACT(YEAR ...)` values alone is wrong, because someone hired in December 2023 hasn't worked a year by January 2024.

## Truncating to periods

Grouping by month, week or quarter requires truncating timestamps to the start of the period:

~~~sql
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
~~~

MySQL lacks `DATE_TRUNC`; use `DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m-01')`. SQLite uses `strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)` or `date(order_date, 'start of month')`. Months with no orders don't appear in the result. To show them with zero, join against a generated series of months, using `generate_series` in PostgreSQL or a recursive CTE elsewhere.

## Formatting dates

Formatting for display uses `TO_CHAR(d, 'DD Mon YYYY')` in PostgreSQL and Oracle, `DATE_FORMAT(d, '%d %b %Y')` in MySQL, and `strftime` in SQLite. Format at the presentation layer when possible, and keep dates as date types in queries, because formatted strings sort and compare as text.

## Time zones

Time zones cause many real-world bugs. Recommended practice:

- store absolute instants in UTC, using `TIMESTAMPTZ` in PostgreSQL, which stores UTC internally
- convert to the user's zone only for display: `created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'`
- be careful when grouping by day: midnight in UTC is 5:30 AM in India, so "orders per day" depends on which zone defines the day

Plain `TIMESTAMP` without a time zone records wall-clock time with no zone attached. It's fine for things like a store's opening hours, but ambiguous for events, since nobody knows which zone 14:30 referred to.

## Filtering by date efficiently

Wrapping a date column in a function prevents index use:

~~~sql
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024        -- scans every row
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'   -- uses an index
~~~

Half-open ranges, inclusive start and exclusive end, are also correct for timestamps at any precision. "The last 30 days" becomes `order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'`.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "orders in the last 7 days", "monthly revenue", "employees hired in 2023" and "average days between signup and first order". Know your dialect's arithmetic and truncation functions, filter with half-open ranges instead of functions on columns, and mention time zones when grouping by day.

lessons.title: CASE Expressions, COALESCE and NULLIF
lessons.description: Conditional logic inside queries: categorizing rows, conditional counts, and safe division.

sections.title: Categorizing With CASE
sections.code:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE
         WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'High'
         WHEN salary >= 65000 THEN 'Medium'
         ELSE 'Entry'
       END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;
sections.explanation: Conditions are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, which is why the bounds only need one side each. Without ELSE, unmatched rows get NULL.

sections.title: Conditional Aggregation (pivot-style counts)
sections.code:
SELECT
  SUM(CASE WHEN department = 'Engineering' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS eng,
  SUM(CASE WHEN department <> 'Engineering' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS others
FROM employees;
-- eng = 3, others = 5
sections.explanation: This pattern turns rows into columns, and it comes up in interviews constantly.

sections.title: NULLIF for Safe Division
sections.explanation: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b, otherwise a. COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument.

sections.question: With the bands above, which band does a salary of exactly 80000 get?
sections.explanation: The first condition, salary >= 80000, is true, and the first match wins.

items: CASE: the first true WHEN wins; add ELSE to avoid NULLs.
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = conditional count.
NULLIF(x, 0) prevents divide-by-zero.

content.theory:
`CASE` brings if-then-else logic into SQL. It returns different values depending on conditions, so you can label rows, bucket numbers, pivot data and count conditionally, all inside a query. `COALESCE` and `NULLIF` are compact shortcuts for common `CASE` patterns involving NULL. This lesson explains both forms of `CASE`, evaluation order, where `CASE` can appear, conditional aggregation, and how `COALESCE` and `NULLIF` relate to `CASE`.

## Searched CASE

The general form tests a series of conditions in order and returns the result of the first true one:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE
           WHEN salary >= 100000 THEN 'senior band'
           WHEN salary >= 60000  THEN 'mid band'
           ELSE 'junior band'
       END AS band
FROM employees;
~~~

## Evaluation order matters

Conditions are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. Ordering from most specific to least specific is essential. If `salary >= 60000` came first, everyone earning 100,000 or more would match it and be labelled "mid band", because they also satisfy the broader condition.

## ELSE and NULL

If no condition matches and there's no `ELSE`, `CASE` returns NULL. That's sometimes intended, but often a bug: in an `UPDATE ... SET salary = CASE ... END` without `ELSE salary`, every unmatched row gets a NULL salary. Include an explicit `ELSE` unless NULL is genuinely what you want.

## The short CASE form

When comparing one expression against several values, the shorter form applies:

~~~sql
SELECT name,
       CASE status
           WHEN 'A' THEN 'Active'
           WHEN 'L' THEN 'On leave'
           WHEN 'T' THEN 'Terminated'
           ELSE 'Unknown'
       END AS status_label
FROM employees;
~~~

This form compares with `=`, so `WHEN NULL` never matches; NULL status falls through to `ELSE`. To catch NULL, use the searched form with `WHEN status IS NULL`.

## Result types

All branches of a `CASE` should return compatible types. Mixing text and numbers, such as `THEN 'none' ELSE salary`, fails in PostgreSQL, which needs one result type. Convert explicitly with `CAST` when branches differ.

## Where CASE can appear

`CASE` is an expression, so it can appear almost anywhere a value can:

- **SELECT**: computing labels or derived values
- **WHERE**: conditional filters, though plain boolean logic is usually clearer
- **ORDER BY**: custom sort orders, such as putting high-priority tickets first
- **GROUP BY**: grouping by computed buckets
- **UPDATE ... SET**: different updates for different rows
- **Inside aggregates**: conditional counting and summing

A custom sort order:

~~~sql
SELECT id, priority FROM tickets
ORDER BY CASE priority WHEN 'critical' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 WHEN 'medium' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END,
         created_at;
~~~

## Conditional aggregation

Putting `CASE` inside an aggregate counts or sums only matching rows, in a single pass:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id,
       COUNT(*) AS total,
       SUM(CASE WHEN salary >= 100000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS high_earners,
       AVG(CASE WHEN gender = 'F' THEN salary END) AS avg_female_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

In the `AVG` example, rows that don't match produce NULL, which `AVG` ignores, so the average covers matching rows only. Using `ELSE 0` there would wrongly count non-matching rows as zeros. PostgreSQL and SQLite also support the standard `FILTER` clause: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE salary >= 100000)`, which reads more clearly.

## Pivoting with CASE

Conditional aggregation turns rows into columns, called pivoting:

~~~sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS yr,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'North' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS north,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'South' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS south
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1;
~~~

Each region becomes a column. This pattern works in every database, unlike dialect-specific `PIVOT` syntax in SQL Server and Oracle.

## Short-circuit behaviour

`CASE` evaluates conditions in order and stops at the first true one, so it can guard against errors:

~~~sql
SELECT CASE WHEN quantity = 0 THEN NULL ELSE total / quantity END FROM order_items;
~~~

Databases generally honour this order for row-level evaluation, though some optimizers may evaluate constant subexpressions early, and aggregates inside `CASE` branches may be computed regardless.

## COALESCE as a CASE shortcut

`COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first non-NULL argument. It's shorthand for:

~~~sql
CASE WHEN a IS NOT NULL THEN a
     WHEN b IS NOT NULL THEN b
     ELSE c END
~~~

Use it for defaults: `COALESCE(nickname, first_name)` for display names, `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` for totals that might be NULL when no rows match.

## NULLIF as a CASE shortcut

`NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when a equals b, otherwise a. It's shorthand for `CASE WHEN a = b THEN NULL ELSE a END`. Its best-known use is avoiding division by zero, `total / NULLIF(count, 0)`, and it also converts sentinel values, such as empty strings, into NULL.

## Readability

Long `CASE` expressions repeated across queries suggest the logic belongs elsewhere: in a lookup table joined to the data, a view or a generated column. A lookup table of status codes and labels is easier to maintain than a `CASE` copied into twenty queries.

## How interviewers test this

Expect tasks such as categorizing salaries into bands, counting rows per category in one query, pivoting rows into columns and avoiding division by zero. Order conditions from specific to general, include `ELSE`, use conditional aggregation for counts, and explain `COALESCE` and `NULLIF` as `CASE` shortcuts.

sections.title: Summarizing the Whole Table
sections.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)      AS n,
       SUM(salary)   AS total,
       AVG(salary)   AS avg_sal,
       MIN(salary)   AS lowest,
       MAX(salary)   AS highest
FROM employees;
-- 8 | 589000 | 73625.0 | 58000 | 92000

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department) FROM employees;  -- 4
sections.explanation: Without GROUP BY, an aggregate treats the whole table as one group and returns exactly one row.

rows: All rows, including rows full of NULLs
Rows where that column isn't NULL

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mixing aggregates with plain columns without GROUP BY: `SELECT name, MAX(salary) FROM employees`. Standard SQL rejects it; SQLite and old MySQL quietly return an arbitrary name.
Using an aggregate in WHERE (`WHERE salary > AVG(salary)`) is invalid. Use a subquery or HAVING.

sections.question: How many rows does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary > 100000 return?
sections.explanation: An aggregate with no GROUP BY always returns one row. COUNT of an empty set is 0 (SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX of an empty set are NULL).

Aggregates can't appear in WHERE.

content.theory:
Aggregate functions summarize many rows into a single value: how many orders, the total revenue, the average salary, the earliest and latest dates. They're the foundation of reporting and analytics in SQL. This lesson explains the five core aggregates, how each treats NULL, the differences between the forms of `COUNT`, using `DISTINCT` inside aggregates, the rules for mixing aggregates with other columns, and statistical aggregates.

## The five core aggregates

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(*)     AS employees,
       SUM(salary)  AS payroll,
       AVG(salary)  AS avg_salary,
       MIN(salary)  AS lowest,
       MAX(salary)  AS highest
FROM employees;
~~~

Without `GROUP BY`, an aggregate query treats the whole table, after `WHERE` filtering, as one group and returns one row. `MIN` and `MAX` work on any type with an ordering: numbers, text (alphabetical) and dates (earliest and latest). `SUM` and `AVG` need numbers.

## The forms of COUNT

| Form | Counts |
|---|---|
| `COUNT(*)` | All rows, including rows with NULLs |
| `COUNT(column)` | Rows where the column isn't NULL |
| `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` | Distinct non-NULL values |
| `COUNT(1)` | All rows; identical to `COUNT(*)` |

A persistent myth says `COUNT(1)` is faster than `COUNT(*)`. Modern databases treat them identically. `COUNT(*)` states the intent most clearly.

Counting all rows in a large PostgreSQL table can be slow, because MVCC means the database must check each row's visibility to your transaction. For an approximate count, PostgreSQL's statistics in `pg_class.reltuples` are instant.

## Aggregates and NULL

Every aggregate except `COUNT(*)` ignores NULL values:

- `SUM` adds only non-NULL values
- `AVG` divides the sum of non-NULL values by the count of non-NULL values
- `MIN` and `MAX` skip NULLs

Over an empty set, or a set of only NULLs, `COUNT` returns 0 and the others return NULL. So a total for a customer with no orders is NULL, not 0; write `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` when a zero is expected.

The NULL rule changes results. If three employees earn 50,000, 70,000 and NULL, then `AVG(salary)` is 60,000, averaging two values. If missing salaries should count as zero, `AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0))` gives 40,000. Both are correct answers to different questions.

## DISTINCT inside aggregates

`DISTINCT` deduplicates values before aggregating:

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders;
~~~

`COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` is common and useful. `SUM(DISTINCT ...)` and `AVG(DISTINCT ...)` are rarely what you want, since two different rows with equal amounts would be counted once.

## Mixing aggregates with other columns

An aggregate collapses many rows into one value. Selecting an ordinary column alongside it raises the question "which row's value?":

~~~sql
SELECT name, MAX(salary) FROM employees;   -- error in standard SQL
~~~

Standard SQL and PostgreSQL reject this: every selected column must be inside an aggregate or listed in `GROUP BY`. MySQL without its `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` mode, and SQLite, accept it and return a value from an arbitrary row. SQLite has a special case: with a single `MIN` or `MAX`, other columns come from the row holding that extreme. Relying on these behaviours produces queries that silently return wrong data elsewhere.

To find who earns the most, use a subquery, ordering or a window function:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary FROM employees
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
~~~

## Aggregates can't go in WHERE

`WHERE` filters individual rows before aggregation, so `WHERE AVG(salary) > 50000` is an error. Filter on aggregates with `HAVING` after `GROUP BY`, or compute the aggregate in a subquery.

## Arithmetic on aggregates

Aggregates combine in expressions:

~~~sql
SELECT SUM(amount) / COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS revenue_per_customer,
       MAX(salary) - MIN(salary) AS salary_range,
       100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'returned' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS return_rate
FROM orders;
~~~

Watch for integer division in ratios, and for division by zero when a count could be 0; `NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0)` guards against it.

## AVG precision

`AVG` of integers returns a decimal in PostgreSQL and MySQL, but SQL Server returns an integer, truncating the result. Cast first when precision matters: `AVG(CAST(rating AS DECIMAL(5, 2)))`. Round only for display: `ROUND(AVG(salary), 2)`.

## Statistical and other aggregates

Databases provide more aggregates for analysis:

| Function | Purpose | Support |
|---|---|---|
| `STDDEV`, `VARIANCE` | Spread of values | PostgreSQL, MySQL |
| `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)` | Median and percentiles | PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server |
| `STRING_AGG` / `GROUP_CONCAT` | Join values into a string | Most databases, different names |
| `BOOL_AND`, `BOOL_OR` | All true, any true | PostgreSQL |
| `ARRAY_AGG`, `JSON_AGG` | Collect values into an array or JSON | PostgreSQL |

The median resists outliers better than the average: one executive's salary can lift the average far above what most employees earn, while the median barely moves. MySQL and SQLite lack a built-in median; it can be computed with window functions.

## Performance

An aggregate over a whole table reads every row unless an index covers it. `MIN` and `MAX` on an indexed column are fast, since the database reads one end of the index. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` on large tables needs sorting or hashing. For dashboards over huge tables, precomputed summary tables or materialized views avoid repeating heavy aggregation.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column) versus COUNT(DISTINCT)", "How do aggregates handle NULL?" and "Why can't I select name with MAX(salary)?" Explain the NULL rules with an AVG example, wrap totals in COALESCE, and fix the mixed-column problem with a subquery or window function.

lessons.title: GROUP BY: One Summary Row per Group
lessons.description: Group rows by one or more columns, and the rule for which columns may appear in SELECT.

sections.title: Headcount and Average Salary by Department
sections.code:
SELECT department,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount,
       AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
sections.explanation: GROUP BY splits the rows into buckets (one per department), then each aggregate runs separately inside each bucket.

sections.title: The Golden Rule
sections.content: Every column in SELECT must either appear in GROUP BY or sit inside an aggregate function. Each group becomes one output row, so a plain column that isn't grouped has many possible values for that row, and the database can't pick one.

sections.title: Grouping by an Expression
sections.code:
SELECT strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS yr, COUNT(*) AS hires
FROM employees
GROUP BY yr
ORDER BY yr;
-- 2020 1 | 2021 1 | 2022 2 | 2023 3 | 2024 1
sections.explanation: SQLite and MySQL allow the alias (yr) in GROUP BY; PostgreSQL does too. SQL Server requires repeating the expression.

sections.question: Which query is valid in standard SQL?
options: SELECT department, name, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department
SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department
SELECT name, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department
SELECT * FROM employees GROUP BY department
sections.explanation: Only option B selects nothing but grouped columns and aggregates.

items: GROUP BY makes one output row per distinct group value.
SELECT only grouped columns and aggregates.

content.theory:
`GROUP BY` splits rows into groups that share values and computes aggregates for each group, producing one summary row per group. It answers questions such as "headcount per department", "revenue per month" and "orders per customer". This lesson explains how grouping works, the rule for which columns you can select, grouping by multiple columns and expressions, how NULL forms its own group, and advanced grouping with `ROLLUP` and `CUBE`.

## How GROUP BY works

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

Conceptually, the database:

1. takes the rows remaining after `WHERE`
2. sorts or hashes them into groups with equal `dept_id`
3. computes `COUNT(*)` and `AVG(salary)` within each group
4. outputs one row per group

If there are four departments, the result has four rows, whatever the number of employees.

## The single-value rule

After grouping, each output row represents a whole group. So the select list may contain only:

- columns listed in `GROUP BY`, which have one value per group
- aggregates, which compute one value per group
- constants, and expressions built from the above

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, name, COUNT(*)      -- error: which employee's name?
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

Each department contains many names, so `name` has no single value per group. PostgreSQL and standard SQL reject this. MySQL without `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` and SQLite accept it and pick a name from an arbitrary row, a source of silently wrong reports.

One standard exception: if you group by a table's primary key, PostgreSQL lets you select other columns of that table, since they're functionally dependent on the key and have one value per group.

## Grouping by multiple columns

Listing several columns creates one group per unique combination:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, job_title, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id, job_title
ORDER BY dept_id, job_title;
~~~

The order of columns in `GROUP BY` doesn't change the groups, only possibly the physical processing. Add `ORDER BY` to sort the output, since `GROUP BY` doesn't guarantee order. Older MySQL versions sorted grouped results implicitly, and code that relied on that broke in MySQL 8.

## Grouping by expressions

You can group by computed values:

~~~sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS hire_year, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date)
ORDER BY hire_year;
~~~

Repeat the expression in `GROUP BY`, or use the alias where your database allows it (PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite do), or group by position, `GROUP BY 1`. Grouping by a `CASE` expression creates custom buckets, such as salary bands.

## WHERE before GROUP BY

`WHERE` filters rows before they're grouped. To count only employees hired since 2020 per department, put the condition in `WHERE`:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

Departments with no qualifying employees disappear from the result entirely, rather than showing zero. To show every department with a zero count, start from the departments table and `LEFT JOIN` employees, then `COUNT(e.id)`, which counts only matched rows.

## NULL forms a group

All rows with NULL in a grouping column fall into one group, even though `NULL = NULL` isn't true. Employees without a department appear as a single row with `dept_id` NULL. Label it with `COALESCE(dept_id::text, 'unassigned')` in reports, or exclude it with `WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL`.

## Counting with joins

Grouping after a join is common and has a trap. Counting orders per customer:

~~~sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
~~~

`COUNT(o.id)` gives 0 for customers without orders, since the left join produces one row with NULL `o.id`. `COUNT(*)` would wrongly give 1. Joining two one-to-many tables before grouping multiplies rows: joining customers to both orders and support tickets produces orders × tickets rows per customer, inflating both counts. Aggregate each child table in a subquery first, then join the results.

## ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS

Reports often need subtotals and grand totals alongside detail rows. `ROLLUP` adds them in one query:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, job_title, SUM(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY ROLLUP (dept_id, job_title);
~~~

This returns totals per department and job title, subtotals per department, and a grand total, with NULL marking the rolled-up columns. `CUBE` produces subtotals for every combination of columns, and `GROUPING SETS` lets you list exactly which groupings you want. The `GROUPING()` function distinguishes rollup NULLs from real NULL values. PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle support all three; MySQL supports `WITH ROLLUP`.

## How the database groups

Databases group with either sorting, which orders rows by the grouping columns and scans for boundaries, or hashing, which builds a hash table keyed by group values. Hashing is usually faster for unsorted data with few groups; sorting helps when an index already provides the order or when the result must be sorted anyway. `EXPLAIN` shows "HashAggregate" or "GroupAggregate" in PostgreSQL.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "count employees per department", "total sales per month" and "departments with more than five employees". State the single-value rule clearly, use `COUNT(column)` with left joins to get zeros, avoid multiplying rows when joining several child tables, and mention `ROLLUP` for subtotals.

content.theory:
`HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, the way `WHERE` filters rows before it. The distinction confuses many learners, but it follows directly from the order in which SQL evaluates a query. This lesson explains what `HAVING` does, how it differs from `WHERE`, when to use each for correctness and speed, and how the full logical query order determines what every clause can see.

## Filtering groups

To find departments with more than five employees:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
~~~

`HAVING` runs after `GROUP BY`, so it sees each group and its aggregates. Groups where the condition is true stay; others are dropped.

## WHERE versus HAVING

| | WHERE | HAVING |
|---|---|---|
| Filters | Individual rows | Groups |
| Runs | Before grouping | After grouping |
| Can use aggregates | No | Yes |
| Can use non-grouped columns | Yes | No, only grouping columns and aggregates |
| Works without GROUP BY | Yes | Yes, treating the whole result as one group |

The rule: conditions about individual rows go in `WHERE`; conditions about aggregates go in `HAVING`.

## Using both

Most real queries use both, each for its own job:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'        -- rows: recent hires only
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 70000             -- groups: high-paying departments
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
~~~

This means "among employees hired since 2020, find departments whose average salary exceeds 70,000". Moving the date condition into `HAVING` would fail, because `hire_date` isn't a grouping column. Moving the average condition into `WHERE` would fail, because aggregates don't exist before grouping.

## Filter early for speed

A condition on a grouping column can technically go in either clause:

~~~sql
-- works, but groups every department before discarding most
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING dept_id = 10;

-- better: discards rows before grouping
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 10 GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

Both return the same result, and many optimizers move such conditions automatically. Writing them in `WHERE` is still better practice: it states intent, and it guarantees the database filters before doing the expensive grouping work, which can also use an index.

## Aliases in HAVING

Standard SQL doesn't allow select-list aliases in `HAVING`, because `SELECT` runs after `HAVING`:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING headcount > 5;     -- works in MySQL and SQLite, fails in PostgreSQL
~~~

Repeat the aggregate, `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`, for portability. Repeating it doesn't compute it twice; the database recognizes the same expression.

## HAVING without GROUP BY

Without `GROUP BY`, `HAVING` treats the whole filtered result as one group:

~~~sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000;
~~~

This returns the count if it exceeds 1,000, or no row at all otherwise. It's rarely needed but legal.

## The full logical order

Every clause's abilities follow from the logical evaluation order:

| Step | Clause | Can see |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `FROM` / `JOIN` | Tables |
| 2 | `WHERE` | Columns of individual rows |
| 3 | `GROUP BY` | Columns of individual rows |
| 4 | `HAVING` | Grouping columns and aggregates |
| 5 | `SELECT` | Grouping columns and aggregates (or row columns without grouping); creates aliases; window functions run here |
| 6 | `DISTINCT` | Output rows |
| 7 | `ORDER BY` | Output columns and aliases |
| 8 | `LIMIT` / `OFFSET` | Sorted output |

Reading down the table answers most "why doesn't this work?" questions. Aliases are created at step 5, so only steps 6 to 8 can use them. Aggregates exist from step 3 onward, so `WHERE` at step 2 can't see them. Window functions are computed at step 5, so neither `WHERE` nor `HAVING` can filter on them.

## Filtering on window functions

Since window functions run after `HAVING`, filtering on their results needs a subquery or CTE:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 3;
~~~

Some databases, including Snowflake, BigQuery and DuckDB, add a `QUALIFY` clause for this, but PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite don't support it.

## Common HAVING patterns

`HAVING` appears in many interview questions:

- **Duplicates**: `GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds repeated emails
- **Thresholds**: customers with total spending above a value, `HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000`
- **Completeness**: customers who bought every product, `HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products)`
- **Conditional counts**: departments with at least two managers, `HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN role = 'manager' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 2`

## How interviewers test this

Expect "WHERE versus HAVING", "find duplicate emails" and "customers with more than three orders", plus "What's the order of execution?" Explain row versus group filtering, put row conditions in WHERE for correctness and speed, repeat aggregates in HAVING for portability, and derive each clause's limits from the logical order.

lessons.title: INNER JOIN: Combining Related Data from Multiple Tables
lessons.description: Master the most important type of SQL join for combining related data.

sections.title: Learning Objectives
sections.content:
After completing this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Explain what INNER JOIN does and why it's essential for relational databases
2. Write INNER JOIN queries using both explicit JOIN syntax and WHERE clause syntax
3. Understand how INNER JOIN differs from other join types (LEFT, RIGHT, FULL)
4. Handle table aliases and ambiguous column names properly
5. Solve real-world problems requiring data from multiple related tables
6. Answer common interview questions about INNER JOIN and query optimization

sections.title: What Problem Does INNER JOIN Solve?
sections.content:
In relational databases, data is normalized across multiple tables to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. For example:

- **Customers** table: customer information
- **Orders** table: order information (references customer)
- **OrderItems** table: items in each order (references order and product)
- **Products** table: product information

The challenge is: "How do I get a complete view of an order including customer details and product information?"

INNER JOIN solves this by combining rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them, returning only the rows where there is a match in both tables.

sections.title: Think About It: The Dating Problem
sections.question: Imagine you have two lists: one of people who like hiking, and another of people who like photography. How would you find people who enjoy both activities?
sections.answerReveal:
You're looking for the intersection of two sets - people who appear in BOTH lists. This is exactly what INNER JOIN does:

- Find rows in Table A that have matching rows in Table B
- Return only those matching pairs
- Discard rows from A that don't have matches in B
- Discard rows from B that don't have matches in A

In database terms: INNER JOIN returns records that have matching values in both tables.

sections.title: INNER JOIN Syntax: Two Approaches
sections.content:
There are two syntactically different but semantically identical ways to write INNER JOIN:

**1. Explicit JOIN Syntax (Recommended)**
```sql
SELECT columns
FROM table1
INNER JOIN table2
    ON table1.column = table2.column
WHERE conditions;
```

**2. Implicit JOIN Syntax (WHERE clause)**
```sql
SELECT columns
FROM table1, table2
WHERE table1.column = table2.column
    AND conditions;
```

**Why explicit JOIN is preferred:**
- Separates join conditions from filter conditions
- More readable, especially with multiple joins
- Less likely to accidentally create cartesian products
- Clearly shows intent to join vs filter
- ANSI standard that works across all major databases

Note: INNER can be omitted - JOIN alone means INNER JOIN in most databases.

sections.title: Simple INNER JOIN Example
sections.code:
-- Tables: Customers and Orders
-- Customers: customer_id, name, email, city
-- Orders: order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount

-- Get customer name with their order details
SELECT 
    c.name AS customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    o.total_amount
FROM Customers c
INNER JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- Equivalent using WHERE clause (not recommended)
SELECT 
    c.name AS customer_name,
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    o.total_amount
FROM Customers c, Orders o
WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
sections.explanation:
This query combines customer information with their orders:

1. **FROM Customers c**: Start with the Customers table (aliased as 'c')
2. **INNER JOIN Orders o**: Join with the Orders table (aliased as 'o')
3. **ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id**: Match rows where customer IDs are equal
4. **SELECT**: Choose which columns to return from both tables

Result: Each row shows one customer's name along with one of their orders.
Customers without orders are excluded. Orders without valid customer_ids are excluded.

iterations.description: Starting state: 3 customers, 3 orders
First customer matches first order
First customer matches second order (Alice has two orders)
Second customer matches his order
Carol has no orders, so she's excluded from results

sections.title: Table Aliases: Why and How to Use Them
sections.content:
Table aliases (like 'c' for Customers, 'o' for Orders) are essential for readable JOIN queries:

**Reasons to use aliases:**
1. **Shorter queries**: 'c.customer_id' vs 'Customers.customer_id'
2. **Better readability**: Especially important with multiple joins
3. **Avoid ambiguity**: When same column name exists in multiple tables
4. **Required for self-joins**: Joining a table to itself

**Best practices for aliases:**
- Use meaningful abbreviations (cust, ord, prod, emp, dept)
- Be consistent throughout the query
- Make aliases obvious (first letter often works)
- Avoid single letters that could be confusing (like 'a', 'b', 'c' without context)

**Example with ambiguous column names:**
```sql
SELECT 
    e.name AS employee_name,
    d.name AS department_name
FROM Employees e
INNER JOIN Departments d
    ON e.department_id = d.id;
```

Without aliases, we'd need: Employees.name and Departments.name - much more verbose.

sections.title: Multiple JOINs: Combining Three or More Tables
sections.code:
-- Get order details with customer and product information
SELECT 
    c.name AS customer_name,
    o.order_date,
    p.name AS product_name,
    oi.quantity,
    oi.price_per_unit
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers o
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
INNER JOIN OrderItems oi
    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
INNER JOIN Products p
    ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2023-01-01';

-- Notice: We can filter after joins or in WHERE clause
sections.explanation:
This query shows how to navigate a typical e-commerce schema:

1. **Orders** (central table) - connects to customers and order items
2. **Customers** - get customer name for each order
3. **OrderItems** - get what was ordered (quantities, prices)
4. **Products** - get product names for each item

The query returns a flattened view where each row represents one item in an order, with all relevant context.

Important: The order of INNER JOINs doesn't matter for correctness (though it can affect performance).

sections.title: Common INNER JOIN Mistakes
items:
Forgetting the ON clause: Results in cartesian product (every row combined with every row)
      Solution: Always specify how tables are related

      Using wrong join columns: Joining on unrelated columns like name to id
      Solution: Understand your schema and foreign key relationships

      Ambiguous column names: SELECT city when both tables have a city column
      Solution: Always qualify column names with table aliases in JOIN queries

      Missing rows due to NULL values: INNER JOIN excludes NULL matches
      Solution: Understand that NULL ≠ NULL in SQL - use LEFT JOIN if you need to keep NULL matches

      Joining too many tables without necessity: Performance degradation
      Solution: Only join tables you actually need for your query

      Confusing INNER with OUTER joins: Getting fewer rows than expected
      Solution: Remember INNER JOIN = intersection, only matching rows

sections.title: When to Use INNER JOIN vs Other Join Types
sections.content:
Understanding when INNER JOIN is appropriate vs other join types:

**Use INNER JOIN when:**
- You only want rows that have matches in BOTH tables
- You're looking for intersections or relationships
- Business logic requires data from both sides to exist
- Examples: Orders with customers, Employees with departments, Products with categories

**Consider LEFT JOIN when:**
- You want ALL rows from the left table, regardless of matches in right
- You need to find missing relationships (e.g., customers without orders)
- You're doing data quality checks
- Examples: All customers (even those who haven't ordered), Products (even those never ordered)

**Consider RIGHT JOIN when:**
- You want ALL rows from the right table (less common - usually rewrite as LEFT JOIN)
- Examples: Rarely needed in practice

**Consider FULL JOIN when:**
- You want ALL rows from both tables, matching where possible
- Examples: Comparing two versions of a dataset, finding discrepancies

**Key insight**: Start with INNER JOIN unless you specifically need to keep non-matching rows from one or both tables.

sections.title: Comparison: INNER JOIN vs Other Join Types
rows: All rows from left + matches from right
All rows from right + matches from left
You need data from both sides
You need complete picture from both sides

traps.question: What's the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
traps.trap: Just saying "INNER JOIN returns matches, LEFT JOIN includes unmatched left rows" without explaining when to use each
traps.solution:
INNER JOIN returns only rows where there's a match in both tables (intersection). LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table (or NULL if no match).

Choose INNER JOIN when you only want complete relationships (e.g., "show me orders with customer information").
Choose LEFT JOIN when you need to see all records from one side regardless of matches (e.g., "show me all customers, and their orders if they have any").

The key is understanding whether missing relationships are meaningful for your question.

traps.question: Can you INNER JOIN a table to itself? When would you do this?
traps.trap: Saying no or not understanding self-joins
traps.solution:
Yes, you can JOIN a table to itself - this is called a self-join. Use it when:

1. **Hierarchical data**: Employees table with manager_id referencing another employee
   ```sql
   SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
   FROM Employees e
   LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
   ```

2. **Comparing records within same table**: Find pairs of employees hired in same month
   ```sql
   SELECT e1.name, e2.name
   FROM Employees e1
   INNER JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.hire_month = e2.hire_month AND e1.id < e2.id;
   ```

3. **Finding missing sequences**: In a table of dates, find gaps

Remember to use aliases to distinguish between the two instances of the same table.

traps.question: How does INNER JOIN handle NULL values in the join columns?
traps.trap: Saying NULL values match each other or getting confused
traps.solution:
In SQL, NULL represents unknown/missing data, and NULL ≠ NULL (NULL compared to anything is NULL/unknown, not true).

Therefore, INNER JOIN treats NULL join column values as non-matching:
- If table1.column IS NULL, it won't match any row in table2
- If table2.column IS NULL, it won't match any row in table1
- Two NULL values do NOT satisfy the join condition

This is why you might unexpectedly lose rows when joining on nullable columns. Consider:
1. Cleaning your data to remove NULLs from join columns
2. Using LEFT JOIN and filtering for NULLs to find missing relationships
3. Using COALESCE to provide default values for NULL join columns (when appropriate)

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: INNER JOIN returns only rows where there's a match in both tables (mathematical intersection)
Always use explicit JOIN syntax with ON clause - never rely on comma-separated WHERE joins
Table aliases are essential for readability and avoiding ambiguous column references
INNER JOIN eliminates rows where join column is NULL in either table
The order of INNER JOINs doesn't affect results (but can affect query performance)
Use INNER JOIN when you need data from both tables; use OUTER joins when you need to keep non-matching rows
Understand your schema's foreign key relationships to write correct JOIN conditions
INNER JOIN is the most commonly used join type in real-world SQL queries

sections.title: Revision Checklist
items: [ ] I can explain what INNER JOIN does and why it's essential for relational databases
[ ] I can write INNER JOIN queries using both explicit and implicit syntax
[ ] I can explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN/RIGHT JOIN/FULL JOIN
[ ] I can properly use table aliases to avoid ambiguous column references

sections.title: Next Topic: LEFT and RIGHT JOINs
sections.content:
Now that you've mastered INNER JOIN, the next step is learning about OUTER joins: LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and FULL JOIN. These join types are essential when you need to keep rows that don't have matches in the other table.

In the OUTER joins section, you'll learn:
- How LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table regardless of matches
- How RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from the right table (less commonly used)
- How FULL JOIN combines both behaviors
- Practical use cases for each join type
- How to combine different join types in complex queries
- Common interview questions about OUTER joins

content.theory:
A join combines rows from two tables based on a related column. Normalized databases split data across tables, such as employees in one and departments in another, and joins put it back together for queries. The inner join, the most common kind, returns only rows that have a match in both tables. This lesson explains how inner joins work, the ON clause, joining several tables, how joins multiply rows, and the older comma syntax you'll still meet.

## Why joins exist

Storing each department's name once, in a departments table, and referencing it by ID from employees avoids repeating the name on every employee row. That's normalization. The cost is that answering "which department does each employee work in?" requires combining the tables at query time. Joins do that.

## The INNER JOIN syntax

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

`ON` states the matching condition. For each employee, the database finds department rows where `d.id` equals the employee's `dept_id`, and outputs one combined row per match. The keyword `INNER` is optional; `JOIN` alone means an inner join.

## What gets dropped

An inner join keeps only matched pairs. Two kinds of rows disappear:

- employees with a `dept_id` that's NULL, or that doesn't exist in departments
- departments with no employees

If the employees table has 100 rows and five employees have no department, the join returns 95 rows. This silent loss is the most important thing to understand about inner joins: when a report seems to be missing data, an inner join that should have been an outer join is a common cause.

## A mental model

Conceptually, a join forms every pairing of rows from the two tables, the Cartesian product, then keeps pairs satisfying the `ON` condition. For 100 employees and 10 departments, that's 1,000 pairs, of which about 100 match. The database doesn't actually build all pairs; it uses indexes and smarter algorithms, covered in the join performance lesson. But the model correctly predicts the result.

## Table aliases and ambiguous columns

When both tables have a column with the same name, such as `name` or `id`, you must say which one you mean. Table aliases keep this short:

~~~sql
SELECT e.id, e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

Selecting `name` without a prefix fails with an "ambiguous column" error. Prefixing every column in a join query, even unambiguous ones, makes queries easier to read and keeps them working if someone later adds a same-named column to the other table.

## USING and NATURAL JOIN

When the join columns have the same name in both tables, `USING` shortens the condition:

~~~sql
SELECT name, dept_name
FROM employees
JOIN departments USING (dept_id);
~~~

`NATURAL JOIN` goes further and joins on every column name the tables share. Avoid it: if someone adds a `created_at` or `name` column to both tables, the join condition silently changes and the query returns wrong results.

## Joining several tables

Joins chain. Each join adds a table, matched against tables already in the query:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department, l.city
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
JOIN locations l ON d.location_id = l.id;
~~~

With inner joins, the order you write them doesn't change the result; the optimizer chooses the actual order. Read multi-table joins as a path through the schema: employee to department to location.

## Joins multiply rows

Each row of the result is one matching pair. In a one-to-many relationship, the "one" side repeats. Joining departments to employees produces one row per employee, with the department's columns repeated on each. That's expected.

Problems arise when joining two one-to-many relationships from the same parent:

~~~sql
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id), COUNT(p.id)
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
JOIN projects p ON p.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name;
~~~

A department with 10 employees and 3 projects produces 30 rows, so both counts report 30. This "fan-out" silently corrupts aggregates. Fix it by aggregating each child table in a subquery before joining, or by using `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, which fixes counts but not sums.

## Filtering in ON versus WHERE

For inner joins, a filter condition can go in `ON` or `WHERE` with the same result:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id AND d.name = 'Engineering';

SELECT e.name FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE d.name = 'Engineering';
~~~

The convention is to put the relationship in `ON` and filters in `WHERE`. For outer joins, the placement changes the result, as the next lesson explains.

## The old comma syntax

Before SQL-92, joins were written by listing tables with commas and putting the condition in `WHERE`:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name
FROM employees e, departments d
WHERE e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

It produces the same result as an inner join, but forgetting the condition creates a full Cartesian product, possibly millions of rows, with no error. Explicit `JOIN ... ON` keeps the relationship next to the table and makes a missing condition obvious. Use explicit joins in new code.

## Joining on non-key columns

Joins don't have to use keys. You can join on any comparable columns, such as matching orders to promotions by date range, covered in the advanced joins lesson. But joins on keys, backed by foreign key constraints and indexes, are fastest and least likely to produce surprising duplicates.

## How interviewers test this

Expect queries joining two or three tables, and questions such as "What does an inner join return?" and "Why does my count look too high?" Explain that unmatched rows are dropped, use aliases, describe fan-out when joining multiple one-to-many tables, and prefer explicit JOIN syntax over commas.

lessons.title: LEFT JOIN: Keeping All Records from the Left Table
lessons.description: Learn how LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched rows from the left table.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: LEFT JOIN (or LEFT OUTER JOIN) returns all rows from the left table, and the matched rows from the right table. If there is no match, the result is NULL on the right side.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: LEFT JOIN is essential for finding missing relationships and keeping complete records from your primary table.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: LEFT JOIN = all rows from left table + matching rows from right table (NULL where no match)

sections.title: Syntax
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT columns
FROM table1
LEFT JOIN table2
    ON table1.column = table2.column;
```

sections.title: Example: Customers and Their Orders
sections.code:
-- Find all customers and their orders (customers without orders show NULL)
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
sections.explanation: Every row from the left table appears in the result. If there's a matching row in the right table, those columns are filled; otherwise they're NULL.

sections.title: Real-World Use
sections.content: Used extensively for data analysis, finding orphaned records, and ensuring complete reporting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing LEFT JOIN with INNER JOIN
Forgetting that unmatched rows produce NULL values
Using WHERE conditions on the right table that unintentionally filter out NULLs

traps.question: How would you find customers who have never placed an order?
traps.trap: Just saying "use LEFT JOIN" without specifying the IS NULL check
traps.solution: Use LEFT JOIN and check for NULL in the order columns: WHERE o.order_id IS NULL

traps.question: What's the difference between LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN?
traps.trap: Thinking there's a difference when there isn't one
traps.solution: Nothing - they're synonymous. OUTER is optional in LEFT/RIGHT/FULL JOIN.

sections.title: Quick Revision
items: LEFT JOIN: Keep all left table rows, fill in right table data where matches exist.

content.theory:
A left join returns every row from the left table, whether or not it has a match in the right table. Where there's no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL. Left joins answer questions inner joins can't: which customers have never ordered, how many orders each customer has including zero, and which records are missing related data. This lesson explains how left joins work, the anti-join pattern, the ON versus WHERE trap, and counting with left joins.

## How LEFT JOIN works

~~~sql
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
~~~

For each customer:

- if they have matching orders, the result has one row per order, as with an inner join
- if they have none, the result still has one row for them, with `order_id` and `amount` set to NULL

The left table is the one written before `LEFT JOIN`. Every one of its rows appears at least once. `LEFT OUTER JOIN` is the same thing; `OUTER` is optional.

## Inner versus left

| Customer | Orders | Inner join rows | Left join rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asha | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| Rahul | 0 | 0 | 1 (with NULL order columns) |
| Meera | 1 | 1 | 1 |

The left join's result always has at least as many rows as the left table.

## Finding rows with no match

The **anti-join** pattern finds left rows that have no match:

~~~sql
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
~~~

The left join keeps every customer, and `WHERE o.id IS NULL` keeps only those whose order columns are NULL: customers who've never ordered. Test a column that can't be NULL in a real match, such as the right table's primary key. Testing a nullable column, such as `o.discount_code`, would also return customers whose orders happen to have no discount code.

`NOT EXISTS` expresses the same thing, often more clearly:

~~~sql
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
~~~

Modern optimizers usually produce the same plan for both.

## The ON versus WHERE trap

For outer joins, where you put a condition changes the result. Suppose you want all customers, with their 2024 orders if any:

~~~sql
-- Wrong: turns the left join into an inner join
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01';
~~~

The left join produces customers with NULL order columns, and then `WHERE` drops them, because `NULL >= '2024-01-01'` is unknown. Customers without 2024 orders vanish. Put conditions on the right table in `ON`:

~~~sql
-- Right: filters which orders match, keeps every customer
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01';
~~~

The rule:

- conditions on the **right** table that decide which rows match go in `ON`
- conditions on the **left** table that decide which rows appear go in `WHERE`

A condition on the left table placed in `ON` doesn't filter the left table at all: every left row still appears, and the condition only affects which ones get matches.

## Counting with left joins

To count orders per customer, including zeros:

~~~sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
~~~

`COUNT(o.id)` counts only non-NULL values, so customers without orders get 0. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, and each unmatched customer has one row, so it would wrongly report 1. Likewise, `SUM(o.amount)` returns NULL for customers without orders; wrap it as `COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0)`.

## Chaining left joins

When chaining joins, an inner join after a left join can undo it:

~~~sql
SELECT c.name, o.id, p.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id;    -- drops customers without orders
~~~

Customers without orders have NULL `o.product_id`, which matches no product, so the inner join drops them. Once a table is left-joined, later joins to it usually need to be left joins too.

## Left join as a lookup

Left joins also attach optional information without losing rows: adding a department name where some employees have none, or a latest-login date where some users have never logged in. Use an inner join only when a missing match should exclude the row.

## Duplicates from left joins

Like inner joins, left joins return one row per match. If a customer has five orders, they appear five times. To attach a single value per customer, such as their most recent order, aggregate or rank the right table first, then join the result.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "customers who never placed an order", "departments with no employees", "count of orders per customer including zero" and "LEFT JOIN versus INNER JOIN". Use the anti-join with a non-nullable column or `NOT EXISTS`, put right-table filters in ON, and use `COUNT(right.id)` rather than `COUNT(*)`.

lessons.title: RIGHT JOIN: Keeping All Records from the Right Table
lessons.description: Understand RIGHT JOIN and when it's useful (spoiler: usually rewrite as LEFT JOIN).

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: RIGHT JOIN (or RIGHT OUTER JOIN) returns all rows from the right table, and the matched rows from the left table. If there is no match, the result is NULL on the left side.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: While RIGHT JOIN is less commonly used, understanding it helps you read others' queries and handle specific scenarios.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: RIGHT JOIN = all rows from right table + matching rows from left table (NULL where no match)

sections.title: Syntax
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT columns
FROM table1
RIGHT JOIN table2
    ON table1.column = table2.column;
```

sections.title: Example: Orders and Their Customer Info
sections.code:
-- Find all orders and their customer info (orders without valid customers show NULL)
SELECT o.order_id, c.name
FROM Customers c
RIGHT JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
sections.explanation: Every row from the right table appears in the result. If there's a matching row in the left table, those columns are filled; otherwise they're NULL.

sections.title: Real-World Use
sections.content: Less common in practice - usually clearer to rewrite as LEFT JOIN by swapping table order.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using RIGHT JOIN when LEFT JOIN would be clearer
Not realizing RIGHT JOIN table1, table2 is equivalent to LEFT JOIN table2, table1
Confusing which table's rows are preserved

traps.question: When would you choose RIGHT JOIN over LEFT JOIN?
traps.trap: Saying RIGHT JOIN is commonly used when it's actually rare
traps.solution: Rarely - usually better to rewrite as LEFT JOIN for clarity. Might be used when the right table is logically your primary focus.

traps.question: Is RIGHT JOIN table1, table2 the same as LEFT JOIN table2, table1?
traps.trap: Thinking they're different operations
traps.solution: Yes, they produce identical results.

sections.title: Quick Revision
items: RIGHT JOIN: Keep all right table rows, fill in left table data where matches exist (usually rewrite as LEFT JOIN).

content.theory:
A right join is the mirror image of a left join: it keeps every row from the right table and fills the left table's columns with NULL where there's no match. Anything a right join does can be written as a left join with the tables swapped, which is why many teams avoid right joins entirely. This lesson explains how right joins work, how to convert them to left joins, when they appear in practice, and how they behave in multi-table queries.

## How RIGHT JOIN works

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

Every department appears in the result. Departments with employees produce one row per employee. Departments with no employees produce a single row with `e.name` set to NULL. Employees without a valid department are dropped, since they're on the left side.

## The equivalent left join

Swapping the table order turns any right join into a left join:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

Both queries return the same rows. The only possible difference is column order in `SELECT *` results, which you avoid by listing columns explicitly.

## Why most people prefer LEFT JOIN

Teams often adopt a convention of using only left joins:

- **Reading order**: queries are read top to bottom, so it's natural for the table whose rows are all kept to come first, in `FROM`
- **Mixing directions is confusing**: a query with both left and right joins forces readers to track which table is preserved at every step
- **Consistency**: one form is easier to review and maintain than two

The SQL standard includes right joins for symmetry, and they're fully supported in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle. SQLite added `RIGHT JOIN` and `FULL JOIN` only in version 3.39, released in 2022, so older SQLite versions reject them.

## Finding unmatched rows

The anti-join works with right joins too. Departments with no employees:

~~~sql
SELECT d.name
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;
~~~

The equivalent left join, `FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ... WHERE e.id IS NULL`, reads more naturally. `NOT EXISTS` is clearer still.

## ON versus WHERE, mirrored

The placement rule mirrors the left join rule:

- conditions on the **left** table, the optional side, go in `ON` to control matching
- conditions on the **right** table, the preserved side, go in `WHERE` to control which rows appear

Putting a left-table condition in `WHERE`, such as `WHERE e.salary > 50000`, removes departments without employees, since their `e.salary` is NULL. The right join silently becomes an inner join.

## Right joins in multi-table queries

Right joins occasionally appear when a query has been built by adding tables to an existing chain, and the author wants to preserve all rows of a newly added table:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department, p.title
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
RIGHT JOIN projects p ON p.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

This keeps every project, even those whose department has no employees. Reasoning about it requires knowing that joins are evaluated left to right: the result of the employees-departments inner join is the left side, and projects is preserved. Rewriting with projects first, followed by left joins, is clearer:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department, p.title
FROM projects p
LEFT JOIN departments d ON p.dept_id = d.id
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

Notice the rewrite isn't mechanical: the original inner join between employees and departments had to become a left join, or projects whose department has no employees would be dropped again. When converting multi-table right joins, check what each join preserves.

## Generated SQL

Right joins also show up in SQL generated by reporting tools and object-relational mappers (ORMs), and in queries written by people used to them. You should be able to read them fluently even if you write left joins yourself.

## Visualizing outer joins

Venn diagrams are often used to explain joins: an inner join is the overlap, a left join is the whole left circle, and a right join is the whole right circle. The picture helps with which rows are kept, but it's imperfect: joins match rows by a condition and can produce multiple rows per match, which Venn diagrams don't show. Think in terms of "every row from this side appears at least once".

## Joins compared

| Join | Keeps unmatched rows from |
|---|---|
| INNER | Neither table |
| LEFT | The left table |
| RIGHT | The right table |
| FULL | Both tables |
| CROSS | Not applicable: every pair, no condition |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What's a right join, and how does it differ from a left join?" and "Rewrite this right join as a left join." Explain that every right join can become a left join by swapping table order, why teams prefer left joins for readability, and how the ON versus WHERE rule mirrors. Mention SQLite's late support for right joins as a portability note.

lessons.title: FULL JOIN: Combining Both Outer Join Behaviors
lessons.description: Learn how FULL JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both tables.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: FULL JOIN (or FULL OUTER JOIN) returns all rows when there is a match in either left or right table. Rows that don't match are filled with NULL values.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: FULL JOIN is useful when you need a complete view of data from both tables, including unmatched records from both sides.

sections.title: Core Concept
sections.content: FULL JOIN = all rows from both tables, with NULLs where no match exists

sections.title: Syntax
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT columns
FROM table1
FULL JOIN table2
    ON table1.column = table2.column;
```

sections.title: Example: Customers and All Orders
sections.code:
-- See all customers and all orders, matched where possible
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM Customers c
FULL JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
sections.explanation: Combines the behavior of LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN: keeps all rows from both tables, matching where possible.

sections.title: Real-World Use
sections.content: Used for comparing datasets, finding discrepancies between two versions of data, and comprehensive reporting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Not realizing FULL JOIN may not be supported in all databases (MySQL doesn't support it natively)
Expecting FULL JOIN to be faster than separate LEFT and RIGHT JOIN queries
Forgetting that unmatched sides will have NULL values

traps.question: How can you simulate FULL JOIN in MySQL which doesn't support it?
traps.trap: Just saying "use UNION" without specifying the exact approach
traps.solution: Use UNION of LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN, or UNION of LEFT JOIN with WHERE IS NULL and RIGHT JOIN with WHERE IS NULL

traps.question: What's the difference between FULL JOIN and INNER JOIN?
traps.trap: Saying FULL JOIN just returns more rows without explaining NULL handling
traps.solution: FULL JOIN includes unmatched rows from both tables (with NULLs); INNER JOIN only includes matched rows.

sections.title: Quick Revision
items: FULL JOIN: Keep all rows from both tables, showing matches where they exist and NULLs where they don't.

content.theory:
A full outer join keeps every row from both tables. Matched rows are combined, unmatched rows from either side appear with NULLs for the other side's columns. It's the tool for reconciling two datasets: comparing two systems' records, finding what exists in one list but not the other, and merging sources that each have gaps. This lesson explains full joins, the reconciliation pattern, NULL handling with `COALESCE`, emulating full joins in MySQL, and cross joins.

## How FULL JOIN works

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
FULL JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
~~~

The result contains three kinds of rows:

- employees matched with their department
- employees with no valid department, with department columns NULL
- departments with no employees, with employee columns NULL

`FULL OUTER JOIN` is the same; `OUTER` is optional. In terms of row counts, a full join returns the inner join's rows plus the left join's extra rows plus the right join's extra rows.

## Reconciling two datasets

Full joins are best known for comparing two sources that should match. Suppose an e-commerce system and a payment gateway each record transactions:

~~~sql
SELECT COALESCE(s.txn_id, g.txn_id) AS txn_id,
       s.amount AS store_amount,
       g.amount AS gateway_amount,
       CASE
           WHEN s.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'missing in store'
           WHEN g.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'missing at gateway'
           WHEN s.amount <> g.amount THEN 'amount mismatch'
           ELSE 'ok'
       END AS status
FROM store_txns s
FULL JOIN gateway_txns g ON s.txn_id = g.txn_id;
~~~

One query classifies every transaction: present in both and matching, present in both with different amounts, or present in only one system. Finance teams run reconciliations like this daily.

## Merging keys with COALESCE

In a full join, the join key can be NULL on either side, depending on which table the row came from. `COALESCE(s.txn_id, g.txn_id)` picks whichever is present, giving one reliable key column. Without it, sorting or grouping by `s.txn_id` would lump all gateway-only rows into one NULL group.

The same idea merges other columns from two sources: `COALESCE(new.email, old.email)` prefers the newer value and falls back to the older one.

## Finding differences only

To list only mismatched keys, filter out matched rows:

~~~sql
SELECT COALESCE(a.id, b.id) AS id
FROM list_a a
FULL JOIN list_b b ON a.id = b.id
WHERE a.id IS NULL OR b.id IS NULL;
~~~

This returns the **symmetric difference**: keys in exactly one of the two tables. For comparing whole rows, rather than keys, set operations such as `EXCEPT` are an alternative.

## Filtering full joins

Filters in `WHERE` apply after the join and can remove the unmatched rows you wanted to keep. `WHERE s.amount > 100` drops every gateway-only row, since its `s.amount` is NULL. Filter each source in a subquery before joining, or include `IS NULL` alternatives in the condition, so the filter applies only where it makes sense.

## Emulating FULL JOIN in MySQL

MySQL doesn't support `FULL JOIN`. Combine a left join with the unmatched rows of a right join:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
UNION ALL
SELECT e.name, d.name
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;
~~~

The first query returns all employees, matched or not. The second adds only departments without employees. Using `UNION ALL` with the `IS NULL` filter avoids duplicating matched rows. Plain `UNION` with an unfiltered right join also works, but it removes duplicates by comparing every row, which is slower and wrongly merges rows that are genuinely identical.

## Performance

Full joins are generally more expensive than inner or left joins. PostgreSQL implements them with merge or hash joins only, and they offer the optimizer fewer opportunities for reordering. They're common in reporting and data pipelines, and rare in latency-sensitive application queries.

## Cross joins

A `CROSS JOIN` returns every combination of rows from two tables, with no condition. Three sizes and four colours produce twelve rows:

~~~sql
SELECT s.size, c.colour
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colours c;
~~~

Cross joins are useful for generating combinations: every product variant, every date paired with every store for a sales report that must show zeros, or a grid of time slots. They're dangerous by accident: two 10,000-row tables produce 100 million rows. An inner join with a missing condition, or the comma syntax without a `WHERE`, silently becomes a cross join.

## Filling gaps with cross joins

A common reporting pattern: show sales for every store on every day, with zero where nothing sold. Cross join stores with a list of dates to build the full grid, then left join the sales data:

~~~sql
SELECT s.id, d.day, COALESCE(SUM(x.amount), 0) AS sales
FROM stores s
CROSS JOIN calendar d
LEFT JOIN sales x ON x.store_id = s.id AND x.sale_date = d.day
GROUP BY s.id, d.day;
~~~

## Choosing the right join

| Question | Join |
|---|---|
| Only rows related in both tables | INNER |
| Everything from one table, related data if any | LEFT |
| Everything from both, showing gaps on either side | FULL |
| Every combination | CROSS |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What does a FULL OUTER JOIN return?", "How do you find records in one table but not the other, in both directions?" and "How do you do a full join in MySQL?" Explain the three kinds of output rows, use COALESCE for keys, show the UNION ALL emulation, and know what a cross join does and how one happens by accident.
