lessons.title: Transactions in SQL: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
lessons.description: Group statements into all-or-nothing units and see a rollback in action.

sections.title: Try a Rollback in the SQL Lab
sections.explanation: Replace ROLLBACK with COMMIT to make the change permanent.

sections.title: A Safe Money Transfer
sections.explanation: The `balance >= 500` condition, plus checking the affected-row count, prevents overdrafts even when two transfers run at the same moment.

sections.title: Rules of Thumb
items: Keep transactions **short**: locks are held until COMMIT.
Never wait for user input inside an open transaction.
Catch errors and ROLLBACK; on deadlock or serialization errors, **retry** the whole transaction.
For the theory (ACID, isolation levels, locking), see the DBMS course's Transactions and Concurrency modules.

sections.question: A transaction updates 3 rows, then the app crashes before COMMIT. What happens to the 3 updates?
options: It depends on the row order
sections.explanation: Uncommitted work is undone. That's atomicity.

items: BEGIN ... COMMIT makes a group of statements atomic; ROLLBACK undoes them.
Keep transactions short and retry on deadlocks.

content.theory:
A transaction groups SQL statements into one unit that either succeeds completely or has no effect. Transactions keep data correct when operations involve several steps, when errors occur partway through, and when many users change data at once. This lesson explains `BEGIN`, `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK`, savepoints, the four isolation levels and the anomalies each prevents, locking for read-modify-write operations, and deadlocks.

## The basic commands

~~~sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
~~~

`BEGIN` (or `START TRANSACTION`) opens a transaction. `COMMIT` makes all its changes permanent and visible to others. `ROLLBACK` discards all changes since `BEGIN`. If the connection drops or the server crashes before `COMMIT`, the database rolls back automatically.

## Autocommit

By default, most databases and drivers run in **autocommit** mode: each statement is its own transaction, committed immediately. Without an explicit `BEGIN`, the two updates above are separate transactions, and a crash between them loses money. Application frameworks usually provide a transaction wrapper, such as Spring's `@Transactional` or Django's `atomic()`, which issues `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` for you.

## Errors inside transactions

In PostgreSQL, any error inside a transaction puts it into an aborted state: every later statement fails until you `ROLLBACK`. MySQL rolls back only the failing statement and lets the transaction continue, so the application must decide whether to roll back. Code that ignores errors and commits anyway can save half-finished work in MySQL.

## Savepoints

A savepoint marks a point inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning everything:

~~~sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id) VALUES (1001, 7);
SAVEPOINT before_items;
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (1001, 55, 2);
-- suppose this fails a stock check
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_items;
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (1001, 56, 2);
COMMIT;
~~~

Savepoints let you retry part of a transaction, and they're how frameworks implement nested transactions.

## Concurrency anomalies

When transactions run at the same time, several anomalies can occur:

| Anomaly | Example |
|---|---|
| Dirty read | T2 reads a balance T1 changed but hasn't committed; T1 rolls back, so T2 used a value that never existed |
| Non-repeatable read | T1 reads a row, T2 updates and commits it, T1 reads again and gets a different value |
| Phantom read | T1 counts orders over ₹1,000, T2 inserts a new one, T1 counts again and gets a different number |
| Lost update | T1 and T2 both read stock = 10, both subtract 1 and write 9; one sale is lost |
| Write skew | Two doctors each check that another doctor is on call, then both go off call, leaving nobody |

## Isolation levels

The SQL standard defines four isolation levels, each preventing more anomalies:

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom read |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read uncommitted | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Read committed | Prevented | Possible | Possible |
| Repeatable read | Prevented | Prevented | Possible (in the standard) |
| Serializable | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

Set the level per transaction:

~~~sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
~~~

Real databases differ from the standard table. PostgreSQL defaults to read committed, never allows dirty reads even at read uncommitted, and its repeatable read also prevents phantoms. MySQL's InnoDB defaults to repeatable read. PostgreSQL's serializable level detects conflicts and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, which the application must retry. SQLite serializes writes with a database-level lock.

## How MVCC provides isolation

PostgreSQL, MySQL's InnoDB and Oracle use **multi-version concurrency control** (MVCC). Updates create new row versions instead of overwriting, and each transaction reads from a snapshot. Under read committed, each statement gets a fresh snapshot; under repeatable read, the whole transaction uses the snapshot taken at its first query. Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. Old versions are cleaned up later, by `VACUUM` in PostgreSQL.

## Preventing lost updates

The read-modify-write pattern is dangerous at read committed:

~~~sql
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 5;      -- application reads 10
UPDATE products SET stock = 9 WHERE id = 5;   -- writes 10 - 1
~~~

Two concurrent sessions can both read 10 and both write 9. Fixes:

- **Atomic updates**: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 5 AND stock > 0`, which reads and writes in one statement
- **Pessimistic locking**: `SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE` locks the row until the transaction ends, so the second session waits
- **Optimistic locking**: store a `version` column, and update with `WHERE id = 5 AND version = 3`; if zero rows change, someone else updated first, so reload and retry
- **Higher isolation**: repeatable read in PostgreSQL detects the conflict and aborts one transaction

## Deadlocks

A **deadlock** occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. T1 locks account 1 and waits for account 2, while T2 locks account 2 and waits for account 1. Neither can proceed. Databases detect deadlocks and abort one transaction with an error. Prevent them by acquiring locks in a consistent order, such as always locking the lower account ID first, and keeping transactions short.

## Keep transactions short

Long transactions hold locks that block other writers, keep old row versions alive so MVCC cleanup can't remove them, and increase deadlock risk. Never wait for user input or call slow external services, such as payment gateways or email providers, while a transaction is open. Do that work outside the transaction, then open a short transaction to record the result.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a transaction?", "Explain isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent", "How do you prevent lost updates?" and "What's a deadlock?" Use a bank transfer for atomicity, the anomaly table for isolation, describe atomic updates, SELECT FOR UPDATE and optimistic locking, and give the consistent lock ordering fix for deadlocks.

lessons.title: Common Table Expressions (WITH)
lessons.description: Name intermediate results to make multi-step queries readable, and chain several CTEs.

sections.title: Why CTEs?
sections.content: A CTE is a named, temporary result defined with WITH at the top of a query. It turns deeply nested subqueries into a readable top-to-bottom pipeline: step 1, step 2, final answer. It exists only for that one statement.

sections.title: Above-Average Earners per Department
sections.code:
WITH dept_avg AS (
  SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department
)
SELECT e.name, e.department, e.salary, d.avg_sal
FROM employees e
JOIN dept_avg d ON d.department = e.department
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal
ORDER BY e.department;
sections.explanation: The same result as the correlated-subquery version, but every step is named and can be read in order.

sections.title: Chaining CTEs
sections.code:
WITH payroll AS (
  SELECT department, SUM(salary) AS total FROM employees GROUP BY department
),
with_budget AS (
  SELECT p.department, p.total, d.budget,
         ROUND(100.0 * p.total / d.budget, 1) AS pct_used
  FROM payroll p JOIN departments d ON d.name = p.department
)
SELECT * FROM with_budget ORDER BY pct_used DESC;
-- Marketing 139000 250000 55.6
-- Engineering 255000 500000 51.0
-- Sales 123000 300000 41.0
-- HR 72000 200000 36.0
sections.explanation: Later CTEs can refer to earlier ones. Separate them with commas and use WITH only once.

sections.question: How long does a CTE's result exist?
options: Only for the single statement it is defined in
sections.explanation: A CTE is scoped to one statement. For reuse across statements, create a view or a temporary table.

items: WITH name AS (...) names a step; chain steps with commas.
CTEs improve readability; performance is usually the same as the equivalent subquery.

content.theory:
A common table expression (CTE) names a subquery at the start of a statement using `WITH`, so the main query can refer to it like a table. CTEs turn deeply nested queries into a readable sequence of named steps, and they can be referenced several times in one query. This lesson explains CTE syntax, chaining multiple CTEs, how CTEs compare with subqueries and temporary tables, how databases execute them, and data-modifying CTEs.

## Basic syntax

~~~sql
WITH dept_avg AS (
    SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY dept_id
)
SELECT e.name, e.salary, d.avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN dept_avg d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_salary;
~~~

`WITH name AS (query)` defines the CTE; the main statement follows. The CTE exists only for that one statement. You can also name its columns explicitly: `WITH dept_avg (dept_id, avg_salary) AS (...)`.

## Why use CTEs

The same logic as a nested subquery:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, e.salary, d.avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) d
  ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_salary;
~~~

For one level, either is fine. As logic grows, nested subqueries force readers to start in the middle and work outwards. CTEs read top to bottom: each step is named, defined, then used. Names such as `active_customers` or `monthly_revenue` document intent.

## Chaining CTEs

Several CTEs are separated by commas, and later ones can reference earlier ones:

~~~sql
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
),
with_growth AS (
    SELECT month, revenue,
           revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
    FROM monthly
)
SELECT month, revenue, change
FROM with_growth
WHERE change < 0
ORDER BY month;
~~~

This builds a pipeline: aggregate by month, compute month-over-month change, then filter to months with declining revenue. Each step can be tested alone by selecting from it, which makes debugging much easier.

## Referencing a CTE more than once

A CTE can be used several times in the main query, which a derived table can't do without repeating it:

~~~sql
WITH dept_stats AS (
    SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id
)
SELECT a.dept_id, a.headcount
FROM dept_stats a
WHERE a.headcount > (SELECT AVG(headcount) FROM dept_stats);
~~~

## How databases execute CTEs

A CTE can be executed in two ways:

- **Inlined**: merged into the main query like a subquery, so the optimizer can push filters into it and use indexes
- **Materialized**: computed once and stored temporarily, then read by the main query

Before version 12, PostgreSQL always materialized CTEs, acting as an **optimization fence**: an outer `WHERE` filter couldn't be pushed inside, so a CTE over a big table could be computed in full even when the outer query needed one row. Since PostgreSQL 12, CTEs referenced once with no side effects are inlined automatically. You can control it explicitly:

~~~sql
WITH big AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT ...) SELECT ...;
WITH big AS NOT MATERIALIZED (SELECT ...) SELECT ...;
~~~

Materializing helps when a CTE is expensive and referenced several times. MySQL 8 and SQLite also decide between merging and materializing. When performance matters, check the plan with `EXPLAIN`.

## Support across databases

CTEs are part of SQL:1999. PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite (since 3.8.3) have long supported them; MySQL added them in version 8.0. Code targeting MySQL 5.7 must use derived tables instead.

## CTEs, subqueries, views and temporary tables

| Tool | Lifetime | Reusable across statements | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Subquery | One place in one query | No | Fine for short logic |
| CTE | One statement | No, but reusable within the statement | Readable pipelines; recursion |
| View | Permanent | Yes | Shared logic for many queries and users |
| Temporary table | Session | Yes, within the session | Can be indexed; good for multi-statement processing |

For a multi-step data job running several statements, a temporary table with an index may outperform repeating a CTE in each statement.

## Data-modifying CTEs

PostgreSQL allows `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` inside a `WITH` clause, combined with `RETURNING`, which enables atomic multi-step operations:

~~~sql
WITH archived AS (
    DELETE FROM orders
    WHERE order_date < '2020-01-01'
    RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO orders_archive
SELECT * FROM archived;
~~~

This moves old orders to an archive table in one statement: the deleted rows flow directly into the insert. All sub-statements see the same snapshot of the data, so a data-modifying CTE doesn't see changes made by its sibling CTEs. MySQL and SQLite don't support data-modifying CTEs.

## CTEs and readability in interviews

In interviews, CTEs make multi-step answers clear: "first I'll compute each customer's total, then rank customers within each city, then keep the top three". Writing each step as a named CTE shows structured thinking and lets you check each step as you go.

## How interviewers test this

Expect multi-step problems where CTEs help, such as "employees earning above their department average" or "months where revenue declined", plus "CTE versus subquery?" Use CTEs to name steps, explain that they exist for one statement only, and mention materialization and the PostgreSQL 12 change for depth.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs: Sequences and Hierarchies
lessons.description: Generate series and walk org charts or category trees with WITH RECURSIVE.

sections.title: Anatomy: Generate 1 to 5
sections.code:
WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (
  SELECT 1                 -- anchor: the starting row(s)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums   -- recursive step: built from the previous rows
  WHERE n < 5              -- stop condition
)
SELECT n FROM nums;
-- 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
sections.explanation: The anchor runs once. The recursive part runs repeatedly on the rows produced by the previous round until it produces no new rows.

sections.title: Setup: Add Managers
sections.code:
-- Run once in the SQL Lab to add a reporting line
ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN manager_id INTEGER;
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 6 WHERE id IN (1, 2);        -- Alice, Bob report to Fiona
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 4 WHERE id IN (3, 5, 6, 8);  -- Charlie, Evan, Fiona, Hannah report to Diana
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 3 WHERE id = 7;              -- George reports to Charlie
-- Diana has no manager (NULL)
sections.explanation: Run this once in the SQL Lab. The data persists in your browser.

sections.title: Walk the Org Chart
sections.code:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL           -- start at the top (Diana)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.level + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, level FROM chain ORDER BY level, name;
sections.explanation: Each round finds the direct reports of the people found in the previous round.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting the stop condition or having a cycle in the data (A manages B, B manages A) loops forever. Add a depth limit such as `WHERE level < 20`.
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL: UNION de-duplicates every round, which is slower (though it can help stop cycles).
SQL Server writes just `WITH` (no RECURSIVE keyword); PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite need `WITH RECURSIVE`.

sections.question: In a recursive CTE, which part runs exactly once?
options: The final SELECT runs once per level
sections.explanation: The anchor seeds the recursion; the recursive member repeats until it returns no rows.

items: Recursive CTE = anchor UNION ALL recursive step, with a stop condition.
Use it for hierarchies (org charts, categories, comment threads) and generated series.

content.theory:
A recursive CTE refers to itself, letting SQL walk hierarchies and generate sequences of any length: an organization chart, a category tree, a bill of materials, or every date in a range. It works by repeatedly applying a step to the previous step's results until no new rows appear. This lesson explains the anchor and recursive parts, how evaluation proceeds, hierarchy traversal with depth and paths, generating sequences, and preventing infinite loops.

## The structure

A recursive CTE has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`:

~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE numbers AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n                 -- anchor: the starting rows
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers     -- recursive part: builds on previous rows
    WHERE n < 10                  -- termination condition
)
SELECT n FROM numbers;
~~~

This returns the numbers 1 to 10. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite require the `RECURSIVE` keyword; SQL Server and Oracle omit it.

## How evaluation works

Despite the name, evaluation is iterative:

1. Run the anchor query. Its rows form the first working set and go into the result
2. Run the recursive part, where the CTE's name refers only to the **previous** working set, not the whole result
3. Add the new rows to the result; they become the next working set
4. Repeat until the recursive part produces no rows

In the example, the working set goes `{1}`, `{2}`, ..., `{10}`. When n is 10, the condition `n < 10` produces nothing, and evaluation stops.

## Walking a hierarchy

The most common use is an employee hierarchy, where `manager_id` references `employees.id`. To find everyone who reports, directly or indirectly, to employee 1:

~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id = 1                       -- direct reports
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id      -- reports of reports
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM reports ORDER BY depth, name;
~~~

The anchor finds direct reports. Each iteration joins employees to the previous level, finding the next level down. The `depth` column counts levels. A self-join can only reach a fixed number of levels; the recursive CTE handles any depth.

## Walking upward

Reversing the join climbs from an employee to the top of the chain:

~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id FROM employees WHERE id = 42
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id
    FROM employees e
    JOIN chain c ON e.id = c.manager_id
)
SELECT name FROM chain;
~~~

This lists employee 42, their manager, their manager's manager, and so on up to the CEO, whose NULL `manager_id` matches nothing and ends the recursion.

## Building paths

Carrying a path string through the recursion shows each row's position in the tree and gives a natural sort order:

~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT id, name, CAST(name AS VARCHAR(1000)) AS path
    FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.id, c.name, CAST(t.path || ' > ' || c.name AS VARCHAR(1000))
    FROM categories c
    JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT path FROM tree ORDER BY path;
~~~

Output looks like `Electronics > Computers > Laptops`. The `CAST` matters: column types are fixed by the anchor, so without widening the anchor's type, longer paths can be truncated or fail. MySQL needs `CONCAT` instead of `||`.

## Generating sequences

Recursive CTEs generate rows that don't exist in any table, such as every date in a month, for reports that must show zero for days without sales:

~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE days AS (
    SELECT DATE '2024-03-01' AS d
    UNION ALL
    SELECT d + 1 FROM days WHERE d < DATE '2024-03-31'
)
SELECT days.d, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM days
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = days.d
GROUP BY days.d
ORDER BY days.d;
~~~

PostgreSQL's `generate_series` function does the same more concisely, but the recursive CTE works in MySQL 8 and SQLite too. Date arithmetic syntax varies: `d + INTERVAL 1 DAY` in MySQL, `date(d, '+1 day')` in SQLite.

## Preventing infinite loops

If the recursive part keeps producing rows, the query never ends. Causes include a missing termination condition and cycles in the data, such as employee A managing B while B manages A. Defences:

- always include a condition that eventually produces no rows, such as `WHERE depth < 20`
- track visited IDs and stop on repeats: in PostgreSQL, keep an array of visited IDs and add `WHERE NOT e.id = ANY(r.visited)`
- use built-in protection: MySQL stops after `cte_max_recursion_depth` iterations (1,000 by default), and SQL Server's default limit is 100, adjustable with `OPTION (MAXRECURSION n)`
- PostgreSQL 14 added a standard `CYCLE` clause that detects cycles automatically

## UNION versus UNION ALL

`UNION ALL` keeps every row and is the usual choice. `UNION` removes duplicates at each step, which can stop recursion over cyclic graphs when the same rows recur, but it costs a duplicate check on every iteration and doesn't help when rows differ only in a depth or path column.

## Performance

Each iteration runs a join between the table and the previous level. An index on the join column, such as `employees (manager_id)`, keeps each step fast. Deep or wide hierarchies produce many rows, so filter what you need early. For hierarchies queried constantly, alternative models such as materialized paths or closure tables store ancestry directly, trading write complexity for faster reads.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "find all subordinates of a manager", "list the chain of command above an employee", "generate dates for a month" and "What stops a recursive CTE?" Describe the anchor and recursive parts and the iteration model, track depth, explain termination, and mention cycle protection.

lessons.title: Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE
lessons.description: Rank rows without collapsing them, how ties are handled, and PARTITION BY.

sections.title: Window vs GROUP BY
Ranking With a Tie
sections.code:
-- Make a tie first: give Bob the same salary as Alice
UPDATE employees SET salary = 85000 WHERE id = 2;

SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 5;
sections.explanation: Undo the change afterwards with: UPDATE employees SET salary = 78000 WHERE id = 2;

sections.title: How They Differ
rows: Tied rows get different numbers (in an arbitrary order)
Splits the rows into n nearly equal buckets

sections.title: Rank Within Each Department
sections.code:
SELECT name, department, salary,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees
ORDER BY department, dept_rank;
-- Fiona Engineering 1 | Alice 2 | Bob 3 | Diana HR 1 | Hannah Marketing 1 | Evan 2 | Charlie Sales 1 | George 2
sections.explanation: Numbering restarts at 1 in each partition.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Filtering on a window function in WHERE (`WHERE dept_rank = 1`) is invalid, because windows are computed after WHERE. Wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.
Using ROW_NUMBER for 'top earners' when ties should be included. Use DENSE_RANK or RANK.

sections.question: Salaries 100, 90, 90, 80. What DENSE_RANK (descending) does 80 get?
sections.explanation: DENSE_RANK: 100 → 1, both 90s → 2, 80 → 3 (no gap). RANK would give 4.

items: Window functions keep every row; OVER(PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) defines the window.
ROW_NUMBER = unique, RANK = gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK = no gaps.
To filter on a window result, wrap the query and filter outside.

content.theory:
Window functions compute a value for each row using a set of related rows, called the window, without collapsing rows the way `GROUP BY` does. Ranking functions are the most used: they number rows, rank them with or without gaps, and split them into buckets. This lesson explains the `OVER` clause with `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY`, the differences between `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK` and `DENSE_RANK`, `NTILE` and percentile ranks, and the top-N-per-group pattern.

## Window functions versus GROUP BY

`GROUP BY` returns one row per group. A window function keeps every row and adds a computed column:

~~~sql
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
FROM employees;
~~~

Every employee row remains, now showing their department's average beside their own salary. That's impossible with `GROUP BY` alone, which would lose the individual rows.

## The OVER clause

`OVER` defines the window:

- **PARTITION BY** splits rows into independent groups; the function restarts in each partition. Without it, the whole result is one partition
- **ORDER BY** orders rows within each partition, which ranking functions need to decide positions

`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)` numbers employees within each department, from highest salary to lowest.

## ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK

The three ranking functions differ only in how they handle ties. For salaries 90,000, 80,000, 80,000 and 70,000:

| salary | ROW_NUMBER | RANK | DENSE_RANK |
|---|---|---|---|
| 90,000 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 80,000 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 80,000 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 70,000 | 4 | 4 | 3 |

- **ROW_NUMBER** gives every row a unique number. Tied rows get different numbers in an arbitrary order unless the `ORDER BY` breaks the tie
- **RANK** gives tied rows the same rank, then skips: after two rows at rank 2 comes rank 4, as in sports standings
- **DENSE_RANK** gives tied rows the same rank without gaps: after two rows at rank 2 comes rank 3

## Choosing the right one

The choice depends on the question:

- "Exactly one row per group, such as one latest order per customer": `ROW_NUMBER`, with a tiebreaker such as `id` for determinism
- "The third highest distinct salary": `DENSE_RANK`, since tied salaries count as one value
- "Competition-style ranks, where two people tied for second push the next person to fourth": `RANK`

Many interview mistakes come from using `ROW_NUMBER` where ties should share a rank, or `RANK` where the question asks about distinct values.

## Top N per group

The most important window function pattern returns the top rows in each group:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees
)
SELECT name, dept_id, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 3;
~~~

Window functions are computed after `WHERE`, so you can't filter on them directly; the CTE computes the ranks first. With `DENSE_RANK`, ties at third place all appear. With `ROW_NUMBER`, you get exactly three rows per department.

## Deduplication with ROW_NUMBER

`ROW_NUMBER` also removes duplicates while keeping one chosen copy:

~~~sql
WITH numbered AS (
    SELECT id, email,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created_at) AS rn
    FROM users
)
DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM numbered WHERE rn > 1);
~~~

This keeps the earliest account for each email and deletes the rest.

## NTILE

`NTILE(n)` divides each partition's ordered rows into n buckets of nearly equal size, numbered 1 to n:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS quartile
FROM employees;
~~~

Quartile 1 holds the top 25% of earners. When rows don't divide evenly, earlier buckets get one extra row: ten rows into four buckets gives sizes 3, 3, 2 and 2. Ties may be split across buckets, since `NTILE` only counts rows.

## Percentile ranks

`PERCENT_RANK()` returns a row's relative position from 0 to 1, computed as (rank − 1) / (rows − 1). `CUME_DIST()` returns the fraction of rows with values at or below the current row. They answer questions such as "what percentile is this student's score in?"

## Ordering inside and outside the window

The `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` only controls how the window is computed. It doesn't sort the final result. Add an outer `ORDER BY` to sort the output. Different window functions in one query can use different partitions and orders.

## Named windows

When several functions share a window, define it once:

~~~sql
SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn,
       RANK() OVER w AS rnk
FROM employees
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC);
~~~

PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite support the `WINDOW` clause.

## Support and performance

Window functions arrived in SQL:2003. PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle have supported them for years; MySQL added them in 8.0 and SQLite in 3.25. Computing a window requires sorting rows by the partition and order columns, so an index matching `(dept_id, salary)` can avoid a separate sort.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "ROW_NUMBER versus RANK versus DENSE_RANK", "top 3 salaries per department", "Nth highest salary" and "remove duplicate rows keeping one". Show the tie table, pick the function that matches the question's treatment of ties, filter through a CTE, and add a tiebreaker for deterministic ROW_NUMBER results.

lessons.title: Analytic Windows: Running Totals, LAG / LEAD, Percent of Total
lessons.description: SUM/AVG over windows, comparing a row with the previous one, and per-group comparisons.

sections.title: Running Total of Payroll by Hire Date
sections.code:
SELECT name, hire_date, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date) AS running_payroll
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_date;
sections.explanation: With ORDER BY inside OVER, the default frame is 'from the first row up to the current row', so SUM becomes a running total.

sections.title: LAG and LEAD: Look at Neighbouring Rows
sections.code:
SELECT name, hire_date,
       LAG(name)       OVER (ORDER BY hire_date) AS hired_before,
       LEAD(hire_date) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date) AS next_hire
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_date;
-- Fiona   2020-03-10  NULL     2021-11-20
-- Diana   2021-11-20  Fiona    2022-01-18
-- ...
-- Charlie 2024-02-01  George   NULL
sections.explanation: LAG reads the previous row and LEAD the next one; the first and last rows get NULL (or a default: LAG(x, 1, 0)). This is the standard tool for month-over-month growth: value − LAG(value).

sections.title: Compare Each Row With Its Group, and With the Total
sections.code:
SELECT name, department, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)          AS dept_avg,
       salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS diff
FROM employees
ORDER BY department, salary DESC;
-- Fiona Engineering 92000 85000 7000 ... George Sales 58000 61500 -3500

SELECT name, salary,
       ROUND(100.0 * salary / SUM(salary) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;
-- Fiona 15.6, Alice 14.4, Bob 13.2
sections.explanation: An empty OVER () means the window is the whole result set.

sections.title: Frames (Advanced)
sections.content:
You can set the frame explicitly:
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a 3-row moving average.
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING covers the whole partition.
RANGE (the default) treats rows with the same ORDER BY value as peers and includes them together; ROWS counts physical rows.

sections.question: Which function gives you the previous month's revenue on the same row as this month's?
sections.explanation: LAG looks back one row in the window order; LEAD looks forward.

items: SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...) = running total; OVER () = the whole result set.
LAG/LEAD compare a row with its neighbours: growth, gaps, streaks.
PARTITION BY lets each row see its own group's statistics.

content.theory:
Analytic window functions compute running totals, moving averages, comparisons with previous rows and shares of a total, all while keeping every row. They replace slow self-joins and correlated subqueries with a single pass over the data. This lesson explains aggregate window functions, frames with `ROWS` and `RANGE`, `LAG` and `LEAD`, `FIRST_VALUE` and `LAST_VALUE`, and percent-of-total calculations.

## Aggregates as window functions

Any aggregate becomes a window function when followed by `OVER`:

~~~sql
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_payroll,
       COUNT(*)    OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_size
FROM employees;
~~~

Without `ORDER BY` in the window, the aggregate covers the whole partition, so every row in a department shows the same payroll.

## Running totals

Adding `ORDER BY` changes the meaning: the aggregate covers rows from the start of the partition up to the current row:

~~~sql
SELECT order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM daily_sales;
~~~

Each row shows the cumulative total up to that date. With `PARTITION BY region`, the running total restarts for each region. The older alternative, a self-join on `b.order_date <= a.order_date`, costs O(n²); the window version is a single sorted pass.

## Frames

The **frame** specifies exactly which rows around the current row the function uses:

~~~sql
AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
~~~

This is a 7-day moving average: the current row plus the six before it. Frame boundaries include:

| Boundary | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` | The first row of the partition |
| `n PRECEDING` | n rows (or values) before the current row |
| `CURRENT ROW` | The current row |
| `n FOLLOWING` | n rows after |
| `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` | The last row of the partition |

## ROWS versus RANGE

Frames come in two main types:

- **ROWS** counts physical rows: `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` means exactly three rows
- **RANGE** uses values of the `ORDER BY` column: rows with equal values are treated as peers and included together

The default frame, when `ORDER BY` is present, is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. This surprises people: if two orders share the same date, both rows show the running total including **both** orders, because they're peers. For a strictly row-by-row running total, specify `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, or add a tiebreaker column to the `ORDER BY`.

`ROWS` frames over gaps in data can also mislead: "6 preceding rows" covers more than a week if some days have no rows. PostgreSQL 11+ supports value-based ranges such as `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which respects calendar time.

## LAG and LEAD

`LAG` reads a value from a previous row, and `LEAD` from a following row, in the window's order:

~~~sql
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM monthly_revenue;
~~~

The first row has no previous row, so `LAG` returns NULL. Optional arguments set the offset and a default: `LAG(revenue, 12, 0)` reads the value from 12 rows back, such as the same month last year, using 0 when none exists. `LAG` and `LEAD` ignore frames; they always count rows within the partition.

Common uses:

- month-over-month or year-over-year growth
- time between consecutive events: `login_time - LAG(login_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_time)`
- detecting changes: rows where `status <> LAG(status)`

## FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE and NTH_VALUE

These return a value from a specific position in the frame:

~~~sql
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS top_earner
FROM employees;
~~~

`LAST_VALUE` has a well-known trap. With the default frame ending at the current row, the "last" value is the current row itself. To get the true last value in the partition, extend the frame:

~~~sql
LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
)
~~~

`NTH_VALUE(name, 2)` returns the second value in the frame, with the same caveat.

## Percent of total

Dividing a row's value by a window total gives its share:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, name, salary,
       ROUND(100.0 * salary / SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id), 2) AS pct_of_dept
FROM employees;
~~~

The same pattern computes market share, a product's share of category revenue, and cumulative percentages for Pareto analysis: `SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) / SUM(revenue) OVER ()` shows how quickly the top products add up to 80% of sales. An empty `OVER ()` means the whole result.

## Combining windows with grouping

Window functions run after `GROUP BY`, so they can operate on aggregated results:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS payroll,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(salary) DESC) AS payroll_rank
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

This ranks departments by total payroll in one query.

## Performance

Each distinct window specification may need its own sort. Queries with several different `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY` combinations sort the data several times. Reusing the same window, through a `WINDOW` clause, lets the database share the work, and an index matching the window's columns can avoid sorting altogether.

## How interviewers test this

Expect running totals, 7-day moving averages, month-over-month growth with LAG, percent of total, and "time since previous event". Know the default RANGE frame and its effect with ties, the LAST_VALUE frame trap, how LAG handles the first row, and why windows replace self-joins for these problems.

lessons.title: Set Operations: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
lessons.description: Combine the results of several queries vertically, and why UNION ALL is usually what you want.

sections.title: Set Operators
rows: Rows from either query, duplicates removed
Rows from either query, duplicates kept
Departments with someone hired before 2022: Engineering, HR
Rows in the first query but not the second
Departments with nobody under 70000: Engineering, HR

sections.title: Examples
sections.code:
SELECT department FROM employees
UNION
SELECT name FROM departments;           -- 4 distinct names

SELECT name FROM departments
INTERSECT
SELECT department FROM employees WHERE hire_date < '2022-01-01';
-- Engineering, HR

SELECT name FROM departments
EXCEPT
SELECT department FROM employees WHERE salary < 70000;
-- Engineering, HR
sections.explanation: Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types. Column names come from the first query.

traps.question: UNION vs UNION ALL?
traps.trap: Saying they're the same, or always using UNION.
traps.solution: UNION removes duplicates, which needs a sort or hash step. UNION ALL just appends the rows. Use UNION ALL unless you specifically need de-duplication: it's faster and doesn't silently drop rows that are legitimately identical.

sections.question: Query A returns 5 rows and query B returns 3 rows; 2 rows appear in both. How many rows does A UNION ALL B return?
sections.explanation: UNION ALL keeps everything: 5 + 3 = 8. UNION would return 6 (if each query has no internal duplicates).

items: UNION de-duplicates; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster.
INTERSECT = in both; EXCEPT/MINUS = in the first but not the second.

content.theory:
Set operations combine the results of two or more queries vertically: stacking rows from one result on top of another, or comparing them. `UNION` combines, `INTERSECT` finds common rows, and `EXCEPT` finds rows in one result but not another. They're the SQL version of set union, intersection and difference from mathematics. This lesson explains each operation, the rules for compatible queries, `UNION` versus `UNION ALL`, duplicate and NULL handling, and how set operations compare with joins.

## Joins versus set operations

Joins combine tables **horizontally**: they add columns by matching rows. Set operations combine results **vertically**: they add or compare rows with the same columns. Use a join when you need data from related tables side by side; use a set operation when you have similar rows from different sources.

## UNION and UNION ALL

`UNION ALL` stacks two results, keeping every row:

~~~sql
SELECT name, email, 'employee' AS source FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT name, email, 'contractor' FROM contractors;
~~~

`UNION` does the same but removes duplicate rows from the combined result.

| | UNION | UNION ALL |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicates | Removed | Kept |
| Cost | Extra sort or hash to deduplicate | No extra work |
| Use when | Duplicates must be eliminated | Sources don't overlap, or duplicates are meaningful |

Default to `UNION ALL`. Deduplication costs time on large results, and when sources can't overlap, such as different years of orders, it's pure waste. Use `UNION` only when you need unique rows. Adding a constant column, like `source` above, labels each row's origin, and also means rows from different sources never count as duplicates.

## Compatibility rules

Queries combined with set operations must be compatible:

- **the same number of columns**
- **compatible types** in each position: you can't combine a number column with a date column without casting
- **column names come from the first query**; aliases in later queries are ignored

Columns are matched by position, not name. If the first query selects `name, email` and the second selects `email, name`, the values are combined into the wrong columns without any error, as long as the types are compatible. List columns explicitly and in the same order.

## Sorting combined results

`ORDER BY` applies to the whole combined result and goes at the end, after the last query:

~~~sql
SELECT name, hire_date FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT name, start_date FROM contractors
ORDER BY hire_date DESC;
~~~

It refers to column names from the first query, or positions. To sort or limit an individual branch, wrap it in parentheses or a subquery.

## INTERSECT

`INTERSECT` returns rows present in both results:

~~~sql
-- customers who bought in both 2023 and 2024
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2023
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024;
~~~

It removes duplicates by default. `INTERSECT ALL` keeps duplicates up to the smaller count, supported in PostgreSQL. The same question can be answered with `EXISTS` or a join with `DISTINCT`; `INTERSECT` often states it most directly. MySQL added `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` in version 8.0.31, so older MySQL versions need the `EXISTS` form.

## EXCEPT

`EXCEPT` returns rows in the first result that aren't in the second:

~~~sql
-- customers who bought in 2023 but not in 2024 (churned)
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2023
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024;
~~~

Oracle calls it `MINUS`. Order matters: `A EXCEPT B` differs from `B EXCEPT A`. Like `UNION` and `INTERSECT`, it removes duplicates unless written `EXCEPT ALL`.

## NULL in set operations

Set operations treat NULLs as equal to each other when comparing rows, unlike `=` in a `WHERE` clause. Two rows `(1, NULL)` are duplicates for `UNION`, match for `INTERSECT`, and cancel out in `EXCEPT`. This makes `EXCEPT` a reliable way to compare whole rows that contain NULLs, where `NOT IN` would fail.

## Comparing two tables

`EXCEPT` in both directions finds every difference between two tables with the same structure, which is useful for verifying data migrations or test results:

~~~sql
(SELECT * FROM expected_results EXCEPT SELECT * FROM actual_results)
UNION ALL
(SELECT * FROM actual_results EXCEPT SELECT * FROM expected_results);
~~~

An empty result means the tables contain the same rows, ignoring duplicate counts.

## Precedence

`INTERSECT` binds more tightly than `UNION` and `EXCEPT`, which are evaluated left to right. `A UNION B INTERSECT C` means `A UNION (B INTERSECT C)`. Use parentheses whenever you mix operations.

## Practical uses

| Task | Operation |
|---|---|
| Combine current and archived records | `UNION ALL` |
| Merge contact lists, removing duplicates | `UNION` |
| Customers active in both periods | `INTERSECT` |
| Churned customers, missing records | `EXCEPT` |
| Emulate a full outer join in MySQL | `UNION ALL` of a left join and unmatched right rows |
| Build rows from constants | `SELECT 'A' UNION ALL SELECT 'B'` |

## Performance

`UNION ALL` is cheap: it streams one result after another. `UNION`, `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` must compare rows, using a sort or hash, which costs memory and time on large results. When equivalent `EXISTS` or `NOT EXISTS` queries can use indexes on the comparison columns, they may be faster. Check plans for large datasets.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "UNION versus UNION ALL", "customers who ordered in one year but not the next", "customers active in both months" and "join versus union". Explain duplicate removal and its cost, the column count and type rules, positional matching, and the NULL behaviour that makes EXCEPT useful for comparing tables.

modules.title: Placement SQL
modules.description: Practice the most frequently asked SQL interview queries.

lessons.title: Nth Highest Salary (the most asked SQL question)
lessons.description: Four ways to find the 2nd or Nth highest salary, and how each one handles ties.

sections.title: Approach 1: MAX Below MAX (2nd highest only)
sections.code:
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
-- 85000
sections.explanation: Simple and handles ties correctly, but it only works for N = 2.

sections.title: Approach 2: DISTINCT + LIMIT / OFFSET
sections.code:
-- Nth highest: OFFSET N - 1 (3rd highest here)
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2;
-- 78000
sections.explanation: DISTINCT is essential. Without it, two people sharing the top salary would make the '2nd highest' equal to the 1st.

sections.title: Approach 3: DENSE_RANK (the most robust)
sections.code:
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE r = 3;
-- 78000
sections.explanation: Works for any N, handles ties, and extends easily to 'Nth highest per department' by adding PARTITION BY department.

sections.title: Approach 4: Correlated COUNT (no window functions needed)
sections.code:
-- Employees in the top 2 distinct salaries
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE 2 > (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary)
           FROM employees x
           WHERE x.salary > e.salary)
ORDER BY salary DESC;
-- Fiona 92000, Alice 85000
sections.explanation: A salary is in the top N if fewer than N distinct salaries are greater than it. This is O(n²), but it works in very old databases.

traps.question: What should the query return when there is no Nth salary?
traps.trap: Returning an empty result when the interviewer expects NULL.
traps.solution: Wrap it so an aggregate always returns one row: `SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1) AS nth`. Ask which behaviour is expected (LeetCode's version expects NULL).

sections.question: If Alice and Bob both earn 85000 and Fiona earns 92000, what is the 2nd highest DISTINCT salary?
sections.explanation: The distinct salaries in descending order are 92000, 85000, 72000, ..., so the second one is 85000.

items: Use DISTINCT or DENSE_RANK so ties don't break the answer.
DENSE_RANK generalizes to any N and to per-group questions.
Clarify the empty-result behaviour with the interviewer.

content.theory:
"Find the Nth highest salary" is the most frequently asked SQL interview question. It looks small, but it tests whether you handle duplicates, missing answers and different database features correctly. There are at least four valid approaches, and interviewers often ask for more than one. This lesson works through each approach, explains how they differ on ties and empty results, and covers the per-department variant.

## The problem

Given an employees table with a salary column, return the Nth highest distinct salary. With salaries 100, 90, 90 and 80, the second highest salary is 90 and the third highest is 80. Duplicates count once. If N exceeds the number of distinct salaries, return NULL rather than no row.

Clarify both points at the start of an interview: whether duplicates count once, and what to return when there's no answer. They decide which approach is correct.

## Approach 1: LIMIT and OFFSET

Sort distinct salaries in descending order and skip N − 1 of them:

~~~sql
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;     -- N = 2
~~~

`DISTINCT` is essential: without it, the two 90 values occupy positions 2 and 3, and `OFFSET 2` would return 90 as the third highest instead of 80.

If fewer than N distinct salaries exist, this returns no rows. To return NULL instead, wrap it in a scalar subquery, which yields NULL when the inner query has no rows:

~~~sql
SELECT (
    SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees
    ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
) AS second_highest;
~~~

In SQL Server, use `OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY`.

## Approach 2: DENSE_RANK

The window function approach names the rule for ties directly:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees
)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 2;
~~~

`DENSE_RANK` gives equal salaries the same rank with no gaps, so ranks map exactly to distinct salary positions. Using `RANK` would fail: the 80 salary would get rank 4, not 3, because two rows share rank 2. Using `ROW_NUMBER` would also fail, since it numbers the duplicate 90s as 2 and 3. Explaining why `DENSE_RANK` is the right choice among the three is often the main point the interviewer wants.

`DISTINCT` in the outer query prevents returning the same salary once per employee who earns it.

## Approach 3: subquery with MAX

For the second highest specifically, a classic answer uses `MAX` twice:

~~~sql
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
~~~

The subquery finds the highest salary; the outer query finds the largest salary below it. This handles duplicates naturally and returns NULL automatically when there's no second salary, since `MAX` of no rows is NULL. It works in every database, including old versions. It doesn't generalize well beyond N = 2 or 3.

## Approach 4: correlated subquery

The general method without window functions counts how many distinct salaries are higher:

~~~sql
SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary
FROM employees e1
WHERE (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary
) = 1;     -- N - 1 higher salaries means e1.salary is the Nth highest
~~~

A salary is the Nth highest when exactly N − 1 distinct salaries are greater. This works everywhere but runs the subquery per row, costing O(n²) without an index, so it suits small tables or databases without window functions.

## Comparing the approaches

| Approach | Handles ties | Returns NULL if missing | Generalizes to N | Portability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LIMIT/OFFSET with DISTINCT | Yes | Only when wrapped in a scalar subquery | Yes | Syntax varies |
| DENSE_RANK | Yes | No row by default; wrap to get NULL | Yes | Needs window functions |
| MAX below MAX | Yes | Yes | Awkward beyond 2 | Universal |
| Correlated COUNT | Yes | No row by default | Yes | Universal, slow |

## As a reusable function

Some interview platforms ask for a function that takes N. In PostgreSQL:

~~~sql
CREATE FUNCTION nth_highest_salary(n INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $f$
    SELECT (
        SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees
        ORDER BY salary DESC
        LIMIT 1 OFFSET n - 1
    );
$f$ LANGUAGE sql;
~~~

`OFFSET` can't be negative, so guard against N less than 1. In MySQL, functions can't use expressions in `LIMIT` directly; you compute `n - 1` into a variable first.

## Nth highest per department

The variant "find the second highest salary in each department" needs `PARTITION BY`:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT dept_id, salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees
)
SELECT DISTINCT dept_id, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;
~~~

Departments with only one distinct salary don't appear. If they should appear with NULL, left join the departments table to this result.

## Testing your answer

Before declaring a solution finished, test mentally with: duplicate top salaries, fewer than N distinct salaries, all salaries equal, NULL salaries (which `ORDER BY` sorts first or last depending on the database, and `DENSE_RANK` ranks), and an empty table. Many submissions fail on exactly these cases.

## How interviewers test this

Expect the second or Nth highest salary, often followed by "Can you do it another way?" and "What if there are duplicates?" Present DENSE_RANK or LIMIT/OFFSET with DISTINCT, explain why RANK and ROW_NUMBER fail with ties, return NULL when no answer exists, and extend to per-department with PARTITION BY.

lessons.title: Find and Delete Duplicate Rows
lessons.description: Detect duplicates with GROUP BY / HAVING, list the extra copies, and delete them while keeping one.

sections.title: Setup
sections.explanation: Run this in the SQL Lab.

sections.title: 1. Which Values Are Duplicated?
sections.code:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS times
FROM emails
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- a@x.com 3
-- b@x.com 2
sections.explanation: GROUP BY the column(s) that define 'duplicate', then keep groups with more than one row.

sections.title: 2. Which Rows Are the Extra Copies?
sections.code:
SELECT id, email
FROM (
  SELECT id, email,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM emails
) t
WHERE rn > 1;
-- 3 a@x.com, 5 b@x.com, 6 a@x.com
sections.explanation: rn = 1 is the copy we keep (the lowest id); everything with rn > 1 is an extra.

sections.title: 3. Delete the Extras, Keep One
sections.explanation: The NOT IN here is safe because MIN(id) is never NULL. MySQL doesn't allow selecting from the table you're deleting from, so there you wrap the subquery in a derived table or use a self-join DELETE.

sections.question: After deleting duplicates, what stops new duplicates from being inserted?
options: A UNIQUE constraint or index on email
sections.explanation: Only a UNIQUE constraint makes the database reject duplicate values.

items: Find: GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
Identify the extras: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY id) > 1.
Delete, then add a UNIQUE constraint.

content.theory:
Duplicate rows creep into tables through repeated imports, retried requests and missing unique constraints. Finding them, removing the extras while keeping one copy, and preventing them from returning are common interview tasks and common real-world chores. This lesson covers defining duplicates, finding them with `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, viewing the full duplicate rows, deleting extras safely in several dialects, and adding constraints so they can't come back.

## Defining a duplicate

First decide what makes two rows duplicates. Rows are rarely identical in every column: each usually has its own `id` and perhaps a different `created_at`. Duplicates are usually rows matching on a **business key**, such as the same email, or the same customer, product and order date. Stating this definition aloud is the first step in an interview answer.

## Finding duplicate values

`GROUP BY` the defining columns and keep groups with more than one row:

~~~sql
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY copies DESC;
~~~

This lists each duplicated email and how many times it appears. For multi-column duplicates, group by all the columns: `GROUP BY customer_id, product_id, order_date`.

Case and spacing can hide duplicates: `'Asha@Mail.com'` and `'asha@mail.com '` are different strings. Group by a normalized form, `LOWER(TRIM(email))`, to catch them.

## Seeing the full rows

To inspect every duplicated row, not only the values, join back to the duplicate list or use a window count:

~~~sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT u.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY email) AS copies
    FROM users u
) t
WHERE copies > 1
ORDER BY email, created_at;
~~~

Reviewing the rows helps decide which copy to keep: perhaps the oldest, the most recently updated, or the one with the most complete data.

## Marking which copy to keep

`ROW_NUMBER` numbers rows within each duplicate group, in the order of your keep rule:

~~~sql
SELECT id, email, created_at,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created_at, id) AS rn
FROM users;
~~~

The row with `rn = 1` is the keeper, here the earliest; rows with `rn > 1` are extras. Adding `id` to the `ORDER BY` breaks ties when two copies share a timestamp, making the choice deterministic.

## Deleting duplicates

Delete the rows whose `rn` is greater than 1:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created_at, id) AS rn
    FROM users
)
DELETE FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1);
~~~

This works in PostgreSQL, SQLite and SQL Server. In MySQL, which doesn't allow selecting from the table being deleted from, wrap the subquery in a derived table, or use a self-join delete:

~~~sql
-- MySQL: keep the lowest id for each email
DELETE u1 FROM users u1
JOIN users u2 ON u1.email = u2.email AND u1.id > u2.id;
~~~

The self-join deletes every row that has another row with the same email and a smaller id, leaving the smallest id in each group.

## Deleting without a unique ID

If rows are fully identical with no distinguishing column, you can't target individual copies by ID. Options:

- PostgreSQL's hidden `ctid` column identifies each row's physical location: `DELETE FROM t a USING t b WHERE a.ctid > b.ctid AND a.col1 = b.col1 AND ...`
- SQLite's `rowid` works the same way
- Copy distinct rows to a new table, then swap: `CREATE TABLE t_clean AS SELECT DISTINCT * FROM t;`, then drop the original and rename

## Doing it safely

Deleting data is risky, so follow the safeguards:

1. Count first: run the `SELECT` version and check how many rows will be removed
2. Run inside a transaction, verify, then commit
3. Back up the affected rows, for example `CREATE TABLE users_dupes_backup AS SELECT ...` of the rows to be deleted
4. Check foreign keys: other tables may reference the duplicate rows, such as orders placed under a duplicate account. Repoint them to the keeper with an `UPDATE` before deleting, or the delete fails or cascades

For large tables, delete in batches to avoid long locks.

## Preventing duplicates

Cleanup is pointless if duplicates return. Add a unique constraint after cleaning:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_users_email UNIQUE (email);
~~~

For case-insensitive uniqueness, create a unique index on `LOWER(email)`. Then make inserts handle conflicts deliberately with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` or an upsert, instead of failing or relying on the application to check first, which is subject to race conditions. For APIs, idempotency keys stop retried requests from creating duplicate records.

## Counting distinct versus total

A related interview question asks how many duplicate rows exist: `SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT email) FROM users` gives the number of extra rows beyond one per email. Note that `COUNT(DISTINCT email)` ignores NULL emails.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "find duplicate emails", "delete duplicates keeping the first", "find duplicate rows across multiple columns" and "how would you prevent duplicates?" Define the business key, use GROUP BY with HAVING to find, ROW_NUMBER with a deterministic keep rule to delete, mention the MySQL self-join form, handle foreign keys, and finish with a unique constraint.

lessons.title: Top-N per Group and Highest Earner per Department
lessons.description: The 'top 2 salaries in each department' pattern with window functions and a correlated alternative.

sections.title: Highest Earner in Each Department
sections.code:
SELECT e.department, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees x
                  WHERE x.department = e.department)
ORDER BY e.department;
-- Engineering Fiona 92000 | HR Diana 72000 | Marketing Hannah 71000 | Sales Charlie 65000
sections.explanation: Ties are included automatically: if two people share the maximum, both are returned.

sections.title: Top 2 per Department
sections.code:
SELECT department, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT department, name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE r <= 2
ORDER BY department, salary DESC;
sections.explanation: Change 2 to any N. Swap DENSE_RANK for ROW_NUMBER if you need exactly N rows even when there are ties.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: `SELECT department, name, MAX(salary) ... GROUP BY department`: SQLite and old MySQL return some name, but not necessarily the one that earns the maximum. Standard SQL rejects it.
Forgetting PARTITION BY ranks across the whole company instead of within each department.

sections.question: To return exactly 2 rows per department even when salaries tie, use:
sections.explanation: ROW_NUMBER assigns unique numbers, so rn <= 2 always gives at most 2 rows per partition.

items: Top-N per group = rank inside PARTITION BY, then filter in an outer query.
Choose ROW_NUMBER vs DENSE_RANK based on how ties should be handled.

content.theory:
Top-N-per-group problems ask for the best rows within each group: the highest earner in each department, the three best-selling products per category, each customer's most recent order. They appear constantly in interviews and reports. Plain `GROUP BY` can't solve them, because it collapses each group into one row of aggregates and loses the other columns. This lesson explains why, then covers the window function solution, its tie-handling choices, and the alternatives using joins, correlated subqueries and lateral joins.

## Why GROUP BY isn't enough

This finds the highest salary per department:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;
~~~

But it can't tell you **who** earns it. Adding `name` to the select list is an error in standard SQL, because a department has many names. In MySQL without strict grouping, or SQLite, it may run and return a name from an arbitrary row, which is a silent bug. The problem needs a way to keep whole rows while comparing within groups.

## The window function solution

Rank rows within each group, then filter:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT e.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn
    FROM employees e
)
SELECT dept_id, name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
~~~

`PARTITION BY dept_id` restarts numbering in each department, `ORDER BY salary DESC` puts the highest first, and `WHERE rn = 1` keeps the top row of each. Change it to `rn <= 3` for the top three. The CTE is necessary because window functions are computed after `WHERE`.

## Choosing how ties behave

The ranking function decides what happens when salaries tie:

| Function | Two employees tied for highest | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `ROW_NUMBER` | Exactly one returned | You need exactly N rows per group |
| `RANK` | Both returned as rank 1; next is rank 3 | Ties should share a position, gaps allowed |
| `DENSE_RANK` | Both returned; next distinct salary is rank 2 | "Top N distinct values" per group |

For "the highest earner in each department", ask whether ties should all be shown. If yes, use `RANK` or `DENSE_RANK`. With `ROW_NUMBER`, add a tiebreaker such as `id` so the same row is chosen every time.

## Each customer's latest order

The same pattern finds the most recent row per entity:

~~~sql
WITH latest AS (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders o
)
SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id, order_date, amount
FROM latest
WHERE rn = 1;
~~~

This is one of the most common patterns in production analytics: latest status per ticket, latest price per product, latest login per user.

## Alternative: join to the group maximum

Before window functions, the standard approach joined to an aggregated derived table:

~~~sql
SELECT e.dept_id, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN (
    SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY dept_id
) m ON m.dept_id = e.dept_id AND m.max_salary = e.salary;
~~~

It returns all employees tied for the maximum, like `RANK`. It works in every database, but it only handles the top 1, not the top N.

## Alternative: correlated subquery

A correlated subquery expresses "salary equals the maximum of my department":

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id);
~~~

For the top N, count how many colleagues earn more:

~~~sql
SELECT dept_id, name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary) FROM employees e2
       WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id AND e2.salary > e.salary) < 3;
~~~

This returns employees with fewer than three distinct higher salaries in their department, the top three distinct salaries, like `DENSE_RANK <= 3`. It's portable but O(n²) without indexes.

## Alternative: lateral join

When groups come from a separate table and N is small, a lateral join with an index can be fastest:

~~~sql
SELECT d.name AS department, t.name, t.salary
FROM departments d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT name, salary FROM employees e
    WHERE e.dept_id = d.id
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    LIMIT 3
) t;
~~~

With an index on `employees (dept_id, salary DESC)`, each department needs only a short index read. PostgreSQL and MySQL 8.0.14+ support `LATERAL`; SQL Server uses `CROSS APPLY`.

## PostgreSQL's DISTINCT ON

PostgreSQL offers a concise top-1-per-group:

~~~sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept_id) dept_id, name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC, id;
~~~

It keeps the first row per `dept_id` in the given order. It's PostgreSQL-only and handles only the top 1.

## Choosing an approach

| Approach | Top N | Ties | Portability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Window function in a CTE | Any N | Your choice of function | Modern databases |
| Join to group MAX | Top 1 only | Returns all tied | Universal |
| Correlated COUNT | Any N | Distinct-value semantics | Universal, slow |
| Lateral join | Any N | One per row unless extended | PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, SQL Server |
| DISTINCT ON | Top 1 only | One per group | PostgreSQL only |

In interviews, lead with the window function approach, then mention one alternative.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "highest paid employee per department", "top 3 products per category by revenue" and "latest order for each customer". Explain why GROUP BY alone fails, use ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK in a CTE, discuss ties explicitly, and offer the join-to-MAX approach for databases without window functions.

lessons.title: Self-Joins: Employees and Their Managers
lessons.description: Join a table to itself to answer 'earns more than their manager' and 'list each employee's manager'.

sections.title: Setup
sections.code:
-- Run once in the SQL Lab to add a reporting line
ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN manager_id INTEGER;
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 6 WHERE id IN (1, 2);        -- Alice, Bob report to Fiona
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 4 WHERE id IN (3, 5, 6, 8);  -- Charlie, Evan, Fiona, Hannah report to Diana
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 3 WHERE id = 7;              -- George reports to Charlie
-- Diana has no manager (NULL)
sections.explanation: Skip this if you already ran it in the Recursive CTE lesson.

sections.title: Employees Who Earn More Than Their Manager
sections.code:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
-- Fiona (92000) earns more than Diana (72000)
sections.explanation: Two aliases of the same table: e plays the employee role and m the manager role.

sections.title: Every Employee With Their Manager (including the top boss)
sections.code:
SELECT e.name AS employee, COALESCE(m.name, '(none)') AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY e.id;
-- Alice Fiona | Bob Fiona | Charlie Diana | Diana (none) | Evan Diana | Fiona Diana | George Charlie | Hannah Diana
sections.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps Diana, who has no manager. An INNER JOIN would drop her.

sections.question: How would you count each manager's direct reports?
sections.answerReveal: SELECT m.name, COUNT(*) AS reports FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id GROUP BY m.id, m.name ORDER BY reports DESC; gives Diana 4, Fiona 2, Charlie 1.

sections.question: Why does listing all employees with their manager need a LEFT JOIN?
options: To keep employees whose manager_id is NULL
sections.explanation: With an inner join, the top-level employee (no manager) has no match and disappears.

items: Self-join = the same table under two aliases with different roles.
Use a LEFT JOIN when the related row may be missing.

content.theory:
Many interview questions involve an employees table where each row's `manager_id` points to another employee in the same table. Answering them requires joining the table to itself, treating one copy as employees and another as managers. This lesson covers the self-join technique and the classic questions: listing each employee's manager, employees who earn more than their managers, managers with the most reports, employees without managers, and walking the full chain of command.

## The self-referencing table

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    salary      NUMERIC(10, 2),
    dept_id     INTEGER,
    manager_id  INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id)
);
~~~

`manager_id` is a foreign key referencing the same table. The top of the hierarchy, such as the CEO, has `manager_id` NULL. This structure, called an **adjacency list**, is the most common way to store a hierarchy in SQL.

## The self-join technique

To compare an employee with their manager, the query needs two copies of the table, each with its own alias:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
~~~

Read `e` as "the employee" and `m` as "the manager". The join condition says the employee's `manager_id` matches the manager's `id`. Getting this direction backwards, writing `e.id = m.manager_id`, swaps the roles and returns each employee paired with their direct reports instead.

## Including employees without a manager

The inner join above drops the CEO, whose `manager_id` is NULL. To list everyone:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, COALESCE(m.name, 'No manager') AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
~~~

## Employees who earn more than their manager

Once both copies are in one row, compare their columns:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
~~~

An inner join is right here: employees without managers can't earn more than a manager they don't have.

## Employees in a different department from their manager

The same shape answers other comparisons:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, m.name AS manager, m.dept_id AS manager_dept
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.dept_id <> m.dept_id;
~~~

## Counting direct reports

To find how many people report to each manager:

~~~sql
SELECT m.id, m.name, COUNT(e.id) AS direct_reports
FROM employees m
JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY direct_reports DESC;
~~~

Here `m` drives the query and `e` supplies the reports. To include employees with zero reports, use `LEFT JOIN` and keep `COUNT(e.id)`, which counts only matched rows. Grouping by the manager's `id`, not only their name, prevents two managers with the same name being merged.

Managers with at least five reports add a `HAVING` clause: `HAVING COUNT(e.id) >= 5`.

## Employees who manage nobody

Find employees whose ID never appears as anyone's `manager_id`:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = e.id);
~~~

Avoid `WHERE e.id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)`: the CEO's NULL `manager_id` is in that list, so `NOT IN` returns no rows at all. This exact trap is a favourite interview follow-up.

## Two levels up

Chaining another self-join reaches the manager's manager:

~~~sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager, gm.name AS grand_manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m  ON e.manager_id = m.id
LEFT JOIN employees gm ON m.manager_id = gm.id;
~~~

Each additional level needs one more join, which works for a known, small depth.

## The full chain with a recursive CTE

For arbitrary depth, such as everyone under a given VP, use a recursive CTE:

~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
    FROM employees WHERE id = 3            -- the VP
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT name, level FROM org ORDER BY level, name;
~~~

The anchor selects the starting person, and each iteration adds the next level of reports. Counting the size of each manager's whole organization, or finding the depth of the hierarchy, builds on this.

## Pairs of colleagues

Self-joins also pair employees sharing a manager:

~~~sql
SELECT a.name, b.name, a.manager_id
FROM employees a
JOIN employees b ON a.manager_id = b.manager_id AND a.id < b.id;
~~~

`a.id < b.id` prevents pairing someone with themselves and lists each pair once.

## Indexes and integrity

Index `manager_id`, since every self-join and recursive step joins on it. The foreign key prevents pointing to a nonexistent manager, but not cycles, such as A managing B while B manages A. A cycle makes recursive queries loop until a depth limit stops them, so applications should validate new manager assignments.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "list employees with their manager's name", "employees earning more than their manager", "managers with the most reports", "employees who aren't managers" and "all subordinates of a manager". Alias the two copies clearly, get the join direction right, use LEFT JOIN when everyone must appear, use NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN, and switch to a recursive CTE for unlimited depth.
