lessons.title: Tuple & Domain Relational Calculus
lessons.description: The declarative counterpart of relational algebra, safe expressions and relational completeness.

sections.title: Algebra vs Calculus
sections.content:
Relational algebra is procedural: you describe the steps (select, then project, then join).
Relational calculus is declarative: you describe what the answer must satisfy, and not how to compute it. SQL is mostly based on tuple relational calculus.

sections.title: TRC vs DRC
rows: { <r, n, b> | <r, n, b> ∈ STUDENT ∧ b = 'CSE' }

sections.title: Quantifiers
sections.content:
∃ (there exists) and ∀ (for all) appear inside the predicate.

Students enrolled in some course:
{ t | t ∈ STUDENT ∧ ∃e (e ∈ ENROLL ∧ e.roll_no = t.roll_no) }

∀ is the calculus version of division, and it maps to NOT EXISTS ... NOT EXISTS in SQL.

sections.title: Safe Expressions
sections.content:
{ t | ¬(t ∈ STUDENT) } means 'every tuple that is not a student'. That is an infinite set, so it cannot be computed. Such expressions are called unsafe.

A safe expression only produces values that appear in the database (its active domain). Safe TRC, safe DRC and relational algebra all have exactly the same expressive power. Any query language that can express all of them is called relationally complete. SQL is relationally complete, and with aggregation and recursion it can do even more.

sections.question: Which statement is true?
options: Relational algebra is more powerful than safe TRC
Safe TRC, safe DRC and relational algebra are equally expressive
DRC can express queries that algebra cannot
sections.explanation: Codd's theorem: relational algebra and safe relational calculus have the same expressive power.

items: Algebra = procedural (how); calculus = declarative (what).
TRC variables are tuples; DRC variables are attribute values.
Unsafe expressions describe infinite results; only safe ones are allowed.

content.theory:
Relational calculus describes a query by stating what the result must satisfy, without saying how to compute it. It comes in two forms, tuple relational calculus (TRC) and domain relational calculus (DRC), and it's the theoretical model behind declarative languages such as SQL. This lesson explains both, the quantifiers they use, and the idea of safe expressions.

## Procedural versus declarative

Relational algebra is procedural: an expression lists steps such as "select, then join, then project". Relational calculus is declarative: you describe the properties of the rows you want, and the system decides the steps.

SQL sits closer to calculus. When you write `WHERE cgpa > 8`, you describe the result, and the optimizer chooses whether to scan the table or use an index. That freedom is what lets the database pick an efficient plan.

## Tuple relational calculus

In TRC, a variable ranges over whole rows. A query has the form `{ t | P(t) }`, read as "the set of tuples t such that P(t) is true".

"All CSE students" becomes:

~~~text
{ t | t ∈ STUDENT ∧ t.branch = 'CSE' }
~~~

To return only some columns, you describe a result tuple built from other tuples. "Names of CSE students" is `{ t | ∃s (s ∈ STUDENT ∧ s.branch = 'CSE' ∧ t.name = s.name) }`.

## Domain relational calculus

In DRC, variables range over single attribute values instead of whole rows. A query lists the values it returns:

~~~text
{ <r, n> | ∃b ∃g (<r, n, b, g> ∈ STUDENT ∧ b = 'CSE') }
~~~

This returns roll number and name pairs of CSE students. DRC inspired Query By Example (QBE), where users fill in a grid that looks like the table. Microsoft Access's query designer works this way.

## Quantifiers

Calculus uses two quantifiers inside conditions:

- **There exists (∃)**: at least one value satisfies the condition. "Students enrolled in some course": `{ t | t ∈ STUDENT ∧ ∃e (e ∈ ENROLL ∧ e.roll_no = t.roll_no) }`
- **For all (∀)**: every value satisfies the condition. "Students enrolled in every core course" uses ∀ over CORE, which is the calculus form of division

In SQL, ∃ maps to `EXISTS`. SQL has no "for all", so you express ∀x P(x) as "there is no x for which P is false", which is the double `NOT EXISTS` pattern.

## Safe and unsafe expressions

Some calculus expressions describe infinite results. `{ t | ¬(t ∈ STUDENT) }` asks for every possible tuple that isn't a student: every combination of every string and number. No database can return that.

An expression is **safe** if its result contains only values that appear in the database or in the query itself (the active domain). Practical query languages accept only safe expressions. SQL guarantees safety by construction, because every value in a result comes from a table in the `FROM` clause or a literal in the query.

## Expressive power

E. F. Codd proved that relational algebra and safe relational calculus can express exactly the same set of queries. A language that can express all of them is called **relationally complete**. SQL is relationally complete, and with aggregation, grouping and recursive queries, it can express things pure algebra and calculus can't, such as counts and transitive closure.

## Why it matters today

You'll rarely write calculus directly. Its value is the way of thinking: describe the result precisely, including what "for all" and "there exists" mean, and let the system find the method. That habit makes tricky SQL, especially "for all" questions and correlated subqueries, far less error-prone.

## Comparison

| | Relational algebra | Tuple calculus | Domain calculus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Style | Procedural | Declarative | Declarative |
| Variables | None (operators on tables) | Whole tuples | Attribute values |
| Influenced | Query optimizers | SQL | QBE |
| Power | Same as safe calculus | Same | Same |

## How interviewers test this

GATE questions ask which statements about expressive power are true, or which calculus expression matches an English query. Remember three facts: algebra is procedural, calculus is declarative, and safe calculus equals algebra in power. Placement interviews rarely go deeper than that distinction.

modules.description: Anomalies, functional dependencies, closures and candidate keys, 1NF to BCNF, 4NF, lossless join and dependency preservation.

lessons.title: Why Normalize? Redundancy and Anomalies
lessons.description: Insertion, deletion and update anomalies shown on one badly designed table.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: Normalization is the process of splitting a table into smaller, well-structured tables so that each fact is stored exactly once. It removes redundancy and the anomalies that redundancy causes.

sections.title: The Three Anomalies
headers: What goes wrong in the table above
rows: Dr. Rao's phone changes. It must be updated in 3 rows; miss one and the data contradicts itself.
A new course CS303 has no students yet. It can't be added without inventing a fake student, because roll_no is part of the key.
Delete the only OS enrollment (Ravi, CS302) and you also lose the fact that Dr. Iyer teaches OS.

sections.title: The Fix
sections.content:
Split by 'what the data is about':
STUDENT(roll_no, name)
COURSE(course_id, course_name, instructor)
INSTRUCTOR(instructor, instructor_phone)
ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id)

Now each fact (a phone number, a course title) lives in one place. Joins bring the full picture back when you need it.

sections.question: Is normalization always good? When would you deliberately denormalize?
sections.answerReveal: For read-heavy workloads where joins are too expensive: analytics warehouses (star schemas), cached counters (likes_count), or precomputed reporting tables. You accept redundancy in exchange for speed, and keep it consistent with triggers, jobs or application logic.

sections.question: You cannot record a new department until at least one employee joins it. This is a(n):
sections.explanation: Being unable to store one fact without another unrelated fact is an insertion anomaly.

items: Redundancy causes update, insertion and deletion anomalies.
Normalization stores each fact once by decomposing tables.
Denormalization is a deliberate performance trade-off, not a design error.

content.theory:
Normalization is the process of organizing tables so each fact is stored exactly once. Its motivation is concrete: tables that repeat facts suffer from update, insertion and deletion anomalies, which silently corrupt data over time. This lesson shows each anomaly on one badly designed table, then shows how splitting the table removes them, and when deliberately keeping redundancy is the right call.

## One table that does too much

Imagine the exam cell keeps everything in a single table:

| roll_no | name | course_id | course_name | instructor | instructor_phone |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | Ravi | CS301 | DBMS | Dr. Rao | 98400 11111 |
| 101 | Ravi | CS302 | OS | Dr. Iyer | 98400 22222 |
| 102 | Meena | CS301 | DBMS | Dr. Rao | 98400 11111 |
| 103 | Arjun | CS301 | DBMS | Dr. Rao | 98400 11111 |

The table works for reading a transcript, and that's why designs like it are common. The trouble appears when the data changes.

## Update anomaly

Dr. Rao changes phone numbers. The number appears in three rows, so three rows must change. If a script updates only the rows for one section, the table now holds two different numbers for the same person. Nothing in the table says which is correct.

Every repeated fact is a chance for copies to disagree. The more rows repeat a fact, the more likely an update misses one.

## Insertion anomaly

A new course, CS303 Computer Networks, is announced, but no student has enrolled yet. The table's key is `(roll_no, course_id)`, and `roll_no` can't be NULL, so the course can't be recorded until someone enrolls. The design forces you to know one fact (an enrollment) before you can store an unrelated fact (a course exists).

## Deletion anomaly

Ravi drops OS, so his CS302 row is deleted. That was the only row mentioning OS, so the database also forgets that Dr. Iyer teaches OS and what his phone number is. Deleting one fact destroyed others that happened to share its row.

## The cause: mixing subjects in one table

All three anomalies share a cause. The table describes several different things (students, courses, instructors and enrollments) in one place, so facts about one subject are tied to rows about another. The fix is to give each subject its own table:

- `STUDENT(roll_no, name)`
- `INSTRUCTOR(instructor, instructor_phone)`
- `COURSE(course_id, course_name, instructor)`
- `ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id)`

Now Dr. Rao's phone number lives in one row, a course exists independently of enrollments, and dropping a course removes only the enrollment. You recover the original wide view with joins whenever you need it.

## Functional dependencies make this precise

"Each subject in its own table" is a guideline; normal forms make it a rule. They're defined using functional dependencies such as `course_id → course_name` (a course ID determines the course name) and `instructor → instructor_phone`. The next lessons show how to find these dependencies and use them to decide exactly how to split a table.

## Redundancy you should keep

Normalization isn't always the goal. Denormalization means keeping redundant data on purpose to make reads faster:

- **Counters**: a `comments_count` column on a post, so a feed doesn't count comments for every post on every page load
- **Analytics**: data warehouses use wide, denormalized star schemas because analysts run large aggregations, and joins at that scale are expensive
- **Historical facts**: an order stores the price paid, even though the product table has a current price, because the invoice must not change when prices do

The difference between denormalization and a bad design is intent and maintenance. Deliberate redundancy has a documented reason and something that keeps the copies consistent: a trigger, a background job, or an update inside the same transaction.

## Costs of over-normalizing

Splitting tables has a cost too. Every split adds a join to queries that need the combined data, and a schema split into dozens of narrow tables can make one screen need five or six joins. Most transactional systems normalize to third normal form or BCNF, and stop there.

## How interviewers test this

The most common question is "What is normalization and why is it needed?" Answer with the three anomalies, each with a one-line example, then say that normalization removes redundancy by splitting tables according to functional dependencies. Mentioning when you'd denormalize shows you understand the trade-off rather than a rule.

lessons.title: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Finding Candidate Keys
lessons.description: Armstrong's axioms, attribute closure, and the step-by-step method for finding all candidate keys.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content:
A functional dependency (FD) X → Y means: whenever two rows agree on X, they must also agree on Y. 'X determines Y.'

Examples: roll_no → name (one roll number has one name). course_id → instructor.
Not an FD: name → roll_no (two students can share a name).

Trivial FD: Y ⊆ X, for example {roll_no, name} → name. It always holds.
Non-trivial FD: Y is not a subset of X.

sections.title: Armstrong's Axioms (and derived rules)
rows: If Y ⊆ X then X → Y
If X → Y then XZ → YZ
If X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z
If X → Y and X → Z then X → YZ
If X → YZ then X → Y and X → Z
If X → Y and WY → Z then WX → Z

sections.title: Attribute Closure X+
sections.content:
X+ is the set of all attributes that X determines. Algorithm:
1. Start with result = X.
2. For each FD A → B, if A ⊆ result, add B to result.
3. Repeat until nothing changes.

If X+ contains every attribute of R, X is a super key. If, in addition, no proper subset of X is a super key, X is a candidate key.

sections.title: Worked Example: R(A, B, C, D, E), F = { A → B, B → C, CD → E }

iterations.description: Attributes that never appear on the right side of an FD can't be derived, so they must be in every candidate key. Start with {A, D}.
Compute (AD)+. Start with AD.
A → B applies (A is in result).
B → C applies.
CD → E applies. Every attribute is reached.
AD is a super key, and every key must contain both A and D, so AD is the one and only candidate key.

sections.title: Shortcut for Finding Candidate Keys
items: Attributes **only on the left side** (or in no FD at all) must be in every key.
Attributes **only on the right side** are never in any key.
Attributes on **both sides** may or may not be in a key: try adding them one at a time to the 'must' set and compute closures.
If the 'must' set's closure already covers R, it is the only candidate key.

sections.question: R(A, B, C) with F = { A → B, B → C, C → A }. Find all candidate keys.
sections.answerReveal: Every attribute appears on both sides, so test each one: A+ = {A, B, C}, B+ = {B, C, A}, C+ = {C, A, B}. All three are candidate keys: {A}, {B} and {C}.

sections.title: Minimal Cover (Canonical Cover)
sections.content:
A minimal cover is the smallest equivalent set of FDs. Steps:
1. Split right sides so each FD has a single attribute on the right.
2. Remove extraneous left-side attributes (in AB → C, drop A if B+ already contains C).
3. Remove redundant FDs (drop A → C if it can be derived from the others).
Minimal covers are used when building 3NF decompositions.

sections.question: R(P, Q, R, S) with F = { P → Q, Q → R }. Which is the candidate key?
sections.explanation: P and S never appear on a right side, so both are required. (PS)+ = {P, S, Q, R} = all attributes, so PS is the only candidate key.

items: X → Y: equal X values force equal Y values.
Use attribute closure to test super keys; minimality makes a super key a candidate key.
Attributes never on a right side are in every candidate key.

content.theory:
A functional dependency (FD) is a rule of the form "if you know X, you know Y". FDs are the mathematical tool behind normalization: they tell you which attributes belong together, what the candidate keys are, and whether a table is in a given normal form. This lesson explains FDs, Armstrong's axioms, attribute closure and the method for finding every candidate key, which is the most tested skill in DBMS exams.

## What an FD says

X → Y means: any two rows that agree on X must also agree on Y. In a student table, `roll_no → name` holds, because one roll number always belongs to one name. `name → roll_no` doesn't hold, because two students can share a name.

An FD is a rule about all valid data, not an observation about today's rows. If today's table happens to have unique names, that doesn't make `name → roll_no` an FD. FDs come from the meaning of the data, which you learn from the organization's rules.

## Trivial and non-trivial FDs

An FD X → Y is **trivial** if Y is a subset of X, such as `{roll_no, name} → name`. Trivial FDs always hold and tell you nothing. Normal forms only care about non-trivial FDs.

## Armstrong's axioms

Three rules let you derive every FD implied by a given set:

- **Reflexivity**: if Y ⊆ X, then X → Y
- **Augmentation**: if X → Y, then XZ → YZ for any Z
- **Transitivity**: if X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z

These axioms are sound (they never derive a false FD) and complete (they derive every true one). Three useful rules follow from them: **union** (X → Y and X → Z give X → YZ), **decomposition** (X → YZ gives X → Y and X → Z), and **pseudo-transitivity** (X → Y and WY → Z give WX → Z).

## Attribute closure

Applying axioms by hand is slow. The practical tool is the **closure** of a set of attributes X, written X+: every attribute that X determines. The algorithm is:

1. Start with result = X
2. For each FD A → B, if every attribute of A is in result, add B to result
3. Repeat step 2 until nothing new is added

If X+ contains every attribute of the relation, X is a super key. If additionally no proper subset of X is a super key, X is a candidate key.

## A worked closure

Take R(A, B, C, D, E) with FDs A → B, B → C and CD → E. Compute (AD)+: start with {A, D}. A → B adds B, giving {A, B, D}. B → C adds C. Now C and D are both present, so CD → E adds E. The result is all five attributes, so AD is a super key.

## Finding all candidate keys

Classify each attribute by where it appears in the FDs:

- **Only on left sides, or in no FD**: must be in every candidate key, because nothing derives it
- **Only on right sides**: never in any candidate key, because something else always derives it
- **On both sides**: may or may not be in a key

Then test: compute the closure of the "must" set. If it covers the relation, it's the only candidate key. Otherwise, add "both sides" attributes one at a time, compute closures, and keep the minimal sets that cover everything.

In the example, A and D appear only on left sides, so every key contains both. (AD)+ is everything, so AD is the only candidate key. If the FDs were A → B, B → C and C → A instead, every attribute appears on both sides, and testing each one shows that {A}, {B} and {C} are all candidate keys.

## Minimal cover

A **minimal (canonical) cover** is the smallest set of FDs equivalent to the original. You compute it in three steps:

1. Split right sides so every FD has one attribute on the right
2. Remove extraneous left-side attributes: in AB → C, drop A if B+ already contains C
3. Remove redundant FDs: drop an FD if the remaining ones still imply it

The minimal cover is the input to the 3NF synthesis algorithm, which builds one table per FD.

## How interviewers test this

GATE and placement tests give a relation and FD set and ask for candidate keys, the closure of a set, or the number of super keys. Classify attributes first, then compute closures. Write each closure step out, since one skipped FD is the usual cause of a wrong answer.

lessons.title: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with Worked Examples
lessons.description: Atomic values, partial dependencies and transitive dependencies, explained and removed step by step.

sections.title: Two Terms You Need First
sections.content:
Prime attribute: an attribute that is part of some candidate key.
Non-prime attribute: an attribute that is not part of any candidate key.

The normal forms are about which attributes are allowed to determine non-prime attributes.

sections.title: The Normal Forms at a Glance
rows: Every column holds atomic (single) values; no repeating groups
Multi-valued cells, lists in one column
1NF + no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a candidate key
2NF + no non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute
For every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a super key

sections.title: 1NF: Atomic Values
sections.content:
Violation: STUDENT(roll_no, name, phones) with the row (101, 'Ravi', '98400..., 97100...').
Fix: move phones to STUDENT_PHONE(roll_no, phone), with one row per phone number.

sections.title: 2NF: Remove Partial Dependencies
sections.content:
Only matters when a candidate key is composite.

ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id, student_name, course_name, grade)
Key: {roll_no, course_id}
FDs: roll_no → student_name, course_id → course_name, {roll_no, course_id} → grade

student_name depends on only part of the key (roll_no). That is a partial dependency, so the table is not in 2NF.

Decompose:
STUDENT(roll_no, student_name)
COURSE(course_id, course_name)
ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id, grade)

sections.title: 3NF: Remove Transitive Dependencies
sections.content:
EMPLOYEE(emp_id, name, dept_id, dept_name)
FDs: emp_id → dept_id, dept_id → dept_name

dept_name depends on emp_id only through dept_id (emp_id → dept_id → dept_name). dept_id is non-prime, so this is a transitive dependency and the table is not in 3NF.

Decompose:
EMPLOYEE(emp_id, name, dept_id)
DEPARTMENT(dept_id, dept_name)

Formal 3NF test: for every non-trivial FD X → A, either X is a super key, or A is a prime attribute.

sections.title: Identify the Highest Normal Form: R(A, B, C, D), F = { AB → C, C → D }

iterations.description: (AB)+ = {A, B, C, D}. A and B never appear on a right side, so AB is the only key.
No FD has only A or only B on the left. So R is in 2NF.

variables.C → D: C is not a super key, D is non-prime

iterations.description: Transitive dependency AB → C → D. R is NOT in 3NF.
Decompose on C → D. Both resulting tables are in BCNF.

traps.question: Explain 2NF with an example.
traps.trap: Defining 2NF as 'no partial dependency' without saying what it is partial to, or giving an example whose key is a single column.
traps.solution: A partial dependency is a non-prime attribute that depends on only part of a composite candidate key. Use ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id, student_name): student_name depends on roll_no alone. Note that a table whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF.

traps.question: Is a two-attribute relation always in BCNF?
traps.trap: Saying 'it depends'.
traps.solution: Yes. Any relation with exactly two attributes is in BCNF: every possible non-trivial FD (A → B or B → A) has a single attribute on the left, and that attribute is then a key.

sections.question: R(A, B, C) with key A and FDs A → B, B → C. R is in:
sections.explanation: The key is a single attribute, so there are no partial dependencies (2NF). B → C is transitive (B is not a key, C is non-prime), so R is not in 3NF.

items: 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependency on a composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependency.
3NF test: for each X → A, X is a super key OR A is prime.
Always find the candidate keys first; every normal-form question depends on them.

content.theory:
The normal forms are a ladder of increasingly strict rules about which attributes may determine which. Each step removes a specific kind of redundancy: 1NF removes multi-valued cells, 2NF removes partial dependencies, and 3NF removes transitive dependencies. This lesson defines each one, shows a table that fails it, and shows the split that fixes it.

## Two terms first

Every normal form question depends on these definitions:

- **Prime attribute**: an attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key
- **Non-prime attribute**: an attribute that belongs to no candidate key

Normal forms restrict how non-prime attributes depend on keys. So the first step of any normal form question is always the same: find all candidate keys.

## First normal form (1NF)

A table is in 1NF if every cell holds a single atomic value and there are no repeating groups. `STUDENT(roll_no, name, phones)` with a cell containing "98400 11111, 97100 22222" violates 1NF.

The fix moves the repeating values into their own table, `STUDENT_PHONE(roll_no, phone)`, with one row per number. Searching by phone number becomes an indexed equality lookup instead of string matching.

## Second normal form (2NF)

A table is in 2NF if it's in 1NF and no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a candidate key. That kind of dependency is called a **partial dependency**, and it can only exist when a candidate key has two or more attributes.

Consider `ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id, student_name, course_name, grade)`, with key `(roll_no, course_id)`. Here `student_name` depends on `roll_no` alone, and `course_name` on `course_id` alone. Both are partial dependencies, so the student's name repeats in every course they take.

The fix moves each partially dependent attribute out, alongside the part of the key it depends on:

- `STUDENT(roll_no, student_name)`
- `COURSE(course_id, course_name)`
- `ENROLLMENT(roll_no, course_id, grade)`

A useful shortcut: if every candidate key has a single attribute, the table is automatically in 2NF.

## Third normal form (3NF)

A table is in 3NF if it's in 2NF and no non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute. That chain is called a **transitive dependency**: the key determines X, and X determines Y.

Consider `PROFESSOR(prof_id, name, dept_id, dept_name)`. Here `prof_id → dept_id` and `dept_id → dept_name`, so the department's name depends on the professor only through the department. Every professor in Computer Science repeats "Computer Science", and renaming the department means updating every professor row.

The fix gives the department its own table: `PROFESSOR(prof_id, name, dept_id)` and `DEPARTMENT(dept_id, dept_name)`.

## The formal 3NF test

The ladder definition helps you remember the idea, while the formal test is what you apply to a relation. For every non-trivial FD X → A, at least one of these must hold:

1. X is a super key, or
2. A is a prime attribute

If some FD fails both conditions, the table isn't in 3NF. This test checks 2NF and 3NF at once, because a partial dependency also fails it.

## A full worked example

R(A, B, C, D) with FDs AB → C and C → D. First, find the keys: A and B never appear on a right side, and (AB)+ = {A, B, C, D}, so AB is the only candidate key. A and B are prime; C and D aren't.

Check 2NF: no FD has only A or only B on the left, so there are no partial dependencies, and R is in 2NF. Check 3NF: in C → D, C isn't a super key and D isn't prime, so R fails 3NF. The highest normal form is 2NF. Splitting on the violating FD gives R1(A, B, C) and R2(C, D), and both are in BCNF.

## A practical habit

When you design tables, you rarely run the formal algorithm. Instead, ask of each column: "What does this fact describe?" If the answer is "the department" while the table is about professors, the column belongs in a department table. That question catches most 2NF and 3NF problems before they exist.

## How interviewers test this

The classic question is "Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with examples". Use one example per form, and define partial and transitive dependencies explicitly. GATE asks for the highest normal form of a relation: find the keys, then apply the formal test FD by FD.

lessons.title: BCNF, 4NF, Lossless Join and Dependency Preservation
lessons.description: The stricter normal forms and the two properties every good decomposition must be checked for.

sections.title: BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)
sections.content:
Rule: for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X must be a super key. Unlike 3NF, there is no 'unless Y is prime' exception.

Classic example where 3NF holds but BCNF fails:
TEACHES(student, subject, teacher)
FDs: {student, subject} → teacher, teacher → subject (each teacher teaches one subject)
Candidate keys: {student, subject} and {student, teacher}

teacher → subject: teacher is not a super key. But subject is prime, so 3NF is satisfied. BCNF is violated.

BCNF decomposition: R1(teacher, subject), R2(student, teacher). The anomaly is gone, but the FD {student, subject} → teacher can no longer be checked inside a single table.

sections.title: Lossless-Join Decomposition
sections.content:
Splitting R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining them back gives exactly R, with no extra (spurious) rows.

Test for a two-way split: the decomposition is lossless if the common attributes form a super key of at least one side:
(R1 ∩ R2) → R1   or   (R1 ∩ R2) → R2

Lossless join is mandatory. A lossy decomposition silently produces wrong data.

sections.title: Lossless Test: R(A, B, C), F = { A → B }

iterations.description: A → B means A is a key of R1. Lossless.
B determines nothing, so it isn't a key of either side. Lossy: joining on B can create spurious rows.

sections.title: Dependency Preservation
sections.content:
A decomposition preserves dependencies if every original FD can be checked using the FDs inside the individual tables, without joining them. Formally: (F1 ∪ F2 ∪ ...)+ = F+.

This is desirable but not mandatory. Without it, enforcing a lost FD needs a join or a trigger on every insert.

sections.title: 3NF vs BCNF Trade-off
rows: Used when no FD would be lost

sections.title: Beyond BCNF: 4NF and 5NF
sections.content:
4NF deals with multivalued dependencies (MVDs). X →→ Y means that for one X there is a set of Y values independent of the other attributes.
Example: EMP(emp, skill, language). Skills and languages are independent, so every skill must be paired with every language, which explodes the number of rows. Fix: EMP_SKILL(emp, skill) and EMP_LANG(emp, language).

5NF (project-join normal form) handles join dependencies that can't be expressed as MVDs. It is rarely asked beyond its definition.

traps.question: Every BCNF relation is in 3NF. Is every 3NF relation in BCNF?
traps.trap: Saying yes.
traps.solution: No. 3NF allows X → A when A is prime even if X is not a super key. BCNF does not. The TEACHES(student, subject, teacher) example is in 3NF but not BCNF.

traps.question: Which property of a decomposition can never be sacrificed?
traps.trap: Saying dependency preservation.
traps.solution: Lossless join. Without it, joining the tables back produces wrong data. Dependency preservation can be traded away for BCNF.

sections.question: R(A, B, C, D) is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(C, D). With FD set { A → B, C → D }, the decomposition is:
sections.explanation: R1 ∩ R2 is empty, so the tables can't be joined back (the join is a Cartesian product): lossy. Each FD lives entirely inside one table, so dependencies are preserved.

items: BCNF: every determinant is a super key. Stricter than 3NF.
Lossless test: the common attributes are a key of at least one side.
3NF can always be lossless + dependency preserving; BCNF can't always preserve dependencies.
4NF removes multivalued dependencies (independent multi-valued facts).

content.theory:
Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is a stricter version of 3NF that removes every redundancy caused by functional dependencies. Reaching it sometimes costs something, so this lesson also covers the two properties every decomposition must be checked for: lossless join, which you can never give up, and dependency preservation, which you sometimes must. It ends with 4NF, which handles a kind of redundancy FDs can't describe.

## The BCNF rule

A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a super key. Compared with the 3NF test, BCNF drops the escape clause "or Y is prime". Every determinant must identify the whole row.

## A table in 3NF but not BCNF

Suppose each teacher teaches exactly one subject, and each student has one teacher per subject. Consider `TEACHES(student, subject, teacher)` with these FDs:

- `{student, subject} → teacher`
- `teacher → subject`

The candidate keys are `{student, subject}` and `{student, teacher}`. In `teacher → subject`, `teacher` isn't a super key, but `subject` is prime, so the table passes 3NF. It fails BCNF.

The redundancy is real: every student taught by Dr. Rao repeats the fact that Dr. Rao teaches DBMS. If Dr. Rao switches subjects, every one of those rows must change.

## Decomposing to BCNF

The BCNF algorithm repeatedly splits on a violating FD X → Y into R1 = X ∪ Y and R2 = R − Y. For TEACHES, splitting on `teacher → subject` gives `TEACHER_SUBJECT(teacher, subject)` and `STUDENT_TEACHER(student, teacher)`. Both are in BCNF, and the repeated fact now lives in one row.

The cost appears immediately. The original rule `{student, subject} → teacher` (a student has one teacher per subject) involves attributes now spread across two tables, so neither table can enforce it alone. That's a loss of dependency preservation.

## Lossless join: the property you can't skip

A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is **lossless** if joining R1 and R2 gives back exactly R, with no extra rows. A lossy decomposition produces spurious rows: combinations that never existed in the original data. That's wrong data, so a lossy decomposition is never acceptable.

For a split into two tables, the test is short. The decomposition is lossless if the common attributes form a super key of at least one side:

- (R1 ∩ R2) → R1, or
- (R1 ∩ R2) → R2

With R(A, B, C) and A → B, splitting into (A, B) and (A, C) is lossless, because A is the key of (A, B). Splitting into (A, B) and (B, C) is lossy: B determines nothing, so joining on B pairs unrelated rows.

## Dependency preservation: the property you can trade

A decomposition **preserves dependencies** if every original FD can be checked inside a single table, without joining. Formally, the union of the FDs that hold within each table implies all the original FDs.

Without preservation, enforcing a lost FD means joining tables or writing a trigger on every insert. That's extra work and a chance for bugs, but the data itself stays correct, which is why this property is the one you can trade away.

## The 3NF versus BCNF trade-off

| Property | 3NF synthesis | BCNF decomposition |
|---|---|---|
| Lossless join | Always achievable | Always achievable |
| Dependency preserving | Always achievable | Not always possible |
| Redundancy from FDs | A little may remain | None |

The practical rule: aim for BCNF. If reaching it would lose an important FD, settle for 3NF and accept a little redundancy, or keep BCNF and enforce the lost rule another way.

## Multivalued dependencies and 4NF

Some redundancy has nothing to do with FDs. Suppose a professor has a set of skills and, independently, a set of languages: `PROF(prof, skill, language)`. To record that the skills and languages are independent, every skill must be paired with every language. Two skills and three languages mean six rows.

This is a **multivalued dependency** (MVD), written `prof ↠ skill`: for one professor there's a set of skills, independent of the other attributes. 4NF requires every non-trivial MVD to have a super key on the left. The fix splits the independent facts: `PROF_SKILL(prof, skill)` and `PROF_LANGUAGE(prof, language)`, giving five rows instead of six, and the savings grow quickly with larger sets.

5NF (project-join normal form) handles join dependencies that MVDs can't express. It rarely appears in practice or in exams beyond its definition.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Difference between 3NF and BCNF" (BCNF removes the "or Y is prime" exception; give the TEACHES example) and "Which decomposition property can't be sacrificed?" (lossless join, because a lossy split produces wrong data). GATE also tests the lossless-join check on two-way splits.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content:
A transaction is a group of database operations that must succeed or fail together, as one logical unit of work.

Transferring Rs. 500 from account A to account B is two writes: debit A, credit B. If the system crashes after the debit but before the credit, Rs. 500 disappears. Wrapping both writes in a transaction guarantees that either both happen or neither does.

sections.title: A Transaction in SQL
sections.explanation: Many clients run in autocommit mode, where every single statement is its own transaction. Use an explicit transaction whenever several statements must succeed together.

Changes are permanently recorded (the commit log record has reached disk)
An error or crash means it can't continue normally
Rolled back; the database is restored to its state before the transaction. It may then be restarted or killed

sections.explanation: After the final statement but before commit is complete, it's partially committed. Recovery will roll it back, so it ends up aborted.

items: A transaction is all-or-nothing: COMMIT makes it permanent, ROLLBACK undoes it.
Five states: active, partially committed, committed, failed, aborted.
SAVEPOINT allows a partial rollback inside a transaction.

content.theory:
A transaction is a group of database operations that the DBMS treats as one indivisible unit: either all of them take effect, or none do. Transactions are how a database stays correct when programs crash, servers lose power, or many users work at once. This lesson explains what a transaction is, how you control one in SQL, and the states a transaction passes through.

## Why one statement isn't enough

Many real actions need several writes. Paying a hostel fee from a student wallet means subtracting from the wallet, inserting a payment record and marking the fee as paid. If the server crashes after the first write, the student has lost money and the college has no record of it.

A transaction wraps all three writes so the database can promise one of two outcomes: everything happened, or nothing did. There's no in-between state for anyone to see or for a crash to leave behind.

## Controlling transactions in SQL

You start a transaction, run your statements, then either commit or roll back:

~~~sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - 4500 WHERE roll_no = 101;
INSERT INTO payment (roll_no, amount) VALUES (101, 4500);
UPDATE fee SET paid = TRUE WHERE roll_no = 101 AND term = '2026-S1';
COMMIT;
~~~

`COMMIT` makes every change permanent and visible to others. `ROLLBACK` discards every change since the transaction began. PostgreSQL writes `BEGIN` instead of `START TRANSACTION`; both mean the same thing.

## Autocommit

Most database clients run in autocommit mode by default: every statement is its own transaction and commits as soon as it finishes. That's convenient for one-off queries and dangerous for multi-step actions, because a failure after the first statement leaves the first change committed. Whenever several statements must succeed together, start an explicit transaction.

## Savepoints

A savepoint marks a point inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning everything:

~~~sql
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO admission (roll_no, course) VALUES (205, 'CSE');
SAVEPOINT after_admission;
INSERT INTO hostel_allotment (roll_no, room) VALUES (205, 'B-112');
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_admission;  -- no room free, keep admission
COMMIT;
~~~

The admission survives while the failed hostel allotment is undone. Savepoints suit long workflows where one optional step may fail.

## The five transaction states

Every transaction moves through these states:

- **Active**: running its reads and writes
- **Partially committed**: the last statement has run, but the changes may still exist only in memory
- **Committed**: the commit record is safely on disk, so the changes will survive any crash
- **Failed**: an error, constraint violation or crash means it can't continue normally
- **Aborted**: the DBMS has rolled back every change, restoring the database to its state before the transaction began

Committed and aborted are the two final states. After an abort, the application can retry the whole transaction (useful after a deadlock) or give up (useful after a constraint violation such as a duplicate roll number).

## Where "committed" happens

The moment of commit is precise: a transaction is committed when its commit record reaches durable storage, not when the `COMMIT` statement is typed and not when the data pages are written. A crash one microsecond after that record is written still preserves the transaction, while a crash one microsecond before rolls it back. The recovery lessons explain how the log makes this possible.

## Keep transactions short

A transaction holds locks or old row versions until it ends. A transaction left open while a user stares at a form blocks other users and prevents cleanup. Do the slow work (user input, network calls) before you start the transaction, then run the database writes quickly and commit.

## Transactions in application code

Applications wrap the statements in a try block, commit on success, and roll back on any error. In Python with a database driver, the pattern looks like this:

~~~python
try:
    cur.execute("UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - %s "
                "WHERE roll_no = %s", (4500, 101))
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO payment (roll_no, amount) "
                "VALUES (%s, %s)", (101, 4500))
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise
~~~

The rollback in the error path is what keeps a failed payment from leaving the wallet debited. Frameworks such as Django and Spring wrap this pattern in a decorator or annotation so you don't repeat it.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a transaction?" with an example, and "What are the states of a transaction?" Use a multi-step example such as a fee payment, explain why the steps must succeed together, and draw the five states with the transitions between them.

sections.title: Scenario
sections.content:

T: read(A); A = A − 500; write(A); read(B); B = B + 500; write(B)

sections.title: ACID Explained
rows: All operations happen, or none do
Crash after write(A): A = 1500, B = 1000, and Rs. 500 vanishes
A transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another
A bug credits B with 5000; the total no longer equals 3000
Concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work
Another transaction reads A = 1500 and B = 1000 mid-transfer and reports a total of 2500

sections.title: The Consistency Nuance
sections.content: Atomicity, isolation and durability are guaranteed by the DBMS. Consistency is shared: the DBMS enforces declared constraints (keys, CHECK, foreign keys), but business rules like 'the total money stays constant' depend on the transaction being written correctly. The C in ACID is partly the programmer's job.

traps.question: Explain ACID with an example.
traps.trap: Reciting the four words without saying what fails when each is missing.
traps.solution: Use the bank transfer. For each property, describe the failure it prevents (lost money on a crash, an inconsistent total, a mid-transfer read, a lost commit) and name the mechanism (undo log, constraints, locking/MVCC, redo log/WAL).

traps.question: Do NoSQL databases support ACID?
traps.trap: Saying 'No, NoSQL is BASE'.
traps.solution: It depends. Many offer single-document or single-key atomicity, and several (MongoDB 4.0+, DynamoDB transactions, FoundationDB) support multi-document ACID transactions. BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) describes the trade-off chosen by many distributed stores.

sections.question: A committed order disappears after a server crash. Which property was violated?
sections.explanation: Durability guarantees that committed data survives failures.

items: Atomicity: all or nothing (undo). Durability: committed means permanent (redo/WAL).
Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after another (locking/MVCC).
Consistency: valid state to valid state, enforced by constraints plus correct transaction logic.

content.theory:
ACID names the four guarantees a transaction gives you: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability. Each one prevents a specific failure, and each is implemented by a specific part of the DBMS. This lesson explains all four with one example, a wallet-to-wallet transfer between two students, because naming the failure each property prevents is what separates a strong interview answer from a recited one.

## The running example

Ravi sends 500 rupees from his campus wallet to Meena's. Ravi has 2000 and Meena has 1000, so the total is 3000 before and must be 3000 after. The transaction reads Ravi's balance, writes 1500, reads Meena's balance, and writes 1500.

## Atomicity: all or nothing

Atomicity means the transaction's writes happen completely or not at all. Suppose the server crashes after writing Ravi's new balance but before writing Meena's. Without atomicity, 500 rupees vanish: Ravi has 1500, Meena still has 1000.

The DBMS prevents this with an undo log. Before changing a value, it records the old value. If the transaction doesn't commit, recovery uses those records to restore every old value, so the crash leaves no trace.

## Consistency: valid state to valid state

Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state. "Valid" combines two kinds of rules:

- **Declared constraints** the DBMS enforces: primary keys, foreign keys, `CHECK (balance >= 0)`
- **Business rules** the transaction must respect: the total money in the system stays the same during a transfer

The DBMS rejects any transaction that violates a declared constraint. It can't know your business rules, so a buggy transfer that adds 600 to Meena while subtracting 500 from Ravi would commit happily. Consistency is therefore a shared responsibility: the DBMS enforces constraints, and the programmer writes correct transactions.

## Isolation: no half-finished views

Isolation means concurrent transactions don't see each other's incomplete work. While the transfer runs, an audit query sums all balances. Without isolation it might read Ravi's new balance (1500) and Meena's old balance (1000) and report 2500, a total that never existed.

The concurrency control system provides isolation, using locks or multiversion concurrency control (MVCC). The ideal is that concurrent transactions produce the same result as running them one after another in some order. The isolation-levels lesson explains how databases let you trade some of that guarantee for speed.

## Durability: committed means permanent

Durability means that once the database reports "committed", the change survives any later crash. If the app shows "Transfer successful" and the server loses power a second later, the transfer must still be there after restart.

The DBMS provides durability with a write-ahead log (WAL): before reporting a commit, it forces the transaction's log records to disk. Data pages can be written later, because recovery can redo any committed change from the log.

## Who enforces what

| Property | Failure it prevents | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Atomicity | Half-finished transfer after a crash | Undo log, rollback |
| Consistency | Rule-breaking data | Constraints plus correct transaction code |
| Isolation | Reading another transaction's half-done work | Locks or MVCC |
| Durability | Losing a committed change after a crash | Write-ahead log, flushed at commit |

## ACID in non-relational databases

"NoSQL means no transactions" is out of date. Many NoSQL systems guarantee atomic operations on a single document or key, and several support multi-document ACID transactions, including MongoDB since version 4.0. Many distributed stores choose BASE instead (basically available, soft state, eventually consistent), trading immediate consistency for availability across data centers. The NoSQL lesson covers that trade-off.

## A crash timeline

Walk through the transfer with a crash at different moments. A crash before the first write leaves both balances untouched. A crash after Ravi's write but before commit is undone by recovery, so both balances return to 2000 and 1000. A crash after the commit record reaches the log is redone by recovery if the data pages were never written, so both balances end at 1500. In no case does anyone observe 500 rupees missing, which is atomicity and durability working together.

## How interviewers test this

The question is almost always "Explain ACID with an example." Use the transfer, and for each letter state the failure it prevents and the mechanism that enforces it. Mentioning that consistency depends partly on the application shows you understand the property rather than the acronym.

T1 sets balance = 0, T2 reads 0, then T1 rolls back. T2 acted on a value that never existed.
T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values, because T2 updated and committed it in between

sections.title: Real-World Defaults
items: **PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server**: READ COMMITTED by default.
**MySQL InnoDB**: REPEATABLE READ by default. Its consistent snapshots plus next-key (gap) locks also block most phantoms.
Higher isolation means fewer anomalies, but more blocking, more aborted transactions to retry, and lower throughput.

sections.title: Setting the Level and Avoiding Lost Updates
sections.explanation: Reading a value into the app, changing it there and writing it back without a lock is the classic lost-update bug.

sections.question: An online ticket system shows 1 seat left, and two users click 'Book' at the same moment. Both see 'confirmed'. Which problem is this, and how would you fix it?
sections.answerReveal: A lost update (or write skew): both read seats = 1 and both wrote seats = 0. Fix it with a conditional atomic update (UPDATE seats SET left = left - 1 WHERE id = ? AND left > 0, then check the affected row count), with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or with SERIALIZABLE isolation plus retrying the transaction that fails.

sections.question: Which is the lowest isolation level that prevents non-repeatable reads?
sections.explanation: REPEATABLE READ guarantees that a row read twice in the same transaction returns the same value.

items: Know the four phenomena: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update.
Each level up the table removes one more phenomenon; SERIALIZABLE removes them all.
Prevent lost updates with atomic UPDATEs or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

content.theory:
Perfect isolation is expensive, so databases let you choose how much of it you need. The SQL standard defines four isolation levels, each allowing fewer anomalies than the one before. This lesson explains the four anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms and lost updates), which level prevents which, and how to prevent the lost update that the standard levels miss by default.

## Why databases offer a choice

Stronger isolation means more waiting and more transactions aborted and retried. A dashboard showing approximate counts doesn't need the guarantees a ticket-booking system needs. Isolation levels let each transaction pick its own trade-off between correctness and throughput.

## Dirty read

A dirty read happens when one transaction reads data another transaction has written but not yet committed. Transaction A sets a student's fee status to paid. Transaction B reads "paid" and issues a hall ticket. Then A rolls back because the payment gateway declined. B acted on a value that never officially existed.

## Non-repeatable read

A non-repeatable read happens when a transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values, because another transaction updated and committed it in between. A report reads a course fee as 50,000 at the start and 55,000 at the end, so its totals don't add up.

## Phantom read

A phantom read happens when a transaction re-runs a query over a range and sees rows appear or disappear, because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching the condition. A count of CSE students returns 120, then 121 a moment later within the same transaction.

The difference from a non-repeatable read: phantoms involve new or removed rows, while non-repeatable reads involve changed values in existing rows.

## Lost update

A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, both compute a new value from it, and the second write overwrites the first. Two clerks each see 10 seats left in an elective, each enrolls one student and writes 9. The correct answer is 8.

## The four standard levels

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom |
|---|---|---|---|
| `READ UNCOMMITTED` | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| `READ COMMITTED` | Prevented | Possible | Possible |
| `REPEATABLE READ` | Prevented | Prevented | Possible |
| `SERIALIZABLE` | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

Each level removes one more anomaly. `SERIALIZABLE` guarantees the result equals some one-at-a-time ordering of the transactions.

## What real databases do

Defaults differ, and so do implementations:

- **PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server** default to `READ COMMITTED`
- **MySQL InnoDB** defaults to `REPEATABLE READ`, and its snapshots plus gap locks also prevent most phantoms
- **PostgreSQL** treats `READ UNCOMMITTED` as `READ COMMITTED`, so dirty reads never happen there
- **PostgreSQL's** `SERIALIZABLE` uses serializable snapshot isolation: it lets transactions run in parallel and aborts one if their combination couldn't happen serially, so your code must retry

## Preventing lost updates

The lost update isn't listed in the standard table, and `READ COMMITTED` allows it. You prevent it in one of three ways:

- **Atomic update**: do the arithmetic in the database, `UPDATE elective SET seats = seats - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND seats > 0`, then check that one row changed
- **Row lock**: read with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, which locks the row until commit, so the second clerk waits for the first
- **Optimistic check**: store a version number, and update with `WHERE version = 5`; if no row changes, someone else got there first, so reload and retry

The atomic update is usually the best choice, because it needs no extra round trip and holds the lock for the shortest time.

## Choosing a level

Most applications run at `READ COMMITTED` and protect their few critical read-modify-write paths with atomic updates or `FOR UPDATE`. Reach for `SERIALIZABLE` when correctness depends on several rows together, such as "at least one doctor must stay on call", and add retry logic for serialization failures.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Explain isolation levels" and "What's the difference between a non-repeatable read and a phantom?" Name each anomaly with a short example and the lowest level that prevents it. Then explain the lost update and the `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` fix, because interviewers use it to check practical experience.

lessons.title: Schedules, Conflict Serializability and Precedence Graphs
lessons.description: Serial vs concurrent schedules, conflicting operations, and how to test serializability with a precedence graph.

sections.title: Schedules
sections.content:
A schedule is the order in which the operations of several transactions run.

Serial schedule: transactions run one after another with no interleaving. Always correct, but slow.
Concurrent (non-serial) schedule: operations are interleaved. Faster, but it might produce a wrong result.

Serializable schedule: a concurrent schedule whose effect equals that of some serial schedule. This is the correctness target for concurrency control.

sections.title: Conflict Serializability Test
sections.content:
1. Draw one node per transaction.
2. For every conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes before Tj's, draw an edge Ti → Tj.
3. If the graph has no cycle, the schedule is conflict serializable. A topological order of the graph gives an equivalent serial schedule.
4. If there is a cycle, the schedule is not conflict serializable.

sections.title: Example: S = R1(A), R2(A), W1(A), W2(A), R1(B), W2(B)

iterations.description: A read by T2 followed by a write by T1 on A.
A read by T1 followed by a write by T2 on A.
That is a cycle.
This interleaving is the lost-update pattern: both read A, then both write it.

sections.title: View Serializability
sections.content:
View serializability is a weaker (more permissive) condition. Two schedules are view equivalent if they have the same initial reads, the same reads-from relationships and the same final writes.

Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but not every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable. The difference comes from blind writes (writes with no earlier read of that item in the transaction). Testing view serializability is NP-complete, which is why real systems use conflict-based methods.

sections.question: S = R1(A), W1(A), R2(A), W2(A), R1(B), W1(B). Is it conflict serializable? If so, what is the equivalent serial order?
sections.answerReveal: Conflicts on A: W1(A) before R2(A) and W1(A) before W2(A), giving T1 → T2. T2 never touches B, so there are no other edges. The graph is acyclic, so S is conflict serializable and equivalent to the serial schedule T1, T2.

sections.question: A precedence graph has edges T1 → T2, T2 → T3 and T3 → T1. The schedule is:
options: Conflict serializable as T1, T2, T3
Conflict serializable as T3, T2, T1
sections.explanation: T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 is a cycle, so no serial order satisfies all the edges.

items: Conflict = different transactions, same item, at least one write.
No cycle in the precedence graph ⇔ conflict serializable; a topological sort gives the serial order.
Conflict serializable ⊂ view serializable; blind writes make up the difference.

content.theory:
When transactions run concurrently, their operations interleave, and some interleavings produce wrong results. Serializability is the formal definition of a correct interleaving: one that's equivalent to running the transactions one after another. This lesson defines schedules, conflicts and conflict serializability, and explains the precedence-graph test that GATE asks about every year.

## Schedules

A schedule is the order in which the operations of several transactions execute. We write R1(A) for "transaction 1 reads A" and W2(B) for "transaction 2 writes B".

A **serial schedule** runs transactions one at a time: all of T1, then all of T2. Serial schedules are always correct, assuming each transaction is correct alone, but they waste time, because one transaction waiting on disk blocks everyone. A **concurrent schedule** interleaves operations to keep the CPU and disks busy. The goal of concurrency control is to allow only concurrent schedules that are as correct as some serial one.

## Serializable schedules

A concurrent schedule is **serializable** if its effect on the database equals the effect of some serial schedule of the same transactions. There are two practical ways to define "equals": conflict equivalence and view equivalence.

## Conflicting operations

Two operations conflict if all three conditions hold:

- they belong to different transactions
- they access the same data item
- at least one of them is a write

Read-read pairs never conflict, because swapping two reads changes nothing. Read-write, write-read and write-write pairs conflict, because their order changes what's read or what's finally stored.

## Conflict serializability

You can swap adjacent operations that don't conflict without changing the outcome. A schedule is **conflict serializable** if such swaps can turn it into a serial schedule. Equivalently, the order of every conflicting pair in the schedule matches the order of the transactions in some serial schedule.

## The precedence-graph test

Checking all swaps is slow, so you build a precedence (serialization) graph instead:

1. Draw one node per transaction
2. For each conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes first, draw an edge Ti → Tj
3. If the graph has no cycle, the schedule is conflict serializable, and a topological sort of the graph gives an equivalent serial order
4. If the graph has a cycle, the schedule isn't conflict serializable

## A worked example

Take S = R1(A), R2(A), W1(A), W2(A). The conflicts on A are: R1(A) before W2(A), giving T1 → T2; R2(A) before W1(A), giving T2 → T1; and W1(A) before W2(A), giving T1 → T2. The edges T1 → T2 and T2 → T1 form a cycle, so S isn't conflict serializable.

This schedule is the lost update: both transactions read A, both write it, and T1's write is overwritten. The cycle in the graph is the formal version of that bug.

## View serializability

View equivalence is a weaker condition. Two schedules are view equivalent if:

- each transaction reads the initial value of the same items in both schedules
- each read gets its value from the same write in both schedules
- the same transaction performs the final write of each item

Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but some view-serializable schedules aren't conflict serializable. The difference always involves **blind writes**, writes to an item the transaction never read. Testing view serializability is NP-complete, so real systems enforce conflict serializability instead, usually through locking or timestamps.

## A schedule that passes the test

Take S = R1(A), W1(A), R2(A), W2(A), R1(B), W1(B). The conflicts on A all run from T1 to T2: W1(A) comes before R2(A) and before W2(A). T2 never touches B, so B adds no edges. The graph has the single edge T1 → T2 and no cycle, so S is conflict serializable and equivalent to running T1 completely, then T2. The interleaving still helps: T2 starts its work on A while T1 moves on to B.

## How serializability connects to practice

Databases don't build precedence graphs at run time. Protocols such as two-phase locking guarantee that every schedule they allow is conflict serializable, so no check is needed. PostgreSQL's serializable mode tracks dangerous patterns of read-write dependencies between transactions and aborts one when a cycle becomes possible, which is the same idea applied dynamically.

## How interviewers test this

GATE gives a schedule and asks whether it's conflict serializable, view serializable, or both. Build the precedence graph, list every conflicting pair, and look for cycles. If there's no cycle, give the serial order from a topological sort. If there's a cycle, check for blind writes before concluding it isn't view serializable either.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: Serializability assumes every transaction commits. Aborts create a new problem: if T2 read data written by T1 and then T1 aborts, T2 based its work on a value that never existed.

sections.title: Recoverability Classes (each is stricter than the one above)
rows: If T2 reads from T1, then T1 commits before T2 commits
Committing based on data that is later rolled back
Cascading rollback (one abort forcing many others)
No transaction reads or overwrites an item until the last transaction that wrote it has committed or aborted
Problems with undoing overwritten values; allows simple undo using before-images

sections.title: Spot the Problem: W1(A), R2(A), C2, A1

iterations.description: A dirty read.
T2's result is now permanent.
T2 has committed using a value that is rolled back. Irrecoverable. To be recoverable, C2 must come after C1.

sections.question: Which relationship is correct?
sections.explanation: Every strict schedule is cascadeless, and every cascadeless schedule is recoverable. The stricter the rule, the smaller the set.

items: Recoverable: commit only after the transactions you read from have committed.
Cascadeless: read only committed data, so there are no cascading aborts.
Strict: don't read or write an item until its last writer finishes. Strict 2PL produces these.

content.theory:
Serializability assumes every transaction commits, but real transactions abort. When one transaction has read data from another that later aborts, the database may be unable to undo the damage correctly. Recoverability classifies schedules by how safely they handle aborts. This lesson explains the three classes, recoverable, cascadeless and strict, and why most real systems produce strict schedules.

## The problem aborts create

T1 writes a student's CGPA as 9.1. T2 reads 9.1 and uses it to grant a scholarship, then commits. Now T1 aborts, because the grade entry was wrong, and the CGPA goes back to 7.8. T2 has already committed a scholarship based on a value that never officially existed, and committed work can't be undone. The database is now inconsistent with no way to fix it automatically.

## Recoverable schedules

A schedule is **recoverable** if a transaction commits only after every transaction it read from has committed. In the example, T2 read from T1, so T2 must not commit before T1 does. If T1 aborts, T2 is still uncommitted and can be aborted too.

A schedule that violates this rule is irrecoverable, and every practical system forbids irrecoverable schedules.

## Cascading rollback

Recoverable schedules can still be costly. Suppose T2 read from T1, T3 read from T2, and T4 read from T3, with none committed yet. If T1 aborts, T2 must abort, which forces T3 to abort, which forces T4 to abort. One failure triggers a chain of rollbacks, called a **cascading rollback** (or cascading abort), wasting all that work.

## Cascadeless schedules

A schedule is **cascadeless** (avoids cascading aborts) if transactions read only committed data. If T2 can't read T1's value until T1 commits, T1's abort never affects T2, and no chain can start. Every cascadeless schedule is also recoverable.

## Strict schedules

A schedule is **strict** if no transaction reads or overwrites a data item until the last transaction that wrote it has committed or aborted. Strictness adds a rule about writes, not only reads.

The write rule matters for undo. Suppose T1 writes A, T2 overwrites A, and then T1 aborts. Restoring A to the value before T1 would wipe out T2's write. In a strict schedule T2 couldn't overwrite A until T1 finished, so undo can restore old values from the log without considering other transactions.

## How the classes nest

The classes form nested sets:

- **Strict** schedules are all cascadeless
- **Cascadeless** schedules are all recoverable
- **Recoverable** schedules are a subset of all schedules

In set notation: strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable. These properties are independent of serializability: a schedule can be serializable but irrecoverable, or recoverable but not serializable. A correct system needs both.

## Spotting the class in an exam schedule

For each read, note which transaction wrote the value and when that writer commits or aborts:

1. If a reader commits before its writer commits, the schedule is **not recoverable**
2. If it's recoverable but some read happens before its writer commits, it's **recoverable but not cascadeless**
3. If all reads are of committed data, check writes: if some item is overwritten before its previous writer finishes, it's **cascadeless but not strict**
4. Otherwise, it's **strict**

## A worked classification

Take S = W1(A), R2(A), W1(B), C1, C2, where C means commit. T2 reads A written by T1, and T2 commits after T1, so S is recoverable. But T2 reads A before T1 commits, so S isn't cascadeless: if T1 had aborted, T2 would have had to abort too. Moving R2(A) after C1 would make the schedule cascadeless, and since no item is overwritten early, also strict.

## What real databases produce

Strict two-phase locking, used by most lock-based databases, holds every exclusive lock until commit or abort, so other transactions can't read or overwrite uncommitted data. That produces strict schedules automatically. MVCC databases achieve the same effect differently: readers see only committed versions, so they never depend on a transaction that might abort.

## How interviewers test this

GATE gives a schedule with commits and aborts and asks which class it belongs to. Apply the four checks in order. Placement interviews ask "What is a cascading rollback and how do you prevent it?" The answer: read only committed data, which strict two-phase locking or MVCC guarantees.

sections.title: Lock Types
sections.content:
Shared (S) lock: needed to read. Many transactions can hold an S lock on the same item.
Exclusive (X) lock: needed to write. Only one transaction can hold it, and no S locks may coexist with it.

Locking alone does not guarantee serializability. If a transaction releases a lock too early, another transaction can sneak in between its operations.

sections.title: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
sections.content:
Every transaction has two phases:
1. Growing phase: it may acquire locks but may not release any.
2. Shrinking phase: it may release locks but may not acquire any new ones.
The moment of its last lock acquisition is its lock point.

Theorem: every schedule produced under 2PL is conflict serializable, in the order of the transactions' lock points.

Basic 2PL does not prevent deadlocks or cascading rollbacks.

sections.title: 2PL Variants
rows: Cascading rollbacks and deadlocks are possible
Hold all X locks until commit or abort
Hold all locks (S and X) until commit or abort
Must know all items in advance; low concurrency

sections.title: Lock Granularity and Intention Locks
sections.content:
Locks can cover a database, a table, a page or a single row. Fine granularity (row) means more concurrency but more locks to manage. Coarse granularity (table) means less overhead but more blocking.

Multiple-granularity locking uses intention locks (IS, IX, SIX) on parents. Before locking a row in X mode, a transaction takes IX on the table, so a transaction wanting an X lock on the whole table can see the conflict immediately, without scanning every row lock.

traps.question: Does 2PL prevent deadlocks?
traps.trap: Saying yes, because it's a locking protocol.
traps.solution: No. Basic and strict 2PL can both deadlock: T1 locks A and waits for B, while T2 locks B and waits for A. Only conservative 2PL avoids deadlock, by taking every lock up front.

2PL (growing, then shrinking) ⇒ conflict serializable.
Strict 2PL is what most real databases use; it still needs deadlock handling.

content.theory:
Locking is the oldest and most widely taught way to keep concurrent transactions correct. A transaction must hold a lock on data before using it, and conflicting locks make other transactions wait. This lesson explains shared and exclusive locks, why locking alone isn't enough, how two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees serializability, and the variants real databases use.

## Shared and exclusive locks

There are two basic lock modes:

- **Shared (S) lock**: required to read. Many transactions can hold S locks on the same item at once
- **Exclusive (X) lock**: required to write. Only one transaction can hold it, and no S locks can coexist with it

| Held \ Requested | S | X |
|---|---|---|
| S | Granted | Wait |
| X | Wait | Wait |

Only shared plus shared is compatible, which is why many readers can work together but a writer needs the item to itself.

## Why locks alone aren't enough

Locking each item while you use it doesn't guarantee serializability. Suppose T1 locks A, updates it, releases the lock, then locks B and updates it. Between T1's release of A and its lock on B, T2 can read the new A and the old B, a combination no serial order would produce. The problem is releasing locks too early, which lets other transactions slip between your operations.

## Two-phase locking

Two-phase locking adds one rule about timing. Each transaction has two phases:

1. **Growing phase**: it may acquire locks but may not release any
2. **Shrinking phase**: it may release locks but may not acquire any new ones

The moment a transaction acquires its last lock is its **lock point**. The key theorem: every schedule produced under 2PL is conflict serializable, and the equivalent serial order is the order of the transactions' lock points.

## What basic 2PL doesn't prevent

Basic 2PL guarantees serializability and nothing more. Two problems remain:

- **Cascading rollbacks**: T1 can release an X lock in its shrinking phase before committing, T2 reads the value, and then T1 aborts
- **Deadlocks**: T1 holds A and waits for B while T2 holds B and waits for A. Neither can proceed, and 2PL's rules don't stop this from happening

## Strict and rigorous 2PL

Real databases use stronger variants:

| Variant | Rule | Adds |
|---|---|---|
| Basic 2PL | Grow, then shrink | Conflict serializability |
| Strict 2PL | Hold every X lock until commit or abort | Strict schedules, no cascading rollbacks |
| Rigorous 2PL | Hold every lock (S and X) until commit or abort | Serial order equals commit order |
| Conservative 2PL | Acquire every lock before starting | No deadlocks, but needs all items in advance |

Strict 2PL is the common choice in lock-based systems. Conservative 2PL is rare, because transactions often don't know which rows they'll touch until they run.

## Lock granularity

A lock can cover a whole database, a table, a page or a single row. Locking rows allows more concurrency but means managing many locks; locking a table is cheap but blocks everyone. Databases usually lock rows and may escalate to a table lock when one transaction holds too many row locks.

## Intention locks

Mixed granularity raises a problem: before taking an X lock on the whole `student` table, how does a transaction know nobody holds a row lock inside it? Scanning every row lock would be slow.

**Intention locks** solve this. Before locking a row in X mode, a transaction places an intention-exclusive (IX) lock on the table. Before locking a row in S mode, it places an intention-shared (IS) lock. A transaction wanting an X lock on the table sees the IX or IS lock and waits, without inspecting any rows. SIX (shared plus intention-exclusive) covers "read the whole table, update a few rows".

## Locking versus MVCC

Pure locking makes readers and writers block each other. Many modern databases, including PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL InnoDB, combine row locks for writers with MVCC for readers, so a long report doesn't block updates. The deadlocks lesson covers MVCC in more detail.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is two-phase locking and what does it guarantee?" and "Does 2PL prevent deadlocks?" The answers: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, and no, only conservative 2PL avoids deadlocks. Mention that strict 2PL is what databases use and why: it prevents cascading rollbacks.
