lessons.title: Deadlocks, Timestamp Ordering and MVCC
lessons.description: Detecting and preventing deadlocks (wait-die, wound-wait), timestamp-based protocols and multiversion concurrency control.

sections.title: Deadlock
sections.content:
A deadlock is a cycle of transactions, each waiting for a lock held by the next one. None of them can ever continue on its own.

T1: lock-X(A) ... waits for lock-X(B)
T2: lock-X(B) ... waits for lock-X(A)

sections.title: Handling Deadlocks
rows: Maintain a wait-for graph (Ti → Tj when Ti waits for Tj); a cycle means deadlock. Abort a victim.
What MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server do. Victim = the youngest or cheapest transaction to roll back.
Abort any transaction that waits too long
Simple, but can abort transactions that weren't deadlocked
Older requester waits; younger requester dies (aborts) and restarts with the SAME timestamp
Older requester wounds (aborts) the younger holder; younger requester waits
Every transaction locks resources in a global fixed order

sections.title: Remembering Wait-Die vs Wound-Wait
sections.content: In both schemes, older transactions get priority and an aborted transaction keeps its original timestamp, so it eventually becomes the oldest and can't starve. Wait-die: old waits for young, young dies. Wound-wait: old wounds young, young waits for old.

sections.title: Timestamp Ordering Protocol
sections.content:
Each transaction gets a timestamp TS(T) when it starts. Each item Q stores R-TS(Q) (the largest timestamp that read it) and W-TS(Q) (the largest timestamp that wrote it).

Read(Q) by T: if TS(T) < W-TS(Q), a younger transaction already overwrote Q, so abort T. Otherwise allow it and update R-TS(Q).
Write(Q) by T: if TS(T) < R-TS(Q) or TS(T) < W-TS(Q), abort T. Otherwise allow it and set W-TS(Q) = TS(T).

No locks means no deadlocks, but transactions may restart often. Thomas's write rule: on a write where TS(T) ≥ R-TS(Q) but TS(T) < W-TS(Q), ignore the outdated write instead of aborting (a younger write has already superseded it and nobody read it in between). This allows some view-serializable schedules.

sections.title: MVCC (Multiversion Concurrency Control)
sections.content:
Instead of overwriting a row, a write creates a new version. Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot: the versions committed when it started (or when the statement started, under READ COMMITTED).

The key benefit: readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Only writer-versus-writer conflicts need locks.

PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle all use MVCC. Old versions are cleaned up later (VACUUM in PostgreSQL, the purge thread in InnoDB).

traps.question: What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock?
traps.trap: Mixing them up with ACID or forgetting circular wait.
traps.solution: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait (the Coffman conditions, shared with operating systems). Breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.

traps.question: How do you reduce deadlocks in an application?
traps.trap: Saying 'use a higher isolation level'. That usually increases them.
traps.solution: Access tables and rows in a consistent order, keep transactions short, add indexes so updates lock fewer rows, and catch the deadlock error and retry the transaction.

sections.question: Under wound-wait, an OLDER transaction requests a lock held by a YOUNGER one. What happens?
sections.explanation: Wound-wait is preemptive: the older transaction wounds the younger holder, which rolls back and restarts with its original timestamp.

items: Deadlock = cycle in the wait-for graph. Real DBMSs detect it and abort a victim.
Wait-die (old waits, young dies) and wound-wait (old wounds, young waits) prevent deadlocks using timestamps.
MVCC: readers and writers don't block each other; this is how modern databases implement isolation.

content.theory:
A deadlock is a cycle of transactions, each waiting for a lock that the next one holds, so none can ever proceed. This lesson explains how databases detect and break deadlocks, the timestamp-based schemes that prevent them, the timestamp-ordering protocol that avoids locks altogether, and multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), the approach most modern databases use for reads.

## How a deadlock forms

T1 locks the `student` row for roll number 101 to update a CGPA, then requests the `fee` row for 101. Meanwhile T2 has locked that `fee` row and now requests the `student` row. T1 waits for T2, and T2 waits for T1. Without intervention, both wait forever.

The four Coffman conditions must all hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion (locks are exclusive), hold and wait (a transaction holds one lock while requesting another), no preemption (locks can't be taken away), and circular wait. Breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.

## Detection with a wait-for graph

Most databases let deadlocks happen and then break them. The DBMS keeps a **wait-for graph** with an edge Ti → Tj whenever Ti waits for a lock Tj holds. A cycle in the graph is a deadlock.

When it finds a cycle, the DBMS picks a **victim**, aborts it to release its locks, and lets the others continue. Victims are chosen to waste the least work: the youngest transaction, the one holding the fewest locks, or the one that's cheapest to roll back. PostgreSQL checks for deadlocks after a transaction has waited for one second (`deadlock_timeout`), and MySQL InnoDB detects them immediately by default.

## Prevention with timestamps

Prevention schemes avoid cycles by deciding, at the moment of a lock request, who may wait. Each transaction gets a timestamp when it starts; a smaller timestamp means older. Two classic schemes use it:

- **Wait-die**: if an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger one, it waits. If a younger transaction requests a lock held by an older one, the younger one dies (aborts) and restarts later
- **Wound-wait**: if an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger one, it wounds (aborts) the younger one and takes the lock. If a younger transaction requests a lock held by an older one, it waits

In both schemes, waits only go in one direction of age, so a cycle can't form. An aborted transaction restarts with its original timestamp, so it eventually becomes the oldest and can't starve.

## Timestamp ordering

The timestamp-ordering protocol avoids locks entirely. Each transaction T has a timestamp TS(T), and each data item Q records R-TS(Q), the largest timestamp that has read it, and W-TS(Q), the largest timestamp that has written it.

The rules force operations into timestamp order:

- **Read(Q) by T**: if TS(T) < W-TS(Q), a younger transaction already overwrote Q, so T aborts. Otherwise the read proceeds and R-TS(Q) is updated
- **Write(Q) by T**: if TS(T) < R-TS(Q) or TS(T) < W-TS(Q), a younger transaction already used or replaced Q, so T aborts. Otherwise the write proceeds and W-TS(Q) becomes TS(T)

Nobody waits, so there are no deadlocks, but transactions may restart often under contention. Thomas's write rule relaxes the second check: if TS(T) ≥ R-TS(Q) but TS(T) < W-TS(Q), the write is outdated and nobody read in between, so it's ignored instead of aborting T.

## MVCC: readers and writers stop blocking

Multiversion concurrency control keeps several versions of each row instead of overwriting it. A write creates a new version tagged with the writing transaction. Each transaction reads from a **snapshot**: the versions committed before it started (in repeatable read) or before each statement started (in read committed).

The practical benefit is large: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. A long attendance report reads a consistent snapshot while teachers keep updating attendance. Only two writers changing the same row still need a lock.

Old versions must eventually be removed. PostgreSQL's `VACUUM` reclaims them, and MySQL InnoDB's purge thread does the same. A transaction left open for hours prevents cleanup, which is another reason to keep transactions short.

## Avoiding deadlocks in application code

Databases detect deadlocks, but you can make them rare:

- **Consistent order**: always lock rows in the same order, such as by ascending roll number
- **Short transactions**: hold locks for as little time as possible
- **Indexes on filtered columns**: an update without a usable index may lock far more rows than it needs
- **Retry on deadlock errors**: treat the victim's error as a signal to retry the whole transaction

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a deadlock and how do databases handle it?" Describe the wait-for graph and victim selection, then the difference between wait-die and wound-wait (who waits, who aborts). Finish with MVCC, since interviewers increasingly ask how PostgreSQL or MySQL avoid read locks.

sections.title: Why Recovery Is Needed At All
sections.content:
For speed, the DBMS changes pages in an in-memory buffer pool and writes them to disk later. So at the moment of a crash:
- Some committed changes may not be on disk yet (a durability risk).
- Some uncommitted changes may already be on disk (an atomicity risk).
Recovery uses the log to redo the first kind and undo the second.

<T1, A, 2000, 1500>     -- <transaction, item, old value, new value>
<T1, B, 1000, 1500>
<T1, commit>
<T2, start>
<T2, C, 700, 600>
-- crash here: T2 has no commit record
sections.explanation: The old value (before-image) allows UNDO. The new value (after-image) allows REDO.

sections.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): The Two Rules
sections.content:
1. Before a modified data page is written to disk, the log records describing that change must already be on disk (this enables undo).
2. Before a transaction is reported as committed, all its log records, including the commit record, must be on disk (this enables redo).
The log is written sequentially, which is fast, so committing requires only a log flush, not writing every changed data page.

sections.question: After a crash, the log shows <T2, start> and <T2, C, 700, 600> with no commit record. Recovery will:
sections.explanation: T2 never committed, so atomicity requires undoing it, restoring the old value 700.

Log records store old values (for undo) and new values (for redo).
WAL: log before data, and log flushed before commit.

content.theory:
Recovery is how a database keeps its atomicity and durability promises when something fails. The central tool is the log, an append-only record of every change, written according to the write-ahead logging (WAL) rules. This lesson explains the kinds of failure a database must survive, why the buffer pool makes recovery necessary, what a log record contains, and why WAL is the rule everything else depends on.

## Three kinds of failure

Each kind of failure loses something different:

- **Transaction failure**: one transaction can't continue, because of a constraint violation, a deadlock or an application error. Only that transaction's work must be undone
- **System crash**: power loss, an operating system crash or a killed database process. Everything in main memory is lost, but the disk survives
- **Media failure**: a disk dies or its data is corrupted. Data on that disk is lost, and recovery needs backups plus archived logs

Logging handles the first two directly. Media failure needs copies on other devices, such as backups and replicas.

## Why recovery is needed at all

Writing every change straight to its place on disk would be far too slow, because disks are thousands of times slower than memory. So the DBMS reads data pages into a memory area called the **buffer pool**, changes them there, and writes them back later.

That speed creates two risks at the moment of a crash:

- A committed transaction's changes might still be only in memory, so durability is at risk
- An uncommitted transaction's changes might already be on disk, because the buffer pool evicted a page early, so atomicity is at risk

Recovery repairs both: it redoes committed changes that didn't reach disk and undoes uncommitted changes that did.

## What a log record contains

The log is an append-only file of records. A typical sequence for a transfer looks like this:

~~~text
<T1, start>
<T1, wallet[101], 2000, 1500>
<T1, wallet[205], 1000, 1500>
<T1, commit>
<T2, start>
<T2, fee[307], unpaid, paid>
~~~

An update record holds the transaction ID, the item, the old value (the before-image, used for undo) and the new value (the after-image, used for redo). Each record also gets a log sequence number (LSN), and every data page remembers the LSN of the last change applied to it. If the crash happened after the last line, T1 committed and must be redone if needed, while T2 never committed and must be undone.

## The write-ahead logging rules

WAL consists of two rules:

1. **Log before data**: before a changed data page is written to disk, the log records describing that change must already be on disk. This guarantees undo information exists for anything that reaches disk
2. **Log before commit**: before a transaction is reported as committed, all its log records, including the commit record, must be on disk. This guarantees redo information exists for anything reported as committed

The log is written sequentially, which disks and SSDs handle well. Committing therefore needs one sequential log flush, not scattered writes of every changed page. That's why WAL makes databases both safe and fast.

## Group commit

Flushing the log for every single commit would limit a busy system to the number of flushes the disk can do per second. Databases use **group commit**: transactions that commit within a few milliseconds of each other share one flush. Throughput rises sharply while each transaction still waits for its own commit record to be durable.

## WAL beyond recovery

The same log has other uses. Replicas apply the primary's WAL to stay in sync, which is how PostgreSQL streaming replication works. Point-in-time recovery restores a backup and replays archived WAL up to a chosen moment, which undoes an accidental `DROP TABLE`. SQLite offers a WAL mode that also lets readers proceed while one writer appends to the log.

## Steal and force policies

Two buffer-pool policies decide what recovery must handle. **Steal** means the buffer pool may write an uncommitted transaction's page to disk to free memory, which requires undo. **Force** means every page a transaction changed is written to disk at commit, which removes the need for redo but makes each commit slow. Almost every real database uses steal and no-force: pages leave memory whenever convenient, and commits only flush the log. WAL is what makes that fast combination safe.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is write-ahead logging and why is it needed?" Explain the buffer pool first, because WAL makes no sense without it, then state both rules and what each guarantees. If asked about crash recovery, describe the redo of committed work and undo of uncommitted work using the log records.

sections.title: The Basic Recovery Rule
sections.content:
Scan the log after a crash:
- A transaction with both <T, start> and <T, commit>: REDO it (its changes might not have reached disk).
- A transaction with <T, start> but no commit or abort: UNDO it (its changes might have reached disk).
Undo goes backwards through the log (newest first). Redo goes forwards (oldest first).

sections.title: Checkpoints
sections.content:
Without checkpoints, recovery would have to replay the entire log since the database was created.

A checkpoint writes all modified buffer pages to disk and adds <checkpoint L> to the log, where L lists the transactions active at that moment.

After a crash, recovery only needs to look at transactions that committed after the last checkpoint (redo them) and transactions in L or started later that never committed (undo them). Transactions that committed before the checkpoint are already safely on disk.

Undo just means discarding the new copies, so no undo log is needed. Drawbacks: data gets fragmented, garbage collection is required, and concurrency is hard. SQLite's rollback journal and copy-on-write file systems use related ideas.

content.theory:
After a crash, the recovery manager reads the log to decide which transactions to redo and which to undo. This lesson explains the two update strategies that determine whether undo is needed, the basic recovery rule, how checkpoints keep recovery fast, and the three phases of ARIES, the algorithm behind recovery in IBM DB2 and Microsoft SQL Server.

## Deferred and immediate update

When may a transaction's changes reach the data pages on disk? Two strategies answer differently:

- **Deferred update**: changes are written to the database only after the transaction commits. Uncommitted work never reaches disk, so recovery needs only redo
- **Immediate update**: changes may be written to disk at any time, even before commit. Recovery needs both undo and redo

Most real databases use immediate update, because forcing every page to stay in memory until commit would exhaust the buffer pool on large transactions. That's why the log stores both old and new values.

## The basic recovery rule

After a crash, the recovery manager scans the log and sorts transactions into two groups:

- **Winners**: transactions with both a start record and a commit record. Redo them, because their changes may not have reached disk
- **Losers**: transactions with a start record but no commit or abort record. Undo them, because their changes may have reached disk

Undo goes backwards through the log, newest record first, so that when a transaction changed the same item twice, the oldest value is restored last. Redo goes forwards, oldest record first, so changes are reapplied in their original order.

## Idempotence

Recovery itself can crash. If power fails again halfway through recovery, the next attempt starts over, so redo and undo must be safe to repeat. Page LSNs make redo idempotent: a log record is reapplied only if the page's LSN is older than the record's LSN, meaning the change isn't already on the page.

## Checkpoints

Without checkpoints, recovery would scan the entire log since the database was created, which could take hours. A checkpoint limits how far back recovery must look. A basic (non-fuzzy) checkpoint does three things:

1. Pause new updates briefly
2. Write all modified buffer pages to disk
3. Append a `<checkpoint L>` record, where L lists the transactions active at that moment

After a crash, recovery starts from the last checkpoint. Transactions that committed before it are already on disk and need nothing. Only transactions in L, or started afterwards, need redo or undo. Real databases use fuzzy checkpoints that don't pause activity, writing pages in the background and recording which pages were still dirty.

## A worked example

The log contains: T1 start, T1 commit, T2 start, `<checkpoint {T2}>`, T3 start, T2 commit, T4 start, then a crash. T1 committed before the checkpoint, so it needs nothing. T2 was active at the checkpoint and committed afterwards, so it's redone. T3 and T4 have no commit record, so both are undone.

## ARIES

ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics), published in 1992, is the standard recovery design. It runs in three phases:

1. **Analysis**: scan forward from the last checkpoint to rebuild the dirty page table (which pages might be out of date on disk) and the transaction table (which transactions were active, the losers)
2. **Redo**: starting from the oldest change that might be missing from disk, reapply every logged change, including those of losers. ARIES calls this "repeating history": the database returns to the exact state at the moment of the crash
3. **Undo**: roll back the loser transactions, newest change first

During undo, ARIES writes a compensation log record (CLR) for each change it reverses. If the system crashes during undo, the next recovery sees the CLRs and doesn't undo the same change twice. Repeating history before undoing is what makes this work cleanly with row-level locks and fine-grained logging.

## Shadow paging

Shadow paging is an alternative that avoids an undo log. The database keeps two page tables. A transaction writes changed pages to new locations and builds a new page table pointing at them, while the old (shadow) table still points at the original pages. Committing means atomically switching one pointer to the new table, and aborting means discarding the new pages.

The design is clean but scales poorly: data becomes fragmented across the disk, garbage collection is needed, and concurrent transactions are hard to support. Copy-on-write file systems and some embedded stores use related ideas.

## How interviewers test this

GATE gives a log with a checkpoint and asks which transactions are redone and which are undone. Mark each transaction as committed before the checkpoint, committed after it, or never committed, then apply the rule. Placement interviews ask "What is a checkpoint and why is it needed?" Answer: it bounds how much of the log recovery has to read.

sections.content:
Disk is read in blocks (pages), typically 4-16 KB. Query cost is measured mainly in block accesses, because reading a block from disk is far slower than processing it in memory.

Without an index, finding one row means scanning the whole table. An index is a separate, smaller structure (search key → pointer to row) that lets the DBMS jump to the right block, just like the index at the back of a textbook.

content.theory:
An index is a separate data structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, the way a textbook's index lets you find a topic without reading every page. To understand indexes, you first need to know how tables sit on disk and why the cost of a query is counted in disk blocks. This lesson covers file organizations, the main index types, dense and sparse indexes, and the block-access calculations GATE asks about.

## Disk blocks are the unit of cost

Disks and SSDs read and write data in fixed-size blocks (pages), typically 4 KB to 16 KB. Reading one byte costs the same as reading the whole block, and reading a block from storage is thousands of times slower than processing it in memory. So database designers count **block accesses**, not comparisons, when estimating query cost.

A table of 30,000 student records at 100 bytes each fills 3,000 blocks of 1 KB. Finding one student by scanning means reading up to 3,000 blocks. Every technique in this lesson exists to cut that number.

## File organizations

The way rows are arranged in the table's file decides the cost of a search before any index exists:

- **Heap file**: rows go wherever there's free space, in no particular order. Inserts are fast, but finding a row means scanning: b/2 blocks on average, where b is the number of blocks
- **Sorted (sequential) file**: rows are kept in order of one key. Binary search finds a row in about log₂(b) block reads, and range queries read consecutive blocks. Inserts are expensive, because rows must shift to keep the order
- **Hashed file**: a hash of the key decides which bucket (block) holds the row, so an equality search reads about one block. Range queries get no help, because hashing scatters neighbouring keys

## Primary, clustering and secondary indexes

Indexes are classified by their relationship to the file's order:

| Index | Built on | File sorted by that field? | Entries |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | A unique ordering key | Yes | One per block (sparse) |
| Clustering | A non-unique ordering field | Yes | One per distinct value (sparse) |
| Secondary | Any other field | No | One per row (dense) |

A file can be physically sorted only one way, so a table has at most one primary or clustering index. It can have as many secondary indexes as you like, each costing extra space and extra work on every insert.

## Dense and sparse indexes

A **dense** index has an entry for every search-key value in the file. A **sparse** index has entries for only some values, usually the first key in each block. To find a key with a sparse index, you locate the last index entry not greater than the key, jump to that block, and scan within it.

Sparse indexes are smaller and work only when the file is sorted on the indexed key. Dense indexes work on any file, and they can answer "does this value exist?" from the index alone.

## A block-access calculation

GATE often asks how much an index helps. Take 30,000 records of 100 bytes, 1,024-byte blocks, and index entries of 15 bytes (key plus pointer), with the file sorted on the key:

1. **Blocking factor**: ⌊1024 / 100⌋ = 10 records per block, so the file has 3,000 blocks
2. **Without an index**: binary search needs ⌈log₂ 3000⌉ = 12 block reads
3. **Sparse primary index**: one entry per data block gives 3,000 entries; ⌊1024 / 15⌋ = 68 entries fit per block, so the index has ⌈3000 / 68⌉ = 45 blocks
4. **With the index**: ⌈log₂ 45⌉ = 6 reads to search the index, plus 1 to read the data block, giving 7

Going from 12 to 7 reads helps, and a multilevel index (an index on the index) cuts it to 3 or 4. That idea, taken to its conclusion, is the B+ tree in the next lesson.

## Clustered and non-clustered indexes

Interviewers use these terms more than "primary" and "secondary". A **clustered** index stores the table's rows in the index's order; in MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server, the leaf pages of the clustered index are the table itself, and it's built on the primary key by default. A **non-clustered** index is a separate structure whose entries point to rows, by a row ID or by the clustered key.

The practical consequence: a range query on the clustered key reads rows stored next to each other, while the same query through a non-clustered index may jump to a different page for every row. PostgreSQL stores tables as heaps and treats every index as non-clustered; its `CLUSTER` command reorders a table once but doesn't maintain the order afterwards.

## Indexes aren't free

Every index costs disk space and memory for its pages. Every `INSERT`, `DELETE` and indexed-column `UPDATE` must update every index on the table. A table with ten indexes makes each insert do eleven writes. Index the columns your frequent queries filter, join and sort on, and drop indexes nothing uses.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is an index and how does it speed up queries?", "Clustered vs non-clustered index", and "Why not index every column?" For the first, mention block reads; for the second, physical order and one-per-table; for the third, write cost and space. GATE asks the block-access calculation, so practice the four steps above.

With a fan-out of 200, three levels can index 200 × 200 × 200 = 8 million keys, so a lookup takes only 3-4 block reads. The top levels usually stay cached in memory as well.

traps.solution: High fan-out means few disk reads (each node is one page). Linked leaves make range queries and ORDER BY cheap, which hashing can't do. They stay balanced under inserts and deletes. And internal nodes hold no data pointers, so more keys fit per page than in a B-tree.

traps.question: Should you index every column?

content.theory:
The B+ tree is the index structure behind almost every relational database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and SQLite all use it as their default index. It stays shallow even for billions of rows, it keeps itself balanced as data changes, and it handles both exact lookups and range queries. This lesson explains why binary trees don't work on disk, how B-trees and B+ trees differ, how insertion keeps the tree balanced, and how to calculate a tree's order.

## Why not a binary search tree

A balanced binary search tree over a million keys has a height of about 20. On disk, each level means reading a different block, so a lookup costs 20 block reads. Binary trees are tall because each node holds one key and two children.

A B-tree makes each node as wide as a disk block. If a node holds 200 keys, it has about 200 children, so three levels cover 200 × 200 × 200 = 8 million keys and four levels cover 1.6 billion. The top levels are small enough to stay cached in memory, so most lookups read only one or two blocks from storage.

## B-trees and B+ trees

Both are balanced trees of wide nodes, and they differ in where the data lives:

| | B-tree | B+ tree |
|---|---|---|
| Data pointers | In internal nodes and leaves | Only in leaves |
| Internal nodes | Keys, data pointers and child pointers | Keys and child pointers only |
| Keys | Each appears once | Internal keys repeat in the leaves |
| Leaves | Not linked | Linked in key order |
| Range query | Needs repeated tree traversal | Find the start, then follow leaf links |

Two advantages make the B+ tree the database standard. Internal nodes hold no data pointers, so more keys fit per node, the fan-out rises and the tree gets shorter. The linked leaves turn a range query such as `WHERE cgpa BETWEEN 7 AND 8` into one descent plus a sequential walk.

## The rules of a B+ tree

For a tree of order p, where p is the maximum number of children per node:

- every internal node except the root has between ⌈p/2⌉ and p children
- the root has at least 2 children, unless it's the only node
- a node with k children holds k − 1 keys that separate the subtrees
- all leaves are at the same depth, so the tree is always perfectly balanced
- leaves hold key and record-pointer pairs, plus a pointer to the next leaf

The minimum-occupancy rule keeps nodes at least half full, which bounds the height. Search, insert and delete all take O(log n) block accesses.

## Insertion and splits

To insert a key, find the correct leaf and add the key in sorted position. If the leaf overflows, split it into two leaves and add a separator key to the parent. The rules for what moves up are specific:

- **Leaf split**: the separator is **copied** up, so it also stays as the first key of the right leaf, because every key must exist in a leaf
- **Internal split**: the middle key is **moved** up and doesn't stay in either half

If the parent overflows, it splits too, and the split can travel up to the root. Splitting the root creates a new root above it, and that's the only way the tree grows taller. All leaves therefore stay at the same depth automatically.

Deletion works in reverse: if a node falls below half full, it borrows a key from a sibling or merges with it, and merges can travel upwards and shrink the tree.

## Calculating the order

GATE gives a block size, key size and pointer size and asks for the maximum order. For an internal node, p child pointers and p − 1 keys must fit in one block. With a 512-byte block, 8-byte keys and 6-byte pointers:

~~~text
p × 6 + (p − 1) × 8 ≤ 512
14p − 8 ≤ 512
p ≤ 37.14, so p = 37
~~~

For a leaf, count key and record-pointer pairs plus one next-leaf pointer: n × (key + record pointer) + pointer ≤ block size.

## Composite indexes and the leftmost prefix

An index on `(dept_id, salary)` is sorted by `dept_id` first, then by `salary` within each department, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. It helps `WHERE dept_id = 5` and `WHERE dept_id = 5 AND salary > 50000`. It can't efficiently help `WHERE salary > 50000` alone, because matching salaries are scattered across every department. That's the **leftmost-prefix rule**, and it decides the column order of every composite index you design.

## How interviewers test this

The classic question is "Why do databases use B+ trees instead of binary trees or hash tables?" Answer with fan-out and block reads (short trees), linked leaves (range queries and sorting), and self-balancing (consistent performance). GATE asks order calculations and the number of keys after a sequence of insertions, so practice drawing splits.

lessons.description: Static and extendible hashing, hash vs B+ tree, covering indexes, and how query planners use indexes.

sections.title: Hash-Based Indexing
sections.content:
A hash function maps a search key to a bucket (one or more blocks). An equality lookup ('WHERE id = 42') costs about one block access.

Static hashing: a fixed number of buckets. As data grows, overflow chains get longer and lookups slow down.
Extendible hashing: a directory of 2^d pointers (d = global depth). When a bucket overflows, only that bucket splits. The directory doubles only when the overflowing bucket's local depth equals the global depth.
Linear hashing: buckets split one at a time in a fixed round-robin order, so no directory is needed.

sections.title: Hash Index vs B+ Tree Index
rows: Memory tables, hash joins, some key-value stores

sections.title: Index Design Checklist
items: **Selectivity**: index columns that filter out most rows (email, order_id), not near-constant ones (is_active).
**Covering index**: if the index holds every column a query needs, the DBMS answers from the index alone (an index-only scan).
**Composite order**: put equality-filtered columns first and range-filtered columns last.
**Functions defeat indexes**: `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025` can't use an index on created_at. Rewrite it as a range: `created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01'`.
**Leading wildcard**: `LIKE '%son'` can't use a B+ tree index.
**Write cost**: each extra index slows down inserts and updates.

sections.question: A query on a 50 million row table uses WHERE status = 'DELIVERED' AND customer_id = 991. 90% of orders are DELIVERED. Which index would you create?
sections.answerReveal: An index on customer_id, or a composite (customer_id, status). customer_id is highly selective. status is not: 90% of rows match it, so an index on status alone is nearly useless and the planner would probably ignore it.

sections.question: Which query can NOT benefit from a B+ tree index on last_name?
sections.explanation: A leading wildcard has no fixed prefix to search the sorted tree for, so the DBMS must scan.

items: Hash indexes are only for equality; B+ trees handle equality, ranges and sorting.
Extendible hashing grows smoothly by splitting buckets and doubling a directory.
Index selective columns, follow the leftmost prefix, and avoid functions on indexed columns.

content.theory:
Hash indexes find a row in about one step when you know its exact key, but they can't help with ranges or sorting. Choosing the right index means matching the structure to the queries you run, then checking that the database actually uses it. This lesson explains static and extendible hashing, compares hash and B+ tree indexes, and gives practical rules for designing indexes and reading a query plan.

## How hash indexing works

A hash function turns a key into a bucket number, and the bucket (one or more blocks) holds the entries for that key. Looking up `roll_no = 2045` means computing the hash, reading the bucket, and scanning its few entries: about one block access, regardless of table size.

The catch is that hashing deliberately scatters keys. Roll numbers 2045 and 2046 land in unrelated buckets, so a query for roll numbers between 2000 and 2100 gets no help from a hash index.

## Static hashing and its problem

Static hashing fixes the number of buckets in advance. As the table grows, buckets fill and spill into overflow chains, and lookups slow down as they follow those chains. Doubling the number of buckets means rehashing every entry at once, which is expensive and blocks the table while it runs.

## Extendible hashing

Extendible hashing grows smoothly. It keeps a directory of 2^d pointers, where d is the global depth, and uses the first d bits of each hash to pick a directory slot. Several slots may point to the same bucket, and each bucket records its own local depth.

When a bucket overflows, only that bucket splits:

1. If its local depth is less than the global depth, split it into two buckets and update the directory slots that pointed to it
2. If its local depth equals the global depth, double the directory first (d increases by 1), then split

Most splits touch one bucket, so growth costs stay small and spread out. **Linear hashing** is a related scheme that splits buckets one at a time in a fixed round-robin order and needs no directory.

## Hash index versus B+ tree

| Query | Hash index | B+ tree index |
|---|---|---|
| `WHERE roll_no = 2045` | About 1 block read | 2 to 4 block reads |
| `WHERE cgpa BETWEEN 7 AND 8` | No help | One descent, then a leaf walk |
| `ORDER BY created_at` | No help | Rows already in order |
| `WHERE name LIKE 'Ra%'` | No help | Works as a prefix range |
| Typical use | In-memory tables, hash joins | Default index almost everywhere |

The B+ tree is a few block reads slower on exact matches, and in exchange it handles everything else. That's why it's the default, and why PostgreSQL's `CREATE INDEX` builds a B-tree unless you ask for `USING hash`.

## Rules for designing indexes

Use these rules when deciding what to index:

- **Selectivity**: index columns that narrow results to few rows, such as `email` or `order_id`. A column like `is_active`, where 95% of rows share one value, rarely helps, because reading most of the table through an index is slower than scanning it
- **Equality before range in composite indexes**: for `WHERE dept_id = 5 AND salary > 50000`, build `(dept_id, salary)`, not the reverse
- **Covering indexes**: if an index contains every column a query needs, the database answers from the index alone, an index-only scan
- **Functions hide columns**: `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025` can't use an index on `created_at`. Rewrite it as a range: `created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01'`
- **Leading wildcards**: `LIKE '%son'` has no fixed prefix, so a B+ tree can't help
- **Foreign keys**: index them, because joins and cascading deletes search on them, and PostgreSQL doesn't create those indexes automatically

## Check the plan

Never assume an index is used; ask the database. PostgreSQL and MySQL show the chosen plan with `EXPLAIN`, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and reports real timings. SQLite uses `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`:

~~~sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'Sales';
~~~

Before an index exists, SQLite reports `SCAN employees`. After `CREATE INDEX idx_dept ON employees(department)`, it reports `SEARCH employees USING INDEX idx_dept (department=?)`. You can run both in the StudyHub SQL Lab.

## When the planner ignores your index

The optimizer estimates costs from table statistics, and it may choose a full scan when your filter matches a large fraction of rows, because sequential reads are faster than many random ones. Stale statistics cause bad choices too: run `ANALYZE` after large data changes so the planner's row estimates match reality.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Hash index vs B+ tree index" (equality only versus equality, ranges and sorting) and a design question such as "Which index would you create for this query?" Talk about selectivity and column order, then mention checking the result with `EXPLAIN`, which shows you've done this on a real database.

Designed for horizontal scaling across many nodes

sections.title: CAP Theorem
sections.content:
In a distributed data store, when a network partition happens (some nodes can't talk to others), you must choose between:
Consistency (C): every read sees the latest write.
Availability (A): every request gets a non-error response.

Partition tolerance (P) isn't optional in a real network, so the practical choice is CP or AP during a partition.

CP: refuse or delay requests rather than return stale data. Examples: HBase, MongoDB with majority writes, etcd/ZooKeeper.
AP: always answer, even if the data may be stale, and reconcile later. Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), CouchDB.

PACELC extends CAP: even with no partition (Else), you trade Latency against Consistency.

sections.title: BASE
sections.content:
BASE is the philosophy of many AP systems:
Basically Available: the system answers even during failures.
Soft state: data may change without new input as replicas sync.
Eventual consistency: if writes stop, all replicas eventually converge.

ACID favors correctness. BASE favors availability and scale.

traps.question: MongoDB or MySQL for an e-commerce app?
traps.trap: Picking one as always better.
traps.solution: Use the access pattern. Orders, payments and inventory need multi-row ACID and relational integrity, so a relational DB fits. A product catalog with varied attributes, sessions or activity feeds can fit a document or key-value store. Many systems use both (polyglot persistence).

traps.question: Does CAP mean you choose 2 of 3 at all times?
traps.trap: Saying 'my system is CA'.
traps.solution: CA only exists on a single node, where partitions can't happen. Any distributed system must tolerate partitions, so the real decision is C versus A while a partition is happening.

sections.question: During a network partition, a system keeps accepting writes on both sides and merges them later. It is choosing:
sections.explanation: It stays available and gives up immediate consistency, reconciling afterwards: AP with eventual consistency.

items: Choose SQL vs NoSQL by consistency needs and access patterns, not popularity.
CAP: during a partition, pick consistency or availability.
BASE = basically available, soft state, eventually consistent.

content.theory:
"SQL or NoSQL?" is one of the most common design questions in interviews, and the honest answer depends on the data and how it's accessed. This lesson compares relational and NoSQL databases, explains the CAP theorem and its extension PACELC, and describes BASE, the consistency model many distributed stores choose. The goal is to make the choice from requirements rather than habit.

## What NoSQL changes

NoSQL is a family of databases that drop some relational features to gain others. Most of them change three things:

- **Data model**: documents, key-value pairs, wide columns or graphs instead of tables joined by keys
- **Schema**: flexible or schema-on-read, so records in one collection can have different fields
- **Scaling**: designed to spread data across many machines from the start

The cost is usually weaker ad-hoc querying, fewer joins, and in many systems, weaker transaction guarantees across records.

## Comparing the two

| | Relational (SQL) | NoSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Schema | Fixed, changed through migrations | Flexible per record |
| Relationships | Joins across tables | Embedding or application-side joins |
| Transactions | Multi-row ACID | Often single-record; some offer multi-record |
| Scaling | Vertical first; sharding is extra work | Horizontal by design |
| Queries | Rich ad-hoc SQL | Optimized for known access patterns |

## Choosing from the requirements

Use the access pattern and consistency needs to decide:

- **Money, inventory, bookings, grades**: relational. You need multi-row transactions and constraints, because a half-applied payment is unacceptable
- **Product catalogs with varying attributes**: document stores fit well, because each product's fields differ
- **Sessions, caches, rate-limit counters**: key-value stores, because every access is "get or set by key" and speed matters most
- **Event logs and time series at hundreds of thousands of writes per second**: wide-column stores spread writes across many nodes
- **Social graphs and recommendations**: graph databases follow relationships many hops deep efficiently

Many systems combine stores, a practice called polyglot persistence. A college platform might keep enrollments in PostgreSQL, sessions in Redis and course search in Elasticsearch.

## The CAP theorem

The CAP theorem concerns distributed data stores, systems that keep copies of data on several machines. It names three properties:

- **Consistency (C)**: every read returns the most recent write, as if there were one copy
- **Availability (A)**: every request to a working node gets a non-error response
- **Partition tolerance (P)**: the system keeps working when the network splits the nodes into groups that can't communicate

The theorem says that while a network partition is happening, a system must give up either consistency or availability. Networks do fail, so partition tolerance isn't optional. The real choice is between C and A during a partition.

## CP and AP systems

A **CP** system refuses or delays requests on the side of the partition that can't confirm the latest data, rather than return stale values. ZooKeeper, etcd and MongoDB with majority writes behave this way. An **AP** system keeps answering on both sides and reconciles the copies afterwards, accepting that some reads are stale. Cassandra, DynamoDB in its default mode and CouchDB behave this way.

A single-node database is often described as "CA", but that only means it has no partitions to tolerate, because it isn't distributed.

## PACELC

CAP says nothing about normal operation, when there's no partition. PACELC extends it: during a **P**artition, choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse, choose between **L**atency and **C**onsistency. Even with a healthy network, waiting for several replicas to confirm a write adds latency. Cassandra and DynamoDB favour low latency by default, while systems such as Google Spanner pay latency for strong consistency.

## BASE

Many AP systems describe their guarantees as BASE:

- **Basically available**: the system answers even during failures
- **Soft state**: replicas may hold different values for a while as updates propagate
- **Eventually consistent**: if writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value

ACID favours correctness at each step. BASE favours availability and scale, and pushes some conflict handling into the application, such as merging two shopping carts edited on both sides of a partition.

## How interviewers test this

For "MongoDB or MySQL for X?", name the access pattern and consistency need first, then the choice. For CAP, state that partitions force a choice between consistency and availability, give one CP and one AP example, and mention PACELC to show you know CAP's limits.

sections.title: Replication Topologies
sections.content:
Leader-follower (primary-replica): all writes go to the leader, which streams changes to followers that serve reads. Synchronous replication waits for a follower to confirm (safer, slower). Asynchronous doesn't wait (faster, but a crash can lose the latest writes, and readers may see stale data).

Multi-leader: several nodes accept writes. Useful across data centers, but conflicting writes must be resolved.

Leaderless (Dynamo-style): clients write to and read from several replicas. With N replicas, W write acknowledgements and R read responses, W + R > N guarantees that reads overlap the latest write.

sections.title: Choosing a Shard Key
rows: Hot spots (all new users land on the last shard)
Range queries hit every shard; changing N moves most keys (use consistent hashing)
Indian users on the Mumbai shard

sections.question: Users complain that their profile edit 'disappears' right after saving, then reappears seconds later. What's happening and how do you fix it?
sections.answerReveal: Replication lag: the write went to the leader, but the follow-up read was served by an asynchronous replica that hadn't caught up. Fix it with read-your-writes consistency: read the user's own data from the leader for a short time after they write, or route their reads to replicas that have reached their last write position.

sections.question: With N = 3 replicas, which (W, R) configuration guarantees that a read sees the latest write?
sections.explanation: W + R must be greater than N: 2 + 2 = 4 > 3. The other options don't guarantee that the read set overlaps the write set.

items: Replication scales reads and availability; sharding scales writes and data size.
Async replication causes lag; use read-your-writes when users must see their own changes.
Shard keys decide hot spots; consistent hashing reduces data movement when nodes change.
Quorum rule: W + R > N.

content.theory:
A single database server eventually runs out of room for reads, writes, data or uptime. Replication, partitioning and sharding are the three techniques for going beyond one machine, and each solves a different bottleneck. This lesson explains how each works, the problems each introduces, and how to choose a shard key, using a growing student platform as the example.

## Start by scaling up

Vertical scaling means moving to a bigger machine: more CPU, more memory, faster SSDs. It needs no code changes and keeps every guarantee of a single database. Its limits are cost, a hard ceiling on machine size, and a single point of failure. Most systems should scale up as far as is affordable before adding the complexity below.

## Replication

Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes. It serves two goals: more read capacity, because replicas answer read queries, and high availability, because a replica can take over if the primary fails.

In **leader-follower** (primary-replica) replication, all writes go to the leader, which streams its changes (often its write-ahead log) to followers. The timing of that stream is a key decision:

- **Synchronous**: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before acknowledging a write. No committed write is lost if the leader dies, but every write gets slower
- **Asynchronous**: the leader acknowledges immediately. Writes are fast, but a leader crash can lose the most recent writes, and followers may serve slightly stale data

Many deployments use one synchronous follower for safety and several asynchronous ones for read capacity.

## Replication lag in practice

Asynchronous followers run behind the leader by milliseconds to seconds. A student updates their phone number, the next page load reads from a follower that hasn't caught up, and the old number appears. The fix is **read-your-writes consistency**: route a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write, or to a follower known to have reached their last write.

## Multi-leader and leaderless replication

**Multi-leader** replication accepts writes at several nodes, for example one per data center. It survives a data center outage, but two leaders can change the same row at once, so the system needs a conflict-resolution rule.

**Leaderless** replication, used by Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra, sends each write to several replicas and reads from several. With N replicas, waiting for W write acknowledgements and R read responses guarantees that a read sees the latest write when W + R > N, because the read set and write set must overlap. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2 satisfies this.

## Partitioning

Partitioning splits one large table into smaller pieces inside one database. PostgreSQL's declarative partitioning can split an `attendance` table by month, so a query for one month reads one partition, and old months can be detached and archived instantly. Partitioning helps manageability and scans, but the data still lives on one server.

## Sharding

Sharding spreads partitions across different servers, each holding a subset of the rows. It's the only one of the three techniques that scales writes and total data size beyond one machine. The cost is complexity:

- **Cross-shard queries**: a query that needs rows from every shard must ask every shard and merge results
- **Cross-shard transactions**: atomic updates spanning shards need distributed protocols such as two-phase commit, which are slow and fragile
- **Rebalancing**: adding a shard means moving data while the system keeps running

## Choosing a shard key

The shard key decides which shard holds each row, and it's hard to change later:

| Strategy | Example | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Range | roll numbers 1 to 1M on shard 1 | Efficient range scans | New rows pile onto the last shard (hot spot) |
| Hash | shard = hash(user_id) mod N | Even spread | Range queries hit every shard |
| Directory | a lookup table maps college to shard | Flexible placement | The lookup service becomes critical |
| Geographic | Indian users on a Mumbai shard | Low latency, data residency | Uneven load across regions |

Plain `hash mod N` moves most keys when N changes. **Consistent hashing** places shards and keys on a ring, so adding a shard moves only the keys between it and its neighbour.

## Choosing among the techniques

Match the technique to the bottleneck: replication for read load and availability, partitioning for tables with hundreds of millions of rows on one server, and sharding only when writes or data size exceed what one server can handle. Sharding too early adds permanent complexity that a bigger server or a read replica would have avoided.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Replication vs sharding" (copies for reads and availability versus splitting data for writes and size), "What is replication lag and how do you handle it?", and the quorum condition W + R > N. For shard keys, discuss hot spots and why consistent hashing helps.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content:
An operating system is the software layer between applications and hardware. It has two jobs:

1. Resource manager: share the CPU, memory, disk and devices fairly and safely among many programs.
2. Abstraction provider: give programs simple interfaces (files, processes, sockets) instead of raw disk sectors, CPU registers and network cards.

The kernel is the core of the OS that is always in memory and runs with full hardware privileges. Shells, desktop environments and system utilities sit on top of it.

sections.title: Core OS Responsibilities
items: **Process management**: create, schedule and terminate programs.
**Memory management**: give each process its own address space and protect them from each other.
**File system**: organize persistent data into files and directories.
**Device / I/O management**: drivers, buffering, interrupts.
**Protection and security**: users, permissions, isolation.
**Networking**: sockets and protocol stacks.

sections.title: Dual-Mode Operation
sections.content:
The CPU has a mode bit.

Kernel mode (mode bit 0): any instruction may run, including privileged ones (I/O, changing page tables, disabling interrupts).
User mode (mode bit 1): privileged instructions are blocked. Trying to run one causes a trap into the OS.

Applications run in user mode. The only ways into kernel mode are system calls, interrupts and exceptions. This stops a buggy or malicious program from taking over the machine.

sections.title: Interrupt vs Trap
rows: A device: timer, keyboard, disk finished, network packet
The running instruction: a system call, divide by zero, invalid memory access
Asynchronous: can arrive at any moment
Synchronous: caused by the current instruction
The timer interrupt that lets the OS preempt a process

sections.question: Which of these must run in kernel mode?
options: Calling a function in your own program
Changing the page table base register
sections.explanation: Changing memory-mapping hardware is privileged. If user programs could do it, they could read any other process's memory.

items: The OS manages resources and provides abstractions; the kernel is its privileged core.
User mode vs kernel mode protects the system; system calls, interrupts and exceptions are the only ways into the kernel.
Interrupts are asynchronous (from devices); traps are synchronous (from instructions).

content.theory:
An operating system (OS) is the software that manages a computer's hardware and gives programs a safer, more convenient way to use it. Without an OS, every program would need its own code to drive the disk, share the CPU with other programs and stay out of their memory. This lesson explains the two jobs an OS does, what the kernel is, and how the hardware's user and kernel modes keep programs from taking over the machine.

## Two jobs: referee and illusionist

An OS does two jobs at once. As a **resource manager** (a referee), it decides which program gets the CPU next, how much memory each one may use, and in what order disk requests are served. As an **abstraction provider** (an illusionist), it hides messy hardware behind clean ideas: a file instead of disk sectors, a process instead of raw CPU registers, a socket instead of a network card's packet buffers.

Each abstraction is an illusion the OS maintains. Your program behaves as if it has the CPU to itself, a private memory starting at address zero, and files that persist forever. Underneath, dozens of programs share one CPU, physical memory is scattered, and disks fail. Most of this course explains how the OS keeps those illusions up.

## What the OS manages

The main subsystems map onto the hardware:

- **Process management**: create, schedule, pause and terminate running programs
- **Memory management**: give each process its own address space and keep processes out of each other's memory
- **File systems**: organize persistent data into files and directories on disks and SSDs
- **Device management**: drive hardware through device drivers, interrupts and buffering
- **Protection and security**: user accounts, permissions, and isolation between programs
- **Networking**: protocol stacks and sockets for talking to other machines

## The kernel

The **kernel** is the core of the OS that's always loaded in memory and runs with full hardware privileges. It contains the scheduler, memory manager, file systems and drivers (depending on the design, as the kernel-architecture lesson explains). Everything else you think of as "the OS", such as the shell, the desktop and system utilities, runs as ordinary programs that ask the kernel for services.

## User mode and kernel mode

The CPU itself enforces the boundary between programs and the kernel. A mode bit records whether the current code is trusted:

- **Kernel mode**: any instruction may run, including privileged ones such as talking to devices, changing memory mappings or disabling interrupts
- **User mode**: privileged instructions are blocked. If a program tries one, the CPU raises an exception and the kernel takes over, usually terminating the program

Applications always run in user mode. That's what stops a buggy game from overwriting the file system or reading another user's passwords from memory.

## Crossing the boundary

User programs enter the kernel in three controlled ways:

- **System calls**: the program deliberately asks for a service, such as reading a file
- **Interrupts**: hardware signals the CPU, for example the timer firing or a disk finishing a read
- **Exceptions (traps)**: the running instruction causes a problem, such as dividing by zero or touching an invalid address

In each case the CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a handler the kernel registered at boot time. A program can't choose an arbitrary kernel address to jump to, so it can only use the doors the kernel built.

## The timer interrupt keeps the OS in charge

If a program runs an infinite loop and never makes a system call, how does the OS regain control? Before starting a program, the kernel programs a hardware timer to interrupt the CPU after a few milliseconds. When the timer fires, control returns to the kernel, which can switch to another program. This **preemption** is why one runaway program can't freeze a modern desktop.

## Interrupts versus traps

| | Interrupt | Trap or exception |
|---|---|---|
| Source | A hardware device | The current instruction |
| Timing | Asynchronous: arrives at any moment | Synchronous: caused by the instruction |
| Examples | Timer, keyboard, disk done, packet arrived | `read()` system call, divide by zero, page fault |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is an operating system?" and "Why do we need user mode and kernel mode?" For the first, name both jobs, resource manager and abstraction provider, with one example each. For the second, explain that privileged instructions are blocked in user mode, so a faulty or malicious program can't damage the system, and that system calls, interrupts and exceptions are the only ways into the kernel.

lessons.description: Batch, multiprogramming, multitasking, multiprocessing, real-time and distributed systems compared.

sections.title: OS Types
rows: Jobs collected and run one after another with no interaction
Several jobs in memory; when one waits for I/O, the CPU switches to another
Multiprogramming plus fast switching with time slices, so every user feels the system responding
Two or more CPUs/cores share memory and run processes in parallel
Tasks must finish within strict deadlines
Many networked machines appear as one system

sections.title: Hard vs Soft Real-Time
sections.content:
Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a system failure (anti-lock brakes, flight control).
Soft real-time: missing a deadline reduces quality but is tolerated (video streaming dropping a frame, online games).

traps.question: What's the difference between multiprogramming and multitasking?
traps.trap: Saying they are the same thing.
traps.solution: Multiprogramming switches jobs only when the running one blocks (for I/O), to keep the CPU busy. Multitasking adds timer-based preemption (time slices), so even CPU-bound programs take turns and interactive users get fast responses.

traps.question: Is multiprocessing the same as multithreading?
traps.trap: Using the terms interchangeably.
traps.solution: Multiprocessing is about hardware: several CPUs. Multithreading is about software: several threads within one process. Threads can run in parallel only when there are multiple CPUs.

sections.question: A car's airbag controller must react within 10 ms every time. It needs a:
sections.explanation: Missing the deadline is a catastrophic failure, which is the definition of hard real-time.

items: Multiprogramming maximizes CPU use; multitasking adds time slices for responsiveness.
Hard real-time: deadlines must never be missed; soft real-time: occasional misses are tolerable.

content.theory:
Operating systems evolved as hardware got cheaper and users wanted different things from computers: first maximum throughput, then fast response, then predictable timing. Each era produced a type of OS that still exists in some form today. This lesson walks through batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing, multiprocessor, real-time, distributed and embedded systems, and explains the goal each design optimizes.

## Batch systems: keep the expensive machine busy

Early computers cost millions and filled rooms, so idle time was waste. Batch systems collected jobs (payroll, scientific calculations) on punched cards, grouped similar ones, and ran them one after another without human interaction. The goal was throughput: jobs completed per hour.

The weakness was idle CPU time. When a job waited for a tape drive, which took milliseconds while the CPU could run millions of instructions, the CPU sat unused.

## Multiprogramming: fill the waiting time

Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory at once. When the running job waits for input or output, the OS switches the CPU to another job that's ready. The CPU stays busy as long as at least one job can run.

Multiprogramming switches only when a job blocks. A job that computes for an hour without doing input or output keeps the CPU the whole time, which is acceptable for batch work and frustrating for interactive users.

## Time-sharing: fast response for many users

Time-sharing (multitasking) adds preemption. Each program gets a short time slice, typically a few milliseconds, and a timer interrupt forces a switch when it expires. Switches happen so often that every user at a terminal feels the machine is responding to them alone.

The goal shifts from throughput to response time. Linux, Windows and macOS are all time-sharing systems, which is why you can type in an editor while a large compile runs in the background.

## Multiprocessor systems: real parallelism

Multiprocessor systems have two or more CPUs (or cores) sharing memory. Several programs truly run at the same instant instead of taking turns. Almost every machine today is multiprocessor: a laptop has 8 to 16 cores and a server can have over 100.

The OS must now schedule work across cores, keep shared data structures safe when two cores update them at once, and decide whether to keep a process on the same core to reuse its cached data.

## Real-time systems: deadlines first

A real-time OS (RTOS) must finish tasks within strict time limits. Speed alone isn't the goal; predictability is. Real-time systems come in two kinds:

- **Hard real-time**: missing a deadline is a failure. An airbag controller, a pacemaker or a car's anti-lock brakes must react within milliseconds every single time
- **Soft real-time**: missing a deadline degrades quality but is tolerated. A video call that drops a frame or a game that stutters for a moment

RTOSes such as FreeRTOS, Zephyr and VxWorks use priority-based preemptive scheduling and avoid features with unpredictable timing, such as swapping memory to disk.

## Distributed systems: many machines as one

A distributed OS (or distributed system) makes a network of computers cooperate, sharing storage and work, and sometimes presenting them as one system. Cluster managers and distributed file systems are modern examples. The goals are scalability and fault tolerance: if one machine fails, the others continue.

## Embedded and mobile systems

Embedded systems run inside devices: washing machines, routers, smart meters. They have limited memory and power and often a single fixed purpose. Mobile OSes such as Android and iOS are time-sharing systems tuned for battery life, touch input and strict app sandboxing.

## Comparing the goals

| Type | Main goal | Example today |
|---|---|---|
| Batch | Throughput | Nightly payroll or report jobs |
| Multiprogramming | CPU utilization | Foundation of every modern OS |
| Time-sharing | Response time | Linux, Windows, macOS |
| Multiprocessor | Parallel throughput | Every multicore machine |
| Real-time | Meeting deadlines | Automotive and medical controllers |
| Distributed | Scale and fault tolerance | Cluster and cloud systems |
| Embedded and mobile | Efficiency, battery | Routers, Android, iOS |

## How interviewers test this

The most common question is "Multiprogramming vs multitasking": multiprogramming switches only when a job blocks, to keep the CPU busy, while multitasking adds timer-based time slices for responsiveness. The second is "Hard vs soft real-time", answered with one example of each.

lessons.title: System Calls
lessons.description: How programs request OS services, the categories of system calls, and what happens during one.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content:
A system call is the programmatic way a user program asks the kernel for a service it can't perform itself: reading a file, creating a process, sending network data.

Programmers usually call a library wrapper (printf → write, fopen → open, in the C standard library) rather than the raw system call.

sections.title: What Happens During read()
sections.code:
1. Program calls read(fd, buf, n)        (user mode, library wrapper)
2. Wrapper puts the system-call number + arguments in registers
3. Executes a trap instruction (syscall / int 0x80)
4. CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the system-call handler
5. Kernel validates the arguments, performs the I/O (may block the process)
6. Return value placed in a register
7. Return-from-trap: back to user mode, execution continues after the call
sections.explanation: Each system call costs a mode switch, which is why programs buffer I/O instead of calling write() for every single byte.

sections.question: Why can't a program simply call a kernel function directly like a normal function?
sections.answerReveal: Kernel code and data live in protected memory that user mode can't access, and kernel functions need privileged instructions. The trap instruction is the controlled gate: the CPU switches mode and jumps only to kernel-defined entry points, so a program can't jump into the middle of kernel code.

sections.question: Which is NOT a system call?
sections.explanation: printf() is a C library function. It formats text in user space and then calls the write() system call.

items: System calls are the API between user programs and the kernel, entered through a trap.
Six categories: process, file, device, information, communication, protection.
Library functions such as printf wrap system calls such as write.

content.theory:
A system call is how a user program asks the kernel to do something it isn't allowed to do itself, such as reading a file, creating a process or sending data over the network. System calls are the official interface between applications and the OS, and every program you've written depends on them, usually through a library. This lesson explains what happens during a system call, the main categories, and why their cost shapes how programs do input and output.

## Why programs can't do it themselves

User programs run in user mode, where instructions that touch devices or change memory mappings are blocked. A program that wants to read a file needs the disk driver, the file system and permission checks, all of which live in the kernel. The only way to reach them is to ask, and the asking mechanism is the system call.

## What happens during `read()`

Calling `read(fd, buf, 100)` in C sets off this sequence:

1. The C library wrapper places the system-call number for `read` and its arguments in CPU registers
2. It executes a special trap instruction (`syscall` on x86-64)
3. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's system-call entry point
4. The kernel checks the arguments: is `fd` an open file, and is `buf` memory this process owns?
5. The kernel performs the read, possibly blocking the process until the disk responds
6. The kernel stores the return value (bytes read, or an error code) in a register
7. A return-from-trap instruction switches back to user mode, and execution continues after the call

Step 4 matters for security. The kernel never trusts pointers from user programs, because a malicious program could pass the address of kernel memory and trick the kernel into overwriting it.

## Library functions versus system calls

Most programmers never write a trap instruction. They call library functions that wrap system calls:

- `printf` formats text in user space, then calls the `write` system call
- `fopen` calls `open`, and `malloc` occasionally calls `brk` or `mmap` to get more memory from the kernel
- Java's `FileInputStream.read` eventually calls `read` through the JVM

The distinction appears in interviews: `printf` isn't a system call, but it uses one.

## Categories of system calls

| Category | UNIX and Linux examples | Windows examples |
|---|---|---|
| Process control | `fork`, `exec`, `exit`, `wait` | `CreateProcess`, `ExitProcess` |
| File management | `open`, `read`, `write`, `close` | `CreateFile`, `ReadFile` |
| Device management | `ioctl`, `read`, `write` | `DeviceIoControl` |
| Information | `getpid`, `time`, `uname` | `GetCurrentProcessId` |
| Communication | `pipe`, `socket`, `shmget` | `CreatePipe` |
| Protection | `chmod`, `chown` | `SetFileSecurity` |

On UNIX-like systems, devices often appear as files, so `read` and `write` work on a terminal, a pipe or a disk file alike. That uniformity is one of UNIX's most influential design choices.

## The cost of a system call

A system call costs far more than a normal function call: switching modes, saving registers, checking arguments, and disturbing the CPU's caches. Writing a 1 MB file one byte at a time would make a million system calls.

That cost is why libraries buffer input and output. The C library's `printf` collects output in a user-space buffer and calls `write` once the buffer fills or a newline reaches a terminal. Java's `BufferedReader` does the same for reads. If your program logs heavily or copies large files, buffering is often the difference between seconds and minutes.

## Watching system calls

On Linux, `strace` prints every system call a program makes. Running `strace ls` shows `openat`, `getdents64`, `write` and many more. It's one of the fastest ways to see why a program is slow or failing, such as a missing configuration file it keeps trying to open. Windows offers Process Monitor for the same purpose.

## Avoiding the trap for hot calls

Some calls run so often that even the mode switch hurts, such as reading the current time thousands of times per second in a game or a database. Linux maps a small page of kernel-provided code, the vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object), into every process. Calls such as `clock_gettime` run there in user mode, reading time data the kernel keeps updated, so they finish without entering the kernel at all.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a system call?" and "Is `printf` a system call?" Describe the trap into kernel mode and the argument checks, then explain that `printf` is a library function that eventually calls `write`. Mentioning buffering as the response to system-call cost shows practical understanding.

lessons.title: Kernel Architectures: Monolithic, Microkernel, Hybrid
lessons.description: How OS components are organized, and the trade-off between speed and isolation.

sections.title: Kernel Designs
rows: All OS services (scheduler, memory, file systems, drivers) in one big kernel address space
Fast: services call each other directly
A driver bug can crash the whole system; large and harder to maintain
Kernel keeps only IPC, basic scheduling and memory; file systems and drivers run as user-space servers
Slower: services talk through message passing
Microkernel-like structure, but many services kept in kernel space for speed
Strict layers; each uses only the layer below
Hard to define the layers; overhead

sections.title: Loadable Kernel Modules
sections.content: Linux is monolithic but modular: drivers and file systems can be loaded and unloaded at run time (lsmod, modprobe). That gives much of the flexibility of a microkernel without the message-passing cost, but modules still run in kernel space, so a buggy module can still crash the system.

sections.question: In which design does a crashing device driver least likely take down the whole OS?
sections.explanation: In a microkernel, drivers run as separate user-space processes, so a crash is contained and the driver can be restarted.

items: Monolithic = fast but less isolated; microkernel = isolated but slower; hybrid = a compromise.
Linux is monolithic with loadable modules; Windows and macOS are hybrids.

content.theory:
Kernel architecture is the decision about which OS services run inside the privileged kernel and which run as ordinary user processes. The choice trades speed against isolation: services inside the kernel call each other quickly but can crash the whole system, while services outside are protected from each other but must communicate through slower messages. This lesson explains monolithic, microkernel, hybrid and layered designs, with the real systems that use each.

## The question every kernel design answers

Every OS has the same list of services: scheduling, memory management, file systems, network stacks and device drivers. A designer must decide which of them run in kernel mode, sharing one address space, and which run in user mode as separate processes. Kernel mode is fast and dangerous; user mode is protected and costs extra communication.

## Monolithic kernels

A monolithic kernel runs all core services in one large kernel address space. The scheduler, memory manager, file systems, network stack and drivers call each other directly as ordinary function calls.

The advantage is speed: reading a file goes from the system-call handler to the file system to the disk driver without any boundary crossings. The disadvantage is that every component shares the kernel's privileges. A bug in one obscure driver can corrupt kernel memory and crash the whole machine, and the kernel's huge code size makes it harder to verify.

Linux and the traditional UNIX kernels are monolithic.

## Loadable kernel modules

Linux softens the monolithic design with **loadable kernel modules**: drivers and file systems that can be added to or removed from a running kernel with `modprobe`, without rebooting. That gives much of the flexibility associated with microkernels. Modules still run in kernel mode, though, so a faulty module can still crash the system.

## Microkernels

A microkernel keeps only the minimum in kernel mode: basic scheduling, address-space management and inter-process communication (IPC). File systems, drivers and network stacks run as user-mode server processes that communicate by passing messages.

Reading a file becomes a conversation: the application sends a message to the file-system server, which sends a message to the disk-driver server, and replies come back the same way. Each message needs the kernel to switch between processes, which costs time.

The payoff is isolation. A crashing driver is one failed process that can be restarted while the rest of the system keeps running. The small kernel is also easier to verify: seL4, a microkernel, has a machine-checked mathematical proof that its code matches its specification. QNX, used in cars and medical devices, and MINIX 3 are microkernels.

## Hybrid kernels

Hybrid kernels start from a microkernel-like structure but move performance-critical services back into kernel mode. Windows NT and its descendants, and Apple's XNU kernel in macOS and iOS (which combines the Mach microkernel with BSD components), are hybrids. In practice they run most services in kernel space, so their behaviour is closer to monolithic than the label suggests.

## Layered design

A layered OS stacks components so each layer uses only the services of the layer below: hardware at the bottom, then memory management, then process management, then file systems, then the user interface. Strict layering makes each layer testable in isolation. In practice it's hard to choose an order, because components need each other in both directions, and every layer crossing adds overhead. Dijkstra's THE system (1968) is the classic example, and modern kernels use layering ideas inside subsystems rather than across the whole OS.

## Comparison

| Design | In kernel mode | Strength | Weakness | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monolithic | All core services | Fast direct calls | One bug can crash all | Linux, traditional UNIX |
| Microkernel | IPC, scheduling, memory | Isolation, verifiability | Message-passing overhead | QNX, seL4, MINIX 3 |
| Hybrid | Most services, microkernel-style structure | Balance | Complexity | Windows NT, macOS XNU |
| Layered | Strict stack of layers | Clean, testable | Hard to order, overhead | THE OS |

## The trend toward isolation in practice

Modern systems borrow microkernel ideas without changing architecture. Linux runs some drivers in user space, eBPF lets small verified programs run safely in the kernel, and virtual machines and containers add isolation layers above the kernel. The core trade-off of speed versus isolation keeps appearing, now at different levels of the stack.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Monolithic vs microkernel": describe what runs in kernel mode in each, then the trade-off between performance and fault isolation. Name Linux as monolithic with loadable modules and Windows or macOS as hybrid. If you mention seL4's formal verification, you show you know why small kernels matter beyond the textbook answer.
