lessons.title: Process, Memory Layout and the PCB
lessons.description: Program vs process, the four sections of a process's memory, and what the Process Control Block stores.

sections.title: Program vs Process
sections.content:
A program is a passive file on disk (an executable). A process is a program in execution: code plus its current activity (program counter, registers, open files, memory).

One program can be running as many processes at once. Three open Chrome windows can mean three separate processes running the same code.

              |        |         |

              |                  |

              |        |         |
              |       Heap       |  malloc / new (grows up)
              +------------------+
              |  Data (globals)  |  initialized + uninitialized (BSS) globals/statics
              +------------------+
 Low address  |   Text (code)    |  machine instructions, read-only

items: A process is a running program: code + data + stack + heap + its CPU state.
The PCB is the kernel's record of a process; context switches save to and restore from it.

content.theory:
A process is a program in execution: the code plus everything that describes its current activity, such as its memory, open files and CPU registers. The process is the OS's main abstraction for running work, and the process control block (PCB) is the kernel's record of each one. This lesson explains the difference between a program and a process, the layout of a process's memory, and what the PCB stores.

## Program versus process

A **program** is a passive file on disk, such as `/usr/bin/python3` or `chrome.exe`. A **process** is an active instance of that program: loaded into memory, with a current instruction, data being changed, and files open.

One program can run as many processes at once. Three terminal windows running Python are three processes executing the same program file, each with its own variables and its own position in the code. Modern browsers go further, running each tab as a separate process so a crashing website can't take down the others.

## The memory layout of a process

Each process sees its own address space, a range of memory addresses that appears to start at zero. The OS divides it into regions:

- **Text (code)**: the machine instructions, usually marked read-only so a bug can't overwrite the program
- **Data**: global and static variables, split into initialized data and BSS (zero-initialized)
- **Heap**: memory allocated at run time with `malloc` or `new`, growing upwards
- **Stack**: one frame per active function call, holding local variables, arguments and return addresses, growing downwards

The heap and stack grow towards each other from opposite ends, which lets either one use the free space between them. Infinite recursion keeps adding stack frames until the stack hits its limit, producing a stack overflow. Allocating memory without freeing it grows the heap until the process runs out, a memory leak.

## The process control block

The kernel tracks every process with a data structure called the **process control block (PCB)**, named `task_struct` in Linux. It contains everything the kernel needs to manage and resume the process:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Process ID and parent ID | Identify the process and its creator |
| State | New, ready, running, waiting or terminated |
| Program counter | Address of the next instruction to run |
| CPU registers | Saved values while the process isn't running |
| Scheduling information | Priority, time used, position in scheduler queues |
| Memory-management information | Page table location, memory limits |
| Open files | Table of files, pipes and sockets the process uses |
| Accounting | CPU time consumed, resource limits |

When a process stops running, the kernel saves its registers and program counter into its PCB. When it runs again, the kernel loads them back, and the process continues as if nothing happened. That save and restore is the context switch, covered in its own lesson.

## Processes form a tree

Every process except the first is created by another process, its parent. On Linux, the first user process (`systemd` or `init`, PID 1) starts system services, which start more processes. Running `pstree` shows this family tree. When a parent exits before its children, PID 1 adopts the orphans, which the fork lesson explains.

## Isolation between processes

Each process has a private address space, enforced by the memory-management hardware. Process A can't read or write process B's memory, even if both run the same program. That isolation is why a crash in one process rarely affects another, and why processes need explicit inter-process communication to share data.

## Seeing processes on a real system

You can inspect processes directly. On Linux, `ps aux` lists them with their IDs, CPU and memory use, and `/proc/<pid>/maps` shows a process's memory regions. On Windows, Task Manager's Details tab shows the same information.

## Process identifiers and limits

Each process gets a process ID (PID), a number the kernel reuses after a process exits and its parent collects its status. Systems cap the number of processes to protect themselves: Linux's `pid_max` has a kernel default of 32,768, and many distributions raise it to 4,194,304 at boot, and per-user limits stop one account from starving the rest. A runaway script that forks endlessly, a fork bomb, is stopped by those limits rather than by luck.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Difference between a program and a process", "What does the PCB contain?" and "Where are local variables stored?" Answer with the passive file versus active instance distinction, list the main PCB fields, and say that local variables live in the stack frame of the function that declared them.

lessons.title: Process States, Queues and Schedulers
lessons.description: The five-state model, suspended states, and long-, short- and medium-term schedulers.

sections.title: Five-State Model
sections.code:
New --admitted--> Ready --dispatch--> Running --exit--> Terminated
                     ^  ^                |   |
                     |  +---interrupt----+   |
                     |   (time slice over)   |
                     |                       | I/O or event wait
                     +--I/O done-- Waiting <-+
sections.explanation: Only Running → Waiting is caused by the process itself (it asks for I/O). Waiting → Running is never a direct transition: the process goes back to Ready first.

Degree of multiprogramming, and the mix of CPU- and I/O-bound jobs
Which ready process runs next (Ready → Running)
Which processes to swap out to disk and back in

sections.title: Suspended States
sections.content:
When memory is tight, the medium-term scheduler swaps a process out to disk:
Ready → Ready-Suspended, and Waiting → Waiting-Suspended.
When it is swapped back in, it returns to Ready or Waiting. This gives the seven-state model.

sections.title: CPU-Bound vs I/O-Bound
sections.content: A CPU-bound process (video encoding) does long computations and has long CPU bursts. An I/O-bound process (text editor, web server) does short CPU bursts between waiting for I/O. A good long-term scheduler admits a mix of both, so neither the CPU nor the devices sit idle.

sections.question: Which transition is NOT possible in the five-state model?
sections.explanation: A waiting process whose I/O finishes moves to Ready and must wait to be dispatched again.

items: States: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated (+ two suspended states).
Long-term: admission; short-term: CPU dispatch; medium-term: swapping.

content.theory:
A process doesn't run continuously from start to finish. It waits for input, gets paused so others can run, and occasionally gets moved out of memory entirely. The process state model describes these stages, and the OS's schedulers decide when a process moves between them. This lesson explains the five-state model, the suspended states, and the three schedulers that control a process's lifecycle.

## The five states

A process is always in exactly one of these states:

- **New**: being created; the OS is setting up its PCB and memory
- **Ready**: able to run and waiting for a CPU
- **Running**: executing instructions on a CPU
- **Waiting (blocked)**: unable to continue until an event happens, such as a disk read finishing or a key press
- **Terminated**: finished; the OS is cleaning up its resources

On a single core, only one process is running at a time; the rest are ready or waiting. A machine with 8 cores can have up to 8 running processes at once.

## The transitions

The transitions between states each have a specific cause:

- **New to ready**: the OS admits the process
- **Ready to running**: the scheduler dispatches it to a CPU
- **Running to ready**: a timer interrupt ends its time slice, or a higher-priority process arrives
- **Running to waiting**: the process requests input or output, or waits for an event
- **Waiting to ready**: the event completes, such as the disk read finishing
- **Running to terminated**: the process exits or is killed

One transition never happens: waiting directly to running. When a waiting process's event completes, it joins the ready queue and must be dispatched again. The scheduler stays in control of who gets the CPU.

## Queues

The OS organizes processes into queues. The **ready queue** holds processes waiting for a CPU. Each device has a **device queue** of processes waiting for it. Scheduling is the job of moving processes between these queues and the CPU.

## Suspended states

When memory runs short, the OS can move a whole process out of memory to disk (swap it out). That adds two states:

- **Ready-suspended**: would be ready, but its memory is on disk
- **Waiting-suspended**: waiting for an event, and its memory is on disk

When memory frees up, the process is swapped back in and returns to ready or waiting. With these, the model has seven states. Modern systems usually swap individual pages rather than whole processes, but the idea of suspension remains.

## Three schedulers

Different schedulers make decisions at different time scales:

| Scheduler | Decision | Frequency | Controls |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long-term (job scheduler) | Which new jobs to admit into memory | Rarely, seconds to minutes | The degree of multiprogramming |
| Short-term (CPU scheduler) | Which ready process runs next | Hundreds of times per second | CPU allocation |
| Medium-term (swapper) | Which processes to swap out and back in | Occasionally | Memory pressure |

The short-term scheduler must be fast, because it runs hundreds of times per second, and time spent choosing is time not spent running programs. The long-term scheduler matters most in batch systems; desktop systems admit nearly every program you launch.

## CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes

Processes behave differently while running:

- **CPU-bound**: long stretches of computation and few input or output requests, such as video encoding or training a model
- **I/O-bound**: short bursts of computation between frequent waits, such as a text editor, web server or database client

A good mix keeps both the CPU and the devices busy. If every process is CPU-bound, devices sit idle; if every process is I/O-bound, the CPU sits idle while everything waits. Schedulers often favour I/O-bound processes, because they use the CPU briefly and then free it, which keeps interactive programs responsive.

## Following one process through its states

A student runs a script that reads a large CSV file and prints a summary. It starts in **new**, is admitted to **ready**, and gets dispatched to **running**. Its first `read` call blocks it in **waiting** until the disk returns data, after which it goes back to **ready**. While it parses rows its time slice expires several times, cycling between **running** and **ready**. When it prints the summary and exits, it moves to **terminated**, and its parent shell collects the exit status.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Draw the process state diagram" and "Which transition is impossible?" Draw the five states with labelled transitions, and point out that a waiting process can't move straight to running. For "long-term vs short-term scheduler", contrast how often each runs and what each controls.

lessons.title: Context Switching
lessons.description: What is saved and restored when the CPU switches processes, and why switches are expensive.

sections.title: What Happens
sections.content:
A context switch is the CPU moving from one process (or thread) to another:
1. A timer interrupt, system call or I/O wait enters the kernel.
2. The kernel saves the current process's registers, program counter and stack pointer into its PCB.
3. The scheduler picks the next process.
4. The kernel loads that process's saved state from its PCB and switches the memory mapping (page-table base register).
5. Execution resumes where that process left off.

sections.title: Why Switches Are Costly
items: **Pure overhead**: no user work happens during the switch (typically microseconds).
**Cache and TLB pollution**: the new process's data isn't cached; switching address spaces often flushes the TLB.
**Thread switches are cheaper** than process switches within the same process, because the address space stays the same.

sections.question: If a context switch takes 1 ms and the Round Robin time quantum is 4 ms, what fraction of CPU time is wasted on switching?
sections.answerReveal: Each cycle is 4 ms of work plus 1 ms of switching, so 1/5 = 20% is overhead. That's why quanta are much larger than switch times (typically 10-100 ms against microsecond switches).

sections.question: Where is a process's state saved during a context switch?
sections.explanation: Registers, the program counter and other CPU state are saved in the PCB and restored from it later.

items: A context switch saves state to one PCB and loads it from another.
It is pure overhead, plus cache and TLB misses afterwards; thread switches are cheaper than process switches.

content.theory:
A context switch is the CPU stopping one process (or thread) and starting another, saving everything needed to resume the first one later. Context switches make multitasking possible, and they're pure overhead: no user work happens while one is in progress. This lesson explains what's saved, what triggers a switch, why switches cost more than their direct time, and why switching threads is cheaper than switching processes.

## Why switch at all

A single core runs one instruction stream at a time. To run dozens of processes "at once", the OS switches between them many times per second. Each process must believe it ran continuously, so the OS must save exactly where it stopped and restore it perfectly later.

## What triggers a switch

Three situations hand control to the kernel, which may then switch:

- **Timer interrupt**: the running process's time slice expired
- **Blocking system call**: the process asked for something slow, such as reading from disk, so it can't continue until the request completes
- **Higher-priority work**: an interrupt makes a more important process ready, and the scheduler preempts the current one

Not every entry into the kernel causes a switch. A fast system call such as `getpid` returns to the same process.

## The steps of a switch

When the kernel decides to switch from process A to process B, it follows these steps:

1. Save A's CPU state (program counter, stack pointer, general-purpose registers) into A's PCB
2. Update A's state to ready or waiting and place it in the right queue
3. Ask the scheduler to choose the next process, B
4. Switch the memory mapping to B's address space, by loading B's page-table base into the CPU
5. Restore B's saved CPU state from B's PCB
6. Return to user mode, continuing B at the instruction where it last stopped

From A's point of view, nothing happened except that the clock jumped forward.

## The direct cost

Saving and restoring registers takes a few microseconds on modern hardware. That's small, but it adds up: a system doing 10,000 switches per second spends time on overhead that grows with the switch rate. This is why schedulers choose time slices of several milliseconds rather than microseconds.

A useful exercise: if a context switch takes 1 ms and the time slice is 4 ms, each cycle spends 1 ms switching and 4 ms working, so 1/5, or 20%, of CPU time is wasted. With a 100 ms slice, the waste falls below 1%, but interactive programs wait longer for their turn.

## The indirect cost: cold caches

The larger cost comes after the switch. The CPU keeps recently used data in fast caches, and it keeps recent address translations in the translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Process B's data isn't in those caches, so its first instructions miss repeatedly and wait for main memory, which is roughly 100 times slower than the L1 cache.

Switching address spaces can also invalidate TLB entries, so every memory access must walk the page tables again until the TLB refills. Modern CPUs reduce this with tagged TLB entries (process-context identifiers on x86), which let entries from several processes coexist.

## Threads switch more cheaply

Threads of the same process share one address space. Switching between them skips step 4 entirely: there's no page-table change and no TLB disruption, and the shared code and data may still be in the caches. That's a large part of why threads are called lightweight, and why a busy server uses a pool of threads rather than one process per request.

## Measuring switches

On Linux, `vmstat 1` reports context switches per second in its `cs` column, and `pidstat -w` breaks them down per process into voluntary switches (the process blocked) and involuntary ones (it was preempted). A high involuntary count suggests too many busy threads competing for too few cores.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a context switch and what's saved during it?" and "Why are thread switches cheaper than process switches?" For the first, list the saved state and the PCB's role. For the second, explain that threads share an address space, so there's no page-table switch and the caches and TLB stay useful. The time-slice overhead calculation is a common follow-up.

With n = 4: 16 processes in total, 15 of them new children.

Short-circuit evaluation: the first child gets 0 from the first fork(), so && stops and it skips the rest. The parent calls the second fork(); that child also gets 0 and skips. Only the parent reaches the third fork(). Parent + 3 children = 4.

Parent finished while the child is still running
Dead, but its PCB entry and exit status remain
The parent calling wait(); if the parent dies, init/systemd reaps it
Adopted by init (PID 1) or a subreaper, which reaps it later

sections.question: How many times is "hello" printed? fork(); fork(); printf("hello");
sections.explanation: Two forks give 2^2 = 4 processes, and each one prints once.

n sequential forks → 2^n processes (2^n − 1 children).
Zombie = finished but not reaped; orphan = parent died first and init adopts it.

content.theory:
On UNIX-like systems, new processes are created by copying an existing one with `fork()` and then, usually, replacing the copy's program with `exec()`. The parent can wait for the child with `wait()`. This pair of steps is unusual, and it explains several behaviours that appear in interviews: fork-counting puzzles, zombie processes and orphan processes. This lesson explains each call and each behaviour.

## fork: one call, two returns

`fork()` creates a new process that's a near-exact copy of the caller: same code, same variables, same open files, and the same position in the program. Both processes continue from the line after `fork()`. The only difference is the return value:

- in the child, `fork()` returns 0
- in the parent, it returns the child's process ID
- on failure, it returns −1 in the parent and no child exists

Programs use that return value to branch: `if (pid == 0)` runs child code, and the else branch runs parent code. The copy is independent, so a variable changed in the child doesn't change in the parent.

## Copy-on-write makes fork cheap

Copying gigabytes of memory for every `fork()` would be slow, and usually wasted, because the child often replaces itself immediately with `exec()`. Modern kernels use **copy-on-write**: parent and child initially share the same physical memory pages, marked read-only. Only when one of them writes to a page does the kernel copy that single page. A fork followed by exec copies almost nothing.

## exec: replace the program

`exec()` (in variants such as `execlp` and `execvp`) loads a new program into the current process, replacing its code, data, heap and stack. The process ID stays the same, and open files stay open unless marked close-on-exec. If `exec()` succeeds, it never returns, because the code that called it no longer exists.

A shell runs a command by combining the two: it forks, the child execs the command, and the parent waits. Separating creation from loading lets the child adjust things in between, such as redirecting its output to a file before exec. That's how `ls > files.txt` works.

## wait: collect the child

`wait()` (or `waitpid()`) makes the parent block until a child exits, then returns the child's exit status. That status tells the parent whether the child succeeded and lets the kernel finish cleaning up the child.

## Counting fork calls

Every `fork()` doubles the number of processes executing the code after it. Three calls in a row, `fork(); fork(); fork();`, produce 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 processes, so a following `printf` prints 8 times. In general, n sequential forks give 2^n processes, of which 2^n − 1 are new children.

Conditions change the count. In `if (fork() && fork()) fork();`, the first child gets 0 from the first fork, so the `&&` short-circuits and that child skips the rest. The parent calls the second fork, whose child also gets 0 and skips. Only the parent reaches the third fork, so the total is 4 processes. For any puzzle with conditions, trace each branch instead of applying the formula.

## Zombie processes

When a child exits, the kernel frees its memory but keeps a small entry in the process table, holding its exit status, until the parent calls `wait()`. A child in this state is a **zombie**: it's dead, but its entry remains.

A few zombies are harmless and disappear when the parent collects them. A parent that creates many children and never waits for them fills the process table, and eventually the system can't create new processes. The fix is to call `wait()`, or to handle the `SIGCHLD` signal and wait for children as they exit.

## Orphan processes

An **orphan** is a child whose parent exits first. The orphan keeps running normally. The kernel re-parents it to PID 1 (`init` or `systemd`), which periodically waits for its adopted children, so orphans never become permanent zombies. Background services are often started as deliberate orphans, a technique called daemonizing.

## Windows takes a different approach

Windows creates processes with one call, `CreateProcess`, which creates a new process and loads a program in a single step. There's no fork-then-exec split, which is simpler to use but less flexible for tasks such as setting up redirection between the two steps.

## How interviewers test this

Expect fork-counting puzzles, "What does fork return?", and "Zombie vs orphan". For counting, use 2^n for sequential calls and trace branches when conditions appear. For zombie versus orphan, say who died first: a zombie is a dead child whose parent hasn't waited; an orphan is a living child whose parent died.

lessons.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
lessons.description: Shared memory vs message passing, pipes, message queues, sockets and signals.

sections.title: Why IPC?
sections.content: Processes have separate address spaces, so they can't read each other's variables. IPC mechanisms let cooperating processes exchange data and coordinate (for example, a shell piping ls into grep, or a browser's tab processes talking to its main process).

sections.title: The Two Models
rows: A memory region is mapped into both processes
The kernel copies messages between processes (send / receive)
Fastest: no kernel involvement after setup
Slower: a system call and a copy per message
The programmer must add it (semaphores, mutexes)

sections.title: IPC Mechanisms
rows: One-way byte stream between related processes, e.g. `ls | grep txt`
Has a name in the file system; unrelated processes can use it
Works within one machine or over a network; the basis of client-server apps
Asynchronous notification with no data, e.g. SIGKILL, SIGINT (Ctrl+C)

sections.question: Two processes on the same machine must exchange large video frames as fast as possible. Best choice?
sections.explanation: Shared memory avoids copying data through the kernel. Add a semaphore or mutex to coordinate access.

items: Shared memory is fastest but needs synchronization; message passing is simpler and safer.
Pipes are one-way; sockets work across a network; signals carry no data.

content.theory:
Processes are isolated by design: each has a private address space, so one process can't read another's variables. Inter-process communication (IPC) covers the mechanisms the OS provides for processes that need to cooperate, such as a shell pipeline or a browser's tab processes talking to its main process. This lesson explains the two IPC models, shared memory and message passing, and the main mechanisms built on them.

## Why processes need IPC

Splitting work across processes has real benefits: isolation (a crash in one doesn't kill the others), security (each process gets only the permissions it needs), and parallelism across cores. Chrome runs each site in its own process for exactly these reasons. But cooperating processes must exchange data, and isolation means they can't do it by sharing variables.

## The two models

Every IPC mechanism follows one of two models:

| | Shared memory | Message passing |
|---|---|---|
| How it works | A region of memory is mapped into both processes | The kernel copies data from sender to receiver |
| Speed | Fastest; no kernel involvement after setup | Slower; a system call and copy per message |
| Synchronization | Your responsibility (semaphores, mutexes) | Built into send and receive |
| Works across machines | No | Yes, with sockets |
| Typical use | Large data on one machine | Small messages, distributed systems |

## Shared memory

With shared memory, two processes ask the kernel to map the same physical pages into both address spaces, using `shmget` or `mmap` on Linux. After that, a write by one process is visible to the other immediately, at memory speed.

The danger is that the kernel no longer coordinates access. If both processes update the same counter at once, they can lose updates, exactly as threads do. Shared memory is always paired with synchronization such as a semaphore, covered in the synchronization module. Databases such as PostgreSQL use shared memory for their buffer cache, with careful locking around it.

## Pipes

A **pipe** is a one-way byte stream: one process writes into one end and another reads from the other. Anonymous pipes connect related processes, typically a parent and child, and the shell uses them for pipelines:

~~~bash
ps aux | grep python | wc -l
~~~

The shell creates two pipes and three processes, connecting each process's output to the next one's input. The kernel buffers data between them (typically 64 KB on Linux) and blocks a writer when the buffer is full or a reader when it's empty, which gives automatic flow control.

**Named pipes (FIFOs)** have a name in the file system, created with `mkfifo`, so unrelated processes can open them like files.

## Message queues

A message queue is a kernel-managed list of discrete messages. Unlike a pipe's continuous byte stream, each message keeps its boundaries and can carry a type or priority, so a receiver can pick messages of a particular type. POSIX and System V both provide message queues.

## Sockets

A **socket** is an endpoint for communication that works between processes on the same machine (UNIX domain sockets) or across a network (TCP and UDP sockets). Sockets are the foundation of client-server programs: a web server listens on a socket, and each browser connection is a socket pair. Because the same interface works locally and remotely, a program can move from one machine to many without changing how it communicates.

## Signals

A **signal** is an asynchronous notification with no data attached beyond its type. `SIGINT` is sent when you press Ctrl+C, `SIGTERM` asks a process to exit cleanly, and `SIGKILL` terminates it immediately and can't be caught. A process can install handlers for most signals, for example to save work before exiting. Signals tell a process that something happened; they don't transfer data.

## Choosing a mechanism

Match the mechanism to the need:

- **Large data, same machine, maximum speed**: shared memory plus a semaphore
- **Streaming output from one process to the next**: a pipe
- **Discrete messages with priorities**: a message queue
- **Client and server, possibly on different machines**: sockets
- **Notifying a process of an event**: a signal

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What are the IPC mechanisms?" and "Shared memory vs message passing". List the mechanisms with one use each, then compare the two models on speed, synchronization and whether they work across machines. Explaining how the shell builds a pipeline from pipes is a strong concrete example.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution that can be scheduled on a CPU. A process can contain many threads, all running inside the same address space.

Example: a word processor might use one thread for typing, one for spell-check and one for auto-save, all working on the same document in memory.

content.theory:
A thread is an independent sequence of instructions inside a process. A process can run several threads, and they all share the process's memory while each keeps its own place in the code. Threads let one program do several things at once without the cost and isolation of separate processes. This lesson explains what threads share, what each owns, and the trade-offs between threads and processes.

## The idea

A process is a container: an address space, open files and other resources. A thread is an activity running inside that container. Every process starts with one thread, and it can create more.

Consider a word processor. One thread responds to your typing, a second checks spelling in the background, and a third saves a backup every few minutes. All three work on the same document in memory. If they were separate processes, each would need its own copy of the document, or a shared-memory arrangement to keep one copy in sync.

## What threads share and what they own

Threads of the same process share everything that belongs to the process, and each keeps what it needs to run independently:

| Shared by all threads | Private to each thread |
|---|---|
| Code (text section) | Thread ID |
| Global and static data | Program counter |
| Heap (dynamically allocated memory) | CPU registers |
| Open files and sockets | Stack (local variables, call frames) |
| Signal handlers, working directory | Thread-local storage |

The private stack is what lets each thread call functions independently. The shared heap is what lets threads cooperate without copying data.

## Why threads are cheaper

Creating a process means building a new address space, page tables and a PCB. Creating a thread needs only a stack and a small thread control block (TCB), because the address space already exists. Switching between threads of one process also skips the page-table switch, so the caches and translation lookaside buffer stay useful. On Linux, creating a thread is commonly several times faster than creating a process, and the gap grows with the size of the process's memory.

## Communication is free, and dangerous

Threads communicate by reading and writing shared variables, with no system call and no copying. That's their biggest advantage and their biggest risk. If two threads increment a shared counter at once, both can read the old value, add one, and write back the same result, losing an update. Shared data needs synchronization, which the synchronization module covers in detail.

## Isolation is weaker

Processes protect each other: a crash in one leaves the others running. Threads offer no such protection. A thread that dereferences a bad pointer causes a segmentation fault that terminates the entire process, killing every thread in it. A thread that corrupts the heap breaks every other thread that uses the heap.

## When to choose which

Choose processes for isolation and threads for cheap sharing:

- **Processes**: untrusted or crash-prone work (browser tabs), separate programs, security boundaries, using several machines
- **Threads**: parallel work on shared data within one program, responsive user interfaces, servers handling many connections

Many systems combine both. Chrome uses a process per site for isolation and many threads inside each process. PostgreSQL uses a process per connection, while MySQL uses a thread per connection: two valid answers to the same design question.

## Threads in practice

In Java, you start a thread by giving a `Runnable` to a `Thread` and calling `start()`. In Python, the `threading` module does the same, though the global interpreter lock (GIL) in standard CPython lets only one thread run Python code at a time, so threads help with waiting on input and output more than with parallel computation. In C, POSIX threads (`pthread_create`) provide the same model.

## Concurrency bugs depend on timing

Thread bugs are hard because they depend on the exact interleaving of instructions, which changes from run to run. A race condition might appear once in a thousand runs, or only on a machine with more cores. Testing alone rarely proves thread code correct; careful design with locks, immutable data and well-tested concurrent collections does.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Process vs thread" and "What do threads share?" Answer with the table: shared code, data, heap and files; private stack, registers and program counter. Then give one trade-off each way: threads are cheaper and share data directly, while processes isolate failures.

content.theory:
Threads can be managed by a library in user space, by the kernel, or by a combination of both. The choice decides whether one blocked thread stalls the whole program and whether threads can use several CPU cores at once. This lesson explains user-level and kernel-level threads and the three ways of mapping one onto the other, with the languages and systems that use each.

## Who knows about the threads?

The central question is whether the kernel knows a thread exists. If it does, the kernel can schedule that thread on any core and keep the others running when it blocks. If it doesn't, the kernel sees only the process, and every scheduling decision about the threads happens in user space.

## User-level threads

User-level threads are created and scheduled by a library inside the process. The kernel sees one schedulable entity. Switching between user threads is a function call within the process, with no system call and no mode switch, so it's fast.

The weaknesses follow from the kernel's ignorance:

- **One blocks, all block**: if one user thread makes a blocking system call such as reading a file, the kernel blocks the whole process, including threads that could have run
- **No parallelism**: the kernel gives the process one CPU at a time, so its threads can't run on several cores at once

## Kernel-level threads

Kernel-level threads are known to and scheduled by the kernel. Each has its own entry in the kernel's scheduling structures. When one blocks on input or output, the kernel runs another thread of the same process, and threads can run truly in parallel on different cores.

The cost is that creating, switching and synchronizing kernel threads involves the kernel, which is slower than a function call in user space. Creating hundreds of thousands of them also uses significant kernel memory, mostly for their stacks.

## Many-to-one

The many-to-one model maps many user threads onto a single kernel thread. It's cheap and portable, and it inherits every weakness of user-level threads: one blocking call stops everything, and there's no parallelism. Early Java "green threads" and some older thread libraries used it. It has mostly disappeared from general-purpose systems.

## One-to-one

The one-to-one model maps each user thread to its own kernel thread. Blocking and parallelism both work correctly, at the cost of kernel involvement for every thread. Linux's POSIX threads (NPTL), Windows threads and Java's traditional platform threads all use one-to-one. It's the default in most systems today because kernels became efficient enough at managing many threads.

## Many-to-many

The many-to-many model multiplexes M user threads over N kernel threads, with M usually much larger than N. A user-space scheduler assigns runnable user threads to the available kernel threads, and when one blocks, the runtime moves the others to different kernel threads. You get cheap user threads and real parallelism together, at the cost of a complex runtime.

Go's goroutines work this way: a Go program can run hundreds of thousands of goroutines over a small pool of kernel threads, roughly one per core. Java 21's virtual threads follow the same idea: millions of lightweight threads mounted on a few carrier threads, with blocking operations automatically unmounting the virtual thread so its carrier can run another.

## Comparison

| Model | Mapping | Blocking call | Parallelism | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Many-to-one | Many user threads to 1 kernel thread | Blocks every thread | None | Early Java green threads |
| One-to-one | Each user thread to its own kernel thread | Blocks only that thread | Yes | Linux pthreads, Windows, Java platform threads |
| Many-to-many | M user threads over N kernel threads | Runtime reschedules others | Yes | Go goroutines, Java virtual threads |

## Why many-to-many is coming back

Servers that handle tens of thousands of simultaneous connections can't afford a kernel thread per connection, but writing them with callbacks is hard to read and debug. Many-to-many runtimes let programmers write ordinary blocking code, one thread per connection, while the runtime keeps the number of kernel threads small. That's the motivation behind both goroutines and Java's virtual threads.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "User-level vs kernel-level threads" and "What happens in the many-to-one model when one thread blocks?" Explain that the kernel only sees one entity, so the whole process blocks. Then name the model your favourite platform uses: one-to-one for Linux and Java platform threads, many-to-many for Go and Java virtual threads.

lessons.title: Multithreading: Benefits, Concurrency vs Parallelism, Thread Pools
lessons.description: Why programs use threads, Amdahl's law, and practical patterns such as thread pools.

sections.title: Benefits of Multithreading
items: **Responsiveness**: the UI thread stays responsive while a background thread works.
**Resource sharing**: threads share memory without IPC.
**Economy**: creating and switching threads is cheaper than for processes.
**Scalability**: work spreads across CPU cores.

sections.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
sections.content:
Concurrency: several tasks make progress over the same period. On one core they take turns (interleaving).
Parallelism: several tasks run at the same instant on different cores.

Concurrency is about structure (dealing with many things); parallelism is about execution (doing many things at once). You can have concurrency without parallelism, but not the reverse.

sections.title: Amdahl's Law
sections.content:
If a fraction S of a program is serial, the maximum speedup with N cores is:
Speedup ≤ 1 / (S + (1 − S) / N)

Example: S = 0.25 (25% serial), N = 4 cores: 1 / (0.25 + 0.75/4) = 1 / 0.4375 ≈ 2.29×. Even with infinitely many cores, the limit is 1 / 0.25 = 4×. The serial part sets the ceiling.

sections.title: Thread Pools
sections.content: Creating a thread per request (for example, per web request) wastes time and can exhaust memory under load. A thread pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue. Java's ExecutorService, web servers and database connection handling all use this pattern.

sections.question: A program is 40% serial. What is the maximum possible speedup with unlimited cores?
sections.explanation: 1 / S = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5×. The serial part can't be sped up.

items: Concurrency = interleaved progress; parallelism = simultaneous execution.
Amdahl's law: the serial fraction limits speedup to 1/S.
Use thread pools instead of a thread per task.

content.theory:
Multithreading lets one program use several CPU cores and stay responsive while waiting for slow work. It also introduces limits that more cores can't fix, and patterns that keep threaded code manageable. This lesson explains the benefits of threads, the difference between concurrency and parallelism, Amdahl's law, and why real programs use thread pools instead of creating a thread per task.

## Four benefits

Threads give a program four advantages:

- **Responsiveness**: a user interface thread keeps reacting to clicks while a background thread loads a file
- **Resource sharing**: threads share memory, so cooperating parts of a program exchange data without copying it
- **Economy**: creating and switching threads is cheaper than creating and switching processes
- **Scalability**: work divided across threads can run on every core of a multicore machine

## Concurrency and parallelism

These two words are often used interchangeably, and they mean different things. **Concurrency** is about structure: several tasks are in progress during the same period, possibly taking turns on one core. **Parallelism** is about execution: several tasks run at the same instant on different cores.

A single-core machine running a music player and a browser is concurrent but not parallel; the OS switches between them. An 8-core machine encoding a video in 8 pieces is parallel. You can have concurrency without parallelism, but parallelism needs concurrency, because you must first divide the work into independent tasks.

## Amdahl's law

Splitting work across more cores helps only with the part that can be split. If a fraction S of a program must run serially, the maximum speedup with N cores is:

~~~text
Speedup ≤ 1 / (S + (1 − S) / N)
~~~

Take a program that's 25% serial on 4 cores: 1 / (0.25 + 0.75 / 4) = 1 / 0.4375, about 2.29 times faster, not 4. With infinitely many cores the limit is 1 / S = 4 times. The serial part sets the ceiling, which is why reducing serial work, such as a single shared lock every thread waits for, often matters more than adding cores.

## Gustafson's view

Amdahl's law assumes a fixed problem size. In practice, people often use more cores to solve bigger problems in the same time, for example simulating a finer grid or training on more data. Gustafson's law describes that case, where the parallel part grows with the machine and speedups scale much better. Both views are correct; they answer different questions.

## Thread pools

Creating a new thread for every task, such as every web request, has three problems. Thread creation costs time on every request. Under a traffic spike the server creates thousands of threads, each with its own stack, and runs out of memory. And with far more runnable threads than cores, the CPU spends its time switching between them instead of working.

A **thread pool** solves all three. It keeps a fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue. Requests wait in the queue when all workers are busy, which bounds memory use and keeps the number of runnable threads near the number of cores. Java's `ExecutorService`, web servers such as Tomcat, and database connection pools all follow this pattern.

## Sizing a pool

For CPU-bound work, a pool about the size of the core count is usually right, since more threads only add switching. For I/O-bound work, threads spend most of their time waiting, so a larger pool keeps the CPU busy. A common estimate is cores × (1 + wait time / compute time). Measure under realistic load rather than trusting any formula.

## Common threading problems

Threads bring their own failure modes:

- **Race conditions**: results depend on timing because shared data isn't protected
- **Deadlocks**: threads wait for each other's locks forever
- **Starvation**: a thread never gets the resource it needs because others always win
- **Contention**: many threads wait on one lock, so adding threads adds waiting instead of speed

Modern practice reduces these by sharing less: immutable data, message passing between threads, and thread-safe collections such as Java's `ConcurrentHashMap`.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Concurrency vs parallelism" and an Amdahl's law calculation. State the distinction with the single-core example, and for Amdahl, show the formula, the numbers, and the 1 / S ceiling. Mentioning thread pools and why they beat one thread per request is a common follow-up in backend interviews.

Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away (a timer interrupt, or a higher-priority process arriving). Every modern general-purpose OS is preemptive.

sections.question: A process arrives at t = 2, needs 4 units of CPU, and completes at t = 11. Its waiting time is:

items: TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT; RT = first run − AT.
Draw the Gantt chart first; every number comes from it.

content.theory:
CPU scheduling decides which ready process runs next. Before comparing algorithms, you need a precise way to measure what "good" means, and that's what the scheduling criteria and timing formulas provide. This lesson defines arrival, burst, completion, turnaround, waiting and response time, explains preemptive versus non-preemptive scheduling, and shows how to compute every metric from a Gantt chart.

## Why scheduling matters

With more ready processes than cores, some must wait. The scheduler's choices decide whether an interactive editor feels instant or sluggish, whether a batch job finishes overnight or by morning, and whether any process waits forever. Different systems want different things, so there's no single best algorithm, only the best fit for a goal.

## Preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling

A **non-preemptive** scheduler lets the running process keep the CPU until it finishes or blocks for input or output. A **preemptive** scheduler can take the CPU away, when a time slice expires or when a higher-priority process becomes ready.

Non-preemptive scheduling is simpler to implement and avoids some synchronization problems inside the kernel, but one long process can make everyone else wait. Every modern general-purpose OS is preemptive, because responsiveness matters more than that simplicity.

## The time definitions

Every scheduling calculation uses these quantities:

| Term | Meaning | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| Arrival time (AT) | When the process enters the ready queue | Given |
| Burst time (BT) | CPU time the process needs | Given |
| Completion time (CT) | When the process finishes | Read from the Gantt chart |
| Turnaround time (TAT) | Total time from arrival to completion | TAT = CT − AT |
| Waiting time (WT) | Time spent ready but not running | WT = TAT − BT |
| Response time (RT) | Time until the process first runs | RT = first start − AT |

For a process that never blocks, waiting time is everything in its turnaround that isn't running. Turnaround minus the time it actually ran (its burst) gives exactly that.

## A worked calculation

A process arrives at time 2, needs 4 units of CPU, first runs at time 5 and completes at time 11. Its turnaround is 11 − 2 = 9, its waiting time is 9 − 4 = 5, and its response time is 5 − 2 = 3.

The difference between waiting and response time matters with preemption. A process can start quickly, giving low response time, then get preempted several times, giving high waiting time. Interactive systems care most about response time, because users notice the first reaction.

## The Gantt chart

A Gantt chart is a timeline showing which process runs during each interval, such as `| P1 0–5 | P2 5–8 | P3 8–9 |`. Every metric comes from it: completion times are where each process's last block ends, and first-start times give response times. Drawing the chart carefully is most of the work in any scheduling question; the arithmetic afterwards is mechanical.

## What schedulers optimize

| Criterion | Goal | Who cares most |
|---|---|---|
| CPU utilization | Maximize | Everyone; an idle CPU is waste |
| Throughput | Maximize (processes finished per unit time) | Batch systems |
| Turnaround time | Minimize | Batch users waiting for results |
| Waiting time | Minimize | The direct target of the algorithm |
| Response time | Minimize | Interactive users |
| Fairness | No process starves | Shared systems |

These goals conflict. Running the shortest jobs first minimizes average waiting time but can starve long jobs. Short time slices improve response time but waste CPU on context switches. Choosing an algorithm means choosing which goals matter most.

## Waiting time is what scheduling controls

A process's burst time is fixed by its code, so the scheduler can't change how long a process computes. What it can change is how long processes wait in the ready queue, which is why waiting time is the standard measure for comparing algorithms in exams.

## Dispatch latency

Switching from one process to another isn't free. The dispatcher saves state, switches memory mappings and restores the next process, and the time this takes is called dispatch latency. Exam problems usually ignore it, but real schedulers account for it when choosing time-slice lengths, because switching too often wastes CPU time.

## How interviewers test this

Exams give a table of arrival and burst times and an algorithm, then ask for average waiting or turnaround time. Draw the Gantt chart first, then fill a table with CT, TAT = CT − AT and WT = TAT − BT for each process. Interviewers also ask "Preemptive vs non-preemptive", answered with what triggers a switch in each.

sections.title: How Can SJF Know Burst Times?
sections.content:
It can't know them exactly. Real systems predict the next CPU burst using exponential averaging:
τ(n+1) = α · t(n) + (1 − α) · τ(n)
where t(n) is the actual length of the last burst, τ(n) the previous prediction, and α (often 0.5) controls how much recent history counts.

sections.question: Which algorithm suffers from the convoy effect?
sections.explanation: In FCFS one long CPU-bound job holds up all the short jobs queued behind it.

items: FCFS: arrival order, convoy effect.
SJF: shortest burst first, optimal non-preemptive average WT.
SRTF: preemptive SJF, optimal average WT, risk of starvation.

content.theory:
First-come-first-served (FCFS), shortest job first (SJF) and shortest remaining time first (SRTF) are the three classic algorithms that order processes by arrival or by length. They're the foundation for every scheduling question, and comparing them shows why the order of execution changes average waiting time so much. This lesson explains each algorithm, its strengths and failures, and how real systems approximate burst lengths they can't know in advance.

## First-come-first-served

FCFS runs processes in the order they arrive, each to completion. It's a single FIFO queue: fair in a narrow sense, never starving anyone, and trivial to implement.

Its weakness is the **convoy effect**. If a long CPU-bound process arrives first, every short process behind it waits for the whole thing. In the course's example workload (P1 arrives at 0 needing 5 units, followed by short jobs P2, P3 and P4), FCFS gives an average waiting time of 4.0, mostly because P3 and P4 wait behind P1 and P2.

The convoy effect also hurts devices. While the long job computes, I/O-bound processes sit in the ready queue instead of keeping the disk busy, so both the CPU and the devices are used poorly.

## Shortest job first

SJF picks the ready process with the shortest next CPU burst. It's non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst.

Running short jobs first is provably optimal for average waiting time among non-preemptive algorithms. The intuition: a job that runs early delays every job behind it by its own length, so putting short jobs first minimizes the total delay. On the example workload, SJF lowers the average waiting time from 4.0 to 3.25.

## Shortest remaining time first

SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, the scheduler compares its burst with the remaining time of the running process, and preempts if the newcomer is shorter. On the example, SRTF lowers the average waiting time further, to 2.25, the best of the three, because short arrivals never wait behind a long job in progress.

SRTF is optimal for average waiting time among all algorithms, but it pays for that with more context switches and the risk below.

## Starvation

Both SJF and SRTF can starve long processes. If short jobs keep arriving, a long job may wait indefinitely, because there's always something shorter to run. FCFS never starves anyone, which is one reason pure SJF is rare in practice. The usual fix, aging, raises a waiting process's priority over time and appears in the priority scheduling lesson.

## Predicting burst times

SJF needs to know the next burst length, and the OS can't know the future. Real systems predict it from history using **exponential averaging**:

~~~text
τ(n+1) = α · t(n) + (1 − α) · τ(n)
~~~

Here t(n) is the measured length of the most recent burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α (between 0 and 1, often 0.5) sets how much weight recent behaviour gets. With α = 0.5, the prediction is the average of the last actual burst and the last prediction, so older bursts fade geometrically. An interactive process that keeps doing short bursts earns a short prediction and gets scheduled quickly.

## Comparison on the example workload

| Algorithm | Preemptive | Average waiting time | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| FCFS | No | 4.00 | Convoy effect |
| SJF | No | 3.25 | Starvation; needs burst estimates |
| SRTF | Yes | 2.25 | Starvation; more switches; needs estimates |

## Where these ideas appear today

Pure FCFS still runs inside many systems where fairness of order matters more than average speed: print queues, network packet queues and most message brokers. SJF's idea survives in schedulers that favour short or interactive work, and in database and web servers that prioritize cheap requests so a few expensive reports can't stall everyone. Shortest-remaining-time thinking also appears in disk and network schedulers that serve the smallest pending transfers first.

## Tie-breaking

When two processes have equal bursts or remaining times, exams usually break ties by arrival time, then by process number. State your tie-breaking rule when you answer, because a different rule can change the Gantt chart and therefore the averages.

## How interviewers test this

Exams ask you to compute average waiting and turnaround times for these algorithms on a given workload, and interviewers ask "Which algorithm minimizes average waiting time?" The answer is SRTF overall and SJF among non-preemptive algorithms. Follow it with the catch: both need burst predictions and can starve long jobs.

sections.content:
Each process gets a fixed time quantum q. If it doesn't finish within q, it is preempted and goes to the back of the ready queue. RR is designed for time-sharing: no process waits more than (n − 1) × q before it runs again.

Queue rule used here (the common exam convention): when a process arrives at the same moment another's quantum expires, the new arrival enters the queue first, then the preempted process.

sections.title: Priority Scheduling
sections.content:
Each process has a priority, and the CPU goes to the highest-priority ready process. (Check the convention in the question: in many textbooks a smaller number means higher priority.) It can be preemptive or non-preemptive.

Problem: starvation. Low-priority processes may never run if higher-priority work keeps arriving.
Solution: aging. Gradually raise the priority of processes that have been waiting a long time, so every process eventually runs.

traps.question: Is SJF a special case of priority scheduling?
traps.trap: Saying no, they're different algorithms.
traps.solution: Yes. SJF is priority scheduling where priority = predicted next CPU burst (shorter means higher priority). FCFS is priority scheduling with priority = arrival time.

content.theory:
Round robin (RR) and priority scheduling address what FCFS and SJF ignore: responsiveness for interactive users and the relative importance of different work. Round robin gives every process a fair turn on a timer, and priority scheduling runs the most important work first. This lesson explains both, how to choose a time quantum, and how aging prevents low-priority processes from starving.

## Round robin

Round robin gives each ready process a fixed time slice, the **quantum** q. A process that doesn't finish within q is preempted and goes to the back of the ready queue, and the next process runs. With n ready processes, no process waits more than (n − 1) × q before running again, which makes response time predictable.

RR is the basis of time-sharing. On the course's example workload with q = 2, its average waiting time is 4.5, worse than SJF's 3.25, but every process starts running within a few units of arriving. For interactive systems, that's the trade worth making.

## The queue rule that decides exam answers

When a process's quantum expires at the same moment a new process arrives, the order in the queue matters. The common exam convention puts the new arrival in the queue first, then the preempted process. Other conventions exist, so state the rule you use, because it changes the Gantt chart.

## Choosing the quantum

The quantum is the single most important design choice in round robin:

- **Too large**: no process is ever preempted, and round robin becomes FCFS, with the convoy effect
- **Too small**: the CPU spends a large share of its time on context switches. With a 1 ms switch and a 4 ms quantum, 20% of CPU time is overhead
- **Rule of thumb**: about 80% of CPU bursts should finish within one quantum, so most interactive work completes in a single turn

Real systems use quanta of roughly 1 to 100 ms, and Linux adjusts slice lengths dynamically based on load.

## Priority scheduling

Priority scheduling assigns each process a priority and always runs the highest-priority ready process. It can be preemptive (a newly ready higher-priority process interrupts the current one) or non-preemptive. Watch the convention in any question: in many textbooks a smaller number means higher priority, and in others the reverse.

Priorities can be internal, computed by the OS from measurable properties such as memory use or the ratio of I/O to CPU time, or external, set by users or administrators. On Linux, the `nice` value lets you lower a process's priority, for example to run a backup without slowing down interactive work.

## Starvation and aging

Priority scheduling's classic failure is **starvation**: a low-priority process may never run if higher-priority work keeps arriving. A well-known story describes a low-priority job found on a shut-down MIT mainframe in 1973 that had been waiting since 1967.

The fix is **aging**: gradually increase the priority of processes the longer they wait. A process might gain one priority level for every few seconds in the ready queue. Eventually even the lowest-priority process becomes the highest and runs.

## Priority inversion

A subtler problem appears when priorities meet locks. A low-priority process holds a lock that a high-priority process needs, and a medium-priority process keeps preempting the low-priority one. The high-priority process waits indefinitely, behind a medium-priority one it should outrank. This **priority inversion** famously caused repeated resets on NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997.

The standard fix is **priority inheritance**: while a low-priority process holds a lock that a high-priority one needs, it temporarily inherits the high priority, finishes its critical section quickly, and releases the lock.

## Connecting the algorithms

Many algorithms are special cases of priority scheduling. SJF is priority scheduling where priority is the predicted next burst, shorter meaning higher. FCFS is priority scheduling by arrival time. Round robin is FCFS with preemption on a timer. Seeing these connections makes it easier to reason about the trade-offs of any new algorithm you meet.

## How interviewers test this

Exams give a workload and a quantum and ask for average waiting time under RR. Interviewers ask "What happens if the quantum is too large or too small?" and "What is starvation and how does aging fix it?" Priority inversion with the Mars Pathfinder example is a strong addition in systems interviews.

lessons.title: Multilevel Queues, MLFQ and Real-World Schedulers
lessons.description: Separate queues per process class, feedback queues that learn behaviour, and how Linux CFS works.

sections.title: Multilevel Queue (MLQ)
sections.content: The ready queue is split into permanent queues by process type, for example system → interactive → batch. Each queue can use its own algorithm (RR for interactive, FCFS for batch). Scheduling between queues is usually fixed priority (lower queues run only when the higher ones are empty) or a time split such as 80% / 20%. Processes never move between queues, so lower queues can starve.

sections.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
sections.content:
Processes move between queues based on how they behave:
- A new process starts in the top queue (highest priority, small quantum).
- If it uses its whole quantum (CPU-bound), it moves down one level (lower priority, larger quantum).
- If it gives up the CPU early (I/O-bound, interactive), it stays high.
- Aging, or a periodic boost back to the top, prevents starvation.

Result: interactive processes get fast response, and CPU-bound jobs still finish. MLFQ is the most general (and most complex) classic scheduler.

sections.title: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler)
sections.content: From kernel 2.6.23, CFS tracks each task's virtual runtime (CPU time used, weighted by its nice value) and always runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime, so the task that has had the least CPU goes next. Tasks are kept in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime, so picking the next task is fast. Since kernel 6.6, CFS is being replaced by EEVDF, which keeps the same fairness idea and adds latency deadlines.

sections.question: In MLFQ, a process that keeps using its full time quantum will:
options: Move up to a higher-priority queue
Move down to a lower-priority queue
Stay in the same queue forever
sections.explanation: Using the full quantum marks it as CPU-bound, so it's demoted. That keeps the top queues free for interactive tasks.

items: MLQ: fixed queues per process class; can starve the lower queues.
MLFQ: processes move between queues based on behaviour; aging prevents starvation.
Linux CFS: run the task with the least virtual runtime, kept in a red-black tree.

content.theory:
Real systems run a mix of work: interactive editors, background services and long batch jobs. No single algorithm suits all of them, so practical schedulers combine several queues and policies. This lesson explains multilevel queues, the multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) that learns each process's behaviour, and how Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) and its successor EEVDF approach the same problem.

## Multilevel queue scheduling

A multilevel queue divides the ready queue into several permanent queues by process type, for example system processes, interactive processes and batch jobs. Each queue can use its own algorithm: round robin for interactive work, FCFS for batch.

The scheduler must also choose between queues. Two approaches are common:

- **Fixed priority**: always serve the higher queue first; batch jobs run only when no interactive process is ready
- **Time slicing between queues**: give each queue a share of CPU time, such as 80% to interactive and 20% to batch

Processes never move between queues in this design. That keeps scheduling decisions cheap, but the scheduler must know each process's type in advance, and lower queues can starve under fixed priority.

## The problem MLFQ solves

The OS usually doesn't know whether a new process is interactive or CPU-bound, and a process can change its behaviour over time. A compiler reads files (I/O-bound), then optimizes code (CPU-bound). The multilevel feedback queue learns each process's behaviour from what it does and adjusts its priority accordingly.

## How MLFQ works

MLFQ uses several queues with decreasing priority and increasing quantum. Its rules are:

1. A new process enters the top queue, which has the highest priority and the shortest quantum
2. If a process uses its entire quantum, it's probably CPU-bound, so it moves down one queue
3. If a process gives up the CPU before its quantum ends, by blocking for input or output, it stays at its current level
4. The scheduler always runs a process from the highest non-empty queue
5. Periodically, every process is moved back to the top queue (a priority boost)

The result: interactive processes, which use short bursts, stay near the top and get fast response, while CPU-bound jobs sink to lower queues with longer quanta, where they run efficiently with fewer switches.

## Defending against starvation and gaming

Rule 5 prevents starvation. Without it, a steady stream of interactive processes could keep CPU-bound jobs at the bottom from ever running. The boost also helps a process whose behaviour changed from CPU-bound to interactive regain a high priority.

A clever program could game rule 3 by blocking for an instant right before its quantum expires, staying at the top forever. Modern MLFQ designs count the total CPU time a process uses at each level, regardless of how many times it blocked, and demote it once it exceeds that level's allowance.

## Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler

From kernel 2.6.23 (2007), Linux scheduled normal processes with the Completely Fair Scheduler. Instead of queues and fixed quanta, CFS tracks each task's **virtual runtime**: the CPU time it has used, scaled by its weight. Tasks with a lower `nice` value (higher priority) have higher weights, so their virtual runtime grows more slowly.

CFS always runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime, the one that has received the least fair share so far. It keeps tasks in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime, so finding the next task is fast. An interactive task that sleeps a lot accumulates little virtual runtime and gets the CPU quickly when it wakes, which produces good responsiveness without MLFQ's explicit rules.

## EEVDF

Linux 6.6 (2023) replaced CFS with EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First). It keeps CFS's fairness accounting and adds a virtual deadline for each task based on its requested time slice. Among tasks that are owed CPU time, it runs the one with the earliest deadline. Latency-sensitive tasks can request shorter slices and get scheduled sooner, which CFS handled only through heuristics.

## Real-time classes

Linux also provides real-time scheduling classes, `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR`, for tasks with strict timing needs. Real-time tasks always run before normal ones, using fixed priorities. They're powerful and dangerous: a runaway real-time task can starve the whole system, so they require elevated privileges.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Explain MLFQ" and "How does the Linux scheduler work?" For MLFQ, state the demotion rule, the stay-high rule for interactive processes and the periodic boost against starvation. For Linux, describe virtual runtime and the red-black tree, and mention EEVDF to show your knowledge is current.

lessons.description: Why count++ is unsafe with threads, and the three requirements every critical-section solution must meet.

sections.title: Race Condition
sections.content:
A race condition happens when the result depends on the timing of threads or processes that share data.

count++ looks like one step, but the CPU runs it as three:
1. load count into a register
2. add 1 to the register
3. store the register back to count
If two threads interleave these steps, one increment can be lost.

iterations.description: A context switch happens before T1 stores its result.
Two increments ran, but count is 6 instead of 7.

sections.title: Critical Section
sections.content:
The critical section is the part of the code that accesses shared data. Every process follows the pattern:
entry section → critical section → exit section → remainder section

A correct solution must satisfy three requirements:
1. Mutual exclusion: at most one process is inside its critical section at a time.
2. Progress: if no process is in the critical section, the choice of who enters next can't be postponed forever, and only the processes trying to enter take part in that choice.
3. Bounded waiting: there is a limit on how many times others can enter before a waiting process gets its turn (no starvation).

sections.question: A solution uses a shared variable turn and lets P0 enter only when turn == 0 and P1 only when turn == 1, flipping turn on exit. Which requirement fails?
sections.answerReveal: Progress. The processes must strictly alternate. If P0 wants to enter twice in a row while P1 is busy in its remainder section, P0 is blocked even though the critical section is empty.

sections.question: Which requirement guarantees that a waiting process won't wait forever while others keep entering?
sections.explanation: Bounded waiting limits how many times other processes can enter before a requesting process gets in.

items: Read-modify-write on shared data is not atomic, so races lose updates.
A correct critical-section solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

content.theory:
A race condition happens when the result of a program depends on the exact timing of threads or processes that share data. Races cause bugs that appear once in a thousand runs and vanish when you add a print statement, which makes them some of the hardest bugs to find. This lesson explains why even `count++` is unsafe with threads, defines the critical-section problem, and states the three requirements every solution must meet.

## Why count++ isn't one step

In source code, `count++` looks like a single action. The CPU executes it as three separate instructions:

1. Load the value of `count` from memory into a register
2. Add one to the register
3. Store the register back to `count`

The OS can switch threads between any two instructions, and on a multicore machine two threads can run these steps at the same moment on different cores.

## Losing an update

Suppose `count` is 5 and two threads each increment it once. Thread 1 loads 5 into its register. Before it stores, thread 2 also loads 5. Thread 1 adds one and stores 6, then thread 2 adds one and stores 6. Two increments ran, and `count` is 6 instead of 7.

Run this a million times in each of two threads and the final count is usually well below two million, with a different total every run. Nothing crashed and nothing reported an error. The data is wrong, silently.

## Races in real systems

The same pattern appears far beyond counters. Two clerks book the last hostel room at once. Two requests withdraw money from the same wallet, each checking the balance before either writes. A program checks that a file doesn't exist, then creates it, while another process creates it in between (a time-of-check to time-of-use race, which attackers exploit). Each case is a read, a decision, and a write that should have been indivisible but wasn't.

## The critical-section problem

A **critical section** is the part of a program that accesses shared data. Every process that uses the shared data follows the same structure:

- **Entry section**: request permission to enter
- **Critical section**: access the shared data
- **Exit section**: announce that it's done
- **Remainder section**: everything else

The critical-section problem is designing the entry and exit sections so that the shared data stays correct.

## The three requirements

A correct solution must satisfy all three conditions:

- **Mutual exclusion**: at most one process is in its critical section at any time
- **Progress**: if no process is in its critical section and some want to enter, the choice of who enters next can't be postponed forever, and only processes trying to enter take part in the decision
- **Bounded waiting**: after a process requests entry, there's a limit on how many times others can enter before it gets its turn

Mutual exclusion protects the data. Progress prevents the system from stalling when the critical section is free. Bounded waiting prevents any one process from starving.

## A broken attempt: strict alternation

Consider two processes sharing a variable `turn`. Process 0 enters only when `turn == 0`, and sets `turn = 1` when it leaves; process 1 does the reverse. This guarantees mutual exclusion, because `turn` can't be both values at once.

It fails progress. If process 0 finishes its critical section and wants to enter again while process 1 is busy elsewhere, it must wait, because `turn` is 1. The critical section is empty, yet process 0 can't use it. The processes are forced to alternate even when one has nothing to do.

## Where solutions come from

Solutions fall into three levels, each covered in the following lessons:

- **Software algorithms**, such as Peterson's solution, use only ordinary reads and writes
- **Hardware instructions**, such as test-and-set and compare-and-swap, perform a read and write as one indivisible step
- **OS and language primitives**, such as mutexes, semaphores and monitors, build on those instructions and add sleeping instead of busy waiting

## Avoid sharing when you can

The surest way to avoid races is to avoid shared mutable data. Give each thread its own data and combine results at the end, pass messages instead of sharing variables, or use immutable objects. When sharing is necessary, keep critical sections as short as possible, so threads spend little time waiting for each other.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a race condition?" and "What are the requirements of a critical-section solution?" Use the count++ example with the three instructions and the lost update, then name mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting with one sentence each. The strict-alternation example is a good way to show why progress matters.
