content.theory:
Locks have to be built from something. Peterson's solution shows that two processes can achieve mutual exclusion using only ordinary memory reads and writes, and atomic hardware instructions such as test-and-set and compare-and-swap make practical locks for any number of threads. This lesson explains both, why Peterson's solution fails on modern hardware without extra care, and when spinning on a lock is a good idea.

## Peterson's solution

Peterson's solution (1981) protects a critical section shared by two processes, numbered 0 and 1. It uses two shared variables:

- `flag[i]`: process i wants to enter
- `turn`: whose turn it is to go first when both want in

To enter, process i sets `flag[i] = true`, then politely sets `turn = j` (the other process). It then waits while `flag[j]` is true and `turn == j`. To leave, it sets `flag[i] = false`.

## Why it works

**Mutual exclusion**: if both processes want in, both set their flags, and both write `turn`. Only one write survives, because `turn` holds a single value, so exactly one process sees `turn` pointing at the other and waits.

**Progress**: if process j doesn't want to enter, `flag[j]` is false, so process i enters immediately.

**Bounded waiting**: when process i is waiting and process j leaves and immediately tries again, j sets `turn = i`, so i goes next. Neither can enter twice in a row while the other waits.

## Why it breaks on modern hardware

Peterson's proof assumes memory operations happen in program order. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder independent reads and writes for speed. If the read of `flag[j]` moves before the write of `flag[i]`, both processes can see the other's flag as false and enter together. A correct implementation today needs **memory barriers** (fences), instructions that stop reordering across them. Peterson's solution is therefore taught for the reasoning it shows, not used as written.

## Atomic hardware instructions

Hardware provides instructions that read and write a memory location as one indivisible step, so no other core can act in between.

**Test-and-set** sets a boolean to true and returns its previous value, atomically. A spinlock is a loop around it:

~~~c
while (test_and_set(&lock))
    ;  // spin: lock was already held
/* critical section */
lock = false;
~~~

The first thread to arrive sees `false` returned, which means it acquired the lock. Every other thread sees `true` and keeps looping until the holder resets `lock`.

**Compare-and-swap (CAS)** takes an address, an expected value and a new value. It stores the new value only if the current value equals the expected one, and returns the old value either way. CAS is the basis of lock-free programming: to increment a counter, a thread reads it, computes the new value, and uses CAS to store it only if nobody changed it in between, retrying otherwise. Java's `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet` works this way.

## What a basic spinlock lacks

A test-and-set spinlock guarantees mutual exclusion but not bounded waiting: an unlucky thread can lose the race every time the lock is released. **Ticket locks** fix this. Each arriving thread atomically takes a ticket number, and the lock serves tickets in order, like a token system at a bank counter.

## Spinning versus sleeping

A spinning thread keeps a core busy doing nothing useful while it waits. Whether that's acceptable depends on the situation:

| Spin when | Sleep (block) when |
|---|---|
| Critical sections are a few instructions | Waits may be long |
| Several cores exist, so the holder is running elsewhere | There's a single core, so spinning stops the holder from running |
| A context switch would cost more than the wait | Many threads compete for the lock |

Operating system kernels use spinlocks for short critical sections, especially in interrupt handlers that can't sleep. Application locks, such as Linux's futex-based mutexes, usually spin briefly and then put the thread to sleep, which combines the advantages of both.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Explain Peterson's solution" and "What is test-and-set or compare-and-swap?" For Peterson, describe `flag` and `turn` and walk through the case where both processes want in. For the hardware instructions, explain atomicity and sketch a spinlock. Mentioning that Peterson's solution needs memory barriers on modern CPUs shows depth.

content.theory:
Mutexes and semaphores are the standard synchronization tools that operating systems and libraries provide on top of atomic instructions. A mutex enforces mutual exclusion; a semaphore is a counter that can enforce mutual exclusion, limit access to a pool of resources, or make one thread wait for another. This lesson explains both, how blocking semaphores work, and the differences interviewers expect you to know.

## Mutex locks

A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) has two operations: `acquire` (lock) and `release` (unlock). A thread acquires the mutex before its critical section and releases it afterwards. If another thread holds the mutex, the caller waits, usually by sleeping rather than spinning, so it doesn't waste CPU.

A mutex has an **owner**: only the thread that locked it should unlock it. That rule lets libraries detect errors, such as a thread unlocking a mutex it doesn't hold, and supports features such as priority inheritance.

## Semaphores

A semaphore, invented by Edsger Dijkstra, is an integer S accessed only through two atomic operations:

- **wait(S)**, also called P or down: decrement S; if the result is negative, block the calling thread
- **signal(S)**, also called V or up: increment S; if threads are blocked, wake one of them

In this blocking implementation, a negative value −k means k threads are waiting. A semaphore remembers signals: if a thread signals before anyone waits, the count rises, and the next wait passes without blocking.

## Three uses of semaphores

The initial value decides what a semaphore does:

| Initial value | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (binary semaphore) | Mutual exclusion | Protect a shared counter |
| N (counting semaphore) | Limit concurrent access to N identical resources | 5 database connections in a pool |
| 0 | Ordering between threads | Make step B wait until step A finishes |

For ordering, thread 1 runs step A then calls `signal(s)`; thread 2 calls `wait(s)` then runs step B. Whichever thread runs first, B can't start until A has finished. This is how threads hand work to each other.

## Counting semaphore values

Exam questions ask for a semaphore's final value after a sequence of operations. Each wait subtracts 1 and each signal adds 1, regardless of order, in the blocking implementation. A semaphore starting at 7, after 20 waits and 15 signals, ends at 7 − 20 + 15 = 2.

## Mutex versus binary semaphore

The two look similar and differ in an important way:

| | Mutex | Binary semaphore |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Protect a critical section | Signal between threads, or protect a section |
| Ownership | Yes; the locker must unlock | No; any thread may signal |
| Typical bug | Unlocking from the wrong thread | Mismatched or missing signals |
| Extras | Priority inheritance, error checking | None |

Use a mutex to protect data and a semaphore to coordinate or count. Using a semaphore as a lock works, but you lose the ownership checks that catch bugs.

## How blocking semaphores are implemented

A blocking semaphore is a counter plus a queue of waiting threads, and the operations on it must themselves be atomic. The kernel protects them with a short spinlock: `wait` takes the spinlock, decrements the counter, and if it went negative, adds the thread to the queue, releases the spinlock and sleeps. `signal` takes the spinlock, increments, and wakes one queued thread. The spinlock is held for only a few instructions, so spinning is acceptable there.

## Common semaphore bugs

Semaphores are powerful, and a single misplaced call breaks them:

- **Swapped operations**: calling `signal` before the critical section and `wait` after it removes protection entirely
- **Missing signal**: one code path forgets to signal, and every later waiter blocks forever
- **Wrong order of waits**: taking two semaphores in different orders in different threads can deadlock, as the producer-consumer lesson shows

Higher-level tools, such as monitors and Java's `synchronized`, exist largely to prevent these mistakes.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Mutex vs semaphore", "What is a counting semaphore used for?" and a final-value calculation. Answer the first with ownership and purpose, the second with a resource pool such as database connections, and the third by summing waits as −1 and signals as +1.

sections.explanation: Order matters: swapping wait(empty) and wait(mutex) in the producer can deadlock. A producer holding mutex while waiting for an empty slot blocks the consumer from ever freeing one.

sections.title: Readers-Writers (readers' preference)
sections.explanation: Many readers can read at the same time, but writers can starve while readers keep arriving. Writer-preference versions fix that, at the cost of starving readers instead.

sections.title: Dining Philosophers
sections.content:
Five philosophers sit around a table with five chopsticks, one between each pair. A philosopher needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat.

Naive solution: everyone picks up their left chopstick, then their right. If all five pick up their left at the same moment, everyone waits forever: deadlock.

Fixes:
- Allow at most 4 philosophers at the table at once (a counting semaphore initialized to 4).
- Asymmetry: odd-numbered philosophers pick up left first, even-numbered pick up right first.
- Pick up both chopsticks only if both are free (check and take inside a critical section, or use a monitor).

sections.question: In the producer-consumer solution, what are the initial values of empty and full for a buffer of size N?
sections.explanation: At the start, all N slots are empty and nothing is full.

items: Producer-consumer: mutex = 1, empty = N, full = 0; wait on the counting semaphore before the mutex.
Readers-writers: the first reader locks writers out, the last reader lets them in; watch for starvation.
Dining philosophers shows how symmetric resource grabbing deadlocks.

content.theory:
Three classic problems capture most of the synchronization patterns you meet in real systems: the bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem, the readers-writers problem and the dining philosophers problem. Each one shows a different danger, such as overflow, starvation or deadlock, and the standard semaphore solutions show how to avoid it. This lesson explains each problem, its solution and the mistake that breaks it.

## Producer-consumer with a bounded buffer

Producers create items and place them in a shared buffer of fixed size N; consumers remove and process them. A print queue, a logging pipeline and a web server's request queue all follow this pattern. Three rules must hold:

- producers must wait when the buffer is full
- consumers must wait when the buffer is empty
- only one thread at a time may modify the buffer's internal structure

## The semaphore solution

Three semaphores enforce the three rules:

- `empty`, initialized to N, counts free slots
- `full`, initialized to 0, counts filled slots
- `mutex`, initialized to 1, protects the buffer itself

A producer calls `wait(empty)` to claim a slot, `wait(mutex)` to lock the buffer, adds the item, `signal(mutex)`, then `signal(full)` to announce a new item. A consumer mirrors it: `wait(full)`, `wait(mutex)`, remove, `signal(mutex)`, `signal(empty)`.

## The ordering trap

The order of the two waits matters. If a producer calls `wait(mutex)` before `wait(empty)` and the buffer is full, it sleeps while holding the mutex. No consumer can then acquire the mutex to remove an item, so nobody ever signals `empty`: a deadlock. The rule is to wait on the counting semaphore first and take the mutex only once you know you can proceed.

## Readers and writers

A shared resource, such as a timetable or a cached configuration, is read often and written rarely. Several readers can safely read at the same time, but a writer needs exclusive access. Treating every access with one mutex would make readers wait for each other for no reason.

## The readers-preference solution

Two semaphores and a counter implement it:

- `rw_mutex`, initialized to 1, gives exclusive access to writers
- `read_count` counts active readers
- `mutex`, initialized to 1, protects `read_count`

A writer waits on `rw_mutex`. A reader increments `read_count` under `mutex`; the first reader also waits on `rw_mutex`, locking writers out. When leaving, a reader decrements the count, and the last reader signals `rw_mutex`, letting writers in.

## Starvation in readers-writers

In the readers-preference version, a steady stream of readers keeps `read_count` above zero, so a waiting writer may never get in. Writers-preference versions block new readers once a writer is waiting, which can starve readers instead. Fair versions queue readers and writers in arrival order. Real libraries provide read-write locks, such as Java's `ReentrantReadWriteLock` and POSIX `pthread_rwlock`, with configurable fairness.

## The dining philosophers

Five philosophers sit at a round table with five chopsticks, one between each pair. Each alternates between thinking and eating, and needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat. The problem models processes that each need several shared resources at once.

The naive solution, where each philosopher picks up the left chopstick and then the right, can deadlock: if all five pick up their left chopstick at the same moment, each waits forever for the right one, held by a neighbour.

## Three fixes for the philosophers

Each fix breaks one of the conditions that allows deadlock:

- **Limit the diners**: a counting semaphore initialized to 4 lets at most four philosophers try at once, so at least one can always get both chopsticks
- **Break the symmetry**: odd-numbered philosophers pick up the left chopstick first and even-numbered ones the right, so a circular wait can't form
- **Take both or neither**: a philosopher picks up chopsticks only when both are free, checking and taking them inside a critical section or a monitor

The second fix is the general principle behind lock ordering in real code: always acquire locks in one global order.

## Patterns behind the puzzles

The three problems map onto everyday engineering:

| Problem | Real-world form | Main danger |
|---|---|---|
| Producer-consumer | Work queues, pipelines | Deadlock from wrong wait order |
| Readers-writers | Caches, configuration, shared indexes | Starvation |
| Dining philosophers | Transactions needing several locks | Deadlock from circular waiting |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Solve the producer-consumer problem with semaphores", with the initial values (`empty` = N, `full` = 0, `mutex` = 1) and the correct wait order. For dining philosophers, explain how the naive version deadlocks and give one fix with the reason it works.

lessons.title: Monitors and Condition Variables
lessons.description: A higher-level synchronization construct, wait/notify, and why you always check conditions in a while loop.

sections.title: Monitor
sections.content:
A monitor is a language-level construct: shared data plus the procedures that operate on it, where only one thread can be active inside the monitor at a time. The compiler or runtime adds the locking, so programmers can't forget a wait() or signal() the way they can with raw semaphores.

Condition variables let a thread wait inside the monitor until something becomes true:
x.wait(): release the monitor lock and sleep until signalled.
x.signal(): wake one waiting thread (it does nothing if none are waiting, unlike a semaphore signal, which is remembered).

sections.title: Java: Every Object Is a Monitor
sections.explanation: Always use while, not if, around wait(). After waking, the condition may already be false again (another thread got there first), and spurious wakeups are allowed.

sections.question: Why must a condition be re-checked in a while loop after wait() returns?
options: The condition may be false again by the time the thread runs
sections.explanation: Another thread may have changed the state between the signal and this thread re-acquiring the lock, and spurious wakeups can also happen.

items: A monitor = shared data + procedures, with automatic mutual exclusion.
A condition-variable signal is lost if nobody is waiting; a semaphore signal is remembered.
Wrap wait() in a while loop.

content.theory:
A monitor is a higher-level synchronization construct that bundles shared data with the procedures that use it, and guarantees that only one thread runs inside at a time. Condition variables let a thread inside a monitor wait until some state becomes true. Monitors exist because a single misplaced semaphore call can break a whole program. This lesson explains monitors, condition variables, signalling semantics, and why every wait belongs inside a while loop.

## Why semaphores aren't enough

Semaphores work, but correctness depends on every programmer placing every `wait` and `signal` correctly. Swap two calls, forget one on an error path, or take two semaphores in the wrong order, and the program races or deadlocks. These mistakes are scattered across the code, so they're hard to find in review.

## What a monitor is

A monitor is a module that contains shared data and the procedures that operate on it. The language or runtime guarantees that at most one thread is active inside the monitor at any time, by acquiring a lock on entry to every procedure and releasing it on exit. You can't forget to lock, because you never write the lock calls yourself.

Java builds this into the language: every object has a monitor lock, and a `synchronized` method acquires it automatically. C# uses the `lock` statement, and Python's `threading.Condition` supports the same pattern explicitly.

## Condition variables

Mutual exclusion alone can't express "wait until the buffer has an item". A condition variable is a queue of threads waiting for some condition to become true. It has two main operations:

- **wait()**: atomically release the monitor lock and sleep; when woken, reacquire the lock before returning
- **signal()** (or `notify`): wake one waiting thread, if any; `broadcast` (or `notifyAll`) wakes all of them

The atomic release-and-sleep in `wait` is essential. If a thread released the lock and then went to sleep in two steps, a signal could arrive between them and be missed, leaving the thread asleep forever.

## Signals aren't remembered

A semaphore counts signals, so a signal with no waiter isn't lost. A condition variable's signal is lost if nobody is waiting at that moment. That's why monitor code always checks the actual state (is the buffer empty?) rather than relying on having received a signal. The condition variable is only a way to sleep efficiently until the state might have changed.

## Always wait in a while loop

Correct monitor code waits in a loop that rechecks the condition:

~~~java
synchronized void put(int x) throws InterruptedException {
    while (count == items.length) wait();  // full: wait
    items[putIdx] = x;
    putIdx = (putIdx + 1) % items.length;
    count++;
    notifyAll();                           // wake consumers
}
~~~

The `while` matters for two reasons. Between the signal and the woken thread reacquiring the lock, another thread may enter and change the state again, for example by filling the slot the signal announced. And the language specifications for Java and POSIX threads allow **spurious wakeups**, where a thread returns from `wait` without any signal. An `if` would proceed on a false assumption in both cases; a `while` checks again.

## Signal semantics

When a thread signals, two threads want to run inside the monitor: the signaller and the woken waiter. Two designs answer who goes first:

- **Hoare semantics**: the waiter runs immediately and the signaller waits. The waiter knows the condition is still true, so an `if` would be safe
- **Mesa semantics**: the signaller continues and the waiter joins the queue for the lock. By the time it runs, the condition may be false again

Almost every real system, including Java, C# and POSIX threads, uses Mesa semantics, which is the deeper reason for the while loop.

## notify versus notifyAll

`notify` wakes one arbitrary waiter, and `notifyAll` wakes every waiter. `notify` is efficient but risky when threads wait for different conditions on the same monitor: it might wake a producer when a consumer was needed, and the woken producer goes back to sleep, leaving everyone waiting. `notifyAll` is safer at the cost of waking threads that immediately sleep again. Java's `java.util.concurrent` package offers `Condition` objects, which let you keep separate wait queues, such as "not full" and "not empty", and signal precisely.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a monitor?", "Why use while instead of if around wait?" and "Difference between a semaphore signal and a condition variable signal". Answer with automatic mutual exclusion, the two reasons for the while loop (Mesa semantics and spurious wakeups), and the fact that condition-variable signals are lost if nobody waits.

lessons.title: Deadlock: The Four Conditions and Resource Allocation Graphs
lessons.description: The Coffman conditions, resource allocation graphs, and the minimum-resources formula.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content:
A set of processes is deadlocked when each one is waiting for a resource held by another process in the set, so none of them can ever continue.

T1 holds the printer and wants the scanner; T2 holds the scanner and wants the printer.

sections.title: The Four Necessary Conditions (Coffman)

A process holds at least one resource while waiting for more
Resources can't be forcibly taken away; they're released voluntarily
A cycle P1 → P2 → ... → Pn → P1, where each waits for the next one's resource

Request edge: P → R (P is waiting for R).
Assignment edge: R → P (an instance of R is held by P).

content.theory:
A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are all waiting for resources held by each other, so none of them can ever continue. Deadlocks freeze parts of a system without any error message, and they're common wherever processes or threads hold several locks or resources. This lesson explains the four necessary conditions for deadlock, how to model one with a resource allocation graph, and how to calculate the minimum resources that guarantee deadlock can't happen.

## A deadlock in everyday terms

Two students need both the department's only projector and its only laptop for a presentation. One takes the projector and goes looking for the laptop; the other takes the laptop and goes looking for the projector. Each waits for the other to finish, and neither will give up what they hold. Nothing moves until someone intervenes.

In software, the same thing happens when thread A locks the `orders` table and requests `inventory`, while thread B holds `inventory` and requests `orders`.

## The four Coffman conditions

In 1971, Coffman and colleagues showed that a deadlock can happen only if all four of these conditions hold at once:

- **Mutual exclusion**: at least one resource can be held by only one process at a time
- **Hold and wait**: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire more
- **No preemption**: resources can't be forcibly taken away; a process releases them voluntarily
- **Circular wait**: there's a cycle of processes, each waiting for a resource held by the next

All four are necessary. Removing any one of them makes deadlock impossible, which is the basis of every prevention strategy in the next lesson.

## Resources and instances

A resource type can have several identical instances: three printers, or a pool of ten database connections. A process requesting a printer can use any free one. The number of instances matters for deadlock analysis, as the graph rules below show.

## Resource allocation graphs

A resource allocation graph (RAG) models the current state:

- processes are circles and resource types are squares, with a dot for each instance
- a **request edge** P → R means P is waiting for an instance of R
- an **assignment edge** R → P means an instance of R is held by P

Reading the graph depends on the number of instances:

- **Every resource has one instance**: a cycle means deadlock, guaranteed
- **Some resources have several instances**: a cycle means deadlock is possible but not certain, because a process outside the cycle might release an instance that breaks it

## A multi-instance example

Suppose resource R has two instances. P1 holds one and requests S; P2 holds S and requests R; P3 holds the other instance of R and isn't waiting for anything. There's a cycle through P1, S, P2 and R, but P3 will finish and release its instance of R. P2 then gets it, finishes, releases S, and P1 proceeds. A cycle existed, yet there's no deadlock, which is why multi-instance graphs need more analysis.

## Minimum resources to guarantee safety

Exams ask: n processes each need at most k units of a resource; how many units guarantee deadlock can't happen? Reason about the worst case. If every process holds k − 1 units and waits for one more, nobody can finish, and that uses n(k − 1) units. One extra unit lets some process complete and release all k units, which lets the others proceed one by one:

~~~text
minimum units = n(k − 1) + 1
~~~

With 3 processes each needing up to 4 units, the answer is 3 × 3 + 1 = 10.

## Deadlock, livelock and starvation

Three related problems are often confused:

| Problem | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Deadlock | Processes wait forever for each other | Two threads each holding a lock the other needs |
| Livelock | Processes keep changing state but make no progress | Two people stepping aside in a corridor, again and again |
| Starvation | One process waits indefinitely while others proceed | A low-priority job never scheduled |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What are the necessary conditions for deadlock?" and "Does a cycle in a resource allocation graph always mean deadlock?" Name all four Coffman conditions with a short example each. For the graph question, answer yes for single-instance resources and "not necessarily" for multi-instance ones, with a reason.

lessons.title: Deadlock Prevention and Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm)
lessons.description: Breaking each Coffman condition, safe states, and a complete Banker's algorithm example.

sections.title: Prevention: Break One Condition
rows: Request every resource at once, or release everything before requesting more
Take resources from waiting processes (practical for CPU and memory)
Not possible for printers or locks mid-use
Number the resources and always request them in increasing order
The most practical approach; used for lock ordering in real code

sections.title: Avoidance: Stay in a Safe State
sections.content:
Avoidance grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state, meaning there is some order (a safe sequence) in which every process can get its maximum need and finish.

Safe state → no deadlock is possible.
Unsafe state → deadlock may happen, but isn't guaranteed.

The Banker's algorithm needs every process to declare its maximum need up front.

sections.title: Banker's Example: Resources A = 10, B = 5, C = 7

iterations.description: P1 can finish and releases its allocation 2 0 0.
Releases 2 1 1.
Releases 0 0 2.
Releases 0 1 0.
Releases 3 0 2 → Work = 10 5 7.
Every process can finish, so the state is safe. Other safe sequences may also exist.

sections.title: Resource-Request Algorithm
sections.content:
When Pi requests resources:
1. If Request > Need, it's an error (it asked for more than it declared).
2. If Request > Available, Pi must wait.
3. Otherwise pretend to grant it: Available −= Request, Allocation += Request, Need −= Request.
4. Run the safety algorithm. If the state is safe, grant it for real; if not, roll back and make Pi wait.

sections.question: An unsafe state means:
sections.explanation: Unsafe doesn't mean deadlocked. It only means the OS can no longer guarantee that every process will finish.

items: Prevention breaks a Coffman condition; ordering resources (no circular wait) is the most practical.
Avoidance (Banker's) grants a request only if a safe sequence still exists.
Need = Max − Allocation; repeatedly pick a process whose Need ≤ Work, then Work += its Allocation.

content.theory:
There are two proactive ways to handle deadlock. Prevention designs the system so that one of the four necessary conditions can never hold. Avoidance allows all four conditions but checks each resource request, granting it only if the system stays in a safe state. This lesson explains how to break each condition, what a safe state is, and how the Banker's algorithm decides whether to grant a request.

## Prevention: break one condition

Each Coffman condition can be targeted, with different costs:

| Condition | How to break it | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Mutual exclusion | Make resources shareable, such as read-only files, or spool output through a single daemon | Impossible for most resources, like locks or a tape drive |
| Hold and wait | Request every resource at once, or release everything before asking for more | Resources sit idle; long waits; starvation |
| No preemption | Take resources from a waiting process and give them to others | Works for CPU and memory; not for a half-printed page |
| Circular wait | Number all resources and always request them in increasing order | Needs discipline; the most practical option |

## Lock ordering in real code

Breaking circular wait is the prevention technique you'll use most. If every thread acquires locks in the same global order, for example by ascending account ID or by table name, no cycle can form, because a thread holding a higher-numbered lock never waits for a lower-numbered one. A transfer between accounts 101 and 205 always locks 101 first, whichever direction the money moves.

## Avoidance: stay in a safe state

Avoidance needs one piece of advance information: each process declares the maximum number of instances of each resource it might ever need. With that, the OS can look ahead before granting a request.

A state is **safe** if there's some order of processes, called a **safe sequence**, in which each process can get its maximum need from the currently available resources plus those released by processes earlier in the sequence. A safe state can never lead to deadlock, because the OS can always run the processes in the safe-sequence order.

An **unsafe** state isn't necessarily deadlocked. It means the OS can no longer guarantee that every process will finish; deadlock may follow if processes request their full maximums.

## The Banker's algorithm data

Dijkstra's Banker's algorithm keeps four tables for n processes and m resource types:

- **Available**: free instances of each resource type
- **Max**: the maximum demand each process declared
- **Allocation**: instances each process currently holds
- **Need**: Max minus Allocation, what each process may still request

The name comes from a bank that never lends out cash in a way that would leave it unable to meet every customer's maximum credit line.

## The safety algorithm

To test whether a state is safe:

1. Set Work = Available and mark every process unfinished
2. Find an unfinished process whose Need is less than or equal to Work in every resource type
3. Assume it runs to completion: add its Allocation to Work and mark it finished
4. Repeat from step 2 until no process qualifies
5. If every process finished, the state is safe, and the order you picked them in is a safe sequence

In the course's worked example, with Available starting at (3, 3, 2), the algorithm finds the safe sequence P1, P3, P4, P0, P2, and Work grows to the full (10, 5, 7) once everything finishes.

## The resource-request algorithm

When process i requests resources:

1. If the request exceeds its Need, raise an error, because it asked for more than it declared
2. If the request exceeds Available, the process must wait
3. Otherwise, pretend to grant it: subtract from Available, add to Allocation, subtract from Need
4. Run the safety algorithm on the pretend state
5. If it's safe, grant the request for real; if not, roll back the pretend changes and make the process wait

## Why avoidance is rare in practice

The Banker's algorithm costs O(m × n²) per request, needs every process to declare its maximum needs in advance, and assumes a fixed number of processes and resources. General-purpose systems can't meet those assumptions: a web server doesn't know how many connections it will open. Avoidance appears mostly in teaching, and in specialized systems with known workloads.

## How interviewers test this

Exams give Allocation, Max and Available tables and ask whether the state is safe, or whether a request should be granted. Compute Need first, then run the safety algorithm step by step, writing Work after each process. Interviewers ask "How would you prevent deadlock in your code?", and the best answer is consistent lock ordering.

lessons.title: Deadlock Detection, Recovery and the Ostrich Approach
lessons.description: Wait-for graphs, detection for multi-instance resources, recovery options, and what real OSs actually do.

sections.title: Detection
sections.content:
Let deadlocks happen, then find them.

Single-instance resources: collapse the RAG into a wait-for graph (Pi → Pj when Pi waits for a resource Pj holds). A cycle means deadlock. Finding a cycle takes O(n²) time.

Multiple-instance resources: run a Banker-like algorithm using current requests instead of maximum needs. Any process that can never be marked finished is deadlocked.

sections.title: Recovery Options
rows: Abort every process in the cycle
Simple, but loses a lot of work
Abort a victim, re-run detection, repeat
Choose by priority, work done, resources held
Take resources from a victim and roll it back to a safe point
Needs checkpointing; avoid picking the same victim every time (starvation)

sections.title: The Ostrich Algorithm
sections.content: General-purpose operating systems such as Linux and Windows mostly ignore deadlocks among user processes, like an ostrich with its head in the sand. Deadlocks are rare, and prevention or avoidance would slow everything down. Applications are expected to avoid them themselves (lock ordering, timeouts). Databases are different: they actively detect deadlocks and abort a victim transaction.

sections.question: Which approach do Linux and Windows mainly use for deadlocks between user processes?
sections.explanation: The cost of prevention or avoidance outweighs how rarely deadlocks happen, so ordinary OSs leave it to applications.

items: Detection: a cycle in the wait-for graph (single instance), or a detection algorithm (multiple instances).
Recovery: abort processes or preempt resources, choosing victims carefully.
Real OSs mostly use the ostrich approach; databases detect deadlocks and kill a victim.

content.theory:
Instead of preventing or avoiding deadlocks, a system can let them happen, detect them, and recover. This is often the most practical choice, because deadlocks are rare and prevention restricts every program all the time. This lesson explains detection with wait-for graphs and with a Banker's-style algorithm, the ways to recover, and why general-purpose operating systems mostly ignore deadlocks while databases handle them actively.

## Detection with single-instance resources

When each resource has a single instance, the resource allocation graph can be simplified into a **wait-for graph**: remove the resource nodes and draw an edge Pi → Pj whenever Pi waits for a resource held by Pj. A deadlock exists exactly when the wait-for graph has a cycle.

Finding a cycle with depth-first search takes O(n²) time for n processes in the worst case. The system runs the check periodically, or when a process has waited unusually long.

## Detection with multiple instances

With several instances per resource, cycles aren't enough. The detection algorithm resembles the Banker's safety algorithm, using each process's current **Request** in place of its maximum Need:

1. Set Work = Available; mark processes holding no resources as finished
2. Find an unfinished process whose Request fits within Work
3. Assume it completes: add its Allocation to Work and mark it finished
4. Repeat until no process qualifies
5. Every process still unfinished is deadlocked

The difference from avoidance is that detection looks at what processes are asking for now, not what they might ask for later.

## How often to run detection

Detection costs CPU time, so how often to run it is a trade-off. Running it on every resource request finds deadlocks immediately but adds overhead to every request. Running it every few minutes, or when CPU utilization drops, which can happen when many processes are stuck, is cheaper but leaves deadlocked processes stuck longer.

## Recovery by terminating processes

Once a deadlock is found, the system must break it. The bluntest option kills processes:

- **Abort every deadlocked process**: certain to work, but discards a lot of completed work
- **Abort one at a time**: kill a victim, rerun detection, and repeat until the cycle is gone

Choosing a victim means weighing several factors: the process's priority, how long it has run and how close it is to finishing, how many resources it holds, and whether it's interactive. Killing a process that has computed for an hour and is nearly done wastes far more than killing one that started a second ago.

## Recovery by preempting resources

The gentler option takes resources away from a victim and gives them to others. Three issues must be handled:

- **Victim selection**: choose which process loses which resources at the lowest cost
- **Rollback**: the victim must return to an earlier safe state, which needs checkpoints, or restart from the beginning
- **Starvation**: if cost always selects the same process, it may never finish, so the number of rollbacks should count as part of the cost

## The ostrich algorithm

General-purpose operating systems such as Linux and Windows mostly ignore deadlocks between user processes, an approach nicknamed the ostrich algorithm after the bird said to bury its head in the sand. The reasoning is economic: deadlocks among user programs are rare, and prevention or avoidance would slow down every program, all the time. When a user program deadlocks, the user or a watchdog kills it, and the application developer fixes the lock ordering.

The kernel itself is a different matter. Kernel developers use strict lock-ordering rules, and Linux includes a validator called lockdep that detects lock-order violations during testing, before they can deadlock in production.

## Databases detect deadlocks actively

Database systems take the opposite approach, because deadlocks between transactions are common: many transactions lock rows in unpredictable orders. PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server all maintain wait-for graphs, detect cycles, and abort a victim transaction, which receives an error. The application is expected to retry it. That's why database client code wraps transactions in retry loops.

## Comparing the strategies

| Strategy | When it acts | Cost | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prevention | Design time; a condition can't hold | Restricts all programs | Lock ordering in applications and kernels |
| Avoidance | Every request is checked | Heavy; needs maximums in advance | Specialized systems, teaching |
| Detection and recovery | After a deadlock forms | Periodic checks; lost work | Databases |
| Ignore (ostrich) | Never | Occasional manual restarts | General-purpose OSes for user processes |

## How interviewers test this

Expect "How does an OS handle deadlocks?" Describe all four strategies with their trade-offs, and say which real systems use each: databases detect and abort victims, general-purpose OSes mostly ignore user-level deadlocks, and applications prevent them with lock ordering.

lessons.title: Address Binding, Logical vs Physical Addresses and the MMU
lessons.description: When addresses are bound, how the MMU translates them, and base/limit protection.

sections.title: Logical vs Physical
sections.content:
Logical (virtual) address: generated by the CPU while running a program. Every process sees its own address space starting at 0.
Physical address: the real location in RAM.

The Memory Management Unit (MMU) is hardware that translates logical addresses to physical ones on every memory access. This lets each process believe it owns the whole memory while the OS places it anywhere.

sections.title: Address Binding Times
headers: Can the process move in memory?
rows: Absolute addresses are written into the code
No: it must load at that exact location

sections.title: Base and Limit Registers
sections.content:
The simplest MMU uses two registers:
physical = base (relocation register) + logical
protection: if logical ≥ limit, trap to the OS (an addressing error).

Example: base = 14000, limit = 3000. Logical address 346 maps to 14346. Logical address 3500 traps.

sections.question: Base = 5000, limit = 1200. Which logical address causes a trap?
sections.explanation: Valid logical addresses are 0 to limit − 1 = 1199. Address 1200 is out of range.

items: The CPU generates logical addresses; the MMU turns them into physical ones.
Execution-time binding (through the MMU) is what lets processes move around in memory.
Base + limit: relocate, then check the bounds.

content.theory:
Every address your program uses is an illusion. The CPU generates logical addresses, and hardware called the memory management unit (MMU) translates each one into a physical address in RAM. That translation is what lets every process believe it owns memory starting at zero, and what keeps processes out of each other's memory. This lesson explains address binding, logical versus physical addresses, and the base-and-limit scheme that introduces relocation and protection.

## Two kinds of address

A **logical address** (also called a virtual address) is what the CPU produces when a program reads or writes memory. Each process has its own logical address space, typically starting at 0. A **physical address** is a real location in RAM chips.

When two processes both access logical address 1000, they reach different physical locations, because the OS sets up a different translation for each. That's the foundation of process isolation.

## When addresses get bound

A program refers to memory symbolically, such as a variable named `total`. At some point, those names must become concrete addresses. That step is **address binding**, and it can happen at three times:

| Binding time | How | Can the process move? |
|---|---|---|
| Compile time | The compiler writes absolute addresses into the code | No; it must load at that exact spot |
| Load time | Addresses are fixed when the loader places the program in memory | Not after loading |
| Execution time | Hardware translates every access as the program runs | Yes, at any time |

Early systems used compile-time binding, which meant a program could only run at one location. Modern systems bind at execution time, which is what makes paging, swapping and memory sharing possible.

## The memory management unit

The MMU is hardware between the CPU and memory that translates every logical address to a physical one, on every access. Software can't afford to do this, because a program makes billions of memory accesses per second. The OS's job is to set up the MMU's translation information for each process and switch it during context switches.

## Base and limit registers

The simplest MMU uses two registers per running process:

- **Base (relocation) register**: the physical address where the process's memory starts
- **Limit register**: the size of the process's memory

On every access, the hardware checks that the logical address is less than the limit, then adds the base:

~~~text
if logical >= limit: trap to the OS (addressing error)
physical = base + logical
~~~

With base 14000 and limit 3000, logical address 346 becomes physical 14346, and logical address 3500 causes a trap, because it's outside the process's memory.

## Relocation and protection together

Base and limit registers give two features at once. **Relocation**: the OS can load a process anywhere, or move it later, by changing the base register, without changing the program. **Protection**: the limit check stops a process from reading or writing outside its region, whether by bug or by design.

Only the kernel may change the base and limit registers. If user code could set them, a program could point its base at another process's memory, so loading them is a privileged instruction.

## The limits of a single base and limit

Giving each process one contiguous region has costs, which the next lessons address. Free memory gets broken into scattered holes as processes come and go (external fragmentation). A process can't easily grow, because the memory after it may be in use. And processes can't share memory selectively, such as a common library. Paging and segmentation replace the single base and limit with finer-grained translation that solves all three.

## Seeing addresses in practice

You can watch logical addresses on a real system. On Linux, printing the address of a local variable in two copies of the same program often shows identical values, because each process has its own address space. Address space layout randomization (ASLR) shifts those addresses between runs, making it harder for attackers to predict where code and data live. Running `cat /proc/self/maps` lists the regions of the current process's address space.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Logical vs physical address", "What does the MMU do?" and a base-and-limit calculation. Explain that the CPU generates logical addresses and the MMU translates them on every access, then show base + logical with the limit check. Mentioning that execution-time binding is what allows processes to move shows you understand why the design matters.

Internal = waste inside blocks; external = waste between blocks.

content.theory:
Contiguous allocation gives each process one continuous block of physical memory. It's the most direct way to share memory between processes, and it teaches the central problem of memory management: fragmentation, where free memory exists but can't be used. This lesson explains fixed and variable partitioning, the first-fit, best-fit and worst-fit strategies, the two kinds of fragmentation, and why paging replaced contiguous allocation.

## Fixed partitioning

The earliest approach divides memory into fixed-size partitions at boot, say four partitions of 8 MB. Each process gets one partition. A 3 MB process in an 8 MB partition wastes 5 MB that nobody else can use. That waste inside an allocated block is **internal fragmentation**. Fixed partitioning also caps both the number of processes and the size of each one.

## Variable partitioning

Variable partitioning gives each process exactly the memory it requests. Memory starts as one large free block, called a hole. As processes arrive, the OS carves blocks out of holes; as they exit, their blocks become holes again, merging with neighbouring holes when possible.

Over time, memory becomes a patchwork of allocated blocks and holes of many sizes. The OS needs a policy for which hole to use for each request.

## Fit strategies

Three classic strategies choose a hole for a request:

- **First fit**: scan the holes in order and take the first one large enough. It's fast, because it stops early
- **Best fit**: take the smallest hole that's large enough. It preserves large holes but leaves tiny leftover slivers
- **Worst fit**: take the largest hole, hoping the leftover is still large enough to be useful. Simulations show it usually performs worst

Using the course's example (holes of 100, 500, 200, 300 and 600 KB, and requests of 212, 417, 112 and 426 KB), best fit satisfies all four requests, while first fit and worst fit both leave the 426 KB request waiting. Studies across many workloads show first fit and best fit perform similarly in memory use, and first fit is faster.

## External fragmentation

Variable partitioning avoids internal fragmentation and introduces **external fragmentation**: enough total free memory exists for a request, but it's split into holes, none large enough. You might have 500 KB free in total but no hole larger than 150 KB, so a 200 KB request fails.

The 50-percent rule describes how bad this gets: with first fit, for every N allocated blocks, about 0.5N blocks are lost to fragmentation, so roughly a third of memory can become unusable.

## Compaction

Compaction moves allocated blocks together so all free space becomes one large hole. It needs execution-time address binding, because every moved process must keep running with new physical addresses, which base registers make possible. It's expensive: the system copies large amounts of memory and pauses processes while doing it. Compaction treats the symptom rather than the cause.

## Internal versus external fragmentation

| | Internal | External |
|---|---|---|
| Where the waste is | Inside an allocated block | Between allocated blocks |
| Caused by | Fixed-size units larger than needed | Variable-size allocation over time |
| Example | A 4 KB page holding 1 KB in a process's last page | 500 KB free in total, but no hole over 150 KB |
| Fix | Smaller allocation units | Compaction, or non-contiguous allocation |

## Why paging won

The root cause of external fragmentation is the requirement that a process's memory be contiguous. Paging removes that requirement: memory is divided into equal fixed-size frames, and a process's pages can occupy any free frames, in any order. Any free frame can satisfy any page request, so external fragmentation disappears. The price is a small amount of internal fragmentation, averaging half a page per process, which is a far better trade.

## Fragmentation beyond the OS

The same ideas apply inside programs. The `malloc` allocator in the C library manages a heap with holes, uses fit strategies, and suffers external fragmentation in long-running programs. Allocators such as jemalloc and tcmalloc group objects by size class to reduce it, which is a form of fixed-size allocation chosen deliberately.

## How interviewers test this

Exams give a list of holes and requests and ask which strategy satisfies all requests. Track the leftover sizes after each allocation. Interviewers ask "Internal vs external fragmentation" and "How does paging solve external fragmentation?" Answer that any frame can hold any page, so there are no unusable holes between allocations.

sections.title: How Paging Works
sections.content:
Logical memory is split into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size. Any page can go into any free frame. A per-process page table maps page number → frame number.

A logical address is split into a page number p and an offset d:

sections.title: TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)
sections.content:
Without help, every memory access needs two accesses: one to the page table and one to the data. The TLB is a small, fast, associative cache of recent page → frame translations inside the MMU.

TLB hit: the frame is found in the TLB, so only one memory access is needed.
TLB miss: walk the page table (an extra memory access), then cache the translation.

Effective Access Time:
EAT = h × (t + m) + (1 − h) × (t + 2m)
where h = hit ratio, t = TLB lookup time, m = memory access time.

sections.explanation: 2 KB = 2^11, so there are 11 offset bits and 16 − 11 = 5 page-number bits (32 pages).

items: Address = page number | offset; offset bits = log2(page size).
Page-table size = number of pages × entry size.

content.theory:
Paging divides a process's logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, so any page can sit in any free frame. It eliminates external fragmentation and is the basis of memory management in every modern OS. This lesson explains how addresses are split and translated, how big page tables get, and how the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) makes translation fast enough to use.

## Pages and frames

Logical memory is divided into **pages**, and physical memory into **frames**, both of the same size, typically 4 KB. Each process has a **page table** that maps page numbers to frame numbers. A process's pages can be scattered across physical memory in any order, while the process still sees one continuous address space.

## Splitting an address

With a page size of 2^n bytes, the low n bits of a logical address are the **offset** within the page, and the remaining high bits are the **page number**. With 4 KB pages (2^12), the bottom 12 bits are the offset.

Translation replaces the page number with the frame number from the page table and keeps the offset unchanged:

~~~text
physical address = frame number × page size + offset
~~~

The offset never changes, because the byte's position within the page is the same as its position within the frame.

## Page-table entries hold more than a frame number

Each page-table entry stores the frame number plus control bits:

- **Valid bit**: whether the page is in memory and part of the process's address space
- **Protection bits**: read, write and execute permissions, so code pages can be made read-only
- **Dirty bit**: whether the page has been modified since it was loaded, so the OS knows whether to write it back
- **Referenced bit**: whether the page was accessed recently, used by page replacement

A write to a read-only page, or any access to an invalid page, traps to the OS. That's how the system catches bugs and implements features such as copy-on-write.

## How big is a page table?

Take a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages. The offset uses 12 bits, leaving 20 bits for the page number, so there are 2^20, about a million, pages. With 4-byte entries, the page table needs 4 MB per process. With 100 processes, that's 400 MB of page tables, most describing memory the processes never use. For 64-bit address spaces a flat table would be astronomically large. Multilevel page tables, covered in the next lesson, fix this.

## The cost of translation

A page table lives in memory. Without help, every memory access becomes two: one to read the page-table entry and one to access the data. That would halve the speed of every program, which is unacceptable.

## The translation lookaside buffer

The TLB is a small, fast cache inside the MMU that holds recent page-to-frame translations, typically 64 to a few thousand entries. On each access:

- **TLB hit**: the translation is in the TLB, so only one memory access is needed
- **TLB miss**: the hardware (or OS) walks the page table, then stores the translation in the TLB for next time

Programs have strong locality, using the same pages repeatedly, so hit rates above 99% are common.

## Effective access time

The effective access time (EAT) measures the average cost of a memory access:

~~~text
EAT = h × (t + m) + (1 − h) × (t + 2m)
~~~

Here h is the hit ratio, t the TLB lookup time and m the memory access time. With h = 0.8, t = 20 ns and m = 100 ns: 0.8 × 120 + 0.2 × 220 = 96 + 44 = 140 ns, compared with 200 ns without a TLB. At a realistic 99% hit ratio, the EAT falls to about 121 ns.

## Sharing pages

Because translation happens per page, two processes can map the same physical frame into their address spaces. Shared libraries such as the C library are loaded once and mapped read-only into every process that uses them, saving large amounts of memory. Copy-on-write after `fork()` uses the same mechanism.

## Huge pages

Larger pages, such as 2 MB or 1 GB on x86-64, mean fewer page-table entries and fewer TLB misses for programs that use large amounts of memory, such as databases and virtual machines. The cost is more internal fragmentation, so systems use huge pages selectively.

## How interviewers test this

Exams ask for the number of page-number bits, the page-table size, or the effective access time. Show each step: offset bits from the page size, page-number bits from the rest, entries × entry size for the table, and the EAT formula with your numbers. Interviewers ask "Why do we need a TLB?", answered with the two-memory-access problem.

lessons.description: Shrinking page tables with hierarchy, inverted tables, and segmentation vs paging.

sections.title: Multilevel (Hierarchical) Paging
sections.content:
Instead of one huge table, page the page table itself. A two-level scheme splits the page number into p1 (index into the outer table) and p2 (index into an inner table).

32-bit address, 4 KB pages: 10 bits p1 | 10 bits p2 | 12 bits offset. Inner tables are created only for regions the process actually uses, so a small process needs only a few KB of page tables instead of 4 MB. x86-64 uses 4 levels (5 on newer CPUs).

The cost: every extra level is another memory access on a TLB miss, which makes the TLB even more important.

sections.title: Inverted Page Table
sections.content: There is one entry per physical frame (not per virtual page), storing <process id, page number>. Its size depends on RAM, not on the size of the address spaces. Lookups need a search, so a hash table is used to speed them up. It was used in some PowerPC and IA-64 systems.

sections.content: Segmented paging combines the two: memory is divided into logical segments, and each segment is paged. You get segment-level protection without external fragmentation. Classic x86 did this; modern 64-bit OSs keep segmentation essentially flat and rely on paging.

sections.explanation: An inverted page table has exactly one entry per physical frame.

items: Multilevel paging saves memory by creating inner tables only for regions in use; each level adds a memory access on a TLB miss.
Inverted page table: one entry per frame.
Segmentation: variable-size logical units with external fragmentation; paging: fixed units with internal fragmentation.

content.theory:
A flat page table for a large address space wastes memory on entries for pages a process never uses. Multilevel page tables solve this by paging the page table itself, and inverted page tables solve it by indexing physical frames instead of virtual pages. Segmentation offers a different view of memory based on the program's logical parts. This lesson explains all three and how modern systems combine them.

## The problem with flat page tables

A 32-bit process with 4 KB pages needs a million-entry, 4 MB page table, even if it uses only a few megabytes. Most of a process's address space is empty: code and data near the bottom, the stack near the top, and a vast unused gap between. A flat table spends entries on every page of that gap.

## Two-level paging

Two-level paging splits the page number into two parts. For a 32-bit address with 4 KB pages, a common split is:

~~~text
| p1: 10 bits | p2: 10 bits | offset: 12 bits |
~~~

The first 10 bits index an **outer page table**, whose entries point to **inner page tables**. The next 10 bits index the chosen inner table, which gives the frame number. Each inner table covers 4 MB of address space and occupies exactly one 4 KB page.

The saving comes from leaving inner tables out. If a region of 4 MB is entirely unused, its outer entry is marked invalid and no inner table exists. A small process might need only the outer table plus two or three inner tables, about 16 KB instead of 4 MB.

## Deeper hierarchies

64-bit address spaces need more levels. x86-64 uses four levels to translate 48-bit virtual addresses, and newer processors support five levels for 57-bit addresses. Each level is a 4 KB page holding 512 entries of 8 bytes, so each level consumes 9 bits of the address.

## The cost of more levels

Every level adds a memory access on a TLB miss: a four-level walk needs four page-table reads before the data access itself. This is why TLB hit rates matter so much, and why processors cache intermediate page-table entries in addition to final translations. Huge pages also help, because a 2 MB page skips the last level entirely.

## Inverted page tables

An inverted page table flips the structure: it has one entry per physical frame rather than per virtual page, storing which process and which page occupy that frame. Its size depends on physical memory, not on the size or number of address spaces, so it stays small however large the virtual address space is.

The catch is lookup. To translate an address, the system must find the entry holding a given process and page number, which would mean searching the whole table. Systems use a hash table keyed on process and page to make lookups fast. Inverted page tables appeared in architectures such as PowerPC and IA-64. Sharing memory is awkward with them, because each frame records only one owner.

## Segmentation

Segmentation divides a process's memory into variable-size logical units that match how programmers think: a code segment, a data segment, a heap and a stack. A logical address becomes a pair: segment number and offset. A **segment table** stores each segment's base and limit, and the hardware checks the offset against the limit, then adds the base.

Segments make protection and sharing natural: mark the code segment read-only and share it between processes running the same program. Because segments vary in size, segmentation suffers from external fragmentation, the same problem as contiguous allocation.

## Paging versus segmentation

| | Paging | Segmentation |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | Fixed-size pages | Variable-size logical segments |
| Visible to the programmer | No | Yes |
| Fragmentation | Internal (last page) | External |
| Address | Page number and offset | Segment number and offset |
| Protection and sharing | Per page | Per logical segment |

## Combining them

Segmented paging divides memory into segments for protection and then pages each segment, avoiding external fragmentation. Older x86 processors used this design. Modern 64-bit operating systems keep segments essentially flat, with base zero and maximum limit, and rely on paging for everything, using page-level protection bits for read-only code and non-executable data.

## How interviewers test this

GATE asks how many levels a page table needs, or how much memory a multilevel table uses. Work out the entries per page (page size divided by entry size), the bits each level consumes, and divide the page-number bits by bits per level. Interviewers ask "Paging vs segmentation", answered with the table above.

sections.title: Virtual Memory
sections.content:
Virtual memory lets a process use more memory than is physically available by keeping only the pages it currently needs in RAM and the rest on disk (the swap area).

Demand paging: a page is loaded only when it is first accessed. Each page-table entry has a valid bit; invalid means 'not in memory' (or not a legal address).

sections.title: Handling a Page Fault
sections.code:
1. Process accesses a page whose valid bit = 0  -> trap to the OS (page fault)
2. OS checks the address: illegal -> kill the process (segmentation fault)
3. Find a free frame (if none, run page replacement to evict one;
   a dirty victim is written back to disk first)
4. Schedule a disk read of the page into the frame (the process blocks)
5. Update the page table: frame number, valid bit = 1
6. Restart the instruction that faulted
sections.explanation: Page faults are very expensive: milliseconds of disk I/O against nanoseconds for RAM.

iterations.description: p = page-fault rate, ma = memory access time.
About 40× slower than a fault-free system.
Fewer than 1 fault per 400,000 accesses. Locality of reference makes this achievable.

sections.title: Copy-on-Write
sections.content: After fork(), the parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. Only when one of them writes to a page does the OS copy that page. This is why fork() followed by exec() is cheap: most pages are never copied.

options: Accesses a page not currently in RAM
Accesses a page in the TLB
sections.explanation: The page is marked invalid in the page table, so the OS must bring it in from disk.

Fault cost dominates: EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·fault_time, so p must be tiny.
Copy-on-write makes fork() cheap.

content.theory:
Virtual memory lets a process use more memory than physically exists by keeping only the pages it's actively using in RAM and the rest on disk. Demand paging loads each page only when it's first touched. This lesson explains how demand paging works, exactly what happens during a page fault, how page faults affect the effective access time, and how copy-on-write makes `fork()` cheap.

## The idea behind virtual memory

Programs rarely need all their code and data at once. A word processor carries spell-check dictionaries, printing code and import filters, but a typical session touches a fraction of them. Virtual memory takes advantage of this: each process gets a large virtual address space, and only the pages in use occupy physical frames. The rest wait in a swap area on disk, or in the program file itself.

The benefits are large: programs can be bigger than physical memory, more programs fit in memory at once, and programs start faster because they don't load everything up front.

## Demand paging

With demand paging, no page is loaded until the process first accesses it. Every page-table entry has a valid bit. When a process starts, its pages are marked invalid (not in memory). The first access to each page triggers a page fault, and the OS loads it. A process that never touches part of its code never loads it.

## What happens on a page fault

When a process accesses a page whose valid bit is 0, the hardware traps to the OS, and the OS runs these steps:

1. Check whether the address is legal for this process. If not, terminate it with a segmentation fault
2. Find a free frame. If none is free, run the page-replacement algorithm to choose a victim, and write the victim to disk first if it's dirty
3. Schedule a disk read to load the page into the frame, and block the process meanwhile
4. When the read finishes, update the page-table entry with the frame number and set the valid bit
5. Restart the instruction that caused the fault, which now succeeds

Restarting the instruction is a hardware requirement: the CPU must be able to undo a partially completed instruction and run it again from the start.

## Page faults are expensive

A memory access takes on the order of 100 ns. Servicing a page fault from disk takes milliseconds, tens of thousands of times longer. The effective access time with page faults is:

~~~text
EAT = (1 − p) × memory_access + p × fault_time
~~~

With a 200 ns memory access, an 8 ms fault time and one fault per 1,000 accesses, the EAT is about 8,200 ns, 40 times slower than a system with no faults. To keep slowdown under 10%, p must be below 0.0000025, fewer than one fault per 400,000 accesses. SSDs shorten fault times, but the gap stays huge.

## Why it works anyway

Those numbers would make virtual memory useless if programs accessed memory randomly. They don't. **Locality of reference** means programs reuse the same pages repeatedly (temporal locality) and access nearby addresses (spatial locality). A loop runs the same instructions on neighbouring array elements, so once its pages are in memory, it runs without faulting.

## Major and minor faults

Not every page fault reads from disk. A **major fault** needs disk input. A **minor fault** happens when the page is already in memory but not yet mapped into this process, for example a shared library page another process loaded, or a page in the file cache. Minor faults cost microseconds rather than milliseconds. On Linux, `/usr/bin/time -v` reports both counts for a program.

## Copy-on-write

After `fork()`, parent and child have identical address spaces. Copying every page immediately would be slow and usually wasted, since the child often calls `exec()` right away. Copy-on-write lets both processes share the same physical pages, marked read-only. When either one writes to a shared page, the write faults, and the OS copies that single page, gives the writer the private copy, and resumes. Pages nobody writes are never copied.

## Memory-mapped files

The same machinery maps files into memory. With `mmap()`, a file appears as a range of addresses; reading those addresses faults pages in from the file, and modified pages are written back. Databases and programs that process large files use memory mapping to let the OS handle caching.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What is a page fault and how is it handled?" and an EAT calculation. List the steps from trap to instruction restart, and in the calculation, convert milliseconds to nanoseconds before multiplying. Explaining copy-on-write as a use of page faults shows you see virtual memory as a general mechanism.

sections.title: Belady's Anomaly
sections.content:
Normally, more frames means fewer faults. With FIFO, adding frames can sometimes cause more faults. The classic string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4 frames.

LRU and OPT are stack algorithms (the pages held with n frames are always a subset of those held with n + 1), so they never show Belady's anomaly.

sections.title: LRU in Practice: Approximations
sections.content:
Exact LRU needs to record the time of every memory access, which is too expensive in hardware. OSs approximate it with a reference bit that the hardware sets when a page is accessed:
Second-chance (clock) algorithm: sweep frames in a circle. If a page's reference bit is 1, clear it and move on (giving it a second chance). If it's 0, evict that page.
Enhanced clock: also uses the dirty bit, preferring clean, unreferenced pages, because they don't need writing back.

sections.question: Which algorithm can suffer from Belady's anomaly?
sections.explanation: FIFO isn't a stack algorithm, so adding frames can increase faults for some reference strings.

items: OPT ≤ LRU ≤ FIFO faults in typical cases; here 7, 9 and 10.
Belady's anomaly affects FIFO, never LRU or OPT.
Real OSs approximate LRU with reference bits (clock / second chance).

content.theory:
When a page fault occurs and memory is full, the OS must evict a page to make room. The choice matters: evict a page that's needed again soon and you cause another fault almost immediately. This lesson explains the optimal algorithm that sets the benchmark, FIFO and its surprising anomaly, LRU and why it works, and the clock algorithm real systems use to approximate LRU cheaply.

## The goal

Page replacement aims to minimize page faults. Each fault costs milliseconds, so even a small improvement in the fault rate makes a large difference in performance. Algorithms are compared on a **reference string**, the sequence of pages a program accesses, with a fixed number of frames.

## Optimal (OPT)

The optimal algorithm evicts the page that won't be used for the longest time in the future. It produces the fewest possible faults for any reference string. In the course's example string with 3 frames, OPT causes 7 faults.

OPT can't be implemented, because the OS doesn't know the future. Its role is as a benchmark: if a practical algorithm comes within a few percent of OPT on real traces, there's little left to gain.

## FIFO

First-in, first-out evicts the page that has been in memory longest. It needs only a queue, so it's cheap. Its flaw is that age says nothing about usefulness: the oldest page might be the most heavily used, such as a page of a frequently called function. On the example string, FIFO causes 10 faults.

## Belady's anomaly

Intuition says more frames should mean fewer faults. FIFO can violate this. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, FIFO causes 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 faults with 4 frames. This is **Belady's anomaly**.

LRU and OPT never show the anomaly, because they're **stack algorithms**: the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1 frames. Adding a frame can only keep more useful pages, never fewer.

## LRU

Least recently used evicts the page that hasn't been accessed for the longest time. It uses the recent past to predict the near future, relying on temporal locality: pages used recently are likely to be used again soon. On the example string, LRU causes 9 faults, between FIFO and OPT, and on real workloads it usually comes much closer to OPT than FIFO does.

## Why exact LRU is impractical

Exact LRU needs the time of every single memory access, or a list reordered on every access. With billions of accesses per second, doing that in software is impossible, and hardware support is too costly. Real systems approximate LRU using one bit the hardware sets cheaply.

## The reference bit and the clock algorithm

Each page-table entry has a **reference bit** that the hardware sets whenever the page is accessed. The **clock algorithm** (second chance) arranges frames in a circle with a pointer, like a clock hand:

1. Look at the page under the hand
2. If its reference bit is 1, clear it to 0 (giving the page a second chance) and advance the hand
3. If its reference bit is 0, the page hasn't been used since the hand last passed, so evict it

Recently used pages keep getting their bits set and survive; idle pages are found and evicted. The **enhanced clock** algorithm also considers the dirty bit, preferring clean, unreferenced pages, because evicting them needs no disk write.

## What Linux does

Linux approximates LRU with active and inactive lists. Pages start on the inactive list and move to the active list when accessed again, and reclaim takes pages from the tail of the inactive list. Recent kernels add a multi-generational LRU that tracks page ages in more detail, improving performance under memory pressure on phones and servers.

## Frame allocation

Replacement can be **global**, choosing a victim from any process, or **local**, choosing only from the faulting process's own frames. Global replacement uses memory more flexibly but lets one process's behaviour hurt others. Most general-purpose systems use global replacement with safeguards against thrashing, the subject of the next lesson.

## How interviewers test this

Exams give a reference string and a frame count and ask for the number of faults under FIFO, LRU and OPT. Draw a table with one column per reference, and mark each fault. Interviewers ask "What is Belady's anomaly?", answered with FIFO, the definition, and the fact that stack algorithms such as LRU are immune.
