modules.description: Replication and sharding, choosing a data store, caching strategies and consistent hashing.

lessons.title: Database Replication, Partitioning and Sharding
lessons.description: Scale reads with replicas and writes with sharding, and handle the problems each creates.

content.theory:
The database is usually the first component to buckle under growth, because app servers scale out easily and data doesn't. Two techniques scale it: replication copies data to more machines to handle more reads and survive failures, and sharding splits data across machines to handle more writes and storage. This lesson explains both, their variants, and the problems they introduce.

## Leader-follower replication

In **leader-follower** (primary-replica) replication, one node, the leader, accepts all writes and streams changes to followers, which serve reads.

~~~text
          writes                 replication log
Client  ------->  Leader  ------------------------>  Followers
Client  <----------------------- reads ---------------  Followers
~~~

Benefits: read capacity grows with each follower, followers can live in other regions for local reads, and a follower can be promoted if the leader fails.

## Synchronous versus asynchronous replication

- **Synchronous**: the leader waits for followers to confirm before acknowledging a write. No data loss on failover, but writes are slower, and a slow follower stalls writes
- **Asynchronous**: the leader acknowledges immediately and replicates in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash can lose the most recent writes, and followers lag behind

Most systems use asynchronous replication, sometimes with one synchronous follower (semi-synchronous) to guarantee at least one up-to-date copy.

## Replication lag

With asynchronous followers, a read may hit a replica that hasn't received the latest write. A user updates their profile, refreshes, and sees the old version. Mitigations:

- **Read-your-writes**: route a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write, or read the user's own data from the leader
- **Monotonic reads**: pin each user to one replica so they never see data go backwards
- **Lag-aware routing**: avoid replicas that report lag above a threshold

## Multi-leader and leaderless replication

**Multi-leader** replication accepts writes at several leaders, often one per region, and syncs them. Writes are fast everywhere, but concurrent writes to the same record conflict and need resolution, such as last-write-wins or merging.

**Leaderless** replication, used by Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra, sends each write to several replicas. With N replicas, a write succeeds after W confirmations and a read queries R replicas. If W + R > N, read and write sets overlap, so reads see the latest acknowledged write. Tuning W and R trades latency against consistency per query.

## Partitioning and sharding

Replication copies all data everywhere, so it doesn't help once writes or total data outgrow one machine. **Sharding** (horizontal partitioning) splits rows across machines, each holding a subset:

- **Range-based**: users A–M on shard 1, N–Z on shard 2. Range queries are efficient, but some ranges get hot
- **Hash-based**: shard = hash(user_id) mod N. Even spread, but range queries hit every shard, and changing N moves most keys; consistent hashing, covered later, fixes the last problem
- **Directory-based**: a lookup service maps each key to its shard. Flexible, but the directory must itself be scaled and highly available

**Vertical partitioning** is different: it splits tables or columns by feature, such as moving the users table and the orders table to different databases. It's a quick first step but has a limit, since each feature's table can still outgrow one machine.

## Choosing a shard key

The shard key decides everything. A good key:

- spreads load evenly, so no shard is hot
- keeps data that's queried together on the same shard
- rarely needs to change

For a chat app, sharding messages by conversation ID keeps each conversation on one shard. Sharding by timestamp sends all new writes to one shard, creating a hotspot.

## Problems sharding introduces

- **Cross-shard queries**: joins and aggregations across shards need application-level fan-out or a separate analytics store
- **Cross-shard transactions**: atomic updates spanning shards need two-phase commit or sagas, both complex
- **Hot keys**: a celebrity's account can overload its shard; split hot keys or cache them
- **Resharding**: adding shards means moving data while serving traffic

Because of these costs, shard only when needed: first add indexes, caching, read replicas and a bigger machine. Many companies run a single well-tuned primary much longer than they expect.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "How would you scale the database?" Walk the ladder: indexes and caching, read replicas for read load, vertical partitioning, then sharding with a justified shard key. Mention replication lag and read-your-writes, and name the cross-shard costs.

sources.title: DeCandia et al., Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)

sections.question: Read replicas mainly help with which load?
sections.explanation: All writes still go to the leader; sharding is needed to scale writes and storage.

traps.question: Shard messages by created_at.
traps.trap: All new writes hit one shard.
traps.solution: Shard by a high-cardinality key such as conversation_id.

traps.question: A user updates their profile and sees the old one.
traps.trap: Reading from a lagging replica.
traps.solution: Serve read-your-writes from the leader after a user's write.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Replication scales reads and adds failover; sharding scales writes and storage.
Asynchronous replication is fast but can lose recent writes and causes lag.
Pick a shard key that spreads load and keeps related data together.
Shard last: indexes, caching, replicas and bigger machines come first.

lessons.title: SQL vs NoSQL: Choosing the Right Data Store
lessons.description: Relational databases, key-value, document, wide-column, graph and object storage, and how to pick.

content.theory:
Choosing a data store is one of the most consequential design decisions, because it shapes queries, scaling and consistency for years. No database is best at everything. This lesson compares relational databases with the main NoSQL families, adds object storage and search engines, and gives a decision approach you can explain in an interview.

## Relational databases

Relational databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL store data in tables with schemas, support joins and SQL, and provide ACID transactions.

Choose them when:

- data is structured and relationships matter, such as users, orders and payments
- you need transactions across multiple rows or tables
- queries are varied and not all known in advance

Their scaling limit is writes on a single primary, which replicas don't fix. With good indexing and hardware, a single primary handles a large share of real-world workloads, and sharding or distributed SQL systems such as CockroachDB, Spanner or Vitess extend it further.

## Key-value stores

Key-value stores such as Redis, Memcached and DynamoDB map a key to an opaque value with O(1) lookups.

- Extremely fast, and straightforward to partition across nodes
- Queries only by key; no rich filtering or joins
- Uses: caches, sessions, rate-limit counters, feature flags, shopping carts

## Document stores

Document stores such as MongoDB and Couchbase store JSON-like documents, each potentially with different fields.

- Flexible schema, and nested data stays together, so one read fetches a whole entity
- Weaker join support; relationships across documents are handled in the application
- Uses: product catalogues with varied attributes, content management, user profiles

## Wide-column stores

Wide-column stores such as Cassandra, HBase and Bigtable organize data by row key into column families, designed for huge write volumes across many machines.

- Linear write scaling, tunable consistency, multi-region replication
- You design tables around queries; ad-hoc queries are hard
- Uses: time series, event logs, messaging history, IoT data

## Graph databases

Graph databases such as Neo4j store nodes and edges directly, making multi-hop relationship queries fast.

- Uses: social graphs ("friends of friends"), recommendations, fraud rings, knowledge graphs
- Less suited to bulk aggregation or plain key lookups

## Object storage and search

Two other stores appear in almost every design:

- **Object storage** such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage holds large binary files: images, videos, backups. It's cheap, durable and effectively unlimited, accessed by key over HTTP. Store the file there and keep only its URL and metadata in the database
- **Search engines** such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch build inverted indexes for full-text search, ranking and faceted filters. They're usually fed from the primary database, not used as the source of truth

## Comparison

| Store | Data model | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relational | Tables, schema | Transactions, joins, flexible queries | Write scaling beyond one primary |
| Key-value | Key → value | Speed, straightforward scaling | Query only by key |
| Document | JSON documents | Flexible schema, nested reads | Cross-document joins |
| Wide-column | Rows and column families | Massive writes, multi-region | Query-driven modelling |
| Graph | Nodes and edges | Relationship traversal | Aggregations |
| Object storage | Files by key | Cheap, durable bulk storage | Not a query engine |

## Polyglot persistence

Real systems combine stores, each for what it does best. An e-commerce platform might use PostgreSQL for orders and payments, Redis for sessions and caching, Elasticsearch for product search, S3 for product images, and a wide-column store for clickstream events. The cost is operational: more systems to run, monitor and keep in sync, usually via change data capture or event streams.

## A decision approach

Ask these questions in order:

1. Do we need multi-row transactions or complex relational queries? If yes, start relational
2. What are the main access patterns? Key lookups suggest key-value; whole-entity reads suggest documents
3. What's the write volume and scale? Massive write rates across regions suggest wide-column
4. Are relationships the core of the queries? Consider a graph database
5. Are there large files or full-text search needs? Add object storage or a search engine

"Use NoSQL because it scales" isn't a reason on its own. State the access pattern and requirement that drives the choice.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "SQL or NoSQL for this system, and why?" Tie the choice to transactions, access patterns and write volume, store media in object storage, and mention polyglot persistence with its operational cost.

sources.title: DeCandia et al., Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)

sections.question: Where should a video-sharing app store the video files themselves?
options: Object storage such as S3, with metadata in a database
In a relational table as BLOBs
sections.explanation: Object storage is cheap, durable and built for large files; the database keeps URLs and metadata.

traps.question: Use MongoDB because NoSQL scales.
traps.trap: No link to requirements or access patterns.
traps.solution: Explain transactions, query shapes and write volume, then choose.

traps.question: Store user-uploaded images in the database.
traps.trap: Bloats the database and its backups.
traps.solution: Put files in object storage and store references.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Relational databases suit transactions and varied queries.
Key-value stores suit fast lookups by key; documents suit whole-entity reads.
Wide-column stores suit massive write volumes; graphs suit relationship queries.
Combine stores per need, and justify each with an access pattern.

lessons.title: Caching Strategies and Pitfalls
lessons.description: Where to cache, cache-aside vs write-through vs write-back, eviction, invalidation and stampedes.

content.theory:
Caching keeps frequently used data in fast storage, usually memory, so most requests avoid slow work such as database queries or remote calls. A good cache can cut latency from tens of milliseconds to under one and reduce database load by an order of magnitude. Caching also introduces its hardest problems: stale data and invalidation. This lesson covers cache layers, update strategies, eviction, invalidation and the failure modes interviewers ask about.

## Where caches live

Caching happens at every layer:

- **Client**: browser caches and mobile app storage
- **CDN**: static and shareable content at the edge
- **Web server / reverse proxy**: cached HTTP responses
- **Application**: an in-process cache in each server, or a distributed cache such as Redis or Memcached shared by all servers
- **Database**: buffer pools and query caches inside the database itself

In-process caches are fastest but each server has its own copy, so data can differ between servers. A distributed cache is shared and consistent across servers, at the cost of a network hop.

## What to cache

Good candidates are read often, change rarely and are expensive to compute: user profiles, product details, rendered page fragments, computed feeds, session data. Data accessed with a skewed distribution benefits most: if 20% of items get 80% of reads, caching that 20% captures most of the benefit.

## Cache-aside (lazy loading)

The application manages the cache directly:

1. Look up the key in the cache
2. On a hit, return it
3. On a miss, read from the database, store the result in the cache with a TTL, and return it

~~~text
value = cache.get(key)
if value is null:
    value = db.query(key)
    cache.set(key, value, ttl=300)
return value
~~~

Only requested data is cached, and a cache failure degrades performance without breaking correctness. Downsides: each miss costs three trips, and data can be stale until the TTL expires or the key is invalidated. Cache-aside is the most common strategy.

## Write-through

Every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always current. Reads are fast and fresh, but writes are slower, and the cache fills with data that may never be read. It's often combined with cache-aside for reads.

## Write-back (write-behind)

Writes go to the cache only, and the cache flushes them to the database asynchronously, often in batches. Writes are fast, but if the cache node fails before flushing, data is lost. It suits high-volume, loss-tolerant data such as view counters, not orders or payments.

## Refresh-ahead

The cache refreshes popular entries before they expire, so users rarely see a miss. It works well when access patterns are predictable, and wastes work when predictions are wrong.

## Eviction policies

Memory is limited, so caches evict entries when full:

| Policy | Evicts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| LRU (least recently used) | The entry unused for longest | The most common default |
| LFU (least frequently used) | The entry used least often | Better for stable popularity |
| FIFO | The oldest entry | Rarely ideal |
| TTL expiry | Entries past their time to live | Bounds staleness |

Redis supports several of these as configurable policies.

## Invalidation

When the underlying data changes, cached copies become stale. Strategies:

- **TTL**: accept staleness up to a bound, such as 5 minutes. Simplest, and often good enough
- **Delete on write**: when data changes, delete the cache key so the next read reloads it. Deleting is safer than updating the cache, because two concurrent updates can write cache values in the wrong order
- **Event-driven invalidation**: publish change events, often from the database's change log, and have cache consumers react

Even with delete-on-write, races exist: a reader can load old data from the database moments before a writer deletes the key, then write the stale value back into the cache. Short TTLs bound the damage.

## Failure modes

- **Cache stampede** (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once, all hitting the database. Fixes: a lock so only one request rebuilds the value, serving stale data while refreshing, or adding random jitter to TTLs
- **Cache penetration**: requests for keys that don't exist always miss and hit the database, sometimes as an attack. Fix: cache "not found" results briefly, or use a Bloom filter
- **Hot keys**: one key gets so much traffic that its cache node saturates. Fix: replicate the key across nodes or keep a local in-process copy
- **Cold start**: after a restart, an empty cache sends all traffic to the database. Fix: warm the cache before taking traffic

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Where would you add caching?", "Cache-aside vs write-through?" and "How do you keep the cache consistent?" Place caches at the right layers, default to cache-aside with TTLs and delete-on-write, and explain stampede protection for hot keys.

sections.question: A popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. What is this called?
sections.explanation: Fix it with a rebuild lock, stale-while-revalidate or TTL jitter.

traps.question: Update the cached value on every write.
traps.trap: Concurrent writes can leave the cache with the older value.
traps.solution: Delete the key and let the next read repopulate it.

traps.question: Use write-back caching for payments.
traps.trap: A cache node failure loses unflushed writes.
traps.solution: Use write-back only for loss-tolerant data such as counters.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Cache data that is read often, changes rarely and is expensive to produce.
Cache-aside is the default; write-through keeps caches fresh; write-back is fast but can lose data.
Delete cache keys on writes and bound staleness with TTLs.
Protect hot keys from stampedes, penetration and node saturation.

lessons.title: Consistent Hashing
lessons.description: Distribute keys across nodes so adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of data.

content.theory:
When data or requests are spread across N servers, the obvious approach, server = hash(key) mod N, breaks badly when N changes: almost every key moves to a different server. Consistent hashing fixes this, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. It underpins distributed caches, Dynamo-style databases, and load balancers that need affinity. This lesson explains the problem, the hash ring, virtual nodes and where it's used.

## The problem with mod N

Suppose 4 cache servers and keys placed with hash(key) mod 4. Adding a fifth server changes the formula to mod 5, and a key's server changes unless hash(key) mod 4 happens to equal hash(key) mod 5. Roughly 80% of keys move.

For a cache, that means a sudden flood of misses that can overload the database. For a database, it means moving most of the data. Either way, scaling becomes dangerous.

## The hash ring

Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto the same circular space, for example 0 to 2³² − 1, arranged as a ring:

1. Hash each server's ID to a position on the ring
2. Hash each key to a position on the ring
3. Assign each key to the first server found moving clockwise from its position

~~~text
          S1
     k3 /    \ k1
       S3      S2
          \  /
           k2
~~~

When a server joins, it takes over only the keys between its position and the previous server's position. When a server leaves, only its keys move to the next server clockwise. On average, adding or removing one of N servers moves about 1/N of the keys.

## Lookup implementation

Keep server positions in a sorted structure, such as a sorted array or a balanced tree (Java's TreeMap). To find a key's server, hash the key and find the smallest position greater than or equal to it, wrapping around to the start of the ring if necessary. With a sorted array and binary search, lookups cost O(log N).

## The imbalance problem

With few servers, random positions divide the ring unevenly: one server might own 40% of the ring while another owns 10%. Uneven ownership means uneven load. And when a server fails, all its keys land on a single neighbour, which may be overwhelmed.

## Virtual nodes

The fix is **virtual nodes**: place each physical server at many positions on the ring, for example 100 to 200, by hashing "S1-0", "S1-1" and so on. Each server then owns many small arcs scattered around the ring.

Benefits:

- **Even distribution**: many small arcs average out, so each server's share approaches 1/N
- **Smooth rebalancing**: when a server leaves, its many arcs spread across many other servers instead of one neighbour
- **Heterogeneous capacity**: a server with twice the capacity gets twice as many virtual nodes

The cost is a larger lookup table, which is negligible in practice.

## Replication on the ring

Dynamo-style databases store each key on the first R distinct physical servers clockwise from its position. Losing one server leaves R − 1 copies, and the ring tells every node where copies live without a central directory.

## Where consistent hashing is used

- **Distributed caches**: client libraries for Memcached and Redis clusters use it so adding a cache node invalidates only a fraction of keys
- **Databases**: Amazon Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak place and replicate data with it
- **Load balancing with affinity**: routing a user or session to the same backend while tolerating backend changes
- **CDNs and content routing**: mapping objects to cache servers within a location

Redis Cluster uses a related approach, fixed hash slots: 16,384 slots assigned to nodes, moved slot by slot during resharding.

## Alternatives

**Rendezvous hashing** (highest random weight) computes a score for each key-server pair and picks the highest, giving similar minimal movement without a ring. **Jump consistent hash** maps keys to numbered buckets with almost no memory. Both are worth naming to show breadth.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "How would you distribute data across cache nodes?" and "What happens when a node is added?" Explain why mod N moves most keys, describe the ring with clockwise assignment, add virtual nodes for balance, and give real systems that use it.

sources.title: DeCandia et al., Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)

sections.question: With consistent hashing and N servers, roughly what fraction of keys move when one server is added?
sections.explanation: Only keys in the new server's arc move; mod N hashing moves most keys.

traps.question: Add a cache node with mod N hashing during peak traffic.
traps.trap: Most keys remap and the database is flooded with misses.
traps.solution: Use consistent hashing so only about 1/N of keys move.

traps.question: Three servers on a ring with one position each.
traps.trap: Uneven arcs give uneven load.
traps.solution: Use many virtual nodes per server.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: hash(key) mod N moves most keys when N changes.
Consistent hashing places keys and servers on a ring; keys go to the next server clockwise.
Virtual nodes even out load and spread a failed server's keys.
Used by Dynamo, Cassandra and distributed cache clients.

modules.title: Async Processing and Reliability
modules.description: Message queues and streams, rate limiting, and patterns that contain failures.

lessons.title: Message Queues and Event Streaming
lessons.description: Decouple services with queues and logs: delivery guarantees, ordering, backpressure and Kafka vs RabbitMQ.

content.theory:
Not every task should happen while a user waits. Sending email, resizing images, updating search indexes and fanning out notifications can run in the background. Message queues and event streams make that possible: producers publish messages, and consumers process them at their own pace. This lesson explains why asynchronous processing helps, queues versus logs, delivery guarantees, ordering and backpressure.

## Why go asynchronous

Asynchronous messaging gives three benefits:

- **Lower latency**: the request returns as soon as the work is queued. Uploading a video returns in milliseconds while transcoding happens later
- **Decoupling**: producers don't need to know who consumes their messages, and either side can be deployed, scaled or fail independently
- **Load levelling**: a traffic spike fills the queue instead of overwhelming downstream services, which drain it at a steady rate

The cost is complexity: eventual consistency, duplicate messages, monitoring queue depth and debugging flows that cross services.

## Queues versus logs

Two main models exist:

| | Message queue | Event log (stream) |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS | Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Redpanda |
| After consumption | Message is removed | Message stays for the retention period |
| Consumers | Compete for messages | Each consumer group reads independently at its own offset |
| Replay | Not possible | Rewind offsets to reprocess history |
| Typical use | Task distribution to workers | Event streaming, multiple subscribers, analytics |

In a queue, each message goes to one worker, which suits jobs like "send this email". In a log, many independent consumers, such as search indexing, analytics and notifications, can each read every event.

## Delivery guarantees

Messages can be lost or duplicated when producers, brokers or consumers fail. Systems offer three levels:

- **At most once**: messages may be lost but never duplicated. Acceptable for metrics where occasional loss doesn't matter
- **At least once**: messages are never lost but may be delivered more than once. The common default
- **Exactly once**: each message's effect happens once. Achievable within some systems, such as Kafka transactions between topics, but end to end it usually means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing

With at-least-once delivery, consumers must be **idempotent**: processing the same message twice must have the same effect as once. Techniques include storing processed message IDs and skipping repeats, or using upserts keyed by a unique ID.

## Acknowledgements and dead letters

A consumer acknowledges a message only after processing succeeds. If it crashes first, the message becomes visible again for another consumer. Messages that fail repeatedly, perhaps because they're malformed, move to a **dead-letter queue** after a few attempts, so they don't block the queue forever and can be inspected later.

## Ordering

Global ordering across a large system is expensive. Kafka guarantees order only within a **partition**, so choosing the partition key decides what's ordered: partitioning by user ID keeps each user's events in order while allowing parallel processing across users. SQS standard queues don't guarantee order; FIFO queues do, with lower throughput.

## Backpressure

If consumers fall behind, queues grow without limit. Monitor **queue depth** and consumer lag, and respond by:

- autoscaling consumers based on lag
- rate limiting producers when queues exceed a threshold
- shedding or deferring low-priority work

A growing queue is an early warning that a downstream service is struggling.

## Choosing between them

Pick a work queue such as SQS or RabbitMQ when each task needs exactly one worker and nobody needs history. Pick a log such as Kafka when several systems react to the same events, when you need to replay events after a bug fix, or when throughput reaches hundreds of thousands of messages per second. Managed services reduce operational effort for both.

## Common patterns

- **Work queue**: background jobs distributed across workers
- **Publish-subscribe**: one event, many interested consumers
- **Fan-out**: one message becomes many, such as a post delivered to thousands of followers' feeds
- **Event sourcing**: store every change as an event, and rebuild state by replaying the log
- **Outbox pattern**: write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the data change, then publish it, so data and events never disagree

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Which parts would you make asynchronous?", "Kafka vs RabbitMQ?" and "How do you avoid processing a message twice?" Move slow, non-blocking work behind a queue, choose a queue or a log by consumer pattern, assume at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, and partition by key for ordering.

sections.question: With at-least-once delivery, what must consumers be?
options: Idempotent, so duplicates have no extra effect
sections.explanation: Retries after failures can deliver a message twice.

traps.question: Kafka guarantees ordering, so all events are in order.
traps.trap: Order holds only within a partition.
traps.solution: Partition by the key whose events must stay ordered.

traps.question: Send the email inside the signup request.
traps.trap: Slow third-party calls add latency and failures to the request.
traps.solution: Queue the email and process it asynchronously.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Queues cut latency, decouple services and absorb spikes.
Queues hand each message to one worker; logs let many consumer groups replay events.
Assume at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent.
Kafka orders messages within a partition, so choose the partition key carefully.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting
lessons.description: Protect services with token bucket, leaky bucket and window algorithms, locally and across a cluster.

content.theory:
Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a period. It protects services from abuse and overload, keeps costs predictable, and ensures one heavy user can't degrade everyone else. "Design a rate limiter" is also a classic interview question in its own right. This lesson explains the main algorithms, how to enforce limits across many servers, and how to communicate limits to clients.

## Why rate limit

- **Prevent abuse**: credential stuffing, scraping and denial-of-service attempts
- **Protect capacity**: keep one client's burst from exhausting shared resources
- **Fairness and cost control**: enforce plan quotas and cap spending on expensive downstream APIs

Limits can apply per user, per API key, per IP address, per endpoint, or globally.

## Token bucket

A bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at R tokens per second. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

- Allows bursts up to B, then a steady rate of R
- Memory-light: store the token count and last refill time per client
- Used widely, including by AWS and Stripe

Refill lazily on each request: compute tokens added since the last request, cap at B, then decide.

## Leaky bucket

Requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate. If the queue is full, new requests are dropped. It smooths traffic into a steady outflow, which suits protecting a downstream system that can't handle bursts, but bursts of legitimate traffic wait or get dropped.

## Fixed window counter

Count requests per client per fixed window, such as each calendar minute, and reject once the count exceeds the limit.

- Cheap: one counter per client per window, for example an atomic increment in Redis with an expiry
- Edge problem: a client can send the full limit at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00, doubling the allowed rate around the boundary

## Sliding window log

Store a timestamp for every request and count those within the last window. It's exact but uses memory proportional to the request rate, which is expensive at high volumes.

## Sliding window counter

A hybrid: keep counts for the current and previous fixed windows, and weight the previous count by how much of it overlaps the sliding window:

~~~text
estimate = current_count + previous_count × (1 − elapsed_fraction_of_current_window)
~~~

It's nearly as accurate as the log, with the memory cost of fixed windows. It's a strong default for APIs.

## Comparing algorithms

| Algorithm | Bursts | Memory | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token bucket | Allowed up to bucket size | Low | Good |
| Leaky bucket | Smoothed out | Low (queue) | Good |
| Fixed window | Double burst at edges | Lowest | Approximate |
| Sliding log | Precise | High | Exact |
| Sliding window counter | Mostly precise | Low | Close to exact |

## Distributed rate limiting

With many API servers, per-server counters let a client exceed the limit by spreading requests across servers. Options:

- **Centralized store**: keep counters in Redis and update them atomically with INCR plus EXPIRE, or with a Lua script that checks and updates in one step to avoid race conditions
- **Sticky routing**: route each client to one limiter instance by consistent hashing
- **Local limits with sync**: each server enforces a share of the limit and periodically syncs, trading accuracy for speed

The centralized Redis approach is the usual interview answer. Mention that the limiter adds a network hop and that if Redis is unavailable you must decide whether to **fail open** (allow requests, preserving availability) or **fail closed** (reject them, preserving protection).

## Where to enforce limits

Limits usually live at the edge, in an API gateway or reverse proxy, so rejected traffic never reaches application servers. Finer, business-specific limits, such as five password attempts per account per hour, live in the application.

## Telling clients

Return **429 Too Many Requests** with a `Retry-After` header, and expose limit headers such as `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. Well-behaved clients back off with exponential delays and jitter instead of retrying immediately.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "Design a rate limiter" or "How would you stop one client overloading the API?" Choose token bucket or sliding window counter with reasons, store counters in Redis with atomic operations, enforce at the gateway, return 429 with Retry-After, and state the fail-open versus fail-closed decision.

sections.question: Which rate-limiting algorithm allows short bursts up to a fixed size while enforcing an average rate?
sections.explanation: A full bucket permits a burst; refills enforce the long-term rate.

traps.question: Each API server keeps its own counter.
traps.trap: Clients exceed the limit by spreading requests across servers.
traps.solution: Use a shared store such as Redis with atomic updates.

traps.question: Read the counter, then write count + 1.
traps.trap: Concurrent requests race past the limit.
traps.solution: Use INCR or a Lua script that checks and updates atomically.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Token bucket allows bursts; leaky bucket smooths traffic.
Fixed windows are cheap but allow double bursts at boundaries; sliding window counters fix this cheaply.
Use atomic Redis operations for limits across many servers.
Return 429 with Retry-After, and decide fail-open vs fail-closed.

lessons.title: Reliability Patterns: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Observability
lessons.description: Keep partial failures contained with timeouts, backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and SLO-driven monitoring.

content.theory:
In a distributed system, something is always failing: a server, a network link, a dependency. Reliability doesn't come from preventing failures; it comes from containing them so one slow component doesn't take down everything. This lesson covers timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation, and the monitoring practices, SLIs and SLOs, that tell you when users are affected.

## Cascading failures

Imagine service A calls service B, and B becomes slow. A's threads wait on B, A runs out of threads, and now A is slow for its own callers. Failures spread upstream like this, called a **cascading failure**. Most reliability patterns exist to break this chain.

## Timeouts

Every network call needs a timeout. Without one, a hung dependency holds resources forever. Choose timeouts from the dependency's measured latency, such as a little above its p99, and make sure the total of nested timeouts fits within the user-facing deadline. Passing a deadline along with each request lets downstream services stop work that no longer matters.

## Retries with exponential backoff and jitter

Many failures are transient, so retrying helps. But naive retries make outages worse: if every client retries immediately, a struggling service receives several times its normal load. Retry safely:

- retry only **idempotent** operations, or use idempotency keys
- use **exponential backoff**: wait 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800 and so on
- add **jitter**, randomizing each wait, so clients don't retry in synchronized waves
- cap the number of attempts, and use a **retry budget**, such as retries limited to 10% of requests

## Circuit breakers

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures:

| State | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Closed | Calls pass through; failures are counted |
| Open | After too many failures, calls fail immediately without contacting the dependency |
| Half-open | After a cool-down, a few trial calls go through; success closes the circuit, failure reopens it |

Failing fast saves resources, gives the struggling dependency time to recover, and lets the caller use a fallback immediately. Libraries such as Resilience4j implement this pattern.

## Bulkheads

Ships have watertight compartments so one breach doesn't sink the ship. In software, **bulkheads** isolate resources: separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency, so a slow payment service can exhaust only its own pool, not the threads serving product pages.

## Graceful degradation and load shedding

When parts fail, serve a reduced experience rather than an error: show cached recommendations, hide the reviews widget, or queue an order for later confirmation. Under overload, **load shedding** rejects low-priority requests early, such as analytics beacons, to keep critical ones, such as checkout, working.

## Redundancy and failover

Run every critical component with redundancy across failure domains: multiple instances, multiple availability zones, and for the highest availability, multiple regions. Test failover regularly; untested failover often fails when it's needed. Chaos engineering, deliberately injecting failures as Netflix's Chaos Monkey does, builds confidence that recovery works.

## SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

Monitoring must answer one question: are users affected?

- A **service level indicator** (SLI) measures user experience, such as the fraction of requests that succeed in under 300 ms
- A **service level objective** (SLO) sets a target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days
- The **error budget** is the allowed shortfall: 0.1% of requests, about 43 minutes of full downtime per month

When the budget is healthy, teams ship features faster; when it's spent, they prioritize reliability work. Google's SRE book popularized this approach.

## Observability

Three signals help you understand a running system:

- **Metrics**: numeric time series, such as request rate, error rate and latency percentiles. The RED method (rate, errors, duration) suits services; the USE method (utilization, saturation, errors) suits resources
- **Logs**: detailed records of events, structured as JSON with request IDs so they can be searched
- **Traces**: the path of one request across services, showing where time is spent, collected with tools such as OpenTelemetry

Alert on symptoms users feel, such as SLO burn rate, rather than on every CPU spike.

## How interviewers test this

Expect "What happens if this service goes down?" and "How do you prevent cascading failures?" Add timeouts everywhere, retries with backoff and jitter for idempotent calls, circuit breakers and bulkheads around dependencies, graceful degradation, and SLO-based monitoring with metrics, logs and traces.

sections.question: Why add jitter to retry delays?
options: So clients don't retry in synchronized waves that overload the service
sections.explanation: Randomized delays spread retries out over time.

traps.question: Retry failed calls immediately, five times.
traps.trap: Synchronized retries multiply load on a struggling service.
traps.solution: Use exponential backoff with jitter and a retry budget.

traps.question: Our health dashboard shows CPU, so we know users are fine.
traps.trap: Resource metrics don't show user experience.
traps.solution: Measure SLIs such as success rate and p99 latency against SLOs.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Every remote call needs a timeout that fits the overall deadline.
Retry only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff, jitter and a cap.
Circuit breakers fail fast; bulkheads isolate resources per dependency.
Define SLIs and SLOs, use error budgets, and alert on user-facing symptoms.

lessons.title: Design a URL Shortener
lessons.description: A full walkthrough: requirements, estimates, ID generation, storage, caching and analytics.

content.theory:
A URL shortener turns a long link into a short one, such as `sho.rt/aZ3kQ9b`, and redirects visitors to the original. It's the most common warm-up design problem because it touches every core idea: estimation, ID generation, read-heavy scaling and caching. This walkthrough follows the four-step framework from requirements to deep dives.

## Step 1: requirements

**Functional:**

- Create a short URL for a long URL, optionally with a custom alias and expiry
- Redirect a short URL to its long URL
- Optional: click analytics per link

**Non-functional:**

- Heavily read-dominated: assume a 100:1 read-to-write ratio
- Redirects must be fast, under about 50 ms at p99 excluding the user's network
- Highly available: a broken redirect breaks every page that links to it
- Short codes shouldn't be guessable in sequence, to avoid enumeration

## Step 2: estimates

Assume 100 million new URLs per month.

- **Writes**: 10⁸ ÷ (2.5 × 10⁶ seconds) ≈ 40 per second
- **Reads**: 100 × 40 = 4,000 per second on average, perhaps 10,000 at peak
- **Storage**: each record (code, long URL up to about 2 KB, owner, timestamps) averages around 500 bytes. Over 5 years: 100M × 12 × 5 = 6 billion URLs × 500 bytes = 3 TB

**Code length**: with 62 characters (a–z, A–Z, 0–9), 7 characters give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations, far more than 6 billion. Seven characters is enough.

## Step 3: high-level design

**API:**

~~~http
POST /api/urls        { "longUrl": "...", "alias": "optional", "expiresAt": "optional" }
-> 201 { "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9b" }

GET /{code}
-> 301 or 302 redirect with Location: <longUrl>
~~~

**Components:**

~~~text
Client -> Load balancer -> Stateless app servers -> Redis cache -> Database
                                         \-> Analytics events -> Queue -> Analytics store
~~~

**Data model**: a table `urls(code PRIMARY KEY, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at)`. Lookups are always by code, a perfect key-value access pattern, so a key-value or wide-column store such as DynamoDB or Cassandra fits well. A relational database with code as the primary key also works at this scale.

## Step 4: deep dive on ID generation

The central question is how to generate unique short codes. Three approaches:

**1. Hash the long URL**, for example MD5 or SHA-256, and take the first 7 Base62 characters. The same URL always produces the same code, which deduplicates. But truncated hashes collide, so you must check the database and retry with a salt on collision, which adds a read to every write.

**2. Counter plus Base62 encoding.** A unique 64-bit number per URL, Base62-encoded, gives a short code with no collisions. The counter must be unique across servers:

- a single database sequence becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure
- **range allocation** fixes this: each app server reserves a block of IDs, such as 1,000,000 at a time, from a coordinator such as ZooKeeper or a database row, then hands them out locally. A crashed server wastes the rest of its block, which is acceptable
- a **Snowflake-style** ID combines timestamp, machine ID and sequence bits, generated locally with no coordination

Sequential IDs produce guessable codes. Shuffle them by encrypting or permuting the number before encoding, so consecutive IDs don't map to consecutive codes.

**3. Pre-generated keys.** A key generation service creates random unique codes ahead of time and stores them in a pool; servers take batches. No collision checks on the hot path, at the cost of another service.

Range allocation with a permutation step is a strong interview answer: no collisions, no coordination per request, and non-sequential codes.

**Custom aliases** go through a uniqueness check; conflicts return 409 Conflict.

## Deep dive: fast redirects

Reads dominate, so cache aggressively. Put code → long URL in Redis with cache-aside. Link popularity is highly skewed, so even a modest cache holds the hot set and serves most redirects. With a 90%+ hit ratio, the database sees a few hundred reads per second. A CDN or edge cache can serve redirects for the hottest links too.

**301 or 302?** A 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, cutting load, but later clicks never reach your servers, so analytics miss them. A 302 (temporary) sends every click through you. Choose 302 if analytics matter, 301 if they don't.

## Deep dive: analytics and expiry

Don't write analytics synchronously in the redirect path. Publish a click event (code, timestamp, country, referrer) to a queue or log such as Kafka, and let consumers aggregate counts into an analytics store. The redirect stays fast even if analytics lag.

For expiry, check `expires_at` on read and return 410 Gone for expired links; a background job purges expired rows later. Cache TTLs must not outlive a link's expiry.

## Scaling and reliability

- App servers are stateless behind a redundant load balancer
- Shard the URL table by hash of the code if one database isn't enough
- Replicate the database and cache across availability zones
- Rate limit link creation per user or IP to stop spam and abuse, and check long URLs against malware lists

## How interviewers test this

Expect the full design with special attention to ID generation, cache strategy and 301 versus 302. Show the estimate that justifies 7 Base62 characters, compare hashing with counters, and keep analytics off the critical path.

sections.question: Why might a URL shortener return 302 instead of 301?
options: So every click reaches the server and can be counted for analytics
sections.explanation: Browsers cache 301s, so repeat clicks bypass the server.

traps.question: Use one auto-increment column for all IDs.
traps.trap: A single sequence is a bottleneck and produces guessable codes.
traps.solution: Allocate ID ranges per server and permute before encoding.

traps.question: Truncate an MD5 hash to 7 characters and you're done.
traps.trap: Truncated hashes collide.
traps.solution: Check for collisions and retry, or use a counter-based scheme.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: 7 Base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes.
Range-allocated counters with Base62 avoid collisions and per-request coordination; permute IDs to avoid guessable codes.
Cache code-to-URL mappings; popularity is highly skewed.
Keep analytics asynchronous through a queue.

lessons.title: Design a News Feed
lessons.description: Fan-out on write vs read, the celebrity problem, feed storage, ranking and pagination.

content.theory:
A news feed shows each user recent posts from people they follow, like the home timelines of Twitter, Instagram or LinkedIn. The central challenge is fan-out: one post must appear in the feeds of every follower, and some users have millions. This walkthrough covers requirements, the fan-out-on-write versus fan-out-on-read decision, the hybrid approach used in practice, storage, ranking and pagination.

## Step 1: requirements

**Functional:**

- Users publish posts (text, images)
- Users follow other users
- Users see a feed of posts from people they follow, newest or ranked first, with infinite scroll

**Non-functional:**

- Feed loads in under about 200 ms
- High availability; slightly stale feeds are acceptable (eventual consistency)
- Read-heavy: feeds are viewed far more often than posts are created

## Step 2: estimates

Assume 300 million daily active users, each opening the feed 10 times and posting 0.5 times per day, with an average of 200 followed accounts.

- **Feed reads**: 3 × 10⁹ per day ≈ 30,000 per second, perhaps 100,000 at peak
- **Posts**: 1.5 × 10⁸ per day ≈ 1,500 per second
- **Fan-out writes**, if every post is copied to every follower's feed: 1,500 × average followers (say 200) = 300,000 feed insertions per second

That last number drives the design.

## Step 3: high-level design

~~~text
Post service -> Posts DB (+ media in object storage)
            \-> Fan-out service -> Feed cache (per-user lists in Redis)
Feed service <- reads feed cache, hydrates post details from post cache
Social graph service: who follows whom
~~~

APIs: `POST /posts`, `POST /users/{id}/follow`, `GET /feed?cursor=...`.

## Fan-out on write (push)

When a user posts, the fan-out service looks up their followers and inserts the post ID into each follower's precomputed feed list, typically a Redis list or sorted set capped at a few hundred entries.

- **Pros**: feed reads are instant, since the feed is already assembled
- **Cons**: writes are expensive, and a user with 50 million followers triggers 50 million inserts, delaying delivery and wasting work for inactive followers

## Fan-out on read (pull)

The feed is built when requested: fetch the list of followed accounts, get each one's recent posts, merge and sort.

- **Pros**: posting is cheap; no wasted work for inactive users
- **Cons**: reads are slow and expensive, since a user following 500 accounts needs 500 lookups and a merge on every feed load

## The hybrid approach

Production systems combine both:

- **Ordinary users** (most accounts): fan out on write to their followers' feed caches
- **Celebrities** (accounts above a follower threshold, such as 100,000): don't fan out. At read time, the feed service merges the precomputed feed with recent posts from the celebrities the user follows
- **Inactive users**: skip pushing to users who haven't logged in recently; build their feed on demand when they return

This bounds write amplification while keeping reads fast. Twitter publicly described a design along these lines.

## Storage

- **Posts**: a sharded store keyed by post ID, with media in object storage behind a CDN. Post IDs from a Snowflake-style generator are roughly time-ordered, which helps sorting
- **Social graph**: follower and following lists, sharded by user ID, often in a wide-column or graph store
- **Feed cache**: per-user lists of post IDs only, not full posts, to keep memory small. The feed service **hydrates** IDs into full posts using a post cache, so edits and deletions appear everywhere

## Ranking

A chronological feed sorts by time. Ranked feeds score candidates by predicted engagement: author affinity, recency, post type and interaction counts. A common pipeline gathers a few hundred candidates from the feed cache and celebrity posts, scores them with a model, and returns the top results. Ranking adds latency, so scores are often precomputed or cached.

## Pagination

Use **cursor-based pagination** with the last seen post ID or timestamp: `GET /feed?cursor=1724400000123&limit=20`. Offset pagination breaks in a feed, because new posts shift every page and cause duplicates.

## Other details

- **New follows**: backfill a few recent posts from the followed account into the follower's feed
- **Deletes**: remove post IDs lazily; hydration skips deleted posts
- **Fan-out queue**: run fan-out through a message queue so posting returns immediately and workers scale independently

## How interviewers test this

Expect "fan-out on write or read?" and "how do you handle celebrities?" Quantify write amplification, propose the hybrid model, store post IDs in per-user feed caches, hydrate posts at read time, and paginate with cursors.

sections.question: How do hybrid feed designs handle accounts with millions of followers?
options: They skip fan-out for them and merge their posts at read time
They fan out to every follower synchronously
They store feeds only in SQL joins
sections.explanation: Pulling celebrity posts at read time avoids millions of writes per post.

traps.question: Fan out every post to every follower.
traps.trap: A celebrity post triggers tens of millions of writes.
traps.solution: Exclude high-follower accounts from fan-out and merge them on read.

traps.question: Store full post objects in each follower's feed list.
traps.trap: Huge memory use, and edits must update millions of copies.
traps.solution: Store IDs and hydrate from a post cache.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Fan-out on write makes reads fast but amplifies writes; fan-out on read does the opposite.
Use a hybrid: push for ordinary users, pull for celebrities, lazy builds for inactive users.
Store post IDs in feed caches and hydrate full posts at read time.
Paginate feeds with cursors, not offsets.

lessons.title: Design a Chat System
lessons.description: Real-time messaging with WebSockets, message routing, storage, ordering, presence and offline delivery.

content.theory:
A chat system such as WhatsApp, Slack or Messenger delivers messages between users in near real time, keeps history, shows who's online, and delivers messages to users who were offline. The challenges are maintaining millions of persistent connections, routing each message to the right server, and storing a huge, write-heavy message history. This walkthrough covers requirements, connections, routing, storage, ordering, presence and group chat.

## Step 1: requirements

**Functional:**

- One-to-one and small group chats (say up to a few hundred members)
- Message history, synced across a user's devices
- Online presence and last seen
- Delivery and read receipts
- Push notifications for offline users

**Non-functional:**

- Low delivery latency, under a few hundred milliseconds
- No lost messages; delivery at least once with deduplication
- Per-conversation ordering
- High availability at massive scale

## Step 2: estimates

Assume 500 million daily active users sending 40 messages each per day.

- **Messages**: 2 × 10¹⁰ per day ≈ 200,000 per second on average, perhaps 1 million at peak
- **Storage**: at about 200 bytes per message, 2 × 10¹⁰ × 200 = 4 TB per day, roughly 1.5 PB per year before replication
- **Connections**: perhaps 100 million concurrent connections at peak. If one server holds about 100,000 to a few hundred thousand idle connections, that's hundreds to a thousand chat servers

The write volume and connection count shape the design.

## Step 3: connections

HTTP is request-response, so the server can't push messages. Options:

- **Polling**: the client asks every few seconds. Wasteful and slow
- **Long polling**: the server holds the request until a message arrives. Better, but connections constantly reconnect
- **WebSockets**: one persistent, full-duplex connection per device. The standard choice for chat

Clients connect through a load balancer to a fleet of **chat servers** that hold WebSocket connections. Chat servers are stateful in one sense: each knows which users are connected to it. Everything else, such as history and user data, lives in shared stores.

## Step 4: routing a message

When Asha sends a message to Ravi:

1. Asha's device sends the message over its WebSocket to chat server A, with a client-generated message ID for deduplication
2. Server A assigns a sequence number for the conversation, persists the message, and acknowledges to Asha (one tick)
3. Server A looks up which server holds Ravi's connection, in a **session registry** such as Redis mapping user ID to server ID
4. If Ravi is online on server B, A forwards the message to B, often through a message bus or direct RPC, and B pushes it down Ravi's WebSocket
5. Ravi's device acknowledges receipt (two ticks); a read event later updates the read receipt
6. If Ravi is offline, the message waits in storage, and a push notification goes through APNs or FCM

~~~text
Asha -> Chat server A -> Message store
                     \-> Session registry: Ravi -> server B
                     \-> Chat server B -> Ravi    (or push notification if offline)
~~~

## Storage

Chat history is write-heavy, append-only and read by conversation, usually the most recent messages. A wide-column store such as Cassandra or HBase fits well: partition by conversation ID and cluster by message sequence or timestamp, so loading recent messages is one sequential read. Facebook Messenger used HBase, and Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB for this workload.

Store media in object storage behind a CDN, sending only the URL in the message.

## Ordering

Clocks across devices disagree, so client timestamps can't order messages reliably. Assign a monotonically increasing **sequence number per conversation** on the server when the message is persisted. Clients display messages by sequence number and detect gaps, requesting missing messages after reconnecting. Global ordering across all conversations isn't needed.

## Offline sync and multiple devices

Each device remembers the last sequence number it has seen per conversation. On reconnect, it asks for everything newer. This handles offline periods, multiple devices and flaky networks with one mechanism. Deduplicate by client message ID, since retries after a lost acknowledgement resend the same message.

## Presence

Presence uses heartbeats: connected clients send a heartbeat every few seconds; if heartbeats stop for, say, 30 seconds, the user is marked offline and last seen is updated. Broadcasting every status change to every contact is expensive for users with many contacts, so systems often fetch presence only for conversations currently on screen.

## Group chat

For small groups, the server fans out each message to all members' connections, looking up each member's server in the registry. Message storage stays per conversation, so history is stored once. Huge channels, as in Slack or Discord, fan out differently, with clients pulling recent messages rather than receiving individual pushes for every member.

## End-to-end encryption

Apps such as WhatsApp and Signal encrypt messages on the sender's device so servers can't read them, using the Signal protocol. The server then routes and stores ciphertext only, which limits server-side features such as search.

## How interviewers test this

Expect connection handling (WebSockets), message routing across servers, storage choice, ordering, and offline delivery. Use a session registry, per-conversation sequence numbers, a wide-column message store, client message IDs for deduplication, and push notifications for offline users.

sources.title: Ilya Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking (free online)

sections.question: How should a chat system order messages within a conversation?
options: With a server-assigned sequence number per conversation
sections.explanation: Device clocks drift; a per-conversation sequence gives a consistent order and detects gaps.

traps.question: Order messages by the sender's timestamp.
traps.trap: Device clocks disagree, so order breaks.
traps.solution: Assign server-side sequence numbers per conversation.

traps.question: Have clients poll for new messages every second.
traps.trap: Huge wasted load and higher latency.
traps.solution: Use persistent WebSocket connections.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Use WebSockets for real-time delivery and a session registry to find each user's server.
Store messages in a wide-column store partitioned by conversation.
Order with per-conversation sequence numbers; sync devices by last-seen sequence.
Deduplicate by client message ID and notify offline users via push.

lessons.title: Design a Notification System
lessons.description: Send push, SMS and email reliably at scale: queues, templates, preferences, retries and deduplication.

content.theory:
A notification system delivers messages to users across channels: mobile push, SMS, email and in-app alerts. Almost every product needs one: order updates, login alerts, reminders, marketing campaigns. The challenges are integrating unreliable third-party providers, respecting user preferences, avoiding duplicates and absorbing huge bursts. This walkthrough covers requirements, architecture, delivery pipeline, reliability and rate limiting.

## Step 1: requirements

**Functional:**

- Send notifications through push (iOS and Android), SMS and email, plus in-app
- Triggered by other services (transactional) or scheduled campaigns (bulk)
- Respect user preferences and opt-outs per channel and category
- Templates with personalization, such as "Hi Asha, your order has shipped"

**Non-functional:**

- Transactional notifications, such as one-time passwords, delivered within seconds
- No lost notifications, and avoid duplicates
- Handle bursts, such as a campaign to 50 million users
- Track delivery status

## Step 2: estimates

Assume 10 million push, 1 million SMS and 5 million emails per day for transactional traffic, with campaigns that occasionally target tens of millions at once. The average rate is low, around 200 per second, but campaigns create bursts far above that. Third-party providers have their own rate limits and costs, especially SMS.

The design must absorb bursts without slowing time-sensitive messages.

## Step 3: high-level architecture

~~~text
Services / Scheduler -> Notification API -> Validation, preferences, templating
                                              -> Priority queues per channel
                                                   -> Channel workers -> Providers (APNs, FCM, SMS gateway, email service)
                                              -> Notification log (status, dedup)
~~~

**Components:**

- **Notification API**: accepts requests like `{ userId, type: "order_shipped", data: {...}, idempotencyKey }`
- **Preference and contact store**: per-user opt-outs, quiet hours, device tokens, phone numbers and emails
- **Template service**: renders localized content per channel
- **Queues**: separate queues per channel and priority, so a huge email campaign can't delay one-time passwords
- **Channel workers**: pull from queues, call providers, record results
- **Notification log**: stores each notification's status for deduplication, retries and analytics

## Step 4: the delivery pipeline

1. A service calls the API with an event and an idempotency key
2. The API validates the request, loads preferences, and drops channels the user has disabled or that fall in quiet hours
3. It renders templates and enqueues one job per channel onto the right priority queue
4. It returns 202 Accepted immediately; delivery is asynchronous
5. Workers dequeue jobs, call the provider, and update the log: sent, delivered, failed

Separating acceptance from delivery lets the API stay fast during bursts while workers drain queues at the rate providers allow.

## Reliability

**Retries**: provider calls fail transiently. Workers retry with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a limit, then move the job to a dead-letter queue for inspection. Some failures are permanent, such as an invalid device token, which should be removed from the user's record rather than retried.

**At-least-once delivery and deduplication**: queues may redeliver a job after a worker crash. Before sending, workers check the notification log for the idempotency key or job ID and skip if already sent. Duplicate SMS messages cost money and annoy users, so this check matters.

**Provider failover**: for critical channels like SMS, integrate two providers and switch when one degrades.

**Persistence**: write each notification to the log before enqueueing, using the outbox pattern, so a crash between the two steps doesn't lose it.

## Rate limiting and user experience

- **Provider limits**: throttle workers to each provider's allowed rate
- **Per-user limits**: cap how many notifications one user gets per hour, and batch low-priority ones into a digest
- **Priorities**: one-time passwords and security alerts jump ahead of marketing
- **Quiet hours and time zones**: schedule campaigns in each user's local time

## Tracking and analytics

Record sent, delivered, opened and clicked events. Providers report delivery through callbacks or webhooks; emails use tracking pixels and link redirects. These events feed dashboards and help prune unengaged users from campaigns.

## Security and compliance

Store contact details securely, honour unsubscribe links (required for marketing email in many jurisdictions), and never include sensitive data such as full card numbers in notification content.

## How interviewers test this

Expect the pipeline design, plus "How do you avoid duplicate notifications?" and "How do you stop a campaign from delaying OTPs?" Use per-channel priority queues, asynchronous workers, preference checks before enqueueing, retries with backoff and dead-letter queues, and idempotency checks against a notification log.

sections.question: How do you stop a 50-million-email campaign from delaying one-time-password SMS messages?
options: Separate queues per channel and priority, with OTPs on a high-priority queue
sections.explanation: Isolating queues keeps bulk traffic from blocking time-critical messages.

traps.question: Call the SMS provider directly inside the API request.
traps.trap: Provider latency and outages hit the caller, and bursts overwhelm the provider.
traps.solution: Queue the job and let rate-limited workers deliver it.

traps.question: A worker crashed after sending; the job is redelivered.
traps.trap: The user receives the SMS twice.
traps.solution: Check the notification log by idempotency key before sending.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Accept requests quickly and deliver asynchronously through queues.
Use separate queues per channel and priority.
Retry transient provider failures with backoff; dead-letter persistent failures.
Deduplicate with idempotency keys and a notification log; respect preferences and quiet hours.

modules.title: More Design Walkthroughs
modules.description: Ride-sharing, video streaming, a web crawler, search autocomplete, payments and file sync.

lessons.title: Design a Ride-Sharing App
lessons.description: Location updates at scale, geospatial indexing, driver matching, trip state and surge pricing.

content.theory:
A ride-sharing app such as Uber, Ola or Lyft matches riders with nearby drivers in seconds, tracks trips live on a map, and handles payments afterwards. The hard parts are ingesting a constant stream of driver locations, finding the nearest available drivers quickly, and managing each trip's state reliably. This walkthrough covers requirements, estimates, geospatial indexing, matching, trip state and surge pricing.

## Step 1: requirements

**Functional:**

- Drivers go online and share their location continuously
- Riders request a ride from a pickup point to a destination and see an estimated fare and arrival time
- The system matches a rider with a nearby available driver, who can accept or decline
- Both parties see each other's live location during the trip
- Payment is charged when the trip ends

**Non-functional:**

- Matching within a few seconds
- Location updates reflected with low latency, around a second or two
- High availability: a failed match means a lost customer
- Consistency where it matters: a driver must never be assigned to two riders at once

## Step 2: estimates

Assume 10 million daily trips and 1 million drivers online at peak, each sending a location update every 4 seconds.

- **Location updates**: 1,000,000 ÷ 4 = 250,000 writes per second at peak
- **Ride requests**: 10⁷ per day ≈ 100 per second on average, perhaps 1,000 at peak
- **Location data size**: each update (driver ID, latitude, longitude, timestamp, status) is about 50 bytes, so 250,000 × 50 bytes = 12.5 MB per second of incoming data

Location updates dominate. They're high volume, short-lived and only the latest value matters, so they belong in memory, not in a relational database row per update.

## Step 3: high-level design

~~~text
Driver app --(WebSocket, location every 4s)--> Location service --> In-memory geo index (Redis)
Rider app --> Ride request service --> Matching service --> queries geo index, offers trip to drivers
Trip service: trip state machine (DB)        Pricing service: fares, surge
Notification/push service                    Payment service (after trip)
~~~

Drivers keep a persistent connection to report location and receive trip offers. The location service updates a geospatial index held in memory. The matching service queries it for nearby available drivers when a request arrives.

## Deep dive: geospatial indexing

"Find available drivers within 2 km" can't be answered efficiently with a plain index on latitude and longitude, because a range on two columns scans too much. Spatial indexes divide the map into cells:

- **Geohash** encodes a location as a string where nearby places share prefixes, such as `tdr1y` for part of Bengaluru. Search the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours, since a nearby driver may sit right across a cell boundary
- **Quadtrees** recursively split regions into four until each cell holds few drivers, adapting to dense city centres
- **H3**, Uber's open-source hexagonal grid, uses hexagons, which have uniform distances to all neighbours

Redis provides built-in geospatial commands (`GEOADD`, `GEOSEARCH`) based on geohashes, which suit this workload. Shard the index by city or region, since riders and drivers are local.

## Deep dive: matching

When a rider requests a trip:

1. Query the geo index for available drivers near the pickup point, expanding the radius if too few are found
2. Rank candidates by estimated time of arrival using road network routing, not straight-line distance, which ignores rivers and one-way streets
3. Offer the trip to the best driver, with a timeout of around 10 to 15 seconds; on decline or timeout, offer it to the next
4. On acceptance, atomically mark the driver unavailable and create the trip

The atomic step is essential. Two matching processes must not assign the same driver to two riders. Use a compare-and-set update on the driver's status, a short-lived lock, or route all matching for a region through a single partition owner.

## Deep dive: trip state

A trip moves through states: requested, matched, driver arriving, in progress, completed, cancelled, paid. Store trips in a durable database with these transitions enforced, because trips are financial records. Each transition emits an event to a stream so pricing, notifications, payments and analytics react independently.

During the trip, location updates flow to the rider through the same real-time channel used for driver tracking. Trip routes are also logged for fare calculation and dispute resolution, written in batches to cheaper storage.

## Surge pricing

When demand outstrips supply in an area, prices rise to attract drivers and temper demand. The pricing service computes, per geo cell every minute or so, the ratio of open requests to available drivers, and maps it to a multiplier. Riders see the price before confirming, and the quoted fare is locked for a short window so it doesn't change mid-request.

## Reliability

- Driver apps buffer location updates during brief network loss
- Location services are stateless apart from the in-memory index, which can be rebuilt from fresh updates within seconds after a failure
- Region-level isolation keeps an outage in one city from affecting others

## How interviewers test this

Expect location ingestion, nearby-driver search and double-assignment prevention. Size the location write rate, keep locations in an in-memory geospatial index sharded by region, search neighbouring cells, rank by ETA, and make driver assignment atomic.

sections.question: Why search a geohash cell and its neighbours when finding nearby drivers?
options: A nearby driver may sit right across a cell boundary
Neighbouring cells are cheaper to query
Geohashes only work in groups of nine
To find drivers in other cities
sections.explanation: Cell boundaries are arbitrary, so a close driver can be in an adjacent cell.

traps.question: Store every location update as a row in PostgreSQL.
traps.trap: 250,000 writes per second of short-lived data overwhelms the database.
traps.solution: Keep the latest location in an in-memory geospatial index.

traps.question: Two riders matched to the same driver.
traps.trap: Non-atomic check-then-assign.
traps.solution: Use compare-and-set on driver status or a single owner per region.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Location updates dominate write volume; keep them in an in-memory geo index.
Use geohash, quadtree or H3 cells, and search neighbouring cells.
Rank candidates by road ETA, not straight-line distance.
Assign drivers atomically so no driver gets two trips.

lessons.title: Design a Video Streaming Platform
lessons.description: Uploads, transcoding pipelines, adaptive bitrate streaming, CDNs and view counting.

content.theory:
A video platform such as YouTube or Netflix accepts uploads, converts them into many formats, and streams them smoothly to millions of devices on networks ranging from fibre to patchy 4G. Storage and bandwidth dominate the cost, and playback quality depends on adapting to each viewer's connection. This walkthrough covers the upload pipeline, transcoding, adaptive bitrate streaming, delivery through CDNs, and metadata and view counts.

## Step 1: requirements

**Functional:**

- Creators upload videos
- Viewers watch videos on web, mobile and TV with smooth playback
- Search, recommendations and comments (out of scope for the core design, but mention them)
- View counts and basic analytics

**Non-functional:**

- Playback starts within about 2 seconds and rarely buffers
- Reads vastly outnumber uploads
- Uploads are durable: a creator's video must never be lost
- Global reach with low latency everywhere

## Step 2: estimates

Assume 500 hours of video uploaded per minute (a figure YouTube has cited publicly) and 1 billion views per day.

- **Raw upload storage**: an hour of HD source video might be 2 to 5 GB. 500 hours per minute × 60 × 24 ≈ 720,000 hours per day, so on the order of petabytes of raw uploads per day
- **Transcoded storage**: each video is stored in several resolutions and codecs, multiplying storage again
- **Egress bandwidth**: 1 billion views × an average of 5 minutes at roughly 3 Mbit/s ≈ 10⁹ × 300 s × 3 × 10⁶ bits ≈ 10¹⁸ bits per day, about 11 Tbit/s on average

Those bandwidth figures mean serving from your own origin servers is impossible. CDNs, and for the largest platforms their own edge caches inside ISPs, are mandatory.

## Step 3: high-level design

~~~text
Upload: Client -> Upload service (pre-signed URL) -> Object storage (raw)
                                  -> Event -> Transcoding pipeline -> Object storage (renditions + manifests)
Watch:  Client -> API (metadata, manifest URL) ; Client -> CDN edge -> Origin storage (on miss)
Metadata DB (videos, channels) ; View events -> Stream -> Counters/analytics
~~~

## Deep dive: uploads

Large files over unreliable networks need care:

- The API issues a **pre-signed URL** so the client uploads straight to object storage such as S3, keeping large transfers off application servers
- **Resumable, chunked uploads** split the file into parts, so a dropped connection resumes from the last chunk instead of restarting
- When the upload completes, storage emits an event that starts processing

## Deep dive: transcoding

The uploaded file is converted into many **renditions**: resolutions such as 240p to 4K, bitrates, and codecs such as H.264 for compatibility and VP9 or AV1 for efficiency. Transcoding is CPU-heavy, so it's parallelized:

1. Split the video into short segments, often a few seconds each
2. Transcode segments in parallel across a fleet of workers, coordinated through a queue or workflow engine
3. Generate thumbnails, extract audio, and run content checks
4. Package segments with **manifest files** that list every rendition

The pipeline is a directed graph of tasks. Failed tasks retry individually without redoing the whole video. The video becomes watchable as soon as a basic rendition is ready, with higher qualities following.

## Deep dive: adaptive bitrate streaming

Modern players use **HLS** (HTTP Live Streaming) or **MPEG-DASH**. Each rendition is cut into segments of 2 to 6 seconds, and a manifest lists them. The player:

- downloads the manifest
- measures available bandwidth and buffer level as it plays
- requests each next segment at the highest quality the connection can sustain, dropping quality when bandwidth falls and raising it when it recovers

Because segments are ordinary HTTP files, any CDN can cache them. Adaptive bitrate is why a video degrades to a lower resolution instead of freezing when you walk into a weak-signal area.

## Deep dive: delivery

Segments and manifests are served from CDN edges near viewers. Popularity is extremely skewed: a small fraction of videos gets most views, so edges hold the hot set while the long tail is fetched from origin on demand. The biggest platforms also place caches inside ISP networks, Netflix's Open Connect being a well-known example, to cut transit costs. Pre-positioning new popular releases at edges before launch avoids a thundering herd on the origin.

## Metadata and view counts

Video metadata (title, owner, renditions, status) lives in a sharded database with a cache in front, since it's read on every play. View counts are high-volume, write-heavy and tolerant of slight delay: clients send view events to a stream, consumers aggregate them in batches, and the displayed count updates every few seconds or minutes. Writing a database row per view would never keep up.

## How interviewers test this

Expect the upload pipeline, transcoding and how streaming adapts to bandwidth. Use pre-signed resumable uploads to object storage, parallel segment-based transcoding into multiple renditions, HLS or DASH with manifests, CDN delivery for the hot set, and batched view counting.

sources.title: Ilya Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking (free online)

sections.question: How does adaptive bitrate streaming avoid buffering on a weak connection?
options: The player requests later segments at a lower quality rendition
The server compresses the whole file again
The video pauses until bandwidth returns
sections.explanation: Each short segment can come from a different rendition based on measured bandwidth.

traps.question: Upload videos through the API servers.
traps.trap: Large transfers tie up application servers.
traps.solution: Issue pre-signed URLs so clients upload straight to object storage.

traps.question: Increment a database counter on every view.
traps.trap: Billions of writes per day on hot rows.
traps.solution: Stream view events and aggregate in batches.

sections.title: Key takeaways
items: Upload directly to object storage with pre-signed, resumable chunked uploads.
Transcode segments in parallel into many resolutions and codecs.
Stream with HLS or DASH so players switch quality per segment.
